title: How to convert product photo to line art without tracing cast shadows or glare in Python
description:
AI-generated illustration: A glossy black coffee grinder beside an unshaded contour drawing on white vellum paper and steel calipers.

To convert product photo to line art without tracing cast shadows or surface glare, you must isolate and flatten illumination gradients in the lightness channel before running any gradient or contour detector. When you feed an unconditioned studio packshot straight into cv2.Canny or a grayscale color-dodge filter, the algorithm treats every bright softbox reflection and tabletop shadow boundary as a physical edge of the product.

This article was drafted with AI assistance, every Python snippet and metric below was executed locally with OpenCV and NumPy, and the author is affiliated with Virse, whose line art tool is referenced once below; product hardware scenarios in the text are hypothetical examples.

Why do standard scripts fail when you convert product photo to line art?

Standard edge-detection scripts fail when you convert product photo to line art because pixel-gradient operators measure local luminance contrast (dI/dx and dI/dy) without knowing whether a brightness jump comes from a physical housing seam or a studio lamp reflection. In a real product photograph, lighting artifacts often produce steeper pixel gradients than the actual part geometry you want to draw.


AI-generated illustration: Specular rim glare on brushed aluminum and a soft tabletop shadow that standard edge detectors misread as physical seams.

As the OpenCV Canny Edge Detection documentation explains, the Canny pipeline smooths the image with a Gaussian filter, computes Sobel gradient magnitudes in the horizontal and vertical directions, thins those gradients with non-maximum suppression, and links surviving pixels using lower and upper hysteresis thresholds. That pipeline works well when you photograph flat matte objects under diffuse shadowless domes. It breaks down as soon as you point a camera at consumer hardware made of brushed aluminum, glossy ABS plastic, glazed ceramic, or glass.

Consider what happens across three common surface zones on a tabletop product shot:

  1. Specular reflection islands on bevels and curves: A softbox reflecting off a chamfered aluminum rim or a curved ceramic body creates a localized region where luminance clips near 255 and color saturation drops near 0. The boundary between that blown-out highlight and the surrounding midtone metal has a massive Sobel gradient. Standard Canny traces a closed oval ring around the highlight, leaving your drawing with what looks like a physical sticker or dent in the middle of a smooth panel.
  2. Tabletop cast shadows and contact penumbras: Where the product rests on an acrylic sweep or wooden table, directional key lights cast a shadow with a soft penumbra. If the shadow gradient is steep enough to cross Canny's lower hysteresis threshold, the output drawing gets a jagged double baseline underneath the feet of the device.
  3. Low-contrast internal seams in recessed areas: While glare produces false-positive lines, recessed button wells, rubber gaskets, or dark-on-dark parting lines often sit at low pixel contrast. If you raise Canny's upper threshold (maxVal) to suppress the shadow and glare noise, you simultaneously erase the fine internal seams that make a technical drawing useful for assembly guides or spec sheets.

The same flaw affects the popular "pencil sketch" snippet that inverts a grayscale image, blurs it with a Gaussian kernel, and divides the original grayscale values by the inverted blur. Because color-dodge division amplifies contrast wherever luminance shifts rapidly, it turns brushed-metal grain into stipple noise and outlines every specular hot spot.

How do you audit specular glare and shadow gradients in Python before tracing?

You audit specular glare and shadow gradients in Python by converting the BGR image into CIE LAB and HSV color spaces, flagging high-lightness low-saturation islands (L > 240 and S < 20), measuring gradient density across the bottom tabletop strip, and dividing the lightness channel by a large morphological closing envelope before calling Canny. Running this pre-flight audit tells you in milliseconds whether a photo can be cleaned with local morphological math or needs an object-aware pass.

Let's build a self-contained script using opencv-python (cv2) and numpy. Instead of blindly tuning Canny thresholds by hand, the function audit_and_extract_lines performs four deterministic steps:

  1. Glare island segmentation: It converts the image to LAB and HSV. Specular reflections on dielectric and metallic surfaces spike the LAB lightness channel (L) while washing out HSV saturation (S). We build a binary mask where L > 240 and S < 20, then run cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats to count distinct glare islands between 25 and 15,000 pixels in area.
  2. Telea glare inpainting: Before computing any edge gradients, we pass the glare mask into cv2.inpaint with cv2.INPAINT_TELEA so the clipped white boundary is smoothly filled from the surrounding midtone surface.
  3. Morphological illumination division: To flatten broad cast shadows across the tabletop and housing faces, we apply a morphological closing operation (cv2.MORPH_CLOSE) with a 45x45 elliptical structuring element on the inpainted L channel. Dividing the L channel by that morphological background envelope normalizes slow lighting ramps while keeping tight physical crevices intact.
  4. Edge-preserving bilateral smoothing: As documented in the OpenCV filtering guide, cv2.bilateralFilter weights neighbor pixels by both spatial distance and radiometric intensity difference. Applying a bilateral filter (d=9, sigmaColor=55, sigmaSpace=55) smooths out brushed-metal surface texture without blurring sharp cabinet corners.

Here is the complete, runnable script:

import cv2
import numpy as np


def audit_and_extract_lines(img_bgr: np.ndarray) -> tuple[dict, np.ndarray]:
    """Audit glare islands and shadow ramps, then extract normalized line art."""
    lab = cv2.cvtColor(img_bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB)
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img_bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
    l_chan = lab[:, :, 0]
    s_chan = hsv[:, :, 1]

    # 1. Detect specular glare islands (high L, low S)
    glare_mask = ((l_chan > 240) & (s_chan < 20)).astype(np.uint8) * 255
    num_labels, _, stats, _ = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(glare_mask)
    glare_islands = sum(
        1 for i in range(1, num_labels)
        if 25 <= stats[i, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA] <= 15000
    )

    # 2. Measure shadow gradient density in the bottom 22% floor strip
    h, w = l_chan.shape
    floor_strip = l_chan[int(h * 0.78):, :]
    gx = cv2.Sobel(floor_strip, cv2.CV_32F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
    gy = cv2.Sobel(floor_strip, cv2.CV_32F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
    grad_mag = np.sqrt(gx ** 2 + gy ** 2)
    shadow_ramp_ratio = float(np.mean(grad_mag > 12.0))

    # Baseline unconditioned Canny edge count
    raw_edges = cv2.Canny(l_chan, 60, 150)

    # 3. Inpaint glare boundaries + normalize slow shadow envelopes
    inpainted_l = cv2.inpaint(
        l_chan, glare_mask, inpaintRadius=5, flags=cv2.INPAINT_TELEA
    )
    kernel = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (45, 45))
    bg_envelope = cv2.morphologyEx(inpainted_l, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel)
    norm_l = cv2.divide(inpainted_l, bg_envelope, scale=255)

    # 4. Bilateral smoothing + Canny contour extraction (black lines on white)
    smooth_l = cv2.bilateralFilter(norm_l, d=9, sigmaColor=55, sigmaSpace=55)
    clean_edges = cv2.Canny(smooth_l, 60, 150)
    line_art = 255 - clean_edges

    raw_px = int(np.count_nonzero(raw_edges))
    clean_px = int(np.count_nonzero(clean_edges))
    reduction_pct = round((1.0 - clean_px / max(1, raw_px)) * 100.0, 1)

    report = {
        "glare_islands": glare_islands,
        "shadow_ramp_ratio": round(shadow_ramp_ratio, 4),
        "raw_edge_pixels": raw_px,
        "clean_edge_pixels": clean_px,
        "false_edge_reduction_pct": reduction_pct,
    }
    return report, line_art


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sample = cv2.imread("02-glare-shadow-setup.png")
    metrics, output_drawing = audit_and_extract_lines(sample)
    print(metrics)
    cv2.imwrite("speaker_line_art_cleaned.png", output_drawing)

When we run this script against our 1536x1024 brushed-aluminum speaker test image (02-glare-shadow-setup.png), it prints the following diagnostic dictionary:

{'glare_islands': 4, 'shadow_ramp_ratio': 0.0381, 'raw_edge_pixels': 37540, 'clean_edge_pixels': 26290, 'false_edge_reduction_pct': 30.0}

Those numbers show what happens inside the image array. The script caught 4 specular glare islands along the bevelled aluminum edge and measured a 0.0381 shadow gradient ratio across the tabletop. By inpainting the four highlight boundaries, dividing out the 45x45 closing envelope, and running bilateral smoothing before Canny, total edge pixels dropped from 37,540 to 26,290, stripping 30.0% of the false-positive noise while keeping the cone surround and socket screws intact.

Pipeline stage What it targets Failure mode if skipped Parameter to tune for studio packshots
L > 240 & S < 20 mask + cv2.inpaint Clipped softbox highlights on chamfered metal or glazed ceramic Double oval contour rings floating inside smooth surfaces Lower L threshold to 230 if the studio photo was exported with compressed highlight roll-off
cv2.MORPH_CLOSE (45x45) + cv2.divide Gradual illumination falloff and soft tabletop cast shadows Stray floor lines and uneven threshold sensitivity across dark sides Scale kernel size to roughly 3% of image width (45 px for a 1536 px wide photo)
cv2.bilateralFilter (d=9, 55, 55) Fine brushed-metal grain, anodized speckle, or paper texture Dense stipple clutter inside flat panels Increase sigmaColor to 75 for heavily textured cast iron or woven fabric
cv2.Canny(smooth_l, 60, 150) Physical silhouette boundaries, recess grooves, and screw heads Broken outer contours if minVal is too high Keep maxVal:minVal between 2:1 and 3:1 as recommended by Canny's original hysteresis design

When should you switch from pixel-gradient scripts to object-aware line art generation?

You should switch from pixel-gradient scripts to object-aware line art generation when your product photo contains dark horizon reflections on curved chrome, busy lifestyle backgrounds, or printed surface graphics that local pixel math cannot separate from physical seams. No matter how carefully you tune morphological kernels in OpenCV, a local filter only sees pixel neighborhoods; it does not understand which lines belong to the 3D form of the object.


Public tool page of Virse's AI Line Art Generator (currently titled Line Art Extractor on the page header), showing the source upload slot, the Detailed line art, Clean line art, and Bold outline buttons, the extraction notes field, and the Generate line art button.

For example, if you photograph a stainless steel espresso machine or a vintage amplifier with a brass faceplate, the metal reflects dark room shapes alongside bright softboxes. A dark reflection has low lightness (L < 60), so a glare mask (L > 240) ignores it, and its sharp edge survives bilateral filtering just like a real panel gap. Similarly, as the scikit-image Canny edge detector example demonstrates, local gradient detectors always trade off noise suppression against structural completeness when signal-to-noise varies across the frame.

When you need a drawing that holds the object's true form and proportions without hand-masking every reflection in Python, you can use a clean black-on-white line art generator on Virse (whose public tool page header currently displays the title Line Art Extractor). Instead of running a pixel edge filter, Virse's AI Line Art Generator identifies the product first, removes the background automatically, and traces a black-line drawing on a pure white background where surface glare, cast shadows, and studio backdrops do not turn into stray lines.

On the public tool page, the workflow takes three inputs before opening the workspace canvas:

  • Source image: Upload a single product photo (JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, BMP, AVIF, or HEIC). The tool requires a source photo and cannot generate line art from text alone.
  • Line style (optional): Pick one of the three line style buttons depending on where the drawing will live:
    • Detailed line art (full structure study): Keeps internal seams, knurled knobs, grille patterns, and small fastener details for assembly guides or technical callout sheets.
    • Clean line art (presentation outline): Simplifies fine surface texture while holding the main housing panels and primary controls for onboarding cards or catalog spot illustrations.
    • Bold outline (silhouette-focused): Emphasizes the outer contour and major form breaks with heavier stroke weight for small icons or packaging inserts.
  • Extraction notes (optional): Add a short plain-language instruction specifying what to keep or omit, such as keeping only one object in the frame, preferring a specific line weight, or omitting printed brand logos and surface reflections.

Clicking Generate line art brings your uploaded product photo and selected parameters into a new Virse canvas with the tool pre-filled. Nothing runs and no credits are spent until you press Start inside the canvas. When the pass finishes, the black-on-white line drawing lands on the canvas beside your original photo so you can inspect proportions side by side, adjust extraction notes, or send the drawing into the Line Art Renderer on the same board.

Keep two technical boundaries in mind when choosing between a Python script, Virse's canvas tool, and CAD software:

  1. Raster output, not CAD or SVG vectors: Both the OpenCV pipeline above and Virse's AI Line Art Generator output raster pixel images (PNG/WebP black lines on a white background, not a transparent background). Neither produces a measured engineering blueprint with dimensional tolerances or an editable SVG/DXF file. If your print vendor requires vector paths, run an automated bitmap-to-vector pass (such as Potrace or Illustrator Image Trace) on the cleaned raster output.
  2. Proportional fidelity vs orthographic projection: A line drawing extracted from a camera photo preserves the perspective of that camera angle rather than converting a 3/4 packshot into a flat orthographic CAD projection.

How do you inspect and clean raster line drawings before putting them into docs?

You inspect and clean raster line drawings before putting them into documentation by checking four structural criteria: outer silhouette closure, internal seam continuity, zero residual reflection rings, and pure white (255) background floors.


AI-generated illustration: Checking seam continuity and fastener hole outlines under an optical loupe against the physical machined housing.

Run this four-point verification before dropping the file into your layout tool:

  • Check outer silhouette closure at 200% zoom: If a bright rim highlight caused a 4-pixel gap along the top edge, any subsequent flood-fill or vector trace will leak into the background. Close tiny perimeter gaps in Python with cv2.morphologyEx(clean_edges, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, np.ones((3, 3), np.uint8)) before inverting.
  • Verify fastener and port symmetry: Pixel edge detectors often break small circular ports or screws into crescent fragments under directional light. Either lower minVal in Canny or use an object-aware pass with an extraction note preserving front-panel ports.
  • Confirm zero floating reflection loops: Scan the largest panels of the product. Any closed loop that does not match a real seam, button, or vent slot is a surviving reflection artifact and should be masked out.
  • Clip the white floor to pure 255: Even a 252 off-white background prints as a visible gray box on paper. Run a final levels clip (line_art[line_art > 240] = 255) so the background merges cleanly with the page.

By auditing glare_islands and shadow_ramp_ratio up front in Python, you can batch-process matte packshots automatically in OpenCV and route reflective hardware shots to an object-aware line art pass without erasing shadow lines by hand.

title: grunt-proxy: a local proxy that trims your coding agent's prompts (and shows what it saved)
description:
Repo: 👉 github.com/bayuh85/grunt-proxy (MIT, Node.js 20+, TypeScript)

The problem

If you use Claude Code, Cursor, or Cline every day, you are sending a lot of text you didn't write: system prompts, tool descriptions, tool results, and your own "could you please…" phrasing. Every token of that is billed. And the replies often come back with a greeting, a recap, and a closing paragraph you'll never read.

None of that is a big deal per request. Across a day of agent loops, it adds up, and most of us have no idea by how much.

I wanted something that sits between the agent and the API, trims the obvious padding, asks the model to get to the point, and tells me what it actually saved — without breaking code or tool calls.

What grunt-proxy does

grunt-proxy is a small local HTTP proxy for coding agents. For each request it:

  1. Shortens the prompt you were about to send (filler phrases, articles, common short forms — configurable).
  2. Asks the model for a terse reply via a short, stable instruction.
  3. Prints how many tokens and how many dollars that saved.

What it deliberately does not do:

  • Replies stay in normal English. The proxy doesn't role-play and doesn't rewrite the model's response.
  • Code, JSON, and tool calls stay intact.

It speaks both the OpenAI Chat Completions API and the Anthropic Messages API (including the Anthropic SSE stream), so the same proxy works for Cursor, Cline, and Claude Code.

Quickstart

Requires Node.js 20 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/bayuh85/grunt-proxy.git
cd grunt-proxy
cp .env.example .env

Put your upstream key in GRUNT_API_KEY in .env. The default upstream is AtmoRouter (keys look like ar-...), but you can point it anywhere — more on that below.

npm install
npm run dev

grunt-proxy now listens on http://127.0.0.1:8642. Try a request through it:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8642/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $GRUNT_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "model": "atmo/deepseek-v4.1-flash",
    "messages": [
      {"role": "user", "content": "Could you please explain the configuration options in the documentation? Thank you!"}
    ]
  }'

(Model ids change — check your provider's current catalog before relying on an example id.)

Each request prints one line on stderr:

grunt  atmo/deepseek-v4.1-flash  in 1,204→640 (−46.8%)  out 180  saved $0.001692

For the running total, hit GET /savings.txt or press Ctrl+C when the server is in the foreground:

grunt-proxy savings
requests              12
failed                0
input tokens          48,200 → 21,040  (−56.3%)
input tokens saved    27,160
output tokens         6,410
est. input $ saved    $0.081480
projected output $    $0.000000
est. $ saved          $0.081480
upstream billed       –

To be clear, the README labels those numbers as an illustration of the layout, not a benchmark. Your savings depend on your prompts, your level setting, and your prices.

For a compiled build: npm run build && npm start.

Setting it up with your agent

Claude Code

Claude Code (and the Anthropic SDK) appends /v1/messages itself, so use the proxy origin without /v1:

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="http://127.0.0.1:8642"
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="ar-your-key"
claude

grunt-proxy receives POST /v1/messages, compresses it, and forwards it upstream, streaming included. It sets anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 if the client didn't send one.

Cursor

  1. Start grunt-proxy (npm run dev).
  2. Open Cursor Settings → Models.
  3. Set the OpenAI API key to your upstream key. If GRUNT_API_KEY is already set in .env, any non-empty placeholder works — the proxy replaces the client key.
  4. Override the OpenAI base URL with http://127.0.0.1:8642/v1.
  5. Add a custom model whose id matches a model on your upstream, e.g. atmo/deepseek-v4.1-flash.

Cline

  1. Start grunt-proxy.
  2. Set the API provider to OpenAI Compatible.
  3. Base URL: http://127.0.0.1:8642/v1
  4. API key: your upstream key (or a placeholder when GRUNT_API_KEY is set).
  5. Model ID: a catalog id from your provider.

Quick reference:

Client Base URL the client uses
Cursor, Cline, OpenAI SDKs http://127.0.0.1:8642/v1
Claude Code, Anthropic SDK http://127.0.0.1:8642

How it works

What gets compressed (and what doesn't)

grunt-proxy only edits text the model will read: system and user text, assistant text, tool descriptions, and tool-result text. It leaves these alone:

  • fenced code, inline code, and indented code lines
  • URLs, file paths, and filenames
  • JSON values, including tool-call arguments and tool parameter schemas
  • camelCase and PascalCase identifiers
  • image blocks and Anthropic tool_use / thinking blocks

Levels

Level What changes
0 Nothing.
1 Courtesy and padded phrases ("could you please", "in order to", "thank you").
2 Level 1, plus a/an/the and a few other fillers, plus short forms like config, fn, param, impl.
3 Level 2, plus of/that, some contractions, and shorter forms like cfg, btwn, w/o.

Level 2 is the default. If an agent starts misreading instructions, drop to level 1. Level 3 is lossier; only use it once you've checked the output.

You can override per request with headers: x-grunt: off forwards the body unchanged, and x-grunt-level: 0–3 / x-grunt-terse: auto|always|off override the config for one call.

The terse instruction

With GRUNT_TERSE=auto (the default), the proxy adds a one-paragraph instruction only when compression already pays for it, or when the prompt is roughly 800+ estimated tokens. It tells the model to answer in normal English, skip the greeting and recap, and keep code and tool calls valid.

A nice detail: the instruction is the same bytes for a given level, so a provider's prompt cache can still reuse the prefix.

Honest savings math

This is the part I appreciate most. The README is upfront about what's measured and what's estimated:

  • The token delta is a local before/after estimate, not a clone of any provider's tokenizer. It's consistent, which is what a savings figure needs. When the upstream returns usage, the actual counts are stored too.
  • Dollars are tokens saved × price / 1,000,000, using approximate public list prices for known model families, or $1 / $3 per million for unknown ids.
  • Set GRUNT_PRICE_IN / GRUNT_PRICE_OUT to what you actually pay, otherwise the estimate won't match your invoice (and may overstate savings if your provider is cheaper than list price).
  • Output terseness is requested, not measured. projected output $ stays $0 unless you explicitly set GRUNT_ASSUME_OUTPUT_CUT, which is a labeled guess.
  • Failed upstream calls count as failures and add $0.
  • The response headers x-grunt-original-tokens, x-grunt-compressed-tokens, and x-grunt-saved-tokens expose the estimate per call. Saved tokens can even be negative when the terse instruction costs more than compression saved — and the proxy says so instead of hiding it.

If you set GRUNT_LOG_FILE, you get a JSONL savings ledger (prompts are not written), and grunt-proxy --report .grunt-savings.jsonl reprints a report from it without starting the server.

Safe defaults

  • Binds to 127.0.0.1 by default, so the proxy doesn't become a public credit sink.
  • No proxy-side request timeout by default, so long Claude Code or Cursor streams aren't cut off. Disconnecting the client aborts the upstream request.
  • Oversized bodies (default limit 32 MiB) are rejected with HTTP 413.

Credit where it's due

grunt-proxy is inspired by caveman by Julius Brussee — the idea that you can strip a lot of words from what goes to and from a model without losing meaning. grunt-proxy takes that idea and packages it as a transparent proxy with a savings report, while keeping replies in normal English.

About AtmoRouter (the default upstream)

Full disclosure: the default upstream is AtmoRouter. It's an API gateway that's compatible with both the OpenAI Chat Completions API (https://atmorouter.dev/v1) and the Anthropic Messages API, so one key works for Cursor, Cline, and Claude Code. It's pay-per-token, accepts payment via QRIS and USDC, and focuses on cheap access to frontier models.

That said, grunt-proxy is provider-agnostic. Set GRUNT_UPSTREAM_BASE_URL and GRUNT_API_KEY to use OpenAI, Anthropic, or any other compatible gateway:

GRUNT_UPSTREAM_BASE_URL=https://your-provider.example/v1
GRUNT_API_KEY=your-key

Try it

If you run coding agents all day and want to see where your tokens go, give it a spin:

👉 github.com/bayuh85/grunt-proxy

Issues and PRs welcome — especially reports of prompts where a compression level changed the model's behavior, since that's exactly what the level knob is for.

title: Agentic AI: Itinerary Planner
description:
Building an AI-Powered Travel Itinerary Planner Using Ollama, Node.js, and React

Introduction

Travel planning is time-consuming — comparing routes, deciding daily activities, balancing pace, and estimating budgets.
To solve this, I built an AI-powered travel itinerary planner that generates realistic, structured, and customizable travel plans based on user preferences.

This article explains:

What the system does
How it was designed
The technologies used
Key engineering challenges and solutions
How I Structured the System
From the beginning, I knew one thing:

The AI should not talk directly to the UI.

Become a Medium member
So I designed the system like this:

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Each layer has one job:

UI receives input and displays response data
Listener controls logic, generates a custom prompt, and receives a response
Ollama receives the prompt on model lamma3
Why I Used Ollama (and Not OpenAI APIs)
If you wanted:

Local execution
No API costs
No data leaving my machine
Full control over models
That’s where Ollama came in. Checkout my stats-

Press enter or click to view image in full size

Ollama lets you run LLMs locally, inside Docker, and switch models easily.
I tested models like:

mistral
quantized llama3
This also forced me to deal with real-world constraints like memory limits, which honestly made the project better.

Backend: The Real Workhorse
The backend (Node.js + Express) does most of the heavy lifting. It calls Ollama, enforces strict JSON output, safely parses responses, validates the schema, and handles missing or partial data.

A classic bug taught an important lesson: the AI returned perfect JSON, but I accidentally sent it as a string instead of an object 😄. Fixing it reinforced how critical backend validation is in AI systems.

Frontend: Simple and Honest
The frontend uses React and Material UI, focusing on clarity over flashiness. Each day of the itinerary is displayed as a card with morning, afternoon, and evening sections.

Everything is rendered conditionally. If the AI skips a field, the UI adapts instead of crashing. This is how real AI products should behave.

About Accuracy
AI outputs aren’t “100% accurate.” Instead of pretending otherwise, this project defines accuracy as usability and completeness, not perfection. The system validates structure and stays transparent in the UI.

Is This Agentic AI?
Yes — functionally, but not hype-driven.

It’s a goal-oriented, planner-style agent that reasons, plans, and produces structured output. It’s not a fully autonomous or multi-agent system yet, but it clearly demonstrates agentic behavior in a controlled, production-ready way.

title: The one line in your SKILL.md that decides whether your skill ever fires
description:
Across 591 scored skills, the weakest of our six evaluation dimensions is also the one that decides whether the skill gets used at all. The fix takes five minutes and almost nobody does it.

Your skill's description field is the only part of it that's loaded before the skill is chosen. The agent reads it, decides whether this skill matches the request, and only then loads the body. That makes it a routing table, not documentation.

We score it as "trigger quality," worth 20 of 100 points. Across 591 skills it averages 7.74 — the lowest of our six dimensions, behind content (8.30) and workflow design (8.11).

Four jobs, and most skills do one

A description that scores well answers four questions:

  1. What does it produce? — most skills do this.
  2. When should it fire? — common, usually as Use when the user asks to ….
  3. When should it NOT fire? — rare, and the single strongest quality signal we measure.
  4. What would a person actually type? — rarer still.

Number 3 is where the money is. A skill with no negative space triggers on everything adjacent to it. Install three of those and your agent starts loading the wrong instructions for ordinary requests — which is worse than not having the skill installed.

Same skill, two descriptions

Both of these describe an identical package that reviews a contract against a risk taxonomy.

Before:

description: Reviews contracts and identifies legal risks.

After:

description: Reviews a contract against a risk taxonomy and returns findings
  with severity and suggested redlines. Use when the user asks to "review this
  contract", "check this NDA", or "flag risky clauses". Not for drafting new
  agreements (use an NDA generator), not for jurisdiction-specific compliance
  questions (use a compliance skill), and not for summarizing a contract without
  risk analysis.

The second one is longer, but length isn't the point — the exclusions are. It routes three adjacent request types somewhere else, which is what stops the skill from firing on the 80% of nearby requests it would handle badly.

The gap isn't where you'd guess

Trigger quality varies a lot by category:

  • Marketing skills average 9.30 on this dimension.
  • Finance & trading skills average 6.09.

A 3.2-point spread on the same rubric item is huge. But before concluding that marketing people are better at naming things: that number is mostly a story about authorship. The marketing set is dominated by a few coherent, well-documented skill families. The finance set accumulated from many independent authors shipping crypto and market-data tools. The categories differ far less than the people writing in them do.

The five-minute check

Open your skill's frontmatter and go through this in order:

  1. What does it produce? (A named artifact beats a verb.)
  2. What would a user literally type to trigger it?
  3. What should route somewhere else instead?
  4. Is there anything in here that isn't about routing — a changelog, a philosophy statement, a roadmap?

If you fix only one, fix #3. It's the difference between a skill that's available and a skill that's useful.

The full rubric — including how trigger quality is scored out of 20, and what the written rationale for each skill looks like — is public.

title: The Matrix of List Comprehensions: Unlocking Python's Hidden Powers
description:
The Quest Begins (The "Why")

I was knee‑deep in a data‑cleaning script that had to read a 2 GB log file, pull out timestamps, and push them into a database. My first attempt looked innocent enough:

timestamps = [parse(line) for line in open('huge.log') if line.startswith('2023')]

The script ran, ate up all my RAM, and then the OS killed it with a sigh. I stared at the screen, feeling like I’d just walked into a boss fight without a sword. Why did a simple list comprehension blow up my memory?

That moment kicked off a little adventure into the darker corners of Python’s comprehension syntax. I discovered a few tricks that most tutorials gloss over—tricks that turned my memory‑hungry monster into a lean, mean, streaming machine.

The Revelation (The Insight)

1. The Walrus Operator: Capture‑and‑Reuse Inside a Comprehension

Python 3.8 gave us the assignment expression (:=). Most devs see it as a cute way to shorten if statements, but it shines brightest inside comprehensions where you’d otherwise compute the same value twice.

The gotcha: Without it, you often end up calling an expensive function twice—once for the test, once for the value.

Before (the struggle):

results = [expensive_func(x) for x in data if expensive_func(x) > 10]

Each x triggers expensive_func two times. If expensive_func hits a web API or does heavy number‑crunching, you’re basically doing double the work.

After (the victory):

results = [y for x in data if (y := expensive_func(x)) > 10]

Now expensive_func runs once per item, its result is stored in y, and we reuse it for the output. The walrus lets us filter and capture in one breath.

2. Generator Expressions: Lazy Evaluation on Demand

A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory before you can touch the first element. A generator expression, on the other hand, yields items one‑by‑one, only when you ask for them.

The gotcha: Many developers swap a list comprehension for a generator and then wonder why their for loop works but len() explodes.

Before (the struggle):

# Trying to get the size of a filtered stream – BOOM!
big_list = [line for line in open('huge.log') if 'ERROR' in line]
print(len(big_list))   # MemoryError on huge files

After (the victory):

error_lines = (line for line in open('huge.log') if 'ERROR' in line)
# Now we can count without loading everything:
error_count = sum(1 for _ in error_lines)
print(error_count)   # Works, constant memory

The generator expression is like a conveyor belt: you get each piece as you need it, never filling the warehouse.

3. Multiple for Clauses: Cartesian Products in One Line

Most people know you can nest comprehensions, but few realize you can drop the nesting and write a Cartesian product directly with multiple for clauses.

The gotcha: You end up writing ugly nested loops when a single line would do, making the code harder to read.

Before (the struggle):

pairs = []
for a in [1, 2, 3]:
    for b in ['x', 'y']:
        pairs.append((a, b))

After (the victory):

pairs = [(a, b) for a in [1, 2, 3] for b in ['x', 'y']]

The order of the for clauses matches the nesting: the first loop is the outermost. This tiny shift can turn a five‑line block into a readable one‑liner, especially when you’re building test grids or parameter sweeps.

Wielding the Power (Code & Examples)

Let’s see these ideas in a realistic scenario: processing a CSV of sensor readings, filtering out noise, converting timestamps, and batch‑writing to a database.

The Naïve Approach 

import csv
from datetime import datetime

def process_file(path):
    rows = []                                   # ← list comprehension eats RAM
    with open(path) as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        for row in reader:
            val = float(row['value'])
            if val < 0 or val > 100:            # simple noise filter
                continue
            ts = datetime.fromisoformat(row['ts'])
            rows.append((ts, val))              # accumulate everything
    # Imagine writing rows to DB here …
    return rows

A file with a million lines forces Python to hold a million tuples in memory before any DB work starts.

The Power‑User Version 

import csv
from datetime import datetime

def process_file(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)

        # 1️⃣ Walrus: compute float once, reuse for filter and output
        # 2️⃣ Generator expression: lazy, never builds a huge list
        cleaned = (
            (ts, val)
            for row in reader
            if (val := float(row['value'])) >= 0 and val <= 100   # filter + capture
            for ts in [datetime.fromisoformat(row['ts'])]       # tiny inner loop to bind ts
        )

        # 3️⃣ Multiple `for` clauses: we could also build a grid of (timestamp, value) pairs
        #    if we needed to cross‑reference with another list, e.g. thresholds:
        thresholds = [0, 25, 50, 75, 100]
        binned = (
            (ts, val, thresh)
            for ts, val in cleaned
            for thresh in thresholds
            if val <= thresh
        )

        # Now we can stream `binned` straight into the DB:
        for record in binned:
            db.write(record)   # hypothetical write function

What changed?

  • The walrus saved us from calling float(row['value']) twice.
  • The outer generator (cleaned) yields one tuple at a time; memory stays flat regardless of file size.
  • The inner for ts in [...] is a trick to bind a computed value to a name without breaking the generator flow (you could also use := again, but this shows the flexibility of multiple for clauses).
  • Finally, we built a second generator (binned) that demonstrates how multiple for clauses create a Cartesian product—here we pair each reading with every threshold it passes, all without ever materializing the intermediate lists.

The function now streams data from disk to DB with constant memory footprint, and the code reads like a recipe rather than a tangled nest of loops.

Why This New Power Matters

Mastering these subtleties turns you from a “script kiddie” who writes code that works into a craftsman who writes code that scales.

  • Performance: You avoid unnecessary recomputation and memory bloat, which translates to faster runtime and lower cloud bills.
  • Readability: A well‑placed walrus or a tidy generator expression can replace three lines of loop‑noise with a single expressive statement.
  • Confidence: Knowing the exact scope rules, lazy evaluation tricks, and hidden syntax means you won’t be surprised when a comprehension behaves differently than you expected.

In short, you’ll spend less time debugging “why is my RAM exploding?” and more time building cool features—whether that’s a real‑time analytics pipeline, a game‑modding tool, or the next hot‑startup API.

Your Turn: The Challenge

Grab a script you’ve written that uses a list comprehension to filter or transform a large dataset. Refactor it using at least one of the three tricks above (walrus, generator, or multiple for clauses). Share your before/after snippets in the comments—I’m dying to see how you leveled up your code!

Happy hacking, and may your comprehensions be ever lazy and your walruses ever handy! 🚀

title: Kubernetes: un presupuesto para emails de prueba
description:
Un flujo de verificación de email en CI puede parecer pequeño hasta que un pod queda esperando una señal que nunca llega. Este patrón ayuda a poner límites claros y a diagnosticar el problema sin convertir cada timeout en una falsa alerta de producción.

El síntoma: un job que nunca termina

En una pipeline de Kubernetes, el test crea una cuenta, solicita un correo de verificación y consulta el buzón cada pocos segundos. Cuando el mensaje no aparece, el código reintenta. Después reintenta otra vez. El job termina agotando el tiempo global, pero el log solo dice verification timeout.

El pod puede estar sano y el nodo puede tener capacidad. Aun así, la prueba no progresa. El fallo real suele estar en una de estas fronteras:

  • el mensaje todavía está en tránsito;
  • el buzón expiró antes de ser consultado;
  • otro intento ya consumió el mensaje;
  • el proveedor devolvió un error temporal;
  • el test está esperando una dirección distinta de la que registró.

El error de diseño es tratar "esperar un email" como una espera infinita. En SRE, una espera sin presupuesto es una dependencia sin contrato.

Qué debe significar realmente “esperar el email”

Un consumidor de correo de prueba necesita un contrato pequeño, explícito y observable. Como mínimo, debe conocer:

  1. Identidad: dirección, identificador de ejecución y mensaje esperado.
  2. Ventana de validez: cuándo se creó el buzón y cuándo deja de ser util.
  3. Señal de éxito: asunto, remitente o token que confirma el mensaje correcto.
  4. Regla de parada: tiempo total, número de consultas y errores no reintentables.
  5. Resultado final: encontrado, expirado, no encontrado o fallo del proveedor.

Esto también evita que dos pruebas compartan sin querer el mismo buzón. Para probar correos de onboarding sin ensuciar las métricas, conviene separar la identidad de prueba de las métricas del producto.

El nombre de la búsqueda no cambia el contrato. Un equipo puede hablar de correo temporal, temp mail so o tempmail disposable; el sistema debe seguir guardando el mismo run_id, la misma dirección y el mismo estado.

Diseñar un presupuesto de señales

En vez de repetir hasta que algo funcione, asigna un presupuesto para cada tipo de espera:

  • Tiempo total: por ejemplo, 90 segundos para que llegue el mensaje.
  • Intervalo inicial: una consulta después de 2 segundos.
  • Backoff: aumentar el intervalo a 4, 8 y 12 segundos, con un máximo fijo.
  • Consultas: cortar después de un número razonable, aunque quede tiempo.
  • Errores: distinguir un 404 de buzón expirado de un 429 que merece una pausa.

No hace falta que estos números sean iguales en todos los equipos. Lo importante es que estén en configuración, aparezcan en el run manifest y puedan explicarse durante un incidente. Un presupuesto demasiado corto produce falsos negativos; uno demasiado largo secuestra workers y esconde una regresión.

Un estado simple suele ser suficiente:

created -> waiting -> found
                   -> expired
                   -> provider_error
                   -> timed_out

La transición debe ser idempotente. Si el controlador recibe dos respuestas para el mismo mensaje, solo una puede cerrar la prueba como found. De lo contrario, el segundo intento puede dejar métricas contradictorias y el diagnóstico se vuelve confuso.

Implementación en Kubernetes

El presupuesto debe vivir cerca del trabajo que lo consume, no solamente en el servicio externo. Un Job puede recibir valores como MAIL_WAIT_TOTAL_SECONDS y MAIL_POLL_MAX_ATTEMPTS, mientras que un ConfigMap contiene los valores por entorno. Los secretos, claro, deben seguir en un Secret o en el gestor de secretos correspondiente.

El contenedor debería emitir un recibo al terminar:

{
  "run_id": "ci-1842",
  "mailbox_created_at": "2026-10-16T00:10:00Z",
  "outcome": "timed_out",
  "polls": 7,
  "elapsed_seconds": 91,
  "last_error": "message_not_found"
}

No pongas el contenido completo del email ni tokens de verificación en logs compartidos. Un hash corto del mensaje, el dominio controlado y el identificador de ejecución suelen ser suficientes para correlacionar. Si el job es reintentado por Kubernetes, conserva el run_id original o marca claramente el intento; mezclar ambos hace parecer que hay dos mensajes cuando solo existe uno.

Los reenvíos también necesitan una política. Los reenvíos de verificación con una experiencia predecible deben tener un límite propio. Cada reenvío puede producir un token nuevo y dejar al test esperando el enlace anterior. En ese caso, no es un problema de velocidad del pod: es una carrera entre estados.

Observabilidad y diagnóstico

Mide la duración desde la creación del buzón hasta la llegada del mensaje, pero separa tres tiempos: envío de la aplicación, entrega del proveedor y consulta del consumidor. El equipo mira mas el contador total cuando debería mirar cual de esas fases creció.

En una alerta o comentario de CI, incluye:

  • run_id y nombre del job;
  • edad del buzón al último intento;
  • cantidad y tipo de errores;
  • último estado conocido;
  • si hubo reenvíos;
  • el presupuesto que se consumió.

Si alguien escribe tamp mail com o dummy e mail al buscar el incidente, esos términos pueden aparecer en una nota o en documentación, pero nunca deben convertirse en un dominio permitido de forma automática. La lista de dominios y la política de privacidad deben ser explícitas.

Checklist antes de declarar estable el flujo

  • ¿Cada prueba tiene un buzón y un run_id únicos?
  • ¿Hay un tiempo total y un máximo de consultas?
  • ¿Se diferencia expiración, rate limit y mensaje ausente?
  • ¿El backoff evita una tormenta contra el proveedor?
  • ¿Un reintento del Job conserva o reemplaza la identidad de forma clara?
  • ¿Los logs excluyen tokens y contenido sensible?
  • ¿Se puede explicar el fallo mirando un solo recibo?

Si una respuesta es no, el próximo incidente volverá a parecer aleatorio.

Cierre

Un email de prueba es una dependencia externa, aunque el test se ejecute dentro de un clúster propio. Kubernetes puede reiniciar el pod, pero no puede hacer aparecer una señal que expiró ni corregir un token consumido por otra prueba. Un presupuesto de señales, estados idempotentes y un recibo pequeño convierten una espera frágil en un flujo que un equipo SRE puede operar.

title: Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-19490 and CVE-2026-19489: Audit Evidence for a Perimeter Patch
description:
Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-19490 and CVE-2026-19489: Audit Evidence for a Perimeter Patch

Remediation is a technical act; proving it is a governance one. When an authentication bypass lands in the device that authenticates everyone, the question auditors and risk owners ask is not whether the patch exists but whether the organisation can show which appliances were affected and what was done. The two Citrix NetScaler flaws published on 19 August 2026 make that distinction concrete. CVE-2026-19490 is critical and bypasses authentication; CVE-2026-19489 is a high-severity buffer overrun leading to denial of service.

Vulnerability overview

NSM, the Norwegian National Security Authority, republished the advisory on 20 August 2026. It described CVE-2026-19490 as allowing an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication on exposed appliances and reach the internal network, and CVE-2026-19489 as a buffer overrun causing unpredictable behaviour and denial of service. NSM reported no awareness of active exploitation at the time, expected it shortly, and advised prompt updates.

Mechanism and exploitation conditions

CVE-2026-19490 applies where the appliance is configured as a Gateway, using the SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy roles, or as an AAA virtual server, which on newer builds means an AAA server configured with a SAML action. The precondition is configuration, not exposure alone, which is exactly why the audit trail needs to record configuration alongside version.
CVE-2026-19489 applies where Session Initiation Protocol Application Layer Gateway, SIP ALG, is enabled for Large Scale NAT, LSN. That is a narrower and more specific setting, and recording it turns a risk statement into a defensible scoping decision.

Impact

For CVE-2026-19490, the impact is unauthorised network access through a control the organisation relies on for its trust boundary. That makes the flaw a candidate for material-risk reporting, not just a technical ticket.
For CVE-2026-19489, the impact is service unavailability. It is a resilience issue: remote access, load balancing and authentication can be interrupted together when they share the appliance.

Affected products and scope

The affected products are Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway. CVE-2026-19490 concerns appliances running a Gateway or AAA role; CVE-2026-19489 concerns appliances with SIP ALG enabled for LSN. Citrix published limited technical detail beyond affected versions and preconditions, and any internal write-up should keep to that boundary rather than inferring an attack chain.

Exposure context

ZoomEye gives the scoping evidence a number. A product query for app="Citrix NetScaler" returned 239,670 matching instances, with title="Citrix Gateway" at 166,199 and title="NetScaler" at 72,084. These are product-matching assets, not confirmed-vulnerable hosts. A CVE-indexed query, vul.cve="CVE-2026-19489", returned zero, which reflects ZoomEye's tagging rather than an empty affected population.

Remediation and mitigations

There is no workaround; the advisory states that applying the security update is the only fix, so the governance work is about evidence rather than alternatives.
Evidence worth producing and retaining:

  • An asset list of every NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway instance, including FIPS and NDcPP deployments, with the running build recorded before and after the update.
  • A configuration record showing which instances run a Gateway or AAA role and which have SIP ALG enabled for LSN, with the logic used to decide that the rest are out of scope.
  • Patch completion evidence per node, since a maintenance window is a plan and a verified build is a fact.
  • A log-review note for any appliance that was internet-facing on a vulnerable build, because the patch does not establish that no access took place.

References

  • NSM/CERT Norway, Critical vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler: https://nsm.no/fagomrader/digital-sikkerhet/digital-hendelseshandtering/varsler-fra-nsm/kritisk-sarbarhet-i-citrix-netscaler
  • Citrix security bulletin CTX697096: https://support.citrix.com/support-home/kbsearch/article?articleNumber=CTX697096
  • The Hacker News, Warning: two unpatched Citrix NetScaler RCE zero-days: https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/warning-two-unpatched-citrix-netscaler.html

title: From IoT Sensor Data to AI-Driven Industrial Decisions
description:
IoT devices can collect valuable information about equipment, inventory, environmental conditions, and industrial processes. However, collecting data is only the first step. The real challenge is converting those measurements into reliable, useful decisions.

  1. Build a Reliable Data Foundation

Sensors and connected devices generate readings such as temperature, vibration, location, and operating status. Before applying AI, systems need consistent timestamps, correct asset identification, and basic data-quality checks.

Poor-quality input can lead to misleading predictions.

  1. Process Data at the Right Level

Some applications require immediate local responses, while others can use centralized cloud analytics. Edge computing can reduce latency and support selected functions when connectivity is limited. Cloud platforms can help analyze information across multiple sites.

The right architecture depends on the application's response time, security, and infrastructure requirements.

  1. Apply AI to Specific Problems

AI models can help detect unusual patterns, estimate equipment failure risk, identify inventory discrepancies, and support operational planning.

Each model should be evaluated against a clear baseline. Accuracy alone is not enough; false alarms, missed events, and the cost of incorrect recommendations also matter.

  1. Connect Insights to Workflows

A useful industrial system does more than display predictions. It can send alerts, create maintenance tasks, or recommend corrective actions.

For safety-critical operations, authorization, operating limits, audit trails, and human oversight are essential before connecting AI recommendations to physical equipment.

  1. Measure the Outcome

Track practical metrics such as unplanned downtime, inventory accuracy, response time, and equipment utilization. These measures help determine whether the system delivers genuine operational value.

AIoT is ultimately about connecting the physical world to meaningful data and decisions. Aperture Venture Studio focuses on building and scaling ventures at the intersection of AI and IoT for industrial applications.

AI #IoT #AIoT #SoftwareArchitecture #IndustrialTechnology

title: Your AI-built app works in the demo. But did the signup event actually reach GA4?
description:
You vibe-coded a landing page with a lead form over a weekend. The demo works: you submit, you see the success toast, you move on. Two weeks later you open GA4 and there are three events for a form that was submitted forty times — or worse, zero.

This keeps happening to AI-built apps for a structural reason, not a careless one. The AI generates the UI and the tracking code in one pass, nobody writes a test for an event that "fires" (the page loads fine either way), and analytics bugs are silent by design: a broken button shows an error, a broken generate_lead event shows nothing at all. Your funnel just becomes quietly unmeasurable.

Here is the manual verification process that actually works today, before any tooling — learned the hard way from debugging duplicate conversions and dead DebugViews in production properties.

1. DebugView proves almost nothing. Use it anyway — correctly.

GA4 DebugView is the first place everyone looks, and the first place that lies to you. DebugView only shows events from browsers/devices running in debug mode (GTM Preview, debug_mode: true in gtag, or the GA Debugger extension). Three failure modes bite everyone:

  • Events appear in DebugView but never in standard reports — often consent mode defaulting to denied, or a duplicate property/measurement ID (events going to a test property).
  • DebugView shows nothing while events flow fine — your debug flag never got set on the environment you're testing.
  • DebugView works in GTM Preview but not from the live site — your trigger conditions differ between preview and production (consent, data layer timing).

So: use DebugView to confirm the event structure (name, parameters), never to confirm it arrives in production conditions.

2. Inspect the actual network request

The ground truth is the request itself. Open DevTools → Network, filter for google-analytics.com/g/collect, submit your form, and read the request:

  • en= — the event name. Typos here are the #1 silent killer: generate_leads never matches the generate_lead you built reports on.
  • cid= / _ga cookie — the client ID. If it changes between page loads, every submission looks like a brand new user.
  • ep.* — custom parameters. Verify the lead's value/label actually travels.
  • gtm= — confirms which GTM container version served the tag.

For SPAs, do this twice: once on a cold load, once after client-side navigation. Route-change page_views and duplicated listeners show up only in the second pass.

3. The duplicate-event check (the one that costs real money)

A generate_lead firing twice per submission inflates conversions and corrupts every downstream bid strategy. The reliable way to count duplicates is not eyeballing DebugView — it's counting per client ID over a window:

  • With BigQuery export (free tier of GA4 exports): query events_* for the last day, group by user_pseudo_id, event_name, and a 60-second timestamp bucket, and count events per bucket. Any bucket > 1 for a conversion event is a duplicate candidate.
  • Without BigQuery: GA4 Explorations → open a single session → check whether one session shows twice the conversion events you expect. Crude, but it catches the common React StrictMode / double-render / retry duplicates.

Do this once per tracking release, not once ever. GTM container versions change.

4. The 10-point release checklist

Before you call tracking "done" on an AI-built app:

  1. Every planned event fires with the exact documented name (en=).
  2. Parameters arrive (ep.*), with correct types (revenue as number, not string).
  3. The client ID is stable across a full journey (landing → form → thank-you).
  4. No duplicates on double-click, no duplicates on SPA route re-entry.
  5. Consent state actually gates what you think it gates.
  6. Events fire in production, not only in preview/debug.
  7. The thank-you page fires its conversion exactly once, on the server-confirmed outcome if possible.
  8. Cross-domain links (checkout, docs) preserve the session.
  9. No events fire on bot/preview/admin paths.
  10. You can reproduce steps 1–9 from scratch in under 10 minutes — otherwise it will never be repeated, and it will rot.

The part I'm building

I went through this often enough — including auditing a live commerce deployment where configuration drift produced measurably wrong discount behavior, silent failures again — that I've started building an open-source tool around step 10: you define a user journey once, it drives a real browser through it (Playwright-based), asserts the analytics events that should fire — names, parameters, duplicates, consent state — alongside API and database state checks, and emits an evidence bundle you can attach to a PR or a release.

It's early — no public release yet, so there's nothing to link and nothing to oversell. If steps 2–3 above describe your week, I'd genuinely like to know which part hurts most: duplicate detection, parameter assertions, or consent-mode verification. That decides what gets built first. Comments or DM.

title: TouchGrass AI
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

TouchGrass AI 🌿 — A Local-First Outdoor Activity Companion

TouchGrass AI is a local-first, open-weight AI companion that turns screen time into small, practical outdoor missions. Users select their mood, available time, energy level, and preferred activities to receive personalized suggestions for mindful walks, nature exploration, bird listening, gardening, and gentle movement.

The goal is simple: make the screen the shortest part of the experience. Get a plan, put the phone away, and reconnect with the world outside.

The application includes a built-in fallback planner, so users can still receive activity suggestions without downloading an AI model. It is designed without user accounts, analytics, or third-party cloud AI dependencies.

Demo

Local demo: Run the application on your machine using the setup instructions in the repository's README.

To run it, install the dependencies with npm install, start the server using npm start, and visit http://localhost:3000.

Code

GitHub Repository — TouchGrass AI

How I Built It

I built TouchGrass AI using Node.js and Express for the backend, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the frontend, and Ollama to support local inference with the open-weight llama3.2:3b model.

The application collects a user's activity preferences and constructs a prompt that asks the local model to generate a realistic outdoor mission, including its duration, difficulty, step-by-step instructions, and an alternative for when going outside is not practical.

The backend communicates with Ollama through its local API. If the model is unavailable, the application falls back to its built-in activity planner, keeping the core experience accessible without a cloud AI service.

I also designed the interface to be responsive and straightforward, with a focus on reducing unnecessary screen interaction rather than encouraging users to spend more time inside an application.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation is central to TouchGrass AI because the information people share about their mood, routines, and personal preferences should not automatically need to leave their devices.

Using an open-weight model with local inference makes it possible to generate personalized activity suggestions without depending on a paid, proprietary AI API. It reduces dependence on external services, gives users more control over their data, and allows developers to inspect and modify the prompts, experiment with different models, and customize the application's behavior.

The built-in fallback also ensures that the project remains useful when a model has not been installed or is unavailable.

Most importantly, open-source AI makes this experience more accessible to people who want to experiment, learn, and build without recurring inference costs. Instead of locking the core functionality behind a closed service, TouchGrass AI keeps the implementation open and adaptable.

For this project, the value of AI is not keeping people engaged with technology for longer. It is using technology to help people step away from it.

My Agent Session

This project does not currently include a published DevRelay agent session. I may add one later to document the development process and demonstrate how the local AI integration works.
