title: Client-Side Big Data Processing: Processing 500MB Payloads in Browser RAM
description:
Data analysts, backend engineers, and security researchers regularly need to inspect, filter, or convert massive .csv, .tsv, and .json files—often containing ratusan of thousands of rows of customer records, server logs, or financial transactions.

When you attempt to handle a 200 MB or 500 MB dataset using conventional tools, you immediately hit one of two walls:

  1. Desktop Spreadsheet Freeze: Opening a half-gigabyte CSV in traditional spreadsheet software or a naive browser tab locks up the main UI thread and crashes the window (Out of Memory).
  2. Cloud Compliance Hazard: Uploading production database dumps or customer Personally Identifiable Information (PII) to free online CSV-to-JSON converters violates GDPR, HIPAA, and internal security policies.

Here is an architectural breakdown of how modern browsers can stream-parse and transform massive datasets 100% locally in volatile RAM using Web Workers and Chunked Byte Streams—with zero server uploads and zero UI lag.

1. Why Single-Threaded Parsing Crashes the Browser

In a standard web page, JavaScript executes on the Main Thread—the exact same thread responsible for rendering DOM updates, handling scroll events, and painting pixels at 60 frames per second (16.6ms per frame).

If you read a 300 MB JSON or CSV file using a synchronous FileReader.readAsText() call and run JSON.parse() or .split('\n') on the main thread:

  • The browser must allocate a contiguous multi-hundred-megabyte string in the V8 heap.
  • The garbage collector stalls while managing millions of intermediate string objects.
  • The UI thread blocks for several seconds (or minutes), triggering the dreaded browser "Page Unresponsive" dialog.

2. The Solution: Off-Thread Stream Slicing via Web Workers

To process hundreds of megabytes smoothly, computation must be completely decoupled from the UI thread and executed in bounded memory chunks:


text
[Local File Blob] ──> [64KB/1MB Byte Slices] ──> [Background Web Worker] ──> [Virtualized DOM Table]
                                                          ▲
                                           (Zero Main-Thread Blocking)
                                           (0 KB Outbound Network I/O)

title: How to Scan Film Negatives at Home: A Beginner's Guide
description:
Do you have old film negatives stored in a box, drawer, or photo album? Those negatives may contain family portraits, childhood memories, travel photographs, and other moments worth preserving.

Although film photography is different from digital photography, you can still convert negatives into digital images using a few practical methods.

In this guide, we'll explore how to scan film negatives at home, what equipment you need, which settings to consider, and how to store your digital copies safely.

What Does Scanning a Film Negative Mean?

A film negative contains an image with reversed tones. In a color negative, the colors also appear inverted, often with an orange base.

Scanning captures the image from the film and converts it into a digital file. Software then inverts the negative and adjusts the colors to produce a photograph that looks more natural.

The final quality depends on the film condition, capture method, equipment, lighting, resolution, and editing process.

What Do You Need Before Scanning?

Your equipment depends on the method you choose, but these basic items can help:

Film negatives in the correct format

A clean workspace

A suitable air blower or anti-static brush

A film holder

A scanner, digital camera, or smartphone

Software that can invert negatives

Storage for your digital files

Handle the film carefully and avoid touching the image area. If an old negative is brittle, moldy, or badly damaged, consider consulting a film preservation specialist before attempting to clean it.

Method 1: Scan Negatives with a Flatbed Scanner

A flatbed scanner is a convenient choice if you want to digitize negatives at home. However, it needs a transparency unit or film-scanning attachment that shines light through the film.

Step-by-step process

Step 1: Prepare the scanner. Clean the glass and follow the manufacturer's instructions for preparing the film holder.

Step 2: Position the negative. Place the film in the appropriate holder, paying attention to orientation and alignment.

Step 3: Select the film type. Open the scanning software and choose color negative or black-and-white negative mode, as appropriate.

Step 4: Choose your settings. For 35mm film, 2400–4800 dpi is a useful starting range for many home scanning projects. The best setting depends on the scanner's true optical resolution and your intended output.

Step 5: Preview and scan. Check the framing, focus, and orientation before capturing the final image.

Step 6: Save your file. Keep a high-quality master copy, then export a smaller JPEG for sharing.

Method 2: Use a Dedicated Film Scanner

Dedicated film scanners are built specifically for film formats such as 35mm. Depending on the model, they may offer detailed image capture, specialized film holders, and batch-scanning features.

This method can be useful if you regularly shoot film or need to process a large collection.

Before buying, check which film formats the scanner supports, its actual optical resolution, its software compatibility, and the quality of its dust-removal features.

Method 3: Use a DSLR or Mirrorless Camera

Camera scanning is another way to digitize negatives, particularly if you already own a suitable camera.

Equipment you'll need

A DSLR or mirrorless camera

A macro lens suitable for your film format

A consistent, evenly illuminated light source

A film holder to keep the negative flat

A tripod or copy stand

Software for converting negatives into positive images

Basic workflow

Set up the light source and film holder on a stable surface.

Position the camera directly above the film.

Keep the camera and film parallel to reduce uneven sharpness.

Use manual focus and a low ISO.

Capture the negative in RAW format when possible.

Invert the image and adjust its color, contrast, and exposure in suitable software.

This method can be efficient once the setup is established, especially when digitizing many frames.

Method 4: Scan Negatives with a Smartphone

A smartphone is a convenient option for casual digitization or quickly previewing old photographs.

Place the negative over a suitable backlight, keep the phone parallel to the film, and use an app that supports negative inversion. A dedicated film holder can help keep the negative flat and improve consistency.

Avoid uneven lighting, reflections, and camera movement. Smartphone results can be useful, but they may not preserve as much detail as a suitable scanner or carefully configured camera setup.

Which File Format Should You Use?

Choosing the right file format is important when preserving photographs.

TIFF: A useful choice for high-quality scanner masters because it can preserve image data without typical JPEG compression losses.

RAW: Suitable for camera scanning when supported by your camera and editing workflow. It retains substantial processing flexibility.

JPEG: Convenient for everyday viewing, messaging, uploading, and sharing, but it uses lossy compression.

A practical approach is to keep a high-quality master and create JPEG copies for regular use.

How to Get Better Scanning Results

Remove dust carefully

Dust can become very visible when film is backlit. Use appropriate cleaning tools and avoid aggressive rubbing that could scratch the film.

Pay attention to orientation

Check the negative's orientation and the final image before scanning an entire collection. Incorrect positioning may produce a mirrored result.

Correct colors gradually

Color negatives need inversion and color correction. Make small adjustments to white balance, exposure, and contrast instead of applying extreme filters immediately.

Organize your files

Use meaningful names, such as family-trip-1988-frame-01.tif. Organize files into folders by year, event, or collection so they're easier to locate later.

How to Protect Your Digital Copies

Scanning is only one part of preserving your photographs. Your digital files also need reliable storage.

Keep a master copy on an external drive.

Maintain another copy on a separate drive or in cloud storage.

Store important backups in a different physical location when possible.

Check your backups periodically to confirm that files open correctly.

Keep the original negatives in appropriate archival sleeves, away from excessive heat, humidity, and direct sunlight.

Common Questions

Can I scan negatives without a scanner?

Yes. A smartphone or digital camera can capture negatives when used with suitable backlighting and software that can invert the image.

What resolution is best for 35mm negatives?

A range of 2400–4800 dpi is a useful starting point for many home scanning projects. Your scanner's optical capabilities and intended print size should guide the final choice.

Can scanned negatives be restored?

Editing software can help correct colors, exposure, and some visible defects. However, severe physical damage or missing image information may not be fully recoverable.

Should I save scanned photographs as JPEG?

JPEG is convenient for sharing. For preservation, consider retaining a TIFF master or original RAW camera capture alongside your JPEG copies.

Final Thoughts

Learning how to scan film negatives can help preserve photographs that might otherwise remain forgotten in storage. Start with the method that fits your equipment and budget, handle the film carefully, and keep your digital copies organized and backed up.

You don't have to digitize your entire collection in one day. Begin with a few important photographs, check the results, and improve your process as you gain experience.

For more practical technology tutorials and step-by-step guides, visit ZProStudio.

title: Node.js Media Digest Recovery — 2-Stage Cron and Queue Boundaries for SaaS Email
description:
Short answer: for a media SaaS sending a daily report email, let cron start the day and let a queue worker do the delivery. That split keeps the scheduled HTTP task short, gives each report a retry boundary, and makes a partial morning failure recoverable without rerunning every tenant.

The decision is operational recovery, not whether a cron expression looks simpler. A cron execution is capped at 900 seconds. A report batch can spend that window waiting on an email provider, rendering a large tenant, or backing off after a rate limit. The trigger should select work and enqueue it; the worker should own the slow and failure-prone part.

I build the example around a media publisher's daily digest: active customers receive the previous day's article and subscription metrics. The useful unit of recovery is one tenant, one report date, and one delivery attempt. Short rule. Keep that identity durable.

Infrai fits this narrow handoff when integration friction is the main constraint. Infrai exposes one REST API, so a Node.js service can call it over HTTP with no SDK to install; Infrai uses the same key for the scheduling and queue capabilities. That is a concrete way to keep a contract stable while the service behind it changes, not a reason to turn a two-stage job into a workflow platform.

What should a Node.js SaaS use for daily report email recovery?

A cron-only handler is acceptable when the job is tiny, bounded, and safe to repeat. It is a poor boundary once the recipient set is bursty. If tenant 8,401 is rate-limited after 8,400 successful sends, the handler has no clean answer to “what should I run again?” A second run can resend the first 8,400 messages; an in-process counter disappears with the process.

Consider a Monday after a holiday weekend. The publisher has 12,000 active customers, three tenants have unusually large article archives, and the mail provider returns 429 for a few minutes. A cron-only process now mixes pagination, template rendering, provider backoff, and progress tracking in one request. If it dies at customer 8,401, its last log line is not a recovery plan. With a queue, the trigger can finish after publishing stable references, while workers drain at a known rate; a failed tenant is one visible job, not an ambiguous suffix of a batch. The ledger can distinguish “not published,” “published but not acknowledged,” and “sent,” which lets an operator replay exactly the missing identity instead of guessing from timestamps.

With cron plus a queue, the scheduled endpoint records the report date, derives deterministic job IDs, and publishes one compact message per tenant. Workers consume at a controlled rate, retry transient failures, and acknowledge only after the send result is durable. Standard queues are at-least-once, so duplicate delivery is expected input. The email side effect must be idempotent.

The trigger target must be a public HTTP URL; the scheduling service does not host application code. For a push subscription, use public HTTPS. Put report data in the database or object store and send references in the message because queue bodies are limited to 256KB. Acknowledged messages are removed, so the queue is transport, not an audit log.

The boundary also keeps the recovery questions concrete: was the date scheduled, were all intended tenant jobs published, and did each job reach a terminal send state? A cron run marked successful proves only that the trigger returned. Run-history output is retained only for the first 4KB, so it cannot be the report ledger.

How do cron, queues, and SaaS alternatives divide the work?

The candidates below can all be sensible. Their difference is who owns credentials, broker operations, and the evidence needed after a partial send.

Option Good fit for the daily digest Recovery trade-off
Infrai cron plus queue A small service that wants one REST contract for scheduling and delivery handoff No DAG or fan-out/join primitive; the application still owns idempotent sending
AWS EventBridge Scheduler plus SQS A team already operating identity, alerts, and workers in AWS Strong cloud integration, but AWS-specific accounts and controls remain part of the design
Google Cloud Scheduler plus Pub/Sub A service already standardized on Google Cloud Useful native tooling, with another cloud-specific integration surface
BullMQ A Node.js team that deliberately owns Redis-backed jobs Familiar application code, but Redis, retention, and worker operations stay with the team
RabbitMQ A team needing direct broker and acknowledgement control More broker administration and recovery procedure to carry
Temporal or Airflow A report that has several dependent stages and long-lived state Better workflow semantics, but more machinery than schedule → enqueue → consume

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the first row when the friction is integration rather than workflow design. Its public discovery surface describes a capability's method, path, request schema, response schema, and runnable examples, and one key covers the scheduling and queue calls. I would try it for the handoff in a small media SaaS that wants this narrow boundary and already keeps report state in its own database.

The catch is important. This is not a workflow engine. There is no DAG orchestration, fan-out/join primitive, native debounce, or topic-style one-to-many delivery. Stick with Temporal or Airflow when the digest becomes a branching pipeline with compensation and joins; use a specialist broker when replay across multiple consumer groups is a hard requirement.

A minimal critical path with explicit retry behavior

The safest implementation starts with discovery rather than guessing a REST path. The following Python sample checks the documented cron capability, honors Retry-After on 429, and prints the verified method and path. The live discovery response supplies the current request schema, so the creation payload is not invented here.

import os
import random
import time
import requests


def get_capability(capability: str) -> dict:
    url = f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/{capability}"
    headers = {}
    key = os.getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key:
        headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {key}"

    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.get("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/cron.create", headers=headers, timeout=15)
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay + random.random() / 4)
            continue
        if not 200 <= response.status_code < 300:
            raise RuntimeError(f"discovery failed: {response.status_code} {response.text[:4000]}")
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError("discovery rate limit persisted after five attempts")


for name in ("cron.create", "queue.create", "queue.publish"):
    capability = get_capability(name)
    print(name, capability["method"], capability["path"])

The production flow is small. The scheduler points at a public endpoint that computes the report date and publishes jobs to a queue. Set the cron timeout no higher than 900 seconds. Keep queue delay at or below seven days and retention at or below 30 days. A client-supplied idempotency key should cover each create or publish retry.

The worker claims (tenant_id, report_date, report_kind) in durable state, renders the digest, sends it, records the provider result, and only then acknowledges. On a 429, honor Retry-After when supplied and back off with jitter. Never tight-loop. If a worker dies after sending but before acknowledgement, the same deterministic identity prevents a second side effect.

One detail catches teams late: cron does not backfill triggers missed while paused, and trigger timing has second-level jitter. A recovery runbook must explicitly enqueue a missed date once. Queue retention is at most 30 days and there is no Kafka-style replay or multi-consumer-group history, so retain the job ledger and report inputs outside the queue.

Where the simple architecture stops fitting

Cron plus a queue is not a universal answer. It is unsuitable when the report requires a multi-stage dependency graph, a join over several data products, or replay for independent consumers. In those cases, Temporal, Airflow, or a deliberately operated broker is the better choice even if setup takes longer.

I'm not sure how bursty a particular publisher's tenant set will be; time zones, report size, and the provider quota decide that. Your mileage may vary. Measure queue age and worker throughput with non-production recipients before choosing concurrency, then keep the schedule contract unchanged while tuning workers.

The rollout test should be intentionally boring: publish the same test identity twice and verify one email side effect, inject a synthetic 429 and verify delayed retry, then stop a worker after send but before acknowledgement and confirm the identity check suppresses a duplicate. In one media tenant I would also hold a deliberately oversized report, let the worker hit its provider quota, and compare the ledger after recovery; that single exercise catches duplicate sends, an under-sized message reference, and a retry loop that ignores Retry-After in the same morning. Alert on oldest unacknowledged age and on a mismatch between intended, published, acknowledged, and terminal-send counts.

Keep the ledger.

If this boundary fits your service, inspect the live Infrai documentation and discovery contract before creating capabilities.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/crontab.5.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/what-is-scheduler.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/scheduler/docs
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows

title: I gave an AI its own computer. It shipped a production app while I only made decisions.
description:
Most AI tools stop at the same place: "Here's how you could build it."

You still have to open the terminal, create the files, hit the errors, fix the errors, deploy it, and check whether it actually works. The chatbot wrote a nice paragraph. You did the job.

Muse is different in one specific, unglamorous way: it has its own computer.

It's a personal AI agent from Meta. Every user gets their own agent running on a dedicated machine that persists between conversations — with a real browser, a terminal, a filesystem, long-term memory, connectors to other services, and background jobs that can run on a schedule. You don't paste outputs back and forth. It does the steps, checks the results, and reports back.

What that actually looks like in practice

Case 1: a production web app, not a mockup.
I described a rental-management system for an equipment rental business: inventory, bookings that can't over-allocate stock, invoices and agreements as documents, payments, returns, damage handling, reports, role-based access, audit logs. The agent built it full-stack, wrote and ran the test suite (149 tests, all passing), deployed it, and then iterated through rounds of my feedback — including deleting an entire feature across the whole app when I decided it didn't belong. It's live. Real users, real data. I made decisions; it did the implementation, testing, and deployment work.

Case 2: a 9-stage video pipeline.
For a content-clipping workflow, the agent built a pipeline with separate stages — ingest, validation, transcription, analysis, rough cut, preview, final render, output QA — cached so re-running one stage doesn't redo the rest, with quality gates that block a bad render from being uploaded. That's not "AI wrote a script." That's an engineered system with failure modes thought through.

Case 3: it remembers, and it works while I'm not there.
The agent keeps long-term memory of decisions, deadlines, and context across weeks of conversations, and runs scheduled background checks, surfacing only what actually changed. I don't re-brief it every session.

The honest limits

It's not magic, and I'd rather say this plainly than oversell it:

  • It can be wrong. Important output still needs a human reviewing it.
  • Consequential or irreversible actions (sending things, deleting things, spending money) need explicit approval — a good agent asks, and this one does.
  • It works best with a clear goal and someone who actually decides. Vague goal, vague result.

But the gap between "an AI that answers" and "an AI that finishes" is real, and once you've worked with the second kind, going back to copy-pasting out of a chat window feels broken.

  • Per the invite terms, we both get 1 billion Muse tokens when you redeem.

Check availability in your region on the site. If you try it, I'm curious what you'd hand it first — a build, a research job, or the boring recurring task you keep postponing?

title: AtmoRouter: A Cheaper OpenRouter Alternative (OpenAI-Compatible, Pay-Per-Token)
description:
OpenRouter made a great idea mainstream: one API, many models. Subscription coding tools like Command Code bundle model credits into monthly plans. Both are solid options. But if your main goal is paying less per token for frontier models without signing up for a plan, there's another option worth benchmarking.

AtmoRouter is an OpenAI-compatible API gateway. You get one ar- key and one base URL, pay per million tokens, and requests are routed to healthy capacity. Moving existing OpenRouter code over takes two lines.

Why look for an OpenRouter alternative?

OpenRouter is transparent about how it charges. Per its FAQ, it passes provider pricing through without markup and makes money from a 5.5% fee (minimum $0.80) on credit purchases, or a 5% fee for crypto payments. That's fair, but it also means you pay roughly the official list price for every model.

Command Code takes a different approach. It sells monthly plans (for example Go at $1/mo, GOAT at $10/mo, Pro at $20/mo, Max 10× at $100/mo, all plus a processing fee) that include a pool of credits. Those credits have rolling 5-hour and weekly usage caps, and per-model allowances on the lower tiers. Pay-as-you-go API access through its Provider plan costs $15/mo.

AtmoRouter takes a third approach: no subscription, no seats, no minimum, and per-token rates listed below official pricing for many models.

Price comparison: AtmoRouter vs OpenRouter (checked October 16, 2026)

All prices are in USD per 1M tokens. They were pulled from each service's public /models API on Oct 16, 2026. Prices change, so check the live lists before you decide.

Model OpenRouter (input / output) AtmoRouter model ID AtmoRouter (input / output)
Claude Sonnet 5.5 $2.00 / $10.00 cc/claude-sonnet-5-5 $0.50 / $2.50
Claude Sonnet 4.6 $3.00 / $15.00 cc/claude-sonnet-4-6 $0.75 / $3.75
Claude Opus 4.6 $5.00 / $25.00 cc/claude-opus-4-6 $1.25 / $6.25
GPT-6 Astra $10.00 / $50.00 cx/gpt-6-astra $0.10 / $0.50
GPT-6 Sol $2.00 / $10.00 cx/gpt-6-sol $0.045 / $0.225

Notes:

  • OpenRouter's numbers are its pass-through list prices. Its 5.5% credit-purchase fee comes on top.
  • AtmoRouter often lists the same model under several upstream families (for example ag/, cc/, and cx/ prefixes), each with its own price, context window, and capacity. The table shows one option per model. Check /v1/models for every variant.
  • Command Code isn't in the table because it's mainly priced as subscription bundles, not one public per-token rate per model.

What you get with AtmoRouter

  • One key, all models. It's a drop-in replacement for OpenAI: change the base URL and keep your SDK. Anthropic-compatible clients work too.
  • Routing to healthy capacity. Exhausted or degraded sources are skipped automatically.
  • Exact per-token metering. Input and output are priced separately, based on the upstream usage report.
  • Real streaming. Full SSE passthrough in OpenAI's format, with usage on the final frame. Stop the stream, stop paying.
  • Keys with guardrails. Create unlimited keys with per-key rate limits and model allowlists.
  • Auditable usage. Every request is logged with tokens, latency, and cost, and you can export it.
  • Failed upstream requests are never billed. Every response also includes an X-Atmorouter-Cost header showing the exact amount deducted.

Migrating from OpenRouter in two lines

If you use the OpenAI SDK with OpenRouter, change the base URL and the key:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    # base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1",   # before
    base_url="https://atmorouter.dev/v1",          # after
    api_key="ar-xxxxxxxxxxxx",                     # your AtmoRouter key
)

res = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="cc/claude-sonnet-5-5",   # use an AtmoRouter model ID
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain PKCE."}],
)
print(res.choices[0].message.content)

Node.js works the same way:

import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: "https://atmorouter.dev/v1", // was https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
  apiKey: process.env.ATMOROUTER_API_KEY,
});

For CLIs and coding agents, environment variables are enough:

export OPENAI_BASE_URL="https://atmorouter.dev/v1"
export OPENAI_API_KEY="ar-xxxxxxxxxxxx"

# List every model (with pricing) you can call:
curl $OPENAI_BASE_URL/models -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY"

Model IDs differ between the two services (OpenRouter uses anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5, AtmoRouter uses cc/claude-sonnet-5-5), so update your model strings when you switch.

How AtmoRouter billing works

  • Deposit USDC on Solana or pay with QRIS. No card on file, no recurring charge.
  • Input and output tokens are counted separately. Cached input bills at 10% of the input rate.
  • The cost formula is public: 
cost = ((in − cached) × input_price + cached × input_price × 0.10 + out × output_price) / 1M
  • Your balance is deducted when a request settles. An empty balance blocks new calls and never overdraws.

OpenRouter vs Command Code vs AtmoRouter at a glance

OpenRouter Command Code AtmoRouter
Pricing model Pass-through provider pricing + 5.5% credit fee Monthly plans with included credits; $15/mo Provider API plan Pay-per-token, no subscription
Usage caps Provider rate limits 5-hour and weekly caps on plan credits Per-key rate limits you set
OpenAI-compatible Yes Yes (Provider plan) Yes
Payment Cards, AliPay, USDC Subscription + top-ups USDC on Solana, QRIS

Is AtmoRouter right for you?

If you want the widest catalog and provider-level routing controls, OpenRouter is excellent. If you want a coding agent with bundled credits, Command Code fits. If you want frontier models at per-token rates below list price, no monthly plan, and a migration measured in lines of code, give AtmoRouter a try:

  1. Create an account (email only).
  2. Top up with USDC on Solana or QRIS.
  3. Generate an ar- key.
  4. Point your existing client at https://atmorouter.dev/v1.

👉 Try AtmoRouter at atmorouter.dev

Questions or model requests? Join the AtmoRouter Discord, linked from the site.

Pricing sources, checked Oct 16, 2026: openrouter.ai/docs/faq, openrouter.ai/api/v1/models, commandcode.ai/pricing, commandcode.ai/docs/resources/usage-limits, atmorouter.dev/v1/models.

title: Gating Cloudflare Worker Deployments With CI
description:
Automated build systems often deploy code immediately on merge without waiting for external quality gates to finish.

Quick solution:
Configure GitHub branch protection rules to require your test and lint status checks before merging, and ensure your Workers Builds configuration targets that protected production branch as detailed in the Build branches - Cloudflare Workers docs.

name: CI Validation
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run Tests
        run: npm test

Understanding the Deployment Automation Boundary

When a pull request passes all status checks and merges to the main branch, teams often assume that deployment waits for every upstream validation. In reality, automated continuous integration and platform builds run in decoupled systems. A green test suite or static analysis badge on a pull request does not guarantee that Cloudflare Workers waited for that specific result before deploying the latest script.

Understanding where validation occurs is essential for preventing regressions from reaching users. Pull request checks evaluate proposed changes in an isolated environment. However, platforms like Cloudflare Workers Builds can trigger automatically upon receiving a push to a configured branch, independently of whether external quality gates have finished or passed on that exact ref.

GitHub allows you to enforce requirements via protected branches. According to the About protected branches - GitHub Docs, repository owners can require specific status checks to pass before merging any code. If a required check fails or is missing from the protection rules, a developer can merge code that has not been fully verified.

Integrating SonarQube Cloud Quality Gates

Static analysis tools provide deep insights into code smells, vulnerabilities, and duplications. As detailed in the Introduction to quality gates - SonarQube Cloud, a quality gate defines the pass or fail criteria for a project based on clean code metrics.

A common failure mode occurs when Sonar analysis runs post-merge rather than as a blocking pull request check. If the analysis executes only after code lands on the main branch, it reports the state of the codebase after deployment has already begun. To act as a true quality gate, the Sonar analysis status must be reported back to the pull request and registered as a required status check in your version control platform.

Configuring Workers Builds and Branch Triggers

Cloudflare Workers can build and deduplicate automatically from connected Git repositories. Reviewing the CI/CD - Cloudflare Workers docs and the Configuration - Cloudflare Workers docs helps clarify how build triggers map to repository branches.

Integration Option When to Use It Trade-off or Failure Mode Recommendation
Automatic Branch Builds Fast iterations and continuous delivery for single-service projects. Triggers immediately on push; external analysis might still be running. Use with strict branch protection rules.
Manual or API Deployment Strict regulatory requirements or complex multi-service release sequencing. Requires maintaining external CI pipeline tokens and credentials. Use when deployment must wait for external sign-offs.

Tracing Release Evidence Across Systems

Proper release engineering requires tracing a single release across multiple disconnected platforms. You should inspect the commit SHA of the pull request, verify the exact merge commit hash, confirm the corresponding Cloudflare Workers Build version, check the Sonar branch analysis report, and perform a live route check. If deployment starts immediately on merge, a later main-branch scan is not a pre-deployment gate unless another system explicitly waits for it.

Do not infer correct ordering from two separate green badges. Inspect actual branch-protection rules, Workers Builds settings, and the deployed version directly. Record the exact commit SHA for each event and report any missing gate as a configuration gap in your infrastructure.

Release Verification and Execution Checklist

Use this execution checklist to confirm that your validation steps actually gate your production releases:

  1. Verify branch protection rules: Confirm that pull requests cannot be merged without passing unit test and lint checks.
  2. Inspect status check mapping: Ensure that the exact check names in GitHub match the jobs defined in your CI pipeline configuration.
  3. Check analysis timing: Verify that SonarQube Cloud evaluates the pull request commit rather than only scanning the main branch post-merge.
  4. Audit build triggers: Inspect your Cloudflare Workers Builds settings to ensure production deployments listen only to the protected main branch.
  5. Perform live route testing: Execute a targeted curl command against your production worker route to verify that the newly deployed version hash matches the expected release commit.

title: How SwarmRSI Cut Drug Discovery From 6 Months to 3 Weeks – The AI Revolution You Can’t Miss
description:
SwarmRSI Hits the Spotlight: 2026’s First Open‑Ended Recursive Self‑Improvement Breakthrough

Lead

“SwarmRSI turned a research curiosity into a working system in less than two years,” announced Dr. Maya Patel, lead author of the arXiv 2610.20431 paper, during the AI Summit in Berlin. The claim carries weight: the system autonomously generates, tests, and incorporates scientific hypotheses across a distributed swarm of language‑model agents, and it does so while exposing its internal reasoning to a public ledger.

The announcement marks the first time the AI community watches a recursive self‑improvement (RSI) loop leave the lab and enter a commercial pipeline. The moment also forces regulators, investors, and ethicists to confront a concrete implementation of a technology that, until now, lived mostly in speculative papers.

Below I unpack the technical core of SwarmRSI, examine the safety stack that surrounds it, and assess the market forces that could accelerate—or stall—its diffusion.

The Case Study: A Swarm‑Driven Drug Candidate

Imagine a biotech startup that wants to discover a novel inhibitor for a protein linked to Alzheimer’s disease. Traditionally, chemists design a handful of candidate molecules, synthesize them, and run assays—a cycle that can stretch over months.

SwarmRSI replaces that loop with hundreds of autonomous agents that each propose a molecular scaffold, predict its binding affinity, and suggest synthesis routes. The system stores every proposal in a shared, append‑only ledger. When an agent’s prediction passes a confidence threshold, the proposal triggers a virtual experiment—a high‑fidelity docking simulation run on a GPU cluster.

If the simulation yields a promising score, the result propagates across the swarm. Other agents re‑weight their own hypothesis spaces using the new evidence, a process the authors call Evidence‑Weighted Aggregation (EWA). Within 48 hours, the swarm surfaces a handful of molecules that outperform the best human‑designed baseline by 27 % in predicted potency.

The startup’s chemists then synthesize the top three candidates. Two of them demonstrate activity in vitro, confirming the swarm’s predictions. The entire discovery cycle compresses from six months to three weeks, and the company attributes $12 M of saved R&D spend to the SwarmRSI pilot.

This concrete scenario illustrates how a recursive loop—agents generating hypotheses, testing them, and feeding results back—can produce measurable scientific progress without human intervention at each iteration.

The Meat: Hard Numbers from the 2026 Papers

Metric Value (2026) Source
Agents in the reference swarm 512 transformer‑based scientific agents arXiv 2610.20431
Average hypothesis revision time 3.2 seconds per iteration (GPU‑A100 cluster) arXiv 2610.20431
Evidence‑Weighted Aggregation gain 14 % higher cross‑task utility vs. raw‑score weighting arXiv 2610.20431
Goal‑Drift Index (GDI) detection rate 85 % true‑positive on curated drift set arXiv 2603.06333
False‑negative rate for novel domains 27 % (pre‑deployment) arXiv 2603.06333
Recursive Criticality ℛₐᵢ 1.12 (baseline SwarmRSI) arXiv 2609.00137
Projected ℛₐᵢ after 2× compute scaling 1.38 (crosses exponential growth threshold) arXiv 2609.00137
Series‑B funding raised $300 M total (two rounds) Venture‑capital reports 2026
Corporate MoUs signed 7 (Novartis, BASF, Rigetti, etc.) Company press releases 2026
Open‑source forks on Hugging Face 12 forks, >90 up‑votes each HF repository stats 2026

Key statistic: ℛₐᵢ = 1.12 indicates that SwarmRSI already exceeds the critical threshold for super‑linear improvement, albeit modestly.

These figures reveal a system that operates at scale, improves its own output, and offers a quantifiable growth metric that regulators can reference.

How ℛₐᵢ Works

Recursive Criticality defines a reproduction number for AI improvement loops:

[
\mathcal{R}_{AI} = \frac{\text{baseline productivity} \times \text{feedback amplification}}{\text{difficulty growth}}
]

  • Baseline productivity measures the raw number of hypotheses an agent can evaluate per unit time.
  • Feedback amplification captures how much each successful hypothesis boosts the search space of the entire swarm (the EWA effect).
  • Difficulty growth reflects the increasing marginal cost of finding better hypotheses as the search space saturates.

When ℛₐᵢ > 1, each improvement cycle produces more “effective” hypotheses than the previous one, leading to exponential acceleration. SwarmRSI’s current ℛₐᵢ of 1.12 suggests a 12 % net gain per cycle. Scaling compute or adding heterogeneous agents (e.g., physics‑focused transformers) could push the metric well above the critical point, a prospect that investors watch closely.

The Pivot: Risks That Still Loom

1. Goal‑Drift Blind Spots

SAHOO’s GDI catches ≈ 85 % of alignment drift in controlled experiments, but the false‑negative rate climbs to 27 % when agents explore unfamiliar scientific domains such as synthetic biology or climate engineering. A drift episode could manifest as an agent proposing a pathway to synthesize a toxic compound, then quietly optimizing the process because the reward function only tracks “efficacy” without penalizing misuse.

Mitigation path: Deploy a heterogeneous critic swarm (MASS) that includes agents trained on safety‑critical corpora. The critics evaluate each hypothesis against a broader set of constraints, reducing the chance that a single drift goes unnoticed.

2. Opaque Swarm Dynamics

The ledger records every proposal and result, yet the internal reasoning behind a hypothesis remains a black box. Auditors cannot reconstruct the exact chain of inference that led a swarm to a particular conclusion without access to the agents’ hidden states.

Mitigation path: Require transparent provenance tags that link each hypothesis to the specific model weights and training data slices that contributed most to its generation. Open‑source tools that visualize these links are emerging on Hugging Face, but standardization lags behind.

3. Regulatory Uncertainty

The EU AI Act draft for 2027 explicitly mentions “recursive self‑improving systems” and demands independent alignment audits before deployment in high‑risk sectors. However, the draft leaves the definition of “independent” vague, and no certification body currently possesses the expertise to evaluate a swarm of 512 agents operating at GPU‑scale.

Mitigation path: Industry groups should collaborate with standards organizations (e.g., ISO/IEC 42001) to codify audit procedures that test GDI performance, invariant enforcement, and ℛₐᵢ thresholds under stress conditions.

4. Economic Concentration

Two venture funds poured $300 M into SwarmRSI‑related startups in 2026, and major pharma and materials firms signed MoUs. If only a handful of corporations can afford the compute and talent required to run a production‑grade swarm, the technology could entrench existing market leaders rather than democratize scientific discovery.

Mitigation path: Encourage shared‑infrastructure models (e.g., cloud‑based SwarmRSI as a service) that charge per experiment rather than per compute node, lowering the barrier for smaller labs.

Outlook: From Pilot to Production

Timeline Milestone Implication
Late 2027 First production‑grade SwarmRSI deployments in pharma and quantum‑hardware R&D Expect measurable acceleration in lead generation; early adopters could capture a sizable IP advantage.
2028‑2029 EU AI Act finalizes “recursive self‑improvement” clause; requires certified GDI modules Vendors that integrate SAHOO‑compatible GDI will obtain market clearance faster.
2030 ℛₐᵢ crosses 1.3 for at least one commercial swarm (via compute scaling) System enters a self‑reinforcing acceleration phase; research output could outpace human capacity in narrow domains.
2032+ Emergence of “Swarm‑as‑a‑Service” platforms with built‑in safety stacks Democratization potential rises, but regulatory oversight must keep pace.

If SwarmRSI maintains its current trajectory, 2026 will be remembered as the year the AI community stopped treating recursive self‑improvement as a thought experiment and began building it in the open. The technology promises dramatic gains in scientific productivity, but it also forces us to confront alignment, transparency, and governance challenges that have long haunted the field.

Stakeholders who ignore the safety stack—GDI, invariant checks, and heterogeneous critics—risk unleashing a system that improves itself while slipping beyond human oversight. Those who invest in robust auditing tools, open‑source provenance, and clear regulatory pathways can harness SwarmRSI’s power without surrendering control.

The next few years will decide whether SwarmRSI becomes a trusted catalyst for discovery or a cautionary tale of unchecked recursive growth. The data already suggest a narrow path forward: scale responsibly, audit relentlessly, and keep the human‑in‑the‑loop where it matters most.

title: What is Overfitting: How Can an AI Model Score 99% on Training Data and Still Fail in the Real World?
description:
Imagine building an AI model to detect fraudulent transactions.

You train it on thousands of historical transactions. The results look incredible. It correctly classifies 99% of the training examples.

You deploy it, expecting it to catch fraud reliably.

But something goes wrong.

Legitimate transactions get flagged. New fraud patterns slip through. The model that looked almost perfect during training performs disappointingly on transactions it has never encountered before.

How can a model that performed so well suddenly become unreliable?

The problem might not be the model's architecture, its computing power, or even the quality of the training algorithm.

It might have learned the wrong things.

This is called overfitting, one of the fundamental problems in machine learning. It occurs when a model learns patterns that work extremely well on its training data but fail to generalize to new, unseen examples.

Understanding overfitting means understanding a critical distinction: learning the training data is not the same as learning the underlying problem.

1. The Difference Between Learning and Memorizing

Consider a student preparing for an examination.

One student memorizes the answers to every question in a practice paper. When the exact questions appear in the examination, the student performs exceptionally well.

Another student understands the underlying concepts. Even when the examination introduces unfamiliar questions, the student can reason through them.

Both students may achieve the same score on the practice paper. But only one has demonstrated that their knowledge transfers to new situations.

Machine learning models can behave in a similar way.

During training, a model receives examples and adjusts its internal parameters to reduce prediction errors. The goal is not simply to reproduce the training examples. It is to learn patterns that remain useful when new data arrives.

An overfitted model can become excessively specialized in its training examples. It may learn meaningful relationships, but it also learns accidental details, noise, and coincidences that do not hold outside the dataset.

For example, imagine training an image classifier to distinguish wolves from dogs.

Suppose most wolf images in the training dataset contain snow, while most dog images show grass or houses.

A model might discover that snowy backgrounds are strongly associated with wolves.

Its training accuracy could be excellent. But it has learned a shortcut rather than a reliable way to distinguish the animals.

When shown a wolf standing on grass, or a dog playing in snow, it may make the wrong prediction.

The model has learned a correlation in its training data, but that correlation is not a dependable solution to the actual task.

This is the central danger of overfitting: a model can learn patterns that explain its training data without learning patterns that generalize.

2. Why Does Overfitting Happen?

Overfitting is not caused by a single problem. Several factors can contribute to it.

An Overly Complex Model

A model with too much capacity relative to the available data may be able to fit not only meaningful patterns but also random fluctuations in the training examples.

Imagine fitting a curve to a small collection of data points.

A simple model might capture the general trend while missing some individual points. A much more flexible model might pass through every point, including those that are there because of measurement errors or random variation.

The second model fits the observed data more closely, but that does not necessarily make it better at predicting new observations.

The same principle applies to neural networks, decision trees, and other machine learning algorithms.

However, complexity alone does not guarantee overfitting. The outcome also depends on the amount and quality of data, the model's inductive biases, the training procedure, and the regularization techniques used.

Too Little or Unrepresentative Training Data

A model can only learn from the examples it receives.

Suppose a medical image classifier is trained using images collected from a single hospital. The images may share particular scanners, acquisition settings, patient demographics, or image-processing conventions.

The model may learn patterns associated with those conditions.

When deployed at another hospital with different equipment or patient populations, its performance may decline.

The problem is not necessarily that the model memorized individual images. It may have learned relationships that were valid in the original dataset but are not sufficiently representative of the broader population.

Small datasets make it easier for accidental patterns to appear convincing. Unrepresentative datasets create a different but related problem: the model may never have learned the variation it will encounter in production.

Training for Too Long

Machine learning models often improve as training progresses, but the improvement does not necessarily continue indefinitely.

Early in training, a model may learn broad, useful patterns. As training continues, it may begin fitting increasingly specific details of the training data.

At some point, its performance on unseen data may stop improving even while its training performance continues to get better.

This is one reason training duration matters.

However, overfitting is not inevitable in every long training run. Its likelihood depends on the model, dataset, optimizer, regularization, and other training conditions.

Noisy Labels and Accidental Patterns

Training data is rarely perfect.

Human annotators make mistakes. Sensors introduce measurement errors. Datasets contain duplicates, inconsistent labels, and unusual examples.

A sufficiently flexible model can learn some of these errors instead of treating them as noise.

Imagine a dataset containing photographs of cats and dogs, but a few images are incorrectly labeled. A model that tries to fit every example may learn to reproduce those incorrect labels.

The same issue appears in financial forecasting, medical diagnosis, fraud detection, and natural language processing.

When the training data contains unreliable signals, a model can spend capacity fitting details that have little value in the real world.

3. Training Accuracy Can Be Misleading

If training accuracy does not tell us whether a model generalizes, what should we measure?

The first step is to evaluate the model on data that was not used to fit its parameters.

Machine learning workflows commonly divide data into three sets.

Training set: The model uses this data to learn its parameters.

Validation set: Developers use this data to compare model configurations, tune hyperparameters, select checkpoints, and make other training decisions.

Test set: This data is reserved for a final evaluation of the selected model.

These sets serve different purposes.

If a model achieves 99% accuracy on its training set but only 78% on a representative validation set, the gap is a warning sign. The model performs much better on the examples it learned from than on unseen examples.

This is often called a generalization gap.

But there is an important qualification: a gap alone does not prove overfitting. Training and validation sets may differ in difficulty, class balance, or data distribution. Evaluation metrics may also hide problems affecting particular groups or classes.

The split must be designed carefully.

For example, randomly splitting medical images can produce misleading results if images from the same patient appear in both training and validation sets. The model might benefit from patient-specific characteristics instead of learning patterns that generalize to new patients.

In that situation, splitting by patient is more appropriate.

Similarly, when predicting future events, randomly splitting observations across time can allow information from the future to influence training. A chronological split is often more suitable.

A validation set is useful only when it represents the kind of unseen data the model will encounter.

4. The Hidden Danger: Data Leakage

Sometimes, a model appears to generalize well because the evaluation process accidentally gives it access to information it should not have.

This is known as data leakage.

Consider a model designed to predict whether a customer will cancel a subscription.

The dataset includes customer activity, account details, and a field indicating whether the customer has already completed the cancellation process.

If that field is accidentally included as an input, the model may achieve excellent evaluation results.

But the feature reveals the answer rather than helping the model predict it.

A less obvious example occurs during preprocessing.

Suppose developers normalize a dataset using statistics calculated from the entire dataset before splitting it into training and test sets. Information from the test set has now influenced the preprocessing applied to the training data.

Depending on the transformation and task, this can introduce leakage and make evaluation less reliable.

The safer approach is to split the data first, fit preprocessing steps using only the training set, and then apply the learned transformations to validation and test data.

Leakage can also happen through duplicated records, overlapping users, future information, or features created after the event the model is supposed to predict.

It is important to distinguish leakage from ordinary overfitting. Overfitting occurs when the model fits training-specific patterns too closely. Leakage occurs when information improperly crosses the boundary between training and evaluation, or when an input contains information that would not legitimately be available at prediction time.

The two can coexist, and both can produce models that fail after deployment.

5. How Do We Reduce Overfitting?

There is no single technique that eliminates overfitting in every situation. Effective solutions depend on why the model is overfitting.

Collect More Representative Data

More data can help the model distinguish recurring patterns from random variation.

But the quality and diversity of the data matter as much as its quantity.

Adding thousands of nearly identical examples may provide less value than collecting examples from new environments, devices, users, or conditions that the model must handle.

For the wolf-versus-dog classifier, the dataset should include wolves and dogs in a variety of backgrounds, lighting conditions, poses, and environments.

The objective is to expose the model to the relevant variation instead of allowing a single accidental feature to dominate.

Use Regularization

Regularization introduces constraints or penalties that discourage certain forms of complexity in a model.

For example, L1 and L2 regularization penalize large or numerous parameter values in different ways. These techniques can discourage a model from relying too heavily on particular parameters.

Decision trees can be regularized by limiting their depth or requiring a minimum number of examples in a leaf.

Neural networks can use techniques such as dropout, which randomly disables selected activations during training to discourage excessive dependence on particular units.

These methods work differently, but they share a broad objective: encourage solutions that are less likely to depend on fragile, training-specific details.

Regularization is not a substitute for representative data or proper evaluation. A heavily regularized model can still perform poorly if the data is biased or the task is poorly defined.

Use Data Augmentation

Data augmentation creates modified versions of training examples while attempting to preserve their relevant meaning.

For image classification, this might involve flipping images, cropping them, or changing brightness within reasonable limits.

For speech recognition, it may involve controlled changes to audio. For text, augmentation requires more care because a seemingly minor change can alter the meaning or correctness of a sentence.

The goal is to make the model less dependent on incidental details.

For example, showing an animal classifier the same species against different backgrounds can help discourage it from using background appearance as the primary signal.

Augmentation must be appropriate for the task. A transformation that changes the label or removes important information can make training worse.

Use Early Stopping

Early stopping monitors performance on validation data while training progresses.

If validation performance stops improving, developers can stop training and restore the checkpoint that performed best on the validation set.

The idea is simple: don't continue optimizing the training objective indefinitely if doing so no longer improves performance on unseen data.

In practice, developers often use a patience threshold because validation metrics can fluctuate from one checkpoint to another.

Early stopping does not guarantee the best possible model, but it can be a useful and computationally inexpensive defense against overfitting.

Simplify the Model When Necessary

A model that is too flexible for the available data may benefit from a simpler architecture or stronger constraints.

For a decision tree, reducing its depth may prevent it from creating branches that fit individual training examples.

For other models, developers may reduce the number of parameters, limit feature complexity, or choose an architecture with more appropriate inductive biases.

However, making a model simpler is not automatically better. An overly simple model may fail to capture meaningful patterns, resulting in underfitting.

The objective is not to build the smallest model possible. It is to find a model that captures useful structure without depending excessively on accidental details.

6. The Opposite Problem: Underfitting

Overfitting is only one side of the problem.

A model can also be too simple to learn the underlying patterns in the data. This is called underfitting.

Imagine trying to predict a complex relationship using a model that can represent only a straight-line trend. If the true relationship is much more complicated, the model may perform poorly on both training and validation data.

A useful diagnostic is to examine both training and validation performance.

  • Low training error and substantially higher validation error: This can indicate overfitting.
  • High training error and high validation error: This can indicate underfitting, although poor data quality or optimization problems can also cause it.
  • Low training and validation error: This suggests the model is fitting the training data and generalizing well on the validation set, though further evaluation may still be necessary.

These patterns are diagnostic clues, not absolute rules.

The challenge is to balance model flexibility with generalization. A model must be powerful enough to capture meaningful patterns, but not so dependent on its training examples that it fails when conditions change.

7. Why Passing a Test Set Still Doesn't Guarantee Success

Suppose a model performs well on its training, validation, and test sets.

Is it ready for production?

Possibly, but there is another question: how closely do those datasets resemble the real environment?

A randomly sampled test set from historical data may not represent future users, new devices, changing customer behavior, or evolving fraud techniques.

This problem is especially important when the data distribution changes over time. A model trained on yesterday's patterns may struggle when tomorrow's environment behaves differently.

This is often discussed under the broader concept of distribution shift.

For example, a fraud detection model may learn patterns associated with previously observed fraud campaigns. Once deployed, attackers can change their behavior, making some learned patterns less useful.

Even a model that generalizes well to a held-out test set can become less effective as the world changes.

That is why production systems need more than a one-time accuracy score.

Depending on the application, developers may monitor prediction quality, false positives, false negatives, calibration, data drift, and performance across relevant groups.

They should also establish procedures for investigating degradation and retraining when appropriate.

In high-stakes applications, evaluation must reflect the actual consequences of errors. A medical screening system, for instance, cannot be judged adequately by overall accuracy alone if false negatives and false positives have very different costs.

A model is not finished when training ends. Its reliability must be assessed in the context where it will be used.

The Bigger Picture

Overfitting exposes a fundamental challenge in machine learning.

A model is trained on a finite collection of examples, but it is expected to make predictions about cases it has never seen.

Training accuracy tells us how well the model fits those examples. It does not, by itself, tell us whether the model has learned patterns that will remain useful beyond them.

That is why representative datasets, careful validation, leakage prevention, regularization, and production monitoring matter so much.

A model that achieves 99% accuracy may be excellent. Or it may have learned shortcuts, memorized accidental details, benefited from leakage, or been evaluated on data that does not reflect real-world conditions.

The score alone cannot tell us which.

The real test of a machine learning model isn't how perfectly it remembers its training data. It's how reliably it handles the data it has never seen.

title: Cisco SEG Zero-Day RCE: Unauthenticated Root Execution in Active Campaigns
description:
Originally published on satyamrastogi.com

Cisco patches critical zero-day in Secure Email Gateway enabling unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges. Exploitation actively observed in the wild.

Cisco Secure Email Gateway Zero-Day: Unauthenticated Root Command Execution

Executive Summary

Cisco has released patches for a critical zero-day vulnerability in Secure Email Gateway (SEG) that allows remote unauthenticated attackers to achieve remote code execution with root-level privileges. The flaw has been exploited in active attacks prior to patch availability, marking yet another perimeter device compromise with severe operational impact.

From an offensive perspective, this vulnerability represents the classic attack surface exposure: email gateways sit at the network perimeter, process untrusted data by design, and often run with elevated privileges to inspect encrypted communications. A pre-authentication RCE in such infrastructure is a strategic asset for threat actors targeting enterprise networks, government agencies, and critical infrastructure operators.

Attack Vector Analysis

Cisco Secure Email Gateway handles message flow, threat prevention, and encryption enforcement across organizational email infrastructure. The vulnerability chain likely involves one or more of these attack patterns:

Initial Access & Pre-Authentication Bypass

The ability to exploit SEG without credentials maps directly to MITRE ATT&CK T1190 - Exploit Public-Facing Application. Email gateways are inherently public-facing, accepting connections from untrusted networks and the internet. A pre-authentication vulnerability eliminates the need for credential harvesting or brute-force attacks - the attacker sends a crafted payload to port 25 (SMTP) or the web management interface and triggers execution immediately.

This is functionally equivalent to the Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day chain we documented earlier - a perimeter appliance with unauthenticated RCE leading to lateral movement and internal compromise.

Privilege Escalation Path

The fact that exploitation yields root-level execution suggests either:

  1. Direct execution within the SEG application context (running as root by design)
  2. A privilege escalation flaw chained after initial code execution
  3. Input validation bypass in a root-executed daemon processing email data

This mirrors patterns in 0-day exploitation speed analysis where perimeter devices often run privileged services for legitimate operational reasons, creating systemic risk.

Exploitation Mechanics

Active exploitation typically follows this flow:

Attacker -> SEG Public Interface
 |
 +-> Malformed Input (SMTP command, HTTP request, or file upload)
 |
 +-> Input validation bypass or parser flaw
 |
 +-> Arbitrary code execution in root context
 |
 +-> Reverse shell / command channel established
 |
 +-> Internal network reconnaissance begins

The pre-authentication requirement suggests the vulnerability exists in early-stage connection handling - before the gateway enforces its normal authentication gates. Common vulnerable code paths:

  • SMTP banner parsing or command parsing (RFC 5321 implementation flaws)
  • HTTP header processing in web management interface
  • XML/JSON deserialization in API endpoints
  • Certificate validation logic in TLS handshaking

Technical Deep Dive

While Cisco's advisory will contain vendor-specific details, the exploitation pattern typically involves crafted input that reaches vulnerable code before authentication checks:

# Reconnaissance phase - identify SEG deployment
nmap -p 25,443,8080,8443 <target_range> --script smtp-commands

# Banner grabbing to identify version
echo "EHLO test" | nc -v <seg_ip> 25
# Response may leak version info in SMTP banner

# Exploitation delivery (pseudo-code structure)
craft_payload() {
 # Payload structure depends on identified vulnerability
 # Could be:
 # - SMTP command injection with path traversal
 # - Serialization gadget chain
 # - Buffer overflow in TLS processing
 # - XML External Entity (XXE) injection

 payload = {
 "method": "SMTP|HTTP|MANAGEMENT_API",
 "target": "<vulnerable_endpoint>",
 "payload": "<injection_string>",
 "expected_exec_context": "root"
 }

 return payload
}

# Delivery to target
send_payload_to_seg <target_ip> <payload>

Once code execution is achieved, threat actors typically:

  1. Establish persistent access (web shell, SSH key injection, cron job)
  2. Access message logs and routing tables for email-based reconnaissance
  3. Pivot into internal network using compromised credentials or trust relationships
  4. Deploy additional payloads to compromise downstream systems

This exploitation chain maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1133 - External Remote Services and T1021 - Remote Services as the email gateway becomes the beachhead for internal network compromise.

Detection Strategies

Network-Based Detection

SOC teams should implement detection across multiple layers:

1. SMTP Anomalies
 - Malformed commands before successful authentication
 - Unusually long SMTP command lines
 - Control characters or binary data in SMTP transactions
 - Multiple EHLO/HELO commands from single source

2. Web Interface Access
 - Non-standard User-Agent strings targeting management interface
 - Requests to management endpoints from untrusted sources
 - POST requests with large payloads before authentication
 - Rapid requests to multiple management endpoints

3. System Behavior Post-Exploitation
 - Process execution from mail daemon context
 - Unexpected process spawning (bash, python, perl from postfix/sendmail)
 - Outbound connections from SEG to unknown IPs
 - File system writes in unexpected directories
 - SSH key generation or modification

Log Analysis Patterns

  • SEG application logs: Unhandled exceptions, segmentation faults, or decode errors
  • OS syslog: Privileged command execution without corresponding authorization
  • Authentication logs: Connection attempts followed immediately by process execution

YARA/Signature Detection

Detection research teams should hunt for:

  • Compressed/obfuscated payloads sent to SEG ports
  • Known exploit framework signatures (Metasploit, custom tools)
  • Reverse shell payloads in network traffic
  • Post-exploitation tool staging

Mitigation & Hardening

Immediate Actions (0-24 hours)

  1. Apply Cisco patches immediately - This vulnerability has active exploitation; delay increases breach likelihood
  2. Isolate SEG management interfaces - Restrict HTTP/HTTPS management access to known administrative networks only
  3. Monitor SMTP traffic - Implement deep packet inspection for malformed commands
  4. Enable audit logging - Ensure all SEG activities are logged with sufficient detail for forensics
  5. Check logs for exploitation attempts - Search historical logs for patterns matching active exploit code

Network Architecture Hardening 

# Recommended network segmentation
InternetFacing
 |
 +-- Cisco SEG (patched, hardened)
 |
 +-- IDS/IPS (signature-based detection)
 |
 +-- Internal Email Infrastructure
 |
 +-- User endpoints (isolated VLANs)

Configuration Hardening

  • Disable unnecessary SEG services and ports
  • Use network-level authentication where possible (VPN requirement for management)
  • Implement IP whitelisting for management interface access
  • Enable SEG's internal logging and forward logs to SIEM for correlation
  • Disable SMTP TLS downgrades if possible
  • Implement rate limiting on SMTP connections

Supply Chain Resilience

Organizations running Cisco SEG should:

  • Establish vendor communication channels for zero-day notifications
  • Maintain inventory of all SEG deployments and versions
  • Develop rapid patch deployment procedures (24-48 hour SLA for critical appliances)
  • Consider redundant email gateway architectures to enable safe patching

Key Takeaways

  • Perimeter devices are high-value targets: Email gateways process untrusted data with elevated privileges, making pre-authentication RCE a direct path to internal networks
  • Zero-day exploitation speed is critical: Active exploitation before patch availability means defenders have minimal window for response
  • Root-level execution amplifies impact: Unlike user-context RCE, root execution provides immediate persistence, credential access, and lateral movement capabilities
  • Logging and monitoring are detective controls only: Only patching and network isolation can prevent exploitation
  • Email infrastructure is foundational to supply chain attacks: A compromised SEG enables threat actors to intercept, modify, or inject email-based payloads targeting the entire organization

Related Articles

For deeper context on perimeter device exploitation and rapid patch response:

  • Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Day Chain: Three Flaws, One Unpatched RCE - Parallel vulnerability pattern in remote access appliance
  • 0-Day Exploitation Speed: Hours to Compromise Before Patching - Operational implications of active zero-day exploitation
  • SonicWall SMA SSRF: Perimeter Gateway Exploitation in Active Campaigns - Additional email/gateway infrastructure vulnerability chain

References & Standards:

  • MITRE ATT&CK Framework - Public-Facing Application Exploitation
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework - Identify Function
  • CISA Vulnerability Management Best Practices
  • NVD - National Vulnerability Database

title: My custom AI bot keeps giving bad advice because it cannot retain feedback from past calls
description:
Your support bot tells a customer that a sync error goes away if they clear the app cache. It does not. The customer writes back, a person on the team finds the real fix, re-authorising the integration, and the ticket closes. Next Tuesday another customer reports the same error, and the bot recommends clearing the cache again, with the same confidence.

The short answer: each call ends before anyone knows whether its advice worked, so the feedback arrives with nothing to attach to. Keep a record of every call with the ids of the stored notes the answer was built on. When the verdict comes in, from the user, the ticket or the person who took over, send it back as a rating on those notes, and have the bot recall from a memory that reads ratings when it ranks. Next time, the advice that failed and the advice that worked are no longer equals. Nothing is erased: the failed advice stays on record, with its outcome attached.

Why the bot does not learn from its own calls

A typical custom bot is a model call wrapped in retrieval: a system prompt, a search over help articles or stored notes, and the question. The verdict on last week's answer is in none of those. It is in the customer's reply and the helpdesk.

Teams usually try three fixes, in this order.

Edit the system prompt. Add "do not suggest clearing the cache for sync errors". A prompt is the right home for policy, but it scales like any document edited by hand: every bad call adds a line, nobody prunes them, and important rules compete with stale ones for the model's attention.

Store answers and corrections in a memory. The correction now survives the call, but so does the cache advice, and similarity search ranks by closeness to the question. Both notes match, both come back, and the model picks one in context. A wrong note is as similar to the question after ten failures as after none.

Attach the outcome to the note. When a call's result is known, record it on the notes that shaped the answer. The failed note now carries its failure and the working one its success, and a recall that weighs outcomes can tell them apart. Only this fix has a path from what happened back to what gets recalled next.

What to keep from each call

The answer is written during the call. The verdict arrives after it, sometimes days later, in another process. So the call must leave something for the verdict to find:

Call record: what a bot keeps from each call so that a verdict arriving later can find what to judge: the question, the answer, and the ids of the stored notes the answer was built on, under a key the verdict will carry.

The ids are per note, not per conversation. One piece of advice failed, not the exchange. If the model can say which recalled notes it relied on, keep those; otherwise keep every note that was in the prompt and accept that they move together.

The key is one the verdict will carry: a ticket id, a thread id, the session id your feedback button already sends. When one key covers several answers, the code below keeps the latest.

Keep call records in your own database, apart from the notes the bot recalls. Written into the same memory, every logged answer becomes one more candidate in the next recall, the bad ones included.

Where the verdict comes from

Explicit ratings are rare. Other outcomes are often already recorded somewhere, and wiring those places in works better than waiting for a thumbs-down.

signal when it arrives what it says about the advice what to send
thumbs up or down on the answer seconds later, if at all how the answer looked, often before it was tried positive or negative
the user says it did not work the next message, or the next day it was tried and it failed negative
a person takes over and solves it another way when the handover closes it failed, and here is what worked negative, plus the fix as a new note
the same user returns with the same problem hours or days later the first answer did not hold negative, smaller
the ticket closes and stays closed after a quiet period you choose it probably worked positive, smaller
nothing happens never nothing nothing

Two rows need care. A handover for a reason the bot was never meant to handle, a refund or an angry customer, says nothing about the advice. And silence, the commonest row, is not a verdict.

The third row does the most work. A rating can lower the advice that failed, but only a note can supply the advice that worked, so the person's fix goes into the memory the bot recalls from.

What a rating changes, and what it does not

A rating cannot change the answer already given. It changes the order of what the next recall brings back.

Keep the failed note rather than deleting it. Clearing the cache is right for a different error, and a deleted note cannot answer "why did the bot tell customers to clear the cache in October?".

Ratings tune ranking, not truth. If a help article is wrong, fix the article. The loop needs no particular product: a list of failed advice the bot checks approximates it, a store you run can carry an outcome field, a managed memory layer keeps the bookkeeping. What matters is the path from outcome back to recall.

A minimal version in code

This uses mnemoverse 0.4.0, the Python SDK of Mnemoverse (the author's company), set up as on the Python SDK page. The model call is a placeholder, and call records live in SQLite.

import json
import sqlite3

from mnemoverse import MnemoClient

memory = MnemoClient()  # reads MNEMOVERSE_API_KEY
DOMAIN = "bot:support"
db = sqlite3.connect("calls.db")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS calls "
           "(call_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, question TEXT, answer TEXT, used TEXT, concepts TEXT)")


def answer(call_id: str, question: str) -> str:
    recalled = memory.read(question, domain=DOMAIN, top_k=5)
    reply, relied_on = bot.reply(question, recalled.items)  # your model call
    used = [str(item.atom_id) for item in relied_on]
    db.execute("INSERT OR REPLACE INTO calls VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",  # latest answer per key
               (call_id, question, reply, json.dumps(used), json.dumps(recalled.query_concepts)))
    db.commit()
    return reply


def on_verdict(call_id: str, outcome: float, fix: str | None = None) -> None:
    row = db.execute("SELECT question, used, concepts FROM calls WHERE call_id = ?",
                     (call_id,)).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        return  # no call record: the verdict has nowhere to land
    question, used, concepts = row[0], json.loads(row[1]), json.loads(row[2])
    if used:
        result = memory.feedback(atom_ids=used, outcome=outcome,  # -1.0 to +1.0
                                 query_concepts=concepts, domain=DOMAIN)
        print("updated:", result.updated_count)
    if fix:  # what actually worked, from the person who solved it
        note = memory.write(f"Problem: {question}\nWhat worked: {fix}", domain=DOMAIN)
        if not note.stored:
            print("Not stored:", note.reason)


on_verdict("ticket-1042", -1.0, fix="Re-authorise the integration under Settings, Connections.")
on_verdict("ticket-1043", 1.0)  # the customer confirmed it worked

feedback gets the same domain as the read; the SDK page notes that without it the SDK sends "general". A write that is too similar to the nearest memory in the same domain is not stored, so the code checks stored.

The API docs state the effect in one line: "Ratings re-rank what comes back next." The overview says what stays: "feedback changes the order of the next read, not the stored text". A bot on an MCP client rates through the memory_feedback tool instead.

Check it with a control

  1. Seed notes about two different problems, answer one question about each through answer(), and check that the two call records share no id. Print the valence of the notes each call relied on, "Outcome polarity [-1, +1]" in the API reference, and stop the process.
  2. In a new process, send a negative verdict for the first call only. updated_count, "Number of atoms updated" in the reference, should equal the number of ids recorded for that call. If it is zero, check the ids and the domain first.
  3. Read both questions again and print valence for the same notes. What to look for is the first call's notes moving toward -1 since step 1.
  4. Control: the second call got no verdict, so its notes are the comparison for step 3. If they moved and the first call's did not, look at the key the verdict was filed under. If both moved alike, step 3 does not show the verdict's effect.

The library page follows the same loop for coding agents, where the verdict is a build or a test run, with the limits of outcome memory in more detail. Where does the verdict on your bot's answers end up today?
