title: Email coding tasks to your own computer
description:
Send an idea by email

You can remember a signup form problem while you are away from your computer. You can email yourself the task from your phone. You send the message from your own Gmail account to your own address with +agents added. Gmail delivers the message to your normal inbox, so you need no new email account.

You write the task in the email body. You can send plain text or HTML email. You can attach files, and atgent gives the saved attachment paths to the agent.

A signup form task can ask an agent to improve confusing parts of the form and run the relevant checks. Your computer can stay at home while you send the task from another device.

Run the task on your computer

You install atgent on the computer that holds your projects. The runner reads your Gmail Sent folder, not your Inbox. It starts Codex or Claude Code in a configured project with your existing sign-in.

Your repositories and agent sign-ins stay on your computer. Task text and results travel through Gmail and your chosen agent provider. Tasks for different projects can run at the same time.

The runner sends Queued, Started and the result as replies in the task thread. The result is the agent's final message as formatted email. Every reply ends with the task ID and the command to open it in your terminal.

Only mail that you send from your own Gmail account can start a task. Mail from other people lands in your Inbox. The runner does not read your Inbox, so their mail cannot start a task. Anyone who can add mail to your Sent folder can also send tasks, so you must protect your Gmail account and its credentials.

Route work with the subject line

The subject line selects the agent, project, model and run mode. Agent names ignore case. Project names are case sensitive. The task body contains the instruction.

Codex: improve the signup form runs Codex in your default project.

Claude: improve the signup form runs Claude Code in your default project.

Codex/website: fix the footer links runs Codex in the project named website in your config.

Claude [opus]: review the auth flow runs Claude Code with the opus model. Replies in the thread keep that model.

Codex/website [gpt-6.1-sol]: fix the build runs Codex in the website project with the gpt-6.1-sol model.

Claude [opus, terminal]: review the auth flow opens Claude Code in a new Terminal window and uses the opus model.

Without a model in brackets, the configured default model runs. Add headless in the brackets to run the task in the background. Add terminal in the brackets to open the task in a Terminal window.

Continue and control the session

You can reply in the same thread to continue the same agent session. The agent keeps the earlier turns. A reply of status returns progress by email. A reply of stop cancels queued turns and stops the running agent. Changes that the agent already made stay in your project.

Approval emails let you approve or deny a blocked action from your phone. Each approval covers one action. You reply directly to the approval email with approve or deny. Silence becomes a denial after the configured timeout.

With approvals off, Codex uses its configured sandbox and approval policy. Claude Code denies actions that need approval by default. You review the work before you publish or deploy it.

When you return to your computer, run atgent list to see each email task with its agent, model and status. Select a task and press Enter to resume the same session in your terminal. The agent then answers in the terminal instead of by email. A reply resumes a Claude terminal session. Codex terminal sessions are not tracked, so a reply opens a new window.

Set up atgent

Install uv first. Then install Codex or Claude Code and sign in. Install the runner with uv tool install atgent. Run atgent init to enter your Gmail address, sign-in method, project folders, installed agents and default models. The setup writes no secret to the config.

Turn on IMAP in Gmail. Create a Google app password, or use your own Gmail OAuth desktop client when app passwords are blocked. Keep the app password in your OS keychain or in the AGENT_MAILBOX_PASSWORD environment variable. Never put it in the config file.

Run atgent doctor to check Gmail over IMAP and SMTP without sending mail. The command also checks that Codex and Claude Code are installed. Run atgent start to start the runner in the background. Its first check skips old Sent mail, so send your first task after that check.

Requirements and licence

atgent needs Gmail with IMAP access, macOS or Linux, Python 3.11 or later, uv, and a computer that stays awake and online. You need Codex or Claude Code installed and signed in. Claude Code needs version 2.1.259 or later.

HTML email, attachments, concurrent projects, approval email replies with both agents, and the login service were tested live on macOS. Linux and Gmail OAuth are unit-tested only.

atgent is free and MIT licensed. Your existing Codex or Claude Code plan and its limits apply.

https://atgent.dev

title: Hosted Metrics Query API for React Dashboard Cards — A Startup Backend Pattern
description:
TL;DR: Put a hosted metrics query API behind the Node.js backend when the job is to fill React cards and time-series charts while retaining enough evidence to reconstruct a marketplace incident. Keep reporting separate from querying, attach a stable incident correlation key to every measurement, and record cost attribution at ingestion time. This is the least complex option for a small team that does not need a full monitoring stack.

For this narrow job, Infrai's concrete advantage is a single API key and one REST API spanning 295 routes in 20 modules; a startup can add other backend capabilities without collecting another provider SDK, credential, and invoice each time. Its public discovery surface requires no key and every documented capability includes runnable examples in 10 languages.

It is not a complete observability system. You still need a separate alerting loop, and you should choose a specialist when distributed traces, session replay, source-map processing, configurable retention, or a downstream export stream is part of the requirement. That boundary matters more than a long feature list.

Should a React dashboard use a hosted metrics query API?

Start with the reconstruction question, not the chart library. For a marketplace, an aggregate saying "checkout failures rose" is useful, but an operator also needs to narrow the event by seller, workflow, region, and a correlation identifier. The raw customer identifier should stay out of metric dimensions; keep a pseudonymous incident key that can be joined to access-controlled application records instead.

The flow is small: jobs and request handlers report measurements to the hosted service; the Node backend queries aggregates for a bounded time range; React receives a deliberately narrow view model. The browser never receives the provider key. During an incident, the same backend query can populate a chart and capture the evidence envelope used in the incident timeline. Picture the concrete recovery path: support reports that seller payouts stalled shortly after a deployment, the operator opens a card scoped to the payout operation and seller tier, and the backend requests the same bounded window shown on screen. The saved correlation key links that aggregate to protected application records. The card establishes when volume changed; the application record establishes which workflow instance needs repair. Neither system is forced to do the other's job, and the evidence envelope preserves the exact window and card definition that informed the decision.

That is enough for many admin panels.

Cost attribution belongs in that model from day one. A useful card is not merely "requests per minute." It can show work by marketplace tenant, operation class, or AI feature, using bounded dimensions that let the founder explain which workload created the bill. Avoid order IDs as metric labels. They make aggregation expensive and turn a metrics store into a poor event database.

Infrai is a reasonable fit for this narrow layer when a startup already wants several backend capabilities behind one REST contract. Its self-describing contract reduces integration work when metrics are one part of the backend, rather than a new platform the team wants to operate.

I would try Infrai for the report-and-query portion of a small marketplace admin panel when minimizing provider glue matters and the team is willing to own alert polling. The primary advantage is breadth behind one consistent contract. The supporting benefit is operational: discovery lets the backend validate the live request shape instead of pinning an undocumented payload in application code.

Implementation walkthrough: discover, validate, then query

The request fields for metrics.query are not declared in the supplied discovery parameters, so guessing names such as from, to, or step would produce confident-looking code that may fail. Use the capability document's JSON Schema as the contract, fail during startup if required fields cannot be satisfied, and keep the provider-specific mapping in one server module.

This TypeScript example is intentionally small and runnable. It fetches the public capability description, prints the live request schema, and verifies that the route is available before your adapter accepts traffic. It does not invent a query payload.

type Capability = {
  id: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  params: unknown;
};

async function loadMetricsQueryContract(): Promise<Capability> {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/metrics.query",
    { method: "GET" },
  );

  if (!response.ok) {
    const body = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
  }

  const capability = (await response.json()) as Capability;
  if (!capability.available || capability.method !== "GET") {
    throw new Error("The metrics query capability is not ready for this adapter");
  }

  return capability;
}

const capability = await loadMetricsQueryContract();
console.log(JSON.stringify({
  id: capability.id,
  path: capability.path,
  requestSchema: capability.params,
}, null, 2));

Run it with Node 20 or newer after compiling as an ES module. The output is the input to the only provider-specific code you should write: validate the desired card query against that schema, call the returned path, check the HTTP status, and convert the response into your internal Series type. Do not forward the upstream envelope directly to React. A stable application contract makes switching providers possible without rewriting every card.

For reporting, use the documented write route and the standard Authorization: Bearer convention, with the key read from process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY. A write retry needs an idempotency key. Rate-limited requests should honor Retry-After and then use exponential backoff; retries without either rule can duplicate measurements or amplify an outage. The platform specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities, but the capability schema should still be checked before treating any individual operation as idempotent.

Keep evidence separately from presentation. Persist an incident record containing the query window, normalized dimensions, correlation key, provider request ID when returned, and the exact card definition version. Seven fields can be more valuable than seven more charts. They tell the next person why a graph looked the way it did.

Failure recovery comes before vendor comparison

Treat the dashboard as an operational client, even if only five people can see it. Give every query a timeout and a bounded retry budget. Retry 429 responses only after respecting Retry-After; retry transient failures with jittered exponential backoff; do not retry ordinary validation failures. Surface stale data with its capture time instead of quietly drawing it as current.

Alerting needs its own worker because query access is not alert delivery. The worker can evaluate a small set of thresholds on a schedule, store the last evaluated window and notification state, and send through the team's chosen notification system. Make its state transition idempotent so a retry cannot page twice. For "the settlement job never ran," add a heartbeat product such as Healthchecks.io; absence is difficult to infer from a stream that was never written.

There is another boundary: live data movement. Without export or subscriptions, polling is acceptable for admin cards and a few thresholds, but it becomes custom plumbing for downstream BI synchronization. Choose a provider with a supported streaming or export path when that pipeline is already on the roadmap.

Short paths win.

The React layer should know only value, series, capturedAt, and an explicit freshness state. The Node layer owns authorization, schema validation, provider errors, attribution dimensions, and query limits. This split prevents a card refresh storm from becoming an unbounded provider workload and keeps credentials out of browser bundles.

Compare five operating models, not five price rows

The fair comparison is about operating model and recovery depth, not a single price row. Published prices change, and a startup can spend more engineering time debating units than it spends running the first month of a small admin panel.

Option Best fit for this marketplace job Trade-off to accept
Infrai A thin report/query layer when metrics sit beside other backend API capabilities No built-in alert delivery, export/subscription stream, distributed trace query, synthetic checks, or session replay
Datadog Teams that want a broader commercial monitoring product and are prepared to manage its ingestion and indexing model More platform and billing concepts than a few internal dashboard cards may justify
Grafana Cloud Teams that want managed dashboards around the Grafana ecosystem and familiar telemetry backends The application still needs a deliberate tenant-cost model and incident evidence contract
Honeycomb Engineers whose investigation depends on high-cardinality event exploration and tracing workflows A specialist investigation model can be more than an admin panel's aggregate cards require
Prometheus Teams that value an open metrics model and are comfortable owning or separately hosting collection, storage, and operations Running it directly conflicts with the goal of minimal infrastructure work

Datadog is the sensible comparison when the admin panel is likely to grow into a company-wide monitoring program. Its pricing page explicitly separates log ingestion and indexing, which is a reminder to model evidence volume and retained searchable data independently. Grafana Cloud deserves a look when the team already thinks in Grafana dashboards and standard telemetry components. Honeycomb is stronger territory when an incident starts with an unknown question and trace-shaped, high-cardinality exploration is central.

Prometheus remains a sound choice when ownership is the point. It is less attractive when the actual requirement is "give three React cards a series by Friday" and there is no one available to operate the stack.

Infrai occupies a narrower spot here. The write/query split is approachable, and one contract can reduce the number of SDKs, credentials, and bills around a small backend. Its limits are concrete: there is no alert or notification route, no metrics export or subscription model, and no synthetic heartbeat monitor. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but there is no distributed trace query or span tree. It also does not provide source-map deobfuscation, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, or session replay.

Pick based on the incident you must reconstruct. If the question is "which tenant and operation drove this spike, and what did it cost?", the thin hosted API can be enough. If the question is "which span across six services caused this user-visible failure?", use a tracing specialist. No amount of dashboard polish closes that gap.

Operational checklist before launch

Before launch, verify the live discovery schema in CI and again at service startup, then refuse traffic if the adapter no longer matches it. Send metrics from the backend, never the browser. Keep label cardinality bounded; tenant tier and operation class are useful, while order ID and raw user ID belong in the incident record. Define the evidence retention requirement with legal review because there is no user-scoped log deletion interface and no configurable retention entry point described here.

Exercise three failure cases: a 429 with Retry-After, an upstream timeout after a report may have succeeded, and a query response too old for the card's freshness budget. Confirm that writes cannot double-apply, charts show stale state, and operators can recover the correlation key. Then test the silent case by withholding a scheduled heartbeat and checking that the external monitor notices.

Finally, write down the exit condition. Move to Datadog or another broad suite when integrated alerting and a deeper monitoring surface outweigh simplicity. Prefer Honeycomb or another tracing specialist when span-level investigation is mandatory. Reach for Grafana Cloud when managed ecosystem compatibility is the priority, or Prometheus when your team explicitly wants to own the metrics path. A hosted query API is a focused decision, not an observability strategy in disguise.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the public Infrai discovery document and use its schema-driven examples to shape the server adapter.

Further reading

  • Infrai public discovery example
  • Datadog pricing and log ingestion model
  • Grafana Cloud documentation
  • Honeycomb documentation
  • Prometheus documentation
  • Healthchecks.io documentation

title: Processing XML in PostgreSQL: Do You Really Need PL/Python?
description:
In my previous article, I explained how a university assignment led me to run Python inside PostgreSQL to validate XML documents against an XSD.

It worked. I completed the assignment, learned something new about PostgreSQL, and moved on.

Two years later, I revisited the project with a different question in mind: how much of that solution actually needed Python?

PostgreSQL already provides functions for generating XML, querying its contents, and extracting values into relational columns. What it doesn't provide natively is validation against an arbitrary XML Schema Definition (XSD).

But while reviewing the original files, I found something I hadn't fully appreciated at the time.

Some XML documents produced by the SQL query didn't satisfy the very XSD they were supposed to follow.

That turned a simple comparison of database features into a more interesting engineering question. Before deciding where XML validation should happen, we need to know whether the document and its schema agree on what valid data looks like.

Let's explore what PostgreSQL can do on its own, what PL/Python added to the original solution, and how I would approach the same decision today.

One assignment, two different problems

Looking back at the assignment, I realized I'd been treating "XML processing" as a single requirement.

It was actually two separate workflows.

The first started with relational data. I needed to query employee records, including their job history, and generate an XML document from the results.

The second worked in the opposite direction. I needed to receive an XML document, validate it against an XSD, extract its values, and insert them into relational tables.

Here's the difference:

GENERATING XML

Relational tables
       |
       v
      SQL
       |
       v
  XML document


RECEIVING XML

  XML document
       |
       v
 XSD validation
       |
       v
  SQL extraction
       |
       v
Relational tables

Both workflows involve XML, but that doesn't mean they require the same tools.

Generating a document is about transforming relational data into an XML structure. Receiving a document may introduce an additional requirement: proving that the document follows a defined schema.

That distinction matters because parsing XML and validating an XML contract are different operations.

PostgreSQL handles much of the first workflow, and part of the second, without needing Python at all.

The unexpected problem in my original assignment

Before getting into the PostgreSQL features, there's a discovery worth discussing.

One of my original SQL queries generated an XML document containing employee details and job history records.

An employee could have no previous jobs, one previous job, or several. The relational data model naturally allowed those possibilities.

The XML Schema, however, didn't account for all of them.

It defined an optional jobHistories container, but once that container appeared, the schema expected exactly one jobHistory element.

Why exactly one?

Because the nested jobHistory declaration didn't specify minOccurs or maxOccurs. In XSD, both default to 1.

That became a problem when I recreated the query using three synthetic employees.

One had no job history, another had one record, and the third had two.

I generated the XML and checked each document against the unchanged historical XSD.

Here's what happened:

Job history records Generated XML XSD result
0 An empty <jobHistory/> element Invalid
1 One populated <jobHistory> Valid
2 Two <jobHistory> elements Invalid

The first failure happened because the query generated an empty jobHistory element. The schema required that element to contain fields such as startDate.

The third failed for a different reason. The XML contained two job history records, but the XSD allowed only one.

And this is the important part: none of those failures meant PostgreSQL had generated malformed XML.

The documents were well-formed. They simply didn't satisfy the contract defined by the schema.

That raises a question the validator cannot answer for us.

Should the schema allow multiple job history records? Or was the query supposed to return only one?

If an employee has no job history, should the document omit the optional container instead of generating an empty record?

Those are questions about requirements and data modeling, not about which XML parser to use.

A validator can tell us when two components disagree. It can't decide which one represents the correct business requirement.

For me, that was the most useful discovery in the retrospective. Before worrying about whether to use PostgreSQL, Python, or something else for validation, I needed to make sure the XML and XSD described the same contract.

The three cases are reproduced in 04-historical-output-xsd-cases.sql.

What PostgreSQL can already do with XML

Now let's look at the operations that don't require Python.

PostgreSQL supports a collection of SQL/XML features for working with XML data directly in SQL.

Rather than listing every function, I'll focus on the ones that mattered for the assignment.

Generating XML from relational data

Suppose we want to generate an XML document containing an employee's name and salary.

We can do that with SQL alone:

SELECT XMLELEMENT(
    NAME employee,
    XMLFOREST(
        'Ada'::text AS "firstName",
        1200.50::numeric AS salary
    )
) AS document;

The resulting XML is equivalent to:

<employee>
  <firstName>Ada</firstName>
  <salary>1200.50</salary>
</employee>

Two functions do the work here.

XMLELEMENT creates an XML element, while XMLFOREST turns SQL expressions into child elements.

For more complex documents, PostgreSQL also provides XMLATTRIBUTES and XMLAGG.

XMLATTRIBUTES lets us add attributes to an element. XMLAGG combines XML values from multiple rows, which is particularly useful when dealing with relationships such as an employee's job history.

In the reconstructed experiment, I used these features to generate documents from employees with zero, one, and multiple job history records.

The example also checks ordering, omitted null fields, and the expected output structure.

You can find it in 01-native-xml-generation.sql.

One detail is worth clarifying: the XML generation itself uses native PostgreSQL functions and doesn't require PL/Python. The reproducible test script also validates the generated document against an example XSD, and that additional validation step does use lxml through PL/Python.

In other words, PostgreSQL builds the document. Python checks whether it follows the chosen schema.

Extracting XML into relational columns

The reverse operation is also supported natively.

Let's say an application sends us this document:

<employee>
  <firstName>Ada</firstName>
  <salary>1200.50</salary>
</employee>

We can turn those values into SQL columns using XMLTABLE:

SELECT employee.first_name, employee.salary
FROM XMLTABLE(
    '/employee'
    PASSING XMLPARSE(
        DOCUMENT
        '<employee>
           <firstName>Ada</firstName>
           <salary>1200.50</salary>
         </employee>'
    )
    COLUMNS
        first_name text PATH 'firstName',
        salary numeric PATH 'salary'
) AS employee;

The result looks like any other SQL query:

first_name salary
Ada 1200.50

XMLPARSE interprets the XML document. XMLTABLE then uses XPath expressions to locate the elements and convert their values into the SQL types we've specified.

We haven't written any Python code.

For extracting known values into relational columns, that's often all we need.

There's more than XMLTABLE

PostgreSQL also provides xpath(), xpath_exists(), and XMLEXISTS for querying XML documents.

Namespaces require some care, though.

In one of my tests, a document used a default XML namespace. A simple XPath expression such as /employee returned no rows because it didn't match the namespace-qualified element.

Declaring an explicit namespace alias through XMLNAMESPACES and then using /e:employee solved the problem.

There's also a limitation worth remembering: PostgreSQL 18's XML querying features rely on XPath 1.0. They aren't a complete XQuery implementation.

Still, these functions cover the generation and extraction operations I needed to demonstrate.

So where does that leave PL/Python?

What PL/Python actually contributed

The first article covered the implementation in detail, so I won't repeat the full validator here.

The key idea was to use PostgreSQL's plpython3u extension to execute Python and its lxml library inside the database server.

That allowed me to validate an incoming XML document against an XSD before extracting and inserting its values.

Looking at the solution today, I can draw a much clearer boundary around what Python was doing.

I didn't need it to build XML elements, execute XPath queries, convert a salary into a numeric column, or insert a row.

I needed it because the assignment required XSD validation inside PostgreSQL.

Those aren't interchangeable capabilities.

PostgreSQL can recognize well-formed XML and perform conversions to SQL types. But that doesn't mean it has verified every rule in an XML schema.

An XSD can define required elements, element ordering, occurrence limits, and accepted data types. PostgreSQL 18 doesn't provide built-in validation of arbitrary documents against those schemas.

PL/Python gave me a way to fill that gap.

It also introduced a different set of responsibilities.

The plpython3u language is untrusted. Python code runs within the PostgreSQL server's process, and creating functions in that language requires superuser privileges.

Deploying this approach means dealing with Python dependencies, function ownership, access permissions, parser behavior, and database-server maintenance.

The reconstructed experiment includes parser restrictions and tests for malformed or potentially problematic inputs. Those checks help make the experiment more controlled, but they don't turn it into a production-ready security design.

For my university assignment, the trade-off was understandable. Keeping the validation inside PostgreSQL was part of the constraint I was trying to satisfy.

In a real application, though, I'd first ask whether the database server was the right place for that responsibility.

What if validation happened in the application?

Here's another approach.

Suppose XML documents arrive through an API or an integration service. That component already has to receive the input, identify the request, and decide how to handle failures.

Instead of sending the XML to PostgreSQL for schema validation, the application could validate it first using an XSD-capable library.

The flow would look like this:

 Incoming XML
      |
      v
 API / Ingestion service
      |
      v
   XSD validation
      |
   Valid?
   /    \
  No    Yes
  |      |
Reject  Extract data
           |
           v
       PostgreSQL

This keeps the XML validation dependencies outside the database server and places input validation closer to the point where the document enters the system.

It also lets PostgreSQL focus on storing and protecting the resulting data.

At first glance, that separation is attractive.

But there's a catch.

Application-side validation only enforces the contract if every relevant write path goes through it.

Imagine that an API checks every incoming XML document, but a batch-processing job can write directly to the same tables.

That job might bypass the validation entirely.

The system therefore needs a clear answer to questions such as who can write to the database, which operations are permitted, and what invariants PostgreSQL must enforce independently.

Moving validation out of the database doesn't remove the need for a trustworthy persistence boundary.

It changes where the responsibility lives.

I haven't implemented or benchmarked an equivalent application-side validator as part of this experiment. So I can't honestly say that it would be faster, more secure, or easier to operate for this particular workload.

Those outcomes would depend on the application's architecture, deployment environment, and security requirements.

Still, it's an alternative I would definitely evaluate before choosing an in-database Python implementation.

So, when would I use PL/Python?

After reviewing the project, I'd start with the actual requirement rather than the available extensions.

Here's how I'd approach the different XML-related tasks:

Requirement Where I'd start
Generate XML from relational rows PostgreSQL's native SQL/XML functions
Extract known fields from XML XMLTABLE or XPath
Validate an XSD inside PostgreSQL Evaluate PL/Python with an XSD-capable library
Validate external XML before persistence An ingestion service or application, with controlled database writes

These aren't universal rules. They're starting points for evaluating a design.

If the task is simply to generate an XML document from existing tables, I'd use the native SQL/XML features first.

If I need to extract a handful of known values from XML, XMLTABLE is a natural option to investigate.

If schema validation must happen inside PostgreSQL, PL/Python becomes a possible solution, but one that needs deliberate consideration of its operational and security implications.

And if I control the application receiving the XML, I'd examine whether that is the more appropriate validation boundary.

Before making any of those choices, however, I'd verify that the schema actually represents the expected document.

The job history mismatch taught me why that step shouldn't be taken for granted.

Choosing a validator won't fix an incorrect contract.

Looking back, what would I do differently?

When I originally developed the assignment, my goal was fairly narrow: validate XML against an XSD while staying with PostgreSQL.

I found a way to do that, and it was a worthwhile technical exercise. It introduced me to PL/Python and encouraged me to explore capabilities I hadn't previously used.

But revisiting the project changed what I consider the most interesting part of the problem.

Today, I wouldn't begin by asking how to run Python in PostgreSQL.

I'd ask what the system needs to guarantee, which component owns that guarantee, and whether the XML schema correctly describes the data we expect to exchange.

Only then would I choose the tools.

The historical mismatch between the generated documents and their XSD makes that lesson particularly clear. The SQL could produce well-formed XML, and the validator could correctly reject it, while the underlying disagreement about the data contract remained unresolved.

That's the difference between making a technical solution work and understanding whether the system is doing the right thing.

PL/Python solved a specific limitation in my original assignment. I wouldn't rule it out today, but I wouldn't reach for it automatically either.

The real engineering decision isn't whether PostgreSQL can execute Python. It's whether executing Python inside PostgreSQL is the right way to meet the system's requirements.

And sometimes, the most useful thing about revisiting an old solution isn't finding a better implementation. It's learning to ask a better question.

Source code and references

The reproducible examples are available in smaje99/postgresql-xml-plpython, published under the GPL-3.0-only license.

The recorded experiments use PostgreSQL 18.6.

  • Native SQL/XML generation
  • XML queries, extraction, and namespaces
  • Historical XML/XSD compatibility tests
  • PostgreSQL 18 XML functions
  • PostgreSQL SQL/XML limitations
  • PostgreSQL XML data type

Version note: As of October 15, 2026, PostgreSQL 19 RC 1 was available. Its development documentation still did not describe built-in XSD validation. I haven't tested these examples on PostgreSQL 19; the experimental results discussed here come from PostgreSQL 18.6. PostgreSQL 19 remains a prerelease, so this observation is provisional.

This article presents a retrospective analysis of an educational experiment, not a universal production architecture recommendation.

title: I Used to Think Software Testing Was Unnecessary. Then I Started Building My Own Project.
description:
I used to think writing unit tests, E2E tests, and maintaining a proper testing suite was unnecessary for most projects.

If developers write the code, can't they just test it themselves?

For a long time, that made sense to me.

Until I started building something of my own.

How It Started

At the end of June, I started building The Last Deploy — an open-source platform where people can learn DevOps and Platform Engineering through hands-on labs.

In the beginning, I made a lot of decisions based on one thing:

If it works, ship it. I'll fix it if something breaks.

I even coded directly on the production server for a while.

Not because it was a good engineering practice, but because it felt faster. There were no users back then, and if I broke something, the consequences didn't feel that serious.

Eventually, I separated development and production environments. That helped, and things worked reasonably well for a while.

But the project kept growing.

And then, people started using it.

The Problem With "I'll Just Test It Manually"

When you're building a small project alone, manually checking whether a feature works can feel sufficient.

You make a change, run the application, try the feature, and if everything looks fine, you move on.

The problem is that your change doesn't exist in isolation.

A change to one part of the codebase can affect something you haven't touched in weeks.

For TLD, that could mean:

  • A lab that worked yesterday suddenly fails to start.
  • An update to the curriculum breaks existing modules.
  • A Docker container fails, but the cleanup process doesn't run correctly.
  • The CLI and backend stop handling an error the way they used to.
  • Something appears to work locally but fails in another environment.

And you might not notice any of it until someone else runs into the problem.

The more a project grows, the harder it becomes to confidently verify everything manually after every change.

That's where I started reconsidering my approach.

Testing One Feature Isn't the Same as Testing Your Application

Suppose I'm updating TLD's lab execution system.

I test the new feature. It works. Great.

But what about everything around it?

What I changed What I still need to verify
Lab execution Do existing labs still run?
Docker environment setup What happens if the container fails to start?
Curriculum sync Are existing modules and labs handled correctly?
Error handling Does the user get a useful error instead of a crash?
CLI/backend interaction Are both sides still communicating correctly?

Manually checking every possible interaction gets harder as the codebase grows.

And relying on memory to remember everything I need to test isn't exactly a reliable strategy either.

That's the difference between checking whether my latest change works and having a system that helps verify whether the application still works.

So, What Am I Learning About Testing?

I've been learning more about different types of tests and how they fit into a software project.

1. Unit tests

Test a small, isolated piece of logic.

For example, checking whether a function correctly validates lab configuration without needing to start an actual lab.

2. Integration tests

Check whether multiple components work together correctly.

For example, verifying that the backend handles a lab execution request and responds appropriately when something fails.

3. End-to-end (E2E) tests

Test a complete flow from the user's perspective.

For example, checking whether a user can initiate a lab and receive the expected result through the application.

4. Regression tests

Verify that functionality that worked previously still works after a change.

This is particularly important for a project like TLD, where a change to shared execution logic could affect multiple existing labs.

How I think about the difference

  • Unit: Does this piece of logic work?
  • Integration: Do these components work together?
  • E2E: Does the complete user flow work?
  • Regression: Did my changes break something that already worked?

Of course, these tests don't guarantee that an application is bug-free. They help catch specific classes of problems before those problems reach users.

And that's already valuable.

What I Want to Do With TLD

I'm not trying to introduce a massive testing framework overnight or chase a particular code coverage percentage.

I want to start with the parts where a regression could have the biggest impact.

My initial focus is on:

  1. Lab execution and cleanup
  2. Curriculum synchronization and local file handling
  3. Error handling and failure scenarios
  4. CLI and backend interactions
  5. Existing functionality that could break when shared code changes

The goal is to gradually build a testing suite that gives me more confidence when making changes.

Something that lets me spend less time worrying about what I might have accidentally broken and more time building what comes next.

What Changed My Mind?

I still believe developers should test their own code. That's an important part of writing software.

But I've started to understand why that alone isn't always enough.

When a project is small, you can often keep most of it in your head. As it grows, that becomes increasingly difficult.

And when real people start depending on what you're building, "it worked on my machine" stops being a satisfying answer.

I don't want TLD to be a project where users have to hope that the latest update didn't break something they were using.

I want to build something that I can keep improving without being afraid of every change.

Because, at the end of the day:

Writing code that works is one thing. Being confident that it keeps working as your project evolves is another.

I'm still figuring out the right testing strategy for TLD, and this is just the beginning.

Follow the project: The Last Deploy on GitHub

I'd love to hear from other developers: At what point did testing stop feeling like overhead and start feeling like a necessity?

title: SEO AI Engineering
description:
Why the Future of SEO Looks More Like Software Engineering

SEO is quietly becoming an engineering discipline.

For years, SEO revolved around familiar activities:

  • Keyword research
  • Content optimisation
  • Internal linking
  • Backlinks
  • Technical audits
  • Rank tracking

These things are not disappearing.

But the environment around them is changing.

Search is becoming multi-engine.

Users increasingly discover information through Google, ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, AI Overviews, recommendation systems, and AI-powered assistants.

At the same time, SEO teams are dealing with increasingly large websites, complex JavaScript applications, thousands of URLs, structured data, log files, APIs, automated publishing systems, and enormous datasets.

The result is the emergence of a discipline I call SEO AI Engineering.

It sits at the intersection of:

SEO + Software Engineering + Data Engineering + AI Engineering

And I believe it represents one of the most important evolutions of technical SEO.

1. SEO Is Moving From Pages to Systems

Traditional SEO often asks:

How do we optimise this page?

SEO engineering asks a different question:

How do we design a system that continuously detects, prioritises, and fixes search visibility problems?

Imagine a website with 500,000 URLs.

Manually checking canonical tags, internal links, indexability, schema markup, and page performance at that scale is impractical.

Instead, an SEO engineer might build a pipeline:

Crawler
   ↓
Data extraction
   ↓
Validation rules
   ↓
Issue classification
   ↓
Priority scoring
   ↓
AI-assisted analysis
   ↓
Recommended fix
   ↓
Automated test
   ↓
Deployment
   ↓
Monitoring

That changes SEO completely.

An audit is no longer necessarily a PDF produced once every six months.

It can become a continuously running quality-control system.

2. Python Will Become Increasingly Useful in SEO

SEO professionals do not need to become full-time software engineers.

But basic programming creates enormous leverage.

Python can automate tasks such as:

  • Checking HTTP status codes
  • Validating canonical tags
  • Analysing internal links
  • Detecting orphan pages
  • Comparing XML sitemaps
  • Extracting structured data
  • Analysing server log files
  • Clustering keywords
  • Monitoring SERP changes

Instead of manually inspecting spreadsheets containing hundreds of thousands of rows, an SEO engineer can build reproducible pipelines.

Here is a simplified example using Python and requests:

import requests

urls = [
    "https://example.com/",
    "https://example.com/products/",
    "https://example.com/blog/",
]

for url in urls:
    try:
        response = requests.get(
            url,
            timeout=10,
            allow_redirects=True
        )

        if response.status_code != 200:
            print(
                f"ISSUE: {url} "
                f"returned {response.status_code}"
            )

    except requests.RequestException as error:
        print(f"ERROR: {url} - {error}")

This is a basic example, not a production crawler.

But the principle is powerful.

A repeatable script can execute checks that would otherwise require substantial manual work.

Simple automation. Massive operational difference.

3. AI Changes the Equation Again

Now add large language models.

Traditional SEO automation is largely deterministic.

For example:

If HTTP status code = 404, flag the URL.

AI systems can assist with tasks that require more contextual interpretation.

Examples include:

  • Analysing page intent
  • Evaluating content similarity
  • Classifying search intent
  • Generating remediation suggestions
  • Detecting unusual content patterns
  • Analysing entity coverage
  • Summarising crawl anomalies
  • Evaluating internal linking opportunities
  • Comparing competitor information architecture

Consider internal linking.

Instead of simply finding pages containing the same keyword, an AI-assisted system could evaluate multiple signals:

Semantic similarity
        +
Topical relationship
        +
Page importance
        +
Anchor-text suitability
        +
Crawl depth
        +
Business priority
        ↓
Suggested internal links

An engineer could combine embeddings, graph analysis, deterministic rules, and LLM-assisted evaluation.

The system could propose links for review rather than automatically inserting them into production pages.

The SEO professional becomes the person designing and validating the system instead of manually discovering every opportunity.

4. The Modern SEO Engineering Stack

A modern SEO engineering environment might include:

Layer Technologies
Data collection Search Console API, GA4, crawlers, server logs
Programming Python, JavaScript, SQL
Data processing Pandas, DuckDB, PostgreSQL
AI LLM APIs, embeddings, vector search
Automation GitHub Actions, scheduled jobs
Testing Pytest, Playwright, custom validators
Monitoring Dashboards, alerts, anomaly detection
Deployment Git, CI/CD, cloud infrastructure

This is where SEO starts to resemble a software engineering workflow.

For example:

SEO specification
      ↓
Git commit
      ↓
Automated SEO tests
      ↓
Build
      ↓
Deployment
      ↓
Production validation
      ↓
Search performance monitoring

Which leads to another concept I believe deserves more attention.

5. Spec-Driven Development for SEO

Software engineers use explicit specifications to define expected system behaviour.

SEO can adopt the same approach.

Instead of writing:

Make sure canonical tags are correct.

Define the expected behaviour in a machine-readable specification.

For example:

page_type: article

canonical:
  required: true
  strategy: self_referencing
  allow_cross_domain: false

indexability:
  expected_status: 200
  robots: index,follow

structured_data:
  required_types:
    - Article
    - BreadcrumbList

These are project-specific rules, not a universal SEO standard.

But once requirements become machine-readable, they can drive automated tests.

For example:

def test_article_seo(page):
    assert page.status_code == 200
    assert page.canonical == page.url
    assert page.is_indexable is True

    assert "Article" in page.schema_types
    assert "BreadcrumbList" in page.schema_types

Here, page represents a parsed page object supplied by a testing framework.

This approach changes the relationship between SEO and development teams.

SEO requirements no longer need to exist exclusively in documents, tickets, and Slack conversations.

They can become part of the engineering workflow.

SEO specifications → automated tests → deployment validation.

And that means fewer regressions reaching production.

6. AI Search Creates an Entirely New Measurement Problem

SEO is expanding beyond traditional rankings.

Brands increasingly want answers to questions such as:

Does ChatGPT mention our company?

Does Gemini recommend our product?

Which sources does Perplexity cite when discussing our brand?

Does changing the prompt change how AI describes us?

These questions require a different measurement infrastructure.

Imagine evaluating a brand across multiple AI systems.

A simplified experimental workflow might look like this:

prompts = [
    "What are the best tools for technical SEO?",
    "Which technical SEO platforms are recommended?",
    "What software helps identify technical SEO issues?"
]

for prompt in prompts:
    for run in range(10):
        response = query_model(prompt)
        save_result(
            prompt=prompt,
            run=run,
            response=response
        )

In this pseudocode, query_model() and save_result() represent functions implemented by the researcher.

The resulting dataset can be analysed for:

  • Brand mention frequency
  • Citation frequency
  • Recommendation frequency
  • Sentiment and framing
  • Claim consistency
  • Source concentration
  • Response volatility

The important point is reproducibility.

AI responses may vary between repeated runs, prompt formulations, model versions, and retrieval conditions.

A single answer is not a reliable measure of overall brand visibility.

AI visibility measurement is not just prompt engineering. It is experimental design, data collection, and statistical analysis.

That makes it an engineering problem.

7. AI Agents Will Transform SEO Investigations

Another major shift will come from AI agents.

Imagine an SEO agent receiving the following task:

Investigate the organic traffic decline affecting /products/.

With appropriate permissions and integrations, the agent could:

  1. Query Google Search Console.
  2. Identify when the decline began.
  3. Detect affected pages and queries.
  4. Crawl the affected URLs.
  5. Inspect canonical and robots directives.
  6. Compare internal linking patterns.
  7. Check recent deployments.
  8. Examine server-side rendering.
  9. Formulate possible explanations.
  10. Produce an evidence-based investigation report.

The agent would not know the true cause automatically.

It would generate hypotheses supported by collected evidence.

A human specialist would still validate the findings and approve changes.

But the workflow becomes significantly more efficient.

Instead of spending hours collecting data, the specialist can focus on interpreting results and making decisions.

This is the difference between using AI to write SEO content and using AI to operate SEO engineering workflows.

8. SEO Professionals Will Become Workflow Designers

This is probably the biggest change.

The valuable skill will not simply be knowing which SEO tools to click.

It will be knowing how to design a reliable process.

Problem
   ↓
Data
   ↓
Specification
   ↓
Automation
   ↓
Validation
   ↓
Decision
   ↓
Monitoring

That mindset scales.

A good SEO AI engineer asks:

  • Can this task be automated?
  • Can this rule be expressed as a specification?
  • Can the result be tested automatically?
  • Can the data be collected through an API?
  • Can AI assist with classification or analysis?
  • Can the recommendation be validated?
  • Can the impact be measured after deployment?

These are engineering questions applied to search visibility.

And they are very different from simply producing another SEO checklist.

9. Will AI Replace SEO Specialists?

I don't think that is the most useful question.

AI will automate many tasks currently performed manually.

But automation creates new responsibilities.

Someone still needs to define:

  • What should be measured
  • Which signals matter
  • What counts as an error
  • How systems should behave
  • How experiments should be designed
  • Whether AI output is trustworthy
  • When automation should stop
  • How SEO requirements interact with product and engineering constraints

The SEO professional of the future may spend less time manually producing recommendations and more time designing systems that generate, test, and monitor those recommendations.

The competitive advantage moves from executing individual tasks to designing reliable systems.

10. What Will the Future SEO Team Look Like?

I can imagine SEO responsibilities evolving into several increasingly specialised disciplines.

SEO Strategist

Search demand, market analysis, competitive positioning, and business prioritisation.

Technical SEO Engineer

Rendering, crawling, indexing, architecture, structured data, and web performance.

SEO Data Analyst

Search Console analysis, server logs, experimentation, forecasting, and statistical evaluation.

SEO AI Engineer

LLM workflows, AI agents, AI visibility measurement, evaluation pipelines, and automation.

SEO Content Engineer

Structured content systems, entity architecture, knowledge organisation, and content operations at scale.

Not every organisation will use these titles.

And smaller teams will combine many of these responsibilities.

But the technical capabilities required for SEO are expanding.

11. The Most Interesting Part? We're Still Early.

Many organisations still operate SEO through spreadsheets, manual audits, isolated recommendations, and disconnected tools.

That leaves enormous room for experimentation.

You can start today:

  1. Learn Python. Automate a repetitive SEO task.
  2. Explore APIs. Connect Google Search Console to your own scripts.
  3. Learn SQL. Analyse SEO data without depending entirely on spreadsheets.
  4. Experiment with embeddings. Explore semantic similarity and topic relationships.
  5. Build SEO tests. Validate technical requirements automatically.
  6. Learn Git and CI/CD. Integrate SEO checks into development workflows.
  7. Study LLM evaluation. Measure AI responses systematically.
  8. Experiment with AI agents. Automate investigations with human review.
  9. Create machine-readable SEO specifications. Turn requirements into executable tests.
  10. Publish your experiments. Share code, datasets, methods, and findings.

You do not need to master all these technologies at once.

Choose one SEO problem.

Build a small engineering solution.

Document it.

Test it.

Improve it.

Then move to the next problem.

Final Thoughts

The future of SEO is not simply about generating more content with AI.

And it is not just about getting mentioned in ChatGPT.

It is about building reliable systems that collect data, understand search visibility problems, test technical requirements, evaluate AI responses, and support better decisions.

Traditional SEO knowledge will remain essential.

But its implementation will increasingly involve code, data pipelines, AI models, automation, and software engineering practices.

The future of SEO is not just optimisation. It is engineering.

And that is why I believe SEO AI Engineering is a discipline worth exploring.

What Do You Think?

If you're a developer, technical SEO specialist, data engineer, or AI practitioner:

What technologies would you include in an SEO AI Engineering stack?

Python? SQL? LLM APIs? Vector databases? CI/CD? Search Console?

And which SEO tasks do you think should become automated first?

I'd love to hear how others see software engineering and search visibility converging.

title: How Databricks is disrupting Retail and E-Commerce with LTAP direct writes: OLTP and OLAP working together without overwhelming your application
description:
Every retailer runs two businesses on two kinds of databases.

The first is the store itself: carts, checkouts, order status, loyalty balances, store-level inventory, and the price a shopper sees on a shelf tag or product page. That’s OLTP, transactional work that has to answer in milliseconds because a customer is waiting.

The second is the intelligence behind the store: demand forecasts by SKU, store, and day; personalization scores for every shopper; optimized prices; assortment plans; and fraud models. That’s OLAP, analytics over billions of rows and years of history.

Retail has gotten very good at the second business. The trouble has always been getting its output into the first one.

Two engines, one platform

Databricks handles these two kinds of work with two engines that sit side by side on the same platform.

The lakehouse is where analytics and AI happen. It combines the low-cost, open storage of a data lake with the reliability and performance of a data warehouse. Data is stored in open Delta Lake tables on cloud object storage, and it’s processed by engines such as Apache Spark and Databricks SQL, which can scan billions of rows in parallel. This is where a retailer’s sales history, loyalty data, supply chain feeds, and clickstream come together, and where forecasting, pricing, and personalization models get built and run. It’s the OLAP side.

Lakebase is where applications live. It’s a fully managed Postgres database built into the Databricks Platform, designed for the fast, high-concurrency reads and writes that apps need: looking up one order, one shopper’s recommendations, or one item’s price, in milliseconds, thousands of times a second. Because it’s standard Postgres, app teams use the tools, drivers, and SQL they already know. Unlike a separate operational database bolted on from outside, Lakebase is governed by the same Unity Catalog as the lakehouse, so permissions, lineage, and the definition of “customer” or “item” stay consistent on both sides. It’s the OLTP side.

Having both on one platform is the starting point. The hard part, and the subject of this article, is moving large volumes of data from the lakehouse into Lakebase without slowing down the applications Lakebase is serving.

The nightly load problem

Here’s a scenario most retail data teams will recognize.

Every night the lakehouse produces something big. It might be a fresh price file for every item in every store, a new set of recommendation scores for millions of shoppers, or a demand forecast covering tens of thousands of SKUs across a couple of thousand locations. That last one alone runs to hundreds of millions of rows and is rebuilt from scratch every cycle.

All of it has to land in the operational Postgres database the apps actually read from, and that’s where it hurts.

In standard Postgres, every write goes through a single primary instance, the same one serving your storefront, store systems, and mobile app. A bulk load competes directly with live traffic for CPU and memory. Teams end up with familiar workarounds: maintenance windows, loads squeezed into the overnight gap before stores open, overprovisioned databases sized for the load instead of the shoppers, and a separate reverse-ETL tool just to manage the pain.

One such customer, loading about 1 billion rows a day through synced tables, needed more than 8 hours per load cycle and had to overprovision infrastructure just to keep their application from degrading. In retail, 8 hours is the whole window between the last online order of the night and the first store opening in the morning.

The fix: Build the data somewhere else, then hand it over

Databricks announced LTAP Direct Writes in Beta on October 8, 2026. It’s a new way to load data into Lakebase Postgres. The headline numbers are 1 TB in under 5 minutes and up to 147x faster heap loading, without consuming the resources your live application depends on.

With Direct Writes, the heavy construction work moves out of the Postgres primary and into Spark, running in parallel:

  1. Parallel page building in sandboxes. Each Spark executor runs its own isolated Postgres instance and builds native Postgres data pages for its slice of the table. The driver assigns non-overlapping ID ranges so the slices never collide.
  2. Frozen binary COPY. Inside each sandbox, data is loaded with binary COPY and FREEZE. Rows are treated as already committed, so there’s no transaction history to maintain.
  3. Checksums on every page. Workers checksum the pages they build, and Lakebase’s pageserver validates them on ingest. A corrupted page can never become the source of truth.
  4. Index building without re-downloading the table. Workers export key columns and row locations to object storage. Postgres’s standard B-tree builder then builds indexes from those, without pulling the full table back down.
  5. One atomic handoff. The Spark driver writes a manifest and makes a single SQL call. The primary records only a small log entry describing the import, not the terabytes of data. The pageserver claims the files, warms them on the local SSD, and atomically swaps them into the visible table at commit.

The result is that the primary barely notices. Your storefront’s Postgres writes a tiny log entry instead of absorbing a terabyte of inserts.

This is what LTAP (Lake Transactional/Analytical Processing) means in practice. OLAP computes the bulk work it’s built for; OLTP keeps serving customers; and both share a single governed copy of the data under Unity Catalog.

What this changes for retail and e-commerce

Faster loads are nice. For retailers, the bigger change is that bulk refreshes no longer constitute an operational event.

Price and promotion changes stop waiting for a window. A full refresh of store-item pricing can land during the business day without slowing down point-of-sale lookups or the product page. Merchandising teams get to act when they decide, not when the loading schedule allows.

Personalization goes from nightly to whenever. If scoring millions of shoppers produces a big table, reloading it in minutes means you can rescore after a campaign launches, after a weather event, or ahead of a holiday weekend, and the app picks up the new scores right away.

Forecasts reach the systems that act on them. SKU-store-day demand forecasts can be served from Lakebase to replenishment apps, store ordering tools and delivery-promise logic, without a separate serving database and a pipeline to feed it.

Reference data rebuilds stop being scary. Item master, store hierarchies, assortment and planogram tables are rebuilt wholesale all the time. Snapshot syncs with Direct Writes make a full rebuild routine instead of a weekend project.

You can retire some reverse-ETL infrastructure. The write-up puts it directly: large bulk-refreshed datasets like nightly scoring tables, fresh feature sets and rebuilt reference data can stay in Lakebase. They no longer need a separate reverse-ETL tool just to avoid the load penalty.

Peak season gets safer. During Black Friday or holiday weeks, the worst thing a data team can do is compete with shoppers for database capacity. Direct Writes means that the bulk load and the checkout surge aren’t competing for the same CPU.

How it fits with synced tables

Direct Writes is an option on synced tables, which keep a Unity Catalog Delta table available in Lakebase as a read-only Postgres table. Synced tables have three modes, and it matters which one you pick:

  • Snapshot does a full refresh on every cycle. Direct Writes speeds up every sync in this mode, so it’s the natural fit for price files, forecasts, scores and reference data that get rebuilt wholesale.
  • Triggered and Continuous use Change Data Feed, so updates after the first load are already incremental. Direct Writes speeds up the initial load, which is often the biggest load you’ll ever do.

That suggests a simple retail split. Use Snapshot with Direct Writes for big tables rebuilt nightly or on demand. Use Continuous for data that changes transaction by transaction, like recent sales for returns lookups or live inventory positions.

Getting started

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/oltp/projects/sync-tables#accelerated-sync-with-ltap-direct-writes

The bottom line

Retail has always had a gap between what the business knows and what the storefront can act on. Moving analytics results into operational systems meant risking the customer experience, so it happened less often, more slowly, and with more infrastructure than anyone wanted.

Direct Writes closes much of that gap for the biggest, most disruptive loads. The lakehouse builds the data in parallel; Postgres accepts it in a single atomic handoff; and shoppers at the shelf, in the app, or at checkout never notice.

That’s the shift: OLTP and OLAP working together, on one platform, without the analytics side overwhelming the application side.

Databricks #Lakebase #Retail #Ecommerce #OLTP #OLAP #Postgres #DataEngineering

title: Your Test Suite Is Growing. But Is It Getting Better?
description:
When a project starts, maintaining automated tests usually feels manageable.

There are a few test cases, execution is quick, and when something fails, finding the reason isn't too difficult.

But as the application grows, things start to change.

More features mean more tests. More tests mean longer execution times. And as the UI and application behaviour change, some existing tests need regular maintenance.

Before long, the team might be dealing with hundreds of tests, repeated failures, and a test suite that takes much longer to run than it used to.

The problem isn't that the test suite is growing. It's whether the team can still trust it.

Imagine running 600 tests and getting 30 failures.

Some might be real bugs. Others could be broken locators, outdated test data, environment issues, or flaky tests.

Now the team has another problem: figuring out which failures actually need attention.

This is something I've been exploring at X360 AI Tech.

Instead of looking at test results as just pass or fail, we're interested in how execution details can help make failures easier to investigate. Test steps, assertions, browser actions, network activity, logs, screenshots, and execution videos can provide useful context about what happened.

The goal isn't simply to add more tests or make every failure disappear.

It's to help the team understand what happened during execution and decide what needs attention.

I also think growing test suites need regular review.

Some tests protect critical business flows and should remain part of the regression suite. Others may be redundant, unstable, or no longer relevant after application changes.

More tests don't automatically mean better coverage. And better coverage doesn't automatically mean better feedback.

For me, a healthy test suite is one that covers important behaviour, runs reliably, and helps developers understand problems without spending hours investigating every failure.

As a test suite grows, maintaining trust in the results becomes just as important as adding new tests.

I'm curious how other teams handle this.

When your test suite starts getting bigger and slower, what do you focus on first: reducing execution time, fixing flaky tests, or removing tests that no longer add much value?

title: Testing Ticket-Sync Boundaries: Duplicate Events, Stale Snapshots and Private Fields
description:
AI disclosure: This article and its code example were generated by an AI agent for Autom Mate. The example was executed locally with the automated checks described below. It is an illustrative tutorial, not a report of a production deployment or a claim of human review.

A two-way ticket integration can fail even when every HTTP request succeeds. A delayed event can restore an old priority. A duplicated delivery can trigger repeated work. An internal note can appear in the wrong system.

Before building a complete connector, test a smaller boundary: which incoming information is allowed to update the integration's local view? A deterministic function makes that policy easier to inspect than a large workflow with several remote side effects.

This example extends Autom Mate's ticket integration test matrix with a runnable Python exercise. It filters snapshots into a local SQLite projection. It sends nothing to Jira or another application.

Write the event contract first

The example assumes that each event contains a full snapshot of the fields owned by its source, plus a strictly increasing version for that source's ticket. It uses separate namespaces for the customer tenant, source system and ticket.

Those assumptions are explicit because real webhook mechanisms differ. Atlassian documents a Jira Cloud webhook identifier that stays the same across retries and is unique within a tenant. That is useful for delivery deduplication, but it does not establish the snapshot version contract used here. See the Jira Cloud webhook documentation.

If your events contain partial patches, discarding an older patch may lose an independent field update. Use an appropriate ordering, per-field versioning or authoritative reconciliation design instead of copying this reducer unchanged.

Separate delivery, ordering and ownership

Three questions need separate answers:

Question Local rule in this example
Have we processed this delivery before? Check tenant, source and event identifier together
Is its snapshot newer? Compare versions within that tenant, source and ticket
Which fields may travel? Apply the source's explicit field allowlist
Does this prove remote delivery? No; the example updates only a local projection

The desk owns priority and service_status. Engineering owns development_status. A field named internal_note is excluded from both projections.

“Development done” may still require deployment or customer confirmation.

Run the filter and its checks

Save this as ticket_snapshot_demo.py:

"""Local snapshot filter: no webhooks, credentials, or remote writes."""
import json
import sqlite3
import unittest

ALLOWED = {
    "desk": {"priority", "service_status"},
    "engineering": {"development_status"},
}


def connect():
    db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    db.executescript("""
        CREATE TABLE seen (
            tenant TEXT, source TEXT, event_id TEXT,
            PRIMARY KEY (tenant, source, event_id));
        CREATE TABLE projection (
            tenant TEXT, source TEXT, ticket TEXT, version INTEGER, data TEXT,
            PRIMARY KEY (tenant, source, ticket));
    """)
    return db


def apply_snapshot(db, event):
    tenant, source = event["tenant"], event["source"]
    if source not in ALLOWED or type(event["version"]) is not int:
        raise ValueError("unsupported source or invalid version")
    key = (tenant, source, event["ticket"])
    with db:
        duplicate = db.execute(
            "SELECT 1 FROM seen WHERE tenant=? AND source=? AND event_id=?",
            (tenant, source, event["id"]),
        ).fetchone()
        if duplicate:
            return "duplicate"
        prior = db.execute(
            "SELECT version FROM projection WHERE tenant=? AND source=? AND ticket=?",
            key,
        ).fetchone()
        result = "stale"
        if prior is None or event["version"] > prior[0]:
            safe = {k: v for k, v in event["fields"].items() if k in ALLOWED[source]}
            db.execute("INSERT OR REPLACE INTO projection VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                       (*key, event["version"], json.dumps(safe)))
            result = "applied"
        db.execute("INSERT INTO seen VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                   (tenant, source, event["id"]))
    return result


def read(db, tenant, source, ticket):
    row = db.execute(
        "SELECT data FROM projection WHERE tenant=? AND source=? AND ticket=?",
        (tenant, source, ticket),
    ).fetchone()
    return json.loads(row[0]) if row else None


class SnapshotTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_duplicate_stale_and_private_fields(self):
        db = connect()
        e = dict(tenant="A", source="desk", ticket="7", id="event-2",
                 version=2, fields={"priority": "high", "internal_note": "test only"})
        self.assertEqual(apply_snapshot(db, e), "applied")
        self.assertEqual(apply_snapshot(db, e), "duplicate")
        old = dict(e, id="event-1", version=1, fields={"priority": "low"})
        self.assertEqual(apply_snapshot(db, old), "stale")
        self.assertEqual(read(db, "A", "desk", "7"), {"priority": "high"})
        db.close()

    def test_tenant_and_source_namespaces_are_separate(self):
        db = connect()
        e = dict(tenant="A", source="desk", ticket="7", id="same-id",
                 version=4, fields={"priority": "high"})
        apply_snapshot(db, e)
        other = dict(e, tenant="B", fields={"priority": "low"})
        self.assertEqual(apply_snapshot(db, other), "applied")
        eng = dict(e, source="engineering", version=1,
                   fields={"development_status": "done", "priority": "low"})
        self.assertEqual(apply_snapshot(db, eng), "applied")
        self.assertEqual(read(db, "A", "desk", "7"), {"priority": "high"})
        self.assertEqual(read(db, "B", "desk", "7"), {"priority": "low"})
        self.assertEqual(read(db, "A", "engineering", "7"),
                         {"development_status": "done"})
        db.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

Run:

python ticket_snapshot_demo.py -v

The first test applies version two, repeats the delivery and then delivers version one. It verifies that the repeated event is recognised, the old snapshot cannot regress priority and the internal note is not stored in the projection.

The second test uses identical event and ticket identifiers across two tenants and two sources. Both namespaces must remain independent. Engineering's attempt to supply a desk-owned priority is filtered out.

Both tests passed with Python 3.12.14 during preparation. They check concrete state rather than merely asserting that a function returned without an exception.

Understand the transaction boundary

The local projection change and the “seen” record are committed together using the connection context manager. Python's sqlite3 documentation explains transaction handling and parameterised statements.

There is no remote call inside that boundary. If you later add an HTTP write after the commit, a process failure can occur between recording the event and delivering the change. If you write before the commit, the destination can accept the change while the local transaction later fails.

A production design needs a deliberate outbound delivery mechanism, such as durable queued work with destination-aware duplicate handling. This exercise does not claim exactly-once delivery across systems.

The code is also a single-consumer teaching example. It does not test concurrent transactions, database contention, persistent restarts or retention of delivery identifiers. Those require their own design and tests.

Test loops at the outbound boundary

Deduplicating an inbound event will not necessarily stop an echo loop. A remote update may create a new event identifier even though it reflects a change the bridge just sent.

Record enough outbound context to recognise that specific reflected change. Compare the relevant fields, origin and version before deciding to ignore it. Avoid dropping every event created by an integration account: that account may legitimately perform work for another service.

A useful integration test sends one allowed field change, captures the resulting destination event and verifies that processing it does not issue the same business change repeatedly. Also send a genuine new change from the same account; the loop control must not discard it blindly.

Extend the acceptance matrix beyond this sample

Before connecting real systems, add tests for:

  • Invalid or unauthenticated senders, including a forged tenant identifier.
  • Private attachments and comments, not only the sample internal-note field.
  • Missing events discovered through reconciliation rather than customer complaints.
  • A moved or deleted destination ticket.
  • Equal versions carrying different payloads, which this simplified example treats as stale.
  • A remote permission change after the local event has been accepted.

Each failed or unproven case needs a visible owner. Passing the local tests is useful evidence for the filter's stated rules, not acceptance of the entire service.

Use the wider ticket integration matrix to plan the remaining service checks.
