title: How to Detect AI Bots Without Blocking Googlebot
description:
Your website is receiving automated requests. Some are from search engines trying to index your pages. Others come from AI crawlers, monitoring tools, scrapers, or malicious scripts.

The challenge isn't identifying every automated request. It's knowing which bots should be allowed and which ones deserve closer inspection.

Block everything that looks automated, and you risk blocking Googlebot or AI search crawlers. Trust every request claiming to be Googlebot, and anyone can bypass your basic filtering rules.

So how do you detect AI bots without blocking legitimate crawlers?

In this guide, we'll cover the different types of bots, build a working bot detection tool using Node.js, test it in VS Code, and explore how IP intelligence can help classify suspicious traffic.

What you'll build: A local Express server that recognizes bot user-agent strings, plus an optional IP Security lookup script that can be tested with sample data.

The basic project is free. No paid API subscription is required to complete the first part.

1. Understand the Different Types of Bots

Not every bot visiting your website is trying to cause problems.

Here's a quick comparison.

Bot Purpose Typical handling
Googlebot Search engine indexing Allow after verification
Bingbot Search engine indexing Allow after verification
OAI-SearchBot ChatGPT search discovery Follow your AI search policy
GPTBot AI model-related crawling Follow your training crawler policy
ChatGPT-User User-triggered page retrieval Evaluate separately
Uptime monitoring bots Website availability checks Allow recognized services
Malicious scrapers Unauthorized extraction or abuse Rate-limit or block when justified

OpenAI, for example, operates different crawlers for different purposes.

According to OpenAI's official documentation, OAI-SearchBot is used for ChatGPT search, while GPTBot crawls content that may be used for training AI models.

ChatGPT-User is different again. It can retrieve web pages in response to a user's action.

The distinction matters because you may want your articles discoverable in AI search without allowing every type of automated crawling.

2. Why User-Agent Detection Isn't Enough

One of the easiest ways to recognize a bot is through its HTTP User-Agent header.

For example, a request might contain:

Googlebot/2.1

Or:

GPTBot/1.4

Your server can inspect that header and classify the request.

But there's a problem.

Anyone can send a request pretending to be Googlebot:

curl -A "Googlebot" https://example.com

The -A option tells curl to send a particular user-agent string.

It doesn't make the request come from Google.

That's why we need to distinguish two concepts:

  • Bot identification: What software does the request claim to be?
  • Bot verification: Does the source actually belong to the claimed operator?

Let's start with identification.

3. Build a Basic AI Bot Detector in Node.js

This section works locally and doesn't require an IP intelligence API key.

We'll use Node.js, Express, and VS Code.

Step 1: Check your Node.js installation

Download Node.js from nodejs.org if it isn't installed.

Open VS Code and select:

Terminal → New Terminal

Run:

node -v

Then:

npm -v

Both commands should display version numbers.

Use Node.js 20 or newer for this project.

Step 2: Create a project folder

In the VS Code terminal, run these commands:

mkdir bot-detection-demo
cd bot-detection-demo

Initialize the project:

npm init -y

Install Express and dotenv:

npm install express dotenv

Then open your project in VS Code using File → Open Folder and select bot-detection-demo.

Step 3: Create the main server file

In the VS Code Explorer, right-click your project folder and select New File.

Name it:

server.mjs

Paste this code:

import express from "express";

const app = express();

const knownBots = [
  "Googlebot",
  "Bingbot",
  "GPTBot",
  "OAI-SearchBot",
  "ChatGPT-User",
  "ClaudeBot",
  "PerplexityBot"
];

function detectBotClaim(userAgent = "") {
  return knownBots.find(bot =>
    userAgent.toLowerCase().includes(
      bot.toLowerCase()
    )
  ) || null;
}

app.get("/check-bot", (req, res) => {
  const userAgent = req.get("user-agent") || "";

  const detectedBot = detectBotClaim(userAgent);

  res.json({
    message: "Bot identification completed",
    botClaim: detectedBot,
    isClaimingKnownBot: Boolean(detectedBot),
    verified: false,
    note: "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
  });
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log("Server running on port 3000");
});

Save the file using Ctrl + S.

This code checks incoming requests against a list of common search and AI bot names.

Notice the field:

verified: false

That's intentional. Our code identifies the claimed bot name but doesn't perform any operator verification.

Step 4: Start the server

In your terminal, run:

node server.mjs

You should see:

Server running on port 3000

Your local server is now running.

Open a second VS Code terminal using the + button in the Terminal panel.

Keep the first terminal running.

Step 5: Test Googlebot detection

In the second terminal, run:

curl -A "Googlebot" http://localhost:3000/check-bot

Expected response:

{
  "message": "Bot identification completed",
  "botClaim": "Googlebot",
  "isClaimingKnownBot": true,
  "verified": false,
  "note": "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
}

The server successfully recognized a request claiming to be Googlebot.

Step 6: Test GPTBot detection

Run:

curl -A "GPTBot" http://localhost:3000/check-bot

The response should contain:

{
  "message": "Bot identification completed",
  "botClaim": "GPTBot",
  "isClaimingKnownBot": true,
  "verified": false,
  "note": "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
}

Step 7: Test OAI-SearchBot

Run:

curl -A "OAI-SearchBot" http://localhost:3000/check-bot

The response should identify:

{
  "message": "Bot identification completed",
  "botClaim": "OAI-SearchBot",
  "isClaimingKnownBot": true,
  "verified": false,
  "note": "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
}

Step 8: Test an ordinary request

Now run:

curl http://localhost:3000/check-bot

Since curl doesn't normally claim to be one of the bots in our list, the response should include:

{
  "message": "Bot identification completed",
  "botClaim": null,
  "isClaimingKnownBot": false,
  "verified": false,
  "note": "User-agent matching does not verify identity."
}

That's it.

You've built and tested a working user-agent-based bot identifier.

But it doesn't detect sophisticated automation with unfamiliar user agents, and it doesn't verify whether a recognized name is genuine.

Let's improve the approach.

4. How to Verify Real Googlebot Traffic

Google recommends verifying its crawlers using DNS or published crawler IP ranges.

The DNS verification process works like this:

  1. Extract the actual client IP address.
  2. Perform a reverse DNS lookup.
  3. Check whether the hostname ends with an approved Google crawler domain.
  4. Perform a forward DNS lookup on that hostname.
  5. Confirm the original IP is among the returned addresses.

For example, Google's documentation shows crawler hostnames under:

googlebot.com

But you shouldn't trust an arbitrary hostname simply because it contains the word google.

The hostname must match Google's documented patterns, and forward DNS must confirm the original address.

Google also publishes official crawler IP ranges.

You can find the complete procedure in the Google crawler verification documentation.

What about OpenAI crawlers?

OpenAI publishes IP ranges for different crawlers:

  • OAI-SearchBot IP ranges
  • GPTBot IP ranges
  • ChatGPT-User IP ranges

If a request claims to be GPTBot, you can compare its actual source IP against the appropriate published ranges.

For production systems, you should regularly refresh these lists and correctly handle IPv4 and IPv6 CIDR ranges.

Also, when your application sits behind a reverse proxy, configure Express's trust proxy setting for your actual trusted proxy infrastructure. Don't blindly trust an incoming X-Forwarded-For header.

5. Detect Unknown Bots Using IP Intelligence

Verifying Googlebot is useful because Google provides official verification methods.

But what about a bot that doesn't identify itself?

Imagine an unknown client makes thousands of requests to your website.

It doesn't claim to be a search crawler. Its user-agent looks ordinary, and you don't recognize the IP address.

In this situation, IP intelligence can provide useful context.

For example, IPGeolocation.io's IP Security API provides information about whether an IP address has been associated with:

  • Automated bot activity
  • Known legitimate bots
  • Brute-force attacks
  • VPNs and proxy networks
  • Tor exit nodes
  • Cloud hosting providers
  • Other security risks

The API can return fields such as:

Field Purpose
is_bot Identifies bot activity associated with the IP
bot_type Describes the bot activity category
bot_operator_name Identifies a known operator when available
is_known_good_bot Indicates a recognized legitimate bot
bot_confidence_score Confidence score for bot activity
threat_score Overall IP risk score
is_known_attacker Indicates known attacker activity

These signals help distinguish a recognized crawler from suspicious automation.

An important limitation is that IP intelligence classifies an address based on available intelligence. It doesn't prove that every individual request from that address came from the same software.

Is the IP Security API free?

The IP Security Lookup feature requires a paid subscription.

According to the current documentation, each successful security lookup costs two API credits. The provider also describes an option to request trial access through customer support.

You can still follow the next example without paid access by using mock security data.

6. Test IP Bot Classification in VS Code

Now we'll create a separate script to inspect security information.

We'll support two testing methods:

  • Mock mode: Uses example data locally and requires no paid subscription.
  • Live mode: Calls the actual IP Security API when your subscription permits it.

Step 1: Create the test file

Inside the same project, create:

test-ip.mjs

Paste:

import "dotenv/config";
import net from "node:net";

const API_KEY = process.env.IPGEOLOCATION_API_KEY;
const mode = process.argv[2] || "mock";
const ip = process.argv[3] || "4.227.36.0";

function classifySecurity(security) {
  if (security.is_known_attacker) {
    return "Review and consider blocking";
  }

  if (security.is_known_good_bot) {
    return "Verify operator before allowing";
  }

  if (security.is_bot) {
    return "Monitor or challenge";
  }

  return "Allow and monitor";
}

const mockSecurity = {
  is_bot: true,
  bot_type: "ai_crawler",
  bot_operator_name: "Example AI Operator",
  is_known_good_bot: true,
  bot_confidence_score: 95,
  threat_score: 10,
  is_known_attacker: false
};

async function getSecurityData() {
  if (mode === "mock") {
    return mockSecurity;
  }

  if (mode !== "live") {
    throw new Error("Use mock or live mode");
  }

  if (!API_KEY) {
    throw new Error(
      "Add IPGEOLOCATION_API_KEY to your .env file"
    );
  }

  if (!net.isIP(ip)) {
    throw new Error("Invalid IP address");
  }

  const url = new URL(
    "https://api.ipgeolocation.io/v3/security"
  );

  url.searchParams.set("apiKey", API_KEY);
  url.searchParams.set("ip", ip);

  const response = await fetch(url, {
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000)
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const error = await response.text();

    throw new Error(
      `API returned ${response.status}: ${error}`
    );
  }

  const data = await response.json();

  if (!data.security) {
    throw new Error("Security object missing");
  }

  return data.security;
}

async function main() {
  try {
    const security = await getSecurityData();

    console.log("\nMode:", mode);

    if (mode === "mock") {
      console.log("Using simulated security data");
    } else {
      console.log("Checked IP:", ip);
    }

    console.log("\nSecurity information:");
    console.log(JSON.stringify(security, null, 2));

    console.log(
      "\nSuggested action:",
      classifySecurity(security)
    );

  } catch (error) {
    console.error("\nTest failed:", error.message);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  }
}

main();

Save the file.

Step 2: Run the free mock test

Open your VS Code terminal and run:

node test-ip.mjs mock

The script should display:

Mode: mock
Using simulated security data

Followed by the sample security information and:

Suggested action: Verify operator before allowing

This verifies your classification logic without making an external API request.

The data is simulated. Don't present this output as real IP intelligence.

Step 3: Configure live API access

If you have access to the paid Security API or an enabled trial, create a file named:

.env

Add:

IPGEOLOCATION_API_KEY=your_actual_api_key

Replace the placeholder with your API key.

Also create .gitignore:

.env
node_modules/

Never publish your real API key in screenshots, code examples, or a GitHub repository.

Step 4: Run a live lookup

Once your account has Security API access, execute:

node test-ip.mjs live 4.227.36.0

This IP appears in IPGeolocation's documentation as an example associated with a recognized AI crawler.

If the request succeeds, you'll receive real security fields and the script's suggested action.

The current classification may differ from the documentation example because IP intelligence changes over time.

Step 5: Understand API access errors

If your account doesn't support the Security API, you may receive an error similar to:

API returned 401:
IP Security Lookup is not supported
on your current subscription.

This doesn't mean your Node.js code is broken.

It means the API received your request but the subscription doesn't permit this feature.

To continue learning, run:

node test-ip.mjs mock

Or check the IP Security API documentation for subscription and trial information.

7. How to Decide Which Bots to Allow or Block

Once you have identification and risk signals, you need a policy.

A sensible starting point looks like this:

Traffic Suggested response
Verified Googlebot Allow indexing of public pages
Verified OAI-SearchBot Follow your AI search visibility policy
Verified GPTBot Follow your AI training access policy
Known monitoring service Allow expected monitoring traffic
Unrecognized automated traffic Monitor or rate-limit
Known malicious activity Investigate or block
Uncertain classification Collect more signals

Don't automatically block every datacenter IP.

Many legitimate crawlers operate from cloud infrastructure.

Similarly, don't automatically trust a bot simply because its IP reputation looks good.

For sensitive endpoints such as login forms, combine IP intelligence with request frequency, failed-login patterns, rate limits, and other behavioral signals.

The examples in this article return suggested actions. They don't implement firewall rules or automatically block requests.

That's intentional because a production blocking decision requires stronger verification and a tested false-positive policy.

8. Use robots.txt to Manage AI Crawlers

Some crawler operators support separate instructions for different purposes.

For example, you might allow Googlebot and OAI-SearchBot while asking GPTBot not to crawl your website.

Your robots.txt file could include:

User-agent: Googlebot
Allow: /

User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Allow: /

User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

This tells compliant crawlers that:

  • Googlebot may crawl public content.
  • OAI-SearchBot may crawl public content.
  • GPTBot should not crawl the site.

Remember that robots.txt is not a security mechanism.

Malicious bots can ignore it.

OpenAI also notes that user-triggered ChatGPT-User requests are different from its automatic crawlers, and ordinary robots.txt rules may not apply in the same way.

When you need actual enforcement, use verified network identity and appropriate server-side access controls.

9. Common Bot Detection Mistakes

Trusting user-agent strings

Anyone can claim to be Googlebot.

A matching string isn't proof of identity.

Blocking every cloud IP

Legitimate crawlers, monitoring tools, and real users may access your website from cloud infrastructure.

Treating all AI bots identically

AI search crawlers, training crawlers, and assistant-triggered fetchers serve different purposes.

Making an IP lookup for every request

External API calls introduce latency and cost.

Cache appropriate results and avoid unnecessary repeated lookups.

Blocking based on a single risk indicator

A flagged IP address doesn't necessarily prove malicious intent for every request.

Use additional signals and provide a way to investigate false positives.

Ignoring API failures

Your website shouldn't become unavailable just because a security intelligence API temporarily fails or your account reaches its limits.

Choose an explicit failure policy. For public informational pages, continuing with monitoring may be reasonable. Sensitive endpoints may require stricter controls.

10. Frequently Asked Questions

How do I detect AI bots on my website?

Start by examining user-agent strings and request logs. Verify recognized crawlers using their operators' published IP ranges or DNS verification methods. For unknown traffic, combine behavioral analysis with IP intelligence.

Can someone fake Googlebot?

Yes. User-agent headers can be changed freely. Google recommends verifying crawler requests using its documented DNS procedure or official IP ranges.

Can I test bot detection without paying for an API?

Yes. The basic Node.js user-agent detector in this article runs locally without an API key. You can also test the classification logic using simulated security data. Real IP Security lookup results require the appropriate API subscription or trial access.

Will blocking AI training crawlers affect Google rankings?

Blocking GPTBot through its specific robots.txt rule doesn't directly block Googlebot. However, broad server or firewall restrictions could accidentally affect search engine access.

Is IP intelligence enough to identify malicious bots?

No. It's one useful layer. Combine it with identity verification, request rates, behavioral patterns, and your website's own access policy.

Final Thoughts

Detecting AI bots isn't simply about checking whether a request contains the word bot.

You need to understand the traffic, identify known crawlers, verify their identities when necessary, and make decisions based on both reputation and behavior.

In this guide, we built a basic bot identifier, tested Googlebot and AI crawler user-agent strings, and added an optional IP Security classification example.

The most important lesson is simple:

Don't block a request just because it looks automated, and don't trust a request just because it claims to be legitimate.

Verify what you can, monitor what you can't, and apply policies that protect your website without unnecessarily restricting search engine access.

How are you handling AI crawlers on your own websites? Are you allowing them, blocking certain types, or monitoring everything first?

title: Estimating Gmail's Promotions tab without pretending to predict it
description:
Every marketer has asked the same question: will this land in Primary or Promotions?

Nobody outside Google can answer that with certainty. Gmail decides the tab using the message content, the sender's history, and how each recipient has engaged with that sender before. Two people on the same list can get the same email in different tabs. Any tool that claims to predict placement is overselling.

When we built the "Gmail tab estimate" in Cresca, we started from that limitation. This post covers what we built, how it works and where it falls short.

What we're actually estimating

The feature does not predict the tab. It estimates how promotional the email looks from its content: the one input to Gmail's decision that the sender fully controls. The UI says this directly. Expand the "Why" panel and the first line reads:

Gmail decides the tab using your content, your sending history and how each person has engaged with you before. This estimates how promotional the email looks.

The output is one of three labels, never a percentage:

  • Likely Primary
  • Could go either way
  • Likely Promotions

We avoided showing a raw score because "73%" suggests a precision we don't have.

Where it runs

The estimate runs entirely in the browser on the rendered HTML, the same markup that will be sent. It's a pure function, so it re-runs whenever the email or subject line changes, inside the AI conversation view, the design editor and the template preview:

const result = useMemo(
  () => analyzeInboxPlacement(html, { subject }),
  [html, subject],
);

Running it on the client made sense. It's quick, it updates as you edit, and it needs no network call. It also keeps us honest, because it's a small set of readable rules rather than a black box.

Step 1: Ignore what every email shares

We parse the HTML with DOMParser and remove nodes that would add noise:

doc
  .querySelectorAll(
    '[data-cresca-footer], style, script, title, [style*="display:none"], [style*="display: none"]',
  )
  .forEach((node) => node.remove());

Every Cresca email gets an automatic compliance footer (unsubscribe link and address), and many have a hidden preheader. Since those are the same on every email, counting them would add noise and hide what the sender can change.

Step 2: Measure the signals

We measure the features that make an email look like a newsletter or campaign rather than a message from a person:

  • Images, ignoring very small ones (48px wide or less, such as social icons), since a logo-sized icon isn't the same signal as a hero banner.
  • Distinct links, excluding mailto:, tel: and in-page anchors.
  • Buttons: links styled as buttons, counted once each even if several selectors match.
  • Coloured blocks: elements with a bgcolor that isn't white or a light grey. We use a simple colour test: a colour is neutral if its RGB channels sit within 24 of each other and all are above 200.
  • Multi-column layout.
  • Sale wording in the subject and body: "% off", "discount", "promo code", "shop now", "limited time", "last chance", "ends tonight" and similar phrases, found with one regex.
  • Text volume: a word count, so we can flag an email that is mostly images.
  • Personal markers: a {{first_name}} token or a greeting like "Hi" or "Hello" at the start.

Step 3: Score it, simply

The score starts at 100. Each signal subtracts a fixed penalty, with heavier penalties for stronger signals:

Signal Penalty
3+ images / 1–2 images 25 / 10
6+ links / 3–5 links 20 / 10
2+ buttons / 1 button 15 / 8
Coloured banners or blocks 15
Multi-column layout 10
3+ sale phrases / 1–2 25 / 10
Under 60 words and at least one image 10
Personal greeting or first-name token +5

The result is clamped to 0–100. A score of 70 or more is "Likely Primary", 45–69 is "Could go either way", and anything lower is "Likely Promotions".

I should be clear about where these numbers came from. They are hand-tuned weights, not a trained model. We based them on Google's public guidance and on how personal email differs from campaign email: personal email is mostly text, with few links, no banners and one column. The weights express a judgment about which signals matter most. They are not measured from Gmail's behaviour, and we don't present them that way.

Step 4: Explain, don't just score

A label alone isn't useful. Every penalty also records a reason and a fix, and the "Why" panel shows them:

  • "4 images: use one image or none, because image-heavy emails look like marketing."
  • "Sale wording: % off, shop now: promotional wording is a strong Promotions signal."
  • "1 button: a plain text link reads more personal than a button."

When there are no penalties, the panel says the email reads like a personal email: mostly text, few links, no banners.

The panel also gives three tips that don't depend on content: send from a person's name, ask readers to reply (replies show Gmail your emails are wanted), and remember that sales and big launches belong in Promotions, which is normal. That last tip matters. A product launch should look like a promotion. We don't want people removing every image from a launch email to chase the Primary tab.

The one-click rewrite

In the AI conversation view, if the estimate isn't "Likely Primary", there's a Rewrite as a plain personal email action. It sends the current email back to the AI agent with an instruction to turn it into a plain, personal-style message. The estimate then re-runs on the new HTML, so you can compare before and after.

What I'd tell anyone building something similar

  1. Name what you can't see. Engagement and reputation aren't visible to a content check. Say so in the UI, not in a footnote.
  2. Prefer labels to percentages when your confidence is coarse.
  3. Every penalty needs a fix. A score without an action just makes people anxious.
  4. Don't fight the user's intent. Some emails are meant to be promotional.
  5. Keep it readable. A rule-based heuristic you can explain beats an opaque model you can't defend when someone asks "why?"

We'll keep tuning the weights as we learn. The design principle stays the same: show people what they control, and be honest about what they don't.

If you want to try it on your own emails, Cresca is free for 30 days at https://www.cresca.xyz, no credit card needed. Build an email with the AI agent or a template and open the "Why" panel before you send.

Lalit Kumar Jangid, founder of Cresca

title: XPath to iOS Class Chain: a converter you can trust, and when it is actually faster
description:
Converted 678 Appium XPath locators to iOS Class Chain, checked every result, and timed the two on a simulator and an iPhone. Here is what changed.

TL;DR

  • Class chain is ~25 % faster than XPath for a typical iOS lookup: 70 ms saved at 100 elements, 676 ms at 2000 (iPhone).
  • It only matters on big screens. On small ones the gain is milliseconds, and on a real project the whole test run was not faster.
  • ~87 % of real XPath locators can be converted. The converter does it with no wrong chains and skips or flags the rest. 
npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests          # preview the diff
npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests --write  # apply it

Contents

  1. What a class chain is
  2. Why converting by hand goes wrong
  3. What the tool does
  4. How I checked that it is right
  5. How much faster is it?
  6. Where the chain is slower
  7. What I took away
  8. Try it

If you run Appium tests on iOS, you have probably heard that XPath is slow and that -ios class chain is faster. I wanted two things I could not find anywhere:

  1. A tool that converts existing XPath locators to class chain without silently changing which element they find.
  2. A real number: how much faster is it, and does that depend on the size of the screen?

This post covers both. The tool is open source: xpath-to-class-chain. In short: the chain was faster in all 240 timed lookups (22–29 %, simulator and iPhone), 489 of 562 real locators have a class chain, and a few shapes (visible, lookups of dozens of elements) get slower, see below.

What a class chain is

A class chain is WebDriverAgent's (WDA's) own locator language for iOS. Like XPath, it is a path of element types. Unlike XPath, each filter is an NSPredicate in backticks:

XPath Class chain
//XCUIElementTypeButton (any depth) **/XCUIElementTypeButton
//XCUIElementTypeCell/XCUIElementTypeButton (direct child) **/XCUIElementTypeCell/XCUIElementTypeButton
[@name="Pay"] [`name == "Pay"`]
[contains(@label,"Total")] [`label CONTAINS "Total"`]
[@name="a" and @label="b"] [`name == "a" AND label == "b"`]
//* (any type) **/*

In a test, it is just another locator strategy:

// WebdriverIO
await $('-ios class chain:**/XCUIElementTypeButton[`name == "Pay"`]').click();

// Java client
driver.findElement(AppiumBy.iOSClassChain("**/XCUIElementTypeButton[`name == \"Pay\"`]")).click();

Why it is faster. For XPath, WDA takes a snapshot of the whole accessibility tree, writes it out as XML, runs the XPath over it with libxml2 and maps the matches back to elements. A class chain skips the XML step: WDA turns it straight into XCTest queries. Both still walk the whole tree, so the gain is a percentage, not a fixed number of milliseconds.

Why converting by hand goes wrong

The two languages look alike but behave differently:

  • Positions. XPath //Button[2] is the 2nd Button under each parent; class chain **/Button[2] is the 2nd of all matches.
  • Order. XPath (//Button)[2] counts matches top to bottom; WDA counts them level by level (breadth-first). No class chain counts like XPath here.
  • Text. == compares exactly, but CONTAINS, MATCHES and [c] compare normalized text (a fullwidth Ｑ equals Q).
  • Errors. The Appium driver turns an invalid chain into "no such element", so a typo looks like a flaky test, not a syntax error.

That last point is the reason for the whole project: a wrong chain does not fail loudly.

What the tool does

It scans a folder (JS/TS, Java, Kotlin, Python, Ruby, C#, PHP, JSON…), converts the XPath locators it finds and prints a diff; --write saves the files. It validates every chain, skips what has no exact class chain (with a reason), warns on approximations, and leaves alone strings passed to an explicit XPath strategy like AppiumBy.xpath("…").

A preview on four shapes that are common in real test code:

- //XCUIElementTypeStaticText[@name="Order total"]
+ -ios class chain:**/XCUIElementTypeStaticText[`name == "Order total"`]

- //*[contains(@type,"XCUIElementTypeButton") and contains(@label,"Add to cart")]
+ -ios class chain:**/XCUIElementTypeButton[`label CONTAINS "Add to cart"`]

- (//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name="product.addToCart"])[2]
+ -ios class chain:**/XCUIElementTypeButton[`name == "product.addToCart"`][2]
! grouped position: WDA counts class chain matches breadth-first, XPath in document order,
  so the element can differ when matches sit at different depths

[skip] skipped_unsupported_logic: //*[@name="Total:"]/following-sibling::*[1]

The first two are exact, the third is the closest chain there is (check it on its screen), and the fourth stays XPath: a class chain has no sibling axis.

How I checked that it is right

Every verdict comes from running the XPath and the chain and comparing what they find:

  1. A WDA emulator. WDA's own class chain and XPath code (v16.14.1), compiled to run on a Mac. It tests each locator on hundreds of generated screens in seconds.
  2. 678 locators: 563 real ones from production test suites (anonymized) and 115 hand-made edge cases.
  3. Real devices. 246 cases on an iOS 27 simulator and an iPhone 13 Pro Max under Appium 3.8.0 and WDA 16.14.1. Where a device disagreed with the emulator, the device won. That is how the breadth-first order was found.

Scoring: an exact chain earns 1 point, an approximation 0.5, a skipped or wrong one 0. Locators that have no class chain at all are not counted; skipping them is the right answer.

Result Value
R, real locators 96.0 of 100
S, edge cases 93.6 of 100
Wrong chains 0

Why not 100? 39 real locators, all positions like (//Button)[2], have only an approximation, worth 0.5. So 96.0 and 93.6 are the maximum this scoring allows, and the converter reaches it.

How R and S are calculated 
R = 100 × Σ points / N    N = 489 real locators that have a class chain
  = 100 × (450 + 39 × 0.5) / 489 = 96.0

S is the same score on the 83 edge cases that have a class chain, split into 9 groups (positions, string functions, escaping, logic…) and weighted by how much each group matters in real test code. Every case, group and weight is in speccases.js.

Each locator with its chain and verdict is in coverage-cases.json; the full method is in the report.

How much faster is it?

On small screens (36–275 elements) the chain was about 20 % faster, but that is only 30–65 ms. So I measured what happens as the screen grows.

Setup: a synthetic Checkout page grown to 100, 500, 1000 and 2000 elements; the 10 most common locator shapes from real tests; targets at the top, at depth 39 and at the end of the page. Each lookup is one cold findElement, median of three passes.

Elements in the tree Simulator, XPath → chain Saved iPhone, XPath → chain Saved
~100 115 → 90 ms 21.9 % 295 → 225 ms 23.8 %
~500 453 → 344 ms 24.1 % 760 → 582 ms 23.4 %
~1000 912 → 677 ms 25.8 % 1.40 s → 997 ms 28.9 %
~2000 1.75 → 1.31 s 25.4 % 2.72 → 2.04 s 24.9 %
  • The saving in percent does not depend on the screen size. The saving in milliseconds grows with it, because both strategies process the whole tree on every lookup.
  • The locator shape and the target's position do not matter. A button at the top costs as much as one at depth 39.

More findings: useFirstMatch, depth limit, simulator vs iPhone
  • [1] and useFirstMatch do not help. An explicit [1] takes the same code path in WDA 16.14.1. useFirstMatch (an Appium setting that makes WDA stop at the first match) was 2.7 % faster at 100 elements and 5.7 % slower at 2000, 15 % slower for deep targets.
  • Nothing deeper than 50 levels is found by either strategy (WDA's default snapshotMaxDepth). The error is a plain "no such element".
  • A real iPhone is 1.5–2.6× slower than the simulator, mostly a fixed per-request cost over USB. The ratio between XPath and chain stays the same.

Where the chain is slower

On the small screens, four shapes were slower as a chain (simulator; the iPhone showed the same):

Locator XPath Chain
//XCUIElementTypeButton[@visible='true'], 32 matches 2.05 s 12.6 s
//XCUIElementTypeCell[@visible="true"]/XCUIElementTypeButton 3.46 s 5.14 s
//XCUIElementTypeButton[@name], 36 matches 1.15 s 1.78 s
/XCUIElementTypeApplication/XCUIElementTypeWindow/XCUIElementTypeButton 0.12 s 0.75 s

visible is the main trap: WDA checks visibility for every candidate. These four cases outweighed all the gains, and over the whole small-screen run XPath was faster in total (53.7 s against 64.8 s). Without them, the chain was 3.8 % faster.

So on small screens XPath is fine. The gain shows up on big trees: long feeds and lists, screens kept alive in a navigation stack or in tabs, off-screen drawers. An iPad with several windows on screen should behave the same way (not measured).

What I took away

Faster lookups do not automatically mean faster tests. On a real project with simple screens, run on Sauce Labs devices (iOS 16, 18, 26), the timed lookups got faster, but the total run time barely changed: a few milliseconds are lost next to app launch, network and waits.

My rule of thumb: convert for speed where the screens are big, and convert lookups of one element by name, label, value or type. Check visible predicates, list lookups and absolute paths first.

Limits

  • Only lookups were measured in a controlled way, not whole tests. With implicit waits or retries, a missed lookup repeats the whole search, so the saving multiplies by the number of attempts.
  • The big screen is synthetic; no production app was benchmarked.
  • One WDA version (16.14.1). Its class chain lookup changed recently (appium/WebDriverAgent PR #1194), so other versions may give other numbers.
  • One phone and one Mac (M1 Pro). Absolute times will differ on yours; the ratio should not.

Try it

You need Node.js 20 or newer, nothing else. Start with the screens that have the most elements: dump the page source of your heaviest screen and count them.

npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests          # preview
npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests --write  # save
npx github:domovou69/xpath-to-class-chain ./tests --json   # report with every skip and warning

Then review the warnings, run your suite, and check each grouped position and visible locator on its screen. Everything behind the numbers in this post (the audit, the emulator, the device app) is in audit/.

Next: can an LLM do this instead?

In part 2 I give the same 678 locators to Claude models (Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, several generations, every effort level) and score them with the same checks. Short version: no model beat the converter on real locators, and a prompt with the rules mattered more than the model or the effort level.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Anthropic: Claude Code helped me build the converter, the test harness and the device benchmark, and analyze the results. All numbers come from real runs.

Mikhail Yesipchuk, SDET/Senior QA Automation Engineer. If you try the converter on your suite, I'd like to hear what it skipped and why: open an issue on GitHub or message me on LinkedIn.

title: On Windows, four processes appending to one file lost 37 of 200 lines
description:
My CI failed with this, only on the Windows runner, on a commit that changed nothing but a few GIFs:

receipts: Unexpected token '\', "\hostedtoo"... is not valid JSON

The same test had passed on that runner a few hours earlier. Here is what it was, because it is a small bug that is easy to ship.

The setup

Receipts runs the tests a change added or edited twice: with the change, and with the changed source files put back the way they were. For pytest it loads a tiny plugin that writes one JSON line per test result into a file, and the Node side reads that file afterwards.

def _emit(record):
    out = os.environ.get("RECEIPTS_PYTEST_OUT")
    if out:
        with open(out, "a", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            fh.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")

One file, opened in append mode, one line per record. Fine, until the project uses pytest-xdist. Then several worker processes run the tests, and at the end every one of them writes a record with the list of modules it imported. Those records are long, full of paths like \hostedtoolcache\windows\Python\.... That is the fragment in the error: the start of a line that got torn in half.

The repro

Four processes, each appending the same long JSON line 50 times to one file:

import json, os, multiprocessing as mp

def worker(out, n):
    rec = {"files": [r"\hostedtoolcache\windows\Python\Lib\m%04d.py" % i for i in range(400)]}
    for _ in range(n):
        with open(out, "a", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
            fh.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    out = "race.jsonl"
    ps = [mp.Process(target=worker, args=(out, 50)) for _ in range(4)]
    [p.start() for p in ps]; [p.join() for p in ps]
    print(sum(1 for _ in open(out, encoding="utf-8")), "lines")

On my Windows machine: 163 lines instead of 200. 37 writes simply vanished. With records of different lengths you also get torn lines instead of clean losses, which is what CI hit.

Why

On POSIX, O_APPEND means "move to the end and write" happens as one step for each write(), so concurrent appenders don't overwrite each other. On Windows, the C runtime emulates append mode: it seeks to the end, then writes. Two processes can both seek to the same end and the second write lands on top of the first. Nothing errors, data is just gone.

It only showed up now because it needs two xdist workers to finish within the same moment. It had been passing for weeks.

The fix

Stop sharing the file. The controlling process keeps out.json, each xdist worker writes out.json.<worker id>, and the reader picks up all of them:

worker = getattr(_config, "workerinput", None)
if worker is not None:
    out = "%s.%s" % (out, worker.get("workerid", os.getpid()))

While I was there, the reader stopped throwing on a line it can't parse: a run killed for hanging can leave a half-written last line, and the records before it still count.

The regression test doesn't try to reproduce the race (that would be a flaky test about flakiness). It checks the mechanism directly: a worker writes to its own file, the controller to the main one, and a torn line at the end doesn't sink the read. It fails on the old plugin and passes on the new one, which, given what the tool is for, felt like the least I could do.

Takeaway

If several processes append to one file, it works on Linux and macOS and loses data on Windows, quietly and rarely. Give each process its own file, or take a lock.

I drafted this post with an AI assistant. The error, the numbers and the code are from the actual CI run, my machine and the commit: https://github.com/syntaxixr/receipts/commit/70bb9b2

title: Remote MCP servers with OAuth: lessons from Claude, ChatGPT and Codex
description:
On October 15, 2026, we launched remote MCP servers for three data products: PMWallets (Polymarket traders ranked by on-chain realized PnL), LPSignal (concentrated-liquidity pools ranked by net APR) and OutcomeTick (historical data and backtesting for Polymarket and Predict.fun crypto up/down markets). They share a design with a protected URL that triggers OAuth and a separate anonymous URL. PMWallets uses Streamable HTTP with stateless JSON responses.

We tested them with claude.ai, Claude Code, Codex CLI and ChatGPT developer mode. Most of what broke was in OAuth discovery and client registration; a code review found one more problem in refresh-token cleanup.

Two URLs: one that returns 401, one that doesn't

Every server has a pair:

Protected Anonymous
PMWallets https://api.pmwallets.com/mcp https://api.pmwallets.com/mcp/public
LPSignal https://api.lpsignal.app/v1/mcp https://api.lpsignal.app/v1/mcp/public
OutcomeTick https://outcometick.com/v1/mcp https://outcometick.com/v1/mcp/public

An MCP client starts the OAuth flow when the server answers 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header pointing at the protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728):

HTTP/2 401
www-authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://api.pmwallets.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp", scope="pmwallets"

If an unauthenticated request gets a 200 and a tool list instead, the client stays anonymous. That rules out one URL that serves public tools to everyone and account tools to signed-in users. Each main URL returns 401 without credentials, and the anonymous tools live at /public, which never asks.

Tool annotations in Codex and claude.ai

On PMWallets, the read tools (leaderboard, entity, market, fills, export_quote and others) carry readOnlyHint: true. The subscription and purchase tools, subscribe, buy_export and cancel_subscription, carry destructiveHint: true. LPSignal's 8 tools and OutcomeTick's 14 are all read-only; neither server has spending tools.

{ "name": "leaderboard",
  "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": true, "destructiveHint": false, "idempotentHint": true } }

In the recorded tests:

  • Codex CLI called PMWallets and OutcomeTick read-only tools without approval flags.
  • claude.ai grouped PMWallets read tools under "Read-only tools" in the connector settings.

Annotations are hints that clients may ignore. For PMWallets purchases, the agent quotes first and waits for the user's consent, and buy_export also requires maxPriceCents, the price cap the user agreed to.

Mention every capability in the server instructions

PMWallets sells past fills of a trader as files, one per wallet per UTC day, covering about the last two months. The tools include export_options, export_quote, buy_export and export_file.

Early on, the server instructions didn't mention history exports, and Claude told a user that history from before the subscription was unavailable, although the export tools were already there. The instructions now say that past fills are sold separately as exports and which tool does what.

OAuth: what the authorization server does

PMWallets runs an OAuth 2.1 authorization server with:

  • Discovery through RFC 8414 (authorization server metadata) and RFC 9728 (protected resource metadata).
  • Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD), where the client_id is a URL hosting client metadata, and Dynamic Client Registration (DCR). LPSignal also supports both; its claude.ai, Claude Code and Codex tests used CIMD. OutcomeTick's Claude Code and Codex tests used CIMD.
  • PKCE with S256 and the RFC 8707 resource parameter. Tokens are not bound to a URL path; MCP-only access is enforced separately.
  • Access tokens that last one hour and are accepted for MCP, not the REST API.
  • Refresh tokens that last 30 days and rotate on every use. Replaying an old token revokes the whole connection, provided the server still retains the record needed to recognize it.
  • RFC 7009 revocation, an authorization page that cannot be framed, and a "Connected AI apps" list where users can disconnect a client.

LPSignal also has one-hour MCP-only access tokens, rotating 30-day refresh tokens, RFC 7009 revocation and a "Connected AI apps" list.

OutcomeTick has separate API keys for its data, smart-money and backtest products. The authorization page has a field for each, and each field accepts only that product's key.

ChatGPT's CIMD document says private_key_jwt

ChatGPT's CIMD document declares:

{ "token_endpoint_auth_method": "private_key_jwt" }

All three products hit a compatibility issue with this declaration. The same document lists none in token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported. Treating ChatGPT as a public client using PKCE worked without implementing RFC 7523 JWT client authentication.

Refresh-token rotation and the cleanup job

Reuse detection depends on retaining records of refresh tokens that have already been exchanged.

PMWallets had a cleanup job that deleted used refresh tokens once they expired. That looks harmless, since an expired token can't be exchanged anyway. But once the row is gone, a replayed token is no longer "used", just unknown. After about 30 days, a replay was rejected as an ordinary bad token, and the connection it belonged to stayed alive.

Codex review found this in PMWallets, and OutcomeTick confirmed the same issue.

A wrong URL that half works

LPSignal and OutcomeTick use /v1/mcp; PMWallets originally used /mcp. A user pasted https://api.pmwallets.com/v1/mcp into ChatGPT. Sign-in succeeded, then ChatGPT showed:

Authentication succeeded, action discovery failed

That route did not exist. Without a token, ChatGPT's POST got a 403 from the Origin check, and the path-specific metadata returned 404. ChatGPT fell back to the root metadata, which described /mcp, and completed OAuth. It then POSTed to /v1/mcp with the token, received 404 and reported a discovery failure.

PMWallets now serves /v1/mcp as an alias with its own protected-resource metadata, with resource set to https://api.pmwallets.com/v1/mcp. The 401 points to that metadata, and the alias is included in the Origin exemption and rate limits.

DNS lookups for URLs users control

PMWallets resolves user-supplied hosts for webhooks and CIMD metadata fetches.

In Node, dns.lookup uses getaddrinfo on the libuv thread pool, which has four threads by default. The same pool runs file system calls and some crypto. A user who controls the hostname can make lookups slow, and a few of them hold up unrelated work in the process. For these lookups we switched to the c-ares-based dns.Resolver, which doesn't use the pool, with an overall deadline.

The second problem was in net.BlockList. We added ::ffff:0:0/96 to block IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses. With that rule in the list, every plain IPv4 address was classified as internal, public hosts included. Convert a mapped address to IPv4 yourself and check it against the IPv4 rules instead.

Reading large files through MCP

PMWallets' export_file streams and decompresses the download, returning only the requested page. A call scans at most 50,000 lines, concurrent reads are limited, and the read aborts when the client disconnects. Without the disconnect check, the server would keep downloading and decompressing after the client had gone away.

Batches and rate limits

All three servers rate-limit MCP requests. LPSignal and OutcomeTick reject JSON-RPC batches. PMWallets accepts up to 10 messages per batch and executes them one at a time.

Connecting

For Claude Code and Codex CLI, add the protected URL:

# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http pmwallets https://api.pmwallets.com/mcp

# Codex CLI
codex mcp add pmwallets --url https://api.pmwallets.com/mcp

Use the LPSignal or OutcomeTick URL from the table to connect those servers. PMWallets was also tested with a claude.ai custom connector and a ChatGPT web developer-mode custom connector. LPSignal supports wallet sign-in with any wallet and has a free account. PMWallets accepts OAuth or a bearer API key; OutcomeTick's authorization page accepts its product-specific keys.

The /public URLs need no account. PMWallets exposes a 20-row leaderboard sample, trader records and market lookups. LPSignal exposes everything except my_account. OutcomeTick exposes coverage and plans, backtest capacity and quotes, strategy checks, and smart-money plans and coverage.

All three are listed in the official MCP Registry (io.github.polymarketwallets/pmwallets, app.lpsignal/lpsignal, io.github.outcometick/outcometick) and have Claude Code plugins. OutcomeTick also ships a local stdio server (ot mcp) with a test that keeps its tool set identical to the remote one. Setup guides: pmwallets.com/ai-agents, LPSignals/lpsignal-mcp, outcometick.com/llms-full.txt.

I build PMWallets, LPSignal and OutcomeTick.

title: Why your Puppeteer PDF shows empty boxes for Arabic, Chinese and Hindi (and how to fix it)
description:
You generate an invoice PDF from HTML. On your laptop it looks perfect. In production, every Arabic, Chinese or Hindi character is an empty box (□□□). No error, no warning, a perfectly valid PDF. Usually a customer is the first to notice.

I ran into this enough times that I wrote down what is going on. Nothing is wrong with your code or with Puppeteer.

The problem

Here is a script that reproduces it. On a machine with suitable fonts the output looks fine. In a slim container you get boxes:

const puppeteer = require("puppeteer");

(async () => {
  const browser = await puppeteer.launch({ args: ["--no-sandbox"] });
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.setContent(
    '<html lang="ar" dir="rtl"><body>' +
    "<h1>فاتورة</h1><p>你好，世界 · नमस्ते</p>" +
    "</body></html>"
  );
  await page.pdf({ path: "invoice.pdf", format: "A4" });
  await browser.close();
})();

Why it happens

Chrome draws text with the fonts installed on the machine that runs it. Your laptop has hundreds. A minimal Docker image, a CI runner or a serverless function usually has a handful of Latin fonts and nothing else.

When no installed font contains a character, Chrome draws the "missing glyph" box and moves on. It does not throw. That is why the classic symptom is "works on my machine, broken in production".

The same is true for Playwright, Selenium or anything else that prints through headless Chrome: the fonts come from the machine, not from the library.

The fix: install Noto fonts in the image

Noto covers Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari (Hindi) and most other scripts. Chinese, Japanese and Korean live in a separate package. On a Debian-based image:

FROM node:20-bookworm-slim

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      fontconfig fonts-noto-core fonts-noto-cjk fonts-noto-color-emoji \
    && fc-cache -f \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Rebuild, then check that the system can see a font for each language:

fc-list :lang=ar family | head -3
fc-list :lang=zh-cn family | head -3
fc-list :lang=hi family | head -3

If one of these prints nothing, that language still has no font. Be aware that the CJK package makes the image noticeably bigger, so if size matters, install it only in the image that renders PDFs.

Fonts are not enough: set lang and dir

Two more details decide whether the result looks right, not just not-broken.

Right-to-left text. For Arabic and Hebrew, put dir="rtl" on the <html> tag (or the container) together with a matching lang. Chrome handles letter joining and mixed-direction text once a font exists, but without dir="rtl" alignment, punctuation and numbers can land in the wrong place.

Chinese vs Japanese. The same Han character can be drawn with a different regional shape depending on the language. Characters like 直 and 骨 are good examples. If the page has no lang, Chrome may pick a font you did not intend, and Chinese text can show up with Japanese shapes. Set lang="zh-CN", lang="zh-TW" or lang="ja", and for mixed documents put lang on the element that holds each piece.

:lang(zh-CN) { font-family: "Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif; }
:lang(zh-TW) { font-family: "Noto Sans CJK TC", sans-serif; }
:lang(ja)    { font-family: "Noto Sans CJK JP", sans-serif; }

Turkish has its own trap: the dotted and dotless İ / ı pair is only upper- and lower-cased correctly when the page declares lang="tr".

Test with a real document

A one-line test hides most problems. Real invoices mix scripts, digits, currency symbols and punctuation. Render one realistic PDF per language in your CI and actually look at it. That is the only way to catch this before a customer does.

If you would rather not maintain this

I built a small hosted API around exactly this problem, because I did not want to maintain Chromium and font packages in every project. You POST HTML and get a PDF back, with Noto fonts for 11 languages already installed (en, tr, es, fr, de, ru, ar, he, zh, ja, hi):

curl -X POST https://getprintoza.com/v1/convert \
  -H "x-api-key: YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"language": "ar", "html": "<h1>مرحبا</h1><p>فاتورة مبيعات</p>"}' \
  --output arabic.pdf

If your HTML contains characters that none of the fonts can draw, the PDF is still created and the response carries an X-Getprintoza-Warnings header listing them. It is a best-effort check, so still look at a few real documents. The free plan is 50 PDFs a month. It is new and run by one person, so I would genuinely like to hear which languages or edge cases still break for you.

The guides behind this article work with plain Puppeteer and Docker, no API needed:

  • Empty boxes in Puppeteer PDFs (Arabic, Chinese, Hindi)
  • Right-to-left layout for Arabic and Hebrew
  • Chinese and Japanese fonts and lang
  • Turkish characters ğ ş ı İ

title: SQL Joins Explained with One Tiny Dataset (Plus 5 Interview Questions)
description:
Most join tutorials show you a Venn diagram and move on. Then an interviewer asks, "Why did your row count go up after the join?" or "Why did your LEFT JOIN behave like an INNER JOIN?", and the diagram doesn't help.

In this post we'll use one small dataset (two tables, ten rows in total) and run every join type on it, so you can see exactly which rows survive. Then we'll work through five interview-style questions that test whether you really understand joins, not just the syntax.

Everything below runs on SQLite 3.39 or newer (and on PostgreSQL). If you're on MySQL, everything works except FULL OUTER JOIN, which MySQL doesn't support. We show the usual workaround below.

The setup

Copy this into any SQL editor:

CREATE TABLE departments (
  id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  city TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE employees (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  dept_id    INTEGER REFERENCES departments(id),
  manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id),
  salary     INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO departments VALUES
  (1, 'Engineering', 'Bengaluru'),
  (2, 'Sales',       'Mumbai'),
  (3, 'HR',          'Pune'),
  (4, 'Legal',       'Delhi');

INSERT INTO employees VALUES
  (1, 'Asha',  1, NULL, 150000),
  (2, 'Ravi',  1, 1,     90000),
  (3, 'Priya', 2, 1,     80000),
  (4, 'Karan', 2, 3,     60000),
  (5, 'Neha',  NULL, 1,  70000),
  (6, 'Arjun', 3, 1,     65000);

Two details are there on purpose, because they're what make joins interesting:

  • Neha has no department (dept_id is NULL).
  • Legal has no employees.

Keep an eye on those two rows. The difference between join types comes down to what happens to them.

INNER JOIN: only matching rows 

SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;
name dept
Asha Engineering
Ravi Engineering
Priya Sales
Karan Sales
Arjun HR

Neha is gone (she matches no department) and so is Legal (it matches no employee). An inner join keeps a row only when the ON condition is true for both sides. JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN.

LEFT JOIN: keep everything from the left table 

SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;

You get the same five rows plus Neha | NULL. Every employee shows up. Where there's no match, the right-hand columns are filled with NULL. Legal still doesn't appear, because departments is the right table here.

RIGHT JOIN: the mirror image 

SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM employees e
RIGHT JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;

Now Legal appears as NULL | Legal, and Neha disappears. In practice most people just swap the table order and write a LEFT JOIN, because it reads more naturally.

FULL OUTER JOIN: keep everything from both 

SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM employees e
FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;

Seven rows: the five matches, Neha | NULL, and NULL | Legal. On MySQL you can get the same result with a LEFT JOIN ... UNION ... RIGHT JOIN of the same two tables.

CROSS JOIN: every combination 

SELECT COUNT(*) AS combos
FROM employees CROSS JOIN departments;

That returns 24 (6 employees × 4 departments). You rarely want this on purpose. Usually it shows up by accident when someone forgets the ON condition. If your result ever has "rows × rows" in it, check your join condition first.

Note: SQL doesn't promise any row order unless you write ORDER BY. Your rows may come back in a different order from the tables above. That's fine.

5 interview questions on joins

These are the kinds of questions that separate "I've used joins" from "I understand joins." Try each one yourself before you read the answer.

1. Find departments that have no employees 

SELECT d.name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.id IS NULL;

Result: Legal. This is the anti-join pattern: LEFT JOIN, then keep only the rows where the right side didn't match. Check a column that can never be NULL in a real match, such as the primary key e.id. NOT EXISTS is an equally good answer, and it's worth mentioning both.

2. List each employee with their manager's name 

SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;

This is a self join: the same table, under two aliases. Interviewers like to ask why it's a LEFT JOIN. The answer: Asha has no manager, and with an INNER JOIN she would disappear from the list.

3. Why did my LEFT JOIN turn into an INNER JOIN?

Compare these two queries:

-- Version A: filter in WHERE
SELECT d.name, e.name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.salary > 70000;

-- Version B: filter in ON
SELECT d.name, e.name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id AND e.salary > 70000;

Version A returns 3 rows (Engineering twice, Sales once). Version B returns 5: the same 3, plus HR | NULL and Legal | NULL.

Why? WHERE runs after the join. The unmatched rows have e.salary = NULL, and NULL > 70000 is not true, so WHERE throws them away. Your LEFT JOIN quietly becomes an inner join. If the question is "show every department, and any well-paid employees in it," the filter on the right table belongs in ON.

4. Count employees per department, including empty ones 

SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) AS wrong, COUNT(e.id) AS headcount
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name;
name wrong headcount
Engineering 2 2
Sales 2 2
HR 1 1
Legal 1 0

COUNT(*) counts rows, and the LEFT JOIN produced one row for Legal (full of NULLs). COUNT(e.id) counts only non-NULL values, which gives the right headcount of 0. Mixing these two up is a classic way to fail this question.

The same idea explains the "why did my row count go up?" question. In a one-to-many join, each department row is repeated once for every matching employee. That's correct behaviour. Just remember it before you SUM a column from the "one" side.

5. Highest-paid employee in each department

Version with a correlated subquery:

SELECT d.name AS dept, e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.salary = (
  SELECT MAX(e2.salary)
  FROM employees e2
  WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id
);

Version with a window function:

SELECT dept, name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT d.name AS dept, e.name, e.salary,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees e
  JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
)
WHERE rnk = 1;

Both return Asha (Engineering), Priya (Sales) and Arjun (HR). A good follow-up to bring up yourself is ties: RANK() keeps every employee tied for the top salary, while ROW_NUMBER() would pick exactly one of them.

A quick mental checklist

Before you run any join, ask yourself:

  1. Which rows must not disappear? That table goes on the left of a LEFT JOIN.
  2. Is this one-to-one or one-to-many? If it's one-to-many, expect repeated rows and be careful with aggregates.
  3. Where does each filter go? Filters on the optional (right) table usually belong in ON.
  4. What am I counting? COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values.

Try it in the browser

Reading about joins only gets you so far. You need to write a few that go wrong. Our hands-on SQL practice has chapters on INNER JOIN, outer joins and NULL handling, with exercises you run in the browser. Nothing to install.

A good exercise: extend the dataset above with a projects table (id, name, dept_id) and write a query that lists every department with its number of employees and its number of projects. If you get inflated counts, go back to question 4.

Happy querying!

— Schoolabe team

title: Why `await Promise.all()` Can Crash Your Database (And How to Throttle Concurrent Async Tasks in Node.js)
description:
It's the most natural-looking line in modern JavaScript:

await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => processOrder(id)));

Fast, concise, parallel. In development with 20 IDs it finishes in a blink. Then a backfill job runs it against 200,000 IDs, and:

  • The database CPU pins at 100%, or too many clients already floods the logs
  • Other endpoints on the same service start timing out
  • The third-party API starts returning 429 Too Many Requests
  • The process runs out of memory, or dies with EMFILE: too many open files

Promise.all didn't do anything wrong. It did exactly what you asked. The problem is that you asked for unlimited concurrency, and you may not have realized it.

This post explains what Promise.all actually does, the specific ways unbounded fan-out hurts a Postgres-backed Node.js service, and several ways to throttle concurrency, from a five-line loop to a proper queue.

The misconception: Promise.all doesn't run things in parallel

Look at what happens in this line, step by step:

const promises = ids.map((id) => processOrder(id)); // (1) every task STARTS here
const results = await Promise.all(promises);        // (2) this only WAITS

An async function begins executing the moment you call it. By the end of step 1, processOrder has been invoked N times, and N operations are already in flight. Promise.all at step 2 does no scheduling or throttling at all. It just waits for the promises that already exist.

So "use Promise.all to run things concurrently" is true, but incomplete. It has no concurrency limit. If the array has 200,000 items, you start 200,000 operations at once.

Two more properties that matter for failure handling:

  • Fail-fast, but no cancellation. If one promise rejects, Promise.all rejects immediately, but the other tasks keep running. Your code has moved on (probably into an error handler) while hundreds of queries are still executing in the background.
  • All results are held in memory until everything finishes.

How unbounded concurrency hurts

1. Connection pool exhaustion and queue pile-up

With pg, the pool has a fixed max (default 10). Extra pool.query() calls don't fail, they wait in a queue:

const pool = new Pool({ max: 10, connectionTimeoutMillis: 2_000 });

// 5,000 queries start simultaneously: 10 run, 4,990 wait in the pool's queue
await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => pool.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [id])));

Consequences:

  • Everyone queued behind this job waits too, including unrelated requests (login, health checks, your API traffic). A single background job can starve the whole service.
  • Waiters beyond connectionTimeoutMillis fail with timeout exceeded when trying to connect, so a job that "should be fine" fails partway.
  • Thousands of pending promises, closures, and queued requests consume memory and add GC pressure.

(We covered this failure family in depth in the post on connection pool starvation.)

2. Overloading the database itself

The pool protects Postgres from connection floods, but only if every task shares it. Two common ways the database still gets crushed:

  • Per-task connections. Code that does new Client() per task, or an ORM/serverless setup creating a pool per invocation, opens one real connection per concurrent task. Each Postgres connection is a separate backend process. Hundreds of them exhaust max_connections and make everything slower, since too many concurrent active queries mean CPU and I/O contention, not speed.
  • Heavy queries in lockstep. Even through a pool, if each query is expensive and your pool is large, saturating the pool means the database runs max heavy queries simultaneously. Concurrency above what the hardware can usefully execute adds queueing and lock contention without adding throughput.

Bulk writes add their own problems: lock contention on hot rows, replication lag on replicas, and WAL volume spikes.

3. Hitting downstream rate limits

Calling an external API for each item with Promise.all is a reliable way to earn 429s, temporary bans, or throttled accounts. The retries then pile on more load.

4. Memory and file descriptors

Each in-flight task holds buffers, response bodies, and promise state. Reading 10,000 files concurrently can hit EMFILE. Fetching 10,000 large responses concurrently can exhaust memory long before the work completes.

5. Retry storms and thundering herds

A brief database hiccup makes thousands of concurrent tasks fail at once, and if each retries on its own, they all retry at once. Bounded concurrency naturally limits how much work is exposed to a failure and how much re-attempts at once.

Reproduce it on purpose

Seeing the failure beats believing it:

// repro.ts
import { Pool } from 'pg';

const pool = new Pool({ max: 10, connectionTimeoutMillis: 2_000 });

const results = await Promise.allSettled(
  Array.from({ length: 5_000 }, () => pool.query('SELECT pg_sleep(0.05)')),
);

const failed = results.filter((r) => r.status === 'rejected');
console.log(`failed: ${failed.length} / ${results.length}`);
console.log((failed[0] as PromiseRejectedResult | undefined)?.reason?.message);
// Typically: many failures with "timeout exceeded when trying to connect"

Each query takes ~50 ms and the pool runs 10 at a time, so the last queries in the queue wait far longer than the 2-second connection timeout. Many fail even though every individual query is trivial. (Exact numbers depend on your machine.)

Fix 1: Process in chunks (simplest) 

// ✅ At most `size` in flight at a time
async function inChunks<T, R>(items: T[], size: number, fn: (item: T) => Promise<R>): Promise<R[]> {
  const out: R[] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i += size) {
    const chunk = items.slice(i, i + size);
    out.push(...(await Promise.all(chunk.map(fn))));
  }
  return out;
}

const results = await inChunks(ids, 10, (id) => processOrder(id));

It's dead simple, but there's an efficiency flaw: each chunk is only as fast as its slowest task. If one task in a chunk takes 5 seconds and the other nine take 50 ms, nine "slots" sit idle for ~5 seconds. With uneven task times this wastes a lot of capacity. The next options keep slots busy continuously.

Fix 2: p-limit (sliding-window concurrency)

p-limit gives you a limiter: wrap each task, and at most N run at once. As soon as one finishes, the next starts.

import pLimit from 'p-limit';

const limit = pLimit(5);

const results = await Promise.all(
  ids.map((id) => limit(() => processOrder(id))),   // note: the function is deferred
);

The crucial detail is limit(() => processOrder(id)). You must pass a function so the task doesn't start until the limiter allows it. Writing limit(processOrder(id)) calls processOrder immediately and defeats the purpose.

Caveats:

  • Recent versions of p-limit (and p-map) are ESM-only. In a CommonJS project, use dynamic import() or pin an older version.
  • The ids.map(...) above still creates N closures and promises up front, which is fine for thousands of items, but for millions you want an iterator-based approach (below).

Fix 3: p-map (map with concurrency built in)

p-map packages the pattern as a single call and has useful error options:

import pMap from 'p-map';

const results = await pMap(ids, (id) => processOrder(id), {
  concurrency: 5,
  stopOnError: true,   // default: reject on first error and stop starting new tasks
});

Set stopOnError: false to run everything and get an AggregateError at the end. Because it accepts iterables, you can feed it a generator or lazily-produced sequence rather than materializing a giant array.

Fix 4: A tiny worker pool with no dependencies

Dependencies are optional. The core idea fits in a few lines: start limit workers, and each one repeatedly pulls the next item until none are left.

export async function mapLimit<T, R>(
  items: readonly T[],
  limit: number,
  fn: (item: T, index: number) => Promise<R>,
): Promise<R[]> {
  const results = new Array<R>(items.length);
  let next = 0;
  let failed = false;

  async function worker() {
    while (!failed) {
      const i = next++;                    // safe: JS runs this synchronously, no race
      if (i >= items.length) return;
      try {
        results[i] = await fn(items[i], i);
      } catch (err) {
        failed = true;                     // tell sibling workers to stop pulling new items
        throw err;
      }
    }
  }

  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, worker));
  return results;
}

const results = await mapLimit(ids, 5, (id) => processOrder(id));

Why next++ is safe without locks: Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread, and there's no await between reading and incrementing next, so two workers can't claim the same index.

The failed flag matters. Without it, when one task throws, Promise.all rejects but the other workers keep pulling new items, continuing to do work nobody's waiting for, which is the "no cancellation" problem from earlier.

If you'd rather collect every outcome instead of failing fast, catch inside the worker and store { status, value | reason } per item, mirroring Promise.allSettled.

Fix 5: Don't load everything into memory first

Throttling the tasks doesn't help if you first load 5 million rows into an array. For big jobs, make the producer lazy so there's a bounded amount of work in memory at any time.

import { once } from 'node:events';

// Page through the source with keyset pagination and process a bounded window
async function backfill() {
  let lastId = 0;
  for (;;) {
    const { rows } = await pool.query(
      'SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000',
      [lastId],
    );
    if (rows.length === 0) break;

    await mapLimit(rows, 8, (row) => processOrder(row.id));
    lastId = rows[rows.length - 1].id;
  }
}

Memory stays proportional to the page size (1,000), not the table size. Keyset pagination (WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT n) also stays fast on deep pages, unlike OFFSET. For CSV or file inputs, the same idea applies with streams: read a line, hand it to a bounded processor, and rely on backpressure instead of buffering the whole file.

Fix 6: Reduce the number of tasks (batch in SQL)

The cheapest concurrent query is the one you don't run. If each task is "update one row", you may not need N tasks at all:

// ❌ 10,000 tasks, even throttled: 10,000 round trips
await mapLimit(updates, 10, (u) => pool.query('UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2', [u.status, u.id]));

// ✅ 1 round trip per 1,000 rows
for (const batch of chunk(updates, 1000)) {
  await pool.query(
    `UPDATE orders o
        SET status = v.status
       FROM unnest($1::bigint[], $2::text[]) AS v(id, status)
      WHERE o.id = v.id`,
    [batch.map((u) => u.id), batch.map((u) => u.status)],
  );
}

Passing arrays and expanding them with unnest lets one statement handle a whole batch. The same pattern works for inserts (INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM unnest(...)), and for very large loads, COPY is faster still. Combine the two ideas: batch to reduce round trips, then throttle the batches.

Fix 7: For big or durable work, use a queue

If the job is huge, must survive restarts, needs retries, or shouldn't block your web process, concurrency control belongs in a job queue rather than in an in-process loop. For example with BullMQ:

import { Queue, Worker } from 'bullmq';

const queue = new Queue('backfill', { connection });
await queue.addBulk(ids.map((id) => ({ name: 'process-order', data: { id } })));

new Worker('backfill', async (job) => processOrder(job.data.id), {
  connection,
  concurrency: 5,                              // per-worker cap
  limiter: { max: 100, duration: 1_000 },      // optional: at most 100 jobs per second
});

You get durable state, retries with backoff, a rate limiter, and the ability to scale by adding workers. Remember that with several workers, the total concurrency is workers × concurrency, so size the sum against your database, not each worker in isolation.

Concurrency limit vs. rate limit

These are different controls, and APIs often need the second:

  • Concurrency limit: at most N operations in flight at once. Protects pools, memory, and database load.
  • Rate limit: at most N operations per time window (for example, 50 requests per second). Protects against 429s.

A concurrency cap of 10 with 20 ms calls is still ~500 requests/second, which may break a 100/s API limit. Libraries such as bottleneck support both concurrency and rate limits in one limiter. Pick based on what the downstream system actually constrains.

How to choose the number

There's no universal value, but there's a sensible way to pick one:

  1. Never exceed what the downstream can serve. For database work, stay below your pool size, and leave headroom for normal traffic, since the pool is shared. If the pool is 10 and the API needs to stay responsive, a background job might get 3 to 5.
  2. Account for every instance. instances × concurrency is the real load. Ten pods each running a 10-wide job is 100 concurrent operations.
  3. Measure. Run the job at concurrency 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and watch throughput and p95 latency. Throughput rises, flattens, then often drops as contention takes over. Choose a value at or just before the knee.
  4. Little's Law helps with intuition: concurrency ≈ throughput × latency. If each query takes 20 ms and you want 250 queries/second, you need about 5 in flight. More than that mostly adds queueing. 
for (const concurrency of [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]) {
  const start = performance.now();
  await mapLimit(sample, concurrency, (id) => processOrder(id));
  const secs = (performance.now() - start) / 1000;
  console.log(`concurrency=${concurrency}  throughput=${(sample.length / secs).toFixed(0)}/s`);
}

Error handling that doesn't leave a mess

  • Prefer Promise.allSettled when partial success is acceptable, so one failure doesn't hide the other results.
  • Add per-task timeouts (AbortSignal.timeout(ms)) so one hung task can't occupy a slot forever.
  • Retry transient errors with backoff and jitter, a bounded number of times, inside the limited task so retries also respect the concurrency cap.
  • Make tasks idempotent. Throttled jobs still get interrupted, rerun, and retried, so processing an item twice should be harmless.
  • Stop cleanly on shutdown. Have workers check a shutdown signal before taking the next item, so a deploy doesn't kill a job mid-task.

Choosing an approach

Approach Slots stay busy? Handles huge inputs? Dependency Best for
Promise.all on everything n/a (unbounded) No None Small, bounded N only
Chunked Promise.all No (waits for slowest) Yes None Simple scripts, uniform task times
p-limit / p-map Yes Moderate (p-map with iterables: yes) Yes (ESM) General-purpose throttling
Hand-rolled mapLimit Yes Moderate None No-dependency code, custom error rules
Lazy paging + limiter Yes Yes Optional Backfills over big tables
SQL batching (unnest) n/a Yes None Many small writes
Job queue Yes Yes Yes Durable, retried, scalable work

Checklist

  • ✅ Ask of every Promise.all(xs.map(...)): how big can xs get? If unbounded, throttle it
  • ✅ Keep a task's concurrency well below your pool size, leaving headroom for live traffic
  • ✅ Pass a function to the limiter, not an already-started promise
  • ✅ Use allSettled or a fail-flag so errors don't leave orphaned work running
  • ✅ Page through big sources instead of loading them whole
  • ✅ Batch small writes with unnest or COPY
  • ✅ Separate concurrency limits from rate limits
  • ✅ Measure throughput at several concurrency levels, and size for all instances combined

Key takeaways

  1. Promise.all doesn't parallelize or throttle. Tasks start the moment you create the promises, and Promise.all just waits.
  2. Unbounded fan-out causes pool starvation, database overload, rate-limit errors, and memory blowups, often while every individual query looks fast.
  3. Throttle with a sliding window: p-limit, p-map, or a small worker pool. Chunking works but wastes slots on uneven tasks.
  4. Reduce the work too. Batch in SQL, and stream or page large inputs rather than materializing them.
  5. Concurrency isn't rate limiting. Know which one your downstream needs.
  6. Pick the number by measurement, accounting for every instance and for the traffic sharing your pool.
  7. Use a real queue when work is large, long-running, or must survive restarts.

Have you been burned by an innocent-looking Promise.all? Tell the story in the comments.

Further reading: p-limit, p-map, bottleneck, and the node-postgres pooling docs.

The practical usefulness of an email account depends on several factors.

Communication Continuity

Organized Correspondence

Account Security

Legitimate Ownership
Clear ownership helps prevent access disputes and ensures that private information remains under the appropriate person's control.

Security Risks of Accounts Obtained From Unknown Sources
Obtaining an email account from an unfamiliar seller or third party can create problems that are difficult to predict.

Uncertain Ownership
The original owner may still control recovery methods or other account-related information. This can make long-term access uncertain.

Recovery Difficulties
If recovery details belong to another person, the current user may be unable to complete verification or restore access.

Privacy Concerns
