Unfamiliar Account Settings
Previous settings may include forwarding rules, filters, connected applications, or other configurations that the new user does not understand.

Unexpected Security Verification
Yahoo may request additional verification when it detects unusual activity or an unfamiliar sign-in environment.

Incomplete Account History
Information provided by a third party may not reveal every previous account change or security concern.

These risks demonstrate why account age should never be treated as a guarantee of safety or reliability.

Yahoo Mail Security Best Practices

Use a Strong, Unique Password

Enable Two-Step Verification

Keep Recovery Information Updated

description:
The threat actor known as Silent Lynx has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

The activity, observed from June 2025 through August 2026, involves four different infection chains that make use of macro-enabled documents, PS2EXE downloaders, GitHub-hosted PowerShell, and crafted WinRAR archives

title: Webhook Hub with Spring Boot: Strategy Pattern, Sub-Strategies and Collection Injection
description:
Introduction

When webhooks are received from third-party systems, technical challenges arise quickly. This article shows how to solve them with the Strategy Pattern in Spring Boot and how a second Strategy Pattern ("Sub-Strategy") represents the event level.

The code in this article comes from a real project and is reduced to the essentials. I left out configuration, error handling, the actual persistence and further details to focus on the integration of the pattern. The starting point is a production hub that receives webhooks from around 20 platforms with more than 25 million requests per month.

The starting point

The hub has a simple task: receive webhooks from third-party systems, validate and store them and, depending on the event, forward them to other systems or execute actions. The platforms differ in many ways:

  • Payload: Every platform has its own JSON format. One puts the event name in event, another in type.
  • Verification: Some sign the body, some send a token, some require a challenge response when the URL is registered.
  • Events: A platform often knows many event types (meeting.ended, recording.completed, ticket.created). Each one has different follow-up actions.
  • Follow-up actions: Some events are only stored, others trigger a download, a call to a CRM or forwarding to a data platform such as Foundry.

In addition, I had my own requirement for the architecture. It should be possible to add new platforms (strategies) and new events (sub-strategies) without changing existing code. The tests should stay simple and clear. Conversely, a strategy or sub-strategy must be removable without affecting the rest of the application.

The challenge

The obvious first approach is a controller with a switch:

switch (platformName) {
    case "zoom" -> zoomHandler.handle(body, headers);
    case "gohighlevel" -> goHighLevelHandler.handle(body, headers);
    // ... 18 more
}

This works for two platforms. With twenty platforms, it becomes a class that knows every platform and has to be changed with every modification. Within a platform, the next branch by event is added, followed by the branch by follow-up action. The result is nested conditions that are hard to understand and hard to test.

Even if every platform is in its own class, like zoomHandler above, the switch remains and still knows every platform. With the second level (event), its complexity would be very high. For this reason I decided against a switch.

The actual challenges were:

  1. Extensibility: A new platform should be a new class, not a change to existing code.
  2. Two levels of branching: First by platform, then by event within the platform.
  3. Multiple follow-up actions per event: An event can be stored, sent to a CRM and forwarded at the same time.
  4. Testability: Every platform and every follow-up action must be testable on its own.

The idea

The solution consists of two levels that use the same mechanism.

Level 1: Strategy per platform. Every platform is a strategy. The strategy stores the received raw data via a RawDataSaveService. The controller only knows an interface and a factory.

Level 2: Sub-Strategy per event. Inside the platform strategy there is a second group of strategies that react to platform and event. The sub-strategies take care of further processing: they often fetch dependent data and store it, for example in Foundry. They are not exclusive: several sub-strategies can match the same event and all of them are executed.

The connecting element: Collection Injection. Spring injects all beans of an interface type as a List<T> into the constructor. The factory therefore does not know any concrete strategy. A new class with @Component is all that is needed.

The first level: Strategies

The interface

The strategy answers two questions: "Am I responsible?" and "What do I do with the payload?".

public interface PlatformStrategyInterface {

    boolean supported(String platformName);

    void handle(String payload, HttpHeaders headers);

    ResponseEntity<String> getResponse();
}

Source: PlatformStrategyInterface

supported is the key. It replaces switch/case and moves the decision into the strategy itself.

The base class

Shared behavior moves into an abstract class. The concrete strategy only passes on its name.

public abstract class PlatformStrategyAbstract implements PlatformStrategyInterface {

    private final String platformName;

    protected PlatformStrategyAbstract(String platformName) {
        this.platformName = platformName;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean supported(String platformName) {
        return this.platformName.equals(platformName);
    }

    @Override
    public ResponseEntity<String> getResponse() {
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.OK).build();
    }
}

Source: PlatformStrategyAbstract

The concrete strategies

A platform is a small class:

@Component
public class ZoomPlatformStrategy extends PlatformStrategyAbstract {

    public static final String NAME = "zoom";

    public ZoomPlatformStrategy() {
        super(NAME);
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(String payload, HttpHeaders headers) {
        // platform-specific processing
    }
}

A new platform is another class of this form. There is no central place where it has to be registered.

The factory with Collection Injection 

@Component
public class PlatformStrategyFactory {

    private final List<PlatformStrategyInterface> strategies;

    public PlatformStrategyFactory(List<PlatformStrategyInterface> strategies) {
        this.strategies = strategies;
    }

    public PlatformStrategyInterface getPlatformStrategy(String platformName) {
        for (PlatformStrategyInterface strategy : strategies) {
            if (strategy.supported(platformName)) {
                return strategy;
            }
        }
        return null;
    }
}

Source: PlatformStrategyFactory

Spring fills strategies at startup with all beans that implement PlatformStrategyInterface. The factory does not have to be changed again.

The controller

The controller is deliberately slim. It knows neither Zoom nor any other platform:

@RestController
public class WebhookPlatformStrategyController {

    private final PlatformStrategyFactory platformStrategyFactory;

    public WebhookPlatformStrategyController(PlatformStrategyFactory platformStrategyFactory) {
        this.platformStrategyFactory = platformStrategyFactory;
    }

    @PostMapping("/{platformName:[a-z]{1,16}}")
    public ResponseEntity<String> save(
        @PathVariable String platformName,
        @RequestBody(required = false) String requestBody,
        @RequestHeader HttpHeaders headers
    ) {
        PlatformStrategyInterface strategy = platformStrategyFactory.getPlatformStrategy(platformName);

        if (strategy == null) {
            return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body(String.format("{\"error\":\"PlatformStrategy [%s] not found\"}", platformName));
        }

        try {
            strategy.handle(requestBody, headers);
        } catch (JacksonException e) {
            return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST)
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body(String.format("{\"error\":\"PlatformStrategy [%s] with JSON error\"}", platformName));
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .body(String.format("{\"error\":\"PlatformStrategy [%s] handle failed\"}", platformName));
        }

        return strategy.getResponse();
    }
}

Source: WebhookPlatformStrategyController

getResponse() is intentionally part of the strategy. Some platforms expect a specific response, for example when verifying a new webhook URL with a challenge. In this case the strategy overrides the method and the controller remains unchanged.

The second level: Sub-Strategies

Up to this point it is the classic Strategy Pattern. However, the platform strategy often has to differentiate further, namely by event. Instead of adding a switch to ZoomPlatformStrategy, the same pattern is repeated one level deeper:

public interface SubStrategyInterface {

    boolean supported(String platformName, String eventName);

    void handle(String payload);
}

Source: SubStrategyInterface

The name stays deliberately generic: Sub only says that the class sits below a platform strategy and is called by it. The platform is not part of the type name because the technique does not depend on it. Here the binding happens through supported(platformName, eventName), and the event is part of the concrete class name (ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy).

Here too, the supported(...) check would be in every class. To avoid writing it again and again, there is a base class, as on the platform level. It holds a map platform -> events and answers supported(...) for all sub-strategies in the same way:

public abstract class SubStrategyAbstract implements SubStrategyInterface {

    // platform -> events the sub-strategy is responsible for
    private final Map<String, Set<String>> supported;

    // Short form: exactly one platform and one event
    protected SubStrategyAbstract(String platformName, String eventName) {
        this.supported = Map.of(platformName, Set.of(eventName));
    }

    // Multiple platforms and/or events
    protected SubStrategyAbstract(Map<String, Set<String>> supported) {
        this.supported = supported;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean supported(String platformName, String eventName) {
        return supported.getOrDefault(platformName, Set.of()).contains(eventName);
    }
}

Source: SubStrategyAbstract

A concrete sub-strategy only passes on to the base class what it is responsible for and implements handle(...):

@Component
public class ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy extends SubStrategyAbstract {

    public static final String STRATEGY = "zoom";
    public static final String EVENT = "meeting.ended";

    public ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy() {
        super(STRATEGY, EVENT);
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(String payload) {
        // follow-up action for this event
    }
}

Source: ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy

The corresponding factory differs in one important point: it returns all matching strategies, not only the first.

@Component
public class SubStrategyFactory {

    private final List<SubStrategyInterface> strategies;

    public SubStrategyFactory(List<SubStrategyInterface> strategies) {
        this.strategies = strategies;
    }

    // returns ALL matching strategies (not just the first)
    public List<SubStrategyInterface> getAllSubStrategies(String platformName, String eventName) {
        return strategies.stream()
            .filter(strategy -> strategy.supported(platformName, eventName))
            .toList();
    }
}

Source: SubStrategyFactory

Where does the event name come from?

So that the factory finds the matching sub-strategy, the platform strategy has to read the event name from the payload. This is the actual difficulty, because every platform names it differently: Zoom sends it in event, GoHighLevel in type and for other platforms it is nested on the second or third level of the JSON.

Instead of searching the JSON manually in every strategy, each platform gets a minimal DTO that only knows the event name. A common interface makes them interchangeable:

public interface EventNameInterface {

    String getEvent();
}

Source: EventNameInterface

@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
public class ZoomRootDto implements EventNameInterface {

    @JsonProperty("event")
    private String event;

    @Override
    public String getEvent() {
        return event;
    }

    // setter
}

Source: ZoomRootDto

@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
public class GoHighLevelRootDto implements EventNameInterface {

    // GoHighLevel sends the event name in "type"
    @JsonProperty("type")
    private String event;

    @Override
    public String getEvent() {
        return event;
    }

    // setter
}

Source: GoHighLevelRootDto

Two details make this robust:

  • @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) makes Jackson ignore all other fields. The DTO stays small and new fields of the platform do not break anything.
  • @JsonProperty("type") maps the platform-specific name to the uniform getEvent(). The difference between the platforms is encapsulated in exactly one place.

The platform strategy stores and calls the sub-strategies 

@Component
public class ZoomPlatformStrategy extends PlatformStrategyAbstract {

    public static final String NAME = "zoom";

    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;
    private final SubStrategyFactory subStrategyFactory;
    private final RawDataSaveService rawDataSaveService;

    public ZoomPlatformStrategy(
            ObjectMapper objectMapper,
            SubStrategyFactory subStrategyFactory,
            RawDataSaveService rawDataSaveService) {
        super(NAME);
        this.objectMapper = objectMapper;
        this.subStrategyFactory = subStrategyFactory;
        this.rawDataSaveService = rawDataSaveService;
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(String payload, HttpHeaders headers) {
        // Read the event name from the payload
        ZoomRootDto dto = this.objectMapper.readValue(payload, ZoomRootDto.class);

        // Store raw data
        this.rawDataSaveService.save(NAME, dto.getEvent(), payload);

        // Call all sub-strategies that support platform + event
        for (SubStrategyInterface subStrategy
                : this.subStrategyFactory.getAllSubStrategies(NAME, dto.getEvent())) {
            subStrategy.handle(payload);
        }
    }
}

Source: ZoomPlatformStrategy

The GoHighLevelPlatformStrategy looks identical except for the name and the DTO. This is intended: the difference between the platforms is in supported(...) and in the DTO, not in the flow. If the pattern is this uniform in practice, it is worth checking whether the flow can be moved into the base class and the strategy only provides the DTO (Template Method).

This has a side effect that is very useful in practice: a sub-strategy can be cross-platform. It does not have to belong to one platform. The platform strategy does not know anything about it.

Example: Multiple sub-strategies for the same event

In addition to the ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy, another action should be executed for meeting.ended (and meeting.started), for example forwarding to Foundry. This is a separate class. ZoomPlatformStrategy and ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy remain unchanged. Because it covers several events, it uses the constructor with the map:

@Component
public class FoundrySubStrategy extends SubStrategyAbstract {

    // platform -> events this sub-strategy is responsible for
    private static final Map<String, Set<String>> SUPPORTED = Map.of(
        "zoom", Set.of("meeting.ended", "meeting.started")
    );

    public FoundrySubStrategy() {
        super(SUPPORTED);
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(String payload) {
        // action for this event
    }
}

Source: FoundrySubStrategy

supported(...) is data-driven instead of hard-coded: which platforms and events are covered is defined in the map. Another platform or event is an additional entry, the check logic in the base class remains the same. Unknown platforms return false via getOrDefault.

If meeting.ended is received, both sub-strategies match. getAllSubStrategies("zoom", "meeting.ended") returns both and ZoomPlatformStrategy calls each one:

ZoomPlatformStrategy.handle(payload)
   ├─ rawDataSaveService.save("zoom", "meeting.ended", payload)
   └─ getAllSubStrategies("zoom", "meeting.ended")
        ├─► ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy.handle(payload)
        └─► FoundrySubStrategy.handle(payload)

That there is no order and a sub-strategy must not influence another is the prerequisite for this (see Pitfalls).

What worked well

New platforms are additive changes. A class is added. No existing class is changed, which reduces the risk of regressions.

Follow-up actions are decoupled. Storing, forwarding to the CRM, downloading a file: each of these is its own sub-strategy. They can be tested individually, added and removed.

Tests are small. A strategy can be instantiated without a Spring context:

class ZoomMeetingEndedStrategyTest {

    private final ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy strategy = new ZoomMeetingEndedSubStrategy();

    @Test
    void test_supported() {
        assertTrue(this.strategy.supported("zoom", "meeting.ended"));
        assertFalse(this.strategy.supported("zoom", "meeting.started"));
        assertFalse(this.strategy.supported("gohighlevel", "meeting.ended"));
    }

    // Further tests
}

The platform strategy is tested with a mocked SubStrategyFactory and a mocked RawDataSaveService. This also covers reading the event name, including the platform-specific property, and storing the raw data:

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class ZoomPlatformStrategyTest {

    @Mock
    private SubStrategyFactory subStrategyFactoryMock;

    @Mock
    private RawDataSaveService rawDataSaveServiceMock;

    @Mock
    private SubStrategyInterface subStrategy1;

    @Mock
    private SubStrategyInterface subStrategy2;

    private ZoomPlatformStrategy strategy;

    @BeforeEach
    void beforeEach() {
        this.strategy = new ZoomPlatformStrategy(new ObjectMapper(), this.subStrategyFactoryMock, this.rawDataSaveServiceMock);
    }

    @Test
    void test_handle_calls_all_sub_strategies() {
        when(this.subStrategyFactoryMock.getAllSubStrategies("zoom", "meeting.ended"))
            .thenReturn(List.of(this.subStrategy1, this.subStrategy2));

        String payload = "{\"event\":\"meeting.ended\",\"payload\":{}}";

        this.strategy.handle(payload, new HttpHeaders());

        verify(this.subStrategy1, times(1)).handle(payload);
        verify(this.subStrategy2, times(1)).handle(payload);
    }

    @Test
    void test_handle_stores_raw_data() {
        when(this.subStrategyFactoryMock.getAllSubStrategies("zoom", "meeting.ended")).thenReturn(List.of());

        String payload = "{\"event\":\"meeting.ended\",\"payload\":{}}";

        this.strategy.handle(payload, new HttpHeaders());

        verify(this.rawDataSaveServiceMock, times(1)).save("zoom", "meeting.ended", payload);
    }
}

The factories are tested with a manually created list:

class PlatformStrategyFactoryTest {

    private PlatformStrategyFactory strategyFactory;

    @BeforeEach
    void beforeEach() {
        this.strategyFactory = new PlatformStrategyFactory(List.of(new TestStrategyDummy()));
    }

    @Test
    void test_getPlatformStrategy() {
        assertInstanceOf(TestStrategyDummy.class, this.strategyFactory.getPlatformStrategy("foobar"));
    }

    @Test
    void test_getPlatformStrategy_not_found() {
        assertNull(this.strategyFactory.getPlatformStrategy("dummy"));
    }
}

For the WebhookPlatformStrategyControllerTest a @WebMvcTest with a mocked factory is sufficient. It only tests the HTTP behavior (200, 400, 404, 500) and whether the factory is called.

The pitfalls

The pattern is simple, but in production there were a few things that are good to know in advance.

The base class becomes a god object

In practice, more and more moved into PlatformStrategyAbstract: verification, persistence, error handling, parsing, several overloaded handle methods. As a result, concrete strategies got five or six constructor parameters that they only pass through.

Solution: Keep the base class small (name and supported). Cross-cutting concerns like verification and persistence belong in their own services or interfaces. Composition is better than inheritance here.

Order is not guaranteed

The List<T> from Collection Injection has no defined order. This is not a problem as long as strategies are independent. As soon as a sub-strategy needs the result of another, it becomes a bug.

Solution: Keep strategies independent. If an order is required, use @Order or Ordered and document it.

Errors in a sub-strategy

If three sub-strategies run one after another and the second throws an exception, the question is: Does the third still run? If the webhook is answered with a 500 and repeated by the sender, the first and third run twice.

Solution: Decide deliberately. Either each sub-strategy catches and logs its own errors, or the payload is persisted first and the follow-up actions run asynchronously via a queue with retry. In production, the latter has partly proven itself: store first, then process.

When the pattern is worthwhile, and when not

For two platforms, a switch is simpler and more straightforward. The pattern is worthwhile when

  • the number of variants grows and new variants are added regularly,
  • variants have different dependencies (their own HTTP client, their own repositories),
  • several teams or people work on different variants,
  • every variant should be testable on its own.

It is less worthwhile when there are two or three fixed variants that never change. In this case an enum map or a switch is easier to read.

Conclusion

  • Strategy Pattern replaces the central switch: every platform decides for itself whether it is responsible (supported).
  • Collection Injection (List<PlatformStrategyInterface>) makes the factory immutable. New strategies register themselves with @Component.
  • Sub-Strategies repeat the pattern on the event level. Multiple matches are allowed there and every match is an independent follow-up action.
  • The pitfalls are not in the pattern itself, but around it: a bloated base class, unclear order and error handling with multiple sub-strategies.

Full example on GitHub

https://github.com/alaugks/article-webhook-hub-spring-strategy-pattern

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: Every Free-Tier Request Returned 200. My Acceptance Probes Still Failed.
description:
Two days ago I moved a small batch job onto a free model endpoint and a free server box, and then I spent most of the next 48 hours asking a much less flattering question than "does it answer?" The question I actually cared about was this: does it answer the same way twice, with the model I asked for, on a box that still has my evidence afterwards? A 200 OK only tells you that a socket accepted bytes, and honestly, that is all it tells you.

Why a status code is not an acceptance test

Most of us treat the first successful response as the end of the integration work, because the integration did work — once, on our laptop, with our one prompt. But a free endpoint is a shared, moving target, and the failures that actually hurt are the quiet ones: a different model behind the same alias, a cached answer served as fresh, a stream that got cut in half and still exited cleanly. None of those raise an exception you can catch.

So instead of a checklist that passes quietly, I wrote four probes that fail loudly.

The setup I kept deliberately small

I did not port a real product onto the free tier. I kept the job tiny on purpose, because the point of the 48 hours was to measure the tier, not to ship anything on it. MonkeyCode offers access to a set of free models and a free server option, and that availability is what the operator told me; the specific models and limits you see in your own account may differ from mine, so check the current list before you plan around it.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

I ran the probe harness on that free server rather than on my laptop, for one boring reason: my laptop sleeps, and a measurement that stops when a lid closes is not a measurement. Everything below is a workflow you can reproduce against any endpoint that speaks an OpenAI-compatible chat shape — just adjust the payload to whatever your provider documents.

The artifact: four probes in one file

The harness does one thing per probe and appends a JSON line, so a failed run leaves a trail instead of a mystery. It uses only the standard library, which means you can drop it on a fresh box without a dependency install.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Free-tier endpoint acceptance probes.
Appends one JSON line per probe to PROBE_OUT.
Assumes an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint; adjust if yours differs.
"""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

BASE = os.environ['ENDPOINT_BASE'].rstrip('/')
KEY = os.environ['ENDPOINT_KEY']
MODEL = os.environ['ENDPOINT_MODEL']
OUT = os.environ.get('PROBE_OUT', 'probe_report.jsonl')


def post(payload, timeout=60):
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f'{BASE}/chat/completions',
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
        headers={'Content-Type': 'application/json',
                 'Authorization': f'Bearer {KEY}'},
    )
    started = time.monotonic()
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as resp:
            raw, status = resp.read().decode(), resp.status
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as exc:
        raw, status = exc.read().decode(), exc.code
    except Exception as exc:  # transport failures are data too
        raw, status = json.dumps({'transport_error': repr(exc)}), 0
    return {
        'status': status,
        'elapsed_ms': round((time.monotonic() - started) * 1000),
        'body_sha256': hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest(),
        'raw': raw[:2000],
    }


def ask(prompt, nonce, timeout=60):
    return post({
        'model': MODEL,
        'temperature': 0,
        'messages': [
            {'role': 'system',
             'content': 'Echo the nonce verbatim first, then answer in one sentence.'},
            {'role': 'user', 'content': f'nonce={nonce}\n{prompt}'},
        ],
    }, timeout)


def body_text(raw):
    try:
        return json.loads(raw)['choices'][0]['message']['content']
    except Exception:
        return ''


def answer_of(raw):
    text = body_text(raw)
    return '\n'.join(ln for ln in text.splitlines() if 'nonce=' not in ln).strip()


def reported_model(raw):
    try:
        return json.loads(raw).get('model', '')
    except Exception:
        return ''


def record(probe, verdict, **evidence):
    line = {'probe': probe, 'verdict': verdict, 'ts': round(time.time(), 3)}
    line.update(evidence)
    with open(OUT, 'a', encoding='utf-8') as handle:
        handle.write(json.dumps(line, sort_keys=True) + '\n')
    print(json.dumps(line, sort_keys=True))

Then the probes themselves, each one short enough to read in a code review.

Probe 1 — is the alias pointing where you think?

A fresh nonce goes into the prompt, and I check that it comes back in the answer. If it does not, I am probably reading a cached or canned response rather than a live call. I also log the model field the response reports, next to the alias I requested, because those two strings are the whole basis of every later assumption I make.

def probe_identity():
    nonce = os.urandom(4).hex()
    result = ask('Name the model you are.', nonce)
    text = body_text(result['raw'])
    record('identity',
           'pass' if result['status'] == 200 and nonce in text else 'fail',
           status=result['status'],
           requested=MODEL,
           reported=reported_model(result['raw']),
           nonce_echoed=nonce in text)

Probe 2 — the same prompt, twice, compared

I send one deterministic prompt twice with different nonces and compare the answers after stripping the nonce line. I am not testing whether the model is "correct" here; I am testing whether my pipeline can expect a stable answer at all. If two runs diverge on a question this small, every diff-based review I build on top of it is noise.

def probe_repeatability():
    prompt = 'State the number of days in a leap year, in five words or fewer.'
    first, second = ask(prompt, 'a' * 8), ask(prompt, 'b' * 8)
    a, b = answer_of(first['raw']), answer_of(second['raw'])
    record('repeatability', 'pass' if a and a == b else 'review',
           first_sha256=first['body_sha256'],
           second_sha256=second['body_sha256'])

Probe 3 — does the box still have my report after a restart?

This is the part people skip, and it is the part that decides whether a free server is usable for scheduled work. Write the report, hash it, restart the box through whatever control your provider gives you, then verify the hash again.

python probe_endpoint.py
sha256sum probe_report.jsonl | tee report.hash
# restart the free server here
sha256sum -c report.hash

If it prints OK, my evidence survived. If it prints No such file or directory, then my evidence lives exactly as long as the process did — which is a perfectly good answer as long as I learned it before the job ran unattended, and not after.

Probe 4 — the stream that ends early

I set a ten-second client timeout on a deliberately unbounded request and record whether the call came back as a clean completion or as something I would have to treat as partial. This is the probe that changed my mind about silent truncation being theoretical: a cut stream can look like a short, confident answer.

def probe_timeout():
    result = ask('Count upwards until told to stop.', os.urandom(4).hex(), timeout=10)
    record('timeout', 'pass' if result['status'] == 200 else 'review',
           status=result['status'], elapsed_ms=result['elapsed_ms'])


if __name__ == '__main__':
    probe_identity()
    probe_repeatability()
    probe_timeout()

What broke during the 48 hours

Failures, in the order I hit them, and none of them were exotic:

  1. A verification script that verified nothing. My first repeatability comparison mutated the prompt list in place between the two calls, so I was comparing two different questions and calling the difference "nondeterminism". The probe was wrong, not the endpoint.
  2. Evidence written outside the directory I downloaded. The report existed, the download missed it, and I almost concluded that the box had wiped my file. Path hygiene is part of the experiment.
  3. A pass verdict from a response I never parsed. I marked a run as passing because the HTTP status was 200, while the body was an error-shaped payload. Status checks belong next to body checks, not instead of them.
  4. A restart I did not perform. I scheduled the verification step and then forgot to actually restart anything, which produced a green result that proved nothing except my own timing.

None of those are endpoint bugs. All of them are the reason I now keep the probe output as a file that a second person can read without me in the room.

The decision table I actually use

Workload After a probe run, acceptable on a free tier? Reasoning
Drafting commit messages, renaming variables, explaining a stack trace Yes, with a human reading the output Failures are small, visible, and cheap to redo
CI steps that must produce the same artifact twice Only with the probe report stored next to the build An alias resolving differently is invisible in logs
A scheduled batch job with nobody watching Not until it checks the reported model and alerts A silent model change is a silent behavior change
Anything containing customer data, secrets, or regulated content No I cannot audit retention or isolation on infrastructure I do not control
Deadline work that needs predictable capacity No Shared free capacity is not a capacity plan

Who should not use this approach

If you need an availability guarantee, a data-processing agreement, or a per-request billing model you can forecast, this workflow will not give you any of those, and a probe report will not substitute for them. If you will not read a JSONL file before trusting a number, the harness just adds a step. And if your prompts contain anything you would not paste into a public issue, do not send them to a tier you have not audited — probe the endpoint with throwaway text instead.

What I would repeat

I would repeat the ordering more than the code: measure the endpoint before writing the feature, on the machine that will run the job, with the verdict written to disk. I would also repeat the four-probe split, because each probe maps to exactly one decision — trust the response, expect stable output, expect persistence, expect clean endings. And I would repeat the small scope: two days of probing a batch job was enough to change how I schedule it.

The one habit worth copying, whether or not you use MonkeyCode at all, is keeping a probe report in the repository beside the code that calls the endpoint. That single file is the difference between "the free tier worked when I tried it" and a claim you can re-check next month.

title: Myth FAQ: Your Free Dev Box Is Not a Staging Environment
description:
You ran the test suite on a free box. Everything passed. Now you want to ship.

Slow down. A green run proves exactly one thing. Your tests exited zero inside that environment.

Here are five environment myths I keep seeing in review comments. Each one has a cheap probe you can rerun.

Myth 1: "It ran here, so it runs in production"

This is the most expensive myth in the pile. People compare a machine to a machine. They should compare a contract to a contract.

Your free box and your production host may share a kernel family. They do not share a support contract. Different libc, different CPU flags, different egress rules.

Probe the runtime fingerprint first:

uname -srm
ldd --version 2>/dev/null | head -n1
python3 -c "import platform; print(platform.libc_ver(), platform.machine())"

Corrected model: a free box is a smoke environment. It is not a fidelity environment.

Myth 2: "A disk is a disk"

Does your data survive a restart? Have you actually tested that, or just assumed it?

The free server option is great for ephemeral work. That is precisely why you should treat its filesystem as cache.

Probe it in two steps:

echo "marker-$(date +%s)" > /tmp/probe-marker
cat /tmp/probe-marker
# now restart the box, then run:
cat /tmp/probe-marker || echo "GONE: treat this path as ephemeral"

Corrected model: any state you cannot rebuild from git is a liability, not an asset.

Myth 3: "My job has the whole machine"

Runtimes report host CPU counts. Cgroup limits usually say otherwise. Your "4 workers" plan becomes 4 workers fighting over 1 CPU.

Probe the limits before you tune anything:

echo "visible CPUs: $(nproc)"
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max 2>/dev/null || true
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max 2>/dev/null || true

Corrected model: size concurrency from the cgroup quota, never from nproc. Visible cores are a rumor. The quota is the contract.

Myth 4: "A free model is a drop-in for my paid model"

This one quietly breaks agent workflows. Prompt behaviour is not portable by default. Tool-call formats, stop sequences, and JSON reliability all drift between models.

Do not trust a leaderboard written by a stranger. Build a ten-prompt eval on your own prompts instead.

Here is the plan, not a benchmark result:

  1. Pull 10 real prompts from your own logs.
  2. Define a pass rule per prompt: exact match, schema-valid, or human-reviewed.
  3. Run the same prompts against each candidate.
  4. Record pass rate and failure class. Never record vibes.

I have not published numbers for this harness, and you should be suspicious of any I did. Your prompts are the only valid test set you own.

Corrected model: model choice is a per-task decision, measured on your data.

Myth 5: "The clock is the clock"

Token expiry, JWT validation, TTL caches, and log ordering all depend on time. A drifting clock becomes a mystery 401 on a Friday.

Probe local time against a reference:

date -u +%FT%TZ
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i '^date:' || true

Corrected model: log timestamps are local evidence, not global truth. Stamp everything in UTC and compare before you blame auth.

The artifact: one probe script, five verdicts

Below is the probe I would run before trusting a free box. Treat it as illustrative. I have not executed it as a controlled benchmark, so read its output as a signal, not as proof.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# fidelity-probe.sh - print JSON-ish facts about the box you are on
set -uo pipefail

j() { printf '  "%s": "%s",\n' "$1" "$2"; }

echo "{"
j "kernel"      "$(uname -sr)"
j "arch"        "$(uname -m)"
j "libc"        "$(ldd --version 2>/dev/null | head -n1)"
j "cpu_visible" "$(nproc)"
j "cpu_quota"   "$(cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"
j "mem_limit"   "$(cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"
j "clock_utc"   "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)"
j "egress_dns"  "$(getent hosts example.com >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo ok || echo blocked)"
j "disk_free"   "$(df -h / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}')"
j "tmp_marker"  "$(cat /tmp/probe-marker 2>/dev/null || echo none)"
echo "}"

Then map each fact to a verdict. A table beats an argument every time:

Probe result Claim it invalidates Safe use of the box
libc differs from prod "same runtime" smoke tests
cpu_quota shows 1 CPU concurrency tuning correctness, not throughput
mem_limit under 2 GB build-time memory claims unit and syntax tests
egress_dns blocked integration tests offline test runs
tmp_marker gone after restart persistence claims cache-only workloads

Five probes cost ten minutes. That is cheaper than one bad incident review.

While you are there, ask three uncomfortable questions. What did this suite never touch? Which assumption breaks on a cold start? Which failure looks identical to success?

Where MonkeyCode fits in this loop

I use MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option for the boring half of this loop. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The free server runs the probe next to the code. The free model access handles triage on the JSON output. I paste the probe result and ask one narrow question: which of these facts invalidate a throughput claim? Then I read the answer and check it myself. The model drafts the verdict table. I still own the verdict.

That split is the whole point. Generate with a free model. Verify with a probe you can rerun.

If you want to test the same loop, start with the script above on whatever box you are renting this month.

Limitations and who should skip this

Be honest about the ceiling of this workflow.

  • It proves environment facts. It does not prove application correctness.
  • Probe output is a snapshot and goes stale when the platform changes.
  • A blocked egress check can be a false negative on some hosts.
  • Free capacity suits smoke tests and triage. It is not a load-test rig.

Skip this if you ship regulated workloads that need signed environment attestation. Skip it if you need hard latency numbers, because that requires a real bench harness on fixed hardware. Skip it if someone already owns environment parity for your team.

The habit worth keeping

Before you trust a green run, ask what that run could not see.

That question is free. It is also the difference between a demo and a decision.

title: Warm, Ordered, Dirty: Replay an Agent Patch's Test Suite Cold Before You Trust the Green
description:
A green suite is evidence about one process, not about the diff. Agent patches tend to pass in whatever environment the agent last left behind: warmed caches, leftover sqlite files, a module that happened to be imported in a convenient order. The cheap counter-move is to replay the same patch in a clean sandbox, with caches off and test order shuffled, K times, and to read a per-node status matrix instead of the final exit code.

This is not a correctness check. It is an honesty check on the environment. A patch that survives it has earned a weaker but real claim: the green was not produced by residue.

1. Three residue classes that manufacture warm greens

Process and cache residue. Pytest writes .pytest_cache/lastfailed, which --lf and --ff consult; CPython writes __pycache__. An agent that reruns on failure can inherit failure position from the previous attempt. Disable the cache provider and bytecode writing for the replay:

python -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python -m pytest -q

Filesystem residue. Golden files, *.sqlite, uploaded fixtures, and tmp/ directories from attempt 4 satisfy assertions in attempt 5. The only reliable detector is a fresh directory per run plus a before/after file listing (Section 2, Step 4).

Import and collection residue. An untracked conftest.py, sitecustomize.py, pytest.ini, or *.pth the agent created can make an import resolve or a collection hook fire. git status --porcelain must be part of your patch freeze, or the patch you test is not the patch you merge.

2. Build a cold sandbox from the diff

Four steps, all reproducible.

Step 1 — freeze the patch as a diff, including new files. Untracked files are invisible to git diff; git add -N (intent to add) makes them appear without staging content. It is reversible with git reset.

cd "$REPO"
git add -N .
git diff HEAD > /tmp/agent.patch
sha256sum /tmp/agent.patch | cut -c1-12

Step 2 — export HEAD and apply the patch, with no untracked residue and no build artifacts.

SANDBOX=$(mktemp -d)
git archive HEAD | tar -x -C "$SANDBOX"
patch -d "$SANDBOX" -p1 --batch < /tmp/agent.patch

Step 3 — run K times with a closed environment and a shuffled order. pytest-randomly gives you a seeded shuffle via --randomly-seed; if you do not want another plugin in the loop, collect the node IDs once and shuffle them yourself into an args file.

K=${K:-5}
mkdir -p "$SANDBOX/runs"
for i in $(seq 1 "$K"); do
  HOME="$SANDBOX/home-$i" TMPDIR="$SANDBOX/tmp-$i" \
  PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
  python -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q -rA \
    --randomly-seed="$i" 2>&1 | tee "$SANDBOX/runs/run-$i.log"
  echo "exit=$?" >> "$SANDBOX/runs/run-$i.log"
done

Plugin-free variant, which also proves that collection itself is order-independent:

python -m pytest --collect-only -q | grep '::' > "$SANDBOX/nodes.txt"
for i in $(seq 1 "$K"); do
  shuf -n "$(wc -l < "$SANDBOX/nodes.txt")" "$SANDBOX/nodes.txt" > "$SANDBOX/nodes-$i.txt"
  xargs -a "$SANDBOX/nodes-$i.txt" python -m pytest -q -rA \
    2>&1 | tee "$SANDBOX/runs/nodes-$i.log"
done

Step 4 — record what the run wrote. A marker file plus -newer gives you the residue list per run.

touch "$SANDBOX/.replay-start"
# ... run the suite ...
find "$SANDBOX" -newer "$SANDBOX/.replay-start" -type f \
  | sed "s|$SANDBOX/||" | grep -v '^runs/' | sort > "$SANDBOX/runs/wrote-$i.txt"

3. Read the matrix, not the exit code

-rA prints one status line per test, which is enough to build a node-by-run matrix. Roughly forty lines of Python:

import collections, glob, json, re

PAT = re.compile(r"^(PASSED|FAILED|ERROR|SKIPPED|XFAIL|XPASS)\s+(\S+)")
matrix = collections.defaultdict(dict)
counts = {}

for path in sorted(glob.glob("runs/*.log")):
    run = re.search(r"run-(\d+)\.log$", path).group(1)
    seen = 0
    for line in open(path):
        m = PAT.match(line)
        if m:
            matrix[m.group(2)][run] = m.group(1)
            seen += 1
    counts[run] = seen

print("collected per run:", json.dumps(counts, sort_keys=True))
for node, runs in sorted(matrix.items()):
    if len(set(runs.values())) > 1:
        print("UNSTABLE", node, json.dumps(runs, sort_keys=True))

Three signatures matter. A node that alternates PASSED/FAILED across seeds is order coupling. A node missing from some runs was never collected, which points at collection-level state. A node that fails in every cold run, when the agent reported green, points at cache residue rather than at your code.

4. From matrix to verdict

Cold replay outcome Reading Action
All runs green, identical collected count, no files outside TMPDIR Patch is order- and residue-independent for this suite Eligible for review, not proof of correctness
One node flips in exactly one of five runs, not reproducible under a pinned seed Flake-class Quarantine with an expiry (Section 5)
One node flips in two or more seeds, or a specific seed reproduces it Order coupling, not flake Block; require isolation through fixtures
Collected count differs between runs Collection side effects in conftest or imports Block; collection must be pure
Files written outside HOME/TMPDIR Hidden state inside the worktree Block; route writes through tmp_path

5. Keep the quarantine honest

The quarantine list is the easiest place to hide a real defect behind the word "flaky". Make it a machine-read file with an expiry and an evidence pointer, and hash the whole file into the verdict record so entries cannot be appended after the replay:

{
  "nodeid": "tests/test_cache.py::test_eviction_order",
  "class": "flake",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-14",
  "evidence": "runs/run-3.log"
}

sha256sum flakefreeze.json >> "$SANDBOX/runs/verdict.txt"

Two rules keep this from rotting. Only a flake-class exit may enter the file; an order-coupling verdict has no path into it. And an entry that reaches expires_at without a new cold replay is treated as a failing test on the next run, because the default outcome of an unreviewed freeze must be failure.

6. Where the free compute fits

The replay loop is K independent suite runs plus one log parser. Every run needs its own sandbox anyway, so the work is trivially parallel and does not want your main CI runner's disk.

That is the gap MonkeyCode's free server option fits into for this workflow: a separate host to run shuffled replays without spending K times your CI minutes, while its free model access covers the tedious part of Section 3 — drafting the status-line parser and the residue classifier. Treat any generated parser as a proposal. It reads build logs and has no way to know whether your -rA output matches the format it assumed, so hand-check one run before you trust the matrix.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The availability claims above (free model access, a free server option) are operator-supplied; I have deliberately not stated quotas, hardware, model names, or durations, because I have no verified numbers for them. Check the current terms before you build a schedule around either.

7. Limitations and who should not use this

Cost scales linearly. K cold replays of a twenty-minute suite is a hundred minutes, and the sandbox export plus patch application adds per-run overhead. Replay the full suite only when the patch touches broad surface; otherwise scope the node list to what the diff can plausibly reach.

Shuffling is a sampler, not a proof. It finds order coupling that a random permutation happens to trigger. Pairwise dependencies between two specific tests can survive every seed you try.

External state is untouched. A shared staging database, a live API, a clock, or a network-dependent fixture is not reset by a fresh sandbox. Cold replay helps only where the state lives in the worktree, the process, or the interpreter cache.

Skip this approach if your suite has legitimate serial ordering with no markers to express it, if you cannot reconstruct the patch as a diff because the agent committed straight to a branch, or if the suite is slow enough that nobody will ever run it K times. A gate that is too expensive to run is a gate that will be switched off within a month.

If you run the loop once, keep the first log where a cold run disagrees with the agent's warm run. That disagreement — not the green — is the artifact worth keeping.

title: The Hidden Cost of Unoptimized REST API Payloads in Node.js
description:
Most REST API performance issues in Node.js apps don’t happen because of heavy queries.

They happen because we send the entire database model down the wire when the client only needs two fields.

Here is what usually happens:
• Database returns 50 columns with nested relations.
• Mongoose or TypeORM serializes the whole object graph.
• JSON.stringify blocks the Node.js event loop for 40ms.
• Network bandwidth gets wasted on metadata the client discards.

Fixing this isn't about rewriting in Rust or upgrading your AWS instance.

It’s about intentional API design:

  1. Project your queries strictly at the SQL/ORM level using DTOs or explicit selects.
  2. Apply pagination limits by default — never trust SELECT *.
  3. Profile your JSON serialization overhead using clinic.js or built-in node --prof.

Fast APIs are built by moving less data, not just writing faster algorithms.

What’s the largest JSON payload you've ever had to debug in production? Let's discuss in the comments.
