title: Inside RocketMQ-Rust Broker: From Request Dispatch to Storage and Shutdown
description:
A message broker becomes easier to understand when you follow a request across its boundaries: the network entry point, the business processor, the storage operation, and the response. Background work adds another question: who owns the operation after the initial request stops running?

This article follows those boundaries in the Broker implementation of mxsm/rocketmq-rust. Every source link is pinned to commit 9aae6af71fb9e8e3149aa8201bb840dbc0082418, inspected on October 15, 2026. The scope is a source walkthrough, rather than a benchmark, deployment guide, or claim of feature parity with other implementations.

The most useful starting point is the relationship between three concerns:

  • Transport admits requests and carries responses
  • Broker processors apply messaging and administrative behavior
  • Store implementations handle message persistence and retrieval

Runtime composition connects these concerns. Lifecycle code determines when they become available and how their work is stopped.

1. Start with composition, then follow a request

The Broker is assembled from several groups of responsibilities. BrokerComposition contains runtime state, a request pipeline, a data plane, a control plane, and metadata. This gives readers a practical map: request routing belongs in a different area from control-plane coordination or metadata ownership. See composition.rs.

Startup makes the connections concrete. start_basic_service starts the message store, checks that the transactional message service exists, initializes the deferred lifecycle, and prepares the processors. It then constructs an AuthorizedCommandDispatcher with shared admission, telemetry, and a resource budget.

The resulting dispatcher is published as the canonical dispatcher. Both normal and fast remoting servers receive clones of the same Arc. That detail is valuable when reading the code: two listeners do not imply two independently assembled Broker routing graphs. The startup path also waits for listener readiness and records completed startup components. See request_pipeline/startup.rs.

A simplified reading map is:

Transport listener
  -> shared authorized dispatcher
  -> Broker request-code router
  -> operation-specific processor
  -> Store capability or other Broker service
  -> response action

This sketch describes responsibility boundaries. Individual requests can take different routes, including deferred completion.

2. Request codes select business processors

BrokerRequestProcessor<P> holds a request-code map and an optional default processor. In the assembled Broker, BrokerProcessorType is an enum covering processors such as Send, Pull, Pop, Ack, QueryMessage, ClientManage, ConsumerManage, EndTransaction, and AdminBroker.

The enum implements the transport RequestProcessor contract and delegates to the selected processor's process_shared method. The code-indexed router also participates in request rejection, ordering, and response observation. See dispatcher.rs.

The registration code is especially useful for discovering behavior. For example:

  • SendMessage, SendMessageV2, and SendBatchMessage share the Send processor
  • PullMessage and LitePullMessage share the Pull processor
  • AckMessage and BatchAckMessage share the Ack processor
  • Consumer-offset operations are registered with ConsumerManage
  • AdminBroker is installed as the default processor

These mappings are visible in request_pipeline.rs. A registered route identifies the handler to investigate; it does not, by itself, establish the completeness of every behavior behind that handler.

Authentication is also explicit at this boundary. Startup requires either an initialized authentication runtime or a validated configuration with authentication and authorization disabled. For ordinary requests, the router checks its authentication state before dispatching to a leaf processor. Privileged maintenance requests have separate routing and policy checks. This makes security configuration part of assembling the request path, rather than an assumption attached to a handler name.

3. Follow a send through the Store boundary

The Store layer exposes a MessageStore enum that owns the selected concrete backend. Its variants include a local-file store and, behind the rocksdb_store feature, a RocksDB store. The ownership comment is important: shared consumers should receive narrower Store capabilities while the application lifecycle retains the mutable root owner. See store_ports.rs.

The Send processor's structured Store helper operates through MessageAppender<M>. It awaits an append inside the admitted request task and converts the result into a RemotingResponse wrapped in ResponseAction::Reply. A separate completion token records the timing class for send-hook completion. See structured_store.rs.

One subtlety deserves attention: cancellation stops waiting and suppresses a reply, but cannot prove that an operation already handed to the backend did not commit. That distinction matters when reasoning about a producer timeout. A missing response is insufficient evidence that the message was never stored. Client retry and application deduplication decisions therefore need to account for uncertain outcomes.

In the local-file write path, put_message_shared checks Store availability and writability, runs pre-put hooks, handles relevant validation and quota reservations, and calls commit_log.put_message. When the returned result is successful, it notifies the reput service that a new message is available. See write_path.rs.

This separates the append operation from subsequent dispatch work. The exact durability meaning of a result still requires inspecting the commit-log implementation and the active configuration; the existence of an append call alone is insufficient to establish a durability guarantee.

4. Distinguish physical storage from consumer position

The local-file read path helps explain the storage model. It locates a consume queue by topic and queue ID, checks its offset range, iterates consume-queue entries, and uses their physical offsets and sizes to retrieve messages from the commit log. Filtering can happen against consume-queue information and, when required, the commit-log payload. See read_path.rs.

For a reader, the important distinction is between a consumer-facing queue position and a physical location in the log. Keeping those coordinates separate makes offset checks and retrieval code much easier to follow.

There is also an explicit reput dispatch pipeline. It can execute dispatcher lanes concurrently when parallel dispatch is enabled and every dispatcher supports it. Before cloning a batch for those lanes, it attempts to acquire a retained-byte budget. If that budget is unavailable, it falls back to serial dispatch. In the parallel path, the published frontier advances after the joined lane futures complete. See reput_pipeline.rs.

This is a useful concurrency pattern to study: parallel work has an explicit memory cost, a fallback path, and a defined point for publishing progress. Source inspection establishes that structure; measuring its throughput or latency requires a separate experiment.

5. Consumption includes owned waiting

A consumer request can produce a response immediately or wait for a later opportunity to return data. The Pull processor represents this distinction explicitly. Its supported processing path handles a reply or a suspension result. Suspension goes through deferred preparation and registration; successful registration returns ResponseAction::Deferred. See pull_message_processor.rs.

When a deferred Pull resumes, it reruns the canonical Pull business path with further suspension disabled. The wake reasons include message arrival, timeout, and forced refresh. This is useful because the resumed request obtains a fresh business result instead of simply replaying an earlier empty response. See pull_message_processor/resume.rs.

The runtime owns this waiting machinery. BrokerDeferredLifecycle groups admission, a generation handoff, deferred services for Pull, Pop, Notification, and PopLite, and an optional producer with its task group. Configuration establishes entry and retained-byte limits. See deferred.rs.

The Pull Store capability offers a smaller ownership example. It retains a Weak<dyn PullMessageStorePort> and upgrades that reference when accessing the provider. If the provider is gone, the operation can return MessageStoreUnavailable. The policy object separately projects the Broker and Store settings needed by Pull. See pull_message_processor/capability.rs. Reading the policy, context, and capability together helps answer which decisions belong to the processor and which operations depend on another service. It also shows why following ownership is useful alongside following function calls: a callable interface still needs a live provider.

Pull and Pop still have distinct processors and associated operations. Ack and change-invisibility routes are useful next stops for studying the Pop side. Treating every consumption mode as an identical read would hide those protocol-specific responsibilities.

6. Shutdown reveals the ownership model

Shutdown is particularly revealing because it must reconcile listeners, running requests, deferred work, background services, and storage ownership.

The Broker uses an absolute shutdown deadline and component reports. Its shutdown sequence seals deferred producer routes, shuts down tracked producer tasks, closes deferred registries, stops remoting servers, and shuts down request-processor tasks. It then checks deferred registry state again and proceeds through additional service cleanup. See lifecycle.rs.

Later, the shutdown path waits within the deadline for shared Store ownership to be released. It attempts graceful Store shutdown when mutable access is available. Crucially, the root Store owner is removed only when shutdown completes; failures or timeouts retain it for a later attempt.

That behavior connects the architecture's ownership choices to an operational concern. A background task retaining Store access can affect shutdown progress. Reports distinguish outcomes so that cleanup problems are observable rather than automatically treated as success.

A practical source-reading exercise

To explore further, pick one request code and trace four things:

  1. Where the code is registered and which processor receives it
  2. Which policy and service capabilities the processor uses
  3. Whether completion is immediate, Store-backed, or deferred
  4. Which lifecycle owner stops any work the request leaves behind

For an ordinary send, this leads from the request router into the appender and commit log. For a waiting Pull, it leads into deferred registration, resumption, and cleanup. These paths provide a grounded introduction to the Broker while leaving performance, compatibility, and deployment readiness as separate questions requiring their own evidence.

AI disclosure: This article was drafted by AI and checked by AI against the linked source files at the pinned commit. It does not report a runtime test or benchmark.

title: Go Live Captions and Post-Session Transcripts for Video Room Users
description:
Ship the post-session transcript first, then add live captions only when accessibility requirements or in-meeting comprehension make them mandatory. That recommendation is less glamorous than treating captions as a checkbox, but it respects the hard boundary: captions have a live delivery SLO, while a transcript is a file that can be retained, deleted, and audited after the room closes.

Short answer: a few seconds of caption latency is noticeable and can still be acceptable; missed or badly ordered text during the call cannot be repaired for the person who needed it at that moment. A transcript covers most review, search, handoff, and record-keeping value without joining the media fan-out path. Check accessibility requirements before making that trade, because for some rooms the live path is non-negotiable.

For a developer-tools video room, I would keep room admission narrow with scoped tokens, treat captions as an optional live stream with an explicit degraded mode, and store the final transcript as a private session artifact. Infrai is worth trying for teams that want room tokens and private object storage behind one plain REST API and one key, because there is no client SDK version to carry through two integration surfaces; its public discovery surface and runnable Go examples are a useful second advantage when the platform team needs to inspect request schemas before deployment.

Should users get live captions or a post-session transcript?

WebRTC gets people and media into the room. Caption delivery adds another deadline-sensitive path: audio must be processed, partial text must reach the right room, and updates must be presented in useful order while the speaker is still talking. A delay of a few seconds is visible, even when users accept it. Capacity planning therefore starts with concurrent rooms and fan-out recipients, not with the eventual transcript size.

Users notice.

The SLOs should differ. For captions, measure useful text delivered during the session and bound end-to-end delay; do not hide a missed live delivery behind a successful transcript written later. For the transcript, measure durable completion after room close, then verify that retention and deletion behave as promised. One cannot substitute for the other.

This is also where the trust boundary becomes concrete. The RTC provider handles room media and scoped admission. A speech processor may receive audio. The realtime transport carries caption events. Object storage retains the finished artifact. Before enabling captions, identify the region used at every step, the processor receiving audio, its retention behavior, and the deletion mechanism. A general API layer does not create audio-residency or contractual guarantees on behalf of a specialist processor.

No hand-waving here.

If a user needs captions to participate, loss during fan-out is an availability failure. If users mainly revisit decisions after a demo or support session, the transcript is the smaller and more defensible first release.

Choose the boundary before choosing the vendor

The operational decision is not a feature tally. It is ownership of data during the call and after it.

Stack Strong fit Boundary the platform team still owns
LiveKit plus Amazon S3 Teams wanting a specialist RTC layer and a separately controlled object-store account Two signups, two credential sets, token-to-object glue, processor-region review, retention, and deletion policy
Daily plus Amazon S3 Teams prioritizing a managed video-room product with separate storage control Two signups, two credential sets, artifact transfer, and evidence that media and stored data follow the required regions
Twilio Video plus Amazon S3 Teams already operating Twilio and AWS trust boundaries Cross-provider credentials, artifact handoff, processor contracts, lifecycle policy, and independent outage planning
Pusher plus Amazon S3 Teams that already use Pusher Channels and only need caption-event fan-out RTC, speech processing, token scope, transcript assembly, retention, and deletion remain separate work
Ably plus Amazon S3 Teams needing a dedicated realtime messaging layer for caption events It is not a video-room or transcription replacement; media admission and the final artifact pipeline still need owners
PubNub plus Amazon S3 Teams with an established PubNub event-delivery architecture Room media, speech processing, private artifact transfer, and cross-provider credentials remain outside that layer
Infrai Teams that value one REST surface for scoped room access and private transcript storage One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface; specialist audio processing and its contractual guarantees remain separate

The combined Infrai approach reduces integration surfaces, not accountability. Live discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules, and room tokens and storage use the same bearer key and base URL. That removes an extra account and credential bridge from this particular handoff. It also concentrates risk, so a platform review should demand region, retention, deletion, and processor evidence before approval rather than infer those properties from API consistency.

LiveKit, Daily, and Twilio remain better choices when their specialist RTC controls, media topology, or existing enterprise agreement decide the architecture. Pusher, Ably, and PubNub are narrower alternatives when the missing component is event fan-out rather than the room itself. Amazon S3 is the clearer storage boundary when the organization already has mature AWS residency, lifecycle, and deletion controls. The right answer can be two vendors. On-call load rises, but contractual and failure domains may be easier to separate.

The limitation is deliberate: Infrai is not suitable when a specialist RTC contract, a separately owned storage account, or independently isolated failure domains are mandatory. This trade-off matters more than reducing the number of credentials.

Put the session artifact behind the same authenticated boundary

The safe implementation issues a scoped room token, gives it to the participant, and uploads only the completed transcript to a private object path. The program below deliberately takes the exact token request as JSON from RTC_TOKEN_REQUEST_JSON; token scope fields must come from the current discovery schema rather than copied prose. It then feeds the token response into the stored audit artifact, demonstrating the handoff without claiming that storage performs speech recognition.

Both writes carry an idempotency key, every request has an explicit method, and 429 responses honor Retry-After or use exponential backoff. The upload never exposes a public URL. In production, keep the token response only if policy permits it; otherwise store a stable, non-secret issuance identifier selected from the documented response schema.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func doWrite(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, endpoint, key, idem string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s returned %d: %s", endpoint, resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s remained rate limited after retries", endpoint)
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    tokenRequest := []byte(os.Getenv("RTC_TOKEN_REQUEST_JSON"))
    bucket := os.Getenv("TRANSCRIPT_BUCKET")
    objectKey := os.Getenv("TRANSCRIPT_OBJECT_KEY")
    transcript := os.Getenv("TRANSCRIPT_TEXT")
    if key == "" || len(tokenRequest) == 0 || bucket == "" || objectKey == "" || transcript == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY, RTC_TOKEN_REQUEST_JSON, TRANSCRIPT_BUCKET, TRANSCRIPT_OBJECT_KEY, and TRANSCRIPT_TEXT")
    }
    if !json.Valid(tokenRequest) {
        panic("RTC_TOKEN_REQUEST_JSON must be valid JSON from the discovery schema")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    tokenResponse, err := doWrite(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/rtc/token/issue", key, "room-token-"+objectKey, tokenRequest)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    artifact, err := json.Marshal(map[string]json.RawMessage{
        "room_token_issue": tokenResponse,
        "transcript":       json.RawMessage(strconv.Quote(transcript)),
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    uploadURL := baseURL + "/storage/object/put/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + url.PathEscape(objectKey)
    if _, err := doWrite(ctx, client, http.MethodPut, uploadURL, key, "transcript-"+objectKey, artifact); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("private transcript artifact stored")
}

The example has one API key and one base URL. The alternative LiveKit-or-Daily-plus-S3 stack needs two signups, two credential sets, a mapping between room identity and object key, and code to cross that provider boundary. Those are manageable costs, but they belong in the on-call estimate.

Verify delivery, retention, and deletion

Verification needs to exercise user outcomes rather than stop at a successful response. Run a room with caption consumers on a stable connection and after a reconnect; observe whether useful live text arrives within the chosen SLO, and keep transcript completion as a separate check. Do not declare caption success because a final file exists.

Storage can wait. Captions cannot.

For the artifact, confirm that an unauthenticated read fails, an authorized read returns the expected session object, and the object sits in the approved region. Then test the documented deletion operation and verify that the object is no longer retrievable. Retention needs an owner, a duration derived from policy, and evidence from the storage boundary; silence is not a retention policy.

Processor review comes last only in this runbook, not in procurement. Record which specialist receives audio, which region it uses, how long it retains inputs and outputs, and how deletion requests propagate. The evidence may force a different stack. That is a valid result.

Capacity tests should cover peak concurrent rooms, speakers per room, and caption recipients per room. Averages are misleading because fan-out load follows the busy room, while transcript storage follows sessions completed over time. Set separate error budgets so dropping captions cannot be disguised by retrying the later upload.

Roll back without losing the meeting record

The rollback switch disables live caption publication while leaving the room and transcript workflow intact. Announce the degraded state in the product, because silently removing an accessibility feature is not an acceptable recovery mode. If captions are required for participation, the rollback is to stop or reschedule the affected session, not to pretend the transcript is equivalent.

Keep transcript uploads idempotent so a retry cannot create competing artifacts. If the combined API boundary is unavailable, queue the completed transcript inside the approved retention boundary and retry later under the same object key; do not move it to an unreviewed public store. Recovery is complete only after the private object is verified and any temporary copy is deleted according to policy.

The decision rule is blunt: default to a post-session transcript for review value, add live captions when in-session need or accessibility makes their delivery SLO worth owning, and select vendors only after their regional, processor, retention, and deletion boundaries survive review. If the single-key boundary fits that review, start with the Infrai documentation.

References

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • LiveKit documentation
  • Daily developer documentation
  • Twilio Video documentation
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Infrai documentation

title: Node.js Error Tracking Admin Page: 4-Stage Fintech Event Cost Attribution
description:
TL;DR: Build the internal console as a narrow four-stage flow: list unresolved error groups, inspect one group, open the event payload, and resolve only after an operator has classified the failure. For a nightly fintech pipeline, attach cost and run identity before that flow begins; the resolve button records triage state, not financial completion. Infrai fits a small team that wants this boundary behind ordinary HTTP and one contract, but it does not replace paging, distributed tracing, source-map processing, replay, or a dead-man check.

The dangerous ambiguity is a quiet run. An empty error inbox might mean the batch succeeded, or it might mean the scheduler never started it. Error tracking can describe observed failures. It cannot prove expected execution.

That distinction is the invariant: the run ledger owns execution and cost; the error inbox owns investigation state. Keep it visible in the data model and in the runbook.

How should a Node.js error tracking admin page list unresolved groups?

The console should begin with unresolved production groups. An operator searches the loaded records by message or environment, selects a group, reads its detail, and then opens a specific event for the stack trace and request metadata. Resolve is the final UI action, but it has intentionally modest semantics: somebody acknowledged or classified the error group. It does not certify that a transfer posted, a reconciliation balanced, or a downstream file arrived.

Consider a batch identified as ledger-import-2026-10-09. Three retries can produce three events associated with one recurring failure. The group is the support team's unit of attention; the individual event is the evidence; the stable batch ID is the finance team's attribution key. Those identifiers belong beside each other on the detail screen, but they are not interchangeable.

I would make the four transitions explicit in the UI:

  1. Inbox: retrieve unresolved groups and show environment, message, recency, and the pipeline run ID when the event provides it.
  2. Group: show the recurring failure context without pretending every event is identical.
  3. Event: expose the stack trace and request metadata used to classify this occurrence.
  4. Resolution: require the operator to return to the pipeline system of record before marking the group resolved.

Cost follows the run ID. Resolution does not rewrite it. Infrai specifies cost, vendor, latency, cache-hit, and request-ID metadata consistently per call, so that metadata can be retained by the run ledger for attribution. It remains accounting context, not proof of application correctness.

Short answer: search and resolve belong in the admin page; execution proof and financial truth do not.

The provider boundary is part of the runbook

The clean handoff starts when the pipeline has already captured an error and ends when the operator changes that error group's triage state. Upstream, the scheduler and queue must preserve a durable run ID and make work idempotent. Downstream, the settlement or reconciliation system decides whether the business operation completed. The dashboard sits between those authorities.

Infrai is a credible option for a compact version of that dashboard. Its breadth is useful here because error tracking can use the same key and REST contract as other backend capabilities rather than introducing another SDK lifecycle. The public discovery surface reports 295 routes across 20 modules, requires no key for discovery, and publishes request and response schemas plus runnable examples. Every documented capability has examples in 10 languages. For a mixed-runtime pipeline estate, that means the on-call engineer can inspect the current contract before provisioning credentials and can keep the Go poller as plain HTTP.

That is a separate advantage from account consolidation. The self-describing contract reduces schema guesswork at the handoff, while the single surface reduces credential, permission, and billing reconciliation around it. The two benefits solve different operational friction.

Teams with a modest internal pipeline console should try Infrai for grouped-error triage when a self-describing HTTP contract and consistent per-call cost attribution matter more than a specialist investigation suite. Keep the recommendation scoped. Built-in threshold alerts, phone or SMS notification, webhook notification, distributed trace queries, span trees, source-map deobfuscation, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, and Session Replay are outside this boundary. There is also no heartbeat or synthetic-monitor feature to detect a job that never ran.

Because notifications are absent, a cron worker can poll the free query API for new critical groups and deduplicate its own notifications. That poller is an adapter, not an incident-management system. It should persist the last observed state, tolerate repeated observations, and fail visibly when its own check cannot complete.

A small Go client with boring failure behavior

The following program deliberately covers only two operations: list groups and resolve a selected group. It uses complete URLs, explicit methods, bearer authentication from the environment, response-body error reporting, and bounded retries for HTTP 429. Retry-After is honored when it contains seconds; otherwise, the client applies exponential backoff.

Reads can be repeated. A resolve retry deserves more caution because it changes state, so the client supplies a stable idempotency key derived from the group ID. Infrai specifies idempotency as a platform convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window. The program still treats the admin database as the durable audit record.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const groupsURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/groups"
const resolveURLTemplate = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/resolve/{error_group_id}"

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, url, key, idempotencyKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        if idempotencyKey != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s returned %d: %s", method, url, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s remained rate limited after 5 attempts", method, url)
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}

    groups, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodGet, groupsURL, key, "")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(groups))

    groupID := os.Getenv("ERROR_GROUP_ID")
    if groupID == "" {
        return
    }
    resolveURL := strings.ReplaceAll(resolveURLTemplate, "{error_group_id}", groupID)
    _, err = call(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, resolveURL, key, "resolve-error-group-"+groupID)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The example does not guess query parameters. That restraint matters elsewhere too: the discovery parameters for log search and metric query are undeclared, so a production client should not invent filters from route names. Use the published discovery schema as the contract and keep client-side search bounded to fields actually returned by the error workflow.

No tight loops. No silent success.

Specialists are better when investigation is the product

Option Practical boundary Strong fit Limitation for this design
Infrai Plain REST error workflow under a broader backend contract Small cross-capability internal console with cost attribution No native alerts, trace tree, symbolication, replay, or heartbeat checks
Sentry Dedicated error-monitoring project and SDK workflow Deep application-error investigation Adds a specialist integration and separate attribution boundary
Rollbar Dedicated error-monitoring workflow Teams centering operations on mature error triage Remains a separate provider contract for the pipeline
Bugsnag Dedicated stability and error workflow Product teams that need specialist diagnostics More specialization than a narrow internal inbox requires
Healthchecks Dead-man monitoring around scheduled work Detecting that the nightly job did not run Does not replace grouped event investigation

Sentry, Rollbar, and Bugsnag should be evaluated first when error investigation is a primary engineering system rather than a small admin feature. The deciding requirements are concrete: source maps, crash symbolication, Session Replay, richer notification behavior, and deeper investigation workflows. A lightweight list-detail-resolve surface should not be stretched into those jobs.

Healthchecks solves a different failure mode and belongs beside any of the error products. The nightly batch sends a heartbeat around expected execution; a missing signal can then raise the silent-failure path that an error inbox cannot observe. This is an intentional second provider boundary. Combining it with error resolution would blur the most important distinction in the system.

Datadog is another reasonable alternative when logs, metrics, alerting, and distributed tracing need to live in a specialist observability platform. Grafana fits teams that deliberately operate dashboards over selected telemetry stores. Both are broader operational choices than the four-stage console described here. Neither should be chosen merely to avoid writing a small admin table, and Infrai should not be chosen when a trace tree or advanced log-query contract is the actual requirement.

Production rules for the 02:00 batch

Start with ownership. The scheduler owns evidence that ledger-import-2026-10-09 started. The worker owns an idempotent business key and records completion in the pipeline ledger. Error capture owns failure evidence. The admin page owns operator acknowledgement. Finance owns whether the ledger balanced.

Then make retries dull. A repeated poll must not create repeated pages. A repeated resolve request must carry the same operation identity. A queue redelivery must not apply a transfer twice. These are separate deduplication domains, even when they share a run ID.

Retention and privacy also need an explicit review. The logging surface has no per-user deletion endpoint, no bulk export endpoint, and no subscription endpoint; retention and cold-storage errors exist, but no configuration entry point is exposed. A fintech team with deletion obligations or long-term evidence requirements should treat that as a selection boundary, not a backlog detail.

Finally, write two runbook checks that pull in opposite directions. If the inbox has a new critical group, inspect an event and correlate its run ID before resolving. If the inbox is empty after the batch window, check the heartbeat and scheduler ledger before declaring success.

Silence is a state to investigate.

The resulting console is intentionally small, and that is defensible when the team needs fast grouped triage rather than a complete observability program. If this boundary fits the system, start with the error grouping, search, and resolve guide and verify the current discovery schema before wiring the client.

Sources

  • https://12factor.net/logs
  • https://docs.sentry.io/product/issues/
  • https://docs.rollbar.com/docs/items
  • https://docs.bugsnag.com/product/error-monitoring/
  • https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/errors/answers/simple-error-grouping-api-compare-rollbar-bugsnag-sentr/

title: I Built My Portfolio Like a Piece of Rack Gear - Zero Dependencies, All Vanilla JS
description:
After 29 years of building software - most of it in PHP, all of it allergic to dependencies - I decided my portfolio should behave less like a resume and more like the gear I love: a production console. Rack units. LEDs that flicker on. A VU meter that actually moves.

The result is bryanhamilton.info, and its last PageSpeed run looked like this: 99 Performance, 100 Accessibility, 100 Best Practices, 100 SEO, 104 KB transferred, 8 requests, 558 ms to load - measured in the browser, not in a lab.

No framework. No build step. No npm. Here's how each piece works, and - because that's where the real lessons live - what broke along the way.

1. The rack: HTML that tells the truth

Each project is a "rack unit" card with three things most portfolios hide: a status LED, an honest status word, and zero marketing.

<article class="rack-card">
  <span class="rack-led"></span>
  <span class="rack-status">RUNS LIVE</span>
  <h3><a href="https://github.com/...">dj-card-preview</a></h3>
  ...
</article>

The LED color is contract law:

  • Green (RUNS LIVE): there is a URL you can click right now and it works.
  • Orange (DOCUMENTED): the code is real and CI-tested, but the live instance is retired.

When a tool's live deployment broke, I didn't take the card down or leave a green LED glowing next to a dead link. I flipped the LED to orange. A portfolio that lies to you once is a portfolio you stop trusting.

2. LEDs that power on like real gear

Real rack equipment doesn't fade in politely when it loads. It boots. So when the rack scrolls into view, the LEDs flicker alive left-to-right, one time, then settle into a slow pulse:

@keyframes rack-boot {
  0%   { opacity: .08; filter: brightness(.4); }
  38%  { opacity: 1;   filter: brightness(2.6); }
  55%  { opacity: .35; filter: brightness(.8); }
  100% { opacity: 1;   filter: brightness(1); }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .rack-boot .rack-card .rack-led {
    animation: rack-boot .9s calc(var(--i, 0) * 70ms) both,
               rack-pulse 2.2s calc(var(--i, 0) * 70ms + .9s) infinite;
  }
}

One IntersectionObserver adds a rack-boot class the first time the rack enters the viewport, sets a --i index on each card, and the stagger is just arithmetic in calc(). The handoff from boot animation to infinite pulse is scheduled by delay, not JS, so there's no race condition to manage.

The part I care about most is the @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) wrapper. Every animation on the site - this one, the terminal intro, the background drift - is gated the same way. Accessibility isn't a checklist item at the end; it's the container everything else lives inside.

3. A scroll progress bar disguised as a Venn diagram

The page background is a fixed Venn diagram: one circle for engineering, one for the people-facing work. The overlap used to just sit there. Now it fills.

.venn-core {
  position: absolute;
  width: calc(min(97vw, 1040px) * 0.30);
  background: radial-gradient(closest-side,
    rgba(0, 210, 255, .17),
    rgba(0, 210, 255, .05) 58%, transparent 72%);
  opacity: var(--vp, 0);
}

var max = document.documentElement.scrollHeight - window.innerHeight;
var p = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, window.scrollY / max));
venn.style.setProperty('--vp', p.toFixed(3));

Eleven lines of JS inside a requestAnimationFrame-throttled, passive scroll listener. As you descend the page, the intersection of the two circles glows brighter until, at the footer, the overlap is fully lit. The site's entire thesis - the engineer who can also talk to humans - is rendered as an opacity value.

That's the trick I'd hand to anyone building a personal site: if your brand has a central metaphor, make the mechanics of the page narrate it. Nobody consciously notices a scroll progress bar inside a Venn diagram. Everybody feels it.

4. The equalizer that actually listens

The signature piece is an 8-bar equalizer that reacts to real audio - not a CSS keyframe fake. When you hover a demo card, it plays a 30-second track preview through the Web Audio API and drives eight canvas bars from the analyser:

const ctx = new AudioContext();
const src = ctx.createMediaElementSource(audio);
const analyser = ctx.createAnalyser();
analyser.fftSize = 64;
analyser.smoothingTimeConstant = 0.8;
src.connect(analyser);
analyser.connect(ctx.destination);

// 8 bars, sampling every other bin of the low half
function draw() {
  analyser.getByteFrequencyData(dataArray);
  for (let i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
    const v = dataArray[i * 2] / 255;
    bars[i].style.height = Math.max(4, v * 80) + 'px';
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(draw);
}

Two lessons worth the tuition:

  1. Autoplay policy is a feature, not a bug. Browsers won't let you play audio until the user interacts. The demo shows a one-time "click anywhere to activate" gate. Fighting this is a losing game; designing around it is a UX opportunity.
  2. A CSS "fake" EQ is detectable in about half a second. If the bars don't move with the kick drum, people feel the lie immediately. fftSize: 64 with smoothingTimeConstant: 0.8 gives you chunky, musical bars instead of noise.

5. The search index I'm proudest of

The site has instant search with keyboard navigation and ARIA combobox semantics, built on a prebuilt JSON index and a tiny client-side scoring function. No server round-trips, no search service. At build time the content gets flattened into one JSON file; at runtime, ~60 lines of JS score and match against it.

I extracted the whole pattern into a standalone repo (instant-search-index) because it's the most reusable thing I've built in years: prebuilt index + scored matching + proper combobox ARIA roles, and it works in anything.

6. What broke (and what it taught me)

No tutorial-style post is honest without the blood.

The 16 KB wall. My host's FTP silently truncates uploads at exactly 16,384 bytes. My resume-builder PHP file is 24,084 bytes. The deploy "succeeded" and produced a corrupt PDF. Diagnosis took byte-counting and MD5 comparisons; the fix was a chunked-upload kit (split the file, base64 the parts, assemble server-side, verify MD5 before writing). The real lesson: when a deploy fails weirdly, compare bytes, not screenshots.

The cache header that ate my deploys. I shipped cache-control: max-age=2592000, immutable on my HTML. That header is meant for fingerprinted assets like app.abc123.js - not for a homepage I edit daily. Result: my browser happily served me a week-old page while I debugged code that was already live. I only proved the code worked by loading the site in headless Chrome, which had no cache. The fix is one .htaccess block:

<FilesMatch "\.html$">
  Header set Cache-Control "public, max-age=0, must-revalidate"
</FilesMatch>

If you take one operational lesson from this post: immutable is for hashed assets. HTML gets max-age=0, must-revalidate. Write that on a sticky note before it costs you an afternoon.

The half-leading PDF. My PDF generator advanced the Y cursor by 48% of the line height, stacking lines on top of each other. I didn't see it for weeks because a separate bug (a missing %PDF-1.4 header) made the file unopenable, masking the layout bug underneath. Fix one bug, meet its friends.

7. Why zero dependencies, seriously

I've been doing this since before frameworks were the default, so take this with the appropriate salt. But the math on this site:

  • 104 KB total. The median framework starter ships more than that before it renders anything.
  • 8 requests. No font carousel, no analytics tag parade.
  • 99-100 across every Lighthouse category - including the one most portfolios fail on purpose: Accessibility, because animations respect reduced-motion and the search is a real ARIA combobox.

Zero-dependency isn't nostalgia. It's a debugging philosophy: when everything in the stack is code you wrote, nothing is someone else's mystery. When the PDF breaks, I can read every line that produced it.

Come kick the tires

The site is live at bryanhamilton.info - scroll slowly, let the rack boot, watch the overlap glow as you reach the bottom. The code is on GitHub, ten repos deep, each one CI-badged and extracted from production code rather than written for show.

And if you build something with any of these patterns - the LED boot, the analyser EQ, the instant search - tell me in the comments. I want to see the racks other people bolt together.

title: Your test passed on retry. Your report should say so.
description:
Most Java test suites have a retry somewhere: an IRetryAnalyzer in TestNG, @RetryingTest from JUnit Pioneer, or Surefire’s rerunFailingTestsCount. Retries keep pipelines green. They also hide information.

When a test fails, gets retried and passes, most reports show one word: Passed. The failure that happened two minutes earlier, along with its stack trace, its API calls and the screenshot of what the browser showed, is gone. The test is flaky, and the report hides it.

The second problem is quieter. To get a useful report, teams end up writing reporting code inside their tests:

`java
test.log(Status.INFO, "Calling POST /users");
test.log(Status.INFO, "Response: " + response.asString());
Allure.addAttachment("Screenshot", new ByteArrayInputStream(png));`

That code isn’t testing anything. People forget to add it, it drifts out of date, and it lands in every test for the rest of the project’s life.

I built Ace Reports to fix both problems. Here’s what it does in Java.

One dependency, no reporting code
xml

`<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.acereports</groupId>
    <artifactId>acereports-junit5</artifactId>  <!-- or acereports-testng / acereports-cucumber -->
    <version>1.1.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

`

There are no listeners to register, no base class and no annotations. Run mvn test as usual, and a single self-contained HTML file appears in TestResults/.

Every attempt keeps its own history

A test that fails and then passes on a retry is shown as flaky, with one tab per attempt. Each attempt keeps:

its own log lines,
its own error and stack trace,
its own API calls,
its own screenshots.

So when attempt 1 timed out and attempt 2 passed, you can see exactly what was different. Pass, fail, flaky and retried counts sit at the top of the report.

API calls are recorded automatically

This is a typical API test with no reporting code in it:

java

`
class UsersApiTest {
private final HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();

@Test
void createsUser() throws Exception {
    HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(
        HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://reqres.in/api/users"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("{\"name\":\"John\"}"))
            .build(),
        HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
    assertEquals(201, response.statusCode());
}

}
`

The report’s API tab for this test shows the method, URL, request body, response body (JSON indented), status code and duration.

REST Assured calls are captured the same way, with no code.
Authorization and cookie headers are never stored.
One limitation: a client created inside the test method itself can’t be reached automatically, so you wrap it once with AceHttpClient.wrap(...).
Screenshots before teardown

The failure screenshot is taken before @AfterEach / @AfterMethod runs, so the browser is still open. Ace Reports finds a Playwright Page or Selenium WebDriver in a field of the test class, a base class or a ThreadLocal by itself. A page that never navigated anywhere (about:blank) is skipped, so a failed API test doesn’t get an empty screenshot.

Cucumber: steps are the log

With Cucumber (JUnit 5 or TestNG runner), each scenario is a row and every step is a line in the log:


GIVEN the login page is open
WHEN I log in as "InvalidUser" with password "admin123"
FAIL Step failed. TimeoutError: Timeout 3000ms exceeded.
SKIPPED Then the dashboard is shown
Scenario Outline rows carry their example values.
Tags become categories.
Images you attach with scenario.attach(...) show up as screenshot tabs.
Writing to the report, when you want to

You never have to, but you can:

java


Ace.info("Submitting payment");
Ace.takeScreenshot("After login");

Each line attaches to whichever test is running on the current thread, so parallel runs keep their logs apart.

Same report in .NET, Java and Python

Ace Reports started in .NET (xUnit, NUnit, MSTest, Reqnroll) and Python (pytest, pytest-bdd). The Java version produces the identical report, which helps when one team works across more than one stack.

Try it
Live demo report: **https://harshadlambate.github.io/AceReportsWebsite/demo.html
**Website and docs: https://harshadlambate.github.io/AceReportsWebsite/
Maven Central: https://central.sonatype.com/namespace/io.github.acereports

I’d like to hear how your team handles flaky tests: do you keep the history of each attempt, or only the final result?

title: Component Architecture & Design Systems
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Kill the Button with thirty boolean props by favoring composition over configuration. Split presentational from container components, set clear prop boundaries, and make design tokens the single source of truth so the codebase scales instead of rotting.

Contents

  • The Button with thirty boolean props
  • The one principle: compose small pieces
  • The picture: how a UI codebase layers
  • Presentational vs container components
  • Composition vs configuration: the trade-offs
  • Over-propped vs composable: the code
  • Design tokens: the source of truth
  • From component library to design system
  • Common mistakes that rot a codebase
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

The Button with thirty boolean props

Open the design-system Slack of any growing company and you will eventually find this message: "hey, does anyone know what isCompactSecondaryGhost does?" The Button started life as a humble little thing. Then someone needed a loading state, so they added isLoading. Then an icon, so hasIcon and iconPosition. Then a destructive variant, a ghost variant, a compact size, a full-width mode, a tooltip-on-disabled hack. Two years later the type signature is a wall.

Button.tsx (the horror)

interface ButtonProps {
  isPrimary?: boolean;
  isSecondary?: boolean;
  isGhost?: boolean;
  isDanger?: boolean;
  isCompact?: boolean;
  isLarge?: boolean;
  isFullWidth?: boolean;
  isLoading?: boolean;
  hasIcon?: boolean;
  iconLeft?: boolean;
  iconRight?: boolean;
  isDisabled?: boolean;
  showTooltipWhenDisabled?: boolean;
  isPill?: boolean;
  isOutlined?: boolean;
  // ...and 15 more, half of which are mutually exclusive
}

Nothing about that compiles wrong. <Button isPrimary isSecondary isGhost /> typechecks perfectly and renders nonsense. The component has become a configuration language nobody designed on purpose. This article is about the discipline that prevents it: composition over configuration, clear component boundaries, prop design that closes invalid states, design tokens, and how all of it rolls up into a reusable component library, a real design system instead of a junk drawer.

📌 Who this is for: You ship features in a React/Vue/Svelte codebase and you have felt the rot, components that fork into copies, props that contradict each other, "don't touch that file" comments. You want the senior-level mental models for keeping a UI codebase healthy as the team and surface area grow. Some component framework experience assumed; the principles are framework-agnostic.

The one principle: compose small pieces

Compose small pieces; don't configure giant ones. Every boolean prop you add is a branch inside the component, every slot you expose is a branch you handed to the caller.

The whole article in one line

A configurable component tries to anticipate every use case and exposes a prop for each one. The component owns all the variation, so it grows without bound. A composable component does one small job well and lets callers assemble it with siblings and children to get variation. The complexity moves out to the call site, where it is visible and local, exactly where the person who needs the variation is already standing.

In the real world In tech
A single molded plastic toy, one fixed shape, no parts A giant component with 30 props: every new need means re-molding the whole thing
A box of LEGO bricks, small, uniform, snap together Small primitives (Box, Text, Stack, Button) you compose into anything
Want a castle and a spaceship from the same bricks Same primitives compose into a form, a card, a toolbar, no new code in the primitive
A brick has studs in standard positions so any two fit Props and tokens are the standard interface that lets pieces snap together predictably

Why composition scales and configuration doesn't.

LEGO won because the interface between bricks is small and uniform. That is the entire trick. Your primitives should have small, uniform interfaces too, then features are assembled, not authored from scratch each time.

The picture: how a UI codebase layers

A healthy frontend isn't a flat pile of components, it's a layered dependency graph. Lower layers know nothing about higher ones. Tokens don't know about buttons; buttons don't know about the checkout page. Dependencies point one way, down.

Design tokens flow up into primitives, which compose into reusable components, which compose into features and pages. Each layer depends only on the layer below.

  1. Define tokens: Name your raw decisions once: color.brand.500, space.4, radius.md, font.size.lg. No component hardcodes a hex or a pixel value, they reference tokens.
  2. Build primitives on tokens: A Box maps props to token-backed styles. A Stack lays out children with a token-based gap. Primitives are the only layer that touches raw CSS.
  3. Compose reusable components: Button, Input, Card are built from primitives. They encode brand decisions (a Button always uses brand color + md radius) but stay generic about content.
  4. Assemble features: LoginForm composes Input + Button + Stack. It knows about your domain; the components below it do not.
  5. Compose pages: Routes wire features together. By the time you reach a page, you are arranging blocks, not writing CSS or fixing a Button.
  6. Theme by swapping tokens: Dark mode and white-label brands change token values, not component code. The whole tree re-themes for free because nothing below references a raw value.

Presentational vs container components

Within the component layer there's a second split worth keeping in your head, even in a hooks-everywhere world. Presentational components take data and callbacks via props and render UI, no data fetching, no global state, no business rules. Container (or "connected") components know where data comes from, they call hooks, read stores, fire mutations, and hand plain props down to presentational children.

The payoff is testability and reuse. A presentational UserCard({ name, avatarUrl, onFollow }) renders identically in Storybook, in a test, and in three different features, because it has no idea where name came from. The container ConnectedUserCard does the useUser(id) plumbing and renders <UserCard {...user} onFollow={follow} />. Keep the wiring thin and shove all the actual UI into the dumb component. Modern code rarely needs two literal files for this, but the boundary, "this component fetches, that one only renders", is what keeps things sane.

💡 Tip: Rule of thumb: if a component both calls useQuery/useStore and contains real layout/markup, it's doing two jobs. Split the data-fetching shell from the presentational core. The core becomes trivially reusable and your design system can ship it.

Composition vs configuration: the trade-offs

Configuration isn't always wrong, a variant="primary" enum prop is fine and good. The danger is when configuration is used to bolt on structural variation that should have been composition. Here's how to tell them apart by their symptoms.

Dimension Configuration (prop-driven) Composition (slot/children-driven)
Adding a use case Add another prop + an internal branch Caller arranges existing pieces, no edit to the component
Symptom of overuse Prop explosion; mutually exclusive booleans Deep nesting at call sites if primitives are too granular
Invalid states Easy to create (isPrimary isGhost) Hard to create, structure enforces validity
Who owns complexity The component (grows without bound) The call site (local and visible)
Best for Finite, enumerable variation (size, color) Open-ended, structural variation (layout, content)
Failure mode A god component nobody dares touch Boilerplate if you under-abstract

Reading the symptoms: when a prop should have been a slot.

Over-propped vs composable: the code

The classic example is a Card. The configured version tries to own every layout decision through props. Watch how fast it rots:

Card.tsx, the configured (rotting) version

interface CardProps {
  title?: string;
  subtitle?: string;
  imageUrl?: string;
  imagePosition?: "top" | "left";
  badgeText?: string;
  badgeColor?: string;
  footerText?: string;
  primaryActionLabel?: string;
  onPrimaryAction?: () => void;
  secondaryActionLabel?: string;
  onSecondaryAction?: () => void;
  showDivider?: boolean;
  isHighlighted?: boolean;
  // every new design = a new prop + a new branch in here
}

function Card(props: CardProps) {
  return (
    <div className={props.isHighlighted ? "card card--hl" : "card"}>
      {props.imageUrl && props.imagePosition === "top" && (
        <img src={props.imageUrl} />
      )}
      {props.badgeText && (
        <span style={{ background: props.badgeColor }}>{props.badgeText}</span>
      )}
      {props.title && <h3>{props.title}</h3>}
      {props.subtitle && <p>{props.subtitle}</p>}
      {props.showDivider && <hr />}
      {/* ...footer, two actions, image-left branch, etc. */}
    </div>
  );
}

Every design tweak edits this file and adds a branch. Now the composable version: Card owns only the box (background, radius, shadow, padding, all from tokens) and exposes slots via children and sub-components.

Card.tsx, the composable version

// Card owns the container styling only. Structure is the caller's job.
function Card({ children, highlighted = false }: {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  highlighted?: boolean;
}) {
  return (
    <div data-highlighted={highlighted} className="card">
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

// Small, focused sub-components, the "compound component" pattern.
Card.Header = ({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) => (
  <div className="card__header">{children}</div>
);
Card.Body = ({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) => (
  <div className="card__body">{children}</div>
);
Card.Footer = ({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) => (
  <div className="card__footer">{children}</div>
);

ProductCard.tsx, composing at the call site

// The variation lives HERE, visible and local. No edit to Card needed.
function ProductCard({ product }: { product: Product }) {
  return (
    <Card highlighted={product.featured}>
      <Card.Header>
        <Badge tone="sale">Sale</Badge>
        <Heading level={3}>{product.name}</Heading>
      </Card.Header>
      <Card.Body>
        <img src={product.imageUrl} alt={product.name} />
        <Text tone="muted">{product.summary}</Text>
      </Card.Body>
      <Card.Footer>
        <Button variant="primary" onClick={buy}>Add to cart</Button>
        <Button variant="ghost" onClick={save}>Save</Button>
      </Card.Footer>
    </Card>
  );
}

Notice what happened. Card will never grow another prop for a new layout. A wishlist card, a comparison card, an empty-state card, all of them reuse the same Card and arrange different children. And Button keeps a single variant enum instead of ten booleans, because enums make invalid states unrepresentable: you literally cannot pass variant="primary" variant="ghost". That is prop design as a safety rail, model the finite axes as enums, the open-ended structure as children.

⚠️ Warning: Prop boundary rule: a component's props are its public API. Once teams depend on a prop, removing it is a breaking change. Add props reluctantly, name them for intent (tone="danger") not implementation (color="#e11"), and prefer children over a content prop whenever the slot might hold arbitrary markup.

Design tokens: the source of truth

A design token is a named design decision stored as data, not baked into code. Instead of #d97706 scattered across forty files, you have color.brand.500 defined once. Tokens are what let a design system stay consistent and re-theme without a rewrite. They usually come in two tiers: primitive tokens (the raw palette, purple.500 = #d97706) and semantic tokens (the meaning, color.action.primary = purple.500). Components reference semantic tokens, so you can repoint color.action.primary to a new shade and every button updates.

tokens.ts, semantic on top of primitive

// Primitive tier: raw values, no meaning yet.
export const palette = {
  purple500: "#d97706",
  pink500: "#ec4899",
  gray900: "#111827",
  gray50: "#f9fafb",
} as const;

// Semantic tier: meaning, mapped to primitives. Components use THESE.
export const tokens = {
  colorActionPrimary: palette.purple500,
  colorTextDefault: palette.gray900,
  colorSurface: palette.gray50,
  spaceSm: "8px",
  spaceMd: "16px",
  radiusMd: "8px",
} as const;

// Dark mode = a different semantic mapping, same primitives + components.
export const darkTokens = {
  ...tokens,
  colorTextDefault: palette.gray50,
  colorSurface: palette.gray900,
} as const;

In practice these are emitted as CSS custom properties (--color-action-primary) so theme switching is a single class on <html> and costs nothing at runtime. Tools like Style Dictionary turn one token source into CSS, JS, iOS, and Android outputs, one decision, every platform. The point isn't the tooling; it's the discipline: no raw values below the token layer.

From component library to design system

People use "component library" and "design system" interchangeably, but they aren't the same. A component library is the code, the reusable Button, Card, Input. A design system is that library plus the tokens, the usage guidelines, the accessibility contract, the documentation, and the shared vocabulary between design and engineering. The library is the artifact; the system is the agreement.

  • Tokens, the single source of design truth (covered above).
  • Primitives + components, composable, token-backed, accessible by default (focus rings, ARIA roles, keyboard handling baked in so feature teams can't forget).
  • Documentation, live examples (Storybook), prop tables, and "do / don't" guidance. Undocumented components get re-invented.
  • Contribution model, how a new component gets proposed, reviewed, and promoted from a feature into the shared library. Without this, everyone forks.
  • Versioning, semver on the package so breaking a prop is a deliberate, communicated event, not a surprise on Monday.

Start smaller than you think. You do not need 80 components on day one. Ship tokens + five primitives + the four or five components every feature actually uses (Button, Input, Card, Modal, Stack). Let real usage pull the next component into existence, promote it after it has been copy-pasted twice, not before.

Common mistakes that rot a codebase

  1. Prop explosion. Bolting structural variation onto a component as booleans until it has 30 props and four mutually exclusive ones. Fix: reach for children/slots and the compound-component pattern before adding a prop.
  2. Premature abstraction. Building a "flexible" generic component for a use case you have exactly once, guessing at the future API. The rule of three: don't extract a shared component until the third real usage shows you the actual shape. Wrong abstractions cost more than duplication.
  3. No tokens. Hardcoded hex codes and pixel values sprinkled everywhere. Dark mode becomes a multi-week migration and brand consistency is a manual code review. Fix: a token layer from day one, even a tiny one.
  4. Copy-paste components. "I'll just duplicate UserCard into AdminCard and tweak it." Now a bug fix has to be applied in two (then five) places and they drift. Fix: compose the shared core, vary via props/children, and a contribution model so the shared version is the easy path.
  5. Mixing data and presentation. Components that fetch and render can't be reused or tested in isolation. Fix: keep the presentational core dumb and push the wiring to a thin container.

Takeaways

The whole article in nine lines

  • Compose small pieces; don't configure giant ones, every boolean prop is a branch you own forever.
  • LEGO beats a molded toy: small, uniform interfaces let you build anything without re-molding.
  • Layer the codebase: tokens → primitives → components → features → pages, dependencies pointing down only.
  • Split presentational (renders props) from container (knows where data lives), the dumb core is the reusable one.
  • Use enums for finite axes (size, variant) and children/slots for open-ended structure; that makes invalid states unrepresentable.
  • Treat props as a public API: name for intent, add reluctantly, prefer children over a content prop.
  • Design tokens are named decisions as data, primitive tier for raw values, semantic tier for meaning; no raw values below the token layer.
  • A component library is the code; a design system is library + tokens + docs + contribution model + versioning.
  • Start small and let real usage (the rule of three) pull abstractions into existence, never the other way around.

Where to go next

Architecture is one of three pillars of a healthy frontend. Once your components compose cleanly, the next questions are where state lives and how the visual layer is built underneath your tokens.

  • Continue the track: the Frontend Engineer path sequences these senior topics with the fundamentals beneath them.
  • Where data lives: State Management in Frontend Apps, the container side of the presentational/container split, in depth.
  • The layer under your tokens: CSS Fundamentals: The Box Model and Layout, what your primitives are actually emitting.
  • Practice: pick your ugliest god-component and refactor it into a compound component this week. Pull the variation out to the call site and watch the prop list collapse.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: 6 GSAP Component Libraries Compared in 2026 (Annnimate, Made With GSAP, Osmo, React Bits, Codrops)
description:
GSAP is an animation engine, not a component library. That is the first thing Google tells you when you search "gsap animation component library", and it is true: GSAP gives you gsap.to(), ScrollTrigger and SplitText, and leaves the hero reveal, the pinned gallery and the page transition to you.

So a small ecosystem of libraries has grown up that sell or give away finished GSAP components. I run one of them (Made for Award), so read this with that in mind. I have tried to be fair, and I link to every site so you can check the current numbers yourself, because prices and counts change.

Here is how the six I know best compare, and who each one is for.

Quick comparison

Library What you get Frameworks Pricing model Free tier
Annnimate ~119 UI components: buttons, menus, scroll, sections, shaders React, Vue, HTML Subscription (quarterly / yearly) + one-time kits 16-component starter pack
Made With GSAP ~121 JS effects: scroll, mouse, drag, infinite Webflow, vanilla JS Subscription (quarterly / annual) A few free effects
Osmo Vault of GSAP/Webflow resources and snippets Webflow, vanilla, some React Subscription Some free resources
React Bits Animated React components, part GSAP, part Motion React Free, open source Everything
Codrops Hundreds of demo tutorials, many on GSAP Vanilla Free Everything
Made for Award 40 award-style components: scroll, hero, preloader, slider, page transition, WebGL React, Next.js One-time ($22, lifetime) 8 free components

Counts are what each site stated in October 2026. Check the links for today's numbers.

1. Annnimate

The most "design system" of the group. Components are organised like a UI kit (Buttons, Menus, Scroll, Sections, Shaders), every component ships in React, Vue and plain HTML, and there is an MCP server so Cursor or Claude Code can pull the real source while it writes code. The studio behind it has built for Coca-Cola and Powerade and the polish shows.

Best for: teams on a subscription budget who want a consistent kit across React and Vue, and who like the AI-editor integration.

Watch out for: it is a subscription, so the components stop coming when you stop paying. Check the licence for client work.

2. Made With GSAP

121 effects and counting, all lightweight JavaScript plus GSAP, with an explicit "no Canvas, no WebGL" rule. The sweet spot is Webflow: effects are packaged so you can paste them into a Webflow project, and the source download covers vanilla sites too.

Best for: Webflow designers and anyone who wants scroll and mouse effects without a build step.

Watch out for: no React or Next.js versions, and no 3D or shader work by design. Subscription pricing.

3. Osmo

Osmo is a resource vault from the people behind a well-known Webflow/GSAP studio: snippets, cloneables, utilities and full sections, with a strong Webflow bias and growing framework support. Less a component library than a toolbox you dip into.

Best for: Webflow-first builders who want the studio's own helpers and patterns.

Watch out for: subscription, and you will still assemble most things yourself.

4. React Bits

Free and open source. A big catalogue of animated React components (text effects, backgrounds, cursors, cards) with a CLI, where some components use GSAP and others use Motion. Quality varies piece to piece, as you would expect from a community project, but for a landing page you can get far at zero cost.

Best for: React developers who want something free today and are happy to adapt.

Watch out for: it is a mix of animation engines, so not everything is "GSAP". Expect to tune timings and clean up for production.

5. Codrops

Not a library, but the original source of most of the effects the libraries sell. Every Codrops demo comes with a tutorial and a GitHub repo, many built on GSAP. The catch is that demos are vanilla and written to teach, not to ship: you port them yourself and you handle cleanup, resize and reduced motion.

Best for: learning how an effect works, and developers who prefer to build their own component from a reference.

Watch out for: licences differ per demo; some assets (fonts, images) are demo-only.

6. Made for Award

This is mine. Made for Award is a GSAP animation component library: 40 production-ready React and Next.js components (scroll animations, hero sections, preloaders, sliders, page transitions and WebGL effects), 8 of them free and the rest unlocked by one $22 lifetime purchase. Every component has a live demo you can open full-screen before you sign in, and the source is TypeScript + Tailwind with props for the content, so a slider takes your slides and a hero takes your headline.

The focus is narrower than Annnimate's: not a UI kit, but the specific award-site pieces (pinned scroll scenes, preloaders, smoke and wave page transitions, three.js heroes) that are the hard part of a portfolio or agency site.

Best for: React and Next.js developers building a portfolio, agency or launch site who want award-style motion without a subscription.

Watch out for: React only, no Vue or Webflow versions, and a smaller catalogue than the subscription libraries.

How to choose

  • Webflow: Made With GSAP or Osmo.
  • React + Vue in one kit, subscription is fine: Annnimate.
  • Zero budget: React Bits, plus Codrops to learn from, plus the free tier of any of the paid ones.
  • React or Next.js, pay once: Made for Award.

Whichever you pick, the thing that matters more than the library is the setup underneath it: register ScrollTrigger once, create animations inside useGSAP with a scope, put Lenis on the GSAP ticker, and refresh after fonts and images load. Every library above assumes you have that right, and most "the component is broken" issues are one of those four.

If I missed a library you use, tell me in the comments and I will add it.
