title: Design the Right Inventory Data Flow: Barcode to Stock Quantity Software Requirements
description:
Inventory applications are only as good as the events and records that they manage. If a warehousing operation misses a scan or logs a transfer late, the application’s view of the physical environment becomes out of date.

For software architects and developers, the question of inventory accuracy begins with inventory events.

  1. Capture inventory events

A basic inventory management cycle consists of events such as

• RECEIVED – warehouse stock arrival

• TRANSFERRED – movement between warehouses

• PICKED – removal for fulfillment

• RETURNED – returned goods acceptance

• ADJUSTED – inventory correction

Each of these inventory events holds a product identifier, quantity, transaction time, location (from and/or to), and an identifier of the associated business document. Event types and accompanying data depend on the firm’s needs.

Event records serve the primary purpose of enabling audits – responding to inquiries about why the quantity changed. If the application has to determine the point-in-time quantity, it reconstructs it from the list of processed events.

  1. Inventory quantity and identification methods

When reading a barcode or RFID tag, always remember that the means of item identification do not ensure inventory accuracy.

The application has to take responsibility for processing and recording a change in quantity. This is where validation and database design come in for ensuring that the inventory application’s logic does not allow errors to happen. For example, using transaction identifiers and avoiding duplicates supports prevention of inventory overstatement due to an incorrectly processed RECEIVED event. The application must recognize duplicates and reject them. Even if scanning the same receiving label twice would not add quantity twice.

  1. Location and status

The quantity that the firm records as available for sale or use is not always the actual physical inventory.

Inventory management systems have to track quantities by location and status. A separate inventory balance arises for each property or geographic location and different statuses (e.g., available, reserved, damaged, or pending repair).

This approach applies particularly to multilocational businesses.

  1. Transactions and concurrency

When two employees have picked the same last piece of inventory, the application must handle the second request as an error. Without the proper locking or transaction mechanisms at the database level, an inventory application will allow the second fulfillment to proceed despite availability issues.

Systems engineers have to evaluate the application’s requirements for concurrency and choose the necessary data isolation level or introduce application-level checks and balances.

  1. Inventory exceptions

It is necessary to design the inventory reporting or alert system to support investigations into rejected transactions, incorrect adjustments, or significant variances between the application’s count and the actual inventory.

Therefore, the application has to support the collection and analysis of inventory exceptions, such as

• Failed inventory transactions or adjustments

• Inventory adjustments or adjustments that were repeated

• Unusual manual adjustments to inventory quantities

• Inventory system connection or synchronization failures

• Varying results from cycle counts and inventory counts

These data assist operations and technical support personnel in identifying and resolving inventory exceptions.

  1. Hardware and systems inventory exceptions

Barcode scanners, computer programs, and mobile devices involved in automatic inventory management operate in varying physical environments and have differing communication stability. Before finalizing the applications, it is necessary to examine edge cases involving reading integrity, connection stability, and hardware interoperability.

Hardware inventory exceptions include duplicate reading of the same label, incorrect reading, or application freezes or failures. On the systems side, exceptions arise when incorrect data are captured or when communication between peripheral devices and the application is hampered.

The Right Inventory Software Architecture Begins With Physical Inventory Activities

Inventory applications are not simple warehouses with goods and quantity values. These applications have to appropriately capture event data, ensure there are no transaction processing errors, reflect the state of physical inventory locations, and provide visibility into exceptions. Inventory management software architects need to design inventory applications according to the firm’s actual events and needs. Always document the required physical inventory activities at the event level.

To learn about the general concepts and components of inventory management systems, visit The Inventory Master.

title: 5 Express.js Transactional Email Service Wrapper Rules — Retry, Queue, and Logging
description:
Choose an Express.js transactional email API by the glue its service wrapper leaves behind: a compliance notice is not done until its request, provider ID, retries, suppression decision, and delivery events can be inspected.

TL;DR: Put a narrow service module between Express and the provider. Enqueue a stable command, check suppression before every attempt, send with an idempotency key, persist the returned ID, and poll status or event APIs into your own audit view. Do not make SMTP the abstraction when the selected capability is API-only.

Option First-call effort Audit path Best fit
Postmark Low Provider API and events A focused transactional-email integration
Resend Low Provider API and events Teams optimizing for a compact developer surface
SendGrid Medium Provider API and event tooling Existing SendGrid estates and broader email workflows
Amazon SES Medium to high AWS services and configuration Teams already operating inside AWS
Infrai Low Returned IDs plus polling APIs Teams that value one REST contract across multiple backend modules

For the edtech case here, integration effort is the deciding factor. Postmark or Resend is the clean runner-up when email is likely to stay a standalone concern. Infrai is a strong fit when the same service will later add SMS or other backend capabilities because it puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key, one wallet, one bill, and one REST API. The interface is pure HTTP, with no SDK required, and its public discovery surface is self-describing. The trade-off is important: email events are pull-only, not webhook-driven.

1. What should an Express transactional email service wrapper log?

A provider receipt is evidence of an accepted API request. It is not the whole compliance record. The application should first create a durable command containing its own stable ID, the learner or guardian reference, notice type, template version, intended recipient, creation time, and current state. Store sensitive fields according to the retention and access rules of the product; an audit log is not permission to copy private data everywhere.

Then queue that command. The HTTP handler can return once the durable job exists, while a worker owns delivery. This boundary matters more than the choice between Express and another Node.js framework. A request handler that sends inline ties user latency and process restarts to a compliance operation.

Queues fail.

Keep the state machine small. queued, suppressed, accepted, and failed can be enough at first; observed delivery events belong in a separate append-only collection keyed by the provider message ID. I benchmark this design by counting moving parts, not by timing a toy fetch: one queue, one wrapper, one audit table, and one polling loop are easier to reason about than provider logic spread through route handlers.

2. Make retries boring and duplicate-safe

Retries need two guards. The worker checks suppression immediately before a send, because a queued address can become invalid later. It also reuses the same client-generated idempotency key for every attempt of the same logical notice. Infrai specifies Idempotency-Key as a platform convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window; do not generate a fresh value inside the retry loop.

Backoff handles congestion. It does not fix a bad recipient, rejected payload, or permanent authorization error. Retry HTTP 429 after Retry-After when supplied, and use exponential delay otherwise. Surface every other non-success body to the queue so its policy can distinguish terminal failures from retryable transport failures.

This is the pitfall I would test first: a worker times out after the remote service accepts a message but before the response reaches Node.js. Without stable idempotency, the next attempt may create another send. With it, retrying the logical command has a defined deduplication boundary.

3. Keep the Node.js wrapper narrow

The wrapper below deliberately accepts a prevalidated payload. The verified material does not specify the send body's fields, so hard-coding plausible-looking names would produce a polished example that may be wrong. Fetch the current request JSON Schema from public discovery during development, validate at the boundary, and keep this runtime module concerned with delivery mechanics.

type JsonObject = Record<string, unknown>;

type SendResult = {
  providerMessageId: string;
  response: JsonObject;
};

type SendOptions = {
  idempotencyKey: string;
  payload: JsonObject;
  extractMessageId: (response: JsonObject) => string;
  maxAttempts?: number;
};

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const apiBaseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!apiBaseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required");

const sleep = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  return Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** (attempt - 1), 30_000);
}

export async function sendTransactionalEmail({
  idempotencyKey,
  payload,
  extractMessageId,
  maxAttempts = 4,
}: SendOptions): Promise<SendResult> {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(new URL("/v1/email/send", apiBaseUrl), {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(payload),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < maxAttempts) {
      await sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt));
      continue;
    }

    const rawBody = await response.text();
    let body: JsonObject;
    try {
      body = JSON.parse(rawBody) as JsonObject;
    } catch {
      body = { rawBody };
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Email send failed (${response.status}): ${rawBody}`);
    }

    const providerMessageId = extractMessageId(body);
    if (!providerMessageId) throw new Error("Email response did not contain a message ID");
    return { providerMessageId, response: body };
  }

  throw new Error("Email send exhausted its retry budget");
}

The caller owns template selection and schema validation, then records providerMessageId beside the original command in the same worker transaction pattern used by the queue. The extraction callback is intentional. It prevents this article from inventing a response field while still making the transport executable with the live schema.

This code has one API route. Good. A wrapper should expose an application operation such as sendComplianceNotice, not reproduce a vendor catalog.

4. Poll for evidence, not vanity metrics

Infrai provides message lookup, message listing, and email event listing, but no webhook event push for this namespace. A lightweight dashboard therefore needs a scheduled poller. Save its cursor or watermark, ingest events idempotently, and join them to the stored provider ID. The resulting view should answer a support question: what did the application request, when was it accepted, and what events were later observed?

Polling sets a real latency floor. If staff need delivery state within seconds, a provider with webhook delivery may be the better choice. If a five-minute audit refresh is acceptable, I prefer polling here because it removes a public callback endpoint, signature validation path, and webhook replay queue from a small service. That is an operational trade-off, not a claim that polling is universally better: the dashboard can only be as fresh as its interval, and a missed run extends that delay.

Do not treat opens as proof that a person read a compliance notice. Apple Mail Privacy Protection prevents senders from learning Mail activity and obscures IP information, so open-derived signals are a poor compliance primitive. Record provider events, but base the business decision on the evidence your policy actually recognizes.

Short version: accepted is not read.

5. Know when the runner-up wins

Choose Postmark when transactional email is the durable boundary and a dedicated provider surface plus event delivery better matches the operational model. Resend deserves the same evaluation for teams prioritizing a small email API. SendGrid makes more sense when the organization already has its templates, event processing, and operational knowledge there; migration glue can cost more than a cleaner greenfield API. Amazon SES fits teams willing to compose AWS infrastructure around delivery because IAM, monitoring, and the rest of the deployment already live there.

Choose the unified REST option when integration count is the dominant cost. The benefit is concrete: one key and a consistent contract can cover email, SMS, and many other production modules, while public discovery publishes request and response schemas and runnable TypeScript examples. There are boundaries. Email has no managed OTP operation, scheduled email has no cancellation operation, and there is no SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. The pending Tencent email vendor also cannot serve as evidence for domestic-China compliance. For SMS, geographic fencing and country-price circuit breakers remain application responsibilities.

No option removes product work. Before committing, run the same acceptance test against each candidate: schema-to-first-call time, number of secrets and packages, duplicate behavior after a forced timeout, suppression handling, audit reconstruction, and event delay. Use a fixed test fixture and record the steps. A glossy five-line send snippet scores only one of those six checks.

For this compliance-notice service, the decision rule stays plain: use a dedicated provider if webhook immediacy or existing email operations dominate; use the broader API surface if avoiding the next integration matters more and polling latency is acceptable.

References

  • Postmark Email API documentation
  • Resend Emails API documentation
  • SendGrid v3 Mail Send documentation
  • Amazon SES SendEmail API documentation
  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection guide
  • Twilio guidance on preventing SMS pumping

title: I wrote down the cause of this leak two months before anyone reported it
description:
At 00:19:25Z on 2026-10-13, wolf-crazy opened issue #251 on YantrikDB, the Rust memory engine for AI agents that I maintain. A host running the engine through yantrikdb-hermes-plugin had collected about 60 directories, roughly 490MB, over about eight days. One potion-2M-<pid> directory per process start. None of them ever removed.

The directories come from BundledEmbedder, the zero-setup default. Its model, potion-base-2M, is about 7.9MB of files compiled into the binary with include_bytes!. The loader, model2vec_rs::StaticModel::from_pretrained, reads from a directory, so the first use in every process writes those bytes to disk. This is what the write looked like:

let temp = std::env::temp_dir()
    .join("yantrikdb")
    .join(format!("potion-2M-{}", std::process::id()));
std::fs::create_dir_all(&temp)
    .map_err(|e| format!("create temp dir {}: {e}", temp.display()))?;

A new directory for every PID, and nothing anywhere in the file that deletes one.

PR #128

wolf-crazy's report cross-referenced PR #128, "process-global model init + download retry." That PR fixed a different bug, a race during concurrent model initialisation. Its commit message says "the extraction path is keyed only on process::id()."

I wrote that PR. I merged it on 2026-08-12.

So the mechanism behind this leak had been sitting in my own words, in my own merged commit, for two months. I'd noticed the PID keying while fixing the race, written it down, and done nothing else with it. It took someone else's disk filling up for it to matter to me.

My reply

I answered 15 minutes and 44 seconds after the issue went up. I grepped the file on origin/main at 3dbb86a for remove_dir_all, impl Drop and TempDir, found none of them, and confirmed the bug.

wolf-crazy had proposed two fixes: cache the extracted model in a stable place keyed by model identity, or remove the directory on drop. I picked the cache, under dirs::cache_dir(), because it also gets rid of the one-copy-per-process-start cost instead of only cleaning up after it. I also gave a stopgap for anyone already sitting on a pile of these:

find "$TMPDIR/yantrikdb" -maxdepth 1 -name 'potion-2M-*' -mtime +1 -exec rm -rf {} +

Remove-on-drop turned out to be a non-starter anyway, and the PR body later explained why: "MODEL is a static OnceLock>, so the model lives for the whole process and a Drop on BundledEmbedder never runs. Cleanup-on-drop cannot fire." That OnceLock is the one #128 introduced.

The first version was already safe

wolf-crazy opened PR #252 at 00:49:28Z. The first commit, 7f60cf0, keyed the extraction directory on a fingerprint of the model's contents and left it under std::env::temp_dir()/yantrikdb/. Every process start reuses one directory. The host still only needs a writable $TMPDIR, same as before. That fixes the leak completely and introduces no new requirement.

At 03:55Z wolf-crazy force-pushed a rework, b9cedc1, moving the directory to <dirs::cache_dir()>/yantrikdb/models/potion-base-2M-<fingerprint>. Their comment on the PR: "reworked along the direction you gave on #251."

That rework is where the risk came in, and it came in through my suggestion.

The review

I reviewed b9cedc1 at 04:21:43Z and requested changes. The main point:

The bundled model is the default path, the one that has to work without network access or setup. Today it only needs a writable $TMPDIR. With this PR it needs a writable cache dir, and hosts where HOME is set but read-only would fail on startup where they work now: systemd units with ProtectHome=read-only, containers with a read-only root filesystem and a tmpfs /tmp, and service users with HOME=/nonexistent. dirs::cache_dir() returns Some in all of those, so the existing None fallback doesn't help.

I asked for the fallback to cover the whole extract step, since "a directory that exists but is read-only fails at the write." My issue reply had said nothing about any of this. I didn't see the problem with my own idea until there was code for it, and the first code for it was this commit.

The second request was about the regression test, which checked !s.contains(&std::process::id().to_string()) against a path that also holds a 64-character hex fingerprint and a model name. Any PID whose digits show up somewhere in that string fails the test for no reason connected to the bug. My review listed them: "PIDs 1–9, 17, 18, 20, 25, 36, 42, 57 and 23 others below 100,000."

I recounted that against the real fingerprint while writing this. It's 18 others, 34 in total. I got the count wrong in the comment asking for the test to be exact.

The same review closed with a note that nothing in the PR cleans up directories that had already leaked, and that we'd cover the cleanup from #251 in the release notes.

The second commit

d37c2c5 landed at 06:47:55Z. It moves extraction into a shared extract_into(dir), and init_model() now looks like this:

fn init_model() -> Result<StaticModel, String> {
    let primary = extraction_dir();
    let dir = match extract_into(&primary) {
        Ok(()) => primary,
        Err(e) => {
            let fallback = std::env::temp_dir().join("yantrikdb").join(dir_name());
            extract_into(&fallback).map_err(|e2| {
                format!(
                    "{e}; temp-dir fallback {} also failed: {e2}",
                    fallback.display()
                )
            })?;
            fallback
        }
    };
    StaticModel::from_pretrained(&dir, None, None, None)
        .map_err(|e| format!("model2vec_rs load: {e}"))
}

Any failure on the cache path, at any stage, retries the whole extraction under $TMPDIR with the same fingerprint-keyed name, and if that fails too, the error carries both causes. wolf-crazy tested it with XDG_CACHE_HOME=/proc/self/nope, a cache directory that resolves but can't be written, and the model-dependent tests passed through the fallback. They reported 2204 passing for cargo test -p yantrikdb --lib and 2215 with --all-features. Across both commits the change is +146/-22.

CI on d37c2c5 started around 06:54Z. The Windows leg finished last, at 07:15:05Z. Everything was green: Linux x86 and ARM, Windows, macOS, Python 3.10.

Where the 18 hours went

I approved at 12:30:57Z: "I read the diff but didn't re-run the suite myself. Between that and CI, this looks ready — queuing it for a final merge decision." That was about five hours and sixteen minutes after CI went green.

The merge came at 18:45:39Z, about six hours after that approval, with one last comment: "CI is green across Linux x86/ARM, Windows, macOS and py3.10. Thanks for the careful work and the quick turnaround, @wolf-crazy."

From issue to merge took 18 hours 26 minutes. wolf-crazy's work fits inside two stretches, 00:49 to 03:55 and 04:21 to 06:48, under six hours combined. CI took about twenty minutes. From 07:15, when the last check passed, to 18:45, the PR was green, reviewed and waiting on me. That's eleven and a half hours, the biggest single block of the whole timeline.

I don't think that's a problem, and I know some maintainers would read it as one. A green CI run and an approved diff from a contributor who had already caught his own regression once is exactly the kind of PR that's safe to leave behind a dozen other things for most of a day. The alternative is merging faster than I actually review, and a stale disk-filling bug that sat unfixed in my own PR description for two months doesn't get worse by sitting reviewed-and-green for half a day more.

The release-notes cleanup I promised hasn't been written yet. The last release was v0.23.2 on 2026-10-02, and nothing has shipped since, this fix included. Until there's a release, the find command from the issue is the only cleanup anyone has.

Pranab Sarkar, Independent Researcher

title: Node.js Marketplace Recovery: Send and Verify SMS OTP with Cooldowns
description:
TL;DR: For a Node.js marketplace password reset with a short expiry, let a hosted service own SMS code issuance and verification, but keep resend cooldowns, IP and device limits, country policy, and delivery polling in the application. The clean boundary is narrow: your service decides whether an attempt may proceed, the provider decides whether the code is valid, and your service changes the account only after verification. A unified provider is worth considering when the same flow touches auth, email, and SMS because the implementation can keep one HTTP contract, base URL, and key. That reduces integration work; it does not remove abuse controls.

A useful postmortem question is not "did the SMS dashboard look healthy?" It is "what page fired when one buyer requested 400 resets against 40 seller accounts?" A graph of successful sends can be green while the reset endpoint is doing exactly the wrong thing. Application admission control is the invariant.

How should a Node.js backend send and verify SMS OTP?

Start before the SMS call. Normalize the phone number, resolve the marketplace account without revealing whether it exists, check the country allowlist, and evaluate counters for the account, IP, and device. A permitted request enters a cooldown and then calls /v1/sms/otp. A submitted code goes to /v1/sms/verify; only successful verification can mint a short-lived reset grant. The SMS response must never directly change a password.

That split is deliberately boring. Hosted send and verify avoid rebuilding token validation, while the application retains the decisions that depend on marketplace risk. The unified option does not provide built-in geographic fencing or per-country cost circuit breakers, so those checks cannot be delegated. Delivery status and events are pull-based rather than pushed by webhook, which means the application must poll when it needs delivery visibility.

The account-to-message handoff should preserve one internal correlation ID, not a vendor-specific message object. The account result supplies the normalized recipient; email suppression preflight consumes that recipient; SMS becomes the fallback transport. With Infrai, auth, email, and SMS calls use the same https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base URL and Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY. Swapping the vendor behind a capability therefore does not force the application contract to change.

Infrai's second, separate integration advantage is its plain REST API, so there is no SDK to install. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. It exposes request and response JSON Schema, billing metadata, and readiness. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. A Node.js gateway and a Go worker can therefore generate the same HTTP contract instead of maintaining two SDK adapters, while paths come from the discovery path field rather than description prose. That removes a concrete upgrade and dependency-review chore from this reset flow.

The page is the test.

I would page on exhausted reset budgets, a sustained delivery-state backlog, and reset grants issued without a matching verification record. I would not page merely because one carrier is slow. That distinction keeps a transport symptom from masquerading as an account-security incident.

Put cooldown policy in code you own

The exact thresholds are business policy, so this sample uses explicit example values rather than pretending they are universal: one attempt every 30 seconds per account, five attempts per 15 minutes per IP, and three per 15 minutes per device. Production counters need a shared store and atomic increments; this in-memory implementation is runnable and useful for tests, but it is not suitable across multiple processes.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type limiter struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    events map[string][]time.Time
}

func (l *limiter) allow(key string, limit int, window time.Duration, now time.Time) bool {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    cutoff := now.Add(-window)
    kept := l.events[key][:0]
    for _, at := range l.events[key] {
        if at.After(cutoff) { kept = append(kept, at) }
    }
    if len(kept) >= limit {
        l.events[key] = kept
        return false
    }
    l.events[key] = append(kept, now)
    return true
}

func admit(l *limiter, account, ip, device, country string, now time.Time) error {
    countries := map[string]bool{"US": true, "CA": true}
    if !countries[country] { return fmt.Errorf("country outside reset policy") }
    if !l.allow("account:"+account, 1, 30*time.Second, now) { return fmt.Errorf("cooldown active") }
    if !l.allow("ip:"+ip, 5, 15*time.Minute, now) { return fmt.Errorf("IP budget exhausted") }
    if !l.allow("device:"+device, 3, 15*time.Minute, now) { return fmt.Errorf("device budget exhausted") }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    l := &limiter{events: make(map[string][]time.Time)}
    fmt.Println(admit(l, "seller-1842", "198.51.100.24", "device-77", "US", time.Now()) == nil)
}

The provider-side half can remain schema-safe without baking undocumented fields into an article. Put the JSON object produced from the live discovery schema in INFRAI_OTP_REQUEST_JSON; this runnable Go caller validates that it is an object, sends it with an explicit method and environment-backed key, honors Retry-After, and reports the real error body. A production service should cap the total retry duration at less than the reset expiry.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_OTP_REQUEST_JSON"))
    var object map[string]any
    if key == "" || json.Unmarshal(payload, &object) != nil || object == nil {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY and a schema-valid INFRAI_OTP_REQUEST_JSON object")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/otp", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", os.Getenv("RESET_ATTEMPT_ID"))

        response, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { panic(readErr) }
        if response.StatusCode >= 200 && response.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return
        }
        if response.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("send failed: status=%d body=%s", response.StatusCode, body))
        }
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
}

The order exposes a real pitfall: this compact example consumes the account budget before discovering an exhausted IP or device budget. In production I would evaluate and commit all counters atomically in one server-side operation, so a rejected request cannot burn only part of the budget. Dashboards hide this. Load tests do not.

Provider calls should load the key from the environment, specify the HTTP method, and surface non-success response bodies. A retry on HTTP 429 should honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter. Write retries need an idempotency key tied to the reset attempt; Infrai specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities. Stop after a bounded number of attempts. Fast retry loops turn throttling into an incident.

Do not log the OTP. Store the attempt ID, account ID, policy decision, provider request ID when returned, verification outcome, and reset-grant ID. Those fields answer the postmortem question without putting an authenticator into the logging system.

Three integrations or one trust boundary

The obvious alternative is Clerk for the account, Resend for email, and Twilio for SMS verification. It is a sensible specialist arrangement, and each component can be selected independently. It also means three signups, three credential sets, three client conventions, and application glue to reconcile recipient identity and suppression state. The marketplace team owns that glue forever.

Option Integration shape Better fit when Cost of the choice
Clerk + Resend + Twilio Three accounts and credential sets; application joins account, email, and SMS state Specialist controls justify separate operational surfaces More credential rotation and reconciliation code
Twilio Verify SMS verification is isolated behind a specialist Carrier tooling and SMS operations dominate Account and email handoffs stay separate
Clerk Account lifecycle is central Identity features matter more than a shared communications contract Email and SMS retain separate boundaries
Resend Transactional email is primary Email deserves an independent specialist It does not collapse the account-to-SMS handoff
Infrai Auth, email, and SMS share one REST surface, key, and bill Low integration effort and a stable provider boundary matter One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface

My recommendation: a small marketplace team should try Infrai for the auth-to-email-to-SMS handoff when reducing integration code is more valuable than deep channel-specific control; the stable HTTP contract is the primary reason, and public self-describing schemas remove the separate cost of maintaining several SDK-shaped adapters. The discovery index reports 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth is not the decision. The decision is whether one boundary makes the reset path easier to reason about at 3 a.m.

The main limitation and trade-off is concentrated dependency. The specialist stack is a better fit when an organization already has mature Clerk, Resend, or Twilio ownership, needs immediate webhook-driven orchestration, or needs voice, WhatsApp, RCS, or SMTP relay. The unified option does not provide those channels. It also has no managed email OTP endpoint, so SMS failure cannot become managed email-code verification; the application must build that flow.

This is not a fit for every team.

Polling changes the incident model

Without webhook pushes, delivery observation is delayed by the poll interval. That is acceptable for a short reset window only if the product treats delivery state as diagnostic, not as proof of possession. Verification remains the gate. Poll at a bounded cadence, stop at a terminal state or expiry, and attach the admission layer's attempt ID.

A growing set of nonterminal messages is actionable because it can consume the useful lifetime of the reset flow. A single delayed message is usually a support event. Page on sustained queue age or a broad verification drop, not every late carrier update. Choose thresholds from the marketplace's actual expiry and traffic distribution, then test them during a controlled failure exercise.

Email fallback has a second boundary. Check suppression before sending recovery email, but remember that vendors can define suppression differently. In the three-vendor design, the team must reconcile those meanings. In the single-contract design, the handoff is smaller, although the lack of managed email OTP still leaves verification logic with the application. Tencent email support is pending, so this design is not evidence of domestic compliance.

When this design does not apply

SMS OTP is practical for shipping a second factor quickly, but it is not the strongest authenticator. NIST's identity guidance treats the public switched telephone network as restricted and asks verifiers to consider signals such as device swap or number porting. High-risk payouts, administrator recovery, and accounts with meaningful stored value deserve a phishing-resistant recovery design rather than a larger pile of SMS rules.

Short expiry is not a substitute for throttling. Nor does successful delivery prove that the intended person controls the number. Keep account-enumeration responses uniform, bind a verified attempt to exactly one reset grant, expire that grant promptly, and invalidate it after use. Those are application invariants regardless of vendor.

If this boundary fits your system, generate requests from the published schemas rather than assumptions.

Sources

  • NIST SP 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines
  • Twilio Verify documentation
  • Clerk documentation
  • Resend documentation
  • RFC 7489: DMARC
  • Infrai machine-readable documentation index

title: Spawning a CLI from Node on Windows is not the same as on a Mac
description:
My Electron app starts other command-line tools: coding agents, git, gh. On a Mac, spawn('claude', args) just works. On Windows, the same line failed in two different ways.

First, most CLIs installed through npm aren't executables on Windows. They're .cmd shims. Since the April 2024 security fix (CVE-2024-27980), Node refuses to start a .cmd without shell: true. With the shell on, every argument goes through cmd.exe, which needs its own escaping and can't carry a line break inside an argument: a multi-line first message to an agent got cut off after the first line. What fixed it: read the npm shim, find the JavaScript file it wraps, and run that with node directly. Other .cmd files go through cross-spawn, which escapes arguments for cmd.exe.

Second, stopping things. When the CLI is a shim, the process you spawned is cmd.exe, and child.kill() ends only that one process. The agent it started keeps running in the background. taskkill /pid <pid> /T /F takes down the whole tree.

Both fixes now live in one helper that every spawn goes through, so nobody on the project (human or agent) calls spawn directly any more.

If you ship a Node or Electron tool that starts other CLIs, test it on Windows early. What else has bitten you there?

title: Four ways I tried to ingest data for my League of Legends hobby project
description:
Intro

Hello fellow devs! This is my first post on dev.to. My name is Rinat, I'm a senior full stack developer and I'm developing professionally and for fun for more than 11 years now.

This spring I started my hobby project Riftmind - a web application that analyzes raw data from videogame League of Legends and extracts useful information. Most of you probably heard of that game - it's one of the most popular multiplayer games with very big esports community (by the way Worlds 2026 starts today!). There's a public Riot API that serves a lot of data that we can use - which champions were picked, which champions were banned, who dealt the most damage, who were dying the most, etc. Currently Riftmind calculates winrates by role, rank and region and shows synergies, counterpicks, analyzes draft.

Every 2 weeks Riot releases new patch with changes to the game - from small to very significant. So for our calculations we constantly need large amount of fresh data, desirable balanced by each rank and this brings me to the point I wanted to talk about in this post. The thing is - in order to find the useful effect - we need a lot of data, so for example to say that champion A is statistically confirmed to be stronger than champion B we need to have at least data from 1000 matches between them (and even then the margin of error is about ±3%), while the effect itself is small - for most matchups it's 1-2%, and only the strongest counterpicks reach 5-8%. Riot API has rate limits for small projects like mine - about 100 calls per 2 minutes for each server. And all the match data goes through only 4 regional servers, so it's roughly 200 match API calls per minute for the whole world (calls about players and ranks go to 14 other game servers, like EUW or NA, each with its own limit). And the worst part - there's no endpoint to fetch matches from certain rank directly, we can only get matches of a certain player and we can also get players from certain rank.

So my goal was to ingest as many matches as possible by making as less API calls as possible.

Architecture

As it is my hobby project that was never intended to bring any money I wanted to minimize my monthly spending on the infrastructure. That's why I split the project into 3 applications - Ingestion, Processing and Published Web App. Ingestion is running 24/7 constantly gathering data from RiotAPI and writing it raw to its own database. Processing is executed by schedule or on demand and it calculates aggregates and copies them to the production database at the end of each run. The published app is running on Render and only has small database that only contains aggregated data. Ingestion and processing I was running at my local PC first (the gathered data could reach about 150GB) and then I moved it to the cheap VPS.

Attempt 1 - crawling the players

So the first idea was simple as the idea but turned out to be very complex at execution - I manually went to the website that had some info about players in each rank, manually selected ones that had many games and used them as seeds - my ingestion worker then fetched all their games, saved info and then moved to the other players from these games (each game always has 10 players). It worked and first month or two the ingestion used this approach. But with time some problems became obvious:

  • I couldn't reliably balance games between ranks. When we fetch the game - we don't know the ranks of all players, we only know the rank of the player whose game we're fetching. And the ranks in the same game can vary quite significantly. And if on the lower ranks it worked fine - on the higher ranks our queue would constantly drift to lower ranks. And making additional calls for each player would be very inefficient for our goal
  • It wasn't clear how to pick who we crawl next - each game adds 10 candidates, how do we maximize the "useful" calls? I had to introduce some scoring for players - considering how many games do we play.

Eventually the logic of crawling grew more and more complex while introducing little to none improvements.

By the time I gave up, the crawler was 1,790 lines of code with 17 settings to tune, and the queue of players had to be capped at 250,000 so it wouldn't grow forever.

Attempt 2 - random sampling from the ladder

This time I tried different approach - Riot API has endpoint to fetch players from any rank - the ladder, a list of all players in a rank, about 200 per page. So we don't need to crawl, we already have list of players we can fetch directly. So algorithm was simpler:

  1. Fetch players from the least represented rank in our data
  2. For every player - fetch their 20 recent match ids, download games from the current patch and stop at the first older-patch game
  3. Put these players on 48-hour cooldown, to wait until they play more games

This approach was way simpler - twice less code, games are ingesting, crawler logic was deleted at the same day.

The problem - most of the players we fetch didn't have any new games. So our ingestion was basically looking at the ladder, taking a random player and asked "did you play any games?" and answer was "no" most of the times.

In numbers: over the last full patch with this approach (16.19, two weeks) a random player gave us only 0.66 new matches on average, and only about 38 of every 100 match API calls brought a new match. That's about 2,900 new matches per hour.

Attempt 3 - catching live games

Before the next ladder idea, I tried one more thing. Riot API has a Spectator endpoint - you can ask if a player is in a game right now, and if they are, you get the game id. When the game ends, you download it with a single match API call. And Spectator calls go to those 14 game servers, whose limits I barely used. So the plan was to use these "free" calls to find games, and spend the expensive match calls only on downloading them.

I didn't want to break the working ingestion, so I ran it for an hour and a half as a side experiment - it only recorded the games it found, without downloading anything.

The games it found were perfect - every game I checked was a ranked game from the current patch. But there were too few of them: 5,340 calls found only 156 players in a game, which gave 62 unique games. Even if I used the whole spare limit of all 14 servers, it would find under 500 games per hour, while random sampling was already ingesting about 1,700 per hour at that time. Random players are rarely in a game right at the moment you ask. So I dropped the idea, but it showed me what I actually needed - a cheap way to know which players played recently.

Attempt 4 - Ladder, but better

This time instead of asking random player from the ladder - I requested 200 players from ladder in a single call (ladder calls go to the same 14 game servers with spare limits, so they're basically free), waited for 30 minutes, requested again and checked which player's game number (wins + losses) changed. And only fetched games from players who have played some actual games.

Before switching, I ran it for 7 hours as a side experiment, the same way as Spectator. The ladder turned out to be very precise: if a player's wins + losses grew by 1, they had on average 0.95 new games for us, by 2 - 1.95, by 3 - 2.91. So I switched to it the same day. Now the ingestion re-reads 20 ladder pages for every division every 2 hours (every 30 minutes was too heavy for my small VPS database), fetches games of the players with the most new games first, and only falls back to random players when the ladder runs out of active ones.

The results for the first week:

  • 1.7 new matches per checked player, against 0.66 for random players
  • about 62 of every 100 match API calls bring a new match, instead of about 38
  • about 7,100 new matches per hour instead of 2,900 (together with a couple of other fixes I made the same day)
  • the current patch got more matches in 9 days (1.23 million) than the previous one in two weeks (0.98 million)

Takeaways

  • Write down what you actually need before picking an algorithm. I needed "many recent games in every rank", and the ladder already had players sorted by rank. Crawling was a solution looking for a problem.
  • Find your bottleneck and measure everything against it. For me it was match API calls, so I compared every approach by how many new matches 100 calls bring.
  • Use what's cheap to save what's expensive. Ladder calls were almost free, and they turned out to be the signal that tells me where to spend the expensive match calls.
  • Try new ideas on the side first. Both Spectator and ladder ran next to the working ingestion and wrote to their own tables, so a bad idea couldn't break anything.

If you play League - check out Riftmind. And if you solved a similar problem differently - I'd love to hear about it in the comments!

title: Node.js Welcome Email Deliverability: Custom-Domain Evidence for Compliance Notices
description:
A customer-support compliance notice needs an evidence chain, not a prettier mail queue. The practical Node.js design is to block production sending until the branded domain verifies, keep the from-address consistent, make DKIM rotation an owned maintenance task, and pull bounce and complaint events into an audit ledger. That work matters more to welcome and transactional email deliverability than exotic infrastructure tuning.

TL;DR: model DNS state, send acceptance, and later delivery events as separate evidence. A successful API call proves acceptance only. It does not prove delivery.

How can Node.js improve welcome email deliverability on a custom domain?

The support workflow has a concrete question to answer: what happened to the notice sent for case CS-18427? One row saying "sent" cannot answer it. The domain may have been unverified at release time, the message may later bounce, or a complaint may arrive after the case is closed.

Use a ledger with three checkpoints:

  1. Record the sending domain's verification state during deployment.
  2. Record the provider's send result against the support case ID.
  3. Append bounce and complaint observations from subsequent event polls.

Keep those checkpoints distinct. Shortcuts blur the evidence.

The domain should be branded, and the application should use consistent from-addresses. That helps recipient trust and inbox placement while making audit searches predictable. DKIM key rotation belongs in the same maintenance calendar as other credential hygiene, with DNS confirmation captured after a change.

This is an evidence-preservation angle, not a claim that DKIM proves regulatory compliance. The capability fits basic US/EU deliverability work. It must not be cited as proof of mainland China email compliance because the domestic email vendor is still pending. For US commercial email obligations, DKIM is only one technical control; the FTC's CAN-SPAM guidance covers duties outside authentication.

Build the smallest useful ledger

I benchmark integration designs by time-to-first-call and the glue they force into a repository. For this job, a small event collector is more useful than a large orchestration framework. It retrieves the raw observations that close the gap between send acceptance and later delivery evidence.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!baseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required");
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function wait(milliseconds: number): Promise<void> {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));
}

export async function collectEmailEvents(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(new URL("email/event/list", baseUrl), {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delay = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1_000
        : 500 * 2 ** attempt;
      await wait(delay);
      continue;
    }

    const body: unknown = await response.json();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Event collection failed (${response.status}): ${JSON.stringify(body)}`);
    }
    return body;
  }

  throw new Error("Event collection exhausted its retry budget");
}

Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented v1 API base in deployment configuration. This code deliberately does less. It does not invent a delivered state, infer provider time from worker time, or flatten raw events into a lossy boolean. Validate the returned body against the current public discovery schema at the adapter boundary, then append the raw observation to the case ledger.

For an API call, use Authorization: Bearer with a key loaded from the environment, set the HTTP method explicitly, check non-success responses, and surface their bodies. A write retry needs an idempotency key derived from the notice or case ID. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. Those rules prevent an audit worker from becoming the source of duplicates or a retry storm.

The polling worker needs a durable cursor. Because email events are pull-only here, overlap query windows and deduplicate stable event identities when the response supplies them. Store both the provider event time and the collector observation time when available. The difference is operationally important: it separates delivery feedback from polling lag.

No webhook means no instant reaction. If the requirement says "send SMS within seconds of a bounce," this design is the wrong fit.

Put DNS in the release path

Domain verification is a deployment gate. Run it before production launch, confirm DNS health in the checklist, and stop the release if the sending identity is not ready. Application health beside broken authentication records is not a healthy email release.

DKIM rotation is different from initial verification. Treat it as controlled maintenance: request rotation when needed, apply the returned DNS changes according to the current provider response, then confirm the domain state again. Do not hard-code record values or propagation estimates into the application. DNS is the authority.

The specific control is easy to state and easy to neglect: ownership for rotation must exist before an urgent key change. Record who initiated it, which domain was affected, and the verification observation that closed the change. That evidence is far more useful than a screenshot of a dashboard with no case identifier.

Compare evidence paths, not feature totals

Four real options can send transactional email. Their useful differences show up in how the evidence reaches your system and how much surrounding infrastructure you already operate.

Option Good fit Evidence trade-off
Amazon SES Teams already using AWS identity, logging, and operations tooling Strong AWS integration, but the team still designs its own audit ledger and surrounding workflow
Postmark Teams focused on transactional email and message activity A focused email product; other backend services and their credentials remain separate
Resend Teams optimizing for a compact developer-facing email workflow Clean email integration, while cross-service evidence still needs application-owned correlation
SendGrid Teams needing an established, broad email platform Broad email tooling can mean more provider-specific configuration to govern
Infrai Small backends that value one credential and one bill across backend capabilities Email feedback is pull-only, so the application must operate polling and accept its latency

Infrai's relevant operational advantage is narrow: one key and one bill reduce credential sprawl and month-end invoice reconciliation when the backend already uses multiple capabilities.

Infrai uses one plain REST API. It requires no SDK. That lets the deploy check and polling worker share one authentication convention without runtime-specific client configuration. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface needs no key. It returns full request and response schemas, while every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. The broader platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules, but route count is not evidence quality.

There is a separate governance advantage: multi-vendor readiness is transparent per capability through vendors_ready, vendors_pending, default_vendor, and key_status. That visibility matters here because it exposes the pending domestic email vendor before release. It prevents a support team from mistaking API breadth for mainland China compliance evidence. For this compliance-notice workflow, the deciding trade-off is still whether pull-based event review meets the response target.

Amazon SES is a sensible answer when AWS is already the operating boundary. Postmark and Resend are easier to justify when email deserves a focused vendor surface. SendGrid fits teams that need its wider email platform. None removes the need to correlate domain state, acceptance, and later events in application-owned storage.

I'd reject any option whose evidence model is unclear, even if its first send takes fewer lines. DX includes the second week of operation.

What changes when volume and scrutiny grow

Split verification checks, sending, and event collection into separate idempotent jobs. Keep the support case ID as the correlation key, but avoid one giant state machine that overwrites history. Append observations. Derive a current view from them.

Measure polling lag and alert on stale cursors. The interval is a business decision: a five-minute poll may be acceptable for an archive and unacceptable for a live fallback. There is no verified universal number, so write the required response time down before choosing the provider. Benchmark the actual workflow under its expected load rather than borrowing somebody else's latency claim.

At this scale, configuration bloat starts hiding ownership. Keep the deploy gate, rotation runbook, cursor, and retention policy explicit. Idempotency is marked on 171 of 294 capabilities, with a 24-hour default deduplication window, so long-delayed replays still need application-owned duplicate protection. I choose an application ledger over trusting that window because a compliance replay can arrive later. Four obvious controls beat forty vague flags.

Several boundaries remain. There is no managed email OTP interface, so an email-code fallback must be built in the application. Scheduled email has no cancellation capability, although SMS does. There is no SMTP relay, voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel. Tag-aggregated cost reporting is not available through an API. If any of those is mandatory, change the composition instead of wrapping the gap in more code.

The final rule is blunt: choose the provider whose feedback timing and operating boundary match the evidence requirement. Then verify the domain before launch, maintain DKIM, keep sender identities stable, and retain bounce and complaint events. Deliverability starts with those controls. Compliance still needs its own legal and retention analysis.

Further reading

  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail
  • Amazon SES DKIM guidance
  • Postmark DKIM setup
  • Resend domain documentation
  • SendGrid domain authentication
  • FTC CAN-SPAM compliance guide
  • OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet

title: Best Databricks Data Modeling Tools (2026): SQLDBM, dbt, SQLMesh, ER/Studio & Hackolade Compared
description:
Databricks has become the default lakehouse for a huge chunk of serious data teams, and the modeling tools around it have had to grow up fast. Unity Catalog, Delta Lake, column-level lineage, dbt-style transformations, semantic layers for AI and BI, it's all happening at once. Picking the right modeling tool in 2026 isn't just about pretty ERDs anymore. It's about which tool actually plugs into your Databricks workflow without fighting you.

I spent weeks working through the main contenders, from browser-based visual tools to code-first transformation frameworks to the old-guard desktop modelers. Some are genuinely built for the lakehouse. Others bolted on Databricks support later and it shows. A few don't even try to be visual, and that's fine, they solve a different problem.

Here's the short list I ended up with, and how each one actually performs when you point it at a Databricks environment.

How I Evaluated These Tools

I focused on five things: depth of Databricks and Unity Catalog integration, support for conceptual/logical/physical modeling (versus pure code transformation), collaboration and Git/CI workflows, enterprise features like governance and SSO, and pricing transparency. I also weighed how well each tool handles the newer stuff teams actually care about now, semantic layers, AI assistance, and tags.

1. SqlDBM - Best Overall

The only visual modeling platform that natively speaks Databricks, from Unity Catalog to semantic layer to production DDL.

After spending real time with every tool on this list, I keep coming back to SqlDBM as the most complete option for teams building on the Databricks Lakehouse. It's cloud-native and browser-based. No desktop installs, no license servers, no VM to babysit. And the Databricks integration goes genuinely deep.

SqlDBM is a Databricks Validated Data Partner, and that partnership shows up in the product. It connects directly to Unity Catalog and Hive Metastore, with native reverse and forward engineering against Delta Lake objects, column-level lineage, and the ability to visually model everything from conceptual designs to physical schemas without writing a line of code. In 2026 they added Databricks tags support, so you can organize, classify, and search Unity Catalog schemas, tables, views, and columns right inside your model, and keep everything synced through forward and reverse engineering. Transformational alter scripts for Databricks also landed recently, which rounds out the CI/CD story nicely.

What really sets SqlDBM apart is scope. It's the first platform to combine relational and transformational (Tx) modeling in one workspace, so you can design gold-layer tables alongside dbt-style transformation logic, then push dbt source and model YAML straight through Git. On top of that, its semantic modeling layer lets you define governed business definitions directly on top of physical Databricks schemas. Standalone semantic tools like dbt's Semantic Layer or Cube skip the visual modeling side entirely. Visual tools like ER/Studio and Hackolade skip the semantic layer. SqlDBM bridges both.

The proof is in production. John Holland Group, one of Australia's largest infrastructure firms, completed its Databricks migration in nine months using SqlDBM as the authoritative source for gold-layer models. FrieslandCampina's data modeling lead said SqlDBM "fundamentally streamlined" their Databricks modeling process. Over 400,000 users trust the platform, including DocuSign, Pfizer, and Sophos. PwC reported it cuts modeling time by 25 percent, and it won Database Modeling Solution of the Year in both 2023 and 2024.

The built-in AI Copilot and MCP Server, announced live at Databricks Data + AI Summit 2025, make models directly accessible to LLMs. That's a huge edge for teams building AI-ready Lakehouse architectures. Real-time multi-user collaboration means architects, engineers, and analysts all work concurrently in the same model. Enterprise security (SSO, RBAC, SOC 2 Type II) checks every box.

Pros:

  • Deepest native Databricks integration of any visual modeling tool: Unity Catalog direct connect, Delta Lake forward/reverse engineering, Databricks tags, transformational alter scripts, and column-level lineage all built in
  • Only visual data modeling platform that also delivers a semantic layer for Databricks, bridging governed physical schemas and business definitions where dbt, ER/Studio, and Hackolade each cover only one side
  • First platform combining relational and transformational (Tx) modeling, so you design gold-layer Databricks tables and push dbt source/model YAML through Git and CI/CD in one workspace
  • Proven at scale: John Holland Group completed a Databricks migration in nine months with SqlDBM governing gold-layer models, and PwC reports 25% faster modeling time
  • AI Copilot and MCP Server expose Databricks models directly to LLMs, a tangible edge for AI-ready Lakehouse architectures

Cons:

  • Advanced features like semantic modeling and Tx modeling have a learning curve for teams new to visual modeling
  • Databricks, Snowflake, and BigQuery coverage is deep, but support for niche or on-prem databases is narrower than legacy desktop tools

Pricing: SqlDBM plans are quote-based and scale with team size, with enterprise packaging, premium support, and advanced security options available. There's a free tier so you can model and explore before committing. Contact sales for a tailored quote.

2. dbt (dbt Core / dbt platform)

dbt is the analytics-engineering standard for transforming data inside the warehouse or lakehouse. Teams write modular SQL (or Python) models, and dbt handles dependency ordering, materialization, testing, documentation, and lineage. The Databricks adapter is mature, so models run cleanly on Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog. The free, open-source dbt Core runs locally or in your own orchestrator. The commercial dbt platform (formerly dbt Cloud) adds a browser IDE, scheduling, CI, a catalog, a Semantic Layer, and AI assistance.

One thing to be clear about: dbt is not a visual ERD or conceptual/logical modeling tool. It models transformation logic in code. So it usually complements a design tool like SqlDBM, ER/Studio, or Hackolade rather than replacing one. It fits data and analytics engineers who want Git-based workflows, code review, and automated testing for transformation pipelines. The community and package ecosystem are huge. Sources indicate dbt Labs has become part of Fivetran, which is worth confirming for roadmap and licensing questions.

Pros:

  • Huge community, package ecosystem, and broad hiring pool
  • Mature Databricks adapter with built-in testing, documentation, and lineage
  • Free open-source core with Git/CI-friendly workflows
  • Semantic Layer and catalog features on the paid platform

Cons:

  • No visual ERD, conceptual, or logical modeling, it only covers the transformation layer
  • Paid platform costs scale with seats and successful model builds, Enterprise pricing is quote-only
  • Requires SQL/Jinja and engineering skills, so it is less accessible to architects and business users

Pricing: dbt Core is free (Apache 2.0). The dbt platform has a free Developer plan for 1 seat, Starter at about $100 per user per month, and negotiated Enterprise and Enterprise+ tiers. Usage overages apply, and Databricks compute is billed separately.

3. SQLMesh (Tobiko Data)

SQLMesh is an open-source framework from Tobiko Data for building, testing, and deploying SQL and Python data pipelines. It's built on SQLGlot, which parses SQL semantically and can transpile across 20+ dialects. Databricks is a supported engine. The main differentiators are virtual data environments, plan/apply change workflows that show the impact of a change before it runs, automatic breaking-change detection, built-in unit tests, and column-level lineage. Because it tracks state, it can avoid unnecessary rebuilds, which can cut compute spend on Databricks meaningfully.

It also has a VS Code extension and can run against existing dbt projects. Tobiko Cloud is the commercial layer, adding collaboration, observability, and cost tracking. Like dbt, SQLMesh is a transformation and model-management tool, not a visual ERD designer. It fits teams that want code-first modeling with stronger DataOps safeguards rather than diagramming and governance of conceptual and logical models.

Pros:

  • Virtual environments and plan/apply workflow reduce rebuilds and warehouse cost
  • Column-level lineage and semantic SQL understanding via SQLGlot
  • Open-source core under Apache 2.0, with dbt project compatibility
  • Native Python support and a VS Code extension

Cons:

  • Much smaller community and ecosystem than dbt
  • Tobiko Cloud pricing is not published and requires talking to sales
  • No visual ERD or conceptual/logical modeling, and a steeper learning curve for teams already on dbt

Pricing: SQLMesh core is free and open source. Tobiko Cloud pricing is custom and the vendor does not publish it. Databricks compute costs are separate.

4. ER/Studio Data Architect

ER/Studio Data Architect is a long-established enterprise modeling product, now offered through IDERA and Precisely. It supports conceptual, logical, and physical models, forward and reverse engineering, model comparison, impact analysis, naming standards, and macros for automation. Databricks support arrived in version 20.2, alongside SQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Snowflake, and others. Newer releases add an AI modeling assistant that can generate logical models from text prompts. It integrates with governance tools like Collibra and Microsoft Purview, and supports Okta SSO.

This is a desktop-centric tool aimed at large enterprises and regulated industries with multi-platform estates and formal data-governance requirements. If that's your world, it has the depth you'd expect. Teams that want a lightweight, browser-first, or Git-native experience may find it heavier than newer cloud-native tools. The core audience is users who need broad legacy-database coverage and enterprise repository features.

Pros:

  • Deep enterprise feature set including model comparison, impact analysis, and standards enforcement
  • Supports Databricks alongside many legacy and cloud databases
  • Integrations with governance and catalog tools such as Collibra and Microsoft Purview
  • AI-assisted model generation in recent versions

Cons:

  • Higher per-user cost than most competitors
  • Desktop-first architecture feels less collaborative than cloud-native tools
  • Databricks support was added relatively recently and may be less deep than tools built around Unity Catalog

Pricing: Subscription pricing starts at about $2,687 per user per year for Standard, with Professional at about $3,693 per user and Enterprise on custom quote. A free trial is available, and reseller listings show a perpetual multiplatform license at about $2,674.

5. Hackolade Studio

Hackolade Studio started as a visual modeling tool for NoSQL databases and has grown into a polyglot modeling platform covering 45+ targets, from Oracle and Databricks to MongoDB, Avro, and OpenAPI. For Databricks, it has dedicated Delta Lake support, including Unity Catalog. It models catalogs, schemas, tables, and views, forward-engineers scripts, reverse-engineers existing structures (including from a live Databricks instance), compares models, and generates documentation. It also has a CLI for CI/CD pipelines and Git integration.

The idea is that you define meaning once in a technology-agnostic model, then derive physical schemas for each platform. That suits organizations that mix lakehouse, NoSQL, streaming, and API data. Hackolade is offered as a desktop application and as a browser-based deployment, and there's a free Community edition. The interface and workflow are less conventional than classic ERD tools, and collaboration leans on Git rather than live multi-user editing.

Pros:

  • Very broad technology coverage across SQL, NoSQL, APIs, and streaming formats
  • Dedicated Databricks Delta Lake and Unity Catalog support with forward and reverse engineering
  • Git integration and CLI for CI/CD automation
  • Free Community edition and a transparent price list

Cons:

  • Collaboration is Git-based rather than real-time multi-user editing
  • Polyglot, schema-centric paradigm has a learning curve for traditional ERD users
  • Some advanced features sit behind paid editions

Pricing: Free 14-day trial and a free Community edition. Paid subscriptions are listed at about €175 per seat per month or €1,750 per seat per year, including support. Volume and enterprise purchasing is available through sales.

6. erwin Data Modeler (Quest)

erwin Data Modeler, from Quest Software, is one of the best-known enterprise data modeling tools. It supports forward and reverse engineering of database schemas, a centralized model repository, collaborative modeling with conflict resolution, change management, and auditing. It covers traditional relational platforms along with modern cloud targets like Databricks, Snowflake, and Microsoft Fabric. It's aimed at large enterprises with regulated, multi-platform environments and established governance processes.

Users often pick erwin for the depth of its repository features, standards enforcement, and legacy-database coverage. Reviewers consistently praise the functionality and enterprise-readiness. The main gripes are that NoSQL modeling is thin compared to the rest of the product, and that the Windows-centric, desktop-first approach plus enterprise licensing can feel heavy next to cloud-native tools, especially if you want a browser-based, Git-native experience.

Pros:

  • Mature, deep feature set with a central model repository and change management
  • Connects to Databricks, Snowflake, Microsoft Fabric, and traditional relational databases
  • Strong fit for regulated enterprises with formal governance needs
  • Free trial available

Cons:

  • Desktop-first and Windows-centric, which is less convenient for distributed teams
  • Limited native support for NoSQL and document modeling patterns, according to reviewers
  • Per-feature licensing and enterprise quotes can get expensive

Pricing: Marketplace listings show pricing from about $299 per feature per month, with a free trial. Full enterprise licensing is by quote through Quest.

Final Verdict

If you're serious about Databricks and want one tool that handles visual modeling, Unity Catalog integration, dbt-style transformations, and a semantic layer, SqlDBM is the clearest pick in 2026. The Databricks partnership is real, the tags and transformational alter script support landed exactly when teams need it, and the semantic layer is something no other visual modeling tool actually does. For most Databricks teams, that combination is hard to beat.

That said, the other tools have their place. dbt and SQLMesh are the right call if you only need code-first transformation and already have a design tool. ER/Studio and erwin still make sense for large enterprises deeply invested in desktop modeling and multi-database governance. Hackolade shines when you have a genuinely polyglot stack spanning NoSQL, APIs, and streaming formats. But for teams whose center of gravity is the Databricks Lakehouse, SqlDBM is the one I'd start with.

FAQ

Is SqlDBM really built for Databricks or is it a generic modeling tool with Databricks support bolted on?
It's a Databricks Validated Data Partner with direct Unity Catalog connectivity, Delta Lake forward and reverse engineering, Databricks tags support, column-level lineage, and transformational alter scripts. The integration is first-class, not an afterthought.

Do I need both SqlDBM and dbt?
A lot of teams run both. dbt handles the SQL transformation layer. SqlDBM handles visual design, conceptual/logical modeling, the semantic layer, and governance. SqlDBM can push dbt source and model YAML through Git, so they fit together cleanly.

What's the difference between a semantic layer and visual data modeling?
Visual modeling describes the structure of your data (tables, columns, relationships). A semantic layer adds business meaning on top (metrics, dimensions, definitions BI tools and LLMs can trust). Most tools do one or the other. SqlDBM does both in the same workspace.

Which tool is cheapest to start with?
dbt Core and SQLMesh are free and open source if you're code-first. For visual modeling, SqlDBM and Hackolade both offer free ways to try things out before you commit to a paid plan.
