title: OPC UA in action: the SLX GridPilot industrial digital twin
description:
OPC UA becomes easier to understand when a command produces an observable response. A power request, a valve opening, a rotating machine and an alarm connect the protocol to process behavior. With SLX GridPilot, Silicon LogiX presents a desktop application for exploring that path: from the nodes of an OPC UA server to the control of two reversible hydroelectric units and their 3D representation.

The starting point is precise: OPC UA communication and the control runtime are real; the plant is simulated. The computer runs clients, three independent servers and the Eclipse 4diac FORTE runtime. Water, rotating machinery, electrical power and equipment faults belong to the numerical model. This software laboratory serves both people approaching industrial automation and engineers evaluating interfaces, information models and diagnostics without connecting physical equipment.

What is OPC UA, and why does it matter in industrial automation?

OPC Unified Architecture is a platform-independent interoperability architecture. In the client-server model, a server exposes information and services that a client can discover and use: variables, objects, methods and events. For industrial automation, its value includes communicating the meaning of data through types and relationships, beyond a list of numeric values.

A unit's speed, for example, can be presented together with its data type, engineering unit, quality and timestamp. A client can browse the model, read a measurement, call a method and receive notifications. GridPilot applies these operations to a visible scenario: two reversible units, U1 and U2, generating electricity or moving water toward the upper reservoir in pumping mode.

A digital twin demonstrator built around OPC UA

The initial OPC UA Studio workspace displays connected servers, monitored items and notifications received in the current sessions. A live operation map distinguishes the client, servers, FORTE control, simulated equipment and feedback path. These indicators help explain which part of the system is working and where the displayed data comes from.

OPC UA Studio in version 0.4.2. Counters describe actual client connections and notifications; the guided tour verifies server responses.
The three local endpoints represent plant services and the two units: opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4840, opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4841 and opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4842. An external OPC UA client can explore the same model and call its methods. The 3D scene receives state through OPC UA, just like the interface indicators. Selecting U1 or U2 highlights the corresponding unit and lets the operator locate it in the plant view.

From command to feedback: what actually happens

Requesting power does not mean that power has already been delivered. Calling SetPower(1.2) on U1's endpoint requests 1.2 MW of generation. The method's initial response confirms that the request has been queued. LastCommand then reports acceptance or rejection, while power, state and actuator positions show the observed outcome. Hydraulic availability and interlocks can limit the result even when a command is accepted.

The coordinator presents the request to FORTE control logic, which manages sequences and operating limits. The numerical model evolves from the actuator targets; the resulting state is published by the servers and returns to the client through subscriptions. The interface therefore distinguishes request received, command accepted and behavior achieved. The same principle applies to Stop(): confirming a stop requires feedback such as zero speed and closed flow-control devices.

Functional architecture of the demonstrator. OPC UA connects the supervisor to the servers; the coordinator uses local connections to control and model components. Calculated state returns to the servers and client, which also updates the 3D scene.

Exploring OPC UA nodes, types and information models

The integrated browser performs actual Browse and Read operations. Users can search for a node, inspect its type, copy its NodeId and examine quality, timestamps and engineering units. Persistent watchlists follow selected variables, while filters help locate measurements whose quality differs from Good.

A NodeId identifies a node within a namespace. GridPilot's application namespace is urn:siliconlogix:gridpilot:v1. A client must resolve its index on the server instead of assuming that a fixed number always identifies the same namespace. This is a practical detail to understand when moving from an example to integration between different applications.

NodeSet2 XML export, alongside JSON and CSV, documents browsed instances, types and method arguments. It describes the information model: it is neither an executable server backup nor a complete recording of its events.

Subscriptions, quality and timestamps: reading data in context

An OPC UA subscription lets a client receive notifications for configured monitored items. The sampling interval concerns observation of the data; the publishing interval governs notification delivery. A numeric deadband defines a change threshold. The server can revise the requested intervals, and GridPilot exposes those values together with the status of individual monitored items.

Watchlists use a dedicated subscription. Coherent plant state arrives in the Snapshot variable, so indicators and the scene do not have to reconstruct a process snapshot by combining independent reads. SourceTimestamp refers to the sample's UTC publication time; SimTime represents simulated process time. Pausing the simulation therefore does not stop the communication clock.

Quality and freshness have visible consequences: uncertain measurements are identified, and state that no longer receives updates is marked stale. Machine animations do not advance beyond the latest confirmed pose. Motion thus helps users read the available telemetry.

OPC UA faults and alarms: acknowledgement is separate from recovery

The demonstrator supports repeatable actuator, sensor, communication and electrical faults. A simulated speed-sensor error also produces an observable quality change on the OPC UA node. Injecting communication loss for a unit actually shuts down its endpoint, allowing users to examine disconnection, reconnection and the controller's response.

The servers expose standard OPC UA OffNormalAlarmType conditions with severity, message, active state and acknowledgement. An operator can acknowledge a condition and add a comment. Acknowledgement does not remove the fault's cause or automatically release the controller latch: recovery must restore the required conditions. This release uses the experimental Alarms & Conditions support in open62541 1.4.14 and makes no claim of OPC UA conformance certification.

Learning through a guided path and observable checks

The OPC UA Studio tour moves from browsing U1 to requesting power, confirming a stop and injecting a sensor fault, followed by alarm acknowledgement and recovery. Each step advances when the expected feedback is observed. Missing or stale data cannot confirm an outcome.

The plant view complements the experience with overview, cutaway and unit-detail modes. Rotation, flow-control devices, flow indicators and electrical activity make it easier to connect a variable to the relevant machine. Graphics represent received state; the numerical model and control logic determine process evolution.

The Plant view places the 3D model beside operator requests and confirmed values. U1 and U2 labels connect each unit card to its location in the plant.

The technology stack: Rust, Slint, Bevy, open62541 and FORTE

The architecture gives each technology a distinct role. Rust is used for coordination, supervision and the numerical engine. Slint provides the desktop interface; Bevy, together with wgpu, handles the 3D scene and glTF models. Interface and visualization share confirmed process state.

open62541 is the C OPC UA stack used for the servers and client adapter. Eclipse 4diac FORTE is a runtime for function-block applications based on IEC 61499. In GridPilot it executes the application block governing startup, stop, reversal and fault handling. The coordinator maintains a fixed 100 ms step and connects control to the numerical model; supervisor-to-device communication goes through OPC UA.

The hydraulic model is lumped and quasi-steady, with constant efficiencies, actuator limits and water/energy accounting. It is suitable for studying the demonstrator and its interfaces. Designing an actual hydro plant requires further modeling and validation: water hammer, cavitation, electrical-grid transients and qualified electrical protections are examples of phenomena outside this model.

Trends, replay and tests for comparing behavior

The Workbench brings together sequence diagnostics, local numeric history, multivariable charts and CSV export. Commands and alarms can be read alongside measurement trends. Recording, replay, pause and temporal seeking support session review, while test plans define scheduled actions and expected results checked against observed feedback.

For industrial software developers, these functions offer a basis for discussing concrete requirements: how to represent unreliable data, when to declare a command complete, what information to export and what conditions to verify after an interruption. Project checks concern the software and demonstrator model; they do not replace commissioning tests on a real plant.

Download GridPilot and discuss a custom OPC UA project

The SLX GridPilot 0.4.2 release provides a portable Windows x64 package. Download the Windows ZIP, extract the complete folder and launch SLX GridPilot.exe. No compiler, package installation, cloud service or field hardware is required. A Vulkan-capable graphics driver is required. The release also includes SHA-256 checksums for checking the download.

Demonstrator endpoints are limited to the local computer, with anonymous access and SecurityPolicy None. OPC UA provides security mechanisms, but configuring certificates, identities, roles and protected communication for production requires dedicated engineering and verification. The package does not include a preconfigured connection to a physical PLC.

The public repository contains operator documentation, selected screenshots, licensing information and publication checks. The Windows ZIP includes the required runtime data, dependency licenses and corresponding third-party sources. GridPilot's application implementations are proprietary and distributed in compiled form; SDK headers and application sources are excluded from the public distribution. The product license permits study and business evaluation; production integration and redistribution of modifications require written permission. Dependency licenses remain independent.

For an industrial application, a next step may be designing an OPC UA information model, integrating devices and PLCs, developing dedicated supervision, or defining interoperability and recovery tests. These are extensions to agree within a specific project, starting with the actual equipment, security requirements and acceptance criteria. To discuss a project with Silicon LogiX, contact us with the process, the data to expose and the operations the software must support.

Further reading and official documentation

These references lead directly to the respective projects and official specifications for the concepts and technologies discussed:

  • OPC UA: the OPC Foundation introduction and online OPC UA specifications.
  • Security and alarms: OPC UA Part 2: Security Model and OPC UA Part 9: Alarms & Conditions.
  • Clients and servers: open62541 1.4.14 documentation, for the version used in the demonstrator.
  • IEC 61499 control: the Eclipse 4diac FORTE runtime.
  • Language: the official Rust website.
  • Desktop interface: the Slint framework.
  • 3D visualization: the Bevy engine.

Originally published at Silicon LogiX.

title: Your HTML-to-PDF Invoices Look Different in Every Tool. Here's Why.
description:
The first time I generated invoice PDFs from HTML, the staging version looked perfect and the production version quietly moved the totals block to page two, alone, like it had been exiled. Same HTML, same CSS, different converter. That day I learned the fact that governs all HTML-to-PDF work: there is no single "HTML to PDF." There are several rendering engines with different subsets of CSS, different default margins, and different ideas about when a page should break. The output differences are not bugs in your markup. They are the engines, being themselves.

The three families you will actually meet

  • Browser engines (headless Chromium via Puppeteer/Playwright, or hosted tools built on it) render your page the way Chrome does — modern CSS, flexbox and grid, web fonts — then print it. If your invoice looks right in Chrome's print preview, this family will treat you best.
  • Dedicated layout engines (WeasyPrint, Prince) implement the CSS paged-media spec more faithfully — running headers, page counters, cross-references — but lag on newer layout CSS.
  • Legacy converters (older wkhtmltopdf builds and friends) use ancient WebKit. Flexbox is partial, grid is a rumor, and every project eventually has the "why is this column the whole page" incident.

My current one-off jobs go through an HTML-to-PDF converter built on a browser engine; in pipelines I pin one engine in the dependency file and treat changing it as a migration, with visual diffs, not an upgrade.

The CSS that actually controls a printed page

Most invoice-print bugs are five properties wearing trench coats:

  1. @page { size: A4; margin: ... } — set the paper and margins in CSS, or accept each engine's defaults, which differ. US Letter vs A4 alone explains a class of "it fits here but not there."
  2. break-inside: avoid on blocks that must not split — totals, signature areas, table rows groups. Without it, every engine breaks content where the page happens to end.
  3. thead repetition — browsers repeat a table's header group on each printed page if you use real thead markup; divs pretending to be headers do not repeat, which is how invoices end up with a page of orphan numbers.
  4. Print color — backgrounds vanish by default in print CSS (print-color-adjust: exact restores the ones you actually want, like a shaded header row).
  5. Fonts the engine can see. A webfont your page loads from a CDN may or may not be fetched by the converter; self-hosting the font or embedding it removes the coin flip, and invoices are not the place for coin flips.

The discipline that ends the surprises

Keep one golden sample — the nastiest invoice you produce: multi-page, long item descriptions, a discount, a tax line, a note in small print — and render it with your pinned engine on every change. Compare page count and eyeball page two; totals drift is visible in seconds. And generate the PDF at the moment of issue with the same engine that renders your preview, so the customer never sees a layout you have not.

HTML-to-PDF is a good architecture — one template, styled with skills your team already has. It just punishes the assumption that print is a screenshot of the screen. Treat the page as a separate medium with its own five rules, pin your engine, and the exiled totals block stays home.

title: Designing Tools Your AI Agent Will Actually Use Correctly
description:
The previous article showed how to wire tools into a Spring AI agent. The mechanics are straightforward — annotate a method, pass it to the ChatClient, done. What's less obvious is that the quality of your tools determines whether the agent works correctly.

A poorly described tool gets called at the wrong time, with the wrong arguments, or not at all. A well-designed tool gets called exactly when it should, with exactly the right input.

The description is an instruction to the model

When you write @Tool(description = "..."), that string isn't documentation for your team. It's a runtime instruction that the model reads before every single request.

The model's decision process looks like this:

  1. What did the user ask?
  2. What tools do I have available? (reads each description)
  3. Do I need a tool to answer this? Which one?
  4. What arguments should I pass? (reads each @ToolParam description)

If your description is vague, the model makes a guess. Sometimes the guess is right. Often it isn't — and because it's a language model, it won't tell you it was guessing. It will just proceed with what seemed most reasonable.

Vague description:

@Tool(description = "Get weather")
public String getWeather(String city) { ... }

The model doesn't know: Is this current weather or a forecast? What does it return — temperature? conditions? Both? What format is the city name expected in?

Clear description:

@Tool(description = "Get the current weather for a city in India. " +
    "Returns temperature in Celsius and sky conditions (sunny, cloudy, rainy). " +
    "Use this when the user asks about current weather or whether to carry an umbrella.")
public String getWeather(
        @ToolParam(description = "City name in English, e.g. Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru") 
        String city) { ... }

Now the model knows exactly when to call it, what it returns, and how to pass the city name. Same method, entirely different instruction.

What to include in a tool description

A useful tool description answers four questions:

What does it do? State the action clearly. "Fetches", "returns", "calculates", "queries" — be specific about the operation.

When should the model use it? This is the most commonly missed part. Add a "use this when..." clause. Without it, the model may skip the tool in cases where it should call it, because it isn't sure the tool applies.

What does it return? Describe the shape of the output. If it returns a price, say what currency. If it returns a date, say what format. If it returns a list, say roughly how many items.

What are the constraints? If the tool only works for certain inputs — cities in India, dates in the future, IDs that exist in the database — say that. The model will avoid calling it in unsupported cases, which prevents unnecessary tool failures.

Example applying all four:

@Tool(description = "Get the cheapest available bus or train ticket price between two cities in India. " +
    "Returns the price in INR and the transport type (bus or train). " +
    "Use this when the user asks about travel cost, ticket price, or how to get between cities. " +
    "Only works for cities with bus or rail connections — does not cover flights.")
public String getTicketPrice(
        @ToolParam(description = "Departure city name in English, e.g. Bengaluru") String from,
        @ToolParam(description = "Destination city name in English, e.g. Mysore") String to) {
    // ...
}

Writing good parameter descriptions

Parameter descriptions are just as important as the tool description. The model constructs arguments from them.

Be specific about format:

// Bad — model doesn't know what format to use
@ToolParam(description = "Date") String date

// Good — model knows exactly what to pass
@ToolParam(description = "Travel date in YYYY-MM-DD format, e.g. 2026-10-15") String date

Specify units:

// Bad
@ToolParam(description = "Budget") int amount

// Good
@ToolParam(description = "Maximum budget in INR, e.g. 5000") int amountInr

Clarify expected values for enums or limited options:

@ToolParam(description = "Seat class: SLEEPER, AC_3_TIER, or AC_2_TIER") String seatClass

When the model knows the exact expected values, it passes valid ones instead of guessing.

Returning results the model can reason about

Your tool's return value is what the model reads next. It uses that text to decide what to do — call another tool, ask a clarifying question, or produce the final answer.

Don't return raw JSON:

// Bad — the model has to parse this in its head
return "{\"temp\":28,\"condition\":\"PC\",\"humidity\":85}";

The model can handle JSON, but it has to mentally parse it first. That's cognitive overhead that introduces errors. Write the return value as natural language.

Return readable sentences:

// Good — the model reads this like a human would
return "Current weather in Mumbai: 28°C, partly cloudy, humidity 85%.";

Include context in the result:

If a tool fetches a price, include what the price is for. The model may call multiple tools and combine results — it needs context in each result to do that correctly.

// Without context — confusing when combined with other results
return "₹3,240";

// With context — clear when combined
return "Flight from Bengaluru to Goa on 2026-11-15: ₹3,240 (economy, non-stop, IndiGo 6E-502).";

Common failure modes

The model answers without calling the tool

This happens when the description doesn't say when to use the tool, and the model happens to know something relevant from training data. It answers directly, skipping the tool entirely.

Fix: add "Use this when..." to the description. Add to the system prompt: "Always use available tools to get current information — do not answer from memory."

The model calls the tool with the wrong argument format

A date tool receiving "15th October 2026" instead of "2026-10-15". A city tool receiving "Blr" instead of "Bengaluru".

Fix: specify the exact format in @ToolParam. Add examples: "e.g. 2026-10-15", "e.g. Bengaluru".

The model calls the wrong tool

Two tools with similar descriptions cause the model to mix them up. A getWeather and a getForecast tool with overlapping descriptions leads to unpredictable choices.

Fix: make descriptions explicitly distinct. State what each tool does NOT do: "Returns current conditions — for forecasts, use getForecast."

The tool returns an error and the model hallucinates a result

The tool throws an exception, returns an empty string, or returns an error message the model didn't expect. The model sees this as an unhelpful result and fabricates what the result probably would have been.

Fix: return meaningful error strings, not exceptions. "Unable to fetch weather for this city — city not found." is something the model can relay honestly to the user. An uncaught exception that surfaces as an empty result is something the model will try to paper over.

How many tools is too many?

There's no hard rule, but there's a practical limit. A model given 20 tools spends more time deciding which one to use. The chance of picking the wrong tool increases. The context window fills with tool definitions.

Keep tools focused. One tool should do one thing. A tool that fetches weather AND attractions AND ticket prices is three tools masquerading as one — split it.

Name tools clearly. The tool name is part of what the model reads. getWeather, getAttractions, getTicketPrice are clear. getData, fetch, process are not.

Remove tools the agent doesn't need. If a tool exists but the current use case will never need it, don't register it. Fewer tools mean faster, more accurate decisions.

Testing your tools

Tool quality is easy to verify. Ask questions that should and shouldn't trigger each tool, then inspect whether the right tools were called with the right arguments.

Three test cases every tool should pass:

Positive case — ask something that clearly requires this tool. Verify it was called and returned a sensible result.

Negative case — ask something unrelated. Verify the tool was NOT called.

Edge case — ask something ambiguous or with unusual input. Verify the arguments the model constructed are valid.

Add logging to each tool method during development:

@Tool(description = "...")
public String getWeather(@ToolParam(description = "City name") String city) {
    log.info("getWeather called with city={}", city);
    // ...
}

The log shows you exactly what the model passed. Wrong argument format? Fix the @ToolParam description. Tool not called at all? Fix the tool description or the system prompt.

What's next

Tools are methods. The agent loop runs them in sequence or parallel. But there's a limit to what single tool calls can do — some problems require a model to plan across many steps, remember intermediate results, and course-correct when something goes wrong. That's where more structured agent patterns come in.

The next article covers memory in agents — how to give your agent context from previous turns so it can handle multi-turn conversations, remember what it learned from earlier tool calls, and build on its own previous answers.

Sham Prakash K — Backend Engineer, 4+ years in Java, Spring Boot, and distributed systems. Building AI backend infrastructure. Writing about what I actually learned, mistakes included.

title: Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies
description:
title: "Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies"
published: true
published_at: "2026-12-28T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [systemdesign, database, scalability, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of system design architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Sharding Keys: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Range-Based Vs Hash-Based Sharding: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Cross-Shard Joins And Distributed Transactions: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Consistent Hashing: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Database Sharding and Partitioning: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling Strategies functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: System design Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Sharding keys, range-based vs hash-based sharding, cross-shard joins and distributed transactions, consistent hashing, and rebalancing shards."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: React state has no type of its own. I gave it one, and it compiles away
description:
In Vue, Solid, and Angular, state has a type of its own: Ref<T>, Accessor<T>, Signal<T>.

In React, the count from useState is just a number. Nothing in the type tells you:

  • that it re-renders the component,
  • that it belongs in the dependency array of an effect,
  • that a closure may be holding an old copy of it.

Those questions are left to you and to lint rules. I wanted the type to answer them, so I built
react-preprocessor.

Status: experimental. The API is still changing. I am posting this to get feedback.

What it looks like

State is Reactive<T>. What is computed from it is Derived<T>.

import { $, reactive } from "react-preprocessor";

type Todo = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean };

export const Todos = ({ owner }: { owner: string }) => {
  const todos = reactive.new<Todo[]>([]); // Reactive<Todo[]>
  const left = todos.derive((list) => list.filter((t) => !t.done).length); // Derived<number>

  reactive.effect(() => {
    document.title = `${owner}: ${$(left)} left`;
  });

  return (
    <ul>
      {todos.each(
        (todo) => todo.id,
        (todo) => (
          <li onClick={() => todo.focus("done").update((done) => !done)}>
            {todo.derive((t) => t.title)}
          </li>
        ),
      )}
    </ul>
  );
};

At build time, this is rewritten into plain React:

import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

type Todo = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean };

export const Todos = ({ owner }: { owner: string }) => {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState<Todo[]>([]);
  const left = todos.filter((t) => !t.done).length;
  useEffect(() => {
    document.title = `${owner}: ${left} left`;
  }, [owner, left]);
  return (
    <ul>
      {todos.map((todo) => (
        <li
          onClick={() =>
            setTodos((prev) =>
              prev.map((item) => (item.id === todo.id ? { ...item, done: !item.done } : item)),
            )
          }
          key={todo.id}
        >
          {todo.title}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

What the preprocessor wrote for you:

  1. The dependency array [owner, left], from what the effect reads.
  2. The nested immutable update, from todo.focus("done").update(...). The item is found by key, not by index, so the update hits the right item even if the list was reordered in the same batch.
  3. The key, from the first argument of todos.each.

The rules

  • There is no get. You cannot pull the value out of a Reactive<T>. You derive from it, or put it in JSX.
  • Using a reactive value as a plain value (`${count}`, if (count)) is a build error with a code frame.
  • Updates are pure functions: update(old => next). set(next) is the shortcut for a constant.
  • Nested state is updated through lenses (focus, each). Unions are narrowed with when and match, and the narrowed value is still writable.

The source is valid TypeScript, so your editor, type checker, and formatter work unchanged.

What it is not

  • Not a runtime library. Reactive<T> exists only at compile time. The output imports only React.
  • Not a performance tool. Memoization is left to the React Compiler, which runs after the preprocessor: 
React + sugar (.tsx)
  ↓ react-preprocessor
plain React (.tsx)
  ↓ React Compiler
optimized React

Low commitment

  • Adopt per file. Files without the sugar are left as they are.
  • See the output. react-preprocessor print src/Todos.tsx prints the plain React a file becomes.
  • Leave any time. react-preprocessor eject src --write rewrites the project to the plain React it compiles to.

It works with Vite, Next.js (Turbopack or webpack), and Babel. It also has a Jotai adapter and an oxlint/ESLint rule.

Try it

  • In the browser: the website lets you edit the examples and see the plain React they become.
  • In a project: pnpm add -D react-preprocessor, then follow the setup in the README.

Feedback wanted

I would like to hear:

  1. Does the Reactive<T> / Derived<T> split make the code easier to read for you, or harder?
  2. Which part of the API feels wrong?

Issues and comments are welcome on GitHub. A star helps other people find it.

title: Building Inventory Applications That Don’t Lose Track Of Their Inventory
description:
Let’s imagine we have an inventory system. Two of its customers decide to order the last remaining unit of a given product at roughly the same time. Does our application allow both of these orders to go through?

This is just one example of a complex series of constraints and rules which go into making an inventory system.

Spreadsheets can be useful, but businesses that want centralized visibility, automation, and protection from mistakes need something more powerful.

Let’s look at some fundamentals of the inventory application development process and consider how engineers can build more robust, reliable tools.

1. Build Inventory Records With Audit Trails

Begin by creating or identifying the data model which our application will use. At the simplest possible level, this might consist of a product ID, product name, SKU, and stock quantity.

In practice, however, it will likely be necessary to track more information. Perhaps we will need to track where inventory is stored, or what products have been reserved for specific customers. Auditing and debugging issues later on will become significantly easier if we leave behind a paper trail of what events occurred and when.

Some examples of this information might include:

• What inventory adjustments have occurred? Has inventory been received from a supplier, sold to a customer, or returned? Has it been transferred from one warehouse to another?

• How did the application reach the state that it is currently in?

• What is the reason for this adjustment? Does it involve an order or reservation?

• What quantity of the given product has been physically affected by this transaction?

• What time did this occur, and what other contextual information might be relevant?

We may also want to associate inventory records with other values, such as an order ID or a customer reserving this product. In a multi-warehouse environment, a given inventory record might also have a location field.

Depending on specific business logic, the data model will take shape. It is important to track all of the relevant adjustments as transactions and build an auditable paper trail.

2. Avoid Overselling With Transactional Integrity

Let’s return to the example of two customers attempting to place an order for the last remaining unit of a product. We want to sell one unit of this product to one customer and prevent the other customer from getting the same item, but it is very difficult to do so if both processes read and write information concurrently.

Using a relational or NoSQL database engine, it might be possible to prevent this sort of issue through transactions and concurrency controls.

The above SQL statement, for instance, will reduce a product’s inventory by 1 if the quantity of this product is at least 1 and prevent any such changes from occurring otherwise.

An application making this request should then be able to determine whether one row was affected (in which case the update was successful) or zero rows (in which case the requested update has failed). This is useful, but there are also additional nuances and edge cases which need to be considered. This includes whether this is the right approach in the context of a reserve-inventory system, what happens if a similar request comes in again later, what occurs when transactions need to be applied concurrently, inventory location and availability, or how this will impact order cancellations.

The point is to ensure that the application itself prevents overselling rather than relying solely on application-layer controls.

3. Automate Inventory Updates With Caution

Inventory automation systems can be immensely helpful. By ensuring that inventory changes occur automatically when certain processes are followed, there is less of a need for manual records or adjustments to go wrong. An automated inventory application might automatically update quantity fields when a purchase is made or an order is processed.

There is a good reason to be cautious, however. The same automation that helps can also hurt if there is no appropriate protection in place. For instance, if the application tries to update inventory again after it has already done so successfully, it will lead to double-counting errors.

We can avoid such issues by including appropriate transaction constraints, such as idempotency keys. Inventory record validation is also important, particularly since we will be working with other systems such as payment processors, order management tools, and warehouses.

4. Barcode Reader And RFID Inventory System Software Requirements

Barcode scanners and RFID (radio-frequency identification) readers offer similar advantages. They allow products to be uniquely identified without requiring human intervention. They are valuable tools in warehouses, as they can help ensure that physical inventory changes are reflected in digital inventory records. They can work in tandem with inventory applications or be incorporated as part of an integrated system.

RFID readers operate differently than barcode scanners and can be further categorized into active and passive variants, depending on whether RFID tags are powered by their own batteries.

An RFID reader will generally operate within a working range (a distance of several centimeters to a few meters) and scan for RFID tags within this area. If RFID tags are affixed to products within this range, it will be possible to obtain unique RFID identifiers for these products.

As with barcode scanners, the specific details will vary depending on the specific use case. Some examples might involve scanning barcodes or QR codes, scanning multiple products at once, determining quantity, or performing inventory verification.

From a software standpoint, such systems should be able to translate a barcode or RFID tag into a given product. The application will also want to verify that the request is legitimate and actually allowed and perform the relevant inventory adjustments for the given RFID or barcode.

It is necessary to choose a method based on the specifics of the inventory environment. RFID systems tend to be more valuable at certain points and less valuable at others. They are generally much more expensive than traditional barcode scanners, for instance, but do not always need to be applied to individual products and can be read without being seen.

5. Inventory Application API: Exposing Product Catalog And Inventory

Inventory applications tend to integrate with a variety of other tools, ranging from e-commerce platforms to enterprise resource planning systems. An API will generally want to expose how inventory information is structured, how requests should be processed, and what error conditions can occur. There are also broader architectural decisions which need to be made as well.

Some important considerations include authorization, authentication, validating incoming requests (particularly IDs), rate limiting, transaction retries, error reporting, and product categorization.

Larger applications, in particular, should consider implementing an event-driven or asynchronous architecture, rather than making direct requests and receiving responses. In practice, asynchronous systems can be even more challenging to develop and are often more error-prone, unless there is a very compelling reason to adopt them. A database and transaction engine will likely suffice for the needs of most applications.

6. Build Inventory Management Reports And Insights To Support Decision Making

Inventory records can be analyzed to produce insights on inventory performance. The application can detect patterns and trends relating to inventory records, such as the most popular products, inventory turnover, or inventory shrinkage.

Historical sales and purchase records, when combined with current inventory records, can help in building forecasts and detecting demand fluctuations.

Reports produced by an inventory application should be focused on answering specific questions. What products are approaching their minimum threshold? What records need to be adjusted? Which products are consistently low-selling or high-selling? Where are the main bottlenecks and delays in operation?

Consistent metrics allow managers and executives to analyze the performance of this application and the state of the business in general, but only if the underlying records are accurate and trustworthy.

7. Test Edge Cases And Failure Scenarios In Inventory Applications

Applications should be tested not only against normal operations, but also against abnormal operations. It is important to have processes in place to manage unexpected problems, such as orders going through which should not have, inventory adjustments canceling each other, or inventory records becoming completely unusable. In the context of inventory applications, a few sample test scenarios might include the following:

• Attempt to reserve the same inventory item for two orders simultaneously.

• Submit the same request several times to an API endpoint.

• Cancel an order that had previously reserved some inventory.

• Return a product and increase its inventory.

• Cancel a warehouse transfer.

• Submit a request to an external API that times out.

• Adjust inventory quantity through an unauthorized or unexpected method.

• Ensure that failed transactions do not leave the system in an inconsistent state.

• Ensure that a few important inventory transactions are properly traceable in case of an incident.

It is important to test the integrity of the system under conditions simulating some of these problems. In practice, inventory errors tend to occur not during normal operation but at the interfaces between systems.

8. Inventory Platforms: Selecting The Best Option For Your Business

Inventory control and management systems vary widely in terms of scale, scope, and capabilities. The choice of one option over another will be informed by the specific needs of the business and its suppliers. Businesses considering this decision should examine its existing procedures and plan accordingly.

The Inventory Master web page offers a number of resources for engineers and managers interested in building or selecting an appropriate toolset. Businesses can use this resource to learn more about the available approaches and select a viable option. Documentation and requirements analysis can help set expectations and ensure that a given selection fits the needs of the business rather than the other way around.

title: Why One Happy Path Beats a Menu of Options When Your User Is an AI Agent
description:
Give an engineer five ways to deploy an app and they'll pick one. When I gave an AI agent several ways, it tried a few, mixed them together, and left me debugging at midnight.

That's the reason agentic-hosting works the way it does. It's an open-source tool I built that turns a Linux server you own into a place AI coding agents can deploy apps and databases on their own. This post explains its main design rule, one way to do each job, and walks through the API calls an agent makes to go from a git repo to a live URL.

⭐ If this is useful, a star on GitHub helps other people find it.

🤖 Give this to your agent: point it at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dennisonbertram/agentic-hosting/main/llms.txt (or the skill) and it can sign up and get going from that one link.

Why fewer options

I used to think "only one way to do it" was a sign of an unfinished product. Heroku, Kubernetes, Coolify, and Dokku all give you lots of settings, because people running servers have strong opinions about how to build and route things.

Agents don't have opinions. They make a guess, and if the guess fails they retry, sometimes with a different guess. Every extra option is another branch they can wander down that I never tested.

So agentic-hosting has one build system, one router, and one choice per database type. If there's only one path, the agent can't find a creative one I didn't plan for. Here's what that looks like in practice.

Building: git repo in, running app out

Apps are built with Nixpacks, a tool that looks at your code and figures out how to package it into a container without a Dockerfile. It's the only build option. You can't upload your own Dockerfile.

Deploying from git takes two calls. First the agent creates a service. The API requires an image field, so for git deploys it sends the placeholder "pending":

POST /v1/services
Authorization: Bearer <api_key>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "my-app",
  "image": "pending",
  "port": 3000
}

Then it starts a build:

POST /v1/services/{serviceID}/builds

{
  "source_type": "git",
  "source_url": "https://github.com/org/repo",
  "source_ref": "main"
}

source_type has to be "git", and source_ref defaults to "main". Only HTTPS URLs from github.com, gitlab.com, bitbucket.org, sr.ht, and codeberg.org are accepted. Anything else gets rejected before the build starts.

While it builds, the agent can watch the logs:

GET /v1/services/{serviceID}/builds/{buildID}/logs?follow=true

Because there's only one build path, the logs always look the same, and when something breaks there's one place to look. In my experience that helps the agent more than which build tool it is.

Routing: you get one URL

Traefik, an open-source proxy, takes incoming web traffic and sends it to the right app. agentic-hosting writes Traefik's config itself. Apps can't set their own routing rules, so a container can't quietly grab another app's traffic.

The URL follows one pattern:

  • By default: http://{serviceID}.localhost
  • If you start the server with --base-domain example.com (or set AH_BASE_DOMAIN): https://{dns_label}.example.com, where dns_label comes from the service name 
GET /v1/services/{serviceID}
# → includes "url": "http://svc_….localhost"
#    or "https://my-app.example.com"

Custom domains aren't supported yet. That's issue #82.

Databases: Postgres or Redis

The type field takes "postgres" or "redis", and nothing else.

POST /v1/databases

{ "name": "my-db", "type": "postgres" }

It takes about 10 to 30 seconds. Then the agent grabs the connection string, adds it to the app's environment variables, and restarts the app:

GET /v1/databases/{dbID}/connection-string

POST /v1/services/{serviceID}/env
{ "DATABASE_URL": "<connection-string>" }

POST /v1/services/{serviceID}/restart

Environment variables are encrypted on disk and hidden in API responses unless you add ?reveal=true.

The smaller limits

The same thinking shows up in small places. Creating a service accepts name, image, port, and optional env, so the agent can't request more memory or CPU. Images come from Docker Hub or the server's own local registry. And if the agent retries a request with the same Idempotency-Key header within 10 minutes, it won't deploy twice.

None of this limits what you can build. It limits how many ways the agent can get there, which is what I wanted.

Try it

With the server running (see the README, or run ./bin/ah --dev --open-registration --port 8080 on your laptop), the agent's path is:

  1. Register to get an API key.
  2. Create a service with "image": "pending".
  3. Start a build from a git URL.
  4. Watch the build logs, then the app logs at GET /v1/services/{id}/logs?follow=true&tail=100.
  5. Create a Postgres or Redis database, set the env var, restart.
  6. Open the service's url.

If you use Claude Code, the repo also has a skill and /ah-deploy, /ah-db, /ah-logs, and /ah-status commands that do the same steps.

Wrapping up

agentic-hosting gives an AI agent exactly one way to build, route, and add a database, which makes its runs a lot more predictable. You run it on your own server, and the agent does the deploying.

  • ⭐ Star agentic-hosting on GitHub so more people find it.
  • 🤖 Give this to your agent: llms.txt to sign up and set up, or the agent skill for daily use.
  • 📖 Read the docs and try the quickstart.
  • 💬 Open an issue with what you'd want your agent to do next.

And if you hand your agent the keys and something breaks, tell me what it was.

title: Why Users Abandon Digital Products Even When They Solve the Right Problem
description:
A digital product can solve a genuine business problem and still struggle to keep users engaged. The features may work correctly, the technology may be reliable, and the product may offer clear value. Yet users can leave when completing a simple task feels unnecessarily difficult.

This often happens because building a useful product involves more than delivering the right functionality.

People also need to understand how it works, find what they need, and complete their tasks without confusion.
The Gap Between Product Value and User Experience

Imagine a small business owner using a new invoicing platform. The application generates accurate invoices, tracks payments, and stores customer details.

However, creating the first invoice requires navigating several menus and filling in fields that are difficult to understand.
The platform solves the business problem, but the experience creates additional work.

This gap can affect onboarding, repeat usage, and customer confidence. Businesses should therefore evaluate not only what their product can do, but also how easily customers can access its value. A clear digital product design approach can help teams connect user needs with meaningful product experiences.

  1. The First Experience Requires Too Much Effort

Users often form an impression of a product during their first few interactions. If registration is complicated, onboarding takes too long, or the next step is unclear, they may leave before discovering the product's benefits.

Teams can improve this experience by identifying the first meaningful action a user wants to complete. Remove unnecessary onboarding steps, explain unfamiliar terms, and provide guidance where users need it.
The objective is not to explain every feature immediately. It is to help users experience the product's value as quickly as possible.

  1. Important Actions Are Difficult to Find

As products grow, teams introduce additional features, settings, and workflows. Without careful planning, the interface can become crowded and navigation can become unpredictable.

A strong UI/UX design process examines how users move through the product and whether the interface supports their goals. Clear labels, logical grouping, consistent controls, and visible next steps can make common tasks easier to complete.

Teams should pay particular attention to actions that users perform frequently. If customers repeatedly search for the same function, the problem may be its placement rather than a lack of functionality.

  1. Features Are Built Without Enough Validation

Product teams sometimes prioritize features because competitors offer them or internal stakeholders believe customers need them. These decisions can introduce complexity without addressing the most important user problems.
Product design helps teams investigate customer needs, evaluate possible solutions, and test assumptions before committing significant development resources.

Early interviews, prototypes, and usability tests can reveal whether a proposed feature solves a meaningful problem. Even simple testing with a small group of representative users can uncover issues that internal reviews overlook.

Businesses planning to improve their product experience can explore UI/UX design and product development services to understand how design and development can support a more usable digital product.

  1. The Interface Does Not Match User Expectations

Users bring familiar expectations from other websites and applications. When common actions behave differently or similar components look inconsistent, people must spend additional effort learning the interface.
For example, a save button should communicate what happens after it is selected. Form errors should explain what went wrong and how to correct it. Navigation should remain predictable across related screens.

Consistent interaction patterns help users build confidence. They also make products easier to maintain as new features are introduced.

  1. Teams Ignore Friction After Launch

Launching a product is not the end of the improvement process. Real users may behave differently from what the team expected during development.
Businesses should review product analytics, support conversations, user feedback, and usability test results to identify recurring problems.

Useful questions include:

Where do users stop during onboarding?
Which tasks generate the most support requests?
Which features receive little engagement?
What causes users to repeat an action or abandon a form?
Which problems affect the most important customer journeys?
These observations help teams prioritize improvements based on evidence rather than assumptions.

  1. Design and Development Work in Isolation

When design decisions are handed to developers without sufficient collaboration, the finished product may differ from the intended experience. Interaction details can be missed, edge cases may remain unresolved, and inconsistent components can emerge.

Designers and developers should collaborate throughout the process. Reviewing requirements together, discussing technical constraints early, and testing implemented screens help prevent avoidable usability problems.
This collaboration is particularly important for complex SaaS platforms, where workflows often involve multiple roles, permissions, and interconnected features.

Turning User Friction Into Product Improvements
Improving retention does not always require a major redesign. A confusing form may need clearer instructions. A complicated workflow may need fewer steps. A poorly understood feature may need better onboarding.

Start by identifying one important user journey, observing where people struggle, and testing a focused improvement. Measure whether the change helps users complete the task more successfully.

A structured approach to UI/UX design and product design can connect these usability improvements with the broader goals of the business. The
emphasis should remain on solving genuine user problems rather than adding features for their own sake.

Conclusion

Users do not abandon digital products only because the products lack useful features. They may leave because the value is difficult to discover, important tasks take too much effort, or the experience fails to meet their expectations.

Understanding these barriers helps businesses make more informed product decisions. By studying user behaviour, validating ideas, improving key workflows, and refining the experience after launch, teams can make digital products more useful and easier to adopt.
