title: Per-Core vs Named User: Choosing a Database Licensing Model
description:
• How vendors actually measure what you pay
  • Real-world cost and scalability trade-offs
  • Where audits bite: compliance traps and vendor perspectives
  • When per-core, named-user, or capacity-based licensing wins (practical case studies)
  • Negotiation levers that reduce audit risk and surprise bills
  • Practical decision checklist and break‑even calculator

Licensing is an architectural decision: it shapes your platform economics, your deployment patterns, and how auditors will read your telemetry. Choose the wrong model and you convert operational scale into steady, escalating license spend and audit exposure.

The signals most teams bring me are predictable: unexpectedly large license true-ups after cloud migrations, an exploding count of named users from service accounts and APIs, or a per-core bill that spikes as you move to larger VMs. Those symptoms hide two root problems — a mismatch between the license metric and the workload footprint, and weak evidence that proves your entitled scope during an audit — both of which drive cost and risk.

How vendors actually measure what you pay

Different vendors translate technical resources into commercial units in distinct ways; your choices are effectively how you convert compute and identity into dollars.

  • Per-core / Processor-based (per-core licensing): Charges map to CPU capacity — physical cores or virtual cores aggregated and adjusted by vendor-specific multipliers. Oracle uses a Processor metric with a published Processor Core Factor Table that converts physical cores (or OCPUs/vCPUs in cloud contexts) into license counts; the table is updated periodically and affects calculation and minimums.
    • Microsoft sells SQL Server in a core-based model (sold in two-core packs) and requires a minimum number of core licenses per physical processor when using physical licensing; virtualization rules differ if you license by VM.
  • Named-user / CAL-style (named user licensing): Licenses are counted per distinct user or device. Oracle’s Named User Plus (NUP) and Microsoft’s Client Access License (CAL) are the canonical examples; these models scale with headcount and require careful treatment of automated service accounts, shared devices, and multiplexing.
  • Capacity-based / subscription / cloud metrics (capacity-based licensing): Vendors or clouds sell capacity units (vCore, vCPU-hour, DTU, PVU) or fully-managed instances billed hourly/monthly. Azure’s vCore model and AWS RDS “license-included” vs BYOL are representative: you either pay a managed, capacity-priced SKU or bring existing licenses under specific rules.
  • Other capacity hybrids (PVU / RVU): IBM DB2 and other enterprise stacks use processor-value units or Authorized User units; PVU maps CPU families to a value table rather than a simple core count.

Table — Quick characteristic comparison

Model What you measure Typical cost driver Good fit Common vendor examples
per-core licensing Physical cores or vCPUs (adjusted by core factor) Core count, core factor, hyperthreading rules High-concurrency, unpredictable user counts, DW/analytics Oracle Processor, SQL Server core-based.
named user licensing Distinct users/devices (NUP/CAL) # of users / devices, service account counts Small fixed teams, known limited user lists Oracle NUP, Microsoft CAL.
capacity-based licensing vCore-hours, instance-hours, PVU Runtime hours, chosen instance class Cloud-native, bursty/ephemeral workloads Azure vCore, AWS RDS license-included, IBM PVU.

Real-world cost and scalability trade-offs

Cost math is rarely the only decision factor, but it’s the easiest place to misjudge long-term outcomes.

  • Predictability vs elasticity: per-core licensing commonly gives predictable capacity pricing for sustained, heavy workloads (big DW clusters, OLTP nodes). That predictability becomes a liability when you scale horizontally with many small VMs: core counts multiply and so do license obligations. The Oracle Processor Core Factor Table can materially change required license counts as CPU families change.
  • Headcount vs concurrency: named user licensing shines when the user population is small, stable, and well-controlled. Hidden costs appear when service accounts, APIs, contractors, and indirect access are counted as users — an easy audit trap. Microsoft’s Server+CAL model is only available for Standard edition and is intentionally intended for environments where counting users/devices is feasible.
  • Elastic cloud and short-lived workloads: capacity-based licensing (vCore, license-included hourly models) converts variable usage to variable cost and removes many inventory headaches — but it can be more expensive for steady-state heavy compute compared to a negotiated perpetual per-core deal or an optimized BYOL + Software Assurance strategy. Azure’s vCore model explicitly supports Licence included and Azure Hybrid Benefit (BYOL) choices that materially change economics.

Practical break-even approach (high level):

  1. Estimate steady-state compute (cores × hours/month) + growth projection.
  2. Estimate named-user population growth and service account count.
  3. Calculate per-month/per-year cost of: per-core, named user, and capacity-based with conservative growth.
  4. Model audit true-up scenarios — add an audit contingency (many teams use 10–30% of license budget as a conservative buffer per year when using aggressive virtualization). Flexera’s industry surveys show audit costs and unexpected fines remain a material line item for many organizations.

Where audits bite: compliance traps and vendor perspectives

Audits find the smallest ambiguities in your environment and convert them into license shortfalls.

  • Virtualization and partitioning: Oracle’s public Partitioning Policy and how LMS treats soft vs hard partitioning is the single biggest surprise for organizations that move to VMware, Hyper-V, or large virtual clusters; Oracle’s practical enforcement often treats a VM running Oracle as “contaminating” the host/cluster unless hard partitioning or explicit contractual carve-outs exist. That interpretation has led to large audit findings.
  • Multiplexing and named users: Multiplexing layers (web servers, API gateways, ETL services) do not reduce named-user counts for many vendors; the licensing rules require counting each distinct user/device or applying vendor-specific multiplexing guidance. Auditors expect proof (logs, identity lists, PoEs).
  • Minimums and rounding rules: Processor and NUP calculations often include minimums per CPU or per processor and explicit rounding rules; a fractional core result rounds up to whole licenses in Oracle’s Processor Core Factor calculation. Overlooking minimums increases license demand unexpectedly.
  • Audit mechanics and evidence: Vendors typically request Proof of Entitlement (PoE), license keys, support CSIs, and environment inventories. Modern audits increasingly correlate telemetry, virtualization metadata, and cloud billing records — poor telemetry equals poor outcomes. Flexera’s 2024 ITAM study reports rising audit fines and persistent visibility gaps that make audit defense harder.

Important: Legal language matters. Oracle’s Partitioning Policy is publicly available but often not contractually incorporated; your Master Agreement / Ordering Documents are the contract you’ll be judged by — don’t assume a vendor policy document protects you unless it’s explicitly part of the deal.

When per-core, named-user, or capacity-based licensing wins (practical case studies)

Below are concise, practitioner-rooted case studies built from patterns I’ve seen across enterprise accounts.

Case A — Small departmental application (ERP bolt-on for HR)

  • Footprint: one DB server, ~150 regular users, predictable daytime traffic, limited API access.
  • Recommendation pattern: named-user licensing (Server+CAL for SQL Server Standard or Oracle NUP) is usually cheaper because per-user count is small and stable; control service accounts and apply an access lifecycle to avoid user sprawl. Confirm minimums (Oracle NUP minimums per Processor apply).

Case B — Global analytics platform and data warehouse

  • Footprint: dozens of cores, heavy parallel queries, many concurrent users and unknown indirect access from BI tools.
  • Recommendation pattern: per-core licensing scales better — you avoid counting every BI user or extract process. Negotiate core counts, core-factor interpretation, and virtualization carve-outs before committing production. Expect to use core factor tables and to defend your virtual host mapping during audits.

Case C — Cloud-native microservices with autoscaling and short-lived DB instances

  • Footprint: transient DBs spun up by CI/CD, serverless/off-peak tiers, unpredictable bursts.
  • Recommendation pattern: capacity-based licensing (vCore/vCPU-hour, license-included DBaaS) typically reduces admin overhead and matches cost to usage. Evaluate BYOL options and hybrid benefits when you have existing on-prem licenses with active Software Assurance or support entitlements. Azure and AWS both publish clear license-inclusion and BYOL guidance.

Each case must be validated by a cost model based on your organization’s lifecycle: projected growth, VM sizing policy, failover topology, and the proportion of machine-to-human access.

Negotiation levers that reduce audit risk and surprise bills

When you negotiate, the right contract language buys you predictability and defensible boundaries.

  • Define the metric precisely in the contract: Processor vs vCPU vs OCPU vs Named User Plus — state the calculation method, rounding, and core-factor application. Reference the exact core-factor table version or freeze the factor for the contract term.
  • Virtualization carve-outs and permitted partitioning: Insist on explicit language that limits license counting to specific hosts or named resource pools, or that recognizes your chosen hard-partitioning technology (and the exact configuration you will run). Avoid relying on a vendor’s generic policy document unless it’s incorporated into the contract.
  • License mobility and cloud portability: Negotiate BYOL terms, movement windows (e.g., 90-day reassignment rules), and permitted cloud providers/regions. Microsoft documents license reassignment rules and Software Assurance benefits for mobility; secure similar language where possible.
  • Audit protocol and limits: Carve out audit timing, scope, notice periods, and frequency. Limit who can perform the audit, require a narrowly defined read-only data set to be delivered, and insist on a dispute-resolution process. Also negotiate an audit remediation cap or fixed schedule for true-ups to avoid open-ended demands.
  • Support uplift caps and price protection: Cap annual support increases, tie renewals to known indices, and get price hold guarantees for a defined period to avoid erosion of initial discounts.
  • Entitlement portability and affiliate coverage: If you operate multiple legal entities or expect M&A activity, put affiliate usage and transferability language into the agreement. Lack of territory/affiliate language is a common post‑audit exposure.

Concrete clause examples to ask for during negotiation (paraphrased, not legal advice):

  • “Processor definition: Processor license obligations shall be calculated using the Inventory listed in Appendix A and the Oracle Processor Core Factor Table dated [YYYY-MM-DD]; any change to core-factor will not apply retroactively during the term.”
  • “Virtualization carve‑out: Licensor confirms that for the customer’s named server cluster identifiers (Appendix B) only the physical processors shown therein are in‑scope for Processor calculations.”
  • “Audit scope: Vendor audit requires 60 days’ notice, limited to once per 24 months, and remediation is limited to an 18‑month look‑back.”

Practical decision checklist and break‑even calculator

Use this checklist as an operational protocol before you sign or renew any large database license.

Checklist — pre-purchase / renewal

  1. Inventory: authoritative list of servers, VMs, CPU families, vCPU → physical mapping, and PoE/support CSI records. collect: hostname, vCPU, physical host, CSI (keep immutable snapshots quarterly).
  2. Identity map: canonical user list, service accounts, API identities; mark service accounts and batch identities separately.
  3. Workload profile: steady-state cores, peak concurrency, duty cycle (hours/day), planned growth.
  4. Audit simulation: run a mock license calculation under each model and add a 10–30% audit contingency.
  5. Contract terms to negotiate: core factor freeze, partitioning carve-out, audit cadence, BYOL mobility, support cap, affiliate coverage.
  6. Evidence pack: PoE, entitlement spreadsheets, virtualization host mapping, change logs, and access logs for named users.

Break‑even calculator (example Python snippet)

# Simple break-even comparator (illustrative only)
def annual_cost_per_core(core_price, cores, support_pct=0.22):
    base = core_price * cores
    support = base * support_pct
    return base + support

def annual_cost_named_user(user_price, users, support_pct=0.22):
    base = user_price * users
    support = base * support_pct
    return base + support

# Example: compare per-core vs named-user
core_price = 10000   # $ per core per year (example)
users = 150
user_price = 500     # $ per named user per year (example)
cores = 4

cores_cost = annual_cost_per_core(core_price, cores)
users_cost = annual_cost_named_user(user_price, users)

print(f"Per-core annual cost: ${cores_cost:,}")
print(f"Named-user annual cost: ${users_cost:,}")

Audit‑readiness commands and sample evidence

  • Count distinct DB users (SQL Server example): 
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT name) AS distinct_logins
FROM sys.server_principals
WHERE type_desc IN ('SQL_LOGIN','WINDOWS_LOGIN','WINDOWS_GROUP');
  • Map VM to host and vCPU mapping (Linux example using lscpu and cloud metadata): 
lscpu | egrep 'CPU\\(s\\)|Model name'
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-type  # AWS instance type mapping

Final operational note: produce a short, signed Proof of Entitlement (PoE) index and store an immutable snapshot quarterly. During audits the difference between a well-documented entitlement and a fuzzy spreadsheet is the difference between a corrective purchase and a multi‑million dollar settlement.

The licensing model you pick will live on your balance sheet and in your audit record long after the architecture review is closed; choose the metric that maps cleanly to your workload, lock the rules into contract language, and make audit-grade evidence an operational output rather than a late-stage scramble.

Sources:
Microsoft — SQL Server licensing guidance - Microsoft’s official documentation describing SQL Server licensing options including Per Core and Server + CAL models, VM and reassignment rules.

Microsoft — Server Virtualization Licensing Guidance - Guidance on license movement, Software Assurance benefits and license mobility across server farms.

Oracle — License Manager / Licensing Metrics - Oracle documentation showing licensing metrics available (Processors, Named User Plus) and how they appear in Oracle License Manager.

Oracle — Processor Core Factor Table (PDF) - The authoritative Oracle core factor table and notes on rounding, cloud mappings, and updates (effective for Processor calculations).

Scott & Scott LLP — How to Understand Oracle’s Use of its Partitioning Policy for Virtualization - Legal analysis of Oracle’s Partitioning Policy and how it is applied in audits.

AWS — RDS for Oracle Licensing Options - AWS documentation on License Included vs Bring Your Own License (BYOL) models for Oracle on RDS.

Flexera — 2024 State of ITAM Report press release - Industry data on audit costs, visibility gaps, and the rising financial impact of software audits.

IBM — DB2 licensing information - IBM documentation describing PVU (Processor Value Unit) and Authorized User licensing models for DB2.

Microsoft Azure — Azure SQL Database pricing and vCore model - Azure’s documentation on the vCore vs DTU purchasing models, serverless and hybrid benefit options.

ISO — ISO/IEC 19770 (Software Asset Management) - The international standard for Software Asset Management (processes and assessment), useful for building audit‑grade SAM processes.

title: Understanding Paint Containment and Composite Layers for Smooth Animations
description:
You’re building a slick UI with smooth animations. You add a subtle transform here, a fade there. But then, boom , your animations stutter. Frames drop, interactions feel sluggish, and your user experience tanks.

You tweak your CSS, add will-change: transform, and suddenly things get smoother. But why? What actually happens under the hood when you add that mysterious CSS property? Or when you add contain: paint? How do those tiny CSS hints help the browser decide to offload rendering work to the GPU?

Let me share what I learned digging into paint containment and compositing layers , the quiet heroes behind buttery smooth animations and frustrating jank.

The moment you realize something’s wrong

I was working on a dashboard with complex nested components and animations. Some animations were jittery, especially when scrolling or interacting with other UI parts.

Opening Chrome DevTools, I checked the Performance tab and noticed a lot of layout and paint work every frame. The GPU wasn’t getting a break.

I suspected compositing layers weren’t being created smartly. If each animated element had its own layer, the browser could push rasterization to the GPU, freeing up the CPU and enabling smooth 60fps animations.

But how does the browser decide what gets its own compositing layer?

What is a compositing layer anyway?

Imagine the browser’s rendering pipeline like an assembly line:

  1. Style: The browser figures out what styles apply to each element.
  2. Layout: Positions and sizes are computed.
  3. Paint: Elements are drawn into bitmaps.
  4. Composite: These bitmaps (layers) are combined to produce the final image.

Most elements are painted into a shared bitmap. But some elements get their own bitmap , a compositing layer. This bitmap can be handed off to the GPU to be transformed or animated independently without repainting the entire page.

When a layer is created, animations like transforms or opacity changes on that layer become super cheap , the GPU just moves or blends that bitmap.

Paint containment: telling the browser to isolate painting

You can hint to the browser when an element should get its own compositing layer by using CSS containment. The contain property lets you declare what aspects of rendering are confined to a subtree.

contain: paint means “hey browser, this element and its subtree won’t affect anything outside their bounding box when painting.”

Why does this matter? Because if the browser knows an element is paint-contained, it can safely create a compositing layer for it. Changes inside won’t force repaints outside.

Consider this example:

.card {
  contain: paint;
  will-change: transform;
}

Here, .card is paint-contained and hints it will be transformed. The browser can create a separate layer for .card and push its rendering work to the GPU.

How paint containment creates layers under the hood

Under the hood, the browser’s rendering engine tracks containment properties during the paint phase.

  • When it hits an element with contain: paint, it creates a new paint layer.
  • This layer is a bitmap snapshot of that subtree.
  • Because it’s isolated, the browser knows repainting this layer won’t affect siblings or ancestors.
  • The compositor can now handle that layer independently.

This is a big win for animations.

If you animate a transform on that element, the browser only needs to update the layer’s position on screen , no repaint or re-layout.

Without containment, the browser might have to repaint a large part of the page every frame.

The GPU angle: why compositing layers matter

Compositing layers are the boundary between CPU-bound painting and GPU-accelerated compositing.

Your browser’s GPU can move, scale, rotate, or fade whole layers very efficiently.

But creating too many layers is also bad , each layer consumes GPU memory and overhead.

The browser tries to balance:

  • Too few layers: More repaint work on CPU, animations jank.
  • Too many layers: GPU memory pressure, possible thrashing.

You can influence this balance with contain, will-change, and other CSS properties.

Debugging paint containment and layers in DevTools

If you suspect your animations are slow due to missing layers, here’s how to check:

  1. Layers panel in Chrome DevTools:

    • Open DevTools > More Tools > Layers.
    • You’ll see a visual map of compositing layers.
    • Animated elements should have their own layers.

  2. Rendering tab > Paint flashing:

    • Enable "Paint flashing" to see what parts of the page repaint during interactions.
    • If large areas repaint during a transform animation, you lack proper containment.

  3. Performance tab:

    • Record a profile while animating.
    • Look for "Recalculate Style" and "Paint" tasks.
    • Excessive painting per frame hints at missing layers.

Practical tips to avoid jank

  • Use contain: paint or contain: layout paint on animated elements or their parents when possible.
  • Add will-change: transform (or whatever property you animate) to hint the browser early.
  • Avoid animating properties that force layout or paint (like width, height, top).
  • Keep your layer tree manageable: don’t paint-contain everything blindly.
  • Test on real devices with DevTools profiling.

Real-world gotchas

  • Not all browsers support all containment types equally.
  • Overusing will-change can backfire and cause memory bloat.
  • Complex shadow DOM or web components might not behave as expected without explicit containment.
  • Sometimes, a parent’s overflow or opacity settings affect layer creation unexpectedly.

Why understanding this matters

When you grasp how paint containment and compositing layers work, you can:

  • Write CSS that helps the browser optimize rendering.
  • Debug tricky animation jank by spotting missing layers.
  • Balance GPU memory usage and CPU load.
  • Build smoother, more responsive UIs.

Next time your animation stutters, pause and inspect your layers. Your GPU will thank you.

Helpful learning resources

  • MDN Web Docs
  • web.dev performance guidance
  • OpenAI developer resources Originally published at Under The Hood. Get the next deep dive in your inbox: subscribe to Under The Hood.

title: I Tested 3 Free, Open-Source Adobe Clones on My Mac. Here Are the Real Numbers.
description:
ArtCraft just open-sourced free Rust rebuilds of Photoshop, Premiere, After Effects and ten more apps. PhotoCraft alone went past 61,000 GitHub stars in about two weeks.

Stars don't edit videos, though. So I installed three of the apps on my Mac mini M4 (16 GB) and gave them real work. Every number below comes from a log I saved on October 15, 2026.

What ArtCraft actually is

ArtCraft is a family of desktop apps that copy the Adobe and Microsoft playbook, released under the Apache 2.0 license:

  • PhotoCraft: Photoshop
  • VectorCraft: Illustrator
  • FilmCraft: Premiere Pro
  • EffectCraft: After Effects
  • LightCraft: Lightroom
  • Plus clones of InDesign, Figma, Word, PowerPoint, Excel, Pro Tools and AutoCAD

When I took my first screenshot the site listed 12 apps. By the time I finished testing, it listed 13. They run on Mac, Windows, Linux and in the browser.

The price gap: Adobe Creative Cloud Pro is US$69.99/month on adobe.com (about $840 a year). ArtCraft is $0.

The catch: most of these repos were created on September 30, 2026. Every app I checked is labelled early alpha or "in development". So the real question is whether you can use them today.

Test 1: PhotoCraft photo edit (0.23 s)

PhotoCraft looks almost exactly like Photoshop: same toolbar, same panels, same layers. The interesting part is that every action is a command, and the app ships its own MCP server. An AI agent or a small script can drive the real app while you watch.

The edit: auto tone, remove background, yellow fill layer behind the subject, two text layers, drop shadow. From the command line (photocraft-cli 0.9.0), the whole thing took 0.23 seconds and saved a real layered PSD with every layer still editable.

The log, trimmed:

{"command":"image.autoTone","result":null}
{"command":"layer.removeBackground","result":{"bounds":[171,56,587,664],"layer":2}}
{"command":"layer.newFillLayer.solidColor","result":{"layer":3}}
{"command":"type.create","result":{"bounds":[838,244,1155,351],"layer":4}}
{"command":"layer.layerStyle.dropShadow","result":{"layer":5}}
real 0.23

What broke: Remove Background left a blue fringe in the subject's hair from the old backdrop. Photoshop's masking still wins here.

Test 2: batch-edit 20 product photos (1.75 s)

The boring test that actually saves time. Picture a small online shop fixing 20 product photos every week. I gave PhotoCraft one action list: auto tone, more vibrance, unsharp mask, resize to 1080 px.

[["image.autoTone",{}],
 ["image.adjustments.vibrance",{"vibrance":35,"saturation":5}],
 ["filter.sharpen.unsharpMask",{"amount":60,"radius":1.2,"threshold":2}],
 ["image.imageSize",{"width":1080}]]

photocraft-cli batch --actions actions.json --in batch-in --out batch-out --format jpg --quality 90

Result: 20 succeeded, 0 failed, 1.75 seconds. In Photoshop you'd record an action for this. Here it's one line in a terminal.

Test 3: FilmCraft 16-second travel reel (12.5 s export)

FilmCraft is a real Premiere clone: source monitor, program monitor, project bin, timeline. I built a 16-second 1080p30 reel from four free Mixkit stock clips, with three cross dissolves and a title.

What broke: one clip was 720p and showed up small in the middle of the 1080p frame. Premiere does the same thing, and one Fill Frame command fixed it.

The export is the nerdy part. FilmCraft doesn't use FFmpeg; its H.264, HEVC, ProRes and AAC codecs are written from scratch in Rust.

filmcraft-cli --project reel/reel.fcproj export out/travel-reel.mp4 --format h264
"frames": 480, "render_fps": 38.3, "seconds": 12.52, "bytes": 38815510

12.5 seconds for 480 frames. The file is chunky, though: 38.8 MB for 16 seconds, so compress it before you upload it anywhere.

Test 4: EffectCraft animated title (0.99 s render)

This one surprised me most. You script EffectCraft with After Effects-style JavaScript: comps, layers, keyframes, easing, Gaussian blur. Here's part of the title script I wrote:

var comp = app.project.items.addComp("Title", 1920, 1080, 1, 4, 30);
var t = comp.layers.addText("OPEN SOURCE");
var o = t.property("Transform").property("Opacity");
o.setValueAtTime(0.3, 0); o.setValueAtTime(0.8, 100);
var blur = t.property("Effects").addProperty("ADBE Gaussian Blur 2");
blur.property("Blurriness").setValueAtTime(0.3, 40);
blur.property("Blurriness").setValueAtTime(1.0, 0);

A yellow bar wipes in, the text blurs into place, and a subtitle fades up. The script ran in 0.08 s, and the 4-second 1080p title (120 frames) rendered in 0.99 s.

All four results

  • PhotoCraft photo edit: 0.23 s, layered PSD (hair fringe after background removal)
  • PhotoCraft batch, 20 photos: 1.75 s, 0 failures
  • FilmCraft 16 s 1080p reel: 12.5 s export, 38.8 MB file
  • EffectCraft 4 s title: script 0.08 s, render 0.99 s

The real use case: automation

ArtCraft isn't replacing a pro editor tomorrow. The strength is that every app has a command line and an MCP server, so agents like Claude can drive them:

  • Make 50 social posts from a spreadsheet
  • Fix every product photo in one go
  • Turn a script into a rough cut
  • Render a title for every video

Adobe gives you a beautiful app. ArtCraft gives you an app that scripts and AI agents can use too, for free.

So, can you cancel Adobe today?

If you're a professional with client deadlines: no. These apps are days old, labelled alpha, and you will hit missing features.

If you're a student, a Linux user, a small business, or a developer who wants to automate creative work: it's already useful.

And if PhotoCraft keeps moving at 61,000 stars in two weeks, Adobe should be a little nervous.

ArtCraft apps: https://getartcraft.com/apps

Not sponsored by or affiliated with ArtCraft or Adobe. Tested on a Mac mini M4 (16 GB), October 15, 2026. Price checked on adobe.com the same day. This article was written with AI assistance from my own test logs and video script.

title: Three Things I Learned Building a Local-LLM Java Repair Tool
description:
I built a tool that uses AI to fix broken Java projects. One of the biggest lessons? You can't just trust what the AI gives you.

Over the past few days, I've been working on CompileLoop, a Java project that uses local LLMs to try and fix broken Maven builds.

The idea is pretty simple. You give it a broken Java project, it sends the build errors to a local code model, gets back a proposed fix, applies that fix in a temporary copy of the project, and runs the build again to see if it actually worked.

If the fix passes validation, you get a patch to review. Your original source code stays untouched.

I'm building this because I want to explore how far we can take AI-assisted software development without blindly trusting the AI to get everything right. I also wanted to build something that goes beyond just sending prompts to a model and hoping for the best.

While working on CompileLoop, I ran into a few interesting problems. Some were things I hadn't really thought about before, and others made me realise that getting an AI model to produce code is only one part of the problem.

Here are three things I learned along the way.

1. The AI can get the fix right and still get the details wrong

One of the first interesting problems I ran into was with unified diffs.

For anyone who hasn't worked with them before, a unified diff is basically a way of describing the changes between two versions of a file. Git uses this format to show changes, and tools can use it to apply patches.

In one of my benchmark cases, the Java compiler complained about a missing semicolon. The model correctly identified what needed to change and produced a diff that looked something like this:

--- a/src/main/java/bench/Adder.java
+++ b/src/main/java/bench/Adder.java
@@ -5,3 +5,3 @@
 public class Adder {
     public int add(int a, int b) {
-        return a + b
+        return a + b;
     }
 }

The actual fix was correct. The problem was that the model got the line counts in the diff header wrong.

A unified diff uses those counts to tell the patch tool how many lines to expect before and after the change. My original implementation rejected the patch if those counts didn't match.

So here I was, looking at a model that had identified the correct fix, but my tool was rejecting it because of a formatting detail.

It happened repeatedly.

Eventually, I realised I needed to handle this differently. Instead of making the model try again every time it got the counts wrong, I changed the patch-handling logic to recalculate those counts from the diff body, similar to what git apply --recount does.

The important part was that I wasn't relaxing the validation of the actual changes. I was correcting a part of the diff that could be calculated deterministically.

My biggest takeaway here is that not every problem needs to be solved by asking the AI to try again.

Sometimes, the better solution is to identify which parts of the output can be corrected safely by normal code.

2. Just because the AI says it fixed something doesn't mean it actually did

This one was interesting because it showed me how important it is to separate what a model says it did from what it actually changed.

I had a Java method declared to return an integer, but its implementation was returning a string:

public int add(int a, int b) {
    return "x";
}

The compiler correctly complained that a String couldn't be converted to an int.

The model returned a summary saying it would fix the method's return type to int. However, the method was already declared to return int.

What the model actually changed was the method body:

public int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

In this case, the diff was correct, but the explanation of the fix wasn't.

At first, this might seem like a small issue. The code was fixed, so why worry about the summary?

The problem is that if you build a tool around AI-generated output, you need to know which parts of that output you can actually trust.

A model can produce a correct patch and an incorrect explanation in the same response. If your tool relies on the explanation instead of examining the actual changes, you could end up making the wrong decision.

That's why CompileLoop validates the patch itself and checks the result by running the build. The model's summary is useful context, but it isn't proof that the fix worked.

For me, the lesson is simple: AI can suggest the solution, but the evidence needs to come from the actual code and the tests.

3. You need to know when to stop asking the AI for help

Another problem I encountered was the model repeatedly producing the same incorrect fix.

The first attempt would fail. CompileLoop would send the model feedback about the failure, and the model would return another patch.

Except the second patch was identical to the first.

Sometimes the third attempt was identical too.

Technically, the tool was doing what I had designed it to do. It had a maximum number of attempts, and it would eventually stop.

But when I looked at what was happening, I realised it was wasting time.

Each attempt involved another model call and another Maven build. If the model wasn't making progress, repeating the process wasn't giving me anything useful.

So I added two conditions to stop the repair loop early:

  • Repeated patches: If the model produces a patch that has already been attempted, the loop stops instead of applying the same failed solution again.
  • Unchanged errors: If two consecutive attempts fail with the same diagnostic information, the loop recognises that it isn't making progress.

For the patch fingerprints, I used Java's String.hashCode() rather than introducing a cryptographic hash. In this case, the fingerprint is only used to compare patches generated by the same process. A collision could cause the tool to stop early, but it wouldn't allow an unsafe patch through.

In my benchmark runs, these stop conditions were triggered 27 times across 60 runs. That included 21 cases where the tool detected a lack of progress and six where the AI provider was unavailable.

That showed me that stopping early wasn't just a theoretical improvement. It was something the tool was actually using.

The lesson I learned is that an AI repair loop needs more than a maximum attempt count. It needs a way to recognise when another attempt is unlikely to help.

Otherwise, you're just spending more time and computing resources asking the same question.

What happened when I tested different models?

I also wanted to see how different local code models performed rather than assuming that a model with a particular parameter count would automatically be better.

I created 20 small Maven projects, each containing one deliberate defect. These covered syntax errors, type mismatches, missing symbols, assertion failures, and bugs involving multiple files.

I tested three models, with three attempts per fixture.

Here are the results from my benchmark:

Model Successful repairs Repair rate Average latency
Qwen2.5-Coder 7B 9/20 45% 29 seconds
Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B 4/20 20% 12 seconds
DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B 1/20 5% 39 seconds

Qwen2.5-Coder 7B performed best overall in these tests.

What surprised me was the result for DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B. It often identified the correct fix in its summary, but its diffs contained context lines that didn't match the actual source files. CompileLoop rejected those patches because they couldn't be applied safely.

This was a useful reminder that choosing a model isn't just about its size or how good its explanations sound. It also matters whether it can produce output in the exact format your system requires.

I also noticed that Qwen2.5-Coder 7B performed better on the test-failure fixtures than on the compilation-failure fixtures. There were only five test fixtures, so I wouldn't make any big claims from that result, but it's an interesting observation worth investigating with a larger benchmark.

The benchmark isn't perfect, and the sample is small. That's exactly why I wanted the results to be available instead of only sharing the successful examples.

The fixtures, runner, and individual result files are committed to the repository. You can reproduce the benchmark by pulling the required Ollama models and running:

bash benchmarks/run.sh

What I actually enjoyed building

Something I've realised while working on CompileLoop is that the AI integration is only one part of the engineering.

A lot of the work is about making sure everything around the model behaves properly.

For example, I had to build:

  • A process runner that executes Maven, handles its output without deadlocking, enforces timeouts, and terminates the process tree when necessary.
  • A parser that turns Maven's output into structured compilation errors and test failures.
  • A patch validator that rejects dangerous or unsupported changes, including path traversal, symlink escapes, and unexpected file operations.
  • A temporary workspace where patches can be applied and tested without modifying the original project.
  • A repair engine that records attempts, checks whether fixes work, and stops when it detects that progress has stalled.

I also wrote tests around these components, including tests that use a fake Ollama server and scripted model responses. That means the test suite can run without downloading a local model.

The project currently has 233 tests, with CI running on Ubuntu and Windows.

These are the parts that make the difference between a simple AI coding experiment and a tool that attempts to handle failures in a controlled way.

There are still things I want to improve. Regression detection is one of them, because fixing one failing test shouldn't mean accidentally breaking another. I also want to introduce stronger isolation for build execution and eventually support other languages beyond Java and Maven.

CompileLoop currently uses a temporary copy to protect the original source tree, but that isn't a security sandbox. Build scripts can execute arbitrary commands, so proper container isolation is still an important next step.

I've documented these limitations rather than pretending the project is more complete than it is.

Building with AI is still engineering

I used Claude during development for architecture discussions, reviewing code, and working through problems when I wasn't sure which approach made the most sense.

But using AI to help build a project doesn't remove the responsibility of understanding what you're building.

I still needed to test the implementation, investigate failures, compare different approaches, and decide which trade-offs were appropriate.

For example, I needed to understand why recalculating diff counts was safe, why the patch itself mattered more than the model's summary, and why stopping repeated attempts was better than blindly continuing.

Those decisions matter because I need to be able to explain and defend them, not just get the code to compile.

I'm still learning as a software engineer, and that's part of why I enjoy projects like this. They give me an opportunity to work through problems that go beyond implementing a feature and to understand how the different parts of a system fit together.

I also think this is one of the more interesting areas of AI-assisted development: not just getting models to write code, but building systems around them that can verify their work and handle their mistakes.

That's ultimately what I want CompileLoop to explore.

The model proposes a fix. The tool checks it. The developer reviews the result.

And if the model keeps getting it wrong, the tool should know when to stop.

Try CompileLoop

The source code, benchmark fixtures, and results are available on GitHub:

github.com/LambdaJedi/compileloop

You can build the project with Maven and run it using a local Ollama model:

git clone https://github.com/LambdaJedi/compileloop.git
cd compileloop

mvn -B -DskipTests package

ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b

java -jar target/compileloop-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar repair \
  examples/broken-compilation-project \
  --model qwen2.5-coder:7b

If you're working on local LLMs, Java tooling, or AI-assisted software development, I'd be interested to hear what you've been building and what problems you've run into.

I'm still developing CompileLoop, so feedback and ideas for improving the approach are welcome.

title: Database Indexing: The Performance Trick Nobody Explained Properly
description:
Here's a scenario I've seen dozens of times.

A developer builds an app. It works great in development with 100 users. Then it goes to production, gets 100,000 users, and suddenly everything is slow. Pages timeout. The database CPU is at 100%. Users are complaining.

The developer starts optimizing code. Caching everything. Adding more servers. Nothing helps.

Then someone looks at the database and says, "Have you tried adding an index?"

One line of SQL later, queries that took 30 seconds now take 30 milliseconds. Problem solved.

Database indexing is the single highest-leverage performance optimization most developers ignore. It's not sexy. It's not a new framework. But it can make your app 100x faster with almost no code changes.

This guide explains how indexes actually work, when to use them, and the mistakes that destroy performance. By the end, you'll understand indexes well enough to speed up any slow query.

Let's make your database fast.

What Is an Index?

An index is a data structure that makes finding data faster.

Think of it like a book index. If you want to find every mention of "authentication" in a 500-page book, you have two options:

  • Without index: Read every page, looking for "authentication" (slow)
  • With index: Look up "authentication" in the back, get page numbers, go directly there (fast)

Databases work the same way.

-- Without index: Database scans EVERY row
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';
-- Checks row 1... nope
-- Checks row 2... nope
-- Checks row 3... nope
-- ... 999,997 more checks ...
-- Checks row 1,000,000... found it!

-- With index: Database jumps directly to matching rows
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';
-- Look up 'john@example.com' in index → Row #847,293
-- Go directly to row #847,293 → Found it!

The difference? O(n) vs O(log n). For a million rows, that's a million operations vs ~20 operations.

How Indexes Work (B-Tree)

Most database indexes use a B-tree (balanced tree) structure.

How a B-tree lookup works:

  1. Start at root node
  2. Compare value, go left or right
  3. Repeat until you find the value
  4. Follow pointer to actual row data

Why it's fast: Each step eliminates half the remaining data. With a million rows:

  • Step 1: 1,000,000 → 500,000
  • Step 2: 500,000 → 250,000
  • …
  • Step 20: Found it!

20 steps instead of 1,000,000. That's the power of indexes.

Creating Indexes

Basic Index 

-- Create index on single column
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);

-- Create index on multiple columns (composite)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at);

-- Create unique index (also enforces uniqueness)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email_unique ON users(email);

When Indexes Are Created Automatically 

-- Primary keys automatically get an index
CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,  -- Index created automatically
    email VARCHAR(255)
);

-- Unique constraints automatically get an index
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT unique_email UNIQUE (email);
-- Index created automatically

-- Foreign keys do NOT automatically get an index in PostgreSQL!
-- (They do in MySQL)
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id)  -- NO automatic index!
);

-- You should create one manually
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);

Which Columns to Index

Always Index These 

-- 1. Foreign keys (JOIN performance)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_comments_post_id ON comments(post_id);

-- 2. Columns in WHERE clauses (filter performance)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_status ON users(status);
CREATE INDEX idx_products_category ON products(category_id);

-- 3. Columns in ORDER BY (sort performance)
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_created_at ON posts(created_at);

-- 4. Columns in GROUP BY (aggregation performance)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_product_id ON orders(product_id);

Don't Index These 

-- 1. Tiny tables (full scan is fast enough)
-- A table with 100 rows doesn't need indexes beyond PK

-- 2. Columns with low cardinality (few unique values)
-- Boolean columns, status with only 3 values
CREATE INDEX idx_users_is_active ON users(is_active);  -- Usually not helpful

-- 3. Columns that change frequently
-- Index must be updated on every change
CREATE INDEX idx_users_last_seen ON users(last_seen_at);  -- Expensive to maintain

-- 4. Columns rarely used in queries
-- Indexes have storage cost and write overhead

The Selectivity Rule

An index is most useful when it narrows down results significantly.

-- HIGH selectivity (good for indexing)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';
-- Returns 1 row out of 1,000,000 = 0.0001% of table

-- LOW selectivity (index might not help)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active = true;
-- Returns 950,000 rows out of 1,000,000 = 95% of table
-- Full table scan might actually be faster!

Composite Indexes (Multi-Column)

Composite indexes cover multiple columns. Order matters!

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at);

How Composite Index Order Works

Which Queries Can Use This Index? 

-- ✅ Uses index (matches left-to-right)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND created_at > '2024-01-01';
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at;

-- ❌ Cannot use index (skips first column)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01';
-- Would need separate index: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date ON orders(created_at);

The Left-Prefix Rule

A composite index can be used for queries that filter on:

  • First column only ✅
  • First + second columns ✅
  • First + second + third columns ✅
  • Second column only ❌
  • Third column only ❌ 
-- Index: (a, b, c)

WHERE a = 1                     -- ✅ Uses index
WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2           -- ✅ Uses index
WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2 AND c = 3 -- ✅ Uses index
WHERE b = 2                     -- ❌ Cannot use index
WHERE c = 3                     -- ❌ Cannot use index
WHERE b = 2 AND c = 3           -- ❌ Cannot use index
WHERE a = 1 AND c = 3           -- ⚠️ Partial: only uses 'a' part

EXPLAIN: See How Queries Execute

The EXPLAIN command shows you exactly how the database executes a query.

Basic Usage 

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';

Output (PostgreSQL):

Seq Scan on users  (cost=0.00..1834.00 rows=1 width=72)
  Filter: (email = 'john@example.com')

Seq Scan = Sequential Scan = Full Table Scan = SLOW!

Now add an index:

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';

Output:

Index Scan using idx_users_email on users  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=72)
  Index Cond: (email = 'john@example.com')

Index Scan = Using the index = FAST!

EXPLAIN ANALYZE (With Actual Timing) 

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com';

Output:

Index Scan using idx_users_email on users
  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=72)
  (actual time=0.025..0.026 rows=1 loops=1)
Planning Time: 0.085 ms
Execution Time: 0.043 ms

Now you can see actual milliseconds!

What to Look For

Common Index Problems

Problem 1: Index Not Being Used 

-- You created an index
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);

-- But this query doesn't use it!
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'john@example.com';
-- Seq Scan!

Why? The index is on email, not LOWER(email).

Fix: Create a functional index.

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users(LOWER(email));

-- Now it works
SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'john@example.com';
-- Index Scan ✅

Problem 2: Wrong Column Order in Composite Index 

-- Index created
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date_user ON orders(created_at, user_id);

-- This query is slow!
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- Seq Scan! The index can't help (wrong order)

-- Fix: Create index with correct order
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_date ON orders(user_id, created_at);

Problem 3: Too Many Indexes 

-- Every index has a cost:
-- • Storage space
-- • Slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (must update all indexes)
-- • Query planner overhead

-- Don't do this!
CREATE INDEX idx_users_a ON users(a);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_b ON users(b);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_c ON users(c);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_ab ON users(a, b);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_bc ON users(b, c);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_abc ON users(a, b, c);
-- 6 indexes to maintain on every write!

-- Instead, analyze your queries and create minimal covering indexes

Problem 4: Type Mismatch 

-- Column is VARCHAR
CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    phone VARCHAR(20)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_phone ON users(phone);

-- But you query with INTEGER
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = 1234567890;
-- Index might not be used! (type conversion)

-- Fix: Use correct type
SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = '1234567890';

Problem 5: LIKE with Leading Wildcard 

CREATE INDEX idx_users_name ON users(name);

-- This uses the index ✅
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'John%';

-- This CANNOT use the index ❌
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE '%John%';
-- Must scan entire index/table because we don't know starting point

-- For full-text search, use proper full-text indexes instead
CREATE INDEX idx_users_name_gin ON users USING gin(to_tsvector('english', name));

Index Types

Different index types for different use cases.

B-Tree (Default) 

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
-- Same as:
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users USING btree(email);
  • Best for: Equality (=) and range queries (<, >, BETWEEN)
  • Use when: Most cases. This is your default choice.

Hash 

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_hash ON users USING hash(email);
  • Best for: Equality only (=)
  • Use when: You only do exact matches, never ranges.

GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) 

-- For array columns
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_tags ON posts USING gin(tags);

-- For full-text search
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_content ON posts USING gin(to_tsvector('english', content));

-- For JSONB
CREATE INDEX idx_users_metadata ON users USING gin(metadata);
  • Best for: Arrays, full-text search, JSONB
  • Use when: You query inside complex data types.

GiST (Generalized Search Tree) 

-- For geometric data
CREATE INDEX idx_locations_coords ON locations USING gist(coordinates);

-- For range types
CREATE INDEX idx_events_duration ON events USING gist(duration);
  • Best for: Geometric/spatial data, range types
  • Use when: PostGIS, geometric queries.

Partial Indexes

Index only rows that match a condition.

-- Full index: includes all 1,000,000 rows
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);

-- Partial index: only includes pending orders (maybe 1,000 rows)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending ON orders(status)
WHERE status = 'pending';

-- Much smaller index, faster to search and maintain!

Use cases:

-- Only index active users
CREATE INDEX idx_users_active_email ON users(email) WHERE is_active = true;

-- Only index recent orders
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_recent ON orders(created_at)
WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01';

-- Only index unprocessed items
CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_unprocessed ON background_jobs(queue, priority)
WHERE processed_at IS NULL;

Covering Indexes (Index-Only Scans)

A covering index contains all columns needed by a query, so the database doesn't need to access the table at all.

-- Query needs: email, name, created_at
SELECT email, name, created_at
FROM users
WHERE email = 'john@example.com';

-- Regular index (must access table for name, created_at)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
-- Index Scan → then fetch name, created_at from table

-- Covering index (includes all needed columns)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_covering ON users(email) INCLUDE (name, created_at);
-- Index Only Scan → no table access needed!

PostgreSQL syntax:

CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table(search_columns) INCLUDE (extra_columns);

Real-World Examples

Example 1: E-Commerce Orders 

-- Common queries:
-- 1. Get user's orders
-- 2. Get orders by status
-- 3. Get recent orders
-- 4. Get user's orders by status

-- Recommended indexes:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status) WHERE status IN ('pending', 'processing');
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created ON orders(created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status ON orders(user_id, status);

Example 2: Blog Posts 

-- Common queries:
-- 1. Get posts by author
-- 2. Get published posts by date
-- 3. Search posts by title
-- 4. Get posts by category

-- Recommended indexes:
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_author ON posts(author_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_published ON posts(published_at DESC) WHERE is_published = true;
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_title_search ON posts USING gin(to_tsvector('english', title));
CREATE INDEX idx_posts_category ON posts(category_id) WHERE is_published = true;

Example 3: User Sessions 

-- Common queries:
-- 1. Get session by token
-- 2. Get user's active sessions
-- 3. Delete expired sessions

-- Recommended indexes:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_sessions_token ON sessions(token);
CREATE INDEX idx_sessions_user_active ON sessions(user_id) WHERE expires_at > NOW();
CREATE INDEX idx_sessions_expires ON sessions(expires_at) WHERE expires_at < NOW();

Index Maintenance

Check Index Usage 

-- PostgreSQL: See which indexes are being used
SELECT
    schemaname,
    tablename,
    indexname,
    idx_scan,      -- Times index was used
    idx_tup_read,  -- Rows read from index
    idx_tup_fetch  -- Rows fetched from table
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
ORDER BY idx_scan DESC;

-- Find unused indexes
SELECT indexname, idx_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0
AND indexname NOT LIKE '%_pkey';

Check Index Size 

-- PostgreSQL: Index sizes
SELECT
    indexname,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexname::regclass)) as size
FROM pg_indexes
WHERE tablename = 'users'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexname::regclass) DESC;

Rebuild Bloated Indexes 

-- PostgreSQL: Rebuild index
REINDEX INDEX idx_users_email;

-- Rebuild all indexes on a table
REINDEX TABLE users;

-- Concurrent rebuild (doesn't lock table)
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_email;

Quick Reference

The Bottom Line

Database indexing is not optional for production systems. It's the difference between "fast" and "unusable."

Remember:

  1. Indexes make reads faster, writes slower. Balance is key.
  2. Use EXPLAIN. Don't guess, look at the query plan.
  3. Index your WHERE clauses. Especially foreign keys.
  4. Composite index order matters. Left-prefix rule.
  5. Monitor index usage. Remove unused indexes.
  6. Start simple. Add indexes based on actual slow queries.

One well-placed index can do more for performance than weeks of code optimization. Learn to use them well.

Your turn 👇

What's the worst slow query you've ever fixed with a single index? I'd like to hear your stories in the comments.

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.

title: Oracle GoldenGate 23ai: Real-Time Replication to the Cloud Without a Downtime Window
description:
Last quarter I migrated a 4TB on-prem Oracle order-management database to OCI Autonomous Database with a change window of exactly zero minutes. No maintenance page, no "please don't place orders between 2 and 4 AM." The tool that made that possible was Oracle GoldenGate 23ai, and if you're still running the classic architecture from a few years ago, the upgrade path itself is worth knowing about before you touch a single extract.

Here's what actually changed, why it matters for cloud migrations specifically, and where I got bitten during setup.

What GoldenGate 23ai actually is

GoldenGate has always done one thing: capture committed changes from a source database's redo/transaction logs and apply them to a target, in near real time, without touching the source workload. 23ai (GA since April 2024, still shipping incremental releases under that name) adds a few things that matter if your target is a cloud database:

  • Microservices architecture is now the only architecture. Classic GGSCI-only deployments are on their way out. Everything runs as a set of REST-managed services (Administration Server, Distribution Server, Receiver Server) fronted by a browser console, managed through adminclient instead of the old ggsci shell alone.
  • AI vector data type support. GoldenGate can now replicate Oracle 23ai VECTOR columns in real time, including to non-Oracle vector stores like pgvector, MySQL HeatWave, and OpenSearch, as long as the embedding algorithm and dimensions match on both sides.
  • Data Streams. DDL and DML changes can be exposed as JSON CloudEvents over AsyncAPI, so a downstream microservice can subscribe to a table's changes without you writing a Kafka Connect pipeline for it.
  • OCI GoldenGate as a managed service. Fully managed deployments across 45+ OCI regions with elastic autoscaling, so you're not babysitting a VM running the hub.

For a straight database migration, the piece that matters most is still the boring one: extract, trail, replicat. Let's build it.

Setting up real-time replication to the cloud

Assume an on-prem Oracle 19c/23ai source and an OCI Autonomous Database (or Oracle on RDS, the pattern is nearly identical) as target. First, enable supplemental logging on the source. Do this at the PDB level, not the CDB root, unless you're specifically doing downstream mining, Oracle explicitly does not recommend root-level capture with a common user for normal replication.

-- Run inside the source PDB, connected as the GoldenGate admin user
ALTER SYSTEM SET ENABLE_GOLDENGATE_REPLICATION=TRUE SCOPE=BOTH;

ALTER TABLE ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER ADD SUPPLEMENTAL LOG DATA (ALL) COLUMNS;

Then, from the admin client (or GGSCI if you're still mid-upgrade), enable trandata and add the extract:

GGSCI> DBLOGIN USERID ggadmin@ORCLPDB1, PASSWORD ******
GGSCI> ADD TRANDATA ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER
GGSCI> ADD EXTRACT EXTORD, TRANLOG, INTEGRATED TRANLOG, BEGIN NOW
GGSCI> ADD EXTTRAIL /u01/ogg/dirdat/ab, EXTRACT EXTORD, MEGABYTES 200

The extract's parameter file is where you actually tell it what to capture:

EXTRACT EXTORD
USERID ggadmin@ORCLPDB1, PASSWORD ******
EXTTRAIL /u01/ogg/dirdat/ab
TRANLOGOPTIONS EXCLUDEUSER GGADMIN
TABLE ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER;
TABLE ORDERS.ORDER_LINES;

On the target side (Autonomous Database, connecting over the wallet TNS alias), add the replicat against a checkpoint table:

GGSCI> DBLOGIN USERID ggadmin@ORCLADB_HIGH, PASSWORD ******
GGSCI> ADD CHECKPOINTTABLE ggadmin.ggchkpt
GGSCI> ADD REPLICAT REPORD, EXTTRAIL /u01/ogg/dirdat/ab, CHECKPOINTTABLE ggadmin.ggchkpt

And its parameter file:

REPLICAT REPORD
USERID ggadmin@ORCLADB_HIGH, PASSWORD ******
ASSUMETARGETDEFS
MAP ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER, TARGET ORDERS.ORDER_HEADER;
MAP ORDERS.ORDER_LINES, TARGET ORDERS.ORDER_LINES;

Start both, watch the lag, and once REPORD reports zero lag against a quiet source, you cut over the application's connection string. That's the whole trick to a zero-downtime migration: the cutover is a DNS/connection-string change, not a data-loading exercise.

GGSCI> START EXTRACT EXTORD
GGSCI> START REPLICAT REPORD
GGSCI> INFO REPLICAT REPORD, DETAIL

Where this requires care

A few things cost me real time on that migration, and I'd rather you skip them:

The classic-to-microservices jump isn't optional anymore. If you're on an older GoldenGate install, plan a separate upgrade step before the migration project, not during it. Trying to learn adminclient REST semantics on the same day you're cutting a production database over is a bad combination.

Autonomous Database needs the wallet, and the wallet needs network ACLs. GoldenGate connects to Autonomous Database over TLS using the downloaded wallet's TNS entry. If your GoldenGate host can't reach the ADB's public or private endpoint, or the ACL on the ADB instance hasn't been opened for that host, you'll get a connection failure that looks like a credentials problem and isn't.

Trail files will eat your disk if replicat lags. On a large initial sync, extract runs ahead of replicat easily. Watch trail directory growth, not just lag in seconds, especially if the target is on a slower network path like a cross-region OCI link.

Vector column replication has real constraints. It's not a magic heterogeneous conversion. Source and target vector dimensions and distance metric need to line up, or you're replicating garbage embeddings that happen to be the right data type.

Root-level capture with a common user works but isn't the recommended path. If you inherited a GoldenGate config that captures from the CDB root, budget time to migrate it to per-PDB extracts before you lean on it for a cloud migration you actually care about.

My take

GoldenGate 23ai's headline features (vector replication, Data Streams, the AI service integrations) are the interesting demo material, but the reason it's worth learning right now is much less flashy: it's the most reliable way I've found to move a live Oracle database to the cloud without asking the business for a maintenance window. The microservices architecture switch is a real cost if you're upgrading from an old classic install, but once it's running, the extract-trail-replicat pattern is the same discipline it's always been, just pointed at a cloud endpoint instead of a second on-prem box.

Further reading

  • Oracle GoldenGate 23ai: What's New
  • Announcing GoldenGate 23ai General Availability
  • Add a Replicat for Autonomous AI Database (OCI GoldenGate)
  • Working with the EXTRACT and REPLICAT utilities of Oracle GoldenGate (AWS RDS docs)

title: Validando CPF dentro do PostgreSQL: função, CHECK constraint e domínio
description:
Transparência: sou fundador da CPFHub, citada no final. O conteúdo é puramente SQL e não depende de nenhum serviço.

Validar CPF só na aplicação deixa uma porta aberta: scripts de importação, outro microsserviço, um UPDATE manual feito às pressas. Se o banco é a fonte da verdade, faz sentido que ele recuse CPFs malformados. Vamos implementar isso no PostgreSQL.

1. Função de validação 

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION cpf_valido(p text)
RETURNS boolean
LANGUAGE plpgsql IMMUTABLE STRICT PARALLEL SAFE AS $$
DECLARE
  d text := regexp_replace(p, '\D', '', 'g');
  soma int;
  dv int;
BEGIN
  IF length(d) <> 11 OR d ~ '^(\d)\1{10}$' THEN
    RETURN false;
  END IF;
  FOR t IN 9..10 LOOP
    soma := 0;
    FOR i IN 1..t LOOP
      soma := soma + substr(d, i, 1)::int * (t + 2 - i);
    END LOOP;
    dv := (soma * 10) % 11 % 10;
    IF dv <> substr(d, t + 1, 1)::int THEN
      RETURN false;
    END IF;
  END LOOP;
  RETURN true;
END $$;

Atenção ao índice: em SQL, substr começa em 1. Para o primeiro DV (t = 9), o peso do primeiro dígito é 10 (9 + 2 - 1); para o segundo (t = 10), é 11.

Marcar como IMMUTABLE permite usá-la em índices e constraints. STRICT faz cpf_valido(NULL) devolver NULL, o que em um CHECK significa "passa", então a obrigatoriedade fica com o NOT NULL.

SELECT cpf_valido('529.982.247-25'),  -- t
       cpf_valido('111.111.111-11'),  -- f
       cpf_valido('529.982.247-24');  -- f

2. Domínio

Um domínio deixa a regra reutilizável em várias tabelas:

CREATE DOMAIN cpf AS char(11)
  CHECK (VALUE ~ '^\d{11}$' AND cpf_valido(VALUE));

CREATE TABLE clientes (
  id    bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  nome  text NOT NULL,
  cpf   cpf  NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  criado_em timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

O ^\d{11}$ dentro do domínio impede gravar com máscara. A aplicação normaliza; o banco garante.

3. Adicionando a uma tabela existente

Em uma tabela antiga, cheia de lixo, não dá para simplesmente criar a constraint. Use NOT VALID:

ALTER TABLE clientes_legado
  ADD CONSTRAINT cpf_ok CHECK (cpf_valido(cpf)) NOT VALID;

Novas linhas e updates passam a ser checados imediatamente. As antigas ficam como estão até você limpá-las:

SELECT id, cpf FROM clientes_legado WHERE NOT cpf_valido(cpf);
-- corrija ou mova para quarentena, depois:
ALTER TABLE clientes_legado VALIDATE CONSTRAINT cpf_ok;

VALIDATE CONSTRAINT usa um lock mais leve que a criação direta, o que importa em tabelas grandes.

4. Normalizando o legado 

UPDATE clientes_legado
SET cpf = lpad(regexp_replace(cpf, '\D', '', 'g'), 11, '0')
WHERE cpf ~ '\D' OR length(cpf) BETWEEN 9 AND 10;

O lpad recupera zeros à esquerda perdidos em exportações para Excel. Antes de rodar, conte quantas linhas serão afetadas e faça em transação.

5. Duplicados disfarçados 

SELECT regexp_replace(cpf, '\D', '', 'g') AS d, count(*)
FROM clientes_legado
GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1;

6. Performance

A função é chamada a cada INSERT/UPDATE da coluna. Em PL/pgSQL ela custa microssegundos; não vai ser o seu gargalo. Se você importa dezenas de milhões de linhas, desabilite a constraint na carga e valide no final.

7. SQLite e MySQL

No MySQL 8, CHECK constraints funcionam, mas não aceitam funções armazenadas. A alternativa é um trigger BEFORE INSERT. No SQLite, registre a função a partir da aplicação (por exemplo, create_function no Python) ou valide na camada de app.

8. E a existência do CPF?

O banco garante que o número é bem formado. Saber se ele existe e a quem pertence depende de uma fonte externa, e isso deve acontecer na aplicação, não em um trigger: uma chamada HTTP dentro de transação segura locks e transforma latência de rede em latência de banco. Um padrão melhor é gravar com status_verificacao = 'pendente' e ter um worker que consulta a API e atualiza a linha.

Sobre a CPFHub

Para esse worker, a API de consulta de CPF oferece consulta individual (GET /cpf/{cpf}) e em lote (POST /cpf/bulk, até 10.000 CPFs por envio, assíncrono), com 50 créditos grátis por mês.

title: Accessibility in React: What Most Developers Skip
description:
Most React accessibility guides tell you to add alt text to images and call it done. That's table stakes. The gaps that actually hurt users with disabilities — and quietly fail WCAG 2.1 AA — are in the dynamic, interactive parts that every modern React app is built on.

This covers focus management, keyboard navigation, ARIA live regions, and a real screen reader testing workflow. Code examples are TypeScript.

Why alt text isn't enough

Static content is easy. Screen readers handle it fine without any developer intervention. The problems start the moment your UI changes without a page reload — a modal opens, a route changes, a toast fires, a combobox filters. At that point, keyboard and screen reader users are on their own unless you handle it explicitly.

The four areas below are where React apps consistently fail audits.

1. Focus management after dynamic content changes

Modals

When a modal opens, focus must move into it. When it closes, focus must return to the trigger element. Neither happens automatically.

import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

interface ModalProps {
  isOpen: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
  triggerRef: React.RefObject<HTMLButtonElement>;
  children: React.ReactNode;
}

export function Modal({ isOpen, onClose, triggerRef, children }: ModalProps) {
  const dialogRef = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (isOpen) {
      dialogRef.current?.showModal();
      // Focus moves to the first focusable element inside
      const firstFocusable = dialogRef.current?.querySelector<HTMLElement>(
        'button, [href], input, select, textarea, [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])'
      );
      firstFocusable?.focus();
    } else {
      dialogRef.current?.close();
      // Return focus to the element that opened the modal
      triggerRef.current?.focus();
    }
  }, [isOpen, triggerRef]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={dialogRef} onClose={onClose}>
      {children}
    </dialog>
  );
}

Use the native <dialog> element. It handles focus trapping and Escape to close by default, and its accessibility semantics are built in. Don't build a <div role="dialog"> unless you have a specific reason — you'll spend twice the effort reproducing what <dialog> gives you for free.

Route changes

Single-page apps are invisible to screen readers on navigation unless you tell them something changed. The browser doesn't announce route transitions the way it announces full page loads.

import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import { useLocation } from 'react-router-dom';

export function RouteAnnouncer() {
  const location = useLocation();
  const announcerRef = useRef<HTMLParagraphElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (announcerRef.current) {
      // Small delay lets the new page content render first
      setTimeout(() => {
        const pageTitle = document.title;
        if (announcerRef.current) {
          announcerRef.current.textContent = `Navigated to ${pageTitle}`;
        }
      }, 100);
    }
  }, [location.pathname]);

  return (
    <p
      ref={announcerRef}
      aria-live="polite"
      aria-atomic="true"
      className="sr-only"
    />
  );
}

Mount this once at the app root. Every route change announces the new page title to screen reader users.

2. Keyboard navigation in custom components

The browser handles keyboard navigation for native elements (<button>, <a>, <input>). The moment you build a custom interactive widget — a combobox, a tab panel, a date picker — you own the keyboard contract entirely.

Tabs (ARIA pattern)

The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide defines the keyboard contract for tabs: Arrow keys move between tabs, Tab moves into the panel, Home/End jump to first/last tab.

import { useState, useRef, KeyboardEvent } from 'react';

interface Tab {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  content: React.ReactNode;
}

interface TabPanelProps {
  tabs: Tab[];
}

export function TabPanel({ tabs }: TabPanelProps) {
  const [activeIndex, setActiveIndex] = useState(0);
  const tabRefs = useRef<(HTMLButtonElement | null)[]>([]);

  function handleKeyDown(e: KeyboardEvent<HTMLButtonElement>, index: number) {
    let nextIndex = index;

    switch (e.key) {
      case 'ArrowRight':
        nextIndex = (index + 1) % tabs.length;
        break;
      case 'ArrowLeft':
        nextIndex = (index - 1 + tabs.length) % tabs.length;
        break;
      case 'Home':
        nextIndex = 0;
        break;
      case 'End':
        nextIndex = tabs.length - 1;
        break;
      default:
        return;
    }

    e.preventDefault();
    setActiveIndex(nextIndex);
    tabRefs.current[nextIndex]?.focus();
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <div role="tablist" aria-label="Content sections">
        {tabs.map((tab, index) => (
          <button
            key={tab.id}
            ref={el => { tabRefs.current[index] = el; }}
            role="tab"
            aria-selected={index === activeIndex}
            aria-controls={`panel-${tab.id}`}
            id={`tab-${tab.id}`}
            tabIndex={index === activeIndex ? 0 : -1}
            onClick={() => setActiveIndex(index)}
            onKeyDown={e => handleKeyDown(e, index)}
          >
            {tab.label}
          </button>
        ))}
      </div>
      {tabs.map((tab, index) => (
        <div
          key={tab.id}
          role="tabpanel"
          id={`panel-${tab.id}`}
          aria-labelledby={`tab-${tab.id}`}
          hidden={index !== activeIndex}
        >
          {tab.content}
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

The tabIndex={-1} on inactive tabs is critical. It means Tab lands on the active tab only — from there, Arrow keys move between tabs and Tab moves into the panel. Without this, keyboard users tab through every tab before reaching the content.

3. ARIA live regions — when to use them and when not to

Live regions announce content changes to screen readers without moving focus. They're useful for status updates (form validation, search results count, toast notifications). They're overused everywhere else.

A reusable announcer 

import { createContext, useCallback, useContext, useState, type ReactNode } from 'react';

type Politeness = 'polite' | 'assertive';

interface AnnouncerContextValue {
  announce: (message: string, politeness?: Politeness) => void;
}

const AnnouncerContext = createContext<AnnouncerContextValue | null>(null);

export function AnnouncerProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [politeMessage, setPoliteMessage] = useState('');
  const [assertiveMessage, setAssertiveMessage] = useState('');

  const announce = useCallback((message: string, politeness: Politeness = 'polite') => {
    // Clearing first lets the same message announce twice in a row
    if (politeness === 'assertive') {
      setAssertiveMessage('');
      setTimeout(() => setAssertiveMessage(message), 50);
    } else {
      setPoliteMessage('');
      setTimeout(() => setPoliteMessage(message), 50);
    }
  }, []);

  return (
    <AnnouncerContext.Provider value={{ announce }}>
      {children}
      <div className="sr-only">
        <p aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">{politeMessage}</p>
        <p aria-live="assertive" aria-atomic="true">{assertiveMessage}</p>
      </div>
    </AnnouncerContext.Provider>
  );
}

export function useAnnouncer() {
  const context = useContext(AnnouncerContext);
  if (!context) throw new Error('useAnnouncer must be used within AnnouncerProvider');
  return context;
}

Use polite for non-urgent updates (search results loaded, item added to cart). Use assertive only for errors that require immediate action — it interrupts whatever the screen reader is saying.

When NOT to use live regions:

  • Don't put them on content that already gets focus (error messages next to inputs — just move focus to the error or use aria-describedby)
  • Don't use them for decorative animations or loading spinners with no meaningful status
  • Don't nest live regions — only the outermost one fires

4. Screen reader testing workflow

Browser DevTools axe checks catch about 30% of real accessibility issues. The rest only surface with a screen reader. Here's a minimal workflow that catches the critical gaps.

Tools:

  • NVDA (free) + Chrome on Windows
  • VoiceOver (built-in) + Safari on macOS/iOS

What to test manually:

  • Tab through every interactive element on the page. Confirm focus order is logical and focus is always visible.
  • Open every modal, drawer, and dropdown with the keyboard. Confirm focus moves in, is trapped, and returns on close.
  • Navigate every custom widget (tabs, combobox, date picker) using only arrow keys and Tab. Confirm the keyboard contract matches the ARIA pattern.
  • Trigger every dynamic state change (form error, toast, search results). Confirm the screen reader announces it.
  • Navigate by headings (NVDA: H key, VoiceOver: Control+Option+Command+H). Confirm the heading structure makes sense out of context.

Chrome DevTools shortcut: Accessibility tree panel (Elements → Accessibility tab) shows you exactly what the screen reader sees for any element. Use it before reaching for a screen reader to catch obvious issues faster.

Practical audit checklist

Run through this before every release that touches interactive UI:

  • All modals use <dialog> or have focus trap + Escape handler
  • Focus returns to trigger element when modal/drawer closes
  • Route changes announce the new page title
  • Custom widgets implement the correct ARIA keyboard pattern
  • tabIndex={-1} on all inactive items in composite widgets (tabs, listbox, menu)
  • Live regions use polite by default; assertive only for blocking errors
  • No nested live regions
  • Every interactive element reachable and operable by keyboard alone
  • Visible focus indicator on every focusable element (not removed by outline: none without a replacement)
  • Heading hierarchy: one <h1>, logical <h2>/<h3> nesting, no skipped levels
  • Form inputs have associated <label> elements (not just placeholder text)
  • Error messages linked to inputs via aria-describedby
  • Tested with NVDA+Chrome or VoiceOver+Safari at least once per release

Key takeaways

  • Static content is the easy part. Dynamic UI — modals, route changes, toasts, custom widgets — is where React apps fail screen reader users.
  • Use <dialog> for modals. It handles focus trap and Escape for free.
  • Every custom interactive widget needs an explicit keyboard contract matching the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide pattern.
  • ARIA live regions announce changes without moving focus — use polite by default, assertive only for blocking errors.
  • A single AnnouncerProvider at the app root handles all live region announcements cleanly.
  • axe DevTools catches ~30% of real issues. Manual screen reader testing with NVDA or VoiceOver is non-negotiable before release.

Originally published at https://suprabhat-dev.com/blog/accessibility-in-react-what-developers-skip/
