title: Mastering API Gateways: Essential Patterns for Scalable Microservices
description:
Introduction

In today's distributed systems landscape, microservices architecture has become a dominant paradigm. While it offers immense benefits like agility, scalability, and independent deployability, managing a growing number of services can quickly become complex. This is where API Gateways step in as a crucial architectural pattern. An API Gateway acts as a single entry point for all client requests, abstracting the underlying microservice landscape and providing a unified interface. This article delves into the essential patterns and considerations for effectively implementing API Gateways, ensuring your microservices architecture is robust and scalable.

The Role of an API Gateway

At its core, an API Gateway serves several critical functions:

  • Single Entry Point: It consolidates multiple microservices into a single, unified API endpoint. Clients don't need to know the location or details of individual services.
  • Request Routing: It intelligently routes incoming requests to the appropriate microservice based on the request path, headers, or other criteria.
  • Protocol Translation: It can translate between different communication protocols, for example, accepting REST requests and forwarding them as gRPC to backend services.
  • Cross-Cutting Concerns: It centralizes common functionalities like authentication, authorization, rate limiting, logging, monitoring, and caching, preventing duplication across microservices.
  • Request/Response Transformation: It can modify requests before they reach the backend or transform responses before they are sent back to the client.

Essential API Gateway Patterns

Several design patterns are fundamental to leveraging API Gateways effectively. Understanding these patterns allows you to build a resilient and performant system. For instance, when dealing with complex real estate platforms or data-intensive applications, the efficiency of your API Gateway directly impacts user experience. Solutions like those found at maxestates.in often rely on sophisticated API Gateway implementations to handle diverse client needs and data retrieval complexities.

Backend for Frontend (BFF)

This pattern involves creating separate API Gateways tailored for specific client types (e.g., mobile app, web app, IoT device). Each BFF can optimize the API calls and data formats for its intended client, improving performance and developer experience for each platform.

Strangler Fig Pattern

While not solely an API Gateway pattern, the Strangler Fig pattern is often implemented in conjunction with an API Gateway. It's a strategy for gradually migrating a monolithic application to microservices. The API Gateway intercepts requests, routing new microservice-based functionality to the new services while still directing traffic for legacy functionality to the monolith. Over time, more functionality is "strangled" from the monolith until it can be retired.

Caching

Implementing caching at the API Gateway level can significantly reduce latency and load on backend services. Frequently accessed, non-dynamic data can be served directly from the gateway's cache, providing a much faster response to clients.

Rate Limiting and Throttling

To protect your backend services from being overwhelmed by excessive requests, rate limiting is essential. The API Gateway can enforce limits on the number of requests a client can make within a specific time window, preventing abuse and ensuring fair usage.

Authentication and Authorization

Centralizing authentication and authorization at the gateway simplifies security management. The gateway can verify user credentials or tokens and determine whether a user has permission to access a particular resource before forwarding the request to the appropriate microservice.

Architectural Considerations

When choosing and implementing an API Gateway, consider the following:

  • Deployment Model: Will it be a standalone service, part of a service mesh, or a managed cloud service (e.g., AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management, Google Cloud API Gateway)?
  • Technology Stack: Choose a gateway technology that aligns with your team's expertise and the needs of your microservices (e.g., Kong, Apigee, Nginx, Envoy).
  • Observability: Ensure your gateway provides robust logging, tracing, and metrics to monitor performance and troubleshoot issues effectively.
  • Scalability and Resilience: The gateway itself must be scalable and resilient, as it's a critical component of your system. Consider strategies like horizontal scaling and circuit breakers.

Conclusion

An API Gateway is an indispensable component of a well-architected microservices system. By understanding and implementing key patterns like BFF, Strangler Fig, caching, rate limiting, and centralized security, you can build a scalable, performant, and maintainable application. Careful consideration of architectural choices will ensure your API Gateway effectively supports your microservices strategy and contributes to the overall success of your application.

Explore the key technical updates, including improved window tiling, TPM-backed full-disk encryption, and a dedicated amd64v3 optimized installer image.

New features in apps and settings

On the apps side, the document viewer now allows users to add handwritten signatures to PDF files. Signatures can be made with a mouse, stylus, touchscreen, or via an imported photo. Taking screenshots has gained more precise control over options via the keyboard, while the sound heard during capture has also been changed.

The main app store has a separate section for additional hardware drivers and media files, while it aggregates details for different app formats. In the system settings, options have been added to automatically disable the touchpad when a mouse is connected, as well as control of auto-rotation on touchscreens. At the same time, the system remembers and restores brightness and color settings for each display separately even after rebooting, while old support for WEP-type wireless networks has been removed.

Hardware support and technical improvements

The new release is based on the GNOME 51 update series, Mesa 26.2 graphics drivers, and Linux kernel 7.3, with a planned nine-month support period. In disk management, full-disk encryption is now available on devices without built-in trusted hardware, requiring the use of a personal PIN or passphrase during installation.

READ ALSO

New Ubuntu 26.10 released with Snapdragon support and new GNOME

The system resource monitor can now display activity for specific AMD processor chips. A separate installation image optimized for the latest processors is available, and an official experimental version has been released for specific new board systems. Finally, the system package management tools offer more informative per-command help.

title: Mastering API Integrations: A Deep Dive with Max Estates
description:
Introduction

In today's interconnected digital landscape, the ability to seamlessly integrate various services and data sources is paramount. APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) serve as the backbone of this connectivity, allowing different software systems to communicate and exchange information. This article will explore the intricacies of API integration, using the real-world example of maxestates.in to illustrate key concepts and best practices. We'll delve into the technical challenges, architectural considerations, and the benefits of robust API integration strategies.

Technical Insights: Building Bridges with APIs

API integration is not merely about making requests and receiving responses; it's about building reliable, scalable, and maintainable connections between disparate systems. For a platform like maxestates.in, which likely deals with real estate listings, property data, and user interactions, integrating with external services can unlock significant value. Consider these common integration scenarios:

Data Synchronization

Maintaining up-to-date property information is critical. This might involve integrating with multiple Multiple Listing Services (MLS) or other data providers. The process typically involves:

  • RESTful APIs: Most modern APIs utilize REST (Representational State Transfer) principles, relying on standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and JSON for data exchange. Understanding these principles is fundamental.
  • Data Mapping: Ensuring that data fields from the source API correctly map to the corresponding fields in your system is crucial. This requires careful analysis of both API schemas.
  • Rate Limiting and Error Handling: External APIs often have rate limits to prevent abuse. Implementing strategies to handle these limits, such as exponential backoff and robust error logging, is essential for preventing service disruptions.

Third-Party Service Integration

Integrating with services like payment gateways, mapping providers (e.g., Google Maps API), or communication platforms (e.g., Twilio for SMS notifications) enhances user experience and operational efficiency. For instance, maxestates.in might integrate with a mapping API to display property locations visually. This involves:

  • Authentication and Authorization: Securely authenticating with third-party services using API keys, OAuth, or other methods is non-negotiable. Proper management of credentials prevents unauthorized access.
  • SDKs and Libraries: Many services provide Software Development Kits (SDKs) or client libraries that simplify the integration process, abstracting away much of the low-level HTTP communication.

Architectural Patterns for Integration

When building complex integration systems, adopting specific architectural patterns can lead to more maintainable and scalable solutions:

  • API Gateway: An API Gateway acts as a single entry point for all client requests, routing them to the appropriate backend services. This can simplify client-side logic and provide centralized cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, and logging.
  • Event-Driven Architecture: For scenarios requiring real-time updates or decoupling of services, an event-driven approach using message queues (e.g., RabbitMQ, Kafka) can be highly effective. When a property listing is updated on maxestates.in, an event can be published, triggering other services to react accordingly.

Conclusion

Effective API integration is a cornerstone of modern software development, enabling platforms like maxestates.in to offer rich functionalities and connect with a broader ecosystem. By understanding REST principles, implementing robust error handling and security measures, and choosing appropriate architectural patterns, developers can build resilient and scalable integration solutions that drive business value and enhance user experiences.

title: Half-open delivery zones: the shared street belongs to exactly one
description:
Draw two delivery zones against the same street and you get a line of addresses sitting exactly on the boundary, and a containment test that is inclusive on both sides hands those doorsteps to two stores at once. Make it exclusive on both sides and nobody gets them. The seam between two zones is not a business question, so a business rule should not be the thing that answers it: the crossing test itself can be half-open, and then a shared edge belongs to exactly one zone by construction.

An overlap is deliberate; a seam is arithmetic

Overlapping coverage is normal, and we design for it. A city-wide hub ring and one store's own ring routinely cover the same district, and which of them serves an address is a rule the business owns: priority, smallest area, nearest store. Our delivery-zones library (https://github.com/shipmindlabs/delivery-zones) keeps that separation. zones_containing collects every match in the order the zones were declared and hands the list to a policy, and the default policy keeps all of them, because picking a winner belongs to the caller rather than to the index.

A seam looks like the same problem and isn't. Two districts cut from one boundary set share an edge, not an area. The addresses along that edge are not contested coverage, they are an artefact of where the arithmetic falls. If a lookup returns both zones for them, a policy will still produce an answer, and the answer will be wrong in a way you cannot see from outside. by_priority(TieBreak.FIRST) ends up resolving the seam by declaration order, so a doorstep changes store the moment somebody appends an unrelated feature to the catalogue file. by_smallest_area(TieBreak.RAISE) compares two districts that have no relationship to each other and picks whichever is smaller, or refuses the order. Neither outcome is a decision anyone made.

So the seam has to be gone before the policy ever runs.

The decision lives in two strict comparisons

The containment test is an even-odd crossing count. You cast a ray east from the position and count how many edges of the ring it crosses. Both of its comparisons are strict, and that is the whole mechanism.

def wraps(self, lon: float, lat: float) -> bool:
    """Even-odd crossing count of a ray running east from the position."""
    inside = False
    for lat_start, lat_end, lon_start, slope in self.edges:
        if (lat_start > lat) != (lat_end > lat):
            if lon < lon_start + (lat - lat_start) * slope:
                inside = not inside
    return inside

The first comparison decides whether an edge spans the ray's latitude at all. Because both halves use a strict >, an edge counts only when exactly one of its endpoints sits strictly above the ray, so an endpoint lying exactly on the ray contributes through the edge that continues upward past it and not through the edge that ends there. A ray passing through a vertex is therefore counted once, a ray grazing a local minimum or maximum is counted twice or not at all, and the parity stays correct with no special case for vertices.

The second comparison decides which side of the edge the position is on, and lon < means a position lying exactly on an edge is treated as being immediately east of it. That single asymmetry is what makes borders half-open. For a ring, the consequence is fixed and you can check it:

position on the ring verdict
southern edge inside
western edge inside
northern edge outside
eastern edge outside

Two zones meeting along a street cannot both claim it, because the street is one zone's eastern or northern edge and the other's western or southern one.

Two rectangles and the street between them 

from delivery_zones import ZoneIndex, zones_from_geojson


def rect(zone_id, store_id, min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat):
    return {
        "type": "Feature",
        "id": zone_id,
        "geometry": {
            "type": "Polygon",
            "coordinates": [
                [
                    [min_lon, min_lat],
                    [max_lon, min_lat],
                    [max_lon, max_lat],
                    [min_lon, max_lat],
                    [min_lon, min_lat],
                ]
            ],
        },
        "properties": {"store_id": store_id, "fee_tier": "standard"},
    }


catalogue = {
    "type": "FeatureCollection",
    "features": [
        rect("west", "store-west", 13.37, 52.51, 13.40, 52.54),
        rect("east", "store-east", 13.40, 52.51, 13.43, 52.54),
    ],
}

index = ZoneIndex(zones_from_geojson(catalogue))

# an address on the shared street, longitude 13.40
[zone.zone_id for zone in index.zones_containing((13.40, 52.52))]  # ["east"]
index.covers((13.40, 52.52))                                       # True

The western zone is not excluded by a cheap pre-filter, incidentally. Its bounding box does contain the position (BoundingBox.contains is inclusive on all four sides), so the lookup has to examine it as a candidate, and the ring is what refuses it. That division is deliberate: an envelope only widens the candidate set, so it can afford to be generous, while the crossing test is the one place where exactness matters. A horizontal seam behaves the same way along latitude. The southern zone's northern edge is outside it and the northern zone's southern edge is inside, so a point on a shared east-west street resolves to the northern zone. For a one-off check against a single polygon, without building an index, there is point_in_polygon.

With the seam closed, the policy recovers its real meaning. More than one match now implies an overlap somebody drew on purpose, which makes by_priority(TieBreak.RAISE) usable as an assertion over the catalogue rather than a dispatch nicety: two zones cover this address and neither claims precedence (priority is 0 when undeclared), so the catalogue is incomplete, and we would rather find that in CI than in a dispatcher's queue.

The seam the test cannot close

Half-open borders decide a shared edge only when it is genuinely shared, when both rings use the same coordinate values along it. Two districts digitised separately, or one of them re-exported through a tool that rounds, leave a sliver nobody covers, and no containment rule can repair that, because the geometry is simply missing. Some of the damage a re-export does is already absorbed. A repeated closing position is discarded when a ring is built, a repeated vertex and an unclosed ring read exactly the same as a clean closed one, and a ring with fewer than three distinct positions raises GeometryError at load instead of quietly dropping out of coverage. A moved coordinate is a different polygon, though, and it will be treated as one.

What we can do is find the hole before a customer does:

from delivery_zones.coverage import scan_coverage

report = scan_coverage(index, spacing=0.0007)
assert report.is_complete, report.describe()

The scan samples a lattice over the envelope of the indexed zones and clusters adjacent misses, so one hole is reported once instead of once per sample, and describe() hands the assertion a line naming how many positions are uncovered, how large the worst gap is and a representative position inside it. Three limits are worth stating plainly rather than discovering later. A gap narrower than the spacing slips between samples. A sample landing exactly on a border falls to whichever side the half-open rule gives it, which is well defined but means a spacing aligned with the rings tells you less than one that isn't. And the default envelope finds holes inside the catalogue, not a district that was forgotten entirely, so for that you pass an explicit area.

What it costs to run

Building the index pays the preparation once. Each ring is flattened into an edge table of (lat_start, lat_end, lon_start, inverse_slope) tuples with horizontal edges dropped, since a horizontal ray never crosses one, which also makes the slope division safe to precompute. The inner loop is then two comparisons and one multiply-add per edge, with no division and no tolerance. Polygons are bucketed into a uniform grid keyed by their envelopes, at most _MAX_GRID_SIDE cells a side, so a lookup examines only the polygons registered in the address' cell and tests each one's bounding box before its rings. An index is a snapshot that prepares every ring once, and when the catalogue changes we build a new one rather than mutating it.

The honest limits are geometric, not performance-related. Coordinates are planar degrees, so nothing wraps at the antimeridian, which a city catalogue does not touch, and we would rather say that out loud than imply coverage we do not have. Polygon area is in square degrees, which does not measure ground area but orders nearby polygons the same way metres would, and that ordering is all that ranking overlaps needs. Distance to a serving store is a great-circle line (EARTH_RADIUS_M = 6371008.8), a line over the ground rather than a route along it. Travel time stays a hook, because streets, traffic and vehicle are not in a polygon, and the constant-speed estimator shipped next to it is for tests and rough delivery tiers, not routing.

Close

The boundary case is the common case here. Every street that separates two zones is made of addresses, and all of them land on the line. A tie-break policy can produce an answer for them, but it cannot produce a stable one, because it is answering a question nobody asked. Make the crossing test half-open and the seam stops being a decision at all, which leaves the policy for the overlaps you actually drew.

title: Ledger errors should name the invariant they protect
description:
A payout worker catches an exception from the ledger and has to decide, with no human in the loop, whether to retry the request, park it, or escalate. If the refusal says "invalid entry", it cannot decide any of those, so the request goes to a dead-letter queue and the string goes to the logs, where a person reads it an hour later and learns exactly as little. A refusal is part of a ledger's interface, and in most systems it is the one part nobody designed.

I have been building payment and custodial systems since 2018, and the error taxonomy is reliably the piece written last and read most. The balance code gets reviewed twice. The exception that stops a write from happening gets a string literal and a shrug. That is backwards: the write that succeeds is self-documenting, since there is an entry you can read. The write that was refused leaves nothing behind except whatever the message said.

Two readers, one string

The message has two audiences with incompatible requirements. The machine wants something narrow and stable: a key it can branch on, which does not move when someone improves the wording. The human wants the opposite, enough context to know whether money is at risk, and whether refusing was the right call.

"Insufficient funds" serves the machine and leaves the human guessing what the ledger was protecting. "The customer's available balance would have gone below zero, so the write was refused" serves the human and is a terrible thing to pattern-match. The usual compromise is a short code plus a wiki page that explains it, and the wiki page is stale within two quarters because nothing fails when it drifts.

In ledger-core (https://github.com/polycratia/ledger-core) I split it differently. The exception class is the branch key. The promise it protects is a class attribute on that class. The message is the two of them joined at raise time, and the bare reason stays reachable on its own.

class InvariantViolated(ValueError):
    """A refused write, carrying the promise that refused it."""

    protects: ClassVar[str] = "a rule of the ledger"

    def __init__(self, detail: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"{detail} \u2014 protects: {self.protects}")
        self.detail = detail


class InsufficientFunds(InvariantViolated):
    """Raised when a reservation or a movement takes more than is available."""

    protects: ClassVar[str] = (
        "available balances stay at or above zero, so the same funds are never spent twice"
    )

There are three of these: UnbalancedEntry, InsufficientFunds, ClosedAccount. Each overrides protects with one sentence written from the ledger's point of view, not the caller's. What reaches a log line is the specific reason and the general promise, separated by an em dash so the two halves stay legible as two halves. What reaches code is the class, plus .detail holding the reason without the promise appended.

That last part matters more than it looks. The promise sentence is editorial copy. Someone will reword it, because it is the sort of thing that gets reworded in review. If callers are storing the full message as a rejection reason on a request row, every rewording changes historical data and any accumulated string matching. .detail is the half that does not carry the editorial text, so it is the half you persist and forward.

Enforced at the one place it can be broken

A promise is only worth printing if it holds where the caller forgot to check. So each of the three is enforced at the single point where it could be violated, and nowhere else pretends to cover it.

Journal.append asks only whether an entry balances. It is not a funds check and does not imply one. The funds check lives in Holds.spend, which computes -effect_on(entry, account), compares that against available(), raises InsufficientFunds if it exceeds it, and only then appends. Closure is enforced where a closed account can actually be touched: in Account._posting, and in Hold.__post_init__.

    def _posting(self, amount: MoneyLike, side: Side) -> Posting:
        if self.closed_at is not None:
            raise ClosedAccount(
                f"account {self.account_id} was closed at {self.closed_at}, "
                f"{side.value} of {amount} is refused"
            )

Putting it there has a consequence worth stating plainly: an Entry.transfer against a closed account raises before the journal appears anywhere in the call stack. The refusal happens while the write is still a value. Same for a one-sided movement: an unbalanced entry never becomes an object, so it cannot be discovered later by something reading the journal. And closing an account refuses new movement without erasing anything, since a closed account's balance still folds from the entries it already has.

Branch on the class, store the detail

With the taxonomy on the classes, the worker's decision is a try block and nothing else:

from ledger_core import ClosedAccount, InsufficientFunds


def settle(holds, entry, account, requests):
    try:
        holds.spend(entry, account=account)
    except InsufficientFunds as refused:
        requests.park(entry.entry_id, reason=refused.detail)
        return "retry_after_funding"
    except ClosedAccount as refused:
        requests.escalate(entry.entry_id, reason=refused.detail, alert=str(refused))
        return "manual"
    return "settled"

The two branches differ because the underlying facts differ. InsufficientFunds is a statement about a quantity that changes: a deposit lands and the same instruction succeeds, so retrying is meaningful. ClosedAccount is a statement about a terminal state, so retrying is guaranteed waste and a human needs to look. The alert carries str(refused), which includes the promise, because the person being woken up has not read this module. The parked row carries refused.detail, because repeating the same promise sentence across ten thousand rows is noise.

Not every refusal is an invariant

The holds module also raises CaptureMismatch, DuplicateHold, HoldNotOpen and UnknownHold. None of them subclass InvariantViolated, and that is deliberate.

Holds.capture skips the funds check entirely: the funds were reserved when the hold was placed, and the reservation is what the balance has been standing behind since. What capture checks is that the amount taken equals hold.amount.amount, raising CaptureMismatch if it does not. That is not a money problem. It is the caller's instruction disagreeing with the caller's own reservation, and collapsing it into InsufficientFunds would make the retry decision wrong: one is worth re-reading a balance for, the other will fail identically forever.

So the dividing question is this: does this refusal protect a promise the ledger makes to everyone, or does it report that the instruction disagrees with state the caller named? The first gets a protects sentence. The second gets a precise message and a plain exception type. That is the only taxonomy rule I have found that keeps working when a new error case shows up six months later.

The test that keeps it honest

Because protects has a default, a subclass that forgets to override it inherits "a rule of the ledger", which is worse than silence, since it looks like a promise and says nothing. One parametrised test closes that:

@pytest.mark.parametrize("violation", [UnbalancedEntry, InsufficientFunds, ClosedAccount])
def test_every_violation_names_what_it_protects(violation: type[InvariantViolated]) -> None:
    assert issubclass(violation, InvariantViolated)
    assert violation.protects != InvariantViolated.protects
    assert violation.protects in str(violation("refused"))

It asserts the override exists and that the sentence actually reaches the message. Since protects is a class attribute, it is readable without raising anything, which means documentation can be generated from the classes rather than maintained beside them.

What I would do differently

First, the default. A ClassVar default makes the base class convenient and makes forgetting silent, and a test is a weaker guard than a definition-time failure. I would check the override in __init_subclass__ so a new invariant without a promise fails at import rather than in CI.

Second, I would write down, in the base class docstring, that the message is for humans and the class is for code. Without that sentence, someone eventually matches on the full string, and then the promise sentence is load-bearing text that cannot be edited.

Third, the gap a refusal cannot close. Holds.place and Holds.spend read available() and then write, as two steps, and the Storage protocol has no transaction, so the atomic pair is left to the backend. InsufficientFunds is then a true statement about what available() was a moment before the append, not a guarantee about what it was during it. Where more than one writer posts to one account, making that pair a single step belongs to the store underneath. A message that names its invariant is honest about the rule, and it cannot be honest about a race the layer below allows. That belongs in the exception's own docstring, next to the promise, so nobody reads the promise as stronger than it is.

A ledger earns trust by what it refuses, and a refusal nobody can act on is barely better than a write nobody checked. Making the promise a class attribute and putting it in the message costs about four lines in one module. What you get for that is that the retry logic and the person on call are reading the same refusal and reaching the same conclusion about it.

title: Yandex problems didn't stop automated programs, according to Cloudflare
description:
Cloudflare analysis reveals that following data center disruptions at Yandex, malicious bot traffic and automated scanning dropped significantly on the affected infrastructure.

However, operators quickly migrated workloads to alternative hosting ASNs like Radist and Selectel, resulting in flat overall attack volumes across targeted sectors.

After the attacks, traffic on Yandex's search and infrastructure services remained at 10% to 15% of normal levels, indicating that the network remains disrupted. While there was a drop in activities such as checking systems for problems, automated systems did not disappear.

This was clearly seen in the case of a gaming company that works with Cloudflare. While attacks from Yandex's systems dropped to zero, the exact same activity began to flow through other networks.

Overall, requests for gaming accounts remained stable over the week, increasing slightly from 167,7 million to 170,1 million. The people behind these programs simply moved their work to other hosting companies once Yandex stopped functioning properly.

title: Building Scalable APIs with Node.js: A Developer's Guide
description:
Introduction: The Rise of Node.js for Backend Development

Node.js has become a powerhouse in the backend development landscape, lauded for its non-blocking, event-driven architecture that excels at building fast and scalable network applications. Its JavaScript-first approach allows developers to use a single language across the full stack, streamlining development workflows and fostering collaboration. Whether you're crafting a simple REST API or a complex microservices architecture, Node.js offers a robust and efficient platform.

Core Concepts for Scalable Node.js APIs

Understanding Asynchronous Operations

At the heart of Node.js's performance lies its event loop and asynchronous I/O model. Unlike traditional threaded models, Node.js handles multiple requests concurrently without blocking the main thread. This is achieved through callbacks, Promises, and the increasingly popular async/await syntax. Mastering these asynchronous patterns is crucial for building APIs that can handle high traffic volumes efficiently.

Leveraging Express.js for Robust Routing

Express.js is the de facto standard framework for building web applications and APIs in Node.js. Its minimalist and unopinionated nature provides a flexible foundation for routing, middleware, and request handling. Setting up a basic Express server involves defining routes for different HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and handling incoming requests and outgoing responses. Middleware functions allow you to execute code at various stages of the request-response cycle, enabling tasks like authentication, logging, and data validation.

Database Integration and ORMs

Scalable APIs often require efficient data persistence. Node.js has excellent support for various databases, including relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL) and NoSQL (MongoDB) options. For relational databases, Object-Relational Mappers (ORMs) like Sequelize or TypeORM can significantly simplify database interactions by mapping database tables to JavaScript objects. For NoSQL databases like MongoDB, libraries like Mongoose provide a schema-based solution to model your application data and offer powerful querying capabilities. Choosing the right database and integration strategy is key to performance. When considering various service providers, it's useful to look at established players in different sectors, for example, understanding the market dynamics by exploring Top Real Estate Companies in Delhi NCR can offer insights into how different entities manage their operations and customer reach, which can indirectly inform strategies for API scaling and service delivery.

Performance Optimization Techniques

To ensure your Node.js API scales effectively, several optimization techniques should be employed:

  • Clustering: Node.js's cluster module allows you to create child processes that share the same server port, effectively utilizing multi-core processors.
  • Caching: Implementing caching strategies (e.g., using Redis or Memcached) for frequently accessed data can drastically reduce database load and improve response times.
  • Load Balancing: Distributing incoming traffic across multiple Node.js instances using a load balancer (like Nginx or HAProxy) is essential for handling peak loads.
  • Code Profiling: Regularly profiling your code to identify bottlenecks and areas for improvement is a proactive approach to maintaining performance.

Conclusion: Building for the Future

Node.js provides a powerful and flexible environment for building scalable backend APIs. By understanding its asynchronous nature, leveraging frameworks like Express.js, integrating databases effectively, and employing performance optimization techniques, developers can create applications that are not only performant but also maintainable and ready to handle future growth. Continuous learning and adaptation to new best practices within the Node.js ecosystem will ensure your APIs remain robust and competitive.

title: Why Is Molecular Dynamics Research Moving to Cloud GPUs?
description:
Molecular dynamics research is moving to cloud GPUs because the hardware available on-premises has stopped keeping pace with the simulations researchers need to run. Molecular dynamics is the computational method used to simulate how atoms and molecules move over time, and it is one of the most GPU-intensive workloads in scientific computing. Labs that built clusters five years ago are still running them today, on the same GPUs, with the same memory limits. The simulations have grown larger. The GPU generations that handle them have moved two cycles ahead. The gap between what the institution owns and what the work needs is widening every year.

Cloud GPUs give research groups access to current GPU generations without capital investment, remove shared-cluster queue time, bill only for compute used, and provide consistent software environments across every team member. These four changes together explain why molecular dynamics labs are shifting from on-premises clusters to cloud infrastructure. Capital budget cycles narrow that gap over eighteen months from approval to installation. Cloud GPUs close that gap in minutes. This is why Yobitel has built a GPU-optimized GROMACS HPC environment on AWS.

What Slows Molecular Dynamics Research Down?

Three infrastructure problems slow molecular dynamics research down before the science even begins: ageing hardware, hidden queue costs, and environment drift across the team.

1. Hardware Generation Gap

On-premises clusters are bought once and run until they are replaced. A cluster purchased in 2021 with NVIDIA V100 GPUs still runs V100s in 2026, while A100, H100, and L4 GPUs have moved through release, widespread deployment, and into standard research use. The institution pays for the cluster regardless of whether it matches the work. Researchers accept the throughput ceiling of hardware that was already ageing when the procurement paperwork cleared.

The memory limit is the harder problem. Older GPU generations carry less memory per card, and molecular dynamics system size is directly constrained by how much GPU memory is available. Three situations push a simulation past what the on-premises hardware can hold:

  • Large membrane-protein complexes that exceed GPU memory per card.
  • Fully solvated biomolecular assemblies that require the workload to split across nodes.
  • Systems that need the memory of a newer GPU generation to avoid communication overhead.

When the workload splits across nodes, communication overhead adds to every step. That overhead increases setup complexity and reduces throughput at the same time.

2. Queue Time as a Hidden Cost

A shared cluster runs on a job scheduler. A researcher submits a job; the scheduler waits for an opening in the queue, and the job starts when resources open. On a busy cluster, that wait lasts hours to days. There is no way to accelerate it without reducing the job, which changes the simulation rather than just the timeline.

The queue does not appear in hardware benchmarks. A cluster rated for high throughput delivers that throughput only to the job that is running. Every job behind it waits, and the researcher who submitted it waits with it. The table below shows the actual time cost of queue delays across common research patterns:

Scenario Clock Time Queue Time Effective Turnaround
Single simulation run 6 hours 48 hours 54 hours
Ten iterative rounds 60 hours 480 hours 540 hours
Grant deadline cycle 2 weeks of compute 4 weeks of waiting 6 weeks total

Queue delay does not appear in any hardware benchmark. It is also the first cost cloud compute eliminates.

3. Environment Consistency Across a Team

On-premises clusters accumulate drift over their operational lifetime. A software update one group installs affects the environment for groups sharing the same nodes. A driver update applied for one application changes the behaviour of another.

GROMACS is sensitive to three configuration variables simultaneously:

  • GPU driver version.
  • CUDA version.
  • Compile flags used to build the binary.

Small differences in any of these produce results that are numerically different even when the scientific inputs are identical. Two researchers with the same input files can get different results for no scientific reason, only because one machine carries a different library version. Reviewers then ask questions the authors cannot answer.

Cloud instances start from a defined image. Every researcher who launches the same AMI gets the same driver, the same CUDA version, and the same GROMACS build. Groups that need to reproduce a result launch the same image rather than reconstructing a software environment from documentation that is often incomplete.

What Does a Cloud GPU Actually Change?

A cloud GPU removes queue time, provides access to current hardware generations, and keeps costs proportional to actual compute used. There is no queue in the shared-cluster sense because the researcher is not competing with other groups for a fixed pool of hardware. The instance terminates when the simulation finishes, and the cost is proportional to the compute used, not to an annual allocation paid regardless of utilisation.

Factor On-Premises Cluster Cloud GPU Instance
Hardware access Fixed at purchase Current generation at launch
Queue time Hours to days Minutes
Scaling Capital request required One configuration change
Cost model Annual regardless of use Hourly per compute used
Environment Drifts over time Defined image at every launch
Reproducibility Depends on cluster state Consistent across every instance

Three things change immediately when a research group moves to cloud GPU instances:

  • Access to current GPU hardware in the week of release, without waiting for a procurement decision.
  • Instance switching that requires changing one field in a launch configuration, not submitting a capital request.
  • Scale-up for a production run or a grant deadline without a request to institutional IT.

How Much Does GPU Generation Affect GROMACS Throughput?

GPU generation affects GROMACS throughput more directly than any other hardware variable, because the engine offloads its heaviest calculations to the GPU and runs faster or slower based on what that GPU can handle.

GPU Workloads GROMACS Offloads

GROMACS offloads the most compute-intensive parts of a molecular dynamics simulation to the GPU, including non-bonded force calculations and particle-mesh Ewald electrostatics. These workloads are highly parallel. GPU generation has a direct and measurable effect on how many nanoseconds of simulation the engine completes per day.

Generation Jump in ns/day.

The throughput differences across GPU generations are not minor:

GPU Generation Relative ns/day Typical Production Runtime
NVIDIA V100 Baseline 8 weeks for large biomolecular system
NVIDIA A100 2 to 3 times V100 3 to 4 weeks
NVIDIA H100 50 to 80 per cent above A100 Under 3 weeks

For a research group running production simulations that need to reach microsecond timescales, those differences determine whether a project completes within a grant period or runs past it. That is not a performance detail. It is a project planning variable.

For a full breakdown of GROMACS GPU workloads and instance configuration, read the GROMACS on AWS technical overview.

Does Cloud Billing Fit Research Workflows?

Yes. Cloud billing fits research workflows because it charges only for compute used, not for time the cluster sits idle. On-premises clusters are funded through capital budgets and amortised over five to seven years. The cost continues regardless of whether the cluster is fully utilised or idle. Periods of low activity do not reduce what the institution paid.

Cloud compute bills by the hour. The difference plays out across the most common research patterns:

Research Pattern On-Premises Cost Cloud Cost
Intensive grant period, then idle Full annual cost regardless Pays only for active compute
Scale-up before publication deadline Capital request, months of lead time Available same day, no approval needed
Continuous year-round simulation Full annual cost Hourly billing, predictable per run
Occasional simulation across the year Full annual cost Proportional to actual use

The model fits the way research actually runs, in cycles of intense simulation followed by analysis and writing, rather than the flat utilisation pattern that justifies a permanent hardware investment. For groups that do not run simulations continuously throughout the year, cloud compute delivers the same throughput at lower total cost than maintaining dedicated hardware.

What Does Moving to Cloud GPUs Look Like in Practice?

Moving to cloud GPUs changes four things at once: hardware access, queue time, cost structure, and environment consistency. These do not operate separately. They compound. A research group that removes queue time also removes the planning uncertainty that comes with it. A group that moves to a defined image also removes the reproducibility questions that configuration drift creates. The gains arrive together, not one at a time.

The move to cloud GPUs is not driven by one advantage. It comes from the combination of four changes that happen at the same time:

  • Access to current GPU hardware in the week of release.
  • Removal of queue time as a constraint on research cycles.
  • Cost proportional to actual compute used.
  • Consistent software environments across every team member.

Research groups that have made the shift report that the primary gain is not raw throughput but the removal of uncertainty around when compute will be available. That change affects how projects are planned and how quickly iterative simulation cycles complete.

Getting started requires less time and expertise than it did three years ago. A pre-configured GROMACS AMI on AWS Marketplace that bundles GROMACS with tested GPU drivers, CUDA, and workflow tools reduces setup time from days to under two hours. The institutional knowledge that previously depended on one HPC administrator is now embedded in a tested image that any team member can launch.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Does moving to cloud GPUs mean losing control over the simulation environment?

No. A cloud instance gives full root access to the machine. Researchers control force field choice, run parameters, system preparation, and every other scientific decision the same way they would on a local machine.

2. Is cloud compute cost-effective for long production runs?

It depends on how the run is structured. A simulation that runs continuously for thirty days on a single instance costs the same as thirty days of on-demand instance time. Spot instances, which AWS offers at sixty to seventy per cent below on-demand pricing for interruption-tolerant workloads with checkpointing, reduce that cost significantly for jobs that can restart from a saved state.

3. Can a cloud GPU instance match a dedicated HPC cluster for multi-node jobs?

For single-node GPU workloads, yes. For jobs that scale across many nodes with high-bandwidth interconnects, a dedicated HPC cluster with InfiniBand fabric still has an advantage. Most molecular dynamics production runs that fit on one to four GPUs run as well or better on cloud instances than on shared cluster hardware.

4. Do I need HPC experience to run GROMACS on a cloud GPU?

Not if the environment is pre-configured. A tested AMI that bundles GROMACS with the required GPU stack removes the compilation and configuration work that previously required HPC expertise. A researcher familiar with GROMACS input files and run parameters can start a simulation without building the software environment from scratch.

title: I built shipshape-cli: a preflight check for JavaScript and React projects before you ship
description:
Most broken builds I've seen weren't caused by hard bugs. They were caused by small things:

  • an import pointing at a file someone renamed
  • an environment variable that never made it into .env.example
  • an empty lint script in package.json
  • a repo with no .gitignore, and node_modules sitting there waiting to be committed

None of these are difficult to fix. They're just easy to miss, and you usually find out at the worst time: when CI goes red, or when a teammate clones the repo and nothing runs.

So I built shipshape-cli, a small preflight check you run before handoff, CI or deployment.

npx shipshape-cli check .

It's on npm now as v0.1.0: shipshape-cli

What it checks

shipshape-cli runs four groups of checks in one pass.

Package configuration. Missing or invalid package.json, invalid package names or versions, empty scripts, no test script, or no build script even though Vite, webpack or Next.js is a dependency.

Import integrity. Relative imports (./ and ../) that don't resolve to a real file. It handles import, export ... from, import(), require() and TypeScript's import type. It also tries the usual extensions and index.* files, the same way your bundler would.

Environment configuration. Variables your code reads through process.env or import.meta.env but that are missing from .env.example, plus entries in .env.example that nothing uses any more.

Project hygiene. No README, no .gitignore, or generated folders like dist or node_modules that aren't ignored.

Here's what it prints for a deliberately broken React app:

IMPORTS
  ✗ IMP001 Cannot resolve import "./components/Footer" (src/App.jsx:2:20)
      Fix: Check the path and file name (including letter case), or create the missing file.

ENVIRONMENT
  ! ENV001 VITE_SENTRY_DSN is referenced but missing from .env.example (src/App.jsx:6:35)
      Fix: Add "VITE_SENTRY_DSN=" with a placeholder value to .env.example.

Summary: 4 errors, 4 warnings, 2 info

Every finding has a rule ID, a file and line, and a suggested fix.

Design decisions

It parses code, it doesn't pattern-match it. Imports and env variables are found with @babel/parser, not regular expressions, so comments and strings that only look like imports don't produce false alarms.

It's strictly read-only. This was the rule I cared about most. A tool you point at your project shouldn't be able to change it, leak it or run it. shipshape-cli:

  • never writes, moves or deletes files
  • never runs npm scripts, installs packages or executes project code
  • never opens your real .env files; it reads only .env.example, and keeps only the variable names
  • makes no network requests and sends no telemetry
  • never prints your source code in its output

All of these are covered by tests.

"Skipped" is not "passed". If a check has nothing to analyse, for example no JavaScript files, it's reported as skipped, never as a green tick. A preflight tool that quietly passes things it never looked at is worse than no tool.

Ignores are never silent. You can leave out intentionally broken folders with a .shipshapeignore file, but every report lists the patterns in use, so nobody can hide a problem without it showing.

Using it in CI

Install it as a dev dependency and add a script:

npm install --save-dev shipshape-cli

{
  "scripts": {
    "preflight": "shipshape check ."
  }
}

The exit codes are built for pipelines: 0 means no errors, 1 means errors were found, and 2 means the scan itself couldn't run. Add --strict to fail on warnings too, or --json for a machine-readable report.

One thing to watch: use npx shipshape-cli, not npx shipshape. The unscoped shipshape package on npm is an unrelated project.

What it doesn't do (yet)

This is a first release, and I'd rather be clear about its limits:

  • Path aliases such as @/components/Button aren't resolved yet, so those imports aren't checked.
  • On macOS and Windows, an import with the wrong letter case still resolves locally, so it isn't caught, even though it will fail on Linux CI.
  • .vue, .svelte and .astro files aren't parsed yet.

Path alias support is the most obvious next step.

Try it 

npx shipshape-cli check .

It needs Node.js 20 or later and works on Node 20, 22 and 24.

  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/shipshape-cli
  • GitHub: https://github.com/Sameera-MHK/shipshape-cli

If you run it on one of your projects, I'd really like to hear what it found, and what it got wrong. Issues and suggestions for new checks are very welcome.

title: How to add a like animation in React (and play it in reverse)
description:
When you come across something you like in an app, a great article, a funny video, a photo that catches your eye, you want to respond, so you hit the like button. If the heart just switches from an outline to a solid icon, it's kind of meh. Okay, I clicked it, but did anything really happen? If the heart fills up and bounces a little, it feels like your tap actually meant something.

I'm not a coder, I'm a motion designer. I create animations like this in After Effects, and I was curious to see how they'd work in a real interface, so I built this button from scratch. This is what I figured out along the way.

Building that bounce in CSS takes keyframes, a scale curve, a color transition and a second set of rules for un-liking. With Lottie, you take the motion a designer made in After Effects as a small JSON file, and React only has to tell it when to play and in which direction.

Here's the whole thing, step by step.

What you need

  • A React app (React 18.2 or newer)
  • A like animation in Lottie format. You can use mine: like.json for light-on-dark UIs, or like-light.json for dark-on-light. It's 3.5 KB and free to use in your projects.

1. Install lottie-react 

npm i lottie-react

This installs lottie-react v3, which brings lottie-web (the player) with it.

2. The component 

import { useState } from "react";
import { useLottie } from "lottie-react";
import likeAnimation from "./like.json";

export function LikeButton() {
  const [liked, setLiked] = useState(false);
  const lottie = useLottie({ src: likeAnimation, autoplay: false, loop: false });

  const toggle = () => {
    lottie.setDirection(liked ? "reverse" : "forward");
    lottie.play();
    setLiked(!liked);
  };

  return (
    <button
      onClick={toggle}
      aria-pressed={liked}
      aria-label={liked ? "Unlike" : "Like"}
      style={{ background: "none", border: 0, padding: 0, cursor: "pointer" }}
    >
      <div ref={lottie.setDisplayRef} style={{ width: 48, height: 48 }} />
    </button>
  );
}

That's it. Drop <LikeButton /> anywhere.

3. How it works

The animation goes from "not liked" on its first frame to "liked" on its last frame. So:

  • autoplay: false and loop: false keep it parked on the first frame until someone taps.
  • On like, we set the direction to "forward" and call play(). The heart fills and bounces.
  • On unlike, we set the direction to "reverse" and call play(). The same motion runs backwards and the heart empties.

The logic is three lines: pick a direction, play, flip the state. Everything else is markup.

aria-pressed tells screen readers the button is a toggle, and the label changes with it, so the animation isn't the only way to know the state.

The easy mistake: restarting instead of reversing

The tempting way to un-like is to jump to the start and play a separate "unlike" animation, or to reset the animation to frame 0. It looks fine when you tap slowly. Now tap twice quickly: the second tap lands while the heart is still bouncing, the animation snaps to its start, and the heart visibly jumps.

Playing in reverse doesn't have this problem. If you tap while the heart is still moving, in either direction, setDirection turns the animation around from exactly where it is, so it always moves smoothly. Try tapping fast in the demo: it never jumps.

One more thing if you're copying from older tutorials. Many of them are written for lottie-react v2, which used animationData and setDirection(-1). In v3 the prop is src and the direction is a word, "forward" or "reverse". If your copied snippet throws or does nothing, that's usually why.

Make it yours: change the color

The heart is orange in my file. Lottie stores colors as numbers inside the JSON, so you can swap them before you pass the animation in:

type Hex = `#${string}`;
const toRgb = (hex: Hex) => [1, 3, 5].map((i) => parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255);

export function recolor<T>(animation: T, colors: Record<Hex, Hex>): T {
  const swaps = Object.entries(colors).map(([from, to]) => [toRgb(from as Hex), toRgb(to as Hex)]);
  const copy = structuredClone(animation);
  const walk = (node: any): void => {
    if (Array.isArray(node)) return node.forEach(walk);
    if (!node || typeof node !== "object") return;
    const k = node.c?.k;
    if ((node.ty === "fl" || node.ty === "st") && Array.isArray(k) && typeof k[0] === "number") {
      const hit = swaps.find(([from]) => from.every((v, i) => Math.abs(v - k[i]) < 0.01));
      if (hit) node.c.k = [...hit[1], k[3] ?? 1];
    }
    Object.values(node).forEach(walk);
  };
  walk(copy);
  return copy;
}

Then, once at the top of your file (outside the component):

const pinkLike = recolor(likeAnimation, { "#FF4A1C": "#E11D48" });

and pass src: pinkLike. The animation uses only two colors, the line (#F2F1ED, or #121212 in the light version) and the accent (#FF4A1C), so two entries are enough to match any brand.

Wrapping up

A like that lands instead of flipping is a small thing, but it's the kind of small thing people feel without being able to name it. With lottie-react it costs you a 3.5 KB file and three lines of logic.

The animation in this post is from Zeltrium, my pack of Lottie UI micro-interactions. Get 5 more free at zeltrium.com.

title: "I Can't Reach the Button" Is Unreproducible on Your Desktop, and `100vh` Is Why
description:
A report comes in: the submit button at the bottom of a full-height section cannot be tapped. You open the page on your desktop. Fine. You open the responsive emulator at the phone's exact dimensions. Also fine. You close the ticket.

The reporter was right, and so were you. The difference is a browser interface neither of you was looking at.

vh is not the height of the screen

It is the height of the screen with the URL bar taken away. Not as a bug, and not as an implementation detail somebody will fix. It is what the unit is specified to mean.

CSS Values and Units Level 4 defines three viewport sizes. The small viewport is "the viewport sized assuming any UA interfaces that are dynamically expanded and retracted to be expanded". The large viewport is the same sentence with the last word changed to "retracted". And then the part that catches people:

The large viewport-percentage units (lv*) and default viewport-percentage units (v*) are defined with respect to the large viewport size.

The default units. vh is lvh. Your 100vh section is laid out as though the URL bar is not there, on a device where it is there until the user scrolls.

So on first paint, before anybody has scrolled, the bottom of that section is underneath the browser chrome. The button is on the page, it is rendered, it has non-zero dimensions, and your tests will say so. It is just not somewhere a thumb can go.

Why it was specified that way

Not an oversight. The alternative is worse.

If vh tracked the bar as it retracted, every full-height element would reflow mid-scroll. Headers would jump, a sticky footer would walk up the screen, and text would reparagraph under the reader's eyes while they were reading it. Pinning vh to the larger of the two sizes buys you a unit that holds still. The cost is that it is wrong by the height of the bar at exactly the moment most people see your page for the first time.

You can see all three at once:

const probe = document.createElement('div');
probe.style.position = 'absolute';   // out of flow, so measuring cannot move the page
probe.style.visibility = 'hidden';
document.body.append(probe);

for (const unit of ['vh', 'svh', 'lvh', 'dvh']) {
  // An unsupported unit is an invalid declaration, which leaves the previous
  // value in place and would print the last unit's number as if it were this one.
  if (!CSS.supports('height', `100${unit}`)) {
    console.log(unit, 'not supported here');
    continue;
  }
  probe.style.height = `100${unit}`;
  console.log(unit, probe.getBoundingClientRect().height);
}

probe.remove();
console.log('innerHeight', window.innerHeight);
console.log('visualViewport', window.visualViewport?.height);

On a desktop browser every number is the same, which is the entire reason this never shows up while you are working. On a phone, before you scroll, svh and lvh differ by the height of the bar and vh sits with lvh.

The fix you reach for is the one the spec warns about

Having found dvh, the obvious move is to swap it in everywhere. The specification gets ahead of you:

The sizes of the dynamic viewport-percentage units are not stable even while the viewport itself is unchanged. Using these units can cause content to resize e.g. while the user scrolls the page.

That is the reflow problem you just opted back into. dvh is right where a resize mid-scroll is genuinely harmless. For anything that has to be reachable without scrolling - a primary action, a dismiss control, a cookie banner's accept button - svh is the honest unit, because it is the one that assumes the chrome is in the way. The layout is slightly short when the bar retracts. Nobody has ever filed a ticket about slightly short.

What the report could not have told you

Here is the part that generalises past this one unit.

Ask the reporter what their viewport was and they will send you a screen size, because that is the number a phone knows about itself. It is the wrong number. What decided the layout was whether a piece of browser furniture was expanded at that moment, which is not a device property, not a setting, and not something they can observe. It depends on whether they arrived from a link or a home screen icon, and on whether they had scrolled yet.

A screenshot does not settle it either. The screenshot shows the visual viewport. Your CSS was reasoning about the large one. Those are the two numbers whose disagreement is the whole bug, and the image contains only one of them.

Which is the shape of most unreproducible reports, once you look at them: the fact that would decide it is not hidden, it is just not a fact the person in front of the problem is able to know they should write down.

title: DigitalOcean costs 30-40% more than Hetzner for Node.js — is the premium worth it?
description:
After benchmarking Hetzner vs DigitalOcean for Node.js, I kept getting the same question: "but what about support and dashboard UX?" Here's what the premium actually buys you, beyond the spec sheet.

Pricing (2026)

Plan vCPU RAM Storage Price/month
Basic 1GB 1 1 GB 25 GB SSD $6
Basic 2GB 1 2 GB 50 GB SSD $12
Basic 4GB 2 4 GB 80 GB SSD $24
Basic 8GB 4 8 GB 160 GB SSD $48

Hetzner CX22 (2 vCPU, 4GB) runs ~€4.35/mo. DigitalOcean's equivalent Basic 4GB is $24/mo — roughly 5x. Premium AMD droplets (NVMe, dedicated thread) cost ~2x the Basic tier on top of that.

What the premium actually buys you

  • Live chat support that responds. This is the real differentiator — tickets get answered in minutes, not the 24-48h typical of budget providers.
  • A dashboard that doesn't fight you. Droplet creation, snapshots, firewalls — all obvious without reading docs.
  • A 1-Click Node.js Marketplace image that pre-installs Node, PM2, and Nginx — saves roughly 15 minutes on initial setup.
  • Managed databases, load balancers, and S3-compatible Spaces in the same dashboard if you need them later.

What it doesn't buy you

Basic plans use shared Intel CPUs with regular SSD, not NVMe — NVMe only comes on Premium droplets. Disk throughput on Basic was clearly the weak point:

Metric DigitalOcean Basic 4GB Hetzner CX22
Express API (light load, EU) 10–18ms 8–15ms
Disk read (sequential) ~500 MB/s ~2,000 MB/s
Price/month $24 ~€4.35

Premium AMD droplets close most of that gap, but then you're paying closer to 6-7x Hetzner's price for comparable performance.

Who this is actually for

  • ✅ You're new to VPS and don't want to debug SSH/firewall issues solo
  • ✅ Client work where "who do we call at 2am" needs a real answer
  • ✅ Short-lived environments — hourly billing is available
  • ✅ You'll actually use managed databases or load balancers later
  • ❌ Pure budget optimization — Hetzner or Contabo give more spec per dollar
  • ❌ Disk-heavy workloads on Basic plans specifically

Verdict

The premium is real, and for client work where support response time matters, I'd pay it again. If you're a solo dev optimizing your own side project's bill, it's genuinely hard to justify over Hetzner on specs alone — the thing you're paying for is the safety net, not the hardware.

Full benchmarks, regions, and Node.js setup steps at vpsfor.dev →

title: How We Built HydroBid: Offline Quoting for Pressure Washing Crews (Capacitor + Dexie)
description:
TL;DR

HydroBid is a Capacitor + React app for pressure washing / soft wash estimates. Quotes and appointments live in IndexedDB (Dexie). PDFs are generated on-device. Calendar reminders use local notifications. No account required for core quoting.

Product page: knoxstudios.net/apps/hydrobid.html

This post is a build log: architecture choices, freemium edges, and Android gotchas—not a feature dump dressed as a tutorial.

Why this app exists

Exterior cleaning crews often bid from the driveway. Cloud-only estimators fail when signal fails. We wanted:

  • Line items with sq ft / linear ft / hour / flat
  • Branded PDF share from the phone
  • Pipeline + calendar so follow-ups don’t die in SMS
  • Wash helpers: chemical mix, area, water usage
  • Local-first data (Dexie), Capacitor for Android

Architecture (high level) 

┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ React 19 + Vite + Tailwind (UI)         │
│  QuoteBuilder · Calendar · Tools · PDF  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Dexie / IndexedDB   │  session drafts   │
│ quotes, appts,      │  photo compress   │
│ settings            │                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Capacitor 8                             │
│ Camera · Filesystem · Share             │
│ Local Notifications · AdMob · RC IAP    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Source of truth = device. AdMob and RevenueCat are side channels; they must never block reading/writing quotes.

Quote model (simplified) 

type QuoteStatus = 'draft' | 'sent' | 'accepted' | 'rejected'

interface LineItem {
  id: string
  label: string
  qty: number
  unit: 'sq_ft' | 'linear_ft' | 'hour' | 'flat'
  rate: number
  amount: number
}

interface Quote {
  id: string
  clientAddress: string
  lineItems: LineItem[]
  photoDataUrls: string[]
  status: QuoteStatus
  price: number
  // ... notes, validUntil, paymentTypes, sentAt, appointmentAt, etc.
}

Always normalize on read: default empty arrays, recompute price from line items. Field apps accumulate messy rows after updates; defensive normalization > perfect migrations alone.

PDF pipeline

  1. Map Quote + company settings → @react-pdf/renderer document (themes: canopy / invoice / simple)
  2. Optionally downscale photos for the PDF (we cap embedded images)
  3. On native: write file → Share plugin
  4. Enforce free-tier unique export quota per month in one module so UI and paywall agree

Lesson: treat the PDF as the customer API. If Share works offline after generation, you’ve won the job-site demo.

Calendar without a backend

  • Store Appointment rows locally (optional quoteId)
  • Derive calendar markers from quote timestamps (sentAt, respondedAt, validUntil) + appointments
  • Export .ics via Filesystem/Share or open a Google Calendar URL when online
  • Rebuild local notifications from DB (T-24h / T-2h for jobs; nudges for drafts/unsent/expiry)
  • Respect quiet hours + max notifications per day so you don’t train users to disable everything

Android 13+ needs POST_NOTIFICATIONS. Exact alarms need the right permission storytelling in the OS settings screen—prime this in onboarding, don’t ambush post-install.

Tools that write back to the draft

Chemical dilution, L×W area, and GPM×time water math live under a Tools tab. Persisting calculator drafts (and “add to quote” actions) keeps wash-specific math inside the same session as the bid.

Small UX win, large retention win: users stop alt-tabbing to random calculator apps.

Freemium edges we encoded early

Free Premium
Ads + PDF generate/share gate Ad-free
Limited unique PDF exports / month Unlimited exports
Up to 2 job photos / quote Up to 6
Basic dashboard Service-mix insights
“Made with HydroBid” on PDF Clean footer + rate hide/customize

Encode limits as constants (FREE_EXPORT_UNIQUE_QUOTES_PER_MONTH, FREE_MAX_QUOTE_PHOTOS). Scattered magic numbers create support tickets.

Onboarding that earns permission

Order that worked for us:

  1. Welcome / problem framing
  2. How it works (quote → PDF → follow-up)
  3. Company profile (logo + default rate)
  4. Notifications prime (why reminders matter)
  5. Soft Premium intro (no hard wall)

Profile-before-paywall means the first PDF already looks like their business.

What I’d tell another indie shipping field tools

  1. Ship offline path first; sync is a sequel.
  2. Compress images before IndexedDB.
  3. One module owns quotas and Premium checks.
  4. Local notifications need a rebuild function you can call after every meaningful write.
  5. Be explicit in store copy about what you don’t do (tax, maps, live CRM)—it reduces 1★ “where’s X?” reviews.

Links

  • App / product page: HydroBid
  • Stack: React 19, Vite, Capacitor 8, Dexie, @react-pdf/renderer, RevenueCat, AdMob

Questions about Dexie schema versioning or PDF photo embedding? Drop them in the comments—happy to compare notes with other Capacitor folks shipping trades apps.

title: CSS-Only Custom Elements for Accessibility (a11y)
description:
In CSS-Only Custom Elements for Layouts, I used undefined custom-element tags to define an API for layout primitives.

That technique can also be used to improve accessibility in your application.

Building visually-hidden

One of the most common accessibility patterns is visually hidden content that remains available to screen readers and other assistive technology.

An element that is merely transparent or moved off-screen is not always equivalent to hidden content. It can still affect layout, receive focus, or be exposed inconsistently. Use a deliberate clipping pattern:

/**
 * Visually hides content while keeping it available to assistive technology.
 */
visually-hidden {
  position: absolute;
  width: 1px;
  height: 1px;
  padding: 0;
  margin: -1px;
  overflow: hidden;
  clip: rect(0 0 0 0);
  clip-path: inset(50%);
  white-space: nowrap;
  border: 0;

  /* Restores visibility while the element or one of its descendants contains focus. */
  &:focus-within {
    position: static;
    width: auto;
    height: auto;
    margin: 0;
    overflow: visible;
    clip: auto;
    clip-path: none;
    white-space: normal;
  }
}

The element can now carry context without changing the visual design:

<button type="button">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 16 16"><!-- icon --></svg>
  <visually-hidden>Open navigation</visually-hidden>
</button>

The button is still the semantic and interactive element. visually-hidden only changes how its child text is presented.

If the element contains a focusable descendant, :focus-within restores the wrapper automatically while that descendant has focus.

NOTE: Do not use this element for content that shouldn't be available to everyone. For that, use the native hidden attribute or display: none.

Building skip-link

Skip links are a useful example because they combine an accessible name, keyboard focus, and visual presentation:

/**
 * A keyboard-accessible link that becomes visible when focused.
 */
skip-link {
  display: block;
}

skip-link > a {
  position: absolute;
  top: 1rem;
  left: 1rem;
  z-index: 1000;
  transform: translateY(-200%);
  padding: 0.5rem 0.75rem;
  background: Canvas;
  color: CanvasText;
  border: 2px solid currentColor;
}

skip-link > a:focus-visible {
  transform: translateY(0);
}

<skip-link>
  <a href="#main-content">Skip to main content</a>
</skip-link>

<header><!-- site navigation --></header>
<main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">
  <h1>Dashboard</h1>
</main>

The target needs a stable id. tabindex="-1" allows a script or a browser to move focus to the main region without adding it to the normal tab sequence.

The custom element does not make the link a skip link. The nested native <a>, its href, and the target relationship do that. The custom element only gives the pattern a discoverable styling hook.

Building reduced-motion

Motion preferences can also be standardized without JavaScript. A common misconception is that prefers-reduced-motion: reduce means every animation and transition must be turned off. The goal is to minimize non-essential motion while preserving information and interaction.

A wrapper can provide a practical boundary for controlling descendant animations, especially in an area of the page that comes from a third-party component or code you do not own:

/**
 * Minimizes non-essential motion for its descendants when requested.
 */
reduced-motion {
  display: contents;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  reduced-motion,
  reduced-motion * {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

<reduced-motion>
  <aside class="toast">Message sent</aside>
</reduced-motion>

This is a policy boundary, not a guarantee that every animation has become accessible. Motion that communicates meaning may need an alternate presentation, and the preference should be respected by JavaScript-driven animation too.

What CSS cannot do

It is tempting to create elements such as <a11y-button>, <a11y-dialog>, or <a11y-live-region> and assume the names communicate their purpose. They do not.

CSS cannot:

  • add a button or other relevant ARIA role, click behavior, or keyboard activation to a generic element.
  • create an accessible name for an unlabeled control.
  • reliably announce changing content to a screen reader.
  • manage focus when a dialog opens or closes.
  • validate a widget's state or keep aria-expanded synchronized.

Use a native element first. Add ARIA only when native HTML cannot express the required relationship or state. Use JavaScript when interaction needs state, focus management, announcements, or event coordination.

Accessibility and the cascade

CSS-only elements have no shadow root, so their styles participate in the global cascade. That makes the API easy to override, but it also means a broad rule can interfere with consumer content.

Keep the base selector low-specificity when possible:

:where(visually-hidden, skip-link) {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

Scope descendant rules narrowly. Target specific interactive elements (a, button, etc.) rather than using broad universal selectors. A small selector surface is easier to audit.

Document the attributes and custom properties as part of the public API. A Custom Elements Manifest can describe CSS-only elements when the stylesheet includes the expected JSDoc comments, even though there is no JavaScript class.

When you should use these

CSS-only accessibility elements are useful when the primitive is about presentation or a reusable styling boundary:

  • A design system can standardize visually hidden content.
  • Templates can make skip links and reduced-motion boundaries discoverable.
  • Native HTML can remain responsible for meaning and interaction.
  • There is no JavaScript cost or custom-element upgrade lifecycle.

Conclusion

CSS-only custom elements can make accessibility patterns visible in markup, but they cannot make an inaccessible structure accessible by naming it.

The strongest design is a division of responsibility: native HTML provides semantics and interaction, ARIA fills specific gaps, JavaScript manages state and focus when required, and CSS handles presentation and user preferences.

When that contract is explicit, a tag and a stylesheet can provide a useful accessibility primitive without pretending to replace the platform.
