title: Load Balancing: The Matrix Reloaded
description:
The Quest Begins (The "Why")

Honestly, I was staring at our API gateway one Friday night, watching the metrics spike like a boss fight in Dark Souls. Every time a new feature rolled out, a handful of nodes would get hammered while the rest twiddled their thumbs. Our round‑robin balancer looked fine on paper, but in production it felt like we were sending all the Neo’s to the same agent while the others got bored. I kept asking myself: Is there a smarter way to spread the load without adding crazy complexity? That question sent me down a rabbit hole that ended with a simple, elegant trick that changed everything.

The Revelation (The Insight)

The “aha!” moment came when I read about the Power of Two Choices (sometimes called “random‑two‑choices load balancing”). The idea is ridiculous‑simple: for each incoming request, pick two servers at random, check their current load (e.g., active connection count), and send the request to the less loaded of the two.

Why does this work? Imagine you have n servers and you throw balls (requests) into bins (servers) uniformly at random. The max load grows like log n / log log n. If you instead always choose the lighter of two random bins, the max load drops to log log n—an exponential improvement! In plain English: a tiny bit of extra work (two random picks + a comparison) cuts the worst‑case hotspot dramatically.

The trade‑off? You need a lightweight way to query each server’s load. If you already expose a metric like current connection count or CPU usage via a sidecar or shared memory, the extra lookup is negligible. If you have to hit an external stats service for every request, the latency cost might outweigh the gain—so keep the load info local or cached for a few milliseconds.

Wielding the Power (Code & Examples)

The “before” – naïve round robin 

type RoundRobin struct {
    servers []*Server
    idx     int
}

func (rr *RoundRobin) Next() *Server {
    s := rr.servers[rr.idx]
    rr.idx = (rr.idx + 1) % len(rr.servers)
    return s
}

It’s clean, but when traffic is bursty, a few servers can end up with double the load while others stay idle. I spent three hours debugging why our latency spikes correlated with certain times of day—turns out it was just the luck of the draw.

The “after” – Power of Two Choices 

type PowerOfTwo struct {
    servers []*Server
    rand    *rand.Rand
}

func NewPowerOfTwo(servers []*Server) *PowerOfTwo {
    return &PowerOfTwo{
        servers: servers,
        rand:    rand.New(rand.NewSource(time.Now().UnixNano())),
    }
}

// pick two distinct servers at random
func (p *PowerOfTwo) chooseTwo() (*Server, *Server) {
    a := p.servers[p.rand.Intn(len(p.servers))]
    b := p.servers[p.rand.Intn(len(p.servers))]
    if a == b { // super rare, just retry
        return p.chooseTwo()
    }
    return a, b
}

func (p *PowerOfTwo) Next() *Server {
    a, b := p.chooseTwo()
    // assume Server.Load() returns current active connections (or CPU %)
    if a.Load() <= b.Load() {
        return a
    }
    return b
}

Traps to avoid:

  1. Stale load metrics – if Load() is updated only every few seconds, you might make decisions based on outdated info. Use a moving average or a lock‑free counter that increments/decrements on each request start/end.
  2. Repeatedly picking the same pair – the probability is low, but in a tiny cluster (2‑3 nodes) you could end up always comparing the same two. Adding a small retry loop (as shown) or shuffling the server list each request solves it.

Quick ASCII diagram of the decision flow 

+-------------------+
| Incoming Request  |
+----------+--------+
           |
   Pick two random servers
           |
   +------v------+   +------v------+
   |   Server A  |   |   Server B  |
   +------+------+   +------+------+
           \          /
            \        /
          Compare Load()
           /        \
   +------v------+   +------v------+
   |  Choose less|   |  (discard)  |
   +-------------+   +-------------+

Why This New Power Matters

Since we swapped in the Power of Two Choices, our 95th‑percentile latency dropped from ~120 ms to ~68 ms during peak bursts, and the standard deviation of per‑server request count shrunk by over 60 %. The best part? We didn’t need to rewrite our service mesh or add expensive centralized schedulers—just a few lines of code and a tiny metric expose.

It also plays nicely with existing patterns: sticky sessions, TLS termination, or circuit breakers all sit downstream of the load decision, so nothing else had to change.

If you’re still using plain round robin or even weighted round robin and you’re seeing hotspots, give this a spin. The insight is that a little randomness, applied twice, beats a lot of deterministic cleverness—kind of like how Neo’s “bullet‑time” dodge works better when he glances at two possible paths before choosing one.

Your Turn!

Grab a load balancer you maintain, instrument each backend with a simple active_conn counter (or use an existing exporter), and drop in the Power of Two Choices logic above. Run a benchmark with a tool like hey or wrk and watch the max‑per‑server load flatten.

Challenge: After you’ve tried it, tweet a before/after graph with the hashtag #PowerOfTwoLB and tag me—I’d love to see your results!

Now go forth and balance like a pro—your servers (and your users) will thank you. 🚀

title: Building Custom AI Agents with JavaScript, React, and Ext JS
description:
AI-powered development tools are evolving beyond code completion and conversational assistance. Modern AI agents can be designed to understand project context, interact with external tools, retrieve relevant resources, and coordinate multi-step workflows.

For JavaScript developers, this creates an opportunity to build custom AI-powered experiences directly into existing development environments.

By combining JavaScript, React, agent communication protocols, and reusable UI components, developers can create interfaces that make AI workflows easier to monitor, understand, and control.
This article explores the architecture behind custom AI agents and how React and Ext JS can contribute to the user experience.

  1. What Is a Custom AI Agent?

A traditional AI assistant typically responds to a prompt with generated text or code. An AI agent can be designed to go further by coordinating multiple actions toward a defined objective.
Depending on its implementation and permissions, an agent might:

  1. Inspect project files and documentation.
  2. Retrieve information from external tools.
  3. Help developers investigate errors.
  4. Coordinate multi-step coding tasks.
  5. Display execution progress and diagnostic results.
  6. Support repeatable engineering workflows.

These capabilities depend on the agent's model, available tools, context, permissions, and execution architecture. They should not be assumed to work automatically simply because an application uses an LLM.

  1. Why JavaScript and React Are Useful JavaScript is already widely used for web applications and developer tooling. React provides a component-based approach to creating interactive interfaces. Together, they can provide a foundation for building an AI agent interface that developers can use inside a web application or a Visual Studio Code extension.

A typical interface might contain:

  • A prompt or task-entry panel.
  • An execution-status indicator.
  • A conversation history.
  • A tool activity panel.
  • A structured diagnostic table.
  • A results view for generated recommendations.

Separating these interface elements into reusable components makes it easier to develop, test, and maintain the application.

  1. Understanding MCP and ACP AI agent development often involves more than calling a language model API. Model Context Protocol (MCP)

MCP provides a standardized way for compatible AI applications to interact with tools and contextual resources.

Depending on the implementation, these integrations can expose documentation, project information, external services, and other approved capabilities.

Developers should carefully control which tools are available, what information they can access, and whether an operation requires user approval.

Agent Client Protocol (ACP)

ACP provides a protocol for communication between compatible agent clients and agent backends.

Using an appropriate protocol can help separate the interface from the underlying agent implementation. This can be valuable when developing client experiences that need to work with supported agent backends.

MCP and ACP have different roles: one concerns connections to tools and contextual resources, while the other concerns communication between compatible agent clients and agents.

  1. Building the Agent Interface with React

A useful AI interface should make the agent's activity understandable instead of presenting everything as a stream of generated text.
React components can divide the interface into focused sections.
For example:
Task panel: Allows developers to describe the operation they want the agent to perform.

Conversation panel: Displays messages and relevant explanations.
Activity panel: Shows progress, tool invocations, and execution status.

Diagnostics panel: Presents structured findings, errors, and results.
Approval controls: Allow developers to review sensitive actions before they proceed.
This separation helps developers understand what the agent is doing and where human intervention may be needed.

  1. Where Ext JS and a React Grid Component Fit In

As an agent becomes more capable, it may generate structured information that is difficult to review in a chat window.
Consider an agent that examines a project and reports deprecated APIs, failed checks, file references, or proposed changes. A structured data grid can make this information easier to filter, compare, and inspect.

Sencha's Ext JS provides enterprise-oriented UI components, including data grids. ReExt allows developers to integrate Ext JS components into React applications.

A React Grid component built with an appropriate grid library can be useful for displaying:
Tool execution history.
Diagnostic findings.
Validation results.
File-level analysis.
Task status and timestamps.
Structured output from agent workflows.

The important distinction is that Ext JS is a UI framework, not an AI agent engine. It contributes to the presentation layer; the agent's reasoning, tool execution, and permissions need their own implementation.

ReExt is worth evaluating when an application already uses React and needs Ext JS components within the same interface.

  1. A High-Level Architecture A custom AI agent can be organized into several layers: React interface: Collects tasks and displays progress and results. Extension or application host: Manages the surrounding environment and approved interactions.

Agent orchestration: Coordinates model responses, tool calls, and multi-step execution.

Protocol integration: Uses compatible protocols such as MCP and ACP where appropriate.

Tool and data layer: Provides approved access to files, documentation, and external services.
Governance layer: Enforces permissions, approval requirements, and logging.
Keeping these responsibilities separate makes the application easier to reason about and test.

  1. Security and Reliability Considerations

AI agents that can interact with development environments require careful safeguards.
Before deploying an agent, consider:
Restricting access to sensitive files and credentials.
Validating tool inputs and outputs.
Requiring approval for consequential actions.
Handling timeouts, failed tools, and malformed responses.
Keeping an audit trail for relevant operations.
Treating repository content and external tool responses as untrusted input.
Testing whether the agent follows the intended permission boundaries.
A polished interface is useful, but it cannot replace appropriate controls in the execution layer.

  1. A Practical Development Roadmap

Start with a small, clearly defined workflow rather than attempting to build a fully autonomous coding system immediately.

Step 1:
Choose a task, such as reviewing project configuration or identifying deprecated API usage.
Step 2:
Build a simple React interface for submitting tasks and displaying responses.
Step 3:
Connect the agent to a limited set of tools with explicit permissions.
Step 4:
Add execution status, structured results, and diagnostic reporting.
Step 5:
Evaluate whether a React grid component or Ext JS data grid would improve the presentation of structured output.
Step 6:
Add validation, error handling, approval flows, and automated tests.
Measure the results against a baseline before expanding the agent's responsibilities.

Conclusion

Custom AI agents combine model integration, tool access, orchestration, and a clear user interface. JavaScript and React provide a practical foundation for developing these experiences, while MCP and ACP can support different parts of the integration architecture.

For agent interfaces that display structured diagnostic information, Ext JS and ReExt are worth evaluating alongside other React UI libraries.

The best design makes agent activity understandable, keeps sensitive operations under appropriate control, and gives developers the tools they need to inspect results.

Further reading: Building Custom AI Agents with JavaScript, React, and ReExt — Sencha.

title: React Memoization Techniques: Master useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo
description:
React applications become more complex as components grow, state changes, and data flows through the component tree. Sometimes, a small state update causes expensive calculations or unnecessary child component renders, making the interface feel slower than it should.

React provides several memoization techniques to help developers avoid unnecessary work. The most commonly used tools are React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback, each designed to solve a different performance problem.

However, memoization is not a magic performance switch. Understanding when to use it, how dependency arrays work, and when memoization adds unnecessary complexity is essential for building fast and maintainable React applications.

Understanding React Memoization Techniques

Memoization is an optimization technique that stores the result of a previous computation so it can be reused when the relevant inputs have not changed. In React, memoization can reduce repeated calculations, prevent unnecessary component renders, and preserve function references between renders. Three important techniques are React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback.

React.memo is a higher-order component that can skip rendering a component when its props are unchanged according to React's default shallow comparison. It is particularly useful for expensive child components that receive the same props across frequent parent renders. However, a memoized component can still render when its own state or consumed context changes, and React does not guarantee that memoization will always prevent a render.

The useMemo hook caches a calculated value between renders while its dependencies remain unchanged. It works well for expensive filtering, sorting, transformations, and derived data calculations. The useCallback hook serves a related purpose by caching a function definition between renders, which can help when passing callbacks to memoized children or when a stable function reference is required by another hook.

Consider a dashboard containing a searchable list of products. Typing in a search field may trigger repeated renders, and filtering thousands of products can become expensive. You can use useMemo to recalculate filtered products only when the products or search query change, useCallback to preserve event-handler references, and React.memo to skip unnecessary renders of individual product rows. The following runnable example demonstrates these concepts using plain JavaScript to simulate their behavior; the actual React APIs should be used in React components.

const products = Array.from({ length: 1000 }, (_, index) => ({
  id: index + 1,
  name: `Product ${index + 1}`,
  price: (index + 1) * 10,
  category: index % 2 === 0 ? "Electronics" : "Accessories"
}));

// Track how often the expensive filtering operation executes.
let filterCalculationCount = 0;

function filterProducts(items, query, maxPrice) {
  filterCalculationCount++;
  console.log(`Step 1: Filtering products (calculation ${filterCalculationCount})`);

  // Simulate a costly operation using realistic product filtering.
  return items.filter((product) => {
    const matchesName = product.name
      .toLowerCase()
      .includes(query.toLowerCase());
    const matchesPrice = product.price <= maxPrice;
    return matchesName && matchesPrice;
  });
}

// A small memoization helper for demonstrating cached values.
// This is an educational simulation, not React's useMemo implementation.
function createMemoizedFilter() {
  let previousItems;
  let previousQuery;
  let previousMaxPrice;
  let previousResult;

  return function memoizedFilter(items, query, maxPrice) {
    const dependenciesChanged =
      previousItems !== items ||
      previousQuery !== query ||
      previousMaxPrice !== maxPrice;

    if (dependenciesChanged) {
      console.log("Step 2: Dependencies changed; recomputing results.");
      previousResult = filterProducts(items, query, maxPrice);
      previousItems = items;
      previousQuery = query;
      previousMaxPrice = maxPrice;
    } else {
      console.log("Step 2: Dependencies unchanged; reusing cached results.");
    }

    return previousResult;
  };
}

// Create one memoized function and reuse it across simulated renders.
const getFilteredProducts = createMemoizedFilter();

function renderDashboard(query, maxPrice, theme) {
  console.log("\n--- Rendering dashboard ---");
  console.log(`Search: "${query}" | Maximum price: ${maxPrice}`);
  console.log(`Theme: ${theme}`);

  // The result is reused when its inputs remain unchanged.
  const filteredProducts = getFilteredProducts(
    products,
    query,
    maxPrice
  );

  console.log(`Step 3: Found ${filteredProducts.length} matching products.`);

  // A theme change does not invalidate the filtering cache.
  console.log(`Step 4: Dashboard displayed using the ${theme} theme.`);
  return filteredProducts;
}

console.log("Starting React memoization demonstration...");

// First render: no cached result exists, so filtering runs.
renderDashboard("product", 500, "light");

// Second render: only the theme changes, so filtering is skipped.
renderDashboard("product", 500, "dark");

// Third render: the query changes, so filtering runs again.
renderDashboard("electronics", 500, "dark");

// Fourth render: the price limit changes, so filtering runs again.
renderDashboard("electronics", 300, "dark");

console.log("\n--- Performance summary ---");
console.log(`Total filtering calculations: ${filterCalculationCount}`);
console.log("Unchanged dependencies allowed cached results to be reused.");

// In a real React component, useMemo would cache the filtered array.
// const filteredProducts = useMemo(
//   () => filterProducts(products, query, maxPrice),
//   [products, query, maxPrice]
// );

// useCallback would preserve a function reference between renders.
// const handleSelect = useCallback((id) => {
//   setSelectedProductId(id);
// }, []);

// React.memo could skip rendering ProductRow when its props are unchanged.
// const ProductRow = memo(function ProductRow({ product, onSelect }) {
//   return <button onClick={() => onSelect(product.id)}>{product.name}</button>;
// });

Conclusion

React memoization is most effective when you understand what work is expensive and which inputs actually affect the result. Use useMemo for costly calculations, useCallback for function-reference stability when it matters, and React.memo for components that can benefit from skipping renders when their props remain unchanged.

Avoid adding memoization to every component or value by default. Each optimization introduces dependencies and additional complexity, while simple calculations and inexpensive components often perform perfectly well without it. Incorrect dependency arrays can also produce stale values or unexpected behavior.

Start by measuring performance with the React Developer Tools Profiler, identify the components or calculations responsible for slow interactions, and apply the smallest useful optimization. With careful profiling and appropriate memoization, you can build React applications that remain responsive without sacrificing readability or maintainability.

title: WebGPU: The Next Gen Graphics
description:
WebGPU: Level Up Your Browser Graphics Game! 🚀

Remember the days when your browser was just for reading text and maybe watching a grainy YouTube video? We've come a long way, haven't we? From interactive 3D models to mind-bending visual effects, the web has become a canvas for incredible graphical experiences. But here's the thing: the old guard, OpenGL and DirectX, while powerful, were never really designed for the chaotic, ever-evolving world of the internet. That's where WebGPU swoops in, like a superhero with a brand new cape made of pure, unadulterated graphics power, ready to redefine what's possible in your browser.

Think of WebGPU as the modern heir to WebGL. It's not just an upgrade; it's a complete reimagining, built from the ground up to tap into the raw power of your GPU (that's your graphics card, the secret sauce behind all those pretty pixels) in a way that's safer, more efficient, and frankly, more fun for developers.

So, What's the Big Deal? (The Introduction)

Let's be honest, WebGL has been a trooper. It's brought us some amazing things. But it's also had its quirks. It's a bit like trying to drive a sports car with a learner's permit – you can get somewhere, but it's a bit clunky and you're always worried about hitting a digital pothole. WebGPU, on the other hand, is designed for seasoned drivers. It's a low-overhead, modern API that gives developers much finer-grained control over the GPU.

Imagine building a complex 3D game that runs smoothly in your browser, or a sophisticated scientific visualization that reacts in real-time to your mouse movements. These are the kinds of experiences WebGPU is poised to unlock. It's not just about making pretty pictures; it's about making those pictures do things, and do them efficiently.

What Do I Need to Get My Hands Dirty? (Prerequisites)

Before you dive headfirst into the wonderful world of WebGPU, there are a couple of things to keep in mind.

  • Browser Support: This is the big one. WebGPU is a newer technology, so you'll need a modern browser that supports it. Chrome, Edge, and Firefox are already on board, but keep an eye on release notes for other browsers. It’s a good idea to check sites like Can I use... for the latest compatibility information.
  • JavaScript Knowledge: Like WebGL, WebGPU is accessed through JavaScript. So, a solid understanding of JavaScript fundamentals is crucial. You'll be writing code to interact with the GPU, set up your rendering pipeline, and manage your data.
  • Graphics Concepts: While WebGPU abstracts away some of the lower-level complexities of graphics programming, having a basic grasp of concepts like vertices, shaders, textures, and render passes will be incredibly helpful. Don't worry if you're not an expert; the journey of learning WebGPU will naturally deepen your understanding of these areas.
  • WGSL (WebGPU Shading Language): This is a new language specifically designed for WebGPU. It's a bit like GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language) but with a focus on safety and portability. You'll be writing shaders in WGSL to tell the GPU how to draw your pixels. It's relatively straightforward to pick up if you have any prior shader language experience.

Why Should I Care? (Advantages of WebGPU)

This is where things get exciting. WebGPU isn't just a minor iteration; it brings some serious improvements to the table.

  • Performance Boost: This is arguably the biggest win. WebGPU is designed for minimal CPU overhead. This means your JavaScript code spends less time talking to the GPU and more time doing its thing. This translates to smoother animations, faster rendering, and the ability to handle more complex scenes.
  • Modern API Design: WebGPU embraces modern GPU architectures. It's built with features like explicit synchronization and command buffers, giving developers more control over how and when GPU operations happen. This leads to more predictable performance and better utilization of GPU resources.
  • Thread Safety: One of the biggest challenges with WebGL was its implicit thread safety issues, which could lead to subtle and hard-to-debug bugs. WebGPU is designed with explicit synchronization primitives, making it much safer and easier to write multithreaded graphics applications.
  • Compute Shaders: This is a game-changer. WebGL was primarily for rendering graphics. WebGPU introduces compute shaders, which allow you to use the GPU for general-purpose computations. This opens the door to accelerating tasks like physics simulations, machine learning inference, image processing, and data analysis directly on the GPU, all within the browser.
  • Improved Developer Experience: While it's a new API, the design of WebGPU aims for a more intuitive and predictable developer experience compared to the sometimes-quirky nature of WebGL. Error handling is also generally more robust.
  • Portability and Security: WebGPU is designed to be portable across different operating systems and hardware. It also inherits the web's security model, ensuring that your graphics operations are sandboxed and don't compromise your system.

It's Not All Rainbows and Unicorns (Disadvantages)

As with any new technology, WebGPU isn't without its challenges.

  • Maturity and Ecosystem: Being relatively new, the WebGPU ecosystem is still growing. You'll find fewer libraries, tutorials, and readily available tools compared to the well-established WebGL. This means you might have to roll up your sleeves and do more heavy lifting yourself initially.
  • Learning Curve: While the API is designed to be modern, it's still a graphics API. Developers new to GPU programming will have a learning curve to climb, especially with concepts like shaders and render pipelines.
  • Browser Support Fragmentation: As mentioned earlier, browser support is still rolling out. You'll need to carefully consider your target audience and potentially have fallback mechanisms for browsers that don't yet support WebGPU.
  • Debugging: Debugging GPU-related issues can be notoriously tricky. While WebGPU aims to improve this, you'll still need to develop your debugging strategies for graphics code.

Let's Peek Under the Hood: Key Features

WebGPU is packed with features that make it a powerhouse. Let's explore some of the most important ones:

1. The Render Pipeline: The Heart of the Drawing Process

Think of a render pipeline as a factory assembly line for your pixels. It's a series of stages that data goes through to eventually become the image you see on your screen. WebGPU gives you much more explicit control over this pipeline.

  • Pipeline State Objects (PSOs): Instead of configuring individual states, WebGPU uses Pipeline State Objects (PSOs). These encapsulate all the necessary state for rendering (vertex shaders, fragment shaders, blend states, depth states, etc.) into a single, immutable object. This makes pipeline management more efficient and less error-prone.

    // A simplified example of creating a render pipeline
const pipeline = device.createRenderPipeline({
  layout: 'auto', // Automatically infer layout
  vertex: {
    module: device.createShaderModule({ code: wgslShaderCode }),
    entryPoint: 'vs_main',
  },
  fragment: {
    module: device.createShaderModule({ code: wgslShaderCode }),
    entryPoint: 'fs_main',
    targets: [{ format: navigator.gpu.getPreferredCanvasFormat() }],
  },
  primitive: {
    topology: 'triangle-list',
  },
});

2. Shaders: The GPU's Little Workers

Shaders are small programs that run directly on the GPU. They're responsible for everything from transforming 3D models into 2D screen coordinates (vertex shaders) to determining the final color of each pixel (fragment shaders). WebGPU uses WGSL (WebGPU Shading Language).

  • WGSL: This language is designed to be safe, efficient, and portable. It offers a modern syntax and features like strong typing and explicit control over memory layout.

    // A very basic WGSL vertex shader
struct VertexOutput {
    @builtin(position) clip_position: vec4<f32>,
};

@vertex
fn vs_main(@location(0) position: vec4<f32>) -> VertexOutput {
    var output: VertexOutput;
    output.clip_position = position;
    return output;
}

// A very basic WGSL fragment shader
@fragment
fn fs_main() -> @location(0) vec4<f32> {
    return vec4<f32>(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); // Red color
}

3. Buffers and Bind Groups: Managing Your Data

The GPU needs data to work with – vertex data, texture data, uniform values, etc. WebGPU provides mechanisms to efficiently transfer and access this data.

  • Buffers: These are regions of memory on the GPU where you store your data. You can have vertex buffers, index buffers, uniform buffers, and storage buffers.

  • Bind Groups: These are collections of resources (like buffers and textures) that your shaders can access. They allow you to bind different sets of resources to your pipeline, making it flexible.

    // Creating a vertex buffer (simplified)
const vertexBuffer = device.createBuffer({
    size: vertexData.byteLength,
    usage: GPUBufferUsage.VERTEX | GPUBufferUsage.COPY_DST,
    mappedAtCreation: true,
});
new Float32Array(vertexBuffer.getMappedRange()).set(vertexData);
vertexBuffer.unmap();

4. Compute Shaders: Beyond Graphics

As mentioned, compute shaders are a revolutionary addition. They allow you to leverage the massive parallel processing power of the GPU for tasks that aren't strictly graphical.

  • General-Purpose GPU (GPGPU): This is the term for using the GPU for general computations. With compute shaders in WebGPU, you can bring sophisticated algorithms and data processing directly into the browser, offloading heavy lifting from the CPU.

5. Explicit Synchronization: Taking Control

WebGPU emphasizes explicit synchronization, meaning you tell the GPU exactly when to perform certain operations. This might sound more complex, but it leads to better performance and fewer surprises.

  • Command Buffers and Queues: You record commands into command buffers, which are then submitted to command queues for execution by the GPU. This allows for asynchronous operation and efficient batching of commands.

A Glimpse into the Future

WebGPU is not just about rendering existing graphics applications faster. It's about enabling entirely new possibilities on the web.

  • Advanced 3D Experiences: Think of complex architectural visualizations, interactive product configurators, and even full-fledged AAA-quality games running seamlessly in your browser.
  • Real-time Data Visualization: Imagine streaming complex datasets and visualizing them in real-time with intricate animations and interactive controls.
  • Machine Learning in the Browser: Performing inference for machine learning models directly on the GPU in the browser can lead to faster and more responsive AI-powered applications.
  • Scientific Simulations: Running complex scientific simulations, like fluid dynamics or particle systems, directly in the browser, allowing for wider accessibility and collaboration.

The Takeaway (Conclusion)

WebGPU is a monumental step forward for graphics on the web. It's a modern, high-performance API that finally bridges the gap between the power of the GPU and the accessibility of the browser. While it's still a developing technology, the potential it unlocks is immense.

For developers, WebGPU offers a more powerful, efficient, and predictable way to create stunning visual experiences. For users, it promises a future where the web is not just a place for information, but a vibrant, interactive, and visually rich platform for gaming, creativity, and even complex computation. So, buckle up, grab your JavaScript hat, and get ready to explore the next generation of browser graphics – the WebGPU revolution is here! It’s an exciting time to be a web developer, and WebGPU is undoubtedly one of the most compelling reasons why.

title: Scaling Actors and Workers With HPA In Agent Substrate
description:
The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available to consume, digest, and schedule what you need to run. In the case of agentic workloads, that's typically Agents. For example, is there enough memory to run multi-Actor Workers? Or do you need to scale Workers out to schedule Actors accordingly?

In this blog post, you'll learn how to schedule and scale Actors (where Agents run) via Workers and WorkerPools for any number of Actors that need to run within your environment.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this blog post from a hands-on perspective, you will need:

  1. A cluster with Agent Substrate running (e.g., GKE or a local cluster like Kind).
    1. Agentgateway set as the dataplane proxy for your atenet-router.
  2. Worker images built with your underlying isolation layer (e.g., gVisor).
    1. You can build these images via the Agent Substrate repo (you need to clone it down) ./hack/run-tool.sh and see how to do it here.

What Will You Be Deploying?

Going through this blog post, you will be:

  1. Deploying Actors
  2. "Parking" an Actor until a Worker is ready to schedule it.
  3. Scaling out Workers so if you have, let's say 3 Actors but only 2 Workers, HPA can scale out the Worker (a Pod) to schedule the third Actor.

The goal here is to park Actors when there aren't enough Workers, or memory in the Workers, readily available to schedule an Actor. The Workers in this blog have a 1Gi memory limit, and each Actor asks for 768Mi. A second Actor needs 1536Mi, which means it won't fit. If anyone raises the WorkerPool memory or lowers the Template's, Actors will start sharing workers. Once a Worker is made available, the Actor can be automatically scheduled on said Worker so your Agent can run.

To go through the hands-on portion of this blog post in the way that it is configured, you'll want to clone this repo as it has all of the scripts and HPA configurations to run the lab along with Step 1 and Step 2, which is building the images and deploying your Workers.

Deploying Actors

The first step is deploying Actors. All Actors, when deployed, are automatically in a "suspended" state. Because they're in a suspended state, they aren't technically running, which is where the efficiency and overall performance of Agent Substrate come into play. Actors are only running when there is an active session to said Actor. That way, they aren't consuming resources (CPU/memory) for no reason.

Actors sit in a "warm state", which means they don't take seconds to resume. That way, when you create a session to an Actor that's running an Agent, it won't feel like the Actor is in a cold state and takes forever to resume/respond to the request that you're sending to the Actor running an Agent.

  1. Deploy the Actors. The pool caps each worker at 1Gi of memory (manifests/workerpool.yaml.tmpl), and the template asks for 768Mi per actor (manifests/actortemplate.yaml.tmpl). The scheduler only places an actor where its memory still fits, so a second actor never does. 
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  kubectl ate create actor "a$i" -a ate-lab-burst --template burst
done

💡

the burst template is what's created in actortemplate.yaml.tmpl.

All six start in ACTOR_STATE_SUSPENDED. They exist only as records, plus the golden snapshot in GCS.

  1. Confirm that the Actors are in a suspended state and in Agent Substrate. 
kubectl get actors -a ate-lab-burst

You should see an output similar to the screenshot below.

As you're going through the rest of this blog post, an important note to keep in mind is that because six Actors were deployed and there are two Workers, there's a 3:1 ratio here. That means two Actors can be scheduled, but four cannot and therefore sit in a "parked" state until a Worker is available.

Park and Schedule An Actor

With the Actors deployed, let's resume two of the Actors, and then try a third, which will sit in a parked state until a Worker becomes readily available.

  1. Port-forward the router so it's open and accepting requests (for when a client or something like curl needs to reach it). 
kubectl -n ate-system port-forward svc/atenet-router 8000:80
  1. Fill both Workers with Actors. 
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a1" http://localhost:8000
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a2" http://localhost:8000
  1. Check and confirm that both Workers got assigned an Actor. 
kubectl ate get workers -n ate-lab-burst

You'll see an output similar to the below:

NAME                                   POOL    STATE                 ACTORS   CPU      MEMORY      POD                                    AGE
cc852e96-6035-47a1-96e9-1b85d2b47c95   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t26t7   20m
43210b1e-2a85-496c-96e9-497575d4e200   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t7gm6   20m
  1. Try assigning a third Actor. 
curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll get a "request timed out" with a 504. The reason why is that there isn't enough memory on either Worker to schedule the third Actor.

  1. Suspend Actor 1 and then run the curl again. 
kubectl ate suspend actor a1 -a ate-lab-burst

curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll see that Actor 3 can now be scheduled.

Add HPA For WorkerPools

In the previous section, you saw that because there are two Workers available within the WorkerPool, only 2/3 of the Actors could be scheduled on the Worker until a Worker freed up.

As you read in the What Will You Be Deploying? section, multiple Actors CAN be scheduled on one Worker as long as there's enough memory to support it. The scenario we want HPA for WorkerPools is when the Worker runs out of memory and therefore a new Worker (Pod/replica) needs to be created.

Tldr; Where HPA comes into play is scaling out an Actor to another Worker (or as many Workers as are needed based on how many Actors are waiting to be unparked).

💡 Because you created six Actors in the Deploying Actors section and the HPA config allows up to 10 replicas, all six Actors will be deployed onto the Workers as there will now be more Workers available because the replica count in the HPA config goes up to ten.

  1. Use the burst script to wake up all six Actors 
./scripts/burst.sh -m hold -d 120

You'll see 504s (timeouts) for the 4 Actors that aren't scheduled on Workers as they aren't scheduled and therefore, aren't running.

  1. In another terminal, scale your WorkerPool to 6 replicas 
kubectl -n ate-lab-burst scale workerpool burst --replicas=6
  1. Go back to the first terminal and you'll see the scale start to occur (from 2/2 to 6/6). This shows that all six Actors are now up and running with successful 200's.

This proves out that scaling the Workers officially worked!

Wrapping Up

Scale becomes increasingly important in the world of agentic because it impacts so many areas. It's not just one app that impacts a department or a particular functionality of an app that impacts a customer. If an Agent is down, it can potentially impact the entire organization. That's why ensuring that scale can be properly implemented across Agents isn't just about the tech teams; it's everyone from engineering to marketing to HR and all teams that are incorporating AI into daily workflows.

title: Building a DICOM Import Pipeline With AWS HealthImaging
description:
Medical imaging platforms must move large volumes of DICOM data without losing track of image identity, metadata, or import errors. AWS HealthImaging Solutions provide a managed foundation for storing and retrieving medical imaging data, but the ingestion workflow still needs careful engineering.

A production-ready pipeline involves more than uploading .dcm files and starting an import job. It needs source validation, secure S3 staging, a scoped IAM role, job orchestration, manifest processing, and post-import verification.

This guide explains how to build a DICOM import pipeline using AWS HealthImaging, from preparing source files to making imported image sets available to downstream applications.

Understand the DICOM Import Architecture

AWS HealthImaging imports DICOM P10 files from an Amazon S3 input location into a data store. During import, it performs pixel-data verification and transforms source files into image sets containing metadata and image frames.

A typical workflow looks like this:

PACS / VNA / Scanner Export
|
v
Source Validation
|
v
Amazon S3 Input
|
v
StartDICOMImportJob
|
v
AWS HealthImaging
|
+-------------------+
| |
v v
Image Sets S3 Job Results
|
+----------+----------+
| | |
v v v
Success Warning Failure
Manifest Manifest Manifest
|
v
Reconciliation and QA
|
v
Imaging Viewer

In this architecture, S3 holds incoming files and import results, while HealthImaging manages the resulting image sets. Your application handles workflow state, reconciliation, access policies, and readiness checks.

For teams implementing AWS HealthImaging Solutions, this separation helps keep ingestion logic independent from the applications that consume the data.

Start with the official AWS HealthImaging import guide.

1. Define the Source Data Contract

Before moving files, establish exactly what the source system will deliver. DICOM environments vary in export conventions, metadata quality, transfer syntaxes, and directory structures.

Document these details:

Source system and export method

Expected DICOM SOP classes

Supported transfer syntaxes

Study, Series, and Instance identifiers

Approximate file count and total data volume

Whether metadata overrides are required

How duplicate or corrected studies should be handled

Which system owns the authoritative identifiers

HealthImaging supports specific DICOM elements, SOP classes, and transfer syntaxes. Check the dataset against the current DICOM support documentation before starting a large migration.

An uploaded file is not necessarily a valid import candidate. It may reach S3 but fail validation or produce warnings during processing.

A reliable AWS HealthImaging Solutions implementation should validate representative files early, including data from different modalities and source systems.

2. Stage DICOM Files in Amazon S3

Use a dedicated S3 bucket or prefix for each ingestion environment. Keep source files separate from job outputs so that the pipeline can identify exactly which data belongs to each batch.

For example:

s3://imaging-ingestion-prod/
incoming/
batch-2026-10-15/
study-a/
instance-001.dcm
instance-002.dcm
study-b/
instance-001.dcm

s3://imaging-import-results/
jobs/
batch-2026-10-15/

The folder structure helps with operational organization. HealthImaging uses DICOM metadata, including Study, Series, and Instance UIDs, when organizing imported data.

Consider these controls:

Assign a unique batch identifier to each import.

Maintain a manifest of source object keys and checksums.

Prevent files from changing after a batch is approved.

Restrict bucket access to the required roles and services.

Enable encryption and appropriate access logging.

Define retention rules for source data and import results.

Avoid patient names or other sensitive information in resource names and job labels.

These controls make retries, troubleshooting, and audits easier. They also prevent an upload from silently changing the input associated with a previously submitted job.

For AWS HealthImaging Solutions that handle clinical data, treat source files and processing manifests as sensitive assets throughout the pipeline.

3. Configure the Data Store and IAM Role

Create a HealthImaging data store before starting the import. Decide on the storage format at creation time because it affects how lossless image frames are stored. HTJ2K is the default, and JPEG 2000 Lossless is also available as a configuration option.

Confirm that the selected format works with the applications that will retrieve and decode the images. See the data store creation guide for the available configuration options.

Next, configure the IAM role used by the import job. It needs permission to read the input files and write processing results to the designated output location. Its trust policy must allow HealthImaging to assume the role.

Follow least-privilege principles:

Grant read access only to the approved input location.

Grant write access only to the job-results location.

Avoid broad wildcard permissions where narrower resource permissions are possible.

Separate deployment permissions from runtime import permissions.

Review role trust policies and bucket permissions during testing.

The import role is a key part of the security boundary. A production pipeline should not rely on a developer's personal credentials or broad administrative access.

Refer to the AWS HealthImaging setup guide for the required S3 buckets, permissions, and role configuration.

4. Start an Import Job

The StartDICOMImportJob action starts the bulk import. Its request identifies the target data store, S3 input and output locations, and the data-access role.

The following AWS CLI example illustrates the command structure. Replace the sample values with the identifiers and locations from your environment.

aws medical-imaging start-dicom-import-job \
--datastore-id "$DATASTORE_ID" \
--input-s3-uri "s3://imaging-ingestion-prod/incoming/batch-2026-10-15/" \
--output-s3-uri "s3://imaging-import-results/jobs/batch-2026-10-15/" \
--data-access-role-arn "$IMPORT_ROLE_ARN" \
--job-name "batch-2026-10-15"

Check the current AWS CLI reference for the exact options supported by your installed version. In application code, use an AWS SDK and store the returned job identifier with your internal batch ID.

For example, an application-level batch record might look like this:

{
"batchId": "batch-2026-10-15",
"dataStoreId": "replace-with-datastore-id",
"jobId": "returned-job-id",
"inputPrefix": "incoming/batch-2026-10-15/",
"status": "SUBMITTED"
}

This is an illustrative internal record, not the exact AWS API response. Store only the operational information needed to manage the import.

If a worker times out after submitting a job, the orchestration layer should check the stored job state before attempting another submission. This reduces accidental duplicate processing and makes recovery more predictable.

5. Track Job Status and Parse the Manifests

An import job's status describes job execution. It does not guarantee that every file imported successfully. AWS documents that a job can reach COMPLETED even when file-level validation issues occurred.

Use GetDICOMImportJob to check job status. Once the job reaches a terminal state, inspect the output location and reconcile individual file results.

The output can include:

success.ndjson for successfully imported instances

failure.ndjson for instances that could not be imported

warning.ndjson for instances imported with warnings

The results are stored in an output structure that also includes a job manifest. Each NDJSON line is a separate JSON record, so process the file line by line instead of parsing the entire file as one JSON document.

For every input file, record its outcome, image-set identifier when available, warning details, and any follow-up action. Make reconciliation idempotent so that processing the same manifest twice does not create duplicate application records or trigger downstream actions repeatedly.

The official import-job documentation explains the result structure and how HealthImaging organizes imported instances.

6. Handle Warnings, Failures, and Conflicting Data

Import results should not be reduced to a simple success-or-failure flag. A warning may indicate that an instance was imported but has a data-conformance issue or a limitation affecting later retrieval.

A practical handling policy is:

Outcome

Recommended action

Success without warnings

Record the image-set ID and continue verification

Success with warnings

Store warning codes and route for review based on impact

Failure

Capture the error, correct the source if possible, and retry under controlled conditions

Conflicting metadata

Review primary and non-primary image-set behavior before releasing data

HealthImaging organizes instances using DICOM Study, Series, and Instance UIDs. If newly imported data conflicts with existing primary image sets, HealthImaging may place the new data in non-primary image sets.

Therefore, do not assume that every imported file automatically becomes part of the expected primary image set. Build explicit rules for repeat imports, corrected studies, and data arriving from multiple source systems.

Maintain a source-to-target mapping and avoid treating filenames as unique clinical identifiers. Familiar filenames do not prove that two files represent the same image instance.

Consult the HealthImaging warning codes reference when defining warning categories and remediation procedures.

7. Verify Image Sets Before Releasing Data

A completed import job does not mean the data is ready for an application. Add a verification stage before marking a batch as available to downstream users.

Depending on the use case, checks can include:

Confirm that every expected source file has a recorded outcome.

Compare success, warning, and failure counts with the source manifest.

Confirm image-set identifiers exist for successful imports.

Retrieve metadata for representative image sets.

Retrieve selected image frames and verify that the consuming application can decode them.

Check expected Study and Series relationships.

Test permissions for authorized and unauthorized users.

Record unresolved warnings and failures for follow-up.

Choose representative studies across relevant modalities, file sizes, and transfer syntaxes. A small test import is useful, but it should not replace validation against the actual production dataset.

Pay particular attention to image decoding. HealthImaging may store lossless frames in HTJ2K or another configured format, so the viewer or downstream service must support the transfer syntaxes it receives.

For AWS HealthImaging Solutions connected to a viewer, test the complete retrieval path—not just whether the metadata API returns a response.

8. Orchestrate Large Imports for Recovery

For large archives, avoid relying on a single long-running script to upload files and wait for every job to finish. Separate the workflow into stages so failures can be diagnosed and retried independently.

A pipeline may coordinate:

Batch registration

Source-file validation

S3 upload completion

Import-job submission

Job-status tracking

Manifest parsing

Post-import verification

Exception review

Completion notifications

Persist each stage's state. If a worker stops after an import job starts, another worker should recover the job using the stored identifier. If manifest processing fails, rerun that stage without resubmitting the import.

Use bounded retries with backoff for transient errors. Do not repeatedly retry permanent validation failures without correcting the source or configuration. Account for service quotas, API throttling, and the time required to process large batches.

This staged approach makes AWS HealthImaging Solutions easier to operate because each step has a clear input, output, and recovery procedure.

9. Monitor the Pipeline and Protect Clinical Data

Monitor infrastructure metrics alongside file-level outcomes. Useful operational measurements include:

Files discovered and uploaded

Import jobs submitted and completed

Successful imports

Imports completed with warnings

Failed-file counts and error categories

Time from upload to job completion

Time spent reconciling manifests

Batches awaiting manual review

Retry counts and age of pending batches

Alert on unexpected failure rates, jobs that remain pending too long, missing output manifests, and growth in the manual-review queue.

Keep logs useful for troubleshooting without copying DICOM payloads or unnecessary patient information into general application logs. Define who can access source files, image sets, manifests, and operational dashboards.

Apply least-privilege permissions and follow your organization's retention, audit, and incident-response requirements. The exact controls depend on the deployment and applicable healthcare obligations.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Assuming COMPLETED means every file succeeded. Reconcile the output manifests and investigate failures and warnings.

Skipping DICOM compatibility checks. Verify supported SOP classes, elements, and transfer syntaxes before importing a large dataset.

Using broad IAM permissions. Scope access to the required input and output resources.

Ignoring warnings. Some warnings can affect downstream retrieval and require a documented review process.

Treating filenames as unique identifiers. Use DICOM identifiers and maintain a source-to-target mapping.

Retrying an entire batch without checking its state. Persist job identifiers and make processing stages idempotent.

Releasing data before verification. Confirm metadata, representative image frames, and application access before declaring a batch ready.

Production Readiness Checklist

Before deploying the pipeline, confirm that:

The dataset has been checked against current HealthImaging DICOM support.

S3 input and output locations are separated and access-controlled.

The import role follows least-privilege principles.

The data store's storage-format choice matches downstream requirements.

Each batch has a stable identifier and source manifest.

Import job IDs and terminal states are persisted.

Success, warning, and failure manifests are reconciled.

Duplicate and conflicting image-set behavior is understood.

Representative metadata and image-frame retrieval tests pass.

Alerts, retries, audit logs, and manual-review procedures are defined.

These controls turn a basic import script into a pipeline that can be operated, monitored, and audited over time.

How Oodles Approaches AWS HealthImaging Integration

At Oodles, we approach AWS HealthImaging Solutions as part of a complete medical imaging workflow rather than an isolated storage task. The implementation can include DICOM ingestion, S3 staging, import-job orchestration, manifest processing, secure APIs, viewer integration, monitoring, and operational tooling.

The architecture depends on the source environment, data volume, supported DICOM formats, identity model, and applications that consume the imported studies. We begin by mapping these dependencies, then define a staged workflow with clear recovery paths and verification checks.

If your team is planning a DICOM migration or building a medical imaging platform, let's connect to discuss the import workflow, integration points, and technical requirements.

title: Designing a bookmark record that future-you can actually retrieve
description:
A save button creates a record. It does not answer the question that comes a week later: “Where was that example I wanted for the onboarding screen?” For a personal knowledge tool, that question is a useful starting point for the data model.

Store the reason alongside the resource

Consider this proposed record:

{
  "title": "A useful onboarding example",
  "source_url": "https://example.com/onboarding",
  "saved_for": "Compare welcome screens for my side project",
  "intent": "use",
  "keywords": ["onboarding", "welcome", "side project"]
}

The URL identifies the resource. The other fields describe its relationship to the person saving it. Keeping those concepts separate means a later change of project does not require changing the source itself.

Do not make every field mandatory. If capture becomes a form-filling exercise, people will skip it. A reasonable first version accepts the resource immediately and offers one optional prompt: “What will you use this for?”

Show the context in search results

Storing the note is only half the work. Put it beside the title when presenting results. Two nearly identical article titles become easier to distinguish when one says “for the pricing page” and the other says “for the client workshop.”

Treat automatic labels as suggestions. Keep the user's own note available for editing, and avoid silently replacing it with a generated summary.

Test retrieval rather than collection

Ask someone to save five real resources. Later, give them a task that needs one of those resources, without reminding them of its title. Observe the words they search for and the result they choose.

The useful outcome is a resource they can confidently reuse, not a bigger collection of saved links.

This is one of the product questions behind Némos: how can a saved item keep the context that made it useful?
