title: Concurrency Programming (10): How BlockingQueue and Channels Work — From Runtime to CPU
description:
Table of Contents

  • 0. What Does This Article Answer Next?
  • 1. How Does the JDK Implement ArrayBlockingQueue?
    • 1.1 Layers
    • 1.2 End-to-End Implementation Path for put / take
    • 1.3 Guarantees at the Runtime / Language Implementation Layer
    • 1.3.1 Atomicity
    • 1.3.2 Visibility and Ordering
    • 1.4 Guarantees at the Hardware Layer
  • 2. How Does Go Runtime Implement Channels?
    • 2.1 Layers
    • 2.2 End-to-End Implementation Path for Channel Communication
    • 2.3 Guarantees at the Runtime / Language Implementation Layer
    • 2.3.1 Atomicity
    • 2.3.2 Visibility and Ordering
    • 2.4 Guarantees at the Hardware Layer
  • 3. How Does CPython Implement queue.Queue?
    • 3.1 Layers
    • 3.2 End-to-End Implementation Path for put / get
    • 3.3 Guarantees at the Runtime / Language Implementation Layer
    • 3.3.1 Atomicity
    • 3.3.2 Visibility and Ordering
    • 3.4 Guarantees at the Hardware Layer
  • 4. The Common Pattern Across the Three Implementations
    • 4.1 Who Can Enqueue or Dequeue? — Mutex / Atomicity
    • 4.2 What If the Queue Is Empty or Full? — Condition / Park / Wakeup
    • 4.3 After Handoff, Why Is the Message Visible? — Release / Acquire
  • 5. Next: How the Two Models Relate

0. What Does This Article Answer Next?

The previous article examined the Atomicity, Visibility, and Ordering guarantees of BlockingQueue, channels, and queue.Queue at the language and standard-library level.

This article examines how Java, Go, and CPython implement those guarantees, from the runtime and OS threads down to the CPU.

1. How Does the JDK Implement ArrayBlockingQueue?

1.1 Layers 

Java Source Code
Example: BlockingQueue.put() / take()
Role: define message handoff and blocking operations
        │
        ▼
JDK Class Library
Example: ArrayBlockingQueue / ReentrantLock / AQS / ConditionObject
Role: maintain queue state, mutual exclusion, and condition waiters
        │
        ▼
JVM Implementation (HotSpot)
Example: Unsafe.park, HotSpot Parker, Continuations
Role: implement low-level thread parking and virtual-thread execution
        │
        ▼
OS Thread / Thread Parking
Example: Platform Thread / Parker; Virtual Thread / Carrier
Role: suspend and resume the relevant execution unit
        │
        ▼
x86-64 Hardware
Example: Atomic Instruction / Cache Coherence / Memory Ordering
Role: provide the hardware foundations for Atomicity, Visibility, and Ordering

1.2 End-to-End Implementation Path for put / take

Within the JDK, these calls follow the paths below:

1.3 Guarantees at the Runtime / Language Implementation Layer

1.3.1 Atomicity

Here, Atomicity means one enqueue or dequeue updates the queue state without interleaving with another thread's queue operation.

Look at the second diagram in section 1.2, “ArrayBlockingQueue put/take control flow”. Both put and take call lockInterruptibly() before enqueue(e) or dequeue(). The array, indices, and count are updated while holding the lock, so other threads cannot modify the queue midway through.

1.3.2 Visibility and Ordering

Here, Visibility means the consumer can see data the producer wrote before enqueueing the message. Ordering means those writes take effect before the consumer reads them.

Look at the first diagram in section 1.2, “ArrayBlockingQueue across implementation layers”. The producer writes message.delta = 1, calls jobs.put(message), and releases the lock (Release). The consumer then acquires the same lock (Acquire), takes the message, and reads delta == 1. The earlier unlock happens-before the later lock acquisition, making the producer's writes visible to the consumer. notEmpty.signal() notifies the waiting consumer.

1.4 Guarantees at the Hardware Layer

At the hardware level, these guarantees rely on atomic instructions, cache coherence, and memory-ordering constraints:

Atomicity
  → Atomic Instruction
  → lock-state updates: LOCK CMPXCHG and related atomic operations

Visibility
  → Cache Coherence
  → cache-coherence protocols on x86-64 CPUs (e.g., MESIF or MOESI)

Ordering
  → Acquire / Release and required Memory Ordering
  → x86-64 memory ordering, locked RMW, and compiler constraints

Source code: ArrayBlockingQueue.java, AbstractQueuedSynchronizer.java, and ReentrantLock.java.

2. How Does Go Runtime Implement Channels?

2.1 Layers 

Go Source Code
Example: jobs <- message / message := <-jobs
Role: define send/receive operations and their synchronization
        │
        ▼
Go Implementation
Example: runtime/chan.go, chansend / chanrecv, hchan, sudog
Role: manage the buffer, waiting goroutines, and sender–receiver pairing
        │
        ▼
Go Runtime / Scheduler (G / M / P)
Example: gopark / goready
Role: park a waiting goroutine and make a notified goroutine runnable
        │
        ▼
OS Thread / Thread Parking
Example: M carrying a G, native waiting under internal lock contention
Role: run goroutines and park or wake OS threads when necessary
        │
        ▼
x86-64 Hardware
Example: Atomic Instruction / Cache Coherence / Memory Ordering
Role: provide the hardware foundations for Atomicity, Visibility, and Ordering

2.2 End-to-End Implementation Path for Channel Communication

First, follow the Go channel communication across implementation layers sequence diagram for an unbuffered channel:

The core send and receive paths are:

2.3 Guarantees at the Runtime / Language Implementation Layer

2.3.1 Atomicity

Here, Atomicity means the channel-state changes and message pairing in one send or receive do not interleave with another goroutine's channel operation.

Look at the second diagram in section 2.2, “Core channel send and receive paths”. The runtime acquires hchan.lock before updating buf, sendx, recvx, and qcount for buffered channels or finding a waiting peer in recvq or sendq for a direct handoff. If communication cannot proceed, gopark suspends the goroutine and releases the lock. Once the other side completes the handoff, goready makes it runnable again.

2.3.2 Visibility and Ordering

Here, Visibility means the consumer can see the producer's writes from before the send after receiving the message. Ordering means those writes take effect before the consumer's reads after the receive.

Look at the first diagram in section 2.2, “Go channel communication across implementation layers”. The producer writes message.delta = 1 and sends the message on an unbuffered channel. sendDirect transfers it to the waiting consumer, which can read delta == 1 after the receive completes. The Go memory model states that a send is synchronized-before the corresponding receive completes. Buffered channels store the message first but follow the same rule.

2.4 Guarantees at the Hardware Layer

At the lowest level, the channel lock relies on atomic instructions and memory-ordering guarantees:

Atomicity
  → Atomic Instruction
  → CAS, exchange, and other atomics used by runtime locks

Visibility
  → Cache Coherence
  → cache-coherence protocols on x86-64 CPUs (e.g., MESIF or MOESI)

Ordering
  → Acquire / Release and required Memory Ordering
  → compiler constraints, x86-64 memory ordering, and locked RMW

Source code: runtime/chan.go, runtime/proc.go, internal/runtime/atomic/atomic_amd64.s.

3. How Does CPython Implement queue.Queue?

3.1 Layers 

Python Source Code
Example: queue.Queue.put() / get()
Role: define enqueue, dequeue, and blocking behavior
        │
        ▼
CPython Standard Library
Example: queue.Queue / threading.Condition / collections.deque
Role: maintain queue state, check conditions, and notify waiting threads
        │
        ▼
CPython Implementation
Example: _thread.lock / PyMutex / Parking Lot
Role: manage atomic lock state and thread parking
        │
        ▼
OS Thread / Thread Parking
Example: native threads, semaphores, platform-specific wait primitives
Role: block and wake threads under contention or while waiting for a condition
        │
        ▼
x86-64 Hardware
Example: Atomic Instruction / Cache Coherence / Memory Ordering
Role: provide the hardware foundations for Atomicity, Visibility, and Ordering

3.2 End-to-End Implementation Path for put / get

First, follow the CPython queue.Queue across implementation layers sequence diagram with a consumer waiting on an empty queue:

The second diagram shows CPython Queue put/get control flow:

3.3 Guarantees at the Runtime / Language Implementation Layer

3.3.1 Atomicity

Here, Atomicity means a put or get checks and updates the queue without interleaving with another thread's queue operation.

Look at the second diagram in section 3.2, “CPython Queue put/get control flow”. Both put and get acquire Queue.mutex before checking the queue and calling deque.append(item) or deque.popleft(). If the queue is full or empty, Condition.wait() releases the lock. After notification, the thread reacquires the lock and checks the condition again before proceeding.

3.3.2 Visibility and Ordering

Here, Visibility means the consumer can see the message contents the producer wrote before enqueueing. Ordering means those writes take effect before the consumer reads them.

Look at the first diagram in section 3.2, “CPython queue.Queue across implementation layers”. The producer writes message.delta = 1, enqueues it with put(message), and releases Queue.mutex (Release). The consumer is notified, reacquires the same lock (Acquire), and reads delta == 1 after get() returns. Releasing and acquiring the lock provides the synchronization; not_empty.notify() notifies the waiting thread.

3.4 Guarantees at the Hardware Layer

One level lower, Queue.mutex is implemented using _thread.lock. Its PyMutex uses atomic operations to acquire the lock; if acquisition fails, the Parking Lot and platform-specific waiting mechanisms can suspend the thread:

Atomicity
  → Atomic Instruction
  → CAS and exchange operations on the PyMutex lock state

Visibility
  → Cache Coherence
  → cache-coherence protocols on x86-64 CPUs (e.g., MESIF or MOESI)

Ordering
  → Acquire / Release and required Memory Ordering
  → compiler-enforced atomic ordering and CPU memory-ordering constraints

Source code: Lib/queue.py, Lib/threading.py, Python/lock.c, Python/parking_lot.c.

4. The Common Pattern Across the Three Implementations

Consider a queue with capacity 2, shared by two producers and two consumers. A correct handoff must address three questions:

Question What can go wrong? Mechanism
How can multiple producers and consumers hand off messages safely? A message may be overwritten or removed twice Mutex / Atomicity
What should happen when a handoff cannot proceed? Consumers cannot take from an empty queue, and producers cannot put into a full one; busy-waiting also wastes CPU Condition / Park / Wakeup
How can the consumer see what the producer wrote? The consumer may receive a message without seeing earlier writes Release / Acquire, Visibility / Ordering

4.1 Who Can Enqueue or Dequeue? — Mutex / Atomicity

Initially, both queue slots are empty, and tail = 0 marks the next insertion position. Without synchronization, both producers can read the same index:

Producer A                    Producer B

Read tail = 0                 Read tail = 0
Write buffer[0] = A           Write buffer[0] = B

Result: both write slot 0, so one message is overwritten

Between reading the insertion position and updating the queue state, another producer may act on the same stale position.

Protect the queue with a mutex. Suppose Producer A acquires the lock first:

Initial queue: [empty, empty], tail = 0

Producer A                    Producer B

Lock acquired                 Try Lock → wait
Read tail = 0
Write slot 0: A
Update tail = 1
Unlock ──────────────────→     Lock acquired
                              Re-read tail = 1
                              Write slot 1: B
                              Update tail = 0
                              Unlock

Final queue: [A, B]

Producer B waits until A releases the mutex, then reads the updated value, tail = 1. It writes to slot 1 rather than overwriting slot 0. Either producer could acquire the lock first; both messages are still enqueued safely.

The same principle applies to competing consumers: checking the queue, taking a message, and updating queue state must happen within one critical section so two consumers cannot remove the same message. The mutex itself uses atomic operations to decide who acquires the lock, giving queue operations their Atomicity.

4.2 What If the Queue Is Empty or Full? — Condition / Park / Wakeup

Mutual exclusion prevents conflicting updates, but a consumer still cannot take from an empty queue, nor can a producer add to a full one.

Queue empty → Consumer waits on notEmpty
Queue full  → Producer waits on notFull

For example, a consumer tries to take from an empty queue:

Consumer                         Producer

Lock → Queue is empty
Register notEmpty wait
Unlock → Park
                                 Lock → Enqueue
                                 signal(notEmpty)
                                 Unlock
Wakeup → Lock
Recheck Queue state
Take message → Unlock

For a full queue, the roles reverse: the producer waits on notFull until a consumer dequeues a message and signals it.

The waiting thread must release the mutex so the other side can change the queue. On waking, it must acquire the lock and check again: another thread may have changed the queue first. Registering a waiter and releasing the mutex must also be coordinated to avoid lost wakeups.

4.3 After Handoff, Why Is the Message Visible? — Release / Acquire

Mutual exclusion and waiting make the handoff possible. The consumer must also see the data the producer wrote before sending the message.

Producer                             Consumer

Writes message.delta = 1
         ↓
Publish [Release] ─── Synchronized handoff ───▶ Receive [Acquire]
                                                        ↓
                                                  Read delta == 1

For a mutex-protected queue, the producer's unlock (Release) happens-before the consumer's subsequent lock (Acquire) on the same mutex. This ensures the consumer can see what the producer wrote before sending the message.

An unbuffered Go channel does not need a message buffer. Instead, it directly pairs the sender and receiver, while ensuring that writes before the send are visible to the receiver.

Together with a message buffer and queue state, these three mechanisms form the core of a bounded blocking queue:

Message buffer + queue state
       +
Mutex: protect an indivisible handoff
       +
Condition: wait and wake when empty or full
       +
Release / Acquire: make messages visible and ordered
       ↓
Blocking Queue

5. Next: How the Two Models Relate

The next article explores how shared memory and message passing relate and work together in practice. Article 12 will conclude the series by bringing the broader picture of concurrent programming together.

This article was first published on ThinkerQAQ's personal blog and syndicated here by the author. The original article may be revised over time; please refer to the personal blog for the latest version.

title: I built a cross-platform Android emulator manager with Tauri 2 + Rust — no Android Studio required
description:
I got tired of three things at once: the Android emulator CLI is tedious, Android Studio is a multi-gigabyte install for just running AVDs, and every decent alternative is either closed-source or expensive. So I built Enmulator — a desktop app that manages Android Virtual Devices end to end, ships on Windows/macOS/Linux, and doesn't need Android Studio installed.

It's Tauri 2 on the backend (Rust, 13 modules), React 18 on the frontend, and it's GPLv3.

What it actually does

  • Create / start / stop / clone / delete AVDs, plus batch operations across multiple devices
  • 66 pre-loaded device profiles across 16 brands (Pixel, Samsung, Xiaomi, OnePlus, realme…)
  • Device identity spoofing: IMEI, operator, phone number, WiFi MAC, timezone, locale
  • Root: adb root for google_apis images, and Magisk via rootAVD for everything else
  • Per-device proxy, GPS mocking, screen recording, clipboard sync, live logcat, a split-panel file explorer
  • A headless REST API (Actix-web) so you can drive it from CI or a script

The whole point was to make emulator setup feel like a product, not a shell-script chore.

Why Tauri instead of Electron

A tool that spawns emulator processes shouldn't eat 300 MB of RAM on its own. Tauri uses the OS webview instead of bundling Chromium, so the installer is small and idle memory is low. The backend being Rust mattered more than I expected: adb calls are blocking Command invocations, and being able to move them off the main thread with plain std::thread — without async ceremony — kept the UI responsive for free.

The tradeoff is real too: the macOS/Windows/Linux build matrix means three toolchains and three sets of platform quirks (more on that below).

Architecture

The Rust side is a flat set of modules, each owning one concern:

  • sdk.rs — locate the Android SDK, adb, emulator, avdmanager binaries
  • avd_manager.rs — create/delete AVDs, write config.ini (resolution, DPI, hardware keyboard)
  • emulator.rs — process management + port allocation (each emulator gets a console port)
  • adb_bridge.rs — the adb shell / install / push / pull wrappers
  • fingerprint.rs — the identity-spoofing engine
  • bypass.rs — build.prop patching for detection bypass
  • extras.rs — GPS, clipboard, screen record, logcat streams
  • api_server.rs — the REST layer

The frontend is a few focused components: a create wizard, per-device cards, an identity panel, the file explorer, quick actions. Nothing clever — state lives in the backend, the UI just calls commands over Tauri's IPC.

The parts that were actually hard

Fingerprint spoofing is a moving target

The naive version is adb shell setprop with the IMEI/operator values. That works for some properties and silently fails for others — and "silently fails" is the worst outcome because the user thinks they're spoofed when they aren't.

The reality on modern Android:

  • ro.product.* (brand, model, manufacturer) are immutable — set at boot by the system image, setprop can't touch them.
  • IMEI/SIM fields (persist.radio.imei, etc.) stopped being settable via setprop around API 29.
  • The reliable route for read-only props is Magisk's resetprop, which patches the property store in memory.

So the identity engine is now Magisk-aware: if the device is rooted with Magisk, it uses resetprop for ro.product.* and ro.build.fingerprint; otherwise it falls back to setprop for the fields that still allow it. The app also reports which fields applied and which failed, instead of one big "success" that might be a lie.

Magisk integration without Android Studio

Rooting an emulator normally means patching the ramdisk. Enmulator bundles rootAVD, which does exactly that: it grabs ramdisk.img from the system image, patches it with Magisk, and pushes it back.

The gotcha I learned: the ramdisk is shared per system image, not per AVD. Root one device on a given image and every AVD using that image is rooted. That's worth documenting loud, because it surprises people.

Also adb root only works on google_apis (non-Play-Store) images — Play Store images reject it outright. So the app offers both paths and tells you which one applies to your image.

Windows wants to show you console windows

Every adb / emulator spawn on Windows popped a black console window. The fix is CREATE_NO_WINDOW (0x08000000) in the process creation flags — one line, but it has to wrap every command invocation, so it went into a shared sdk::new_command() helper used everywhere.

Windows also likes to prepend \\?\ to long paths, which broke resolving the rootAVD submodule. dunce::canonicalize fixed it by stripping the prefix.

Shipping three platforms from one repo

The release pipeline is a GitHub Actions matrix (ubuntu / windows / macos) that produces a .deb, .AppImage, .msi, and .dmg with stable filenames, then uploads them to the release. The thing that bit me: the default GITHUB_TOKEN can't update a release — it needs permissions: contents: write in the workflow. Took a failed run to learn that.

I also did a git history cleanup before open-sourcing: the repo's .git was 483 MB because old target/ and node_modules blobs were stuck in history. git filter-repo brought it to 6.7 MB. Same code, 72× smaller clone.

Honest limitations

  • ARM64 system images only run natively on Apple Silicon — x86_64 everywhere else.
  • The detection-bypass and fingerprint features are for testing on software you own/are authorized to test. There's a disclaimer in the README for a reason.
  • This is a solo project, so some edges (snapshot management, exotic device configs) are rougher than a team-built tool.

Try it

Repo: github.com/engnzdl/enmulator

Installers for macOS / Windows / Linux are on the releases page. If you poke at it and hit something, open an issue — and if it's useful, a star helps others find it.

Built with Tauri 2, Rust, and React. GPLv3.

title: Why Your Team Needs a Multi-Cloud Database Inventory
description:
Quick question: how many database instances is your team running right now?

Not an estimate. The exact number, across all your cloud providers, all your accounts, all your regions.

If you can answer that in under 10 seconds without opening a console, you have a database inventory. Most teams don't.

TL;DR

A multi-cloud database inventory is a single, always-current list of every database instance your organization runs — across AWS, GCP, MongoDB Atlas, and on-prem. Without one, you're flying blind. 1DataCloud automates this without agents or manual tracking. Try it free →

The Hidden Complexity Problem

Ten years ago, most companies had a simple database setup: a few MySQL or PostgreSQL instances, maybe a replica or two, running in a single data center or a single AWS account. One person knew where everything was.

Today, the landscape looks completely different:

  • Multiple cloud providers. AWS for most workloads, GCP for analytics (BigQuery is hard to replace), maybe Azure for a legacy integration, MongoDB Atlas for flexibility.
  • Multiple accounts per provider. Separate AWS accounts for prod, staging, dev, each product team, each regulated workload.
  • Multiple regions. Latency requirements, data residency laws, disaster recovery — all push toward multi-region deployments.
  • Multiple engine types. Relational, document, key-value, column-family, graph. Often in the same organization, sometimes for the same product.

The result is that "where are our databases?" is no longer a question with an obvious answer. And the consequences of not knowing are real.

What Happens Without a Database Inventory

You forget what you have

Databases created for a project that ended. Test instances that were supposed to be temporary. Replicas that were promoted and then the original was never cleaned up. Without an inventory, these accumulate silently — incurring cost, creating attack surface, and holding data that shouldn't be held.

Security gaps appear

A database that isn't in your inventory isn't in your patching cycle. It isn't reviewed during access audits. It might be publicly accessible. It might have a root password that was never rotated. You don't know, because you don't know it exists.

Onboarding is painful

Every new engineer needs to learn "the landscape" from whoever holds the tribal knowledge. This takes weeks, it's always incomplete, and it walks out the door when that person leaves.

Incident response slows down

When something breaks at 2 AM, you don't want to be asking "which database is connected to which service?" That mapping should already exist. Without an inventory, you're reconstructing it under pressure.

Compliance becomes a project

GDPR, SOC 2, HIPAA — all of them require knowing where data is stored. If you don't have a database inventory, every compliance audit becomes a weeks-long archaeology project.

What a Database Inventory Actually Contains

At minimum, a useful database inventory answers these questions for every instance:

Field Why it matters
Cloud provider Determines which tools and APIs apply
Account / project Determines ownership and billing
Region Affects latency, data residency, DR planning
Engine and version Drives patching and end-of-life planning
Instance size Capacity planning and cost optimization
Status Running? Stopped? Rebooting?
Multi-AZ / HA Risk assessment
Publicly accessible Security posture
Connected services Impact radius for incidents
Schema metadata What data is actually stored there

The last two are the hardest — and the most valuable.

Why Multi-Cloud Makes This Harder

If you were on a single cloud provider with a single account, an inventory is manageable. You can use native tools (AWS Resource Explorer, GCP Asset Inventory) to get a reasonable view.

The moment you span providers, those native tools stop helping. AWS doesn't show your GCP instances. GCP doesn't know about your MongoDB Atlas clusters. Neither knows about your on-prem PostgreSQL.

This forces teams into one of three bad options:

  1. Manual spreadsheets. Updated when someone remembers. Always out of date. Doesn't scale.
  2. Home-built tooling. Scraping APIs from each provider, aggregating results, building a UI. This is weeks of engineering time that solves a problem that isn't your core product.
  3. Ignoring it. Accepting the risk and operational friction as a cost of doing business.

None of these are good options when you're trying to move fast.

What an Automated Inventory Looks Like

The right solution connects directly to each cloud provider's API, discovers instances automatically, and presents them in a unified view that stays current without manual updates.

This is what 1DataCloud does.

Connect once, discover continuously:
Add your AWS IAM credentials, GCP service account, MongoDB Atlas API key, or on-prem connection strings. 1DataCloud queries each provider's management APIs and builds a unified inventory automatically.

What it discovers today:

  • AWS: RDS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server), Aurora, Redshift, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune
  • GCP: Cloud SQL, Spanner, BigQuery, Firestore, Bigtable
  • MongoDB Atlas: clusters across all projects
  • On-prem: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB

Coming soon: Microsoft Azure (SQL Database, Cosmos DB, Azure PostgreSQL)

No agents required:
Everything is read-only and API-based. Nothing is installed on your database nodes. Existing cloud security primitives (IAM roles, service accounts) are used directly.

Schema metadata included:
Click any instance and browse its tables, columns, data types, and indexes. This is the layer that turns an inventory from a list of instances into a map of where your data lives.

The Organizational Benefits

Beyond the operational improvements, a database inventory changes how the organization relates to its data infrastructure:

Engineering teams stop wasting time on "what's running where?" and start spending it on things that matter.

Security teams get a complete surface area to audit — without a months-long discovery exercise before every review.

Data teams know where the data they need actually lives, without filing tickets to find out.

Leadership can make capacity, cost, and risk decisions based on a complete picture, not a best guess.

Getting Started

If you don't have a database inventory today, the fastest path to one is to stop trying to build it manually and connect to a tool that maintains it automatically.

1DataCloud is free to start — connect up to 3 database instances across any provider, no credit card required.

If your team is managing more than that, Pro and Enterprise tiers support unlimited instances across all providers with shared organizational access and RBAC.

👉 1datacloud.ai

👉 Start free

One More Thing

Once you have an inventory with schema metadata, natural language querying becomes possible. Instead of "I know the data exists somewhere in our infrastructure" being the beginning of a long search, it becomes the beginning of a question: "How many active users do we have across all our regional databases?"

That's what Query1AI is for — but you need the inventory first.

Does your team have a database inventory today? How do you maintain it? Genuinely curious what approaches people are using at different scales.

title: Migrating On-Prem SQL Server to Azure SQL PaaS: How We Cut Infrastructure Costs by 25%
description:
At S&P Global Market Intelligence I helped migrate on-premise SQL Server databases to Azure SQL PaaS. Our team moved between 10 and 50 databases to Azure SQL Managed Instance. The headline result was a reduction in infrastructure costs of about 25%. The more important result was that the people using those databases barely noticed it happened.

Here's what I learned about doing a migration like that well.

1. Inventory before you plan

Before choosing a target, list everything that touches the database: ETL jobs, reports, linked servers, SQL Agent jobs, cross-database queries, CLR assemblies. PaaS options don't support every on-prem feature in the same way, and you want to find the gaps on a spreadsheet, not in production.

Microsoft's Data Migration Assistant and Azure Migrate help here, but they don't know about the Excel workbook someone in finance refreshes every Monday. Talk to users.

2. Pick the right PaaS flavour

Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance trade compatibility against simplicity. Managed Instance keeps more instance-level features (Agent jobs, cross-database queries), so it suits lift-and-shift. Single databases are simpler and can be cheaper, but may need refactoring. Decide per workload, not per estate. We went with Managed Instance, which kept most instance-level features in place and meant fewer changes to existing code.

3. Right-size, don't copy

Most of the savings came from not paying for capacity we didn't use. On-prem servers are sized for peak load plus growth plus fear. In the cloud you can measure actual usage and scale. Look at real CPU, memory and IO over several weeks before choosing service tiers.

4. Migrate in waves

Start with low-risk databases: development, reporting copies, internal tools. Each wave teaches you something about networking, permissions or performance that makes the next wave smoother.

5. Test the boring things

Performance gets attention. In our migration, the real problems came from elsewhere:

  • Connection strings hard-coded in old applications and reports
  • SSIS packages and SQL Agent jobs that needed reworking to run against Azure
  • Jobs that relied on local file paths on the old servers

Also worth checking: time zone and collation differences, firewall rules and private endpoints.

6. Define "done" with the users

A migration isn't finished when the data moves. It's finished when every report, job and application works as before and the old servers are switched off. Agree that checklist with stakeholders up front.

The takeaway

Cloud migration savings come mostly from right-sizing and retiring infrastructure. Keeping users happy comes from inventory, testing and communication. Neither is glamorous, and both matter more than the migration tooling.

title: Load Testing: Read the Queue Behind Successful Bookings
description:
A booking endpoint can keep returning success while concurrent users wait much longer. Lab 15 makes that behavior visible with a local HTTP server, a constrained work pool, and a small Go load generator.

Load testing reveals how latency changes when demand competes for limited resources.

Fast bookings can queue under load

One successful booking does not explain concurrent behavior. Lab 15 sends POST /booking to a local HTTP server, comparing low and high concurrency to expose queueing and latency distributions. It models bounded work slots, not a production database.

Two scenarios share one server

The demo uses five simulated database slots and a 20 ms base query. Smoke runs two VUs; stress runs 50. Both run for two seconds, sequentially, with the same endpoint and booking body. These are demonstration settings, not production capacity targets.

Each VU waits before sending again

Each VU has one goroutine and sends its next request after the previous attempt finishes. There is no think time, ramp-up, or arrival-rate scheduler. This is a closed loop: slower responses reduce each VU's request rate.

A buffered channel bounds simulated work

A buffered channel acts as a semaphore. Handlers acquire a token before simulated query work and release it with defer. Full capacity makes additional handlers wait; there is no explicit bounded waiting queue or overload rejection policy.

select {
case s.semaphore <- struct{}{}:
case <-r.Context().Done():
    return
}
defer func() { <-s.semaphore }()

The database pool is simulated

There is no SQL driver, real query, booking table, or database transaction. A timer simulates work. ActiveConnections returns len(semaphore): acquired slots, not waiting handlers, TCP connections, or real database telemetry.

Random slow work amplifies queueing

activeReq includes waiting and working POST handlers. After admission, when activeReq exceeds capacity, a 10% random branch multiplies query duration by 25. The demo's 20 ms becomes 500 ms. Stress results therefore combine queueing with deliberately injected slow work.

if atomic.LoadInt64(&s.activeReq) >
    int64(s.cfg.MaxDBConnections) {
    if rand.Float32() < 0.10 {
        dur = s.cfg.DBQueryDuration * 25
    }
}

Context bounds the test lifetime

Run uses context.WithTimeout for the configured duration and passes that context to each HTTP request. A five-second client timeout also applies. The server checks cancellation while acquiring a slot and waiting for simulated work; it does not return a dedicated overload response.

Canceled attempts are not all counted

Request-construction and client.Do errors are counted only while ctx.Err() is nil. End-of-test canceled attempts can be omitted. TotalRequests is recorded success samples plus counted errors, not every attempt started.

if err != nil {
    if ctx.Err() == nil {
        errs++
    }
    continue
}

Success follows an HTTP status rule

The runner drains and closes response bodies. Status >=400 increments errors; status <400 records success latency, which is broader than a 2xx-only rule. JSON business fields are not validated, and body-read errors are ignored.

Latency includes reading the body

Timing starts before client.Do and ends after the successful response body is drained and closed. It is not query-only time. DNS, dialing, TLS, first-byte wait, pool wait, and body transfer are not separately measured.

Percentiles use successful samples only

Failed responses and transport errors have no latency samples. Percentiles, average, min, and max use successful samples only. With no successes, latency fields remain zero; that does not mean the service responded instantly.

RPS includes counted errors

Total is len(latencies)+errors. RPS divides that total by Run's actual elapsed duration after goroutines finish, so it is not success-only throughput. With no total requests, an empty Result is returned, including zero Duration.

total := len(latencies) + errors
res.RPS = float64(total) /
    totalDuration.Seconds()

Percentiles select a floored index

The calculator copies and sorts samples, then selects int((n-1)*p/100) without interpolation. For the test fixture 1–100 ms, P50=50 ms, P95=95 ms, and P99=99 ms. Other tools may use different percentile conventions.

idx := int(float64(len(sorted)-1) *
    (pct / 100.0))
return sorted[idx]

A fixture makes the calculation explicit

The 1–100 ms fixture has min 1 ms, max 100 ms, and average 50.5 ms. time.Duration retains nanosecond units, so division does not force whole-millisecond rounding. These are calculated fixture values, not HTTP performance measurements.

Small samples make the tail coarse

With one 42 ms sample, every percentile is 42 ms. Small datasets can map several tail percentiles to the same sample and may exclude the maximum under this formula. Sample count and method matter when interpreting precision.

Average and tail answer different questions

Average summarizes all successful samples; P95 selects a high-ranked sample. Unit tests verify ordered percentile invariants. The integration test separately checks stress P95 exceeds stress average; that relationship is not guaranteed for every possible distribution.

Demo numbers are recorded examples

The repository records a sample smoke P95 of about 21.37 ms and stress P95 of about 1.357 s, with zero counted errors. These are historical example results, not a fresh measurement. Random spikes and scheduling vary; omitted canceled attempts also qualify the zero-error interpretation.

Transport settings are not a full generator audit

MaxIdleConns and MaxIdleConnsPerHost are both 1000; these are idle-connection retention settings, not proof that every client bottleneck is eliminated. All successful latencies are retained per VU, merged, copied, and sorted, so memory grows with collected samples.

A booking response is not a real transaction

Non-POST methods receive 405. Completed POST requests return 201, confirmed, and the fixed ID BK-1001. Request JSON is not decoded or validated, and there is no persistence, authentication, idempotency, or unique booking creation.

Tests establish specific behaviors

Five metric tests cover fixtures, empty input, one sample, RPS, and ordering. Seven integration tests cover load comparison, HTTP 500, method rejection, dial errors, cancellation, slot limits, and total-count invariants. They do not prove queue fairness or maximum capacity.

The lab bottleneck is known by design

The slot bottleneck is deliberately constructed. In production, rising P95 alone does not isolate application queues, database work, network, or external dependencies. The runtime has no exporter, tracing, or automated SLA threshold; the demo prints summaries.

Rerun and interpret in context

The module declares Go 1.22 and uses the standard library. Go is unavailable in this authoring environment, so source and assertions were inspected without rerunning tests. Recorded repository results are prior-run evidence. Load testing reveals how latency changes when demand competes for limited resources.

cd labs/15-load-testing
go test -v ./...
go test -race ./...
go run ./cmd/demo

Source

Software Engineering Lab 15, snapshot commit 82af988b89439fa92b1200406c5afbd59ce72a56. Source: README, runner, metric calculator and tests, server, integration tests, demo, execution record, and go.mod. Code excerpts belong in their original package context.

title: EyeZen v1.2.0: Bringing Local-First Workspace Customization to the Browser
description:
EyeZen v1.2.0: Bringing Local-First Workspace Customization to the Browser

EyeZen v1.2.0 is officially available!

After building the desktop foundation of EyeZen with Rust, Tauri 2, React and TypeScript, I've reached a new milestone: a functional browser edition with local settings persistence and a dedicated documentation website.

Why a web edition?

EyeZen started as a desktop application focused on workspace personalization, comfort preferences, profiles and break routines.

However, many features—such as changing themes, creating profiles and organizing break reminders—don't require access to native operating-system APIs.

Version 1.2.0 makes these capabilities accessible directly from a browser.

What's new in v1.2.0?

1. EyeZen Web

The browser edition includes ten appearance themes, nine starter workspace profiles, customizable profiles, scheduled routines, break reminders and accessibility preferences.

Users can personalize their environment without installing the desktop application.

2. Persistent local browser settings

A major part of this release involved implementing reliable browser persistence.

EyeZen stores settings locally, validates saved data and handles malformed records rather than silently overwriting them.

Settings can also be exported and imported as JSON.

The web and desktop editions use compatible settings schemas, although synchronization is manual rather than automatic.

3. Permission-aware reminders

EyeZen supports optional in-app break reminders and notification functionality.

Browser notification permission is requested through an explicit user interaction.

Reminders depend on the active application or browser tab and remain subject to browser and operating-system restrictions.

4. A new documentation website

Version 1.2.0 also introduces comprehensive public documentation.

It covers:

  • Application features and configuration
  • Web versus desktop compatibility
  • Installation and setup
  • Privacy and local storage
  • Architecture and accessibility
  • Troubleshooting and frequently asked questions

5. Maintaining honest platform boundaries

The browser edition cannot tint unrelated desktop windows, enumerate physical monitors or change hardware brightness.

The installed desktop application retains optional software-based visual tint overlays on supported environments.

Neither edition claims medical benefits or hardware-level display calibration.

Communicating these differences clearly is important when building trustworthy cross-platform software.

Built with open technologies

The project uses:

  • Rust and Tauri 2 for native desktop functionality
  • React and TypeScript for the interface
  • Vite for web builds
  • GitHub Actions for automated builds and deployment
  • GitHub Pages for the static browser application and documentation

EyeZen is open source under the Mozilla Public License 2.0.

Try EyeZen

Web edition: https://sanskarin.github.io/EyeZen/

Documentation: https://sanskarin.github.io/EyeZen/docs/

GitHub release: https://github.com/sanskarIN/EyeZen/releases/tag/v1.2.0

Source code: https://github.com/sanskarIN/EyeZen

What's next?

EyeZen will continue evolving through better workspace customization, platform compatibility, accessibility improvements and stronger real-device testing.

If you use EyeZen or work with Rust, Tauri, TypeScript or cross-platform applications, I'd welcome your feedback and contributions.

What would you prioritize next for EyeZen?

title: Your Website Feels Slow? Start by Finding the Actual Bottleneck
description:
A website can look perfectly fine during development and still feel slow when someone opens it on their phone or uses it over a weaker internet connection.

The first reaction is often to blame the server or upgrade the hosting plan. Sometimes that helps, but it is not always the real problem.

A page can be slow because of oversized images, render-blocking JavaScript, third-party scripts, or a large amount of work happening in the browser. Making random changes without identifying the cause can waste time and make the code harder to maintain.

Here is a practical way to investigate website performance before jumping into fixes.

1. Check What the Browser Is Actually Loading

Start by opening your website in Chrome and launching DevTools. Go to the Network tab, reload the page, and look at the requests being made.

Pay attention to a few things:

  • Are images much larger than their displayed size?
  • Are several JavaScript files being loaded before the page becomes usable?
  • Are third-party scripts taking a long time to respond?
  • Are there requests that repeatedly fail or take unusually long?

The Network tab gives you a better starting point than guessing based on how the page feels.

Also, test a few important pages rather than checking only the homepage. A product page with multiple images and scripts may behave very differently from a simple landing page.

2. Find Out Whether the Problem Is on the Server or in the Browser

A slow page does not always mean the server is slow.

If the initial document takes a long time to arrive, investigate server response time, database queries, caching, and backend processing.

If the document arrives quickly but the page still takes a long time to become usable, look at JavaScript execution, image loading, fonts, and layout work.

The distinction matters because the solutions are different. Optimizing database queries will not fix a huge image, and compressing images will not solve a slow database request.

3. Pay Attention to Images

Images are an easy place to find unnecessary page weight.

For example, a product card might display an image that is only 300 pixels wide while downloading a file several times larger than necessary. Multiply that across a page containing dozens of products, and the extra data can add up.

A few things worth checking:

  • Resize images to suit their actual display dimensions.
  • Consider modern formats such as WebP or AVIF.
  • Use responsive images where appropriate.
  • Lazy-load below-the-fold images when suitable.
  • Avoid lazy-loading the main image that needs to appear immediately.

Do not compress everything blindly. The goal is to reduce unnecessary data while keeping images clear enough for their intended use.

4. Look for JavaScript That Does Too Much

JavaScript can affect both loading performance and how quickly a page responds to user actions.

A page might download a relatively small script but then spend too much time executing it. Large dependencies, unnecessary event handlers, and expensive calculations can all contribute to the problem.

Use the Performance panel in Chrome DevTools to record a page load or an interaction. Look for long tasks and repeated layout calculations.

If a script is doing work that is not needed immediately, consider whether it can be deferred, split into smaller pieces, or run only when the relevant feature is used.

The right solution depends on what the recording actually shows. Removing a library without understanding its role can introduce bugs without meaningfully improving performance.

5. Measure More Than Just Load Time

A single loading-time number does not explain the entire user experience.

Google's Core Web Vitals provide three useful measurements:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): How quickly the main content becomes visible. The good threshold is 2.5 seconds or less.
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP): How quickly the page responds visually to user interactions. The good threshold is 200 milliseconds or less.
  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): How much unexpected layout movement occurs. The good threshold is 0.1 or less.

These measurements help identify different types of problems. A page might display its main content quickly but still respond poorly when someone clicks a button.

You can read Google's explanation in the Core Web Vitals documentation.

6. Test the Fix Instead of Assuming It Worked

Once you identify a likely bottleneck, make one meaningful change and measure again.

For example, if an image is responsible for a large portion of the page weight, optimize that image and compare the results. If JavaScript execution is the issue, profile the page after changing the relevant code.

Try to keep test conditions consistent. Network speed, caching, device performance, and third-party services can all influence measurements.

Tools such as PageSpeed Insights can help you examine performance reports and identify potential improvements. Browser DevTools is useful when you need to investigate the cause in more detail.

Remember that a lab test and real-user data serve different purposes. A page may perform well on your computer but behave differently for users with older devices or slower connections.

A Better Way to Approach Performance Work

Website optimization becomes much easier when you stop treating every slow page as the same problem.

First, reproduce the issue. Then collect evidence, identify the likely bottleneck, make a focused change, and measure the result.

You will not always find a dramatic improvement in the first attempt. Sometimes the issue comes from several small problems rather than one obvious mistake.

But a repeatable debugging process is more useful than making random changes or upgrading infrastructure before you know what needs fixing.

The goal is not simply to make a performance score look better. It is to build a website that loads reliably, responds quickly, and works well for the people using it.

title: The first stable version 1.0 of Strata for Linux has been released
description:
Strata 1.0 is now available, marking the first stable release of the Rust-based, GTK4 file manager.

Designed for Linux environments like Omarchy, version 1.0 introduces session-restoring tabs, large directory optimizations, and sandboxed file previews using Bubblewrap.

Three display modes and keyboard control

Strata supports three different layouts for browsing files: icon view, traditional list view, and columns that allow for easy navigation into deeper folders.

For those who prefer not to use the mouse, navigation includes shortcuts inspired by the well-known Vim text editor, customizable shortcuts, and quick file search based on the letters of their name.

File previews and security

The program has a preview system that supports images, RAW photos, PDF files, text documents, source code, as well as audio and video files. For greater security, previews based on internal analysis tools are isolated using special containment mechanisms.

READ ALSO

title: ISO 27018 for Cloud Engineers: Protecting Customer PII in Public Cloud Services
description:
Cloud-based applications can process personal information across databases, APIs, administrative interfaces, backups, and external service providers. For Indian SaaS companies and IT service providers working with enterprise customers, understanding these data paths is essential to evaluating privacy risks.

ISO/IEC 27018 focuses on protecting personally identifiable information (PII) processed by public cloud service providers acting as PII processors.

The standard's relevance depends on the service model, processing activities, and applicable certification scope. Here are several technical areas that cloud teams should examine when considering PII protection.

  1. Map PII Across the Service Architecture

Identify where customer PII enters the platform, which components process it, where it is stored, and how it moves between systems.

Include application databases, APIs, support tools, logs, backups, and relevant third-party services. This view can reveal data flows that are not apparent from a high-level infrastructure diagram.

The purpose is to understand the processing environment and establish which controls are relevant to the service.

  1. Review Identity and Access Boundaries

Evaluate how employees, administrators, service accounts, and external providers access personal information.

Relevant technical considerations include authentication, role-based permissions, privileged access, access reviews, credential management, and logging. Permissions should reflect operational requirements rather than grant unnecessary access to customer data.

For multi-tenant platforms, examine whether application logic, storage, APIs, and administrative interfaces preserve the intended separation between customers.

  1. Examine Encryption and Data Lifecycle Controls

Encryption can reduce the risk of unauthorised disclosure when PII is stored or transmitted. Its effectiveness also depends on key management, access restrictions, configuration, and the systems in which the information is processed.

Data lifecycle controls deserve similar attention. Determine how retention periods are defined, how customer information is returned or deleted, and how backups or replicas affect deletion practices.

The applicable arrangements should reflect customer agreements and relevant legal obligations.

  1. Understand Subprocessor Dependencies

Cloud services may rely on external infrastructure, monitoring, hosting, and analytics providers. These dependencies can affect where personal information is processed and which parties can access it.

Maintain visibility into relevant subprocessors and clarify the responsibilities established by applicable agreements. Material changes to the service provider chain may require a review of the existing privacy arrangements.

  1. Distinguish ISO 27018 From ISO 27001

ISO/IEC 27001 establishes requirements for an information security management system. ISO/IEC 27018 focuses on privacy considerations for PII processing in applicable public cloud environments.

The standards address different requirements. Certification to ISO 27001 alone does not establish conformity with ISO 27018.

Technical teams should understand which service boundaries and processing activities fall within the certification scope being considered.

Connecting Technical Evidence With Certification Scope

Access controls, data-flow information, retention practices, and subprocessor arrangements all contribute to understanding how PII is protected. Their relevance should be evaluated against the actual cloud service and applicable requirements.

Organisations can explore ISO/IEC 27018 certification and related governance services when determining how cloud privacy assurance fits their certification priorities.

For cloud engineers, the key principle is straightforward: privacy controls need to reflect the real architecture, the information processed, and the responsibilities defined for the service.

title: Ito: Build Terminal UIs in Lua!
description:
Architecture of Ito: Bridging Lua and Terminal Graphics

The landscape of terminal user interface (TUI) development has been dominated by abstractions that favor either high-level runtime environments (Node.js) or systems-level paradigms (Rust/C++). While Ratatui provides a robust immediate-mode rendering loop for Rust developers, the barrier to entry for rapid prototyping often remains high due to the necessity of compilation steps and strict type safety. Ito represents a departure from this pattern, shifting the TUI development lifecycle into the Lua runtime while maintaining high-performance rendering via a Rust-based core.

The Problem of Execution Contexts

In typical TUI libraries, the state management and rendering logic are bound to the host language’s threading model and memory management. To build a library that feels like a natural extension of a Neovim-centric workflow, one must address the impedance mismatch between a high-level scripting language and the raw byte-stream manipulation required for terminal escape sequences.

Ito addresses this by utilizing a "Core-Provider" architecture. The core is an engine written in Rust, which acts as the terminal driver, managing the virtual buffer, input event polling, and ANSI sequence serialization. Lua serves as the domain-specific language (DSL) for component orchestration, layout calculation, and style definition.

The Core Rendering Pipeline

At the heart of Ito is a custom canvas implementation. Unlike traditional terminal libraries that rely on existing wrappers (like ncurses or termion), Ito implements a double-buffered grid system. This allows for differential updates: rather than redrawing the entire screen on every frame, the engine calculates the diff between the back buffer and the front buffer, emitting only the minimal set of ANSI escape codes required to reconcile the state.

// Simplified representation of the Ito buffer reconcile logic
impl Buffer {
    pub fn diff(&self, previous: &Buffer) -> Vec<Operation> {
        let mut ops = Vec::new();
        for (y, row) in self.cells.iter().enumerate() {
            for (x, cell) in row.iter().enumerate() {
                if cell != &previous.cells[y][x] {
                    ops.push(Operation::MoveCursor(x as u16, y as u16));
                    ops.push(Operation::Write(cell.content.clone()));
                }
            }
        }
        ops
    }
}

By offloading this logic to Rust, Ito maintains a sub-millisecond frame time, which is critical for smooth animations and high-frequency UI updates. The Lua runtime interacts with this system through a strictly defined foreign function interface (FFI), ensuring that overhead remains negligible.

The Lua Integration Layer

The design philosophy of Ito is to provide minimal, composable primitives. In Lua, this manifests as a declarative tree structure. Every element in Ito is a node, and layouts are handled by hierarchical constraints.

Consider the implementation of a basic panel structure in Lua:

local ito = require("ito")

local root = ito.container({
    layout = "vertical",
    children = {
        ito.text("System Monitor", { color = "blue", bold = true }),
        ito.progress({ value = 0.75, width = "100%" }),
        ito.button("Restart", { on_click = function() print("clicked") end })
    }
})

ito.render(root)

The underlying bridge translates these Lua tables into the Rust internal component tree. By utilizing LuaJIT, the performance penalty is essentially non-existent for the majority of UI tasks, as the heavy lifting of terminal output is performed in the compiled binary.

Decoupling Logic from Display: The Canvas Abstraction

One of the more unique engineering choices in Ito is the separation of the TUI library from the physical terminal adaptor. During development, it became evident that testing UI layouts required a more robust debugging mechanism than standard terminal output.

We developed a custom canvas implementation that renders the TUI logic into an HTML5 Canvas via WebAssembly. This was achieved by abstracting the output layer:

  1. Terminal Adaptor: Standard ANSI escape sequence emission.
  2. Canvas Adaptor: Converts the internal grid buffer into WebGL-accelerated drawing commands for a browser context.

This allows developers to experiment with complex layouts in the browser at uji.sh/ito before deploying them to the local terminal environment. This portability ensures that "ricing" a UI becomes a visual, iterative process rather than a cycle of recompilation and terminal toggling.

Handling Input Events

Input management in TUIs is notoriously difficult due to terminal signal handling (SIGINT, SIGWINCH). Ito uses a non-blocking poll loop in Rust that captures input events and pushes them into a thread-safe MPSC (multi-producer, single-consumer) channel.

The Lua runtime monitors this channel periodically. When an input event (e.g., Key(Enter)) is received, Ito invokes the registered callback within the Lua VM context:

ito.on_event("key", function(key)
    if key == "q" then
        ito.quit()
    end
end)

This event-driven model keeps the main UI thread responsive, even when the Lua script is performing heavy data processing or waiting on external IO.

Memory Safety and GC Interaction

Interfacing Lua with Rust presents specific challenges regarding garbage collection. If a Lua object is passed to Rust, there is a risk that the Lua GC might collect it while the Rust side still maintains a pointer to it.

To mitigate this, Ito employs a handle-based system. When a component is created in Lua, Rust returns an integer identifier (handle). The Rust core manages the actual component lifecycle in a stable memory segment, while Lua only maintains the identifier. When the component is garbage collected in Lua, it sends a finalizer event to the Rust side to safely deallocate the associated memory.

Optimization and Future Trajectories

The current version of Ito is optimized for low-latency feedback. Future development is focused on three areas:

  1. Reactive State Binding: Implementing a Lua-side observable pattern that automatically triggers re-renders when data structures change, reducing the boilerplate required for state management.
  2. Extended ANSI Support: Moving beyond basic 16-color support toward full TrueColor (24-bit) implementation and under-the-hood optimization for terminal multiplexers like tmux.
  3. WebAssembly Tooling: Enhancing the llms.txt integration to ensure that AI coding assistants can generate valid Ito layouts by understanding the hierarchical constraints and component API of the library.

Conclusion

The creation of Ito was born from the realization that existing TUI frameworks often impose too much structure at the expense of flexibility. By decoupling the performance-critical rendering engine from the stylistic configuration layer, we have enabled a development loop that feels as fluid as configuring a Neovim plugin. Whether you are building a dashboard, a terminal-based system monitoring tool, or an experimental interface, the ability to control the terminal environment with pure Lua offers a degree of customization previously reserved for lower-level languages.

For those interested in leveraging professional engineering support to integrate these high-performance interface patterns into your own infrastructure, please visit https://www.mgatc.com for consulting services.

title: Convert STEP to GLB and enforce a 3D asset budget
description:
A CAD file is useful for manufacturing. A web page needs a mesh it can download and display. Between those two steps, it helps to put a limit on the asset you ship.

This walkthrough uses two MIT-licensed tools I maintain: step2glb for STEP conversion and glbscope for GLB inspection and build budgets. The first runs on Node.js. The second is written in Rust.

The example uses a small public test fixture, so you can reproduce the result without uploading private CAD files to a service. It demonstrates the workflow; it is not a performance benchmark.

1. Install the published versions

Use Node.js 22 or later and a current Rust toolchain:

mkdir cad-to-web
cd cad-to-web
npm init -y
npm install --save-exact step2glb@0.2.0
cargo install glbscope --version 0.3.0 --locked

Keep package-lock.json in your project. Use npm ci on later build runs.

Download the two-tetrahedra fixture from a fixed source revision:

curl -fL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/M1chlCZ/step2glb/2a19b844150b7057aa4b425577b4f8881754b655/test/fixtures/two-tetrahedra.step -o sample.step

You can use your own .step or .stp file instead. Both tools process files locally. Installing the packages and downloading this fixture need network access.

2. Convert the model 

npx step2glb inspect sample.step
npx step2glb build sample.step --out sample.glb --preset web

inspect prints an assembly manifest. build writes a Draco-compressed GLB and prints a JSON summary. The web preset uses coarser tessellation and lower quantization precision than the high-detail preset. Check the result visually before you use it for a real product.

In my local run with these published versions, the output was 3,356 bytes, with 8 triangles, 24 vertices, and 5 nodes. A second build of the same fixture produced identical bytes. Those numbers describe this tiny fixture, not a typical CAD assembly.

The output uses metres. Occurrence IDs come from hierarchy paths, so renaming a part does not change its ID. Moving a part to a different hierarchy path can change it.

3. Set a budget

Create budget.toml:

max_bytes = 2_000_000
max_triangles = 120_000
max_nodes = 400

These are example limits. Choose limits for your users and viewer. A small product preview and a detailed assembly viewer have different needs.

Run the check:

glbscope --budget budget.toml sample.glb

The sample passes. To prove that the gate works, temporarily set max_bytes = 3_000 and run it again. The 3,356-byte sample fails with exit code 1 and a finding that identifies the exceeded byte budget.

The exit codes make this usable in CI:

Code Meaning
0 No findings or baseline regression
1 A budget finding or baseline regression
2 An input, parse, or argument error

Keep the check as a normal build step so a nonzero result stops the job.

One detail matters for compressed assets: step2glb requires KHR_draco_mesh_compression in its output. If you set allowed_extensions in the budget, include that extension. A viewer also needs a Draco decoder to display the model.

4. Keep a readable build report 

glbscope --format markdown --budget budget.toml sample.glb > model-report.md
glbscope --json sample.glb > baseline.json

The Markdown report is convenient as a build artifact. Commit a baseline when you want to review later growth:

glbscope --baseline baseline.json sample.glb

A file-size increase, triangle-count increase, or new finding causes a regression result. Run from the same working directory with the same paths, and update the baseline only when the change is intended. SARIF output is also available for code-scanning integrations.

What this check does not prove

An asset budget measures structural properties. It does not measure frame rate, confirm visual quality, or replace a full glTF validator and a test in your actual viewer. Draco reduces download size but adds decoding work. A low triangle count alone does not guarantee a fast page.

step2glb also has hard limits, including 2 million triangles and a 16 MiB output file. It converts STEP geometry to a web mesh; it does not preserve the editable CAD feature history.

For a real model, inspect the converted shape, test it on a representative device, and then set your budget. The useful automation is catching unintended growth before it reaches that device.

Source and full options: step2glb · glbscope. Reproducible files that expose conversion or reporting problems are welcome.

AI disclosure: this article was prepared with AI assistance. The commands, budget pass/fail, decoded mesh bounds, and repeated-build result were checked locally with the published package versions on October 15, 2026.

title: A background refresh must not move the row under your cursor, so our table renders the snapshot it loaded with
description:
Nakodo finds creators on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok for a brand, scores each one and emails the good fits. The part of the app this post is about is the boring part: the table of what it has found so far, which the owner of the campaign reads, sorts, filters and ticks boxes in while the pipeline behind it is still adding rows.

The page is a server component. A small client component polls an endpoint for a fingerprint of the campaign's data and calls router.refresh() when it changes:

export function AutoRefresh({ campaignId, every = 30_000 }: { campaignId: string; every?: number }) {

Thirty seconds on the campaign's own pages, five on the outreach page while a draft is being written. Each quiet check doubles the wait, and the timer stops while the tab is hidden. (That endpoint and its fingerprint were their own post; this post is about what the refresh does to the page it lands on.)

router.refresh() is lovely. It re-renders the server component, keeps client state, and the new rows appear. It is also, in a sorted table, a small act of violence: the pointer is over row 14, a creator two rows up finishes being scored, the sort is by score, and row 14 is now a different creator. The checkbox you were about to tick belongs to someone else.

The list is not rows

The component takes rows as a prop and never renders it directly. On first render it captures a Map of the two fields the list sorts on:

type Snapshot = Map<string, { score: number | null; stage: string }>;

const snapshotOf = (rows: ResultRow[]): Snapshot =>
  new Map(rows.map((r) => [r.channelId, { score: r.score, stage: r.stage }]));

Then the list it renders is built from rows and the snapshot together:

const { shown, changed } = useMemo(() => {
  const shown: ResultRow[] = [];
  let changed = 0;
  for (const r of rows) {
    const s = snapshot.get(r.channelId);
    if (!s) {
      changed++;
      continue;
    }
    const same = s.score === r.score && s.stage === r.stage;
    if (!same) changed++;
    shown.push(same ? r : { ...r, score: s.score, stage: s.stage });
  }
  return { shown, changed };
}, [rows, snapshot]);

Three things fall out of that loop.

A row the snapshot has never seen is not rendered. It is counted.

A row whose score or stage has moved is rendered with the old score and stage. Every other field is the fresh one: a name, an avatar, a thread status, a view count. Only the two values the order depends on are held back, because they are the two that can move a row.

Everything else about the refresh still works. Counts in the header update, the "waiting on you" box updates, a creator whose conversation has advanced shows its new badge. The row simply stays where it is.

The banner is the whole feature 

{changed > 0 && (
  <div role="status" className="...">
    <span>{plural(changed, w.one, w.many)} found or updated since this list loaded.</span>
    <Button
      size="xs"
      variant="outline"
      onClick={() => {
        setFresh(new Set(rows.filter((r) => !snapshot.has(r.channelId)).map((r) => r.channelId)));
        setSnapshot(snapshotOf(rows));
      }}
    >
      Show them
    </Button>
  </div>
)}

Two setState calls in that order. fresh is the set of ids that were not in the old snapshot, so it has to be computed before the snapshot is replaced. Re-snapshotting is what admits the new rows, because shown is derived from the snapshot.

The rows in fresh arrive with a highlight and a mark:

@keyframes row-arrive {
  0% { opacity: 0; background-color: var(--selected); box-shadow: inset 2px 0 0 var(--color-cyano-600); }
  12%,
  40% { opacity: 1; background-color: var(--selected); box-shadow: inset 2px 0 0 var(--color-cyano-600); }
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .row-arrive {
    animation: row-arrive 2.4s ease-out calc(var(--i, 0) * 50ms) backwards;
  }
}

--i is the row's index in the visible list, Math.min(i, 10), so twelve new rows stagger over half a second instead of over six. backwards is what makes the delay work: without it a row with a 500ms delay is fully visible for 500ms, then starts its own fade-in from nothing. The mark next to the name is labelled "New since this list loaded", so the highlight is not the only way to know.

The banner's role="status" costs one attribute and means the count is announced instead of appearing silently.

Two things that look like mistakes

A setState during render.

const [snapshot, setSnapshot] = useState(() => snapshotOf(rows));
if (snapshot.size === 0 && rows.length > 0) setSnapshot(snapshotOf(rows));

That is React's own documented pattern for adjusting state when props change, not a mistake, and it is here because of a real sequence: a campaign's page opens seconds after it was created, when the first search has not returned anything, so rows is empty and so is the snapshot. The first batch to arrive would otherwise be twenty rows of "found since this list loaded" against an empty table, with a button to see them. An empty snapshot is not a snapshot, so it takes whatever arrives next. An effect would do the same thing one paint later, which is one paint of an empty table with a full banner over it.

useOptimistic over the derived list, not over the prop.

const [optimistic, setOptimistic] = useOptimistic(shown, (state, change: { ids: string[]; skipped: boolean }) => {
  const ids = new Set(change.ids);
  return state.map((r) => (ids.has(r.channelId) ? { ...r, skipped: change.skipped } : r));
});

Setting a creator aside is a server action. The optimistic layer sits on top of shown, so while the action is in flight the row greys out immediately, and when the action settles and the page refreshes, the optimistic state is dropped onto a list that still has the same ordering. If useOptimistic wrapped rows, the row would grey out and then jump.

Paging works the same way, without an effect:

const [page, setPage] = useState({ key: "", limit: PAGE });
const limit = page.key === fromParam ? page.limit : PAGE;

fromParam is the serialized filters. If they differ from the key the limit was raised under, the limit is PAGE again. Changing a filter resets paging to the first fifty by arithmetic rather than by a useEffect watching the filters.

What it costs

The table is deliberately stale, and the banner is the only signal. If you walk away with the tab open and come back, the list is as it was, with a count over it. We think that is the right trade for a table you work in with a pipeline running underneath, but it is a trade: there are two values for a creator's score in the client for as long as you leave the banner alone.

The other cost is that "changed" conflates two events: a new creator, and a creator whose score moved. One sentence covers both ("found or updated"), because splitting them meant a sentence with two numbers in it and nobody needs that in a notification bar.

Go and look

You cannot see this page without an account, and that is itself checkable:

$ curl -sI https://nakodo.app/campaigns | grep -iE "^HTTP|^location"
HTTP/2 307
location: /login?next=%2Fcampaigns

What is public is the explanation of what the table is showing: how Nakodo works walks through the brief, the search and the parts of the fit score, which are the score and stage columns the snapshot is holding steady. The pricing page has the row that makes the count interesting, "Creators shown per campaign: Best 20 on Free, All on the paid plans", because the free plan's hidden rows are counted by the same predicate the table filters on.

If you have a table that re-renders from the server while somebody is using it, the pattern is four lines: snapshot the fields the order depends on, render from the snapshot, count the difference, and let the person decide when to take it.
