title: Why Java Developers Use Maven (and Not javac by Hand)
description:
When I wrote my first real Java project, I had a folder of .java files, a folder of JAR files I had downloaded by hand and a very long javac command that I kept in a text file. When a teammate cloned the project, it didn't compile on their machine. Their JAR versions were different, their folders were different and the command had to be changed.

That's the problem Maven solves. You describe your project in one file, and one short command builds it the same way on every machine: it downloads the libraries, compiles the code, runs the tests and packages everything into a JAR or WAR.

In this post, we'll cover what build tools are, why we need them, how Maven works, what pom.xml is, the full archetype:generate command, Maven's terms (group id, artifact id, version, packaging), dependencies, goals, repositories and the three build lifecycles. I've drawn the important pictures in text so you can see how the pieces fit.

A note about versions: I'm using Maven 3.9.x, the stable line at the time of writing. Everything here works the same in newer versions.

Part 1: Build tools and why we need them

What is a build tool?

A build tool is a program that automates the steps between your source code and a finished, runnable application. Instead of running those steps by hand, you describe them once, and the tool repeats them exactly the same way every time.

The journey of your code

Every Java project goes through the same steps:

   source code        byte code          unit tests          package            build output
    (.java)    -->    (.class)    -->    (JUnit)     -->    (zip it up)  -->   .jar or .war
       |                  |                  |                   |
    you write          javac             check that         deployable
                       compiles          the code works     format
  • Compile: javac turns .java files into .class bytecode.
  • Test: unit tests check that your code behaves correctly.
  • Package: the .class files and resources are bundled into one file. A JAR (Java ARchive) is for libraries and normal applications. A WAR (Web ARchive) is for web applications that run on a server like Tomcat.

Doing it by hand

Without a build tool, here's what a tiny project with one library needs:

javac -cp lib/gson-2.11.0.jar -d out src/com/example/App.java
java  -cp out:lib/gson-2.11.0.jar com.example.App
jar cf app.jar -C out .

(On Windows, the classpath separator is ; instead of :.)

That's already awkward for one library and one file. Now imagine 200 files, 30 libraries, tests and three developers. The real problems are:

  • Downloading libraries by hand. You have to find each JAR, pick a version and put it in a folder.
  • Libraries need other libraries. Library A needs B, which needs C. You'd have to find all of them yourself.
  • Version clashes. Two libraries need different versions of the same one. This is nicknamed "JAR hell."
  • "Works on my machine." Everyone's folders and versions are slightly different.
  • Long manual steps. Compile, test and package in the right order, every time.

Dependency management

A dependency is a library your project needs. Dependency management means the tool finds, downloads and organizes those libraries for you. You just say what you need, with a name and a version, and the tool does the rest, including the libraries that your libraries need.

   WITHOUT a build tool                        WITH Maven

   you --> search the web for gson.jar         you --> write 5 lines in pom.xml
   you --> download it, copy to lib/                    |
   you --> find the jars gson needs                     v
   you --> fix the classpath by hand           Maven --> downloads gson + what it needs
   you --> repeat for every library                     and puts them on the classpath

The popular build tools

  • Ant: an early tool. You write every step yourself in build.xml. Flexible, but a lot of manual work.
  • Maven: you follow standard conventions and describe the project in pom.xml. Dependencies are built in. This is what we're learning.
  • Gradle: similar goals to Maven, but build files are written in Groovy or Kotlin code instead of XML, and it's known for fast, incremental builds.

All three are used in real projects. Maven is the most common starting point, and its ideas (repositories, coordinates, lifecycles) show up everywhere.

Part 2: What is Apache Maven?

Apache Maven is a build automation and dependency management tool, mostly used for Java. Its name comes from a word meaning "accumulator of knowledge." The key idea is the POM (Project Object Model): a file called pom.xml that describes your project.

What does Maven do?

  1. Project structure. It gives every project the same standard folder layout.
  2. Dependencies. It downloads the libraries you list, and the ones they need.
  3. Unit tests. It runs your tests (for example, with JUnit) automatically.
  4. Compile. It compiles your code with the right Java settings.
  5. Package. It builds a deployable file (JAR or WAR).

And a few more: it can install the result into your local library folder, deploy it to a shared server, and generate project reports and documentation.

How does Maven do it?

Maven works on two simple ideas:

1. Convention over configuration. If you put files in the standard places and follow the standard naming, you don't have to configure anything. Maven already knows where your code and tests are, and where to put the output.

2. Plugins do the real work. Maven itself is a small "coordinator." It reads your pom.xml, decides which steps to run in which order, and hands each step to a plugin. The compiler plugin compiles, the surefire plugin runs tests, the jar plugin builds the JAR.

Here is what happens when you type one command:

   mvn package
      |
      v
   1. Maven reads pom.xml
      |
      v
   2. Works out the lifecycle: validate -> compile -> test -> package
      |
      v
   3. For each step, runs the plugin goal attached to it
        compile  ->  compiler plugin   (javac)
        test     ->  surefire plugin   (runs JUnit tests)
        package  ->  jar plugin        (builds the .jar)
      |
      v
   4. Needs a library or plugin? Looks in the local repository,
      and downloads it from the internet if it's missing
      |
      v
   5. Puts all results in the "target" folder

Install and check

Maven needs a JDK, and the JAVA_HOME environment variable should point to it. After installing Maven, check it:

mvn -v

You'll see something like this (your numbers will differ):

Apache Maven 3.9.x
Maven home: /opt/maven
Java version: 17.0.x, vendor: ...

Look at the Java version line. Maven uses whichever JDK it finds, so make sure it's the one you intend.

The standard project structure

Every Maven project looks like this:

   my-app/
   |-- pom.xml                      <- the project description
   |-- src/
   |    |-- main/
   |    |    |-- java/              <- your application code (.java)
   |    |    +-- resources/         <- config files, images, etc.
   |    +-- test/
   |         |-- java/              <- your unit tests
   |         +-- resources/         <- files used only by tests
   +-- target/                      <- created by Maven: all build output
  • src/main is code that goes into your finished application.
  • src/test is code that only checks it. It's never packaged.
  • target is created by Maven. It holds the compiled classes, test reports and the JAR. You can delete it any time and nothing is lost.

Because everyone uses this layout, you can open any Maven project in the world and find your way around.

pom.xml

The POM (Project Object Model) is the heart of a Maven project. Here's a small but complete example:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
                             http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">

  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>my-app</artifactId>
  <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>jar</packaging>

  <name>my-app</name>

  <properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
      <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
      <version>5.11.0</version>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
        <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>3.5.0</version>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>

What each part means:

  • modelVersion: the version of the POM format. It's always 4.0.0.
  • groupId, artifactId, version: the project's identity (we'll explain them in a moment).
  • packaging: what kind of file to build (jar is the default).
  • name: a friendly name for humans.
  • properties: settings and variables. maven.compiler.release is the Java version to compile for (set it to your JDK version, like 17 or 21), and the encoding avoids platform surprises.
  • dependencies: the libraries you need.
  • build / plugins: extra configuration for the build. Here we pin the test plugin version, which also makes sure JUnit 5 tests are found. Pinning plugin versions makes builds repeatable.

Behind the scenes: your POM is tiny

Your pom.xml looks short because it inherits from a hidden built-in file called the Super POM. It holds all the defaults: the folder layout, the repository address and the default plugins. Maven merges the Super POM and your POM into one effective POM. You can see the full result:

mvn help:effective-pom

It's long, but it shows you everything Maven is actually using.

Creating a project: mvn archetype:generate

You can create the folders and pom.xml by hand, but Maven can generate a ready-made project from a template. That's what archetype:generate does. Here's the full command:

mvn archetype:generate \
  -DgroupId=com.example \
  -DartifactId=my-app \
  -DarchetypeArtifactId=maven-archetype-quickstart \
  -DarchetypeVersion=1.5 \
  -DinteractiveMode=false

(On Windows Command Prompt, write it on one line without the \ characters.)

Let's break it down piece by piece:

  • mvn: runs Maven.
  • archetype:generate: this is plugin:goal. It means "use the archetype plugin and run its generate goal."
  • -D: sets a property. Each option is written as -Dname=value.
  • -DgroupId=com.example: the group id of your new project (usually your reversed domain or company).
  • -DartifactId=my-app: the name of your project. Maven also creates a folder with this name.
  • -DarchetypeArtifactId=maven-archetype-quickstart: which template to use. The quickstart template makes a simple Java project with a sample class and a sample test.
  • -DarchetypeVersion=1.5: the version of that template. Version 1.5 generates a project that uses JUnit 5. (If your Maven can't find it, remove this option, and Maven will pick a version for you.)
  • -DinteractiveMode=false: don't ask questions. Without it, Maven asks you for the template version, the package name and a final confirmation.

Two extra options you may see:

  • -Dversion=1.0-SNAPSHOT: the starting version (this is already the default).
  • -Dpackage=com.example.app: the Java package for the sample classes. If you skip it, it defaults to the group id.

The first run downloads the archetype and some plugins from the internet, so it takes a little while. When it finishes, you'll see BUILD SUCCESS, and this project:

   my-app/
   |-- pom.xml
   +-- src/
        |-- main/java/com/example/App.java
        +-- test/java/com/example/AppTest.java

The generated App.java is a simple "Hello World" with a main method. Open the generated pom.xml and check the Java version property. If it's older than your JDK, change maven.compiler.release to your Java version (for example 17 or 21).

Maven terminology

Archetype

An archetype is a project template. It's a pattern for creating new projects, like a "starter kit." Besides maven-archetype-quickstart, there are archetypes for web applications and more.

Maven coordinates: groupId, artifactId, version

Every project and library in the Maven world is identified by three values, called its coordinates (or GAV):

  • groupId: who it belongs to. Usually a reversed domain, like Java packages: com.example, org.junit.jupiter.
  • artifactId: the name of the project or library: my-app, gson.
  • version: which version: 1.0-SNAPSHOT, 2.11.0.

Together they point to exactly one thing, anywhere in the world:

   com.google.code.gson : gson : 2.11.0
        groupId          artifactId   version

The coordinates also decide where the file lives in a repository, which is just a folder path:

   com.example : my-app : 1.0-SNAPSHOT
         |
         v   dots in groupId become folders
   com/example/my-app/1.0-SNAPSHOT/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

Version: SNAPSHOT vs release

  • A version that ends in -SNAPSHOT (like 1.0-SNAPSHOT) means work in progress. It can change as you keep developing. Maven treats it as "may have a newer build," and can check for updates.
  • A version without -SNAPSHOT (like 1.0.0) is a release. It's a fixed, finished version. Once a release is published to a public repository such as Maven Central, it can never be changed or replaced.

A typical life of a version: 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT while you build it, then you publish 1.0.0 (the release), then you start 1.1.0-SNAPSHOT for the next work. A good tip is to follow a clear numbering scheme, such as major.minor.patch.

Packaging type

packaging tells Maven what to build from your project. It also decides which plugin goals run at each step of the lifecycle.

  • jar (the default): a library or a normal application.
  • war: a web application for a server like Tomcat.
  • pom: no code of its own. Used for parent projects that group other projects.
  • ear: an enterprise application (less common today).

Maven dependencies

A dependency is declared with its coordinates:

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.google.code.gson</groupId>
    <artifactId>gson</artifactId>
    <version>2.11.0</version>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
</xml>

Save the file, and Maven downloads the library the next time you build. Now you can use it in your code right away:

import com.google.gson.Gson;
import java.util.Map;

public class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Gson gson = new Gson();
        System.out.println(gson.toJson(Map.of("name", "Asha")));
    }
}

Output:

{"name":"Asha"}

No JAR downloads and no classpath editing.

Scope: when is the dependency needed?

The <scope> tag says when a library is needed:

  • compile (default): needed to compile and run. It's packaged with your app.
  • test: only for compiling and running tests, like JUnit. Not packaged.
  • provided: needed to compile, but the server provides it when running (for example, the servlet API on Tomcat). Not packaged.
  • runtime: not needed to compile, but needed when running (for example, a database driver).

Using the right scope keeps your final package small and clean.

Transitive dependencies

Libraries often depend on other libraries. If you add library A, and A needs B, Maven fetches B too. These are called transitive dependencies. You can see the whole tree:

mvn dependency:tree

[INFO] com.example:my-app:jar:1.0-SNAPSHOT
[INFO] +- com.google.code.gson:gson:jar:2.11.0:compile
[INFO] \- org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:jar:5.11.0:test
[INFO]    +- org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter-api:jar:5.11.0:test
[INFO]    ...

(The list is trimmed here. Maven also shows the libraries that each one needs, indented underneath.)

What if two libraries need different versions of the same third library? Maven uses a simple rule: the version nearest to your project wins. If they're equally near, the first one declared wins.

   my-app
     |-- lib-a 1.0
     |      +-- lib-b 2.0      (two steps away)
     +-- lib-c 1.0
            +-- lib-b 1.5      (two steps away: a tie, so the first one, 2.0, wins)

   To take control, declare lib-b yourself in your pom.xml. A direct dependency is nearest.

Maven goals and phases

Here's an important distinction:

  • A goal is one specific task done by a plugin. It's written as plugin:goal, like compiler:compile or surefire:test.
  • A phase is a named step in a lifecycle, like compile or test. Each phase has goals attached to it.

When you run a phase, Maven runs every earlier phase first, then the goals attached to that one. You can also run a goal directly, like mvn archetype:generate.

The commands you'll use most:

  • mvn clean: deletes the target folder, so you start fresh.
  • mvn compile: compiles the main code.
  • mvn test: compiles, then runs the unit tests.
  • mvn package: runs the tests, then builds the JAR (or WAR).
  • mvn install: packages, then copies the result into your local repository, so other projects on your machine can use it.
  • mvn deploy: uploads the package to a remote repository for others to use.

Here is what a run looks like. This is a trimmed mvn package:

[INFO] --- resources:3.x:resources (default-resources) @ my-app ---
[INFO] --- compiler:3.x:compile (default-compile) @ my-app ---
[INFO] Compiling 1 source file with javac [debug release 17] to target/classes
[INFO] --- surefire:3.5.0:test (default-test) @ my-app ---
[INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] --- jar:3.x:jar (default-jar) @ my-app ---
[INFO] Building jar: /.../my-app/target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

(Version numbers on your screen will differ.) Each --- plugin:version:goal --- line is one goal running. You can see Maven working through the lifecycle: resources, compile, test, jar.

Testing with JUnit

Let's write a real class and test. Create src/main/java/com/example/Calculator.java:

package com.example;

public class Calculator {
    public int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

And the test, src/test/java/com/example/CalculatorTest.java:

package com.example;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class CalculatorTest {
    @Test
    void addsTwoNumbers() {
        assertEquals(5, new Calculator().add(2, 3));
    }
}

mvn test

[INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

Now break the test on purpose, by changing 5 to 6, and run mvn package:

[ERROR] Tests run: 1, Failures: 1, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD FAILURE

Look what didn't happen: no JAR was created. The test phase failed, so Maven stopped before the package phase. That's the value of the lifecycle: broken code can't become a package by accident.

Maven's test plugin finds tests by name. By default it looks for classes named *Test, Test*, *Tests or *TestCase, in src/test/java.

Running your JAR

After mvn package, your JAR is in target/. If you try to run it like a normal application:

java -jar target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

no main manifest attribute, in target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar

The JAR doesn't say which class has main. You can run it by naming the class:

java -cp target/my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar com.example.App

Or make the JAR runnable by telling the jar plugin about your main class, in pom.xml:

<build>
  <plugins>
    <plugin>
      <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
      <artifactId>maven-jar-plugin</artifactId>
      <version>3.4.2</version>
      <configuration>
        <archive>
          <manifest>
            <mainClass>com.example.App</mainClass>
          </manifest>
        </archive>
      </configuration>
    </plugin>
  </plugins>
</build>

(If your app uses outside libraries, you'd need another plugin, such as the shade or assembly plugin, to bundle them into one "fat" JAR.)

Maven repositories

A repository is a storage place for libraries and plugins, organized by their coordinates. Maven uses three kinds:

  • Local repository: a folder on your own computer, by default ~/.m2/repository. It's a cache of everything you've downloaded, plus anything you install.
  • Central repository: Maven Central, the huge public repository on the internet. It's where most open-source libraries live, and Maven uses it by default.
  • Remote repository: any other server. Companies often run their own (with tools such as Nexus or Artifactory) for private libraries, and to cache Central.

When Maven needs a library, it follows this search:

   Need gson 2.11.0
        |
        v
   1. Local repository  (~/.m2/repository)  --- found? ---> use it (no internet needed)
        | not found
        v
   2. Remote repositories you configured (company server)  --- found? ---+
        | not found                                                      |
        v                                                                v
   3. Maven Central (internet)  --- found? ---> download ---------> save a copy in
                                                                      the local repository

Because of that last step, each library is downloaded only once. Later builds use the local copy, and you can even work offline with mvn -o.

How the lifecycle phases connect to repositories:

  • install copies your JAR into the local repository.
  • deploy uploads it to a remote repository (you must configure the server address and your login).

You can configure repositories, mirrors and passwords in a settings.xml file in your .m2 folder.

The Maven build lifecycle

A build lifecycle is a fixed sequence of phases. Maven has three built-in lifecycles: default, clean and site.

1. The default lifecycle (building your project)

These are the main phases, in order:

   validate --> compile --> test --> package --> verify --> install --> deploy
  • validate: checks that the project is correct and the needed information is there.
  • compile: compiles the source code in src/main/java.
  • test: runs unit tests, using the compiled code. The tests don't need to be packaged.
  • package: bundles the compiled code into the packaging type (JAR, WAR).
  • verify: runs any extra checks on the package, like integration tests and quality rules.
  • install: copies the package into the local repository.
  • deploy: copies the final package to a remote repository for sharing.

(The real lifecycle has more phases in between, such as generate-sources, process-resources and test-compile. The ones above are the ones you'll use directly.)

The key rule: when you run a phase, Maven runs all the phases before it, in order.

   mvn compile   runs:  validate, compile
   mvn test      runs:  validate, compile, test
   mvn package   runs:  validate, compile, test, package
   mvn install   runs:  validate, compile, test, package, verify, install

You never need to run mvn compile and then mvn test separately. Just run the last phase you want.

What runs in each phase?

Each phase has plugin goals attached, and which ones depend on your packaging type. For a normal jar project:

   PHASE        GOAL THAT RUNS               WHAT IT DOES
   compile      compiler:compile             javac on src/main/java
   test         surefire:test                runs the unit tests
   package      jar:jar                      builds the .jar
   install      install:install              copies it to ~/.m2
   deploy       deploy:deploy                uploads to a remote repository

   For packaging "war":   package runs  war:war  instead of  jar:jar

This answers the question "how does Maven know what to do?" The packaging type chooses which goals are attached to which phases. That's why <packaging> matters.

2. The clean lifecycle

This one cleans up. It has three phases: pre-clean, clean and post-clean. In practice you use only clean, which deletes the target folder.

mvn clean

It's the way to get rid of old compiled files, so nothing stale is left behind. You'll often combine it with the default lifecycle:

mvn clean package

Maven runs clean (the clean lifecycle) first, then the default lifecycle up to package.

3. The site lifecycle

This one creates project documentation and reports. Its phases are pre-site, site, post-site and site-deploy.

mvn site

It generates a website describing your project (test reports, dependency lists, and so on) in target/site. It's optional, and less common in day-to-day work than the other two.

What's inside target/ after a build? 

   target/
   |-- classes/                      <- compiled main code (.class)
   |-- test-classes/                 <- compiled test code
   |-- surefire-reports/             <- test result reports
   +-- my-app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar       <- the packaged result

A few tips and commands

  • Skip tests when you must (for example, to package quickly): mvn package -DskipTests. This still compiles the tests. -Dmaven.test.skip=true skips compiling them too. Don't make this a habit, since tests are your safety net.
  • Run one test class: mvn test -Dtest=CalculatorTest
  • Force re-download of snapshots and failed items: mvn package -U
  • Work offline: mvn -o package
  • See the dependency tree: mvn dependency:tree
  • See the full merged POM: mvn help:effective-pom

Which one should I use?

  • mvn package, verify or install? Use package to build the JAR. Use verify when you also want the extra checks. Use install when another project on your machine needs this one as a dependency.
  • mvn clean package or just package? Use clean when you want a guaranteed fresh build, for example after renaming or deleting files, so old .class files don't linger.
  • JAR or WAR? A JAR for libraries and normal applications. A WAR for web apps that go on a server like Tomcat. (Frameworks such as Spring Boot also build runnable JARs with an embedded server.)
  • SNAPSHOT or release? Use -SNAPSHOT while developing. Publish a release version when something is finished and tagged, because releases never change.
  • Which scope? test for testing libraries, provided for things the server gives you, runtime for things only needed when running, and compile for everything else.
  • Archetype or generator website? For plain Java, an archetype is great. For Spring Boot projects, most people use the Spring Initializr website, which creates a ready Maven project.
  • Maven or Gradle? Both work well. Maven is more standard and predictable. Gradle is more flexible and often faster on big builds. Learning Maven first gives you the concepts that both share.

Common mistakes

  1. JAVA_HOME or Java version problems. If mvn -v shows the wrong Java, or fails, fix JAVA_HOME. Also set maven.compiler.release in pom.xml to match your JDK.
  2. Running java -jar on a JAR with no main class. You get "no main manifest attribute." Set the main class in the jar plugin, or run it with -cp and the class name.
  3. Wrong folders or test names. Code outside src/main/java, or tests outside src/test/java or not named like *Test, are silently ignored. "No tests to run" usually means this.
  4. Skipping tests all the time. -DskipTests hides real problems. Use it rarely.
  5. Version surprises. Using SNAPSHOT dependencies in something you release, or two libraries needing different versions of a third. Check with mvn dependency:tree, and declare the version you want directly.
  6. Stale or broken builds. Old classes in target/ or a half-downloaded file in ~/.m2 can cause strange errors. Run mvn clean, and use -U to force a fresh download.

Quick recap

  • A build tool automates compile, test, package and dependency handling, so builds are repeatable on every machine.
  • Dependency management means you declare what you need, and the tool downloads it, including what your libraries need.
  • The code journey: .java → .class → unit tests → package → .jar / .war.
  • Maven follows convention over configuration. It reads pom.xml, runs the lifecycle, and uses plugins to do each step.
  • The standard layout: src/main/java, src/main/resources, src/test/java, and output in target/.
  • pom.xml holds the project's identity (groupId, artifactId, version, packaging), properties, dependencies and plugins. It inherits defaults from the Super POM.
  • mvn archetype:generate creates a project from a template. -D options set properties.
  • Coordinates (groupId:artifactId:version) identify anything uniquely. -SNAPSHOT means in development, and a release never changes.
  • Packaging (jar, war, pom) decides what is built.
  • Goals are plugin tasks (plugin:goal). Phases are lifecycle steps. Running a phase runs all earlier ones.
  • Repositories: local (~/.m2), central (Maven Central) and remote (company servers). install goes to local, deploy goes to remote.
  • Lifecycles: default (validate → compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy), clean (deletes target) and site (generates documentation).

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: generate a project with the archetype:generate command from this post. Add the Calculator class and CalculatorTest, run mvn test, and then break the test on purpose and run mvn package to see that no JAR gets built. Fix it, run mvn clean package, and find your JAR in target/. Finally, run mvn dependency:tree and mvn help:effective-pom and see how much Maven was doing for you.

For a bonus experiment, add the Gson dependency, print some JSON from your App, and then look inside ~/.m2/repository/com/google/code/gson to see the exact folder path your coordinates turned into.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Implementing Distributed Tracing in Go with OpenTelemetry
description:
When a request fails in a distributed system, you end up grepping through five different log files across five services trying to figure out what happened. Logs tell you what, but not where — which service added 800ms of latency, or where an error actually originated across the call chain. Distributed tracing solves this by recording the full lifecycle of a request across service boundaries, and OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for doing it without locking into a specific backend.

What OpenTelemetry Is (and What It Isn't)

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is not a backend — it's an instrumentation framework. It standardizes how you collect traces, metrics, and logs, and ships with:

  • An API — the interface your code calls
  • An SDK — the implementation (samplers, exporters, propagators)
  • A Collector — optional intermediary that receives, processes, and routes telemetry
  • Exporters — Jaeger, Zipkin, Datadog, Grafana Tempo, and others

You instrument your code once against the OTel API. You can route data to any backend by swapping the exporter. The instrumentation stays the same.

Initializing the Tracer Provider

Install the necessary packages:

go get go.opentelemetry.io/otel
go get go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace
go get go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracegrpc
go get go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/instrumentation/net/http/otelhttp

Then initialize the tracer at startup:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "log"

    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracegrpc"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/resource"
    sdktrace "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace"
    semconv "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.21.0"
    "google.golang.org/grpc"
)

func initTracer(ctx context.Context) (func(context.Context) error, error) {
    exporter, err := otlptracegrpc.New(ctx,
        otlptracegrpc.WithEndpoint("localhost:4317"),
        otlptracegrpc.WithInsecure(),
        otlptracegrpc.WithDialOption(grpc.WithBlock()),
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    res, err := resource.New(ctx,
        resource.WithAttributes(
            semconv.ServiceName("order-service"),
            semconv.ServiceVersion("1.2.0"),
        ),
    )
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }

    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
        sdktrace.WithBatcher(exporter),
        sdktrace.WithResource(res),
        sdktrace.WithSampler(
            sdktrace.ParentBased(sdktrace.TraceIDRatioBased(0.1)),
        ),
    )
    otel.SetTracerProvider(tp)
    return tp.Shutdown, nil
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    shutdown, err := initTracer(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer shutdown(ctx)

    // start your HTTP server here
}

A few details worth noting:

  • WithBatcher is what you want in production — it buffers spans and sends them in batches rather than flushing on every span end
  • WithInsecure() is fine when the Collector runs on the same host; use TLS everywhere else
  • The resource is metadata attached to every span emitted by this service — service name and version at minimum

Instrumenting Business Logic

The OTel API follows a simple pattern: create a tracer once per package, call Start to open a span, and End it when the operation is done.

package handler

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"

    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/codes"
)

var tracer = otel.Tracer("github.com/yourorg/order-service/handler")

func ProcessOrder(ctx context.Context, orderID string) error {
    ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "ProcessOrder")
    defer span.End()

    span.SetAttributes(
        attribute.String("order.id", orderID),
        attribute.String("order.region", "eu-west-1"),
    )

    if err := validateOrder(ctx, orderID); err != nil {
        span.RecordError(err)
        span.SetStatus(codes.Error, "order validation failed")
        return fmt.Errorf("validate: %w", err)
    }

    span.AddEvent("order validated")

    if err := chargePayment(ctx, orderID); err != nil {
        span.RecordError(err)
        span.SetStatus(codes.Error, "payment failed")
        return fmt.Errorf("charge: %w", err)
    }

    span.SetStatus(codes.Ok, "")
    return nil
}

func validateOrder(ctx context.Context, orderID string) error {
    _, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "validateOrder")
    defer span.End()
    // validation logic
    return nil
}

func chargePayment(ctx context.Context, orderID string) error {
    _, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "chargePayment")
    defer span.End()
    // payment logic
    return nil
}

The critical discipline: pass ctx down through every function call. OpenTelemetry stores the active span in the context. Drop the context and child spans lose their parent — you end up with disconnected orphan spans instead of a coherent tree.

HTTP Middleware and Outbound Calls

For HTTP servers, the contrib package handles span creation automatically per request:

import (
    "net/http"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/contrib/instrumentation/net/http/otelhttp"
)

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("/orders", ordersHandler)

    handler := otelhttp.NewHandler(mux, "http-server",
        otelhttp.WithMessageEvents(otelhttp.ReadEvents, otelhttp.WriteEvents),
    )
    http.ListenAndServe(":8080", handler)
}

This creates a span per request, attaches standard HTTP attributes (method, route, status code), and — crucially — extracts incoming trace context from headers. If an upstream service already started a trace, your service joins that trace rather than starting a new one. That's what makes cross-service tracing work.

For outbound calls, wrap the HTTP client transport:

client := &http.Client{
    Transport: otelhttp.NewTransport(http.DefaultTransport),
}
resp, err := client.Get("https://inventory-service/items/42")

The transport injects the current trace context into the outgoing traceparent header automatically.

Sampling Strategy

Recording every span in a high-traffic service is expensive. The options in order of practical usefulness:

AlwaysSample — every request is traced. Fine for development or low-traffic services. Not for production at scale.

TraceIDRatioBased(0.05) — traces 5% of requests. Inexpensive, but you can miss rare events.

ParentBased(TraceIDRatioBased(0.1)) — respects the sampling decision of the upstream service. If the caller sampled this trace, you continue it. If not, you don't start one. This is the correct default for production: it keeps traces coherent across service boundaries without every service independently deciding whether to sample.

One real-world wrinkle: you want to always trace errored requests regardless of the base sample rate. The OpenTelemetry Collector supports this with its tailsampling processor, which can override the head-based decision after a trace completes. This is more complex to operate but gives you both cost efficiency and full fidelity on failures.

One operational note: span attributes can easily capture sensitive data — JWT fragments, query parameters, internal IDs. Before deploying to production, check what your instrumentation is recording. A security hardening checklist for your environment is a practical starting point for what to review.

The Takeaway

Distributed tracing in Go with OpenTelemetry breaks down to four steps: initialize a TracerProvider with a batching exporter, propagate ctx everywhere, use contrib middleware for protocol-level spans (HTTP, gRPC, database drivers), and configure ParentBased sampling for production.

The diagnostic value comes from the attributes and events you attach to spans — not just the default fields. span.SetAttributes(attribute.String("order.id", id)) is what turns "payment service returned an error" into "payment failed on order #4521 in eu-west-1 at 14:03:22." That's the difference between tracing and useful tracing.

title: Go vs Python for High-Throughput LLM Proxies: Benchmarking Both
description:
TL;DR

  • In sustained 5,000 requests-per-second benchmarks, Go-based proxies introduce as little as 11 microseconds of processing overhead per request, whereas Python proxies typically add between 500 microseconds and several milliseconds.
  • Python proxies running on asyncio and Uvicorn encounter severe event loop latency and memory bloat under heavy server-sent events (SSE) streaming concurrency due to Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) contention and per-coroutine object allocations.
  • Bifrost, an open-source AI gateway written in Go, sustained 9.5 times higher throughput and 54 times lower tail latency (p99) than Python-based LiteLLM on identical hardware under saturated load.
  • While Python remains the standard for machine learning prototyping and model training, Go provides the concurrency primitives, memory efficiency, and predictable garbage collection necessary for production AI infrastructure.

Production AI systems routing thousands of requests per second often discover that the proxy sitting between client applications and upstream model providers introduces more latency instability than the models themselves. As teams scale autonomous agents, multi-tenant software platforms, and high-frequency inference pipelines, the programming language chosen for the intermediary routing layer dictates operating costs, tail latencies, and service reliability. Bifrost, a high-performance open-source AI gateway written in Go by Maxim AI, and LiteLLM, a popular Python-based proxy server, represent two divergent architectural philosophies for solving this problem. This analysis examines head-to-head benchmark results across both runtimes, evaluating how Go and Python handle concurrent connection spikes, streaming token delivery, and resource utilization.

Why Runtime Architecture Dictates LLM Proxy Performance

A high-throughput LLM proxy operates primarily as an intelligent network router that intercepts HTTP/2 requests, parses JSON payloads, enforces rate limits, evaluates caching layers, and streams server-sent events across long-lived TCP sockets. Unlike typical REST microservices that complete requests in 10 to 50 milliseconds, an LLM gateway holds open connections for seconds or minutes while upstream providers generate output tokens.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                          Client Application                             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                          HTTP POST /v1/chat/completions
                                     v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        High-Throughput LLM Proxy                        |
|                                                                         |
|  [Authentication & Virtual Keys] -> [Semantic Cache Lookup]             |
|  [Rate Limiting & Routing Rules] -> [Provider Selection & Failover]     |
|                                                                         |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
|  | Concurrency Engine: Goroutines (Go) vs Asyncio Event Loop (Python) |  |
|  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                          Upstream Inference Call
                                     v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|             Upstream Providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock)             |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+

When handling ten concurrent requests, the performance difference between Go and Python is negligible because upstream inference latency dominates total turnaround time. However, when traffic scales to thousands of concurrent requests across hundreds of internal teams, the runtime characteristics of the proxy become the primary bottleneck.

Under heavy concurrency, Python proxies must navigate the constraints of the CPython runtime, specifically the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) and single-threaded cooperative multitasking. Go, by contrast, compiles directly to native machine code and schedules lightweight execution units across all available CPU cores using an internal runtime scheduler. When a gateway must parse thousands of streaming chunks per second while simultaneously evaluating authentication keys and tracking token quotas, these architectural differences compound into measurable latency penalties.

Concurrency Models: Goroutines vs Python Asyncio

Go uses goroutines, which are user-space execution threads managed by the Go runtime rather than the host operating system. A newly allocated goroutine requires approximately 2 kilobytes of memory stack space, allowing a single binary to comfortably manage hundreds of thousands of concurrent routines simultaneously. The Go runtime scheduler uses an M:N model, mapping M goroutines onto N operating system threads distributed across available CPU hardware cores. When a goroutine initiates network input or output, the Go netpoller parks the goroutine and assigns the operating system thread to other active workloads without blocking.

// Representative Go gateway worker pattern
func handleRequest(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    ctx := r.Context()

    // Non-blocking routing and authentication
    targetProvider, err := router.SelectProvider(ctx, r.Header.Get("Authorization"))
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusTooManyRequests)
        return
    }

    // Forward request upstream using Go's optimized transport pool
    resp, err := targetProvider.RoundTrip(r)
    if err != nil {
        fallbackProvider.ExecuteFallback(w, r)
        return
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    // Stream chunks directly with minimal buffer allocation
    io.Copy(w, resp.Body)
}

Python web proxies depend on the asyncio framework and asynchronous server gateway interface (ASGI) web servers such as Uvicorn or Hypercorn. Python concurrency uses cooperative multitasking executed on a single system thread. The event loop maintains a queue of coroutines and advances each task whenever an await expression yields control during an I/O operation.

# Representative Python asyncio proxy handler
@app.post("/v1/chat/completions")
async def handle_request(request: Request):
    headers = dict(request.headers)
    body = await request.json()

    # Validation and routing logic execute on the event loop
    provider = await router.select_provider(headers.get("authorization"))

    # Upstream call yields execution back to the loop
    async def stream_generator():
        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            async with client.stream("POST", provider.url, json=body) as response:
                async for chunk in response.aiter_bytes():
                    yield chunk

    return StreamingResponse(stream_generator(), media_type="text/event-stream")

The fundamental limitation of Python's model in an LLM gateway is that coroutines yield control only at explicit I/O pause points. Any CPU-intensive operation performed by the gateway, such as JSON serialization, regular expression evaluation, cryptographic signature verification, or token counting, executes synchronously on the event loop thread. If parsing a large JSON payload takes 2 milliseconds of pure CPU execution, every other connection waiting in the event loop is stalled for those 2 milliseconds. Under sustained high throughput, these brief computational pauses cause task queue backups, resulting in connection timeouts and escalating tail latency.

Benchmark Methodology and Test Environment

To measure the real-world overhead introduced by each runtime architecture, benchmarks were structured to isolate proxy processing latency from external cloud variability. External model endpoints introduce jitter, rate limits, and network volatility that skew measurements. Consequently, the test topology substituted upstream providers with a deterministic mock server that replied with consistent token payloads and configurable delays.

The evaluation compared Bifrost, compiled with Go 1.24, against LiteLLM running on Python 3.12 with Uvicorn workers and uvloop enabled. Both proxies were deployed on dedicated AWS EC2 instances running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS within a private virtual private cloud (VPC). Benchmarks were executed across two separate compute profiles:

  1. t3.medium instance: 2 virtual CPUs, 4 gigabytes of memory, baseline network burst performance.
  2. t3.xlarge instance: 4 virtual CPUs, 16 gigabytes of memory, up to 5 Gbps network bandwidth.

Traffic generation was handled by distributed k6 client instances deployed on separate EC2 nodes within the same availability zone to minimize network transit variance. The load profile simulated real-world enterprise traffic patterns, ramping from 500 requests per second (RPS) to a sustained 5,000 RPS. Each request submitted an OpenAI-compatible payload requesting a streaming chat completion, with the mock backend returning a 10-chunk response simulating a total inference duration of 1.5 seconds.

Latency and Throughput Under Sustained Load

The performance metrics collected during sustained load testing highlight a significant divergence between compiled Go infrastructure and interpreted Python services. When traffic was applied at 5,000 requests per second, the gateway overhead, defined as the time added by the proxy exclusive of backend response time, was measured alongside tail latency and error rates.

Performance Metric LiteLLM (Python, t3.medium) Bifrost (Go, t3.medium) LiteLLM (Python, t3.xlarge) Bifrost (Go, t3.xlarge)
Max Sustained RPS 44.8 RPS 424.0 RPS 480.0 RPS 5,000.0 RPS
Success Rate @ Target Load 71.4% (degraded) 100.0% 88.2% (degraded) 100.0%
Gateway Added Overhead (Mean) ~500 µs to 7.5 ms 59 µs ~350 µs to 3.2 ms 11 µs
P90 Latency (Overall) 14.20 s 1.62 s 3.85 s 1.58 s
P99 Latency (Overall) 90.72 s 1.68 s 18.40 s 1.61 s
Average Queue Wait Time 820.00 ms 47.13 µs 145.00 ms 1.67 µs
Peak Resident Memory 372 MB 120 MB 1,480 MB 3,340 MB (configured pool)

On the t3.medium configuration under saturated load, the Python proxy experienced significant event loop contention. As incoming connection rates outpaced the event loop's ability to dispatch coroutines, the request queue backed up, causing the overall p99 latency to climb to 90.72 seconds before connections dropped with HTTP 504 gateway timeout errors. Bifrost on the same t3.medium hardware maintained a 100% success rate, preserving a p99 latency of 1.68 seconds (representing 1.5 seconds of simulated model generation plus only 180 milliseconds of total queueing and transport latency).

On the larger t3.xlarge system, Bifrost scaled smoothly to 5,000 requests per second. At this operating volume, published benchmarks document that Bifrost added only 11 microseconds of internal routing overhead per request. The average queue wait time dropped to 1.67 microseconds, while JSON marshaling took 26.80 microseconds. By contrast, the Python proxy on t3.xlarge hit an architectural throughput wall near 480 requests per second, requiring horizontal pod autoscaling across multiple container replicas to handle equivalent load.

Memory Footprint and Garbage Collection in Streaming Pipelines

In an LLM proxy, memory consumption is largely governed by how the runtime handles streaming response buffers. Server-sent events require the proxy to receive small string fragments from upstream providers, inspect or log them, and flush them immediately to downstream HTTP clients.

Python's memory management introduces high overhead during streaming operations. In CPython, every string fragment, dictionary, and HTTP chunk is allocated on the heap as a complete PyObject. A single 20-character text token wrapped in an SSE data frame generates multiple object allocations, each carrying internal reference counts and type descriptors. Furthermore, Python's memory allocator rarely releases heap memory back to the host operating system immediately; instead, it retains allocated arenas for future Python objects. Under thousands of concurrent streams, memory consumption climbs steadily, increasing pressure on the generational garbage collector. When cyclic garbage collection cycles trigger, they momentarily pause the interpreter thread, compounding event loop delays.

Go Runtime Memory Pipeline:
[Incoming Socket] ---> [Pre-allocated Buffer Pool] ---> [Zero-Copy Parser] ---> [Client Socket]
                                  ^                            |
                                  +----- sync.Pool Reuse ------+

Python Runtime Memory Pipeline:
[Incoming Socket] ---> [C-String] ---> [PyUnicode Object] ---> [PyDict Chunk] ---> [GC Tracked Heap]

Go manages streaming pipelines with significantly higher memory efficiency. The Go standard library and production frameworks allow developers to use memory pools (sync.Pool) to recycle byte buffers across independent requests. Rather than allocating new objects for incoming response chunks, Go reuses fixed-size byte slices, completely bypassing dynamic heap allocation for the steady-state data path.

As detailed in the Bifrost benchmarking documentation, Bifrost allows operators to configure explicit buffer and worker pool sizes to balance memory limits against maximum throughput. While Bifrost used 3,340 megabytes of memory on t3.xlarge during the 5,000 RPS benchmark, that allocation consisted of pre-allocated buffers specifically sized to handle 20,000 queued requests with zero runtime allocations. Under baseline operational conditions on t3.medium, its memory footprint remained at a compact 120 megabytes.

CPU Efficiency, Connection Pooling, and Worker Contention

Efficient network proxying requires extracting maximum throughput from every available CPU cycle. In multi-core server environments, Go and Python take opposing paths to hardware utilization.

Because CPython enforces the GIL, running a Python proxy across a multi-core machine requires spinning up multiple independent worker processes using process managers like Gunicorn. For example, a 4-vCPU instance typically runs 4 to 8 separate worker processes. While this strategy bypasses the GIL across processes, it introduces operational drawbacks:

  • Isolated Connection Pools: Each Python worker maintains its own distinct pool of HTTP/2 connections to upstream providers. Ten workers querying OpenAI cannot share keep-alive connections, resulting in duplicate TCP handshakes, redundant TLS negotiations, and higher connection overhead.
  • Process Memory Duplication: Each worker process loads its own copy of the Python interpreter, imported libraries, routing tables, and in-memory caches, multiplying baseline memory overhead.
  • Inter-Process State Synchronization: Tracking shared state across workers, such as global rate limits, virtual key quotas, or circuit breakers, requires an external caching layer like Redis. Accessing an external Redis store over local sockets introduces additional network round-trips for every incoming request. 
Multi-Process Python Model (Gunicorn / Uvicorn):
[Worker 1 (PID 101)] ---> [Isolated HTTP Pool] ---> Upstream Provider
[Worker 2 (PID 102)] ---> [Isolated HTTP Pool] ---> Upstream Provider
[Worker 3 (PID 103)] ---> [Isolated HTTP Pool] ---> Upstream Provider
(State shared only via external Redis / IPC)

Single-Process Go Model (Bifrost):
[Goroutine Pool] ===> [Shared HTTP/2 Connection Pool] ===> Upstream Provider
(State shared natively in-process via atomic primitives and mutexes)

Bifrost operates as a unified, multi-threaded binary. A single Go process manages connections across all available CPU cores. All incoming requests share a centralized HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 transport pool, maximizing socket reuse and minimizing upstream handshake latency. Internal state, including token bucket rate limits and quota tallies, is tracked in-process using atomic memory primitives and low-contention synchronization constructs, eliminating mandatory dependencies on external caching instances for single-node deployments.

Extending Gateway Control to the Endpoint

As organizations scale their AI infrastructure, governance challenges extend beyond centralized server deployments into local developer environments and endpoint devices. Beyond routing, Bifrost applies governance and security controls (virtual keys, budgets, guardrails, audit logs) centrally, and Bifrost Edge extends that same governance and security to AI traffic on employee machines, with endpoint enforcement on each device.

                                  +---------------------------------------+
                                  |     Bifrost AI Gateway (Go Core)      |
                                  |  - Centralized Control Plane          |
                                  |  - Policy Engine & Audit Logs         |
                                  |  - Virtual Keys & Budgets             |
                                  +---------------------------------------+
                                                      ^
                                                      | Enforces Unified Policies
                                                      | via Local Routing Agent
                                                      v
                                  +---------------------------------------+
                                  |       Bifrost Edge (Endpoint)         |
                                  |  - Desktop Apps (Claude, ChatGPT)     |
                                  |  - Coding Agents (Cursor, CLI tools)  |
                                  |  - Local MCP Server Discovery         |
                                  +---------------------------------------+

When platform teams deploy gateways solely as centralized cloud services, ungoverned AI usage often emerges on client laptops. Developers install desktop chat clients, run terminal coding agents, and connect local tools using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) without configuring proxy base URLs. Bifrost Edge, currently in alpha, operates as a lightweight endpoint agent that transparently routes desktop and CLI traffic through the central Bifrost policy engine. This combined architecture ensures that guardrails, data loss prevention rules, and spend limits apply consistently across cloud microservices, developer terminals, and desktop interfaces.

Feature Matrix: Go vs Python in Production Infrastructure

Choosing between Go and Python for an LLM gateway involves balancing runtime raw throughput against developer ecosystem familiarity. Python excels during initial experimentation, whereas Go dominates high-scale infrastructure deployments.

Capability / Attribute Python AI Proxies (e.g., LiteLLM) Go AI Gateways (e.g., Bifrost) Engineering Impact
Primary Concurrency Primitive Single-threaded asyncio event loop Multi-threaded M:N goroutine scheduler Go eliminates head-of-line blocking on CPU-bound operations.
Execution Format Interpreted bytecode (CPython VM) Statically linked native machine binary Go binaries launch instantly and deploy with zero runtime dependencies.
Per-Request Memory Overhead High (multiple heap-allocated PyObjects) Low (stack allocations, buffer pools) Go reduces memory consumption by 60% to 80% under sustained concurrency.
Multi-Core Scaling Requires multiple Gunicorn OS worker processes Scales natively within a single OS process Go shares connection pools and internal routing state across all cores.
Streaming Pipeline Efficiency Event loop context switching on every chunk Non-blocking zero-copy socket streaming Go maintains flat p99 tail latency during token generation.
Observability Overhead Tracing middleware adds CPU cycles to event loop Native OpenTelemetry and Prometheus exporters Go exports metrics concurrently without stalling the request path.
Ecosystem Extensibility Vast library of Python AI/ML packages Systems-level performance with Go/WASM plugins Python enables faster script prototyping; Go guarantees operational stability.

For organizations evaluating infrastructure investments, the architectural choice correlates with long-term cloud hosting bills. A proxy that handles 5,000 RPS on a single 4-vCPU Go instance requires dozens of scaled Python pods behind an external load balancer to achieve comparable throughput. The LLM Gateway Buyer's Guide provides an expanded framework for evaluating gateway capacity against organizational traffic projections.

Production Capabilities: Beyond Raw Proxying

While high-throughput network proxying is essential, an enterprise gateway must execute complex policy checks on every passing request. If security and governance rules introduce substantial latency, the benefits of a compiled runtime are quickly lost.

Bifrost implements a comprehensive suite of enterprise capabilities directly within its compiled Go core:

  • Drop-in SDK Replacement: Bifrost functions as a drop-in replacement for major AI development kits. Applications migrating from direct provider APIs or Python proxies adjust only their base URL parameters without rewriting application logic.
  • Dynamic Failover and Load Balancing: When upstream providers return rate-limit errors or experience service interruptions, Bifrost executes automatic fallbacks to secondary models or healthy API keys with zero application downtime.
  • Semantic Caching: To cut redundant inference costs, Bifrost provides native semantic caching, evaluating query intent in memory before routing requests upstream.
  • Hierarchical Governance: Security teams configure virtual keys that enforce granular spend budgets, rate limits, and access permissions across projects, departments, and external clients.
  • Model Context Protocol Support: As an enterprise MCP gateway, Bifrost coordinates autonomous tool calls, exposing centralized tools to AI models while managing authentication and filtering permissions.
  • Unified Observability: Comprehensive request logs, distributed OpenTelemetry traces, and native Prometheus metrics are exposed via Bifrost's built-in observability suite without degrading gateway throughput. 
// Example: Initializing the Bifrost Go core with custom routing and fallback policies
package main

import (
    "context"
    "log"
    "github.com/maximhq/bifrost/core"
    "github.com/maximhq/bifrost/core/providers"
)

func main() {
    gateway, err := bifrost.NewGateway(&bifrost.Config{
        Port: 8080,
        RoutingStrategy: bifrost.StrategyLowestLatency,
    })
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Failed to initialize Bifrost: %v", err)
    }

    // Register multi-provider fallback chain
    gateway.RegisterRoute("production-chat", &bifrost.RouteConfig{
        Primary:   providers.AnthropicClaude35Sonnet,
        Fallbacks: []providers.Provider{providers.OpenAIGpt4o, providers.BedrockLlama3},
        TimeoutMs: 2500,
    })

    log.Println("Bifrost gateway listening on :8080")
    gateway.ListenAndServe()
}

Teams migrating from Python-based infrastructure can review specific migration strategies on the Bifrost LiteLLM alternatives page, which details configuration translation and parity benchmarks.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does an LLM proxy need low latency when LLM responses take several seconds?

An LLM proxy handles token streaming across thousands of concurrent clients. If the proxy adds several milliseconds of overhead to every incoming token chunk, streaming jitter increases, client buffers stall, and server connection queues rapidly exhaust available memory. Low gateway latency preserves application responsiveness and prevents the proxy itself from becoming a single point of failure under unexpected traffic spikes.

Can Python's asyncio performance be fixed using multiple worker processes?

Running multiple worker processes via process managers such as Gunicorn allows Python to utilize multiple CPU cores, but it does not resolve per-process event loop bottlenecks. Each worker maintains its own isolated connection pool, multiplying memory consumption and preventing unified connection reuse. Furthermore, coordinating shared state across multiple Python workers requires external caches like Redis, which introduces additional network latency to every request.

When is a Python-based LLM proxy suitable for an engineering team?

Python proxies are suitable for early-stage prototyping, internal proof-of-concept deployments, and environments where total traffic remains below a few dozen requests per second. Teams with dedicated Python platform engineers often prefer Python proxies initially because they can inspect, debug, and patch routing logic directly using familiar scripting tools without needing to compile binaries.

How does Go prevent head-of-line blocking in streaming LLM responses?

Go uses an internal scheduler that multiplexes lightweight goroutines across multiple operating system threads. When a goroutine waits for the next token chunk over a network socket, the Go runtime automatically parks that routine and executes active workloads on the freed thread. This prevents CPU-bound tasks, such as JSON parsing or cryptographic operations, from delaying network packet processing for other active client streams.

What hardware is required to run a high-throughput Go LLM gateway?

A compiled Go gateway such as Bifrost operates comfortably on modest hardware. In published benchmarks, a standard AWS EC2 t3.xlarge instance (4 vCPUs and 16 GB RAM) sustained 5,000 requests per second with only 11 microseconds of internal gateway latency. Even a smaller t3.medium instance (2 vCPUs and 4 GB RAM) reliably handles hundreds of concurrent streaming requests without connection degradation.

How does Bifrost handle upstream provider rate limits?

Bifrost manages provider rate limits through intelligent load balancing, key pooling, and automated fallback rules. When an upstream provider returns an HTTP 429 status code or encounters temporary downtime, the gateway immediately reroutes the pending request to an alternative API key, model tier, or secondary cloud provider without returning an error to the calling client application.

Choosing the Right Infrastructure Foundation

Building scalable generative AI applications requires treating the routing and governance layer as critical production infrastructure rather than an afterthought. While Python remains an exceptional language for model experimentation, data science, and pipeline orchestration, its runtime constraints create significant hurdles when deployed in high-concurrency network proxies.

Go delivers the structural advantages required for modern AI workloads: true multi-core concurrency via goroutines, minimal memory footprints through native buffer pooling, and sub-millisecond request processing. Engineering teams evaluating high-throughput AI gateways can request a Bifrost demo to explore enterprise governance capabilities or review the source code on the Bifrost GitHub repository.

Sources

  • Python Asyncio Architecture and Event Loop Specification
  • Bifrost Performance Benchmarking Suite and Methodology
  • PEP 703: Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython
