title: Every contrast failure on our site is the same Tailwind feature, and measuring it needs a canvas
description:
I ran a contrast audit over 10 public pages of our quiz app. The headline is boring in a useful way: the palette is fine, the base text colour measures 6.29:1 against the page background, and every single failure comes from one Tailwind feature used in one specific way.

Getting that answer took two attempts, because the first measurement was wrong in an interesting way.

The naive snippet lies, and it lies confidently

The usual way to script this is to read getComputedStyle(el).color, pull the numbers out with a regex, and compute relative luminance. Mine said our body copy was failing at 1.17:1, which would be invisible text, which it plainly is not.

The reason is that Tailwind v4 ships colours in modern colour spaces. The computed value of one of our text colours is:

oklab(0.682949 0.0000312328 0.0000136495 / 0.7)

A regex grabbing the first three numbers reads that as rgb(0.68, 0.00003, 0.00001), which is black, so a light grey on a dark background came out as a catastrophic failure. Every oklab and oklch value in your stylesheet will do this to a naive parser, and because it fails toward "terrible contrast" you get a report full of urgent nonsense.

The fix is to let the browser do the conversion. A canvas will accept any CSS colour string and hand you back sRGB bytes, alpha included:

const cv = document.createElement('canvas'); cv.width = cv.height = 1
const ctx = cv.getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true })

const resolve = (css) => {
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, 1, 1)
  ctx.fillStyle = css
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 1, 1)
  const d = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, 1, 1).data
  return [d[0], d[1], d[2], d[3] / 255]
}

Two more pieces and it is a real audit. Composite the text colour over its background, because a semi-transparent colour is not a colour until you know what is behind it:

const over = (fg, bg) => fg.slice(0, 3).map((c, i) => Math.round(c * fg[3] + bg[i] * (1 - fg[3])))

And walk up the ancestors to find the first opaque background, because the element's own is almost always transparent:

const bgOf = (el) => {
  let n = el
  while (n) {
    const c = resolve(getComputedStyle(n).backgroundColor)
    if (c[3] > 0.95) return c.slice(0, 3)
    n = n.parentElement
  }
  return [23, 23, 23]   // our page background
}

Then the standard luminance and ratio formulas, filtered to elements that own a non-empty text node, so you measure text and not wrappers. With that, the 1.17:1 phantoms disappeared and the real failures showed up.

What the real failures are

Across those 10 pages, every element that failed WCAG AA for normal text was styled with a Tailwind slash opacity modifier, and in every case the same colour without the modifier passes comfortably.

page class size ratio instances
a quiz questions category page text-muted-foreground/60 14px 3.08:1 60
pricing text-muted-foreground/50 14px 2.52:1 2
pricing text-muted-foreground/70 12px 3.73:1 2
a guide page text-muted-foreground/70 14px 3.73:1 1
everything else text-muted-foreground 14 to 18px 6.29:1 passes

Seven of the ten pages had zero failures. The feature grid, the venue solution pages, the comparison tables, the tools, the about page and the legal pages all pass, because they use the palette as declared.

The repository has 24 of these modifiers on text colours, at nine different strengths: /30, /40, /50, /60, /70, /80 and a few on an inverted colour. Not one of them was a considered decision about contrast. They are all the same two second thought, which is "this line should be quieter than the one above it", expressed by reaching for the nearest dial.

That is what makes this a satisfying bug class. There is no palette problem to solve, no colour to rechoose and no design review to run. The design system is correct and the failures are 24 local overrides of it.

The 60 instances are the worst of it, and the most forgivable

The page with sixty failures is a category page full of sample quiz questions, where each one carries an "Answer:" label in text-muted-foreground/60. The intent is obvious and reasonable: the label is scaffolding, the answer beside it is the content, so the label gets dimmed. At 14px and 3.08:1 the result is a word that some people simply cannot read, repeated sixty times down one page.

The honest fix is not more opacity. It is to stop using colour for that distinction: make the label smaller, or uppercase and letter-spaced, or an actual <dt>, and leave its colour at the strength the palette already picked. Dimming is the laziest of the four ways to say "this is secondary", and the only one that costs legibility.

Same story on the pricing page, where the features a plan does not include are rendered at /50 and come out at 2.52:1. Those lines are doing real work: they tell you what you are not getting. A struck-through or icon-marked list item at full contrast says it better than a faint one, and says it to everybody.

Two more findings, neither about colour

No skip link, and seven tab stops before the content. Every content page has one <main> and exactly seven focusable elements ahead of it: the header navigation and its menu trigger, plus the breadcrumb trail. Thirty-four to thirty-five focusable elements per page in total. Keyboard users therefore tab through the same seven controls on every page before reaching a single word of the article. The legal pages, which use a compact footer and a reduced header, have one. A skip link is four lines of HTML and CSS and I have no excuse.

Zero references to prefers-reduced-motion. The repository mentions it nowhere, while every public page carries a scroll-driven animation in its footer. That one is a watermark at five per cent opacity, so the practical harm is small, but a codebase with an animation runtime in it and no reduced-motion query anywhere is not making a choice, it is just not looking.

What passed, since an audit that only lists faults is not an audit

  • Exactly one <h1> per page, and across all 10 pages, zero heading level jumps. One content page runs h1, h2, h3, h3, h3, h2, h3, h3 ... for 28 headings without skipping a level.
  • Every input on the tools pages is associated with a real <label for>, four for four on the scoresheet form.
  • Decorative SVGs are aria-hidden, including the big footer watermark, so a screen reader is never told the word "PubTrivia" at the end of every page.
  • lang="en" on the root element, and focus-visible ring styles on the shared button and link components rather than an outline: none with nothing to replace it.
  • One inconsistency worth fixing: the logo image is alt="PubTrivia logo" on content pages and alt="logo" on the auth pages. Both are non-empty, neither is wrong, and they should match.

Run it on our pages, or yours

Paste the resolver plus the ratio maths into a console on any of these and sort the results:

  • pub-trivia.app/quiz-questions/music is the page with sixty hits. Search the DOM for text-muted-foreground/60 and every match is an "Answer:" label.
  • pub-trivia.app/pricing is the four-hit page, and the two worst elements are the features each plan leaves out, at 2.52:1.
  • pub-trivia.app/guides/how-to-host-a-pub-quiz has exactly one failure, the "Last reviewed" date under the title, and it is a good example of the class: a line that is genuinely minor, dimmed one notch too far.
  • pub-trivia.app/tools/scoresheet-generator is the control. Four labelled inputs, a button, no opacity modifiers, nothing below 4.5:1, and it generates a printable sheet in your browser so you can tab through the whole flow with a keyboard and see where a skip link would have helped.

If you take one thing from this: audit with the browser's own colour conversion, not a regex, and then group your failures by the CSS feature that produced them rather than by page. Ours collapsed into a single line of advice, which is that an opacity modifier on a text colour is a contrast decision wearing a styling costume.

title: microservices
description:
question
Model Microservice

This repo is intended as a starter project for anyone intending to write a new microservice. It demonstrates the following key features:
A basic gradle spring-cloud project
Integration with the service directory
Implementing a REST service with tests
Calling microservices in DWS fabric using webclient and feign.
After cloning you should, at the very least, change the following things before you import it into your IDE.
Change the package name from modelmicroservice to something more appropriate.
Edit settings.gradle and change the rootProject.name property name to your service name.
Edit src/main/resources/application.yaml and change spring.application.name to the name of your project. Review the other properties in this file.
Edit gradle.properties and review all the properties commented with TODO.
Generate a keystore for local testing. More info: Guide
This repo will never be finished. As we evolve our capability and update recommended versions this repo will change and evolve accordingly.
Auto-generated documentation

Swagger
Code Quality: SonarQube

Follow these steps to run a SonarQube instance locally to measure your code quality.
docker-compose -f src/main/docker/sonar.yml up
./gradlew sonar
Visit SonarQube Dashboard
Spring Boot 3

The model-microservice is now (Aug 2023) built against spring boot 3.

i need to understand properly what this repo is for
And what all technical knowledge should i have to use this and understand everything properly
what skills do i need to learn

gemini response
Of course. Based on the documentation you provided, here is an explanation of the "Model Microservice" repository and the skills needed to use it effectively.
What is this Repository For?
This repository serves as a starter project or template for developers who need to create a new microservice. Its primary purpose is to provide a standardized, pre-configured foundation that includes best practices and essential integrations, saving developers time and effort during the initial setup phase.
Instead of starting from an empty project, you can clone this repository and have a functional service skeleton that already demonstrates key capabilities:

Foundation: It's a project built with Gradle and the Spring Cloud framework, which are standard for building distributed systems.
Service Discovery: It includes integration with a "service directory," allowing your new service to register itself and discover other services within the network.
API Implementation: It provides a template for creating a RESTful API, complete with example tests, which is the standard way microservices communicate.
Inter-Service Communication: It shows how to call other microservices using two popular methods: WebClient (a modern, reactive web client) and Feign (a declarative web service client).
Modern Framework: The project is updated to use Spring Boot 3, ensuring it leverages the latest features and performance improvements.

In short, this repository is a blueprint that helps you bootstrap a new microservice quickly while adhering to established architectural patterns and tooling.
Technical Knowledge and Skills Required
To fully understand and effectively use this starter project, you should have a solid grasp of the following technologies and concepts. They are listed in order of importance, from foundational to specific.

  1. Foundational Skills These are the core competencies you'll need before you can work with the specifics of the repository.

Java Programming:

Description: The project is written in Java. You need strong proficiency in the language, including object-oriented principles, data structures, and core libraries. Familiarity with features from Java 17 or later is beneficial, as Spring Boot 3 requires it.
Why it's needed: To write the business logic, controllers, services, and repository layers of your microservice.

RESTful APIs:

Description: Understanding the principles of Representational State Transfer (REST). This includes concepts like resources, URIs, HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), status codes, and data formats like JSON.
Why it's needed: Microservices primarily communicate via REST APIs. You will be building and consuming them.

Microservice Architecture:

Description: A conceptual understanding of why and how applications are broken down into smaller, independent services. This includes concepts like service discovery, configuration management, fault tolerance, and API gateways.
Why it's needed: This repository is a tool for implementing this architectural style. Knowing the "big picture" helps you understand the purpose of each feature (like service directory integration).

  1. Core Frameworks & Tools These are the specific technologies used directly in the repository.

Spring Framework / Spring Boot 3:

Description: This is the most critical framework. You should understand the core concepts of Spring, such as Dependency Injection (@Autowired), Inversion of Control (IoC), and aspect-oriented programming. For Spring Boot specifically, know how it simplifies configuration with auto-configuration, starters, and the application.yaml file.
Why it's needed: The entire application is built on Spring Boot. You'll use its annotations (@RestController, @Service, etc.) and configuration mechanisms daily.

Gradle:

Description: A build automation tool used to manage project dependencies, run tests, and build the application artifact. You should understand the structure of build.gradle and settings.gradle files and how to execute common tasks like gradlew build.
Why it's needed: You need to interact with Gradle to build the project, manage its libraries, and run tasks like the SonarQube analysis.

Spring Cloud:

Description: A sub-project of Spring that provides tools for building distributed systems. The repository mentions "service directory" integration, which is a core feature of Spring Cloud (often implemented with Netflix Eureka or Spring Cloud Consul).
Why it's needed: To make your service work correctly within a larger ecosystem of microservices.

  1. Specific Skills & Tooling These are skills for specific tasks mentioned in the repository's documentation.

Web Clients (WebClient and Feign):

Description: WebClient is a non-blocking, reactive client for making HTTP requests, part of the Spring WebFlux project. Feign is a declarative client that lets you define an API client by creating a simple Java interface.
Why it's needed: Your service will likely need to communicate with other services. The repository provides examples of both, and you should understand the trade-offs between them (e.g., reactive vs. blocking, verbosity vs. simplicity).

Docker and Docker Compose:

Description: Docker is a platform for creating, deploying, and running applications in containers. Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications.
Why it's needed: The repository uses Docker Compose to run a local instance of SonarQube for code quality analysis. Basic knowledge of docker-compose up is required to follow the instructions.

API Documentation (Swagger/OpenAPI):

Description: Swagger (now known as the OpenAPI Specification) is a standard for documenting REST APIs. Tools like Springdoc-openapi can automatically generate this documentation from your code.
Why it's needed: To provide clear, interactive documentation for the API your service exposes, making it easy for other developers to understand and use.

Code Quality (SonarQube):

Description: A platform for continuous inspection of code quality to perform automatic reviews with static analysis of code to detect bugs, code smells, and security vulnerabilities.
Why it's needed: To ensure your code meets quality standards. You'll need to know how to run the analysis and interpret the results on the SonarQube dashboard.

question 2
explain with a simple example of a microservice that can be build with this starter template
how would it be different when this template was not present

gemini response
Of course. Let's walk through a simple, practical example of a microservice you could build with this template and then compare the development process with and without it.
Simple Example: A "Currency Exchange Rate" Microservice
Let's imagine you need to build a microservice called exchange-rate-service. Its sole purpose is to provide the current exchange rate between two currencies (e.g., USD to EUR).
What the Microservice Does:

Exposes a REST API Endpoint: It will have an endpoint like GET /api/v1/rates. You can query it with parameters, for example: GET /api/v1/rates?from=USD&to=EUR.
Returns a JSON Response: A successful request would return a simple JSON object:
json{
"fromCurrency": "USD",
"toCurrency": "EUR",
"rate": 0.95,
"timestamp": "2026-10-15T10:00:00Z"
}

Gets Data from Another Service: This exchange-rate-service doesn't calculate rates itself. It fetches them from a central, authoritative source, let's call it the market-data-provider service.
Registers Itself: It announces its presence on the network so other services (e.g., a trade-booking-service) can find and use it.

How You Would Build This Using the "Model Microservice" Template
Following the instructions in the repository, the process would be streamlined:

Clone and Rename:

You clone the model-microservice repository.
You perform the initial setup:

Change the package name from modelmicroservice to com.db.trading.exchangerate.
Edit settings.gradle to set rootProject.name = 'exchange-rate-service'.
Edit application.yaml to set spring.application.name: exchange-rate-service.

Result: You now have a working, buildable Spring Boot project correctly named and configured.

Define the API Endpoint:

You would create a new Java class, ExchangeRateController.java.
Using Spring's annotations (which are already in the project's dependencies), you define the endpoint. The template already has an example controller you can adapt.

java@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/rates")
public class ExchangeRateController {
// ... inject your service here

@GetMapping
public Rate getRate(@RequestParam String from, @RequestParam String to) {
    return exchangeRateService.getExchangeRate(from, to);
}

}

Call the market-data-provider Service:

The template already includes WebClient and Feign as dependencies and provides examples of how to use them.
You could create a Feign client interface to declaratively define how to call the other service. The setup is already mostly done for you.

java@FeignClient(name = "market-data-provider")
public interface MarketDataProviderClient {
@GetMapping("/data/forex")
BigDecimal getRate(@RequestParam("pair") String currencyPair);
}

Your service logic would then simply call this Java interface, and Spring Cloud would handle the underlying HTTP request, service discovery, and response parsing.

Testing and Quality:

The template includes a testing framework (JUnit 5) and example tests for REST controllers. You can follow this pattern to write your own tests quickly.
To check your code quality, you just run the provided commands: docker-compose -f src/main/docker/sonar.yml up and ./gradlew sonar. The configuration is already done.

Run the Service:

You run the main application class. Because the template includes the Spring Cloud service discovery client, your service will automatically register itself with the service directory upon startup.

Key takeaway: The template provides the scaffolding. You don't spend time on setup, configuration, or figuring out which libraries to use. You focus almost immediately on writing the business logic for your specific service.

How It Would Be Different Without the Template (Starting from Scratch)
If this starter template did not exist, you would have to perform all of the following steps manually.

Project Initialization:

Go to a tool like start.spring.io or use your IDE's project wizard.
Manually select the project type (Gradle), language (Java), and Spring Boot version.
Dilemma: Which version of Spring Boot is standard? Is it compatible with the company's internal libraries? The template pre-answers this.
Manual Dependency Selection: You would need to manually add every single dependency:

Spring Web (for REST controllers)
Spring Boot Actuator (for health checks)
Spring Cloud Starter Netflix Eureka (or a similar client for service discovery)
Spring Cloud Starter OpenFeign (for the Feign client)
Spring Boot Starter Test (for testing)
Lombok (optional, for less boilerplate code)
Springdoc OpenAPI (for Swagger documentation)

Problem: You need to know exactly which dependencies are required and ensure their versions are compatible with each other. This is a common source of errors. The template provides a tested, known-good set of dependencies.

Configuration:

Create the application.yaml file from scratch.
Manually add configuration for the server port, application name, and the address of the service directory.
Manually configure logging patterns and levels.
The template provides a well-structured application.yaml with comments and placeholders for standard properties, which you would have to look up or guess.

Implementing Inter-Service Communication:

You would need to manually configure the Feign client or WebClient. This involves adding annotations like @EnableFeignClients to your main application class and potentially creating configuration beans for things like timeouts, retries, and error handling. The template would have this already set up.

Setting up Code Quality and Documentation:

SonarQube: You would need to find the correct SonarQube Docker image, write your own docker-compose.yml file, and configure the Gradle SonarQube plugin from scratch in your build.gradle file, connecting it to the Docker container.
Swagger: You would have to add the dependency and potentially write Java configuration beans to customize the generated API documentation (e.g., adding security definitions or metadata).

Build Logic:

You would write a build.gradle file from scratch. The template's gradle.properties and build.gradle files contain standardized version management, plugin configurations, and other best practices you would otherwise have to implement yourself.

In summary, without the template, a developer would spend a significant amount of time on boilerplate setup, configuration, and dependency management. This process is error-prone and leads to inconsistencies between microservices.
The template's value is that it encapsulates all of these initial decisions and configurations into a reusable, best-practice starting point, dramatically accelerating development and promoting standardization.

question 3
what things should i learn in proper sequence so that i completely understand each step of creation of a microservice with this template, so that i may understand the things used and also maybe later able to create a new microservice like this manually by my own

gemini response
Excellent question. Building a solid understanding requires a structured approach. Learning these concepts in the right order will ensure you grasp not just how to use the template, but why it is designed the way it is. This will empower you to use it effectively and eventually build a similar service from scratch.
Here is a recommended, sequential learning path, broken down into logical phases.

Phase 1: The Bedrock - Core Programming and Concepts
Start here. Without these fundamentals, the frameworks and tools in the later phases will be difficult to comprehend.

Java (Intermediate to Advanced):

What to Learn: Don't just learn the syntax. Focus on Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) principles (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism), interfaces, abstract classes, collections (Lists, Sets, Maps), and exception handling. Since Spring Boot 3 uses Java 17+, familiarize yourself with modern Java features like Records, var for local variables, and the Stream API for data manipulation.
Why: The entire application is written in Java. A deep understanding is non-negotiable for writing clean, efficient business logic.

HTTP and RESTful APIs:

What to Learn: Understand the client-server model of the web. Learn the core HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), what they semantically represent, and the importance of HTTP status codes (e.g., 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error). Grasp the core principles of REST: resources, statelessness, and using JSON as a data format.
Why: This is the universal language of microservices. You will be designing, building, and consuming REST APIs.

Phase 2: The Engine - The Spring Framework
This is the most critical framework in the template. Master it, and you're halfway there.

Spring Core Concepts:

What to Learn: Focus on the two pillars of Spring: Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection (DI). Understand what the Spring "Application Context" or "IoC Container" is. Learn the most common annotations: @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Autowired.
Why: Spring manages the lifecycle of your objects (beans). Understanding DI is fundamental to how all the pieces of a Spring application are wired together.

Spring Boot:

What to Learn: Understand how Spring Boot simplifies Spring development. Focus on auto-configuration (how it automatically configures beans based on the JARs on your classpath), starter dependencies (e.g., spring-boot-starter-web), and externalized configuration using application.yaml or application.properties. Learn to build a simple REST controller using @RestController and @GetMapping/@PostMapping.
Why: The template is a Spring Boot project. This knowledge will allow you to understand how the service starts, how its configuration is managed, and how to add new API endpoints.

Gradle (Build Tool):

What to Learn: You don't need to be an expert, but you must understand the basics. Learn the purpose of build.gradle (declares dependencies and tasks) and settings.gradle (defines project structure). Know how to execute common tasks from the command line: ./gradlew build (compiles and packages the code), ./gradlew test (runs tests), and ./gradlew bootRun (runs the application).
Why: Gradle is the tool used to build, test, and manage all the libraries your project needs. You will interact with it constantly.

Phase 3: The Ecosystem - Connecting Microservices
Once you can build a standalone service, this phase teaches you how to make it part of a larger distributed system.

Microservice Architecture Concepts:

What to Learn: Before diving into the tools, understand the "why." Learn about key patterns like Service Discovery (how services find each other), Centralized Configuration (managing configuration for many services), and Fault Tolerance (e.g., circuit breakers).
Why: This provides the context for why tools like Spring Cloud are necessary.

Spring Cloud & Service Discovery:

What to Learn: Focus on the role of a "Service Directory" or "Discovery Server" (like Eureka, which is a common choice). Understand that when your service starts, it registers its name and address with this central server. When it needs to call another service, it asks the server for that service's address. Learn the annotations that enable this, like @EnableDiscoveryClient.
Why: In a microservice environment, you don't hardcode IP addresses. Service discovery allows services to find each other dynamically. The template is pre-configured for this.

Communicating Between Services (Feign & WebClient):

What to Learn:

Feign: Understand it as a "declarative" REST client. You create a Java interface, add annotations, and Spring Cloud automatically implements it for you. It's clean and easy to read.
WebClient: Learn this as the modern, more powerful way to make HTTP requests in Spring. It is non-blocking and reactive, which can be more efficient, but has a slightly steeper learning curve.

Why: Your microservice will inevitably need to call other microservices. The template provides examples of both, and you need to understand how to use them to fetch data.

Phase 4: The Polish - Professional Tooling & Practices
These tools ensure your microservice is maintainable, well-documented, and high-quality.

Testing in Spring:

What to Learn: Learn how to write unit tests for your services (@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)) and integration tests for your REST controllers (@SpringBootTest with @AutoConfigureMockMvc or WebTestClient). Understand the difference between mocking dependencies and running a test with a full application context.
Why: The template includes a testing setup. Writing automated tests is crucial for ensuring your service works correctly and doesn't break when you make changes.

API Documentation (Swagger/OpenAPI):

What to Learn: Understand that tools like Springdoc-openapi scan your @RestController code to automatically generate interactive API documentation (a Swagger UI page). Learn how to add annotations (@Operation, @ApiResponse) to make this documentation more descriptive.
Why: Good documentation makes your service easy to use for other developers and teams. The template automates the setup.

Docker & Docker Compose:

What to Learn: Understand what a Docker container is (a lightweight, portable package of an application and its dependencies). Learn the basics of Docker Compose for running multi-container applications from a single docker-compose.yml file. You only need to know how to run docker-compose up to start.
Why: The template uses this to run external dependencies locally, like the SonarQube database and server. This avoids complex local installations.

Code Quality (SonarQube):

What to Learn: Understand that SonarQube is a static analysis tool that scans your code for bugs, vulnerabilities, and "code smells" (bad practices). Learn how to run the Gradle task (./gradlew sonar) and how to interpret the dashboard to identify areas for improvement in your code.
Why: This helps you maintain high code quality and write more secure, robust applications.

By following this path, you will progressively build the knowledge required to not only use the template, but to understand its value and replicate its functionality on your own.

title: Five ways to say "wait" in one Next.js app, and the sign-in form uses none of them
description:
Our app has 18 <form> tags across 16 files, every one of them posting to a server action. I went looking for how each of them tells you it is working, and found five different answers, one of which is "it does not".

The five patterns

One: a shared component wrapping useFormStatus. It exists, it is good, and it is imported by two files:

export function FormSubmitButton({ icon, children, className, ...props }) {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus()
  return (
    <Button type="submit" disabled={pending} className={className} {...props}>
      {icon && (
        <span className="inline-flex shrink-0">
          {pending ? <Loader2 className="h-4 w-4 animate-spin" /> : icon}
        </span>
      )}
      {!icon && pending && <Loader2 className="h-4 w-4 animate-spin shrink-0" />}
      {children}
    </Button>
  )
}

Its own doc comment states the rule it is built around: the leading icon is replaced by a spinner while pending, and the label text stays put, so the button does not change width mid-submit. Three call sites, in the two pack editor pages.

Two: useFormStatus inlined into a local sub-component. Three files do this, each with its own flavour. The sign-up form swaps the label instead of the icon:

function SubmitButton() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus()
  return (
    <Button className="w-full mt-4" type="submit" disabled={pending}>
      {pending ? 'Creating account…' : 'Sign up'}
    </Button>
  )
}

Which is to say it breaks the shared component's one rule, in the same codebase, four lines of code later. In practice it gets away with it because the button is w-full, so a wider label cannot move anything.

Three: useTransition. Two files, where the submit is not the only thing that has to go quiet. One of them binds isPending to eight different controls, because a half-finished dialog with one spinner and seven live buttons is worse than no spinner.

Four: a useState boolean. One form, set manually around an async call. It predates the others, and it is the version every React developer writes before learning useFormStatus exists.

Five: nothing. Eight of the sixteen files render a plain <Button type="submit"> and no pending anything. That list includes the sign-in form, the forgot-password form, the password-reset form, the sign-out form in the header menu, and three of the four account settings forms.

So the app has a purpose-built component for this exact problem, and the four forms a stranger is most likely to meet are the ones not using it.

Pending state and error state are not the same hook

The eight forms with no pending feedback are not careless. They all use useActionState, which is why they feel finished:

const [formState, formAction] = useActionState(loginUser, { message: '' })

That gives you the action's return value, so the form can raise a toast when sign-in fails. useActionState also returns a pending flag as its third element, which these call sites never destructure, because the thing they were written to solve was error display.

useActionState answers "what came back". useFormStatus answers "is something in flight", and it answers it from inside the form, which is why it wants a child component. Having solved the first question, it is very easy to believe you have solved the second.

Reading which pattern a page shipped, from outside

You do not need the source for this. Both pages are public, and the client chunk carries the answer.

Load pub-trivia.app/signup, open the Network tab, filter to JS, and search the chunks for Creating account. One hit, in a 3,254 byte chunk, and the surrounding code is the whole pattern in one line:

let {pending:a} = (0,l.useFormStatus)(),
    o = a ? "Creating account…" : "Sign up";

Now do the same on pub-trivia.app/login, searching for Sign In. The compiled form is there, built from the same primitives, and its button has no binding at all:

(0,r.jsx)(n.Button, { className:"w-full mt-4", type:"submit", children:"Sign In" })

Fifteen JS files on each page. One of them changes its label while a server action runs and one of them cannot, and the diff is visible without reading a line of our repository.

While you are in there, note the (0,r.c)(3) call at the top of those components. That is the React Compiler's memo cache, which this project turns on with reactCompiler: true in next.config.mjs. It is a good reminder that none of this is about saving renders. The compiler already handles that. The missing piece in those eight forms is purely what the human sees in the second after they click.

The fix, and why it is not one line

FormSubmitButton is a drop-in, so each of the eight is a two-line change: import it, swap the <Button type="submit">. The reason it is still a list of eight is that the three sign-in and reset forms sit in client components that were written before the shared button existed, and each of them has to be checked for the layout-shift rule the shared component promises and the local copy ignores. A button that is w-full can swap its label safely. A button sized by its text cannot, and three of these are not full width.

The real lesson is cheaper than the fix: if your codebase has a component whose entire job is pending state, grep for its import count before you trust that the problem is solved. Ours said two.

Forms to poke at on the live site

  • pub-trivia.app/login and pub-trivia.app/signup are the two sides of this post. Same primitives, same server action plumbing, different answers to "is it working", and you can tell which is which from the shipped JavaScript.
  • pub-trivia.app/tools/scoresheet-generator is the control case: four labelled inputs and a button that produces a printable PDF entirely in your browser. Nothing is posted anywhere, so there is no pending state to show, and the form is honest about that by having none. It is also the quickest way to see what these three primitives, Label, Input and Button, do without any of the hooks above.

title: Langages de programmation les mieux payés en 2026 : ce que disent vraiment les chiffres
description:
L'essentiel en une minute

Les langages de programmation les mieux payés ne sont pas les mêmes selon la source que vous ouvrez. Dans le dernier classement mondial publié par Stack Overflow (2024), Erlang est premier, en dollars. Dans le baromètre français de Silkhom, c'est Rust, en euros brut annuel. Les deux ont raison, parce qu'ils ne mesurent pas la même chose.

Cet article sépare donc les classements : chaque chiffre a sa source, son année, son échantillon et son unité, et les dollars du monde ne côtoient jamais les euros de France dans un même tableau. C'est une synthèse de sources publiques consultées le 12 octobre 2026 : nous n'avons mené aucune enquête de salaires.

Points clés

  • Le dernier classement mondial par langage publié par Stack Overflow date de 2024 : Erlang est en tête avec 100 636 $ de médiane annuelle, devant Elixir et Clojure. Les éditions 2025 et 2026 n'affichent pas ce classement sur leurs pages de résultats.
  • Les langages de niche montent en tête parce que peu de gens répondent : en 2023, Zig était premier avec 273 répondants, contre 30 777 pour JavaScript.
  • En France, le baromètre Silkhom 2026 place Rust en tête à Paris, de 90 à 105 k€ brut annuel fixe pour un senior, devant Go, de 70 à 95 k€.
  • Le pays pèse plus que le langage : un développeur back-end déclare 175 000 $ de médiane aux États-Unis et 71 929 $ en France dans l'édition 2025 de Stack Overflow.
  • Apprenez un langage pour le métier qu'il ouvre. Le même Rust vaut de 48 à 70 k€ dans l'embarqué chez Silkhom.

Les sources et leurs unités

Un classement de salaires par langage ne vaut que par sa fiche technique. Avant de lire un chiffre, cherchez quatre choses : qui a répondu, combien de personnes, en quelle année, et ce que le montant contient. Voici les sources de cet article, avec ce qu'elles mesurent vraiment.

Source Année Échantillon Unité Limite principale
Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2024 65 437 répondants, 185 pays ; 23 352 réponses sur le salaire Médiane annuelle en dollars, primes et avantages inclus Aucun effectif par langage publié
Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2023 47 883 réponses sur le salaire Médiane annuelle en dollars Trois ans d'âge
Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025 49 009 répondants, 177 pays ; 1 026 réponses pour la France Médiane annuelle en dollars, par métier et par pays Aucun classement par langage
JetBrains, State of Developer Ecosystem 2025 24 534 développeurs, 194 pays Pourcentage lié aux développeurs les mieux payés Catégorie non définie dans le billet
Silkhom, Salaires Informatique 2026 Plus de 25 000 candidats, de 2019 à 2026 Fourchettes en k€ brut annuel fixe Données d'un cabinet de recrutement
Licorne Society 2026 Non publié k€ brut annuel, Paris et Île-de-France Cabinet de recrutement, méthode peu détaillée
Blog du Modérateur 2026 Reprend le baromètre Silkhom Moyennes en euros par poste Source de seconde main

La première ligne mérite une précision. Stack Overflow demande la rémunération totale annuelle, « salaire, primes et avantages, avant impôts et déductions » (notre traduction), puis convertit les réponses en dollars au taux du 11 juin 2024 (méthodologie 2024, consultée le 12 octobre 2026). Ce n'est ni un fixe, ni un salaire français.

Silkhom fait l'inverse : du fixe seulement, en euros, sur trois zones françaises, à partir des recrutements du cabinet (Silkhom, 30 juin 2026). Comparer ces deux mondes ligne à ligne n'a pas de sens.

Monde : les langages de programmation les mieux payés selon Stack Overflow

Le dernier classement mondial par langage que Stack Overflow affiche date de 2024, et Erlang y est premier avec 100 636 $ de médiane annuelle. La section « Top paying technologies » repose sur 23 352 réponses, soit 35,7 % des participants (Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2024, consulté le 12 octobre 2026).

Rang Langage Médiane annuelle 2024 Part des répondants qui l'utilisent
1 Erlang 100 636 $ 0,9 %
2 Elixir 96 000 $ 2,1 %
3 Clojure 95 541 $ 1,2 %
5 Ruby 90 221 $ 5,2 %
7 Scala 88 619 $ 2,6 %
12 Go 76 433 $ 13,5 %
13 Rust 76 292 $ 12,6 %
18 Swift 75 184 $ 4,7 %
27 Python 67 723 $ 51 %
30 TypeScript 65 907 $ 38,5 %
31 Kotlin 65 815 $ 9,4 %
33 C++ 64 444 $ 23 %
39 JavaScript 63 694 $ 62,3 %
41 Java 61 714 $ 30,3 %
46 PHP 49 586 $ 18,2 %

Les rangs suivent l'ordre d'affichage de la page, qui liste 49 technologies. Les parts d'usage viennent de la section « Most popular technologies » de la même édition.

Les cinq premiers langages retenus ici sont utilisés par moins de 6 % des répondants chacun. Les trois langages les plus répandus hors HTML/CSS et SQL, à savoir JavaScript, Python et TypeScript, sont tous sous les 68 000 $.

Et les éditions 2025 et 2026 ?

Elles ne publient pas ce classement sur leurs pages de résultats. L'édition 2025, fondée sur 49 009 réponses de 177 pays, donne le salaire médian par type de poste, pas par langage (Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025, consulté le 12 octobre 2026).

L'édition 2026 repose sur 30 903 réponses valides de 169 pays, recueillies du 23 juin au 5 août 2026. Sa méthodologie décrit bien une conversion des rémunérations en dollars annuels, mais nous n'avons trouvé aucun classement par langage sur ses pages Work et Technology (méthodologie 2026, consultée le 12 octobre 2026).

Méfiez-vous donc d'un tableau « Stack Overflow 2026 » par langage : soit il recalcule les données brutes sans le dire, soit il reprend 2024.

Pourquoi des langages de niche arrivent en tête

Les langages de niche dominent parce que leurs médianes reposent sur peu de réponses, données par des profils plus expérimentés que la moyenne. L'édition 2023 est la dernière à afficher le nombre de répondants par langage, et elle rend le mécanisme visible (Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2023, consulté le 12 octobre 2026).

Cette année-là, Zig était premier avec 103 611 $ pour 273 répondants, devant Erlang, à 99 492 $ pour 522 réponses. JavaScript, avec 30 777 réponses, était à 74 034 $.

Notre calcul. JavaScript comptait 113 fois plus de répondants que Zig en 2023 (30 777 contre 273). Un an plus tard, la médiane de Zig tombe à 75 332 $, soit 27,3 % de moins. Mais Go recule aussi, de 17,6 % (de 92 760 $ à 76 433 $), et Python de 13,5 % (de 78 331 $ à 67 723 $), sur de grands échantillons. La plus grande part de la baisse est donc commune. Zig recule de 10 à 14 points de plus que Go et Python : l'écart supplémentaire tient à la taille de l'échantillon (273 réponses en 2023, effectif 2024 non publié).

Stack Overflow note d'ailleurs qu'en 2024 seuls Nim, Erlang et Apex voient leur médiane monter, toutes les autres technologies reculant (édition 2024). Une baisse aussi générale évoque, selon nous, un changement de population répondante plus qu'un marché en chute.

Trois raisons expliquent la prime apparente des petits langages :

  • L'ancienneté. C'est l'explication qu'avance Stack Overflow en 2023 : les années d'expérience restent, écrit l'enquête, le facteur déterminant des salaires élevés. Peu de développeurs débutent en Erlang.
  • Le domaine. Erlang et Elixir servent les systèmes distribués, Scala le traitement de données à grande échelle. On paie le secteur.
  • Le pays. Les réponses ne viennent pas des mêmes pays pour chaque langage, et tout est converti en dollars.

JetBrains, éditeur d'outils de développement, publie un constat voisin. Son enquête 2025, menée d'avril à juin auprès de 24 534 développeurs de 194 pays, écrit que Scala « arrive en tête parmi les développeurs les mieux payés avec 38 %, alors que 2 % seulement des développeurs l'utilisent comme langage principal » (notre traduction, JetBrains, octobre 2025). Le billet ne précise ni sur quelle population porte ce pourcentage, ni où commence la catégorie des mieux payés.

Verdict : un langage rare en tête d'un classement signale une population rare, souvent senior. Il ne promet pas ce salaire à celui qui l'apprend demain.

France : les grilles en euros, brut annuel fixe

En France, Rust est le langage le mieux payé du baromètre Silkhom 2026 : de 90 à 105 k€ brut annuel fixe à Paris pour un senior. Le cabinet précise que ses fourchettes sont des moyennes à pondérer selon la structure de l'entreprise (Silkhom, 30 juin 2026).

Poste (intitulé Silkhom) Junior, Paris Confirmé, Paris Senior, Paris
Développeur Rust 50 à 70 70 à 90 90 à 105
Développeur Go 40 à 55 55 à 70 70 à 95
Développeur Flutter 40 à 52 52 à 70 70 à 85
Développeur iOS 40 à 45 52 à 60 68 à 75
Développeur .Net 38 à 45 45 à 55 55 à 75
Développeur Java 38 à 43 43 à 58 58 à 72
Développeur Fullstack JS 38 à 45 45 à 55 55 à 70
Développeur Cobol 35 à 42 42 à 52 52 à 70
Développeur C (embarqué) 41 à 45 43 à 48 48 à 70
Développeur Android 40 à 45 50 à 55 58 à 65
Développeur PHP 38 à 45 45 à 52 52 à 60
Développeur Python 38 à 43 45 à 60 43 à 58 (coquille probable)

Fourchettes en milliers d'euros, brut annuel fixe, colonne Paris. Deux réserves de lecture. Les tranches d'expérience de Rust sont plus longues que les autres : junior jusqu'à 3 ans, confirmé de 3 à 7 ans, senior à partir de 7 ans, contre 2 et 5 ans ailleurs. Et la fourchette senior de Python est publiée sous celle des confirmés : nous la reprenons telle quelle, c'est probablement une coquille.

Le cabinet résume lui-même la tendance : un développeur Java ou Python « s'établit autour de 45 k€, en léger recul », et « ce qui se paie, en 2026, ce n'est plus la maîtrise d'un langage, mais la rareté et l'exigence » (Silkhom). Le Blog du Modérateur, qui a eu accès aux moyennes, donne 70 800 € pour le développeur Rust, nouvelle entrée du baromètre, et un recul de 1,1 % pour Java comme pour Python (Blog du Modérateur, 7 juillet 2026).

Une seconde grille, celle du cabinet Licorne Society, ne recoupe celle de Silkhom qu'en partie pour Paris et l'Île-de-France. Elle donne 45 k€ pour un junior et 70 k€ pour un senior d'environ 5 ans en Python, en Go et en Ruby on Rails, 42 et 65 k€ en Java, 40 et 60 k€ en PHP (Licorne Society, mise à jour du 10 août 2026). Java et PHP y sont dans les fourchettes de Silkhom. Python, en revanche, y est placé au niveau de Go, ce que Silkhom ne fait pas. Elle ne publie ni taille d'échantillon ni ligne Rust.

Ces deux cabinets de recrutement décrivent leurs clients et leurs candidats, pas l'ensemble des développeurs français. Pour le détail par ville et par niveau d'expérience, notre grille des salaires des développeurs en France fait ce travail : nous ne le répétons pas ici.

Verdict : en France, Rust et Go sont les deux seuls langages dont le haut de fourchette senior parisienne dépasse 90 k€ chez Silkhom. L'écart avec Java ou PHP est réel, mais il se joue sur un petit nombre de postes.

Ce qui pèse autant ou plus que le langage

Le pays pèse nettement plus que le langage ; le métier, la zone, l'ancienneté et l'employeur pèsent du même ordre. Les sources citées permettent de le mesurer, avec une limite : le pays et le métier viennent de l'édition 2025 de Stack Overflow, le langage de l'édition 2024, faute de mieux.

Le pays. Dans l'enquête 2025 de Stack Overflow, un développeur back-end déclare une médiane de 175 000 $ aux États-Unis, de 87 011 $ en Allemagne, de 71 929 $ en France et de 22 086 $ en Inde (Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2025). Le rapport est de 2,4 entre les États-Unis et la France, et de 7,9 entre les États-Unis et l'Inde.

Le langage, pour comparer. Dans le classement 2024, une autre édition, l'écart va de 24 % entre Go et Java jusqu'à un rapport de 2,0 entre Erlang et PHP. Chez Silkhom, le milieu de la fourchette senior parisienne de Rust dépasse celui de PHP d'environ 74 %. Le langage n'est donc pas négligeable : il pèse moins que le pays, pas moins que le reste.

Le métier. Pour la France en 2025, l'architecte logiciel déclare 81 210 $, l'ingénieur données 78 890 $, le développeur back-end 71 929 $ et le développeur full-stack 58 007 $. L'écart entre architecte et full-stack atteint 40 %. L'onglet France repose sur 1 026 réponses, et les effectifs par métier ne sont pas publiés.

Le domaine d'application. Chez Silkhom, le développeur Rust d'applications et de services vaut de 90 à 105 k€ à Paris en senior. Le développeur Rust embarqué, lui, est aligné sur le développeur C : de 48 à 70 k€.

La zone. Un développeur Go senior passe de 70 à 95 k€ à Paris à une fourchette de 55 à 70 k€ dans les grandes villes et de 50 à 55 k€ en régions, selon le même baromètre. Pour Java, le senior va de 58 à 72 k€ à Paris et de 45 à 55 k€ dans les grandes villes comme en régions.

L'ancienneté. En Java à Paris, la fourchette passe de 38 à 43 k€ pour un junior à une fourchette de 58 à 72 k€ pour un senior, soit 24,5 k€ de plus au milieu des fourchettes. À niveau senior, passer de Java à Go en ajoute 17,5 et passer à Rust applicatif 32,5, selon notre calcul. Cinq années d'expérience rapportent donc à peu près autant qu'un passage de Java à Go, et moins qu'un passage à Rust applicatif.

Le type d'employeur. Licorne Society estime qu'à 5 ans d'expérience, un développeur touche 65 k€ en startup en phase de démarrage, 75 k€ en scale-up et 60 k€ en grand groupe ou en ESN, toujours à Paris et en Île-de-France.

Un dernier facteur bouge vite. Silkhom attribue le tassement des postes Java et Python à une production de code standard « en partie absorbée par les assistants de génération de code » (Silkhom). JetBrains relève de son côté que 85 % des développeurs utilisent régulièrement des outils d'IA et que 68 % s'attendent à ce que leur employeur l'exige bientôt. Savoir coder plus vite avec l'IA devient un prérequis.

Verdict : si vous cherchez une hausse, le pays et la zone passent en premier. Le métier, l'ancienneté, l'employeur et le langage jouent ensuite à armes à peu près égales.

Quel langage apprendre selon votre objectif

Le bon langage dépend du poste visé, pas du haut d'un classement. Ce tableau relie chaque objectif aux chiffres des sources citées, sans promettre un salaire.

Votre objectif Langage à privilégier Ce que disent les sources
Trouver un premier poste JavaScript, TypeScript ou Python Les plus utilisés en 2024 hors HTML/CSS et SQL : 62,3 %, 38,5 % et 51 % des répondants de Stack Overflow
Viser le haut des grilles françaises Rust ou Go Les deux seuls langages dont le haut de fourchette senior parisienne dépasse 90 k€ chez Silkhom
Travailler dans la donnée ou l'IA Python Le Data Engineer s'établit près de 58 k€ en moyenne, parmi les deux plus fortes hausses du baromètre Silkhom
Faire du mobile Swift, Kotlin ou Dart avec Flutter Senior à Paris : iOS de 68 à 75 k€, Flutter de 70 à 85 k€, Android de 58 à 65 k€
Maintenir des systèmes anciens Cobol Senior à Paris de 52 à 70 k€, mais salaire moyen en recul de 5,8 % sur un an selon Silkhom

Pour un premier poste, nous retenons la part d'usage déclarée, faute de données sur le volume d'offres. Notre guide pour apprendre Python part de zéro, et le tutoriel pour créer une API REST avec Node.js et Express couvre le versant JavaScript.

Go et Rust se justifient comme second langage, une fois un métier acquis. Dans l'enquête JetBrains 2025, ce sont les deux langages que les développeurs veulent le plus adopter ensuite : 11 % citent Go, 10 % Rust (JetBrains). Go mène vers l'infrastructure : notre introduction à Kubernetes donne le contexte.

Deux leviers complètent le langage. Une certification pèse dans les métiers du cloud, comme l'explique notre comparatif des certifications AWS, Azure et GCP. Et le statut change l'unité de compte : si vous envisagez de devenir développeur freelance, vous raisonnerez en tarif journalier, pas en brut annuel.

Verdict : un langage courant pour entrer, un langage rare pour se distinguer, dans cet ordre.

Ce que nous n'avons pas pu vérifier

Plusieurs éléments manquent ou restent incertains :

  • Un classement mondial par langage pour 2025 ou 2026. Les pages de résultats de Stack Overflow n'en affichent pas. Nous n'avons pas recalculé les données brutes.
  • Le nombre de répondants par langage en 2024. La page ne le donne pas. Les effectifs cités viennent de l'édition 2023.
  • Le sens exact des 38 % de Scala chez JetBrains. Le billet ne définit ni la population mesurée ni la catégorie des mieux payés.
  • La hausse exacte du Data Engineer chez Silkhom. La page donne 10,4 % dans son texte et 10,2 % dans son tableau, le Blog du Modérateur 10,1 % : nous n'en retenons aucune.
  • Le volume d'offres d'emploi par langage. Nous n'avons consulté aucune donnée d'offres : les conseils pour un premier poste reposent sur la part d'usage.
  • Les tarifs journaliers des freelances par langage. Le baromètre des tarifs de Malt n'était pas accessible lors de la rédaction : aucun tarif journalier n'est cité ici.
  • Les salaires français en TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift ou Scala. Silkhom raisonne par poste (Fullstack JS, Android, iOS).
  • Une enquête française par langage avec un échantillon représentatif. Nous n'en avons pas trouvé : les deux grilles citées viennent de cabinets de recrutement.

Questions fréquentes

Quel est le langage de programmation le mieux payé en 2026 ?

Cela dépend du périmètre. Dans le monde, le dernier classement publié par Stack Overflow, celui de 2024, place Erlang en tête avec 100 636 $ de médiane annuelle. En France, le baromètre Silkhom 2026 place Rust devant, de 90 à 105 k€ brut annuel fixe à Paris pour un senior.

Rust est-il vraiment mieux payé que Python en France ?

Oui dans la grille Silkhom 2026, qui affiche à Paris de 70 à 90 k€ pour un développeur Rust confirmé et de 45 à 60 k€ pour un développeur Python confirmé. Mais les tranches d'expérience diffèrent, de 3 à 7 ans pour Rust et de 2 à 5 ans pour Python, et le Rust embarqué plafonne à 70 k€.

Pourquoi JavaScript est-il si bas dans les classements ?

Parce que presque tout le monde l'utilise. En 2024, 62,3 % des répondants de Stack Overflow déclarent JavaScript, débutants compris. Sa médiane de 63 694 $ décrit donc une population très large, alors que celle d'Erlang décrit 0,9 % des répondants.

Peut-on comparer un salaire américain en dollars et un salaire français ?

Pas directement. Stack Overflow mesure une rémunération totale, primes et avantages inclus, convertie en dollars. Les grilles françaises donnent un fixe brut annuel en euros.

À propos de l'auteur

title: 7 CSS Myths Beginners Should Stop Believing
description:
If you're learning CSS, you've probably heard a lot of advice.

Some of it is helpful.

Some of it is incomplete.

And some of it is simply a myth.

The problem is that beginners often don't know which is which.

You might hear someone say:

“You need to memorize CSS properties.”

Or:

“CSS is just for making websites look pretty.”

Or perhaps:

“Just add more margin if something isn't aligned.”

So you try it.

And suddenly you're staring at your stylesheet wondering why everything has moved 47 pixels to the left. 😂

CSS becomes much easier to learn when you understand how it actually works, rather than relying on random rules you've heard from other people.

Let's clear up seven common CSS myths beginners should stop believing.

Myth #1: “You Need to Memorize Every CSS Property”

This is one of the first traps beginners fall into.

You see developers writing CSS quickly and think:

“They must have every property memorized.”

Not necessarily.

CSS has a large number of properties, values, layout techniques, and combinations.

Trying to memorize everything isn't the most useful way to learn.

Instead, focus on understanding the important concepts.

For example, learn what these do:

color
background
font-size
margin
padding
width
height
display
position
flex
grid

But don't feel like you have failed because you forgot a property.

Even experienced developers look things up.

The important skill is knowing what you're trying to accomplish and knowing how to find the appropriate CSS solution.

A better learning approach

Instead of:

“I must memorize everything.”

Think:

“I need to understand the concepts and know how to find the details.”

Learn.

Practice.

Build.

Reference documentation when necessary.

That's a much more realistic approach to learning CSS.

Myth #2: “CSS Is Just About Changing Colours”

This myth probably comes from the fact that colour is one of the easiest CSS properties to demonstrate.

You write:

h1 {
color: blue;
}

And immediately see a change.

But CSS goes far beyond colours.

CSS controls many aspects of how a webpage is presented, including:

Layout

How elements are arranged on the page.

Spacing

The space inside and around elements.

Typography

Fonts, sizes, weights, line height, and text presentation.

Sizing

How wide or tall elements are.

Alignment

How elements are positioned relative to one another.

Positioning

Where elements appear within the page.

Responsive design

How layouts adapt to different screen sizes.

Animations and transitions

How visual changes happen over time.

CSS can even dramatically change the layout of the same HTML without changing the underlying HTML structure.

So saying CSS is “just colours” is like saying a house is just paint.

Colour is one part of the presentation.

CSS controls much more.

Myth #3: “Good CSS Means Using Lots of Effects”

This is another common beginner mistake.

You discover:

Box shadows
Gradients
Animations
Transitions
Transforms
Glowing effects

And suddenly you want to use all of them.

😂

The result might look impressive to you for five minutes.

But good CSS isn't about using as many effects as possible.

A website can have:

simple colours
clean spacing
consistent typography
sensible layouts
subtle interactions

…and still look professional.

In fact, adding unnecessary effects can make an interface harder to understand.

Imagine a website where every button moves, every heading animates, every card has multiple shadows, and every section has a different gradient.

There may be plenty happening visually.

But that doesn't automatically mean the design is better.

Good CSS should have a purpose.

Ask:

Does this style improve clarity?

Does it improve usability?

Does it support the visual hierarchy?

Does it help the user understand what to do?

If the answer is no, you may not need the effect.

Sometimes the most professional CSS is the CSS you barely notice.

Myth #4: “You Need a Framework Before You Can Learn CSS”

Frameworks can be extremely useful.

But you don't need a CSS framework before learning CSS itself.

Imagine trying to learn how a car works by only learning how to drive one specific model.

You might get around.

But your understanding of what's happening underneath may be limited.

The same idea applies to CSS.

Before depending heavily on a framework, it's useful to understand fundamental CSS concepts such as:

Box Model

Flexbox

Grid

Positioning

Responsive Design

Cascade

Specificity

Inheritance

Once you understand these concepts, frameworks become easier to understand because you can recognize the CSS ideas behind the tools.

Frameworks aren't the enemy.

The issue is using a tool without understanding the underlying concepts.

Learn the foundation first.

Then use tools to become more productive.

Myth #5: “If Something Doesn't Align, Just Add More Margins”

This one deserves special attention.

Because almost every beginner eventually does it.

Your element is too far to the left.

You add:

margin-left: 20px;

Still wrong?

Try:

margin-left: 40px;

Still wrong?

Maybe:

margin-left: 80px;

😂

Congratulations.

You've moved the problem instead of solving it.

Margins aren't bad.

They're an important part of CSS.

The problem is using them to compensate for an issue you haven't identified.

If something isn't aligned correctly, the real problem might be:

Flexbox
Grid
Padding
Width
Height
Box sizing
Alignment properties
Positioning
Document flow

Instead of asking:

“What margin should I add?”

Ask:

“Why is this element not where I expect it to be?”

That question will take you much further.

Myth #6: “Responsive Design Can Be Added Later”

Imagine building an entire website for a desktop screen.

Everything looks perfect.

Then you open it on your phone.

And suddenly:

The text is too large.

The buttons don't fit.

The navigation breaks.

Images overflow.

The layout becomes difficult to use.

Now you're trying to repair a structure that wasn't designed with smaller screens in mind.

Responsive design is about creating interfaces that adapt to different screen sizes and devices.

That doesn't mean every website needs a completely different design for every device.

It means you should think about how your layout behaves as the available space changes.

A website may be viewed on:

📱 Smartphones

📱 Tablets

💻 Laptops

🖥️ Desktop monitors

Different screen sizes create different layout challenges.

Responsive thinking should happen during development.

Don't treat it as a final decoration you add after everything else is finished.

Think about:

Flexible widths
Relative units
Media queries
Flexible layouts
Responsive images
Mobile navigation
Text scaling
Content hierarchy

The earlier you consider responsiveness, the easier it becomes to build a layout that adapts naturally.

Myth #7: “CSS Is Only for Designers”

This is another misunderstanding.

CSS is certainly important for visual design, but it isn't exclusively a “designer thing.”

CSS is a core part of frontend development.

If you're building websites, you need to understand how HTML structure becomes a usable interface.

A frontend developer might need to understand:

Layout
Spacing
Responsive behaviour
Typography
Component styling
Positioning
Accessibility considerations
Browser rendering
CSS architecture

You don't have to become a professional visual designer to learn CSS.

But understanding CSS can make you a much more capable frontend developer.

A simple way to think about the core frontend technologies is:

HTML → Structure

CSS → Presentation and Layout

JavaScript → Behaviour and Interactivity

Each has a different primary responsibility, but they work together.

So, What Should Beginners Actually Focus On?

If you shouldn't memorize everything, add endless effects, depend immediately on frameworks, or solve every problem with margins…

What should you learn?

Start with the fundamentals.

  1. Understand the Box Model

Learn how:

Content → Padding → Border → Margin

affect the size and spacing of elements.

This alone will help explain many layout problems.

  1. Learn Selectors

Understand how to target elements using:

Element selectors
Classes
IDs
Attribute selectors
Descendant relationships

Selectors are fundamental to writing effective CSS.

  1. Learn Flexbox

Flexbox is extremely useful for arranging elements along one dimension.

Learn concepts such as:

display: flex
justify-content
align-items
flex-direction
gap
flex-wrap

Don't just memorize the properties.

Understand what problem Flexbox is solving.

  1. Learn CSS Grid

Grid is useful for two-dimensional layouts.

Understand:

Rows
Columns
Gaps
Grid areas
Flexible tracks

Again, focus on the concept rather than memorizing every possible combination.

  1. Understand the Cascade and Specificity

This becomes extremely important as your stylesheets grow.

Learn why one rule may override another.

Understanding specificity can save you from repeatedly adding random CSS or reaching for !important.

  1. Learn Responsive Design

Understand how your layout behaves when the available space changes.

Practice building interfaces that work across different screen sizes.

  1. Practice Debugging

This is one of the most valuable skills you can develop.

When your CSS doesn't work, don't immediately rewrite everything.

Ask:

What did I expect?

What actually happened?

Which rule controls this element?

Is another rule overriding it?

What does the browser's Developer Tools show?

The goal isn't simply to make the problem disappear.

The goal is to understand why it happened.

The Bigger Lesson About Learning CSS

Many beginners approach CSS as if the goal is to memorize a huge list of commands.

But CSS isn't really about memorization.

It's about understanding relationships.

You need to understand how:

HTML elements + CSS selectors + properties + values + the cascade + layout systems

work together.

Once you understand those relationships, learning new CSS techniques becomes much easier.

You don't need to know everything.

You need a solid foundation and a willingness to investigate when something doesn't work.

Don't Be Afraid to Break Things

One of the best ways to learn CSS is to experiment.

Change a value.

See what happens.

Remove a property.

See what changes.

Try Flexbox.

Break the layout.

Fix it.

Change the width.

Resize the browser.

Watch the layout respond.

Use Developer Tools.

Inspect the element.

Try something different.

Every experiment teaches you something.

And sometimes the mistake teaches you more than the successful result.

Final Thoughts

CSS has a reputation for being frustrating.

And yes, sometimes it can be.

But many frustrations become easier once you stop relying on myths and start understanding the fundamentals.

You don't need to memorize every property.

CSS isn't just about colours.

More effects don't automatically mean better CSS.

You don't need a framework before learning the basics.

More margins aren't always the solution.

Responsive design shouldn't be an afterthought.

And CSS isn't only for designers.

Instead:

Understand the fundamentals.

Build real projects.

Experiment.

Debug your mistakes.

Use documentation when you need it.

Keep improving.

The goal isn't to become someone who never makes CSS mistakes.

The goal is to become someone who knows how to understand and solve them.

And that is a much more useful skill.

Which CSS myth did you believe when you first started learning?

Share it in the comments. 👇

Someone else learning CSS may be believing the same thing.
