title: Standard Chartered Crypto Trading UAE: BTC/ETH in the Bank App (VARA, Eligibility, Custody)
description:
The short answer

Standard Chartered crypto trading UAE went live on 14 October 2026: eligible Professional Investor clients of Standard Chartered Bank UAE can buy and sell Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH) in AED or USD through the SC Mobile app, with the bank managing custody and settlement in a closed-loop model (no transfers of crypto into or out of the bank). The bank holds a VARA VASP licence for Broker-Dealer Services under reference VL/26/08/003 (issued 24 August 2026), conditioned to serve Qualified Investors. The bank's own Key Facts Statement sets eligibility (UAE residency, age above 21, Professional Investor with risk-profile rating above 5 and a banking relationship of AED 4 million and above, eligible AED or USD account), order bounds (USD 50 to USD 50,000 per trade or AED equivalent), and pricing (spread of up to 2.00% in the quoted price; no separate transaction or custody fee). This is a product and regulatory reading for UAE banks and fintechs — not a price forecast and not financial advice.

Key facts, with dates and primary sources

  • Launch, 14 October 2026: Standard Chartered announced "the UAE's first cryptocurrency trading offering by an international bank" and "a global first for Standard Chartered", enabling affluent clients to buy and sell BTC and ETH "directly through their existing Standard Chartered bank accounts" with "end-to-end custody and settlement through a closed-loop model", in collaboration with SC Ventures-backed Zodia Markets, and "regulated by the Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA)". First available to "Professional Investor clients in the UAE". (Standard Chartered press release, 14 October 2026)
  • VARA public register (verified 15 October 2026): VASP name Standard Chartered Bank; reference VL/26/08/003; licence type VASP Licence; licensed activity Broker-Dealer Services; licence issued 2026/08/24; licence condition Permitted to serve Qualified Investors; status Active; principal place of business Standard Chartered Tower, Downtown Dubai; CMA registration CMA-VASP-0100000-0066. (VARA public register — Standard Chartered Bank)
  • Product page (SC UAE): "Standard Chartered Bank, UAE is licensed by the Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA) to offer Broker-Dealer services under reference number VL/26/08/003." Eligibility listed as Professional Investor clients only, valid Client Investor Profile, existing eligible USD or AED account. Crypto transfers to or from SC are not supported. Market orders via Request for Quote (RFQ) with a 6-second price hold. Minimum order USD 50 or AED equivalent. Trading 24/7. Pairs: BTCUSD, BTCAED, ETHUSD, ETHAED. Execution-only; no investment advice. (SC UAE Crypto Trading product page)
  • Key Facts Statement (English PDF, bank primary): "This product is available only to existing Standard Chartered UAE clients with a valid UAE residency and above the age of 21 years" and "only to clients with an investor classification termed as 'Professional Investor' by the bank". "Professional Investors are defined as clients who have an investor risk profile rating more than 5 and with a banking relationship of AED 4 million and above." Minimum order USD 50; maximum USD 50,000 per trade (or AED equivalent). "A spread of up to 2.00% is levied on the final price shown to the client. There are no other transaction fees, custody fees or other hidden charges." Clients "do not have the ability to transfer their crypto holdings in or out of the SC Ecosystem." (Crypto KFS — English PDF; Arabic KFS)
  • Same-week VARA full licence for Rain MENA FZE (verified on register 15 October 2026): Rain MENA FZE, reference VL/26/10/001, VASP Licence for Exchange Services and Broker-Dealer Services, licence issued 2026/10/05, status Active. Rain's own announcement dated 13 October 2026 describes the licence as covering exchange and broker-dealer including margin trading, and serving retail, qualified and institutional investors (company website path returned 404 from this network on 15 October; cite VARA register as authority for licence fields, and Fintech News UAE / company PR as secondary for the margin and investor-class claims). (VARA public register — Rain MENA FZE)
  • Comparison products already live in the UAE: Liv (Emirates NBD Group) crypto via the Liv X app, "in partnership with Aquanow ME FZE, which is regulated by VARA under license number VL/24/01/001". (Liv Crypto). ruya offers Shari'ah-compliant Bitcoin investing in-app with Fuze documentation linked on the product page. (ruya Bitcoin Investment)

What happened on 14 October 2026 — and what did not

The SC release is careful about what it claims. It is a wealth product for affluent clients, not a retail exchange. It is BTC and ETH only. It is UAE first, with "plans to expand to other markets over time" and no timetable. It sits beside existing SC capabilities the bank already named: crypto ETFs through cash equities, and crypto exposure through structured products and OTC derivatives. The novelty is the consumer-facing spot buy/sell inside the same bank account and mobile app, with the bank as custodian and broker-dealer under a Dubai VARA licence.

What the release does not do is publish the Key Facts Statement numbers. Those live on the UAE product site and in the KFS PDF: the AED 4 million relationship threshold, the risk-profile floor, the 2% spread, the USD 50–50,000 order band, the 6-second RFQ, and the no-transfer rule. Product and compliance teams should treat the press release as the "why we launched" document and the KFS as the "what the client actually gets" document. This article uses both, and prefers the KFS wherever they differ in specificity.

Samir Subberwal (Global Head, Wealth Solutions) framed the launch as bringing digital assets "into our core wealth offering" with "security, trust and confidence that comes from investing through a regulated and trusted institution". Rola Abu Manneh (CEO, UAE, Middle East and Pakistan) called the UAE "a natural choice" given regulation and digital-asset leadership, and named the UAE as one of SC's "four global wealth hubs". Those quotes matter for positioning; they do not replace the KFS for product design.

Four UAE models for crypto inside a banking relationship

The MENA product question is not "is Bitcoin legal in the UAE?" Arabic search already clusters around that ("hal masmuh tadawul al-umlat al-raqamiya fi al-imarat" — is crypto trading allowed in the Emirates). The sharper question for banks and fintechs is: which model of crypto-in-the-bank are you building, because the licence, the custody, the withdrawal rights, the fee disclosure and the failure states all change with the model.

1. Closed-loop bank custody and broker-dealer (Standard Chartered). The bank holds the VARA Broker-Dealer licence, executes the trade, and custodies the asset inside its own ecosystem. The client never receives a withdrawable on-chain balance. Upside: one relationship, one app, institutional custody language (SC describes FIPS 140-2 Level 4 HSMs, segregated wallets, 1:1 client assets). Downside for the client: no self-custody exit; liquidation if the banking relationship ends. Downside for the product team: every disclosure must make the closed loop unmistakable before the first buy.

2. Bank app fronting a VARA-licensed broker (Liv × Aquanow). Liv's public crypto page says the experience runs "in partnership with Aquanow ME FZE, which is regulated by VARA under license number VL/24/01/001", with an Emirates NBD Group trust frame and a "zero trading fee" claim subject to terms. The bank brand owns the UX; a separate VASP owns the regulated activity. Product implication: the offer screen must name the licensed entity, not only the bank brand, and the fee claim must survive the fine print (spread, FX, network costs).

3. Shari'ah-compliant Bitcoin via an Islamic bank app (ruya × Fuze). ruya's Bitcoin Investment page positions Shari'ah-compliant digital investments in-app, with Fuze documentation linked and a standard VA risk disclaimer (full loss possible; no financial-protection scheme). Product implication: the Shari'ah structure and the VA risk warning must share the same first screen; a badge alone is not enough.

4. Regional VASP / exchange with a full VARA licence (Rain MENA FZE). The VARA register entry for Rain MENA FZE (VL/26/10/001, issued 5 October 2026) lists Exchange Services and Broker-Dealer Services. That is a different product shape from a bank closed loop: an exchange licence is built for a venue, order books and (per Rain's own announcement, secondary) margin and multi-investor classes. Banks watching Rain should not copy the exchange UX into a Broker-Dealer-only banking app; the licence categories are not interchangeable.

A fifth institutional pole sits beside these retail/wealth models: bank-grade digital-asset custody and markets rails (Zodia Markets for SC's trading rail; Zodia Custody's ADGM work on tokenised securities was covered in secondary reporting around 12–14 October 2026 — re-verify Zodia's own release before treating any VoP claim as settled). The product lesson is that "custody" in a press release can mean three different things: closed-loop retail holdings inside a bank, institutional settle-with-your-own-custodian spot, and FSRA-regulated digital-securities custody. Label which one you mean on the screen.

Eligibility gating UX: Professional Investor, risk profile, and "why you can't see this yet"

The SC product page FAQ already documents the empty state: if a client cannot see crypto on the SC Mobile app, it is because they are not deemed a Professional Investor or do not meet "other criteria as required by the bank". Registration requires PI classification, Client Investment Risk Profile meeting internal requirements, and up-to-date TIN / FATCA / CRS. The KFS adds the quantitative floor: risk-profile rating more than 5 and banking relationship of AED 4 million and above, plus UAE residency and age above 21, plus an eligible AED or USD account (joint accounts and term deposits excluded; conventional or Saadiq eligible).

That is a product-design brief, not a legal memo:

  1. Pre-qualify before the marketing tile. Showing a "Trade crypto" tile to a mass-affluent client who will fail the PI gate creates a complaint and a VARA marketing-risk problem. Prefer a soft gate: the tile appears only after the CIP/PI status is known, or the tile opens a clear "not available yet" sheet rather than a broken apply flow.
  2. Explain the gate in Arabic and English, with the bank's own definitions. "Professional Investor" and "Qualified Investor" (the VARA licence condition language) are not consumer phrases. The empty state should say what is missing in plain language: residency, age, account type, risk-profile step, or relationship threshold — without inventing thresholds the KFS does not state. SC's public KFS does state AED 4 million and risk rating above 5; if your bank uses different internal numbers, publish your KFS numbers, not SC's.
  3. Separate "can sell existing holdings" from "can buy again". SC's FAQ says that if eligibility changes, the client can still sell existing holdings but must meet criteria again to buy. That is a concrete state machine: holdings view + sell enabled; buy disabled with reason. Most banking apps fail this and show a generic error.
  4. Do not bury the relationship-manager path. SC routes classification questions to the RM or (+971) 600 5080 00. For a gated wealth product, the escalate-to-human path is part of the UX, not a support afterthought.

Our earlier work on UAE Open Finance and AI agents and AI agents for banks stressed consent and explainability when software initiates access. Crypto eligibility is the same pattern with a different regulator: the client must understand why a capability is hidden before they trust the bank when it appears.

Disclosure screens: spread-in-price, no external withdrawal, volatility, deposit-protection framing

VARA marketing and conduct expectations, and ordinary banking conduct, converge on one screen: the pre-trade confirmation. For a closed-loop bank crypto product, the confirmation must make five things impossible to miss:

  1. Cost as spread, not "zero fees". SC advertises "No transaction fees. No custody fees." The KFS simultaneously states a spread of up to 2.00% on the final price. Both statements can be true; the UX that shows only the first is not. Show the locked RFQ price, the implied spread band, and an example in AED and USD. A "zero commission" headline next to a 2% embedded spread is exactly the pattern consumer-protection teams flag in other asset classes.
  2. No external withdrawal. "Can I transfer my SC crypto holdings? No." belongs on the first buy screen, not only in an FAQ. Clients arriving from exchange mental models will assume a withdraw button exists.
  3. Not a bank deposit. The KFS warns of total or substantial loss and that crypto rates fluctuate. Secondary coverage (CoinDesk, Altcoin Buzz and others) emphasises that holdings are not deposit-protected. The bank's own client-facing pages stress execution-only and VA risk; product teams should still put a plain-language "this is not a deposit and is not covered by deposit protection" line on the confirmation if legal agrees — and if legal will not sign that line, do not imply deposit-like safety through visual design (safe vault icons next to BTC balances are a common failure).
  4. Volatility and quote expiry. The 6-second RFQ hold is a UX feature: it forces a conscious accept. When the quote expires, say "price refreshed" and show the delta, not a silent re-lock.
  5. Bilingual parity. Arabic search intent for "tadawul al-umlat al-raqamiya fi al-imarat" is legal and how-to heavy. Disclosure that exists only in English fails the clients who need it most. Ship AR and EN strings from the same source keys.

Related reading on trust and Arabic-first flows: seven fintech trust signals and write onboarding in Arabic first.

Order limits, 24/7 trading, and failed-order states

From the KFS and product FAQ, the order machine is:

  • Market orders only (no limit / stop published).
  • RFQ: price held 6 seconds; accept within window or get a refreshed quote.
  • Min USD 50, max USD 50,000 per trade (or AED equivalent).
  • Cannot cancel once executed.
  • Sell proceeds to eligible USD/AED account in real time (per FAQ).
  • Email confirmation within 2–3 minutes; otherwise call support.
  • Service 24/7 subject to planned maintenance; contact centre also 24/7 on the published number.

Product checklist for any bank copying this shape:

  • Limit-aware amount entry: disable amounts outside the band before RFQ, with the band shown in the client's funding currency.
  • Funding-account picker: exclude joint and term-deposit accounts in the UI, matching the KFS, rather than failing after quote.
  • Partial fill / LP failure: SC's risk disclosure notes settlement may be delayed or fail due to liquidity-provider issues. Design an explicit failed-order state with a reference ID, not a spinner that times out into the home screen.
  • Banking hours vs crypto hours: the ledger is 24/7; relationship-manager callbacks are not. Set expectations on advice (there is none — execution only) and on when a human can help with eligibility.
  • Currency switch AED/USD: SC markets seamless switching for deposits and withdrawals between AED and USD. Show FX impact if the funding currency differs from the pair, even when the "fee" line is zero.

Closed-loop custody as a product, not a slogan

SC's custody copy on the product page is unusually specific for a retail wealth page: FIPS 140-2 Level 4 HSMs, air-gapped signing, segregated wallets, 1:1 client assets, SOC/ISO 27001 language. That is good for trust if the client understands the trade-off: institutional custody inside the bank, no self-custody exit.

Design consequences:

  • Portfolio screens should label holdings as "held by Standard Chartered — not transferable on-chain" rather than mimicking an exchange wallet address UI.
  • Offboarding / account-closure must explain forced liquidation risk (the KFS warns that account closure can require liquidation at a loss). That screen is as important as onboarding.
  • Statements: password-protected monthly email statements on the first working day of the next month (per KFS). In-app history under Transactions is the day-to-day surface; keep them consistent.
  • Incident UX: if the bank suspends access because ID documents are stale (KFS warning), the client needs a path to update documents without discovering the freeze only when they try to sell into a crash.

For regional contrast on stablecoin and card rails — different products, same need for plain-language custody and issuance UX — see Reap × Visa stablecoin cards and Foloosi's CBUAE IPA.

Regulatory map: who regulates what in the UAE

A short map for product teams (verify against the regulator pages before you ship copy):

  • VARA (Dubai): virtual-asset service providers across Dubai mainland and free zones except DIFC. SC's Broker-Dealer VASP licence and Rain's Exchange + Broker-Dealer licence sit here. Marketing, disclosures and investor-class conditions follow VARA rulebooks for the licensed activity.
  • CBUAE: banks and payment tokens / payment services under federal central-bank rules. SC Bank UAE remains a CBUAE-licensed bank; the crypto brokerage activity described here is the VARA-licensed overlay the bank itself discloses.
  • SCA / CMA: capital-markets promotion and related registrations; SC's product page notes CMA licensing for promotion activity and shows a CMA-VASP registration number on the VARA register entry.
  • ADGM FSRA / DIFC DFSA: free-zone financial services regimes with their own VA frameworks — relevant when your custody or tokenisation rail is in those zones (Zodia Custody / institutional products), not when your client is on SC Mobile under a Dubai VARA Broker-Dealer licence.
  • Federal overlays: UAE PDPL for personal data in onboarding and CIP; tax/FATCA/CRS declarations that SC already lists as registration blockers.

Do not collapse "crypto is legal in the UAE" into one sentence without naming the licence class. Arabic how-to content that says only "masmuh" (allowed) without naming Broker-Dealer vs Exchange vs Payment Token is how users end up on the wrong product.

What UAE banks and Saudi / Egypt teams can and cannot copy

Can copy as product patterns (with your own licence):

  • KFS-first publishing: put eligibility, spread, order limits and no-transfer rules in a dated Key Facts Statement linked from the product page, in EN and AR.
  • RFQ with short quote hold as a volatility and consent device.
  • Eligibility empty states that name the missing criterion.
  • Closed-loop vs withdrawable wallet as an explicit product choice, disclosed up front.
  • Naming the licensed legal entity on the trade screen (bank or partner VASP).

Cannot copy without the right licence and entity:

  • Offering exchange-style order books or margin under a Broker-Dealer-only banking licence.
  • Serving retail clients under a "Qualified / Professional Investors only" licence condition.
  • Implying deposit protection or bank-guarantee language for VA holdings.
  • Moving client VA to a third-party VASP without the permissions and disclosures that requires.
  • Reusing SC's AED 4 million / risk-rating >5 thresholds as if they were law; they are SC's published product criteria.

Saudi and Egypt teams reading this for inspiration should map to SAMA / local VA rules and FRA / CBE respectively — the SC pattern is a UAE VARA + bank stack, not a portable licence. Open-finance consent patterns for agent-driven payments remain a separate design track; see agentic payments UX in MENA and open banking consent UX.

Metrics a product team should instrument from day one

  • Funnel: tile seen → eligibility pass → CIP complete → first RFQ → first fill.
  • Quote-accept rate within 6 seconds vs refresh count (are quotes too wide?).
  • Spread realised vs the "up to 2%" ceiling (compliance and fairness).
  • Failed RFQs / LP errors by hour (24/7 ops).
  • Sell latency to fiat credit.
  • Empty-state reasons mix (PI vs risk profile vs account type vs documents).
  • Complaints tagged "thought I could withdraw" and "thought fees were zero".
  • AR vs EN help-centre deflection on eligibility.

A readiness checklist for a UAE bank product team

If you are scoping a peer product, use this as a go/no-go list before engineering capacity is booked:

  1. Dated bilingual Key Facts Statement covering eligibility, cost, order limits and transfer rules.
  2. Confirmation screen that shows spread-in-price, not only a "no fees" badge.
  3. Eligibility empty state that explains the missing criterion in Arabic and English before the apply flow.
  4. Licensed entity name and licence reference in the trade-screen footer.
  5. State machine for sell-allowed / buy-blocked when eligibility changes.
  6. Account-closure path that explains possible forced liquidation.
  7. Instrumentation for funnel, realised spread, LP failures and "thought I could withdraw" complaints.
  8. Legal sign-off on any deposit-protection wording before vault iconography ships.
  9. Bilingual QA on every error string, including quote expiry and LP failure.
  10. 24/7 maintenance playbook with customer-visible status copy.

Why Arabic search intent matters for this launch

Google autocomplete on 15 October 2026 for the Arabic seed "tadawul al-umlat al-raqamiya fi al-imarat" clustered around platforms, law, penalties, whether trading is allowed, and best platforms. English seeds for "standard chartered crypto" still skew toward price predictions and research, while "uae crypto trading" and "is crypto trading legal in uae" show consumer how-to intent. The Arabic gap is not another price article; it is a plain explanation of licence class, eligibility, closed-loop custody and cost-in-spread, written so a product team and a cautious client can both use it. Relative X activity on 14 October UTC for Standard Chartered + UAE/VARA + bitcoin/ether/crypto showed a sharp same-day spike versus the prior week — a reminder that news demand and product-documentation demand peak together, and documentation that ships a day late still ranks.

Limits of this article / what we could not verify

  • We read the English KFS PDF and the SC UAE product page on 15 October 2026 from the box. We did not complete an authenticated SC Mobile session, so in-app microcopy and exact empty-state strings are inferred from the public FAQ and KFS, not screenshotted.
  • The Client Agreement PDFs are linked from the product page; we downloaded the English agreement for archive but this article relies on the KFS and product FAQ for client-facing numbers rather than reproducing agreement clauses.
  • "No deposit protection" is widely stated in secondary coverage; the KFS stresses loss risk and that this is not advice, and the product is clearly a VA holding rather than a deposit — we do not invent a statutory citation we did not open. Teams should confirm the exact deposit-protection wording with counsel before shipping it.
  • Rain's company announcement URL returned 404 from this network on 15 October 2026; licence fields are taken from the VARA public register. Margin trading and retail/qualified/institutional permission are attributed to Rain's 13 October announcement as reported by Fintech News UAE and similar outlets — treat as secondary until the company page is reachable again.
  • Zodia Custody ADGM / tokenised money-market claims from 12–14 October secondary coverage were not re-verified against a Zodia primary PDF on 15 October; we mention the custody-map idea without asserting those licence details.
  • Liv's "zero trading fee" is the public marketing claim with "terms apply"; we did not retrieve Liv's full fee schedule.
  • CBUAE Rulebook pages have been intermittently unreachable from this network on recent days; we do not assert Payment Token article numbers in this piece.
  • This is not financial advice. It is a product, UX and regulatory reading for teams building or competing with bank-distributed crypto.

Frequently asked questions

Who can use Standard Chartered crypto trading in the UAE?

Per the bank's Key Facts Statement: existing Standard Chartered UAE clients with valid UAE residency, age above 21, classification as Professional Investor (investor risk-profile rating more than 5 and banking relationship of AED 4 million and above), and an eligible AED or USD account. Joint and term-deposit accounts cannot fund trades or receive sale proceeds. The VARA licence condition on the public register is "Permitted to serve Qualified Investors."

What does it cost — are there really no fees?

The product page and KFS say there are no separate transaction or custody fees. The KFS also states that a spread of up to 2.00% is levied on the final price shown to the client. Cost is in the price, not on a fee line. Minimum order USD 50; maximum USD 50,000 per trade (or AED equivalent).

Can I withdraw Bitcoin to my own wallet?

No. The KFS and product FAQ state that clients cannot transfer crypto holdings into or out of the Standard Chartered ecosystem. It is a closed-loop buy, hold and sell service inside the bank.

Is crypto trading legal in the UAE, and who regulates Standard Chartered's offering?

Virtual-asset activity in Dubai is regulated by VARA. Standard Chartered Bank holds an active VARA VASP licence VL/26/08/003 for Broker-Dealer Services (issued 24 August 2026). The bank remains a CBUAE-licensed bank. Other activities (payment tokens, free-zone regimes, federal promotion rules) sit under different authorities — the licence class matters.

How is this different from Liv Crypto or ruya Bitcoin?

SC is a closed-loop bank Broker-Dealer with in-house custody under its own VARA licence. Liv's public page presents crypto in the Liv X app in partnership with Aquanow ME FZE (VARA VL/24/01/001). ruya presents Shari'ah-compliant Bitcoin investing in-app with Fuze documentation. Different licence shapes, custody models and target clients — compare the KFS and partner disclosures, not only the bank brand.

Sources

  • Standard Chartered press release, 14 October 2026: Standard Chartered unveils first-of-its-kind cryptocurrency trading solution for affluent clients
  • Standard Chartered UAE product page: Crypto Trading
  • Key Facts Statement (English): Crypto-KFS-English.pdf
  • Key Facts Statement (Arabic): Crypto-KFS-Arabic.pdf
  • Cryptocurrency Service Client Agreement (English): PDF
  • VARA public register — Standard Chartered Bank (VL/26/08/003): vara.ae
  • VARA public register — Rain MENA FZE (VL/26/10/001): vara.ae
  • Liv Crypto (Aquanow ME FZE, VL/24/01/001): liv.me
  • ruya Bitcoin Investment: ruyabank.ae
  • Secondary context only: CoinDesk, 14 October 2026; Fintech News UAE on Rain (14 October 2026)
  • Hero photograph: King Abdullah Financial District, Riyadh — Ahmed (Wikimedia Commons), CC BY-SA 4.0; file page

title: Processing 10k Concurrent RFID Payments at the Edge: Go, SQLite WAL, and EPC Gen 2
description:
When engineering fintech and access control infrastructure for large-scale physical events, standard cloud architectures eventually hit a hard physical wall.

Under the Saudi Vision 2030 events strategy, mega-summits in Riyadh and Jeddah regularly process upwards of 10,000 delegates. At these scales, the operational realities of a crowded convention center break traditional web systems:

  1. Saturated Networks: As thousands of delegates stream through the doors, local cellular macrocells congest and venue Wi-Fi suffers catastrophic packet loss.
  2. Concurrency Bursts: 80% of gate traffic and 60% of food and beverage (F&B) purchases happen during narrow 30-to-45-minute windows (e.g., morning ingress and keynote breaks)[cite: 14].

If your event analytics platform or POS system relies on a synchronous HTTP handshake to a remote PostgreSQL database to open a turnstile or process a payment, it will fail under burst load.

To guarantee sub-second transaction times and zero gate downtime, we redesigned our RFID attendee tracking and cashless event payments architecture entirely around Edge Persistence and Dual-Frequency hardware.

Here is how we built it.

1. Dual-Frequency Credentials (UHF + HF)

The foundation of our architecture is a single physical smart credential (either a sub-3-second on-demand thermal badge or a durable silicone wristband).

We abandoned optical QR codes entirely. Instead, each credential contains a dual-frequency inlay with two distinct memory chips:

  • Passive UHF EPC Gen 2 (865–868 MHz): Used strictly for zero-contact spatial tracking. Overhead RFID portals read these tags at distances up to 8 meters. Using dynamic Q-algorithm arbitration (Frame-Slotted ALOHA), a single portal can resolve up to 400 tag collisions per second, tracking venue capacity and sponsor dwell times without attendees ever breaking stride.
  • Near-Field HF (13.56 MHz / NFC): Used for explicit intent actions, such as tapping to process a cashless payment at a vendor terminal or tapping to access a restricted ministerial VIP lounge.

2. Offline-First POS Architecture with SQLite WAL

If a vendor's Point-of-Sale terminal has to query an external cloud API to verify a wristband's wallet balance, the F&B queue will grind to a halt the moment venue Wi-Fi drops.

We pushed the financial ledger down to the edge. Each physical POS terminal and gate controller runs an embedded SQLite database in Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode[cite: 14].


sql
-- POS Edge Node Initialization
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;
PRAGMA temp_store = MEMORY;

-- Local Ledger Schema
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS edge_transactions (
    txn_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    wallet_uid TEXT NOT NULL,
    vendor_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    amount INTEGER NOT NULL, -- Stored in base currency units (Halalas)
    epoch_ms INTEGER NOT NULL,
    sync_state INTEGER DEFAULT 0
);
Sub-Millisecond Tap-to-PayWhen a delegate taps their wristband to buy a coffee:The local NFC reader validates the cryptographically signed offline balance directly from the HF chip's secure memory sector.   

The transaction is appended to the local SQLite WAL companion file in under 4 milliseconds.   The physical UI updates instantly, completing the transaction.

A background Go daemon running on the terminal continuously monitors network health. When the internet connection is stable, it asynchronously flushes the committed transactions in batches to our central cloud API. If the internet drops, the terminal keeps selling.

3. Cloud Ingestion with Go & Redis StreamsTo handle the asynchronous telemetry bursts coming from hundreds of offline-resilient edge nodes, we use a Go-based ingestion layer backed by Redis Streams[cite: 14].Gopackage main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "[github.com/redis/go-redis/v9](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/v9)"
)

var ctx = context.Background()
var rdb *redis.Client

type SyncBatch struct {
    Transactions []CashlessTxn `json:"transactions"`
}

func ingestEdgeBatch(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    var batch SyncBatch
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&batch); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, err.Error(), 400)
        return
    }

    pipe := rdb.Pipeline()
    for _, txn := range batch.Transactions {
        // Push to in-memory Redis Stream buffer
        pipe.XAdd(ctx, &redis.XAddArgs{
            Stream: "stream:cashless_ingestion",
            Values: map[string]interface{}{
                "txn_id": txn.TxnID,
                "wallet": txn.Wallet,
                "amount": txn.Amount,
                "vendor": txn.VendorID,
            },
        })
    }

    if _, err := pipe.Exec(ctx); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "Ingestion Failed", 500)
        return
    }

    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
}
By pushing telemetry directly into an in-memory stream buffer, we completely decouple our primary PostgreSQL database from the extreme write contention caused by hardware synchronization bursts.4. Live Command via WebSocketsA worker pool consumes the Redis Streams, applies idempotent deduplication logic based on the txn_id, and computes rolling spatial and financial aggregations.

These metrics are then broadcasted via WebSockets directly to our KSA custom reporting dashboard. 

Event directors and financial controllers gain instant visibility into live vendor settlements, peak F&B purchasing windows, and civil defense hall capacities, all without aggressively polling the database.

ConclusionBuilding physical event technology requires acknowledging that venue networks will fail[cite: 1, 14]. By treating cloud connectivity as an eventual luxury rather than a strict requirement, we guarantee continuous ingress and revenue generation.

To explore how these architectures are deployed in the field across GCC exhibitions, review the hardware integration models behind StampIQ's cashless payments for events and their real-time event analytics platform.

title: I Looked at Countdown Timers as a Shopper and a Web Developer
description:
I noticed something about the way I shop online: when a website tells me an offer is about to expire, I suddenly feel like I need to make a decision.

A product I wasn't particularly interested in can start looking tempting when a message appears saying, "Only 10 minutes left."

That got me thinking about something beyond shopping. How much can a small element of web design influence the decisions we make online?

I wanted to explore the relationship between countdown timers and impulse buying, look at how these timers work from a web development perspective, and understand what makes an online shopping experience helpful rather than unnecessarily stressful.

The Same Product Feels Different With a Countdown Time

I compared two shopping scenarios to understand how the presence of a timer might affect my thinking.

In the first scenario, I find a jacket online without any special offer or deadline. I can check its price, compare alternatives, read reviews, and decide whether I actually need it.

In the second scenario, I find the same jacket with a countdown timer showing that a discount will soon expire.

Suddenly, my attention shifts. Instead of asking whether the jacket is worth buying, I start thinking about whether I'll miss the deal.

The product hasn't changed. The interface has.

This wasn't a controlled experiment, and I didn't measure actual purchases. It was a way to examine how urgency might influence my own decision-making.

Still, it left me with a useful question: would I want this product just as much if the timer weren't there?

Why Countdown Timers Matter in E-Commerce UX

Countdown timers are widely used in flash sales, seasonal promotions, and limited-time offers. From a web development perspective, they're relatively simple interface elements that can have an important effect on how users experience a website.

They communicate urgency, draw attention to a deadline, and encourage users to consider an offer before it expires.

When the deadline is genuine, that information can be useful. If a promotion really ends at midnight, displaying the remaining time helps shoppers understand the offer's terms.

The problem arises when urgency becomes more important than clarity.

A timer that resets every time someone refreshes a page, or an offer that repeatedly claims to be ending soon, can make it difficult for shoppers to understand whether a deadline is real.

That's where I think developers need to look beyond whether an interface element attracts clicks. They should also consider whether it gives users accurate information and allows them to make informed decisions.

Research published in the Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics has examined the relationship between countdown timers and impulse buying in online group-buying situations. This provides useful context for understanding why urgency deserves attention in e-commerce design.

It doesn't mean every timer causes an impulse purchase, but it does raise an interesting question about the responsibility that comes with designing persuasive interfaces.

A Simple JavaScript Countdown Timer

I also wanted to look at the technical side of the feature.

At its simplest, a JavaScript countdown calculates the time remaining and updates the display at regular intervals. Here's a basic example:

Offer ends in 10:00

let remainingSeconds = 10 * 60;

const countdown = document.getElementById("countdown");

const interval = setInterval(() => {
const minutes = Math.floor(remainingSeconds / 60);
const seconds = remainingSeconds % 60;

countdown.textContent =
  `Offer ends in minutes:`+`{String(seconds).padStart(2, "0")}`;

remainingSeconds--;

if (remainingSeconds < 0) {
  clearInterval(interval);
  countdown.textContent = "Offer period ended";
}

}, 1000);

This is only a front-end demonstration. The timer starts again if the page is reloaded, so it shouldn't be used as the source of truth for a real promotion.

For a production e-commerce website, I'd use a fixed deadline supplied by the server, calculate the remaining time from that deadline, and verify the promotion's validity on the server when the user checks out.

That distinction matters because a timer should accurately represent the offer, not simply create the appearance of scarcity.

What I'd Consider Before Adding a Countdown to a Website

If I were implementing a countdown timer for an online store, I'd consider a few things beyond the visual design.

1. Is the deadline real?

The timer should represent an actual promotion end time. A countdown that resets indefinitely can mislead users.

2. What happens when the timer reaches zero?

The website should clearly explain that the offer has ended and ensure that the displayed price and checkout conditions reflect the actual promotion.

3. Does the timer improve the user experience?

A useful deadline indicator provides information. Repeated pop-ups, flashing messages, or exaggerated warnings can distract users from comparing products and understanding the offer.

4. Is the timer accessible?

Frequently announcing every second to screen readers would be disruptive. The implementation should communicate important changes without creating unnecessary accessibility problems.

These details might seem small, but they influence whether the feature feels informative or manipulative.

How I Apply This Thinking When Shopping

Thinking about the design behind countdown timers also changed the questions I ask myself before buying something.

When I come across a limited-time offer, I try to step back and consider whether I wanted the product before seeing the promotion.

I also compare the final price, check delivery costs, and think about whether the purchase fits my budget.

While exploring ways to make more deliberate shopping decisions, I came across the Impulse Buying Evaluator Tool created by shopping platform RabattDigga. It connects with the question I was exploring: how can shoppers pause and reconsider a purchase instead of reacting immediately to an offer?

For example, if I see a jacket advertised at 30% off, I'd ask myself whether I was already planning to buy one and whether the final price is genuinely competitive.

If I can't answer those questions, waiting is often more sensible than rushing to checkout.

I've found one principle particularly useful to remember: saving money on something unnecessary is still spending money.

Four Questions I Ask Before Buying a Limited-Time Deal

I've started using four simple questions when an online offer makes me feel pressured to act quickly.

1. Did I Want This Before Seeing the Timer?

If the product was already on my shopping list, the discount might be worth investigating.

If I discovered it only because of a countdown banner, I think more carefully about why I want it.

2. Is the Discount Actually Worth It?

A large percentage discount doesn't automatically mean a good price. Comparing similar products, delivery charges, and recent price history can help put the offer into perspective.

3. Would I Still Buy It Tomorrow?

For non-essential purchases, waiting can help distinguish genuine interest from temporary excitement.

4. Does It Fit My Budget?

I consider the total checkout cost instead of focusing only on the advertised savings. A discount isn't useful if it pushes me to spend money I need for something else.

What This Taught Me About Web Development and Shopping

The interesting thing about countdown timers is that they sit at the intersection of technology, psychology, and design.

A developer can implement a timer in just a few lines of JavaScript. But deciding how that timer should behave, what it communicates, and whether it helps users make informed choices requires more thought.

From a shopper's perspective, the lesson is equally simple: urgency isn't the same as value.

A countdown can tell me when an offer ends, but it can't tell me whether I need the product or whether buying it makes financial sense.

I don't think countdown timers are inherently bad. When they're accurate and transparent, they can communicate useful information. The challenge is designing them in a way that respects the person using the website.

Key Takeaway

The next time I see a countdown timer, I'll try to evaluate the product before thinking about the deadline.

I'll compare the price, consider whether I actually need it, and decide whether it fits my budget.

And if the offer expires while I'm thinking, I haven't necessarily missed a bargain. I may simply have avoided an unnecessary purchase.

As someone interested in web development, I also think it's worth remembering that the interfaces we build can influence real decisions. Good UX shouldn't just encourage people to click faster; it should help them understand what they're choosing.

If you build e-commerce websites, how do you approach countdown timers? Do you see them as useful UX elements, or do you think they can create unnecessary pressure? I'd be interested to hear how other developers approach this trade-off.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

hybrid v1.17.0

On September 14, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, 1.17.0.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a minor release: The container images used in minor releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a minor via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) support

Apigee hybrid now supports Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open protocol that lets agentic AI applications use your APIs as tools through managed MCP endpoints. Apigee hybrid routes, authorizes, and secures these MCP tool calls the same way it manages your other APIs, so you don't need to run or maintain your own MCP servers.

MCP support is an optional feature that is not enabled by default. You must explicitly enable it in your Apigee hybrid configuration.

For more information, see Model Context Protocol (MCP) overview, Enable MCP for Apigee hybrid, and the MCP quickstart.

Feature

Root CA certificate rotation

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 lets you rotate the root certificate authority (CA) certificate that anchors trust for TLS communication between your runtime components. You can now replace the root CA before it expires, without downtime.

For more information, see Rotate the root CA.

Feature

TLS 1.3 support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 adds support for TLS 1.3, a newer version of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol that offers faster connection handshakes and stronger security than earlier TLS versions.

For information about configuring TLS on the ingress gateway, see Configuring TLS and mTLS on the Apigee ingress gateway.

Feature

Forward proxy support for AI policies

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 adds forward proxy support for AI policies, such as the Model Armor and semantic caching policies. Outbound calls from these policies can now be routed through an HTTP forward proxy.

For more information, see Configure a forward proxy, Get started with the Model Armor policies, and Get started with semantic caching policies.

Feature

Semantic cache Private Service Connect (PSC) endpoint support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 adds Private Service Connect (PSC) endpoint support for semantic caching. The semantic caching policies can now reach their backing services over a Private Service Connect endpoint, which keeps that traffic on your private network.

For more information, see Configure semantic caching over Private Service Connect.

Feature

Semantic cache distance measure support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 adds support for non-default Vertex AI Vector Search distance measures in the SemanticCacheLookup policy. A new optional <DistanceMeasureType> element accepts DOT_PRODUCT_DISTANCE (the default, and the existing behavior), COSINE_DISTANCE, SQUARED_L2_DISTANCE, and L1_DISTANCE. The policy compares <Threshold> in the direction the declared measure implies, so declaring a non-default measure requires re-tuning the threshold in the same edit.

For more information, see SemanticCacheLookup policy.

Feature

Reduced service account permissions

Apigee hybrid v1.17.0 reduces the Google Cloud IAM permissions that Apigee service accounts require. Service accounts that use Cloud Storage now require only the storage.objects.get and storage.objects.create permissions rather than the broader Storage Admin (roles/storage.admin) role. The Cassandra components also no longer run with the privileged: true security context.

For more information about service accounts, see Create service accounts.

Security

Various security and CVE fixes are included in this release.

Backup and DR

Feature

You can now monitor restore jobs for Filestore instances directly from the Backup and DR Jobs page in the Google Cloud console. When you trigger a restore on a Filestore instance, Backup and DR automatically tracks the job progress and status.

For more information, see Restore a Filestore instance from a backup vault and Monitor backup and restore jobs in Google Cloud console.

BigQuery

An updated version of the Simba ODBC driver for BigQuery is now available.

Feature

Metadata for BigQuery Graph is automatically ingested and searchable in Knowledge Catalog. This feature is available in preview.

Feature

You can now include a WHERE clause inside of an aggregate function call to filter your aggregate function input using a boolean expression. This feature is in Preview.

Bigtable

Feature

You can use the Google Cloud console to create, list, and query parameterized views for your Bigtable instances. You can also configure view parameters and run queries in Bigtable Studio. This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Create and manage parameterized views.

Cloud Logging

Feature

Starting with version 2.71.0, you can use an Ops Agent configuration option to export your metrics, logs, and traces by using the OpenTelemetry-based Telemetry API rather than by using the Cloud Monitoring API, Logging API, or Trace API. For more information, see Use the Telemetry API.

Cloud Monitoring

Feature

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Feature

You can use the pg_textsearch extension in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL to perform full-text search using the industry-standard BM25 (Best Matching 25) scoring algorithm for highly accurate relevance scoring.

This extension requires PostgreSQL 17 or later and is supported on PostgreSQL release R20260712.01_06 or later.

For more information, see Full-text search using pg_textsearch.

Cloud SQL for SQL Server

Starting on October 13, 2027, SQL Server 2017 will reach end of life (EOL) and Microsoft will stop releasing security updates. Cloud SQL for SQL Server will stop supporting SQL Server 2017 after this date.

For more information, see Database versions and version policies.

Cloud Workstations

Compute Engine

Feature

For more information, see Create and manage regional disks.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

  • Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (gemini-2.5-flash-image): Deprecated and scheduled for retirement on March 15, 2027 (extended from October 2, 2026). Migrate to Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image).
  • Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image): Retirement date is scheduled for June 28, 2027 or later.

For more information, see Gemini model versions and lifecycle.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.7.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Network stream resilience: Improved CLI session stability with automatic reconnection and transient error recovery during long-running scans and remediation workflows.
  • Configuration uniformity: Standardized directory exclusion rules across configuration files and CLI scanning flags under scan_config.exclude_dirs.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed an issue where cm report incorrectly categorized DISMISSED findings as OPEN in the summary table.
    • Resolved sandbox permission denial errors by preventing child worker processes from attempting to create internal session logs on disk.
    • Hardened sandbox command policy to prevent directory traversal and file inspection outside the designated repository root into adjacent directories.

For more information, see CodeMender documentation.

Cyber Verification Program for Claude is available in Preview

Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program (CVP) is available in Preview on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. CVP enables verified organizations to use supported Claude models (Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Opus 5) for legitimate defensive cybersecurity tasks with default dual-use restrictions lifted.

For more information, see Cyber Verification Program for Claude.

This feature is in public preview. You can now use GoogleSQL in Search to query your security data in Google SecOps, offering a flexible and powerful industry-standard alternative to YARA-L 2.0. GoogleSQL is optimized for broad data exploration, statistical aggregation, and deep-dive ad hoc investigations. You can query telemetry tables including but not limited to UDM events, entity graphs, detection rules, and case management data—using either standard declarative SQL or the linear, sequential Piped SQL syntax.

For more information, see Get started with GoogleSQL.

MANDIANT_ACTIVE_BREACH_IOC,MANDIANT_FUSION_IOC, andOPEN_SOURCE_INTEL_IOC` feeds are being removed

The MANDIANT_ACTIVE_BREACH_IOC, MANDIANT_FUSION_IOC, and OPEN_SOURCE_INTEL_IOC feeds are deprecated in favor of the GTI_IOC feed. After March 18, 2027, we will be removing the MANDIANT_ACTIVE_BREACH_IOC, MANDIANT_FUSION_IOC, and OPEN_SOURCE_INTEL_IOC feeds. For more information, see Knowledge Catalog overview.

When adding a new Google Cloud Compute Engine, container, or VM Monitoring Point, Cloud Network Insights lets you generate Google Cloud CLI commands in the Google Cloud console to download Monitoring Point installation bundles.

Parameter Manager supports CRC32C checksums to verify data integrity when you add or access parameter versions.

For more information, see Data integrity assurance.

Data Security Posture Management is deprecated. It will be shut down on February 1, 2027. Learn more about the controls and alternative detection capabilities.

Vertex AI Search

Agent Search: Search query add-ons for configurable pricing (GA)

Search query add-on specifications (searchAddonSpec) for configurable pricing are generally available (GA) in the v1 API. You can use searchAddonSpec when you want to save money by turning off add-ons for individual search requests made programmatically.

Change

For the July 2026 data release (published mid-September 2026), we have upgraded the carbon model to version 17 and implemented the following updates:

Updating Scope 1 & 3 Emissions from Google's Corporate Footprint

  • Allocation factor refresh: Updated Scope 1 and Scope 3 allocation factors using company-wide data from the 2026 Google Environmental Report.
  • Methodology application: For details on how corporate Scope 1 and Scope 3 emissions are distributed across cloud products and services, refer to the non-electricity emission sources section of the methodology documentation.

Updating Inputs for Scope 2 Market-Based Emissions Calculations

  • Updated annual renewable electricity allocation percentages in accordance with the 2026 Google Environmental Report.
  • Refreshed background annual emissions factors using updated government data sources across Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3. Note that Scope 2 location-based emissions continue to be calculated using hourly greenhouse gas emission factors. Learn more in the Scope 2 market-based allocation documentation.
  • Incorporated marketplace purchases of Granular Certificates covering a significant portion of electricity load across carbon-intensive regions.
  • Granular certificate purchases represent market-based accounting allocations. Customers seeking to minimize emissions are encouraged to prioritize regions with high Carbon Free Energy (CFE) scores for new workloads.

Regional Accounting & Boundary Updates

  • Aligned European clean energy matching boundaries with updated RE100 criteria.
  • Corrected country mapping configurations in annual emission factor scripts to resolve historical data discrepancies across select Asian market regions (e.g., asia-east2, asia-northeast3).

To correct your July emissions data, schedule a manual data backfill for the month.

Canonical mode provides higher data fidelity by explicitly labeling every BSON type to prevent precision loss during data exchange.

Filestore

Feature

Small capacity Filestore instances for the Regional service tier are generally available (GA). Small capacity instances start at 100 GiB and scale in 1 GiB increments, providing an option for development, testing, and applications with low traffic or basic storage needs.

Feature

Filestore agent volumes provide managed, high-density elastic NFS storage backed by regional volume pools for stateful AI agent sandboxes, autonomous agent fleets, and multi-agent developer environments.

The Filestore agent volumes feature is available to all Google Cloud customers for evaluation and non-production use. To request access for your Google Cloud project, submit the Filestore agent volumes access request form. Announcement

New minor engine versions released for the retail line of business within the v004.005, v004.009, and v004.010 version lines (aml-retail.default.v004.005.202608-000, aml-retail.default.v004.009.202608-000, and aml-retail.default.v004.010.202608-000). These versions extend support for the major engine version and include no significant changes compared to the previous minor versions.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.16.10

On September 17, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.16.10.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.16.10.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
556750755 Fixed an issue where EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) dropped or truncated events following a large (>16 KB) event under load on the http-adaptor datapath.
547712217 Fixed an issue where EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) responses larger than 16 KB could be truncated or corrupted across socket reads.
519729209 Fixed a SAML XML Signature Wrapping (XSW) vulnerability in the ValidateSAMLAssertion policy.
514384893 Hardened the Script policy to block server-side request forgery (SSRF) to link-local addresses.
505645076 Fixed a security issue in the OAuthV2 policy to prevent unauthorized token injection via HTTP form parameters.
505543289 Fixed thread-safety issues in the Netty client connection pool and channel lifecycle.
503817773 Improved security in the OAuthV2 policy implicit grant redirect_uri validation.
502268966 Apigee hybrid now supports optional decoding of percent-encoded path separators (%2F and %5C) before flow selection via the request.path.decode.encoded.separators proxy property.
480770263 Fixed an issue in the SpikeArrest policy to handle edge cases that previously caused NullPointerException and 500 errors.
472526232 Improved SAML assertion validation in the ValidateSAMLAssertion policy against entity and comment injection.
470375542 Fixed a memory leak in WSFrameDecoder that could result in a spike in 503 responses with no_healthy_upstream errors.
449228485 Apigee hybrid now supports configuring custom Kubernetes PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable or maxUnavailable) values for Apigee hybrid components in your overrides.yaml file.
402250928 Apigee hybrid now supports routing outbound calls from AI policies, such as the Model Armor and semantic caching policies, through an HTTP forward proxy.

Feature

Kubernetes 1.36 support

Apigee hybrid v1.16.10 adds support for Kubernetes 1.36 on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Google Distributed Cloud Virtual for VMware (vSphere), Google Distributed Cloud Virtual for bare metal, Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, and Rancher Kubernetes Engine (RKE2).

For more information, see Supported platforms.

Feature

Forward proxy support for AI policies

Apigee hybrid v1.16.10 adds forward proxy support for AI policies, such as the Model Armor and semantic caching policies. Outbound calls from these policies can now be routed through an HTTP forward proxy.

For more information, see Configure a forward proxy, Get started with the Model Armor policies, and Get started with semantic caching policies.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Change

Cloud SQL for MySQL now automatically enables point-in-time recovery (PITR) in a separate, asynchronous operation after disaster recovery (DR) switchover and replica failover operations complete. Because PITR enablement no longer blocks switchover and replica failover, these operations complete faster, helping you reduce your recovery time.

For more information, see Use advanced disaster recovery (DR).

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL now automatically enables point-in-time recovery (PITR) in a separate, asynchronous operation after disaster recovery (DR) switchover and replica failover operations complete. Because PITR enablement no longer blocks switchover and replica failover, these operations complete faster, helping you reduce your recovery time.

For more information, see Use advanced disaster recovery (DR).

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4D machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by AMD EPYC Turin processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4D instances are purpose-built for low core usage and high storage density workloads such as:

  • SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • Data analytics and data warehouses
  • Search
  • Parallel file systems for AI/ML

The Z4D machine series delivers up to 3 TB of memory and 42,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4D also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4D instances are available in predefined standardlssd and highlssd machine shapes.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Gemini Enterprise

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini Code Assist availability update for subscriptions

If you're getting a new Gemini Enterprise Standard or Plus subscription or renewing an existing subscription online, the subscription no longer includes access to Gemini Code Assist features. Existing subscriptions that include Gemini Code Assist features can still access the features until the end of their subscription term.

Instead of Gemini Code Assist, you can use Antigravity for IDEs with AI developer tools. For more information, see AI developer tools overview.

If you're still looking to use Gemini Code Assist with your Gemini Enterprise licenses, you can obtain a new Gemini Enterprise subscription that includes Gemini Code Assist by contacting Google Cloud sales.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Voice input for the chat box

You can speak your queries and prompts to Gemini Enterprise. Use the microphone button to record your voice, review and edit the transcribed text, and then submit the text.

This feature is generally available (GA). To make voice input available to users, a Gemini Enterprise administrator must turn on the Enable speech-to-text toggle in the Google Cloud console.

For more information, see the following:

  • Manage web app features
  • Chat with the assistant

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini Omni Flash supports stateful and streaming video generation (Preview)

Gemini Omni Flash supports stateful (store: true) and server-sent event (SSE) streaming (stream: true) video generation in the Interactions API in Preview. You can temporarily store generated videos and interaction state on the server, stream status updates and final outputs over an SSE connection, or retrieve completed asynchronous interactions using unary or streaming GET requests.

For more information, see Generate videos from text.

Google Cloud Armor

Feature

Cloud Armor managed rulesets protect your backend services and APIs from a wide range of web application threats using threat signatures which are automatically kept up-to-date. For more information, see Managed rules overview. This feature is available in Preview.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.34.900-gke.135 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade a cluster. Google Distributed Cloud 1.34.900-gke.135 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.900-gke.135:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between Reconciling and Running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density than the user cluster.
  • Updated etcd to v3.5.33-0-gke.3 to address security vulnerabilities CVE-2026-46595 and CVE-2026-39821.
  • Fixed an issue where gkectl diagnose and preflight validations failed to locate PersistentVolume datastores for user clusters deployed in a separate vSphere datacenter from the admin cluster (cpNodesInAdminDatacenter: true).
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a cluster could get stuck because the node pool controller attempted to recreate machine resources while deletion was in progress.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.34.900-gke.135 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.34.900-gke.135 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.900-gke.135:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where the status for Ingress resources was not updated when using bundled Ingress.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster had a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.
  • Updated etcd to v3.5.33-0-gke.3 to address security vulnerabilities CVE-2026-46595 and CVE-2026-39821.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a cluster could get stuck because the node pool controller attempted to recreate machine resources while cluster deletion was in progress.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.18 will roll out to Looker (original) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected deployment start: Monday, September 21, 2026
  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 4, 2026

Looker 26.18 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where custom content theme fonts were improperly applied to the Look edit mode bar. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where downloading a dashboard as a CSV or ZIP file could result in a 500 error if any dashboard elements lacked an explicit title. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where links created using the LookML link parameter could return a 500 error if no label was specified. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dashboard filter token chips didn't display an active highlighted background when a filter value was selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the Git connection test could fail to recognize Git credentials as sufficient if a branch protection rule on the Git provider restricted temporary branches. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where analytic models that referenced cross-database, schema-qualified, or dot-delimited table names failed to compile in BigQuery and Snowflake DDL generation. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where custom tooltips in Single Record visualizations appeared at the bottom of the Explore panel rather than directly beneath the selected row. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dashboard filter tokens and popover menus could fail to inherit fonts from custom themes. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dragging series between Y-axes on pivoted Cartesian charts could cause the Explore page to crash or prevent visualization configurations from being saved. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed in Explores where you couldn't scroll within the Chart Config Editor dialog when editing JSON visualization configurations. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where scheduled PDF deliveries to Cloud Storage could produce corrupted files and unexpectedly replace spaces in filenames with underscores. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where attempting to visualize pivoted query results in SQL Runner resulted in a TypeError configuration error. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

API requests that target a LookML project whose files or directories aren't found on the instance now return a 404 Not Found error instead of a 500 Internal Server Error.

Fixed

In Conversational Analytics, the Open in Explore button and sidebar exploration links are now hidden or disabled with explanatory tooltips when you lack explore permissions for the underlying model.

Fixed

The embed preload page now supports custom theming using the theme URL query parameter.

Fixed

Donut Multiples visualizations now automatically hide overlapping value labels.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed in self-service analytics where CSV and Excel uploads to BigQuery and Snowflake could fail or corrupt data when files contained multiline headers, leading numeric characters, UTF-8 BOM markers, or special characters. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where creating a shared branch based on the production branch in a bare repository project could initialize from stale remote commits, causing the Looker IDE to immediately report the branch as being behind production. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where scheduled deliveries intermittently failed with permission errors such as Cannot send all results because user permissions were incorrectly cached across scheduled jobs on worker threads. This feature now performs as expected.

NetApp Volumes

Feature

Organization Policy Service custom constraints are available for Google Cloud NetApp Volumes. You can use custom constraints to control how NetApp Volumes is used in your organization. For example, you can restrict storage pool or volume capacity, or enforce that storage pools are created only with Premium or Extreme service levels.

For more information, see Custom organization policy constraints.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

For Exadata Database Service, Oracle Database@Google Cloud is available in europe-west12 (Turin, Italy) region.

For a list of supported locations, see Supported regions and zones.

Secure Web Proxy

Feature

Secure Web Proxy supports distributed tracing by integrating with Cloud Trace. With distributed tracing, you can track the lifecycle of outbound requests from internal workloads through your Secure Web Proxy gateways to external endpoints. This integration helps you detect latency bottlenecks and troubleshoot connectivity errors.

This feature is available in Preview.

Spanner

Feature

Spanner queues are generally available (GA). Spanner queues provide transactional messaging to help you manage asynchronous work. The feature pairs this capability with the scalability and reliability of Spanner, letting you build event-driven applications. For more information, see the Spanner queues overview.

Cloud Healthcare API

Feature

General availability: You can now bulk-delete specific FHIR resources by resource ID. In the projects.locations.datasets.fhirStores.bulkDelete method, set the new gcsSource.uri field to a Cloud Storage file or wildcard pattern that lists the resources to delete. Each line must use the format {resourceType}/{resourceId}, for example Patient/123. The gcsSource field can't be used with the type or until filters. For more information, see Bulk-deleting FHIR resources by resource ID.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

Managed workload identity for backend mTLS is generally available for the following Application Load Balancers:

  • Global external Application Load Balancers
  • Regional external Application Load Balancers
  • Cross-region internal Application Load Balancers
  • Regional internal Application Load Balancers

The key benefits are as follows:

  • Streamline certificate management: Automated certificate and trust management for backend mTLS through seamless integration with Certificate Authority Service and Certificate Manager.

  • Eliminate operational toil: Certificates are automatically rotated based on the workload identity pool's configuration, removing the complexity and manual bottleneck of private key provisioning and maintenance.

  • Improve visibility and governance: Gain visibility into communication between distributed services and proactively apply governance to workloads across environments.

For more information, see Backend mTLS with managed workload identity overview
