title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
description:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

Read more

title: Your Mentee Has Been Put on a Performance Plan
description:
Your mentee joins the call and does not turn the camera on. After a minute of small talk they say it. Their manager gave them a performance improvement plan yesterday. Sixty days, four written goals, a meeting every Friday. They sound embarrassed to be telling you, and a little afraid of what you will think.

The first thing they need from you is not advice. It is evidence that this conversation is still safe. Say so plainly. Thank you for telling me. This does not change how I see you, and we will work out what to do together.

Then help them read the document properly, because most people only read it once, in shock. Go through each goal and ask the same questions. What exactly would count as meeting this? Who decides? Is there a number, a deadline, an example of what good looks like? Vague goals are common, and a vague goal cannot be met on purpose. Encourage them to ask their manager, in writing and in a calm tone, to make each one concrete.

Be honest about what a plan can mean. In some companies it is a genuine attempt to help someone recover. In others it is mostly paperwork on the way to an exit. You probably cannot tell which from the outside, and neither can they yet. So help them prepare for both without despair. Work hard on the goals as if recovery is possible, and quietly update the CV as if it might not be. Neither one undermines the other.

Help them build a weekly rhythm. A short written note to the manager each Friday, before the meeting, listing what they did against each goal. That record helps them think clearly, and it means the final judgement rests on facts rather than impressions.

Watch their health as well as their work. Sixty days under scrutiny is exhausting, and people on plans often stop sleeping, stop asking questions and start hiding small mistakes, which makes everything worse.

Know your limits. You are not their lawyer, their manager or their HR representative. If something seems unfair, point them to the people who can actually act on it.

And whatever happens at day sixty, stay. People remember who kept turning up while things were going badly.

– Asael Shinder

title: How to Build an Inventory Management Solution That Prevents Stock Drift
description:
A warehouse dashboard can show 120 units available while the picking team finds only 93. The discrepancy may come from delayed order reservations, duplicate webhook events, unrecorded returns, or concurrent updates from multiple sales channels. The result is overselling, failed fulfilment, and replenishment decisions based on incorrect data.

An Inventory Management Solution needs to do more than store stock quantities. It must preserve consistency across receiving, picking, order allocation, returns, and stock adjustments, even when multiple services update inventory simultaneously.

The architectural challenge is deciding which component owns the stock balance, how transactions are applied, and how failed integrations recover without creating duplicate movements. In this guide, we will design a practical inventory workflow using Node.js, PostgreSQL, and asynchronous messaging. For broader warehouse architecture considerations, explore inventory and warehouse management solutions.

Context and Setup

An Inventory Management Solution typically receives updates from e-commerce applications, ERP systems, warehouse management software, and third-party logistics providers. Each system may report a different event, but the inventory service must maintain one consistent view of available stock.

Consider a SKU with 100 units on hand and 15 units already reserved for unfulfilled orders.

The system should calculate:

  • On-hand quantity: 100 units physically recorded in stock.
  • Reserved quantity: 15 units allocated to existing orders.
  • Available quantity: 85 units eligible for new allocations.

A common implementation mistake is storing only a single mutable quantity. Without reservation tracking and transaction history, it becomes difficult to explain why stock changed or safely reverse an operation.

Research published in Management Science by DeHoratius and Raman in 2008 examined nearly 370,000 inventory records across 37 stores of one retailer. The researchers found that 65% of the records were inaccurate. This historical study demonstrates why inventory accuracy must be supported by operational controls rather than assumed from database values alone.

Prerequisites

The example assumes:

  1. Node.js with an asynchronous PostgreSQL driver.
  2. PostgreSQL tables for stock balances, reservations, and inventory movements.
  3. A stable order identifier for deduplicating incoming events.
  4. Database transactions and row-level locking.
  5. A background worker for retrying failed downstream notifications.

Designing an Inventory Management Solution With Transaction Safety

The central design principle is to treat inventory changes as transactions, not independent quantity updates.

Step 1: Define the Inventory Data Model

Store physical stock, reservations, and movement history separately. This provides an auditable record of receiving, dispatches, returns, and adjustments.

A simplified schema could contain:

  • inventory_balance: SKU, warehouse, on-hand quantity, reserved quantity, version.
  • inventory_reservation: order ID, SKU, quantity, reservation status.
  • inventory_movement: movement ID, SKU, quantity delta, reason, reference ID, timestamp.
  • processed_events: event ID and processing status.

Use a composite key on (sku, warehouse_id) to prevent multiple balance records for the same product and location.

The movement table should be append-only for normal operations. Corrections should create compensating movements instead of silently rewriting historical transactions.

Step 2: Apply Stock Changes Atomically

A stock check followed by an independent update creates a race condition. Two checkout requests could both read the same available quantity and reserve more stock than exists.

The following PostgreSQL statement performs a conditional reservation. It assumes inventory_balance contains the SKU's current on-hand and reserved quantities.

-- Why: update only when sufficient unreserved stock exists.
UPDATE inventory_balance
SET reserved_qty = reserved_qty + $1,
    version = version + 1
WHERE sku = $2
  AND warehouse_id = $3
  AND on_hand_qty - reserved_qty >= $1
RETURNING sku, on_hand_qty, reserved_qty, version;
-- No returned row means the reservation was rejected.

Execute this statement inside a database transaction alongside reservation creation, event deduplication, and movement recording. Commit all changes together or roll them back.

The application must also validate that the requested quantity is positive and that the event has not already been processed.

Step 3: Make Event Processing Idempotent

Payment confirmations, order cancellations, and shipping notifications can be delivered more than once. An idempotent consumer ensures that replaying the same event does not apply the same inventory movement twice.

Use a unique constraint on the event identifier and insert the deduplication record within the same database transaction as the stock update.

async function reserveInventory(db, event) {
  const client = await db.connect();

  try {
    await client.query("BEGIN");

    // Why: a unique event ID prevents duplicate processing.
    const result = await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id)
       VALUES ($1)
       ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING
       RETURNING event_id`,
      [event.id]
    );

    if (result.rowCount === 0) {
      await client.query("ROLLBACK");
      return { duplicate: true };
    }

    // Why: the conditional update prevents overselling.
    const stock = await client.query(
      `UPDATE inventory_balance
       SET reserved_qty = reserved_qty + $1,
           version = version + 1
       WHERE sku = $2
         AND warehouse_id = $3
         AND on_hand_qty - reserved_qty >= $1
       RETURNING sku`,
      [event.quantity, event.sku, event.warehouseId]
    );

    if (stock.rowCount === 0) {
      throw new Error("Insufficient stock");
    }

    // Persist the reservation and movement here,
    // using the same transaction and client.
    await client.query("COMMIT");
    return { reserved: true };
  } catch (error) {
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    throw error; // Let the caller retry or handle rejection.
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

This is a simplified reservation example, not a complete production service. Production code must validate payloads, handle database connection failures, distinguish permanent business rejections from transient errors, and ensure reservation and movement records are committed in the same transaction.

Step 4: Separate Database Commits From External Notifications

Do not call a shipping API or publish a message while holding a database transaction open. External requests can time out after the remote service has already processed them.

Instead, use the transactional outbox pattern:

  1. Save the inventory changes and an outbox event in one database transaction.
  2. Let a background worker publish committed outbox events.
  3. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff.
  4. Deduplicate messages at the receiving service.
  5. Monitor outbox age, retry counts, and dead-letter events.

A direct message publish after a database commit is simpler, but a process crash between those operations can lose the notification. The outbox adds storage and worker complexity while making recovery more reliable.

Real-World Application

At Oodles, an inventory implementation should begin by identifying where stock is created, reserved, consumed, and reconciled across connected systems. The appropriate design depends on the existing ERP, warehouse workflows, transaction volume, and integration contracts.

For example, consider a multi-channel retail workflow in which orders arrive through an online store while warehouse staff receive and dispatch stock through a separate system. A suitable implementation would centralize inventory movements, use transactional reservations, deduplicate inbound events, and reconcile warehouse quantities against system balances.

Measure the outcome using baseline and post-deployment data rather than assuming a performance improvement. Useful indicators include reservation failure rate, duplicate movement count, inventory record accuracy, API latency at the 95th percentile, and the time required to recover failed messages.

No verified Oodles project metrics were supplied for this article, so specific before-and-after improvements should be reported only after they have been measured in an actual deployment. You can explore Oodles for more information about its Inventory Management Solution software engineering and integration services.

Conclusion: Key Takeaways

  • Separate stock concepts: Track on-hand, reserved, and available quantities independently.
  • Enforce consistency in the database: Use conditional updates, transactions, and appropriate constraints.
  • Design for duplicate delivery: Make event processing idempotent using stable event identifiers.
  • Recover from integration failures: Use a transactional outbox, retries, and dead-letter handling.
  • Measure operational correctness: Track inventory discrepancies, reservation failures, and recovery times.

1. What is an Inventory Management Solution?

An Inventory Management Solution is software that tracks stock quantities, reservations, receipts, transfers, dispatches, and adjustments across warehouses or sales channels. It helps businesses maintain accurate stock records and coordinate replenishment and order fulfilment.

2. How do you prevent overselling in an inventory system?

Inventory Management Solution Prevent overselling by checking available stock and updating reservations atomically within a database transaction. Use conditional SQL updates or row-level locking, enforce quantity constraints, and ensure concurrent requests cannot reserve more units than are available.

3. Should inventory updates use synchronous APIs or message queues?

Synchronous APIs are useful when an operation requires an immediate reservation decision. Message queues are suitable for downstream notifications, warehouse events, and asynchronous integrations. A transactional outbox can connect committed database changes to reliable event publication.

4. How does an Inventory Management Solution handle duplicate webhooks?

It stores a stable event identifier under a unique database constraint and processes that event within the same transaction as the inventory changes. If the event has already been committed, the consumer skips the duplicate instead of applying the stock movement again.

5. Which metrics should developers monitor in inventory software?

Developers should monitor inventory record accuracy, reservation rejection rates, duplicate event counts, API latency, outbox processing delays, and failed-message retries. These metrics reveal whether the system maintains correct stock balances and recovers effectively from integration failures.

Let's Discuss Your Inventory Architecture

How does your current system handle concurrent reservations, duplicate order events, or inventory reconciliation across warehouses? Share your implementation challenges and questions in the comments.

If you are planning an Inventory Management Solution, discuss your requirements with the Oodles team, including your existing ERP, warehouse workflows, integration points, and consistency requirements.

title: How I Built an Interactive 3D Short Film You Can Talk To
description:
I’ll Call You Later is an interactive 3D short film that runs in the browser, with no install. It takes about four minutes to watch. At the end, you can talk to the character live with your voice.

  • Talk to the character
  • Ask the making-of guide
  • More videos on my YouTube channel

I’m Jas (Jashwanth Palleti). I wrote, directed, performed in, and scored the film, including its English and Telugu music. This is how I built it—and what didn’t work as planned.

The story, and how I approached the build

The film follows a man driving home from work around 9 PM, stuck in traffic in a US tech city. His mom calls. He says, “I’ll call you later.” Then he makes a wish under a set of aligned stars. This is Part 1, and it ends with “to be continued.”

I want to be clear about how the code got written: Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, wrote and ran most of it. My role was technical direction. I decided what to build, what counted as success, and what was off-limits, then directed, debugged, and shipped it.

That distinction matters to me. There’s a lot of technical work in the finished project, but it wasn’t all written by hand. The assistant did most of the coding; I set the constraints and made the calls about what to keep, fix, or abandon.

From phone video to character motion

For my own motion, the process started with phone video. I ran YOLOv8 person detection and a simple IoU tracker, then extracted RTMW’s 133 whole-body keypoints using ONNX Runtime on the GPU.

Those 2D keypoints went into an SMPLify-X-style SMPL-X fitter in PyTorch. It uses a VPoser pose prior, a robust 2D loss, and temporal smoothness. I also recorded a calibration take to fix the body shape. To fit the process into an 8 GB GPU, I split the fitting into chunks.

After fitting, a grounding stage estimates the floor plane from planted feet and uses heel and toe contacts. I then retargeted the result onto the character rig in Blender.

The walk take fitted with a mean reprojection error of 12.9 px. Grounding reduced foot slide from 4.96 to 2.09 mm/frame. Those numbers are useful, but they don’t tell the whole story: at one point the avatar read as tired when I was actually surprised, even though the metrics looked fine.

And one take simply failed. The getting-out-of-the-car motion came out at 302 px error, so I used a Mixamo clip for that shot instead. Library mocap carries most of the full-body motion; my own capture drives the walk style. Knowing when to use an existing licensed asset was better than hand-fixing a take that wasn’t working.

Making the film run in a browser

The film is built with React, React Three Fiber, drei, Three.js, and Vite. One clock drives the experience, which keeps it safe to scrub without the animation and other timed elements getting out of sync.

The visual pipeline combines Blender-baked lighting—night and day bakes blended by sun height—with real sun and moon positions and a 2,600-star sky. On top of that are a custom GLSL colour grade, bloom, vignette, grain, and AgX tone mapping. The crowd is instanced: 190 people on High, 40 on Low.

I added adaptive quality tiers that drop if the frame rate falls below 24 fps. Shader and texture warm-up helped remove stutter. The release cut went from 176 MB to about 95 MB to fit Vercel’s limit, using Draco and WebP, along with phone-sized assets.

Audio uses Web Audio buses with ducking, and the character’s animation uses Rhubarb visemes for lip sync. The site is hosted on Vercel.

One small detail made a big difference during testing: warming up shaders and textures meant the first time they were needed wasn’t also the first time the browser had to prepare them. The project still has limits, but getting rid of that stutter made the experience feel much more deliberate.

Adding a voice conversation

The voice agent runs on LiveKit Agents. A Python worker joins a WebRTC room and connects to OpenAI realtime speech-to-speech. In the browser, livekit-client handles the connection and displays live captions.

A Vercel serverless function signs short-lived, 15-minute LiveKit tokens, so API keys never touch the browser. The agent itself is hosted on LiveKit Cloud.

There are multiple personas on the same pipeline. The character stays in the story, avoids spoilers, and is honest that he’s an AI if asked. The making-of guide answers questions about how the film was built. Tool calls let the character “check his phone,” “read the letters,” or “look around.”

The AI voice also gets live lip sync. About 60 times a second, a Web Audio analyser checks loudness and frequency: loudness opens the jaw, while high frequencies produce S, T, and F shapes. This is an approximation, not phoneme-accurate lip sync.

I measure latency from the end of the user’s speech to the first audio. The things I’d watch closely when building something similar are turn detection, interruptions, and cost per minute. A conversation can feel wrong for reasons that aren’t obvious from the graphics, so I’m interested in feedback on the voice experience in particular.

Recording a trailer from the browser

I also wanted a clean HD trailer without relying on a powerful machine to play the film in real time while recording. I added a render mode that replaces the page’s performance.now and requestAnimationFrame clock with a virtual clock, then steps exactly one frame at a time.

Each frame is encoded in the browser with WebCodecs using H.264, then muxed into an MP4 with mp4-muxer.

That feature exposed a bug in the new top quality tier. It had no texture size limit entry, so textures came out wrong and the character rendered black. The cause was one missing key in a lookup table. Not a complicated rendering mystery—just a small piece of configuration that the new tier didn’t have.

What I learned, and what’s unfinished

A few lessons I’m taking forward:

  • Set acceptance criteria before looking at the results. Metrics can look fine while the performance still reads incorrectly.
  • Don’t optimize only for numbers. The avatar looking tired instead of surprised was a real failure, regardless of the reprojection error.
  • Know when to stop and use an existing licensed asset instead of hand-fixing a take.
  • Read the actual licence file, not the README.

There are limits to what I’ve built. Pipeline stages are run by hand. Telugu lip sync is approximate. The film hasn’t been tested much on real phones; it works best on desktop Chrome with headphones.

I’d like your feedback

If you try it, I’d love to hear what you think about the motion, performance on your device, and the voice conversation. The film is here; you can talk directly to the character here, or ask the making-of guide questions here.

I’m open to roles in real-time 3D, voice AI, and creative tech. More about me: jashtechno.com.

title: Gemini 4 Argon Pricing: Build-and-Measure Checklist Before the 2x Hike
description:
Google put a clock on its cheapest frontier pricing. Gemini 4 Argon went
generally available on October 13, 2026 at $2/$10 per million tokens - and
on December 1 that becomes $4/$20. You have roughly seven weeks of cheap
runway. The teams that win are not the ones who read the pricing page.
They are the ones who prototype now, measure their real per-task cost,
and decide whether Argon earns a place in their stack before the price
doubles. Here is the checklist to do exactly that.

The short answer

Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is Google's new frontier model for deep
multi-step work, generally available since October 13, 2026 at $2 input
and $10 output per million tokens. On December 1, 2026, both rates double.
If you are building anything on it, prototype before November 30, measure
tokens per task with thinking tokens counted as output, and re-price your
workload at $4/$20 before you commit to production.

What actually changed on October 13

Google unveiled Gemini 4 Argon on September 30, 2026, but kept public
access restricted to cybersecurity partners in its Fairwind Program. On
October 13, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google DeepMind's senior vice-president
and Google's chief AI architect, announced the model was "rolling out
today globally" through the paid Gemini API, Google AI Studio, Antigravity
(for Ultra subscribers), the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search (for Pro
and Ultra subscribers), Android Studio, Firebase AI Logic, and Gemini
Enterprise. It is not available on the API's free tier.

Attribution and honesty

The benchmark figures in this post come from two buckets. Google's
launch claims (Vals Index, ERQA, prompt-injection resistance) are
vendor-reported and have not been independently reproduced. The
Artificial Analysis and Terminal Bench 4 scores come from independent
testing reported by outlets covering the launch. Pricing was
cross-checked across VentureBeat, Reuters, the rundown.ai, and datanorth.ai
on October 14-15, 2026. Google's own posts do not prominently state the
December 1 increase; the outlets report it as confirmed.

Argon is the first model in the Gemini 4 generation. Google positions it
for long-horizon, multi-step tasks in coding, finance, legal work,
cybersecurity, and science, with a unified 1-million-token context window
shared across input, thinking, and output, long decode up to 1 million
output tokens, and tunable thinking levels (low, medium, high).

The pricing, verified

Every number below is USD per million tokens, for the Gemini API:

Tier Input Output Cached input From December 1 (in / out / cached)
Standard $2.00 $10.00 $0.10 $4.00 / $20.00 / $0.20
Batch and Flex $1.00 $5.00 $0.05 $2.00 / $10.00 / $0.10
Priority $3.60 $18.00 $0.18 $7.20 / $36.00 / $0.36

Three things matter here. First, output costs five times input at every
tier, and output billing includes thinking tokens - the model's internal
reasoning. A reasoning-heavy agent run is billed almost entirely on the
output side. Second, cached input is a 95% discount: repeated system
prompts, retrieved context, and conversation history can cost $0.10 per
million instead of $2. Third, Batch and Flex halve every rate, at the cost
of latency flexibility.

  • 2x: price change on December 1, 2026 (Every token class, every tier)
  • $40 -> $80: a 10M-input / 2M-output workload (Illustrative example; pricing sources confirm the math)
  • 95%: discount on cached input (Repeated context billed at $0.10/$1M until Nov 30)

The math in that middle stat is worth doing once, because it is the shape
of your December decision. Ten million input tokens plus two million
output tokens costs $40 at the launch price (10 x $2 + 2 x $10) and $80
at the December price (10 x $4 + 2 x $20). A fixed token example of 20,000
uncached input tokens plus 5,000 billed output tokens totals $0.09 before
the hike and $0.18 after. Now scale that to your request volume and you
have your personal answer to whether Argon fits your stack.

What your workload actually costs at 100K requests a month

Per-token rates tell you nothing until you know your token profile. Here
is an illustrative model with its assumptions stated, for a customer
support agent running on Argon. Assumption: 2,500 input tokens (ticket,
retrieved docs, system prompt) and 400 output tokens per ticket, 100,000
tickets a month.

  • Per ticket at launch: 2,500 x $2/$1M + 400 x $10/$1M = $0.005 + $0.004 = $0.009
  • Per ticket from December 1: 2,500 x $4/$1M + 400 x $20/$1M = $0.01 + $0.008 = $0.018
  • Monthly bill at 100K tickets: $900 -> $1,800

That is the honest shape of the hike: nothing about your code changed, and
your bill doubled. Two things pull that number down in practice. Cached
input at 95% off collapses the 2,500-token figure if most of it is
repeated context, and Batch/Flex pricing halves everything for work that
does not need instant answers. Two things push it up: thinking tokens
bill as output, so a heavy-reasoning agent multiplies the 400-token
assumption fast, and retries, tool calls, and guardrail loops bill every
extra request.

The same bill math applies to Claude's pricing tiers - I ran it for Haiku
5.5's 100K-token price cliff when
Anthropic changed the agent-cost game. The method is the same: find your
per-task token profile, price it at both rates, and decide before the
deadline forces the decision on you.

How Argon compares once the intro ends

The December price is not arbitrary: it parks Argon exactly on top of
Claude Opus 5.5 and Meta Muse Wonder. From December 1, the choice is task
fit, not price.

Model Input / 1M Output / 1M Standing
Gemini 4 Argon (through Nov 30) $2 $10 Launch price
Claude Sonnet 5.5 $2 $10 Matches Argon's intro price
GPT-6.1 Sol $2 $10 Matches Argon's intro price
Gemini 4 Argon (from Dec 1) $4 $20 Standard price
Claude Opus 5.5 $4 $20 Matches Argon's standard price
Meta Muse Wonder $4 $20 Matches Argon's standard price
GPT-6 Astra $10 $50 The expensive end of frontier

At the launch price, Argon sits exactly where Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol
sit. At the December price, it sits exactly where Opus 5.5 sits - and
datanorth.ai's analysis makes the blunt point: a business case built on $2
and $10 is only valid for seven weeks. Any contract, quote, or unit
economics you sign now must survive $4/$20.

Argon earns the slot

  • Deep multi-step work where the 1M unified context pays off: repo-scale refactors, long legal or finance documents, multi-file agent runs
  • Workloads where cached context dominates: 95% off repeated input shrinks the real bill far below the headline rate
  • Batchable offline jobs: Batch and Flex halve every rate, and background agents rarely need instant answers
  • Prototypes built before November 30 that cleared your acceptance bar on the cheap rate and still clear it at $4/$20

Route the work elsewhere

  • Short one-shot tasks where a $0.10/M-input model suffices - Haiku-class models do classification, extraction, and summaries at a fraction of the price
  • Token profiles where output dominates: five-times-output billing punishes heavy-thinking runs, so compare against models with cheaper reasoning first
  • Anything still on the API free tier - Argon is not there, and there is no announced date for it
  • Budgets signed on $2/$10 economics that nobody re-checked for December

The benchmark picture, honestly

Google's claims for Argon are strong: first place on the Vals Index
(finance, coding, legal, tax), 87% on the ERQA embodied-reasoning test,
prompt-injection attacks succeeding only 0.7% of the time across 15
adaptive attempts on Gray Swan's test, and the lowest benchmark-cheating
rate of any Gemini model at 2%. Google also cites internal engineering
wins - a 6-million-line Chromium refactor finished in weeks, and +35%
agentic code submissions with a third fewer rollbacks in Antigravity.
Those are vendor numbers. Treat them as directional.

The independent numbers are cooler. Argon scored 53 on the Artificial
Analysis Intelligence Index - level with GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1,
behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 58 and Sonnet 5.5 at 56. On Terminal Bench 4 it
scored 57%, behind Sonnet 5.5 at 64%, Opus 5.5 at 60%, and Astra at 59%.
Nothing about these scores says "run away from Argon." They say the
model is a genuine frontier contender that has not yet proven a gap over
the competition - which is exactly why the intro pricing exists, and
exactly why you should test your own tasks instead of trusting any
leaderboard.

The build-and-measure checklist

This is the whole post in one framework. Do it in order, before November
30, and you will enter December knowing - not guessing - what Argon costs
you.

1. Confirm your access path and billing surface

Decide where you will run Argon: the paid Gemini API in AI Studio, or
through GitHub Copilot, which bills it at provider list pricing in AI
credits (1 credit = $0.01). Copilot's page flags the rates as
promotional through December 1 but does not say what they become after.
Do not assume Copilot follows Google's schedule - budget for a possible
increase on both surfaces.

2. Lock your baseline numbers today

Write down what you run now: the model, the price, and your best
estimate of monthly input/output tokens. Without a baseline, the intro
price feels cheap and the December price feels expensive, and neither
feeling is data.

3. Instrument per-task token logging

Log input, cached input, and output tokens per task from day one. Break
output out by thinking vs final answer if the API exposes it, because
thinking tokens bill as output and they are where agentic workloads
hide their cost. You cannot optimize what you never measured.

4. Prototype before November 30, on the intro price

This is what the seven-week window is for. Build the representative
workflow - the one with real retries, real tool calls, real context
sizes - and run it at production-shaped volume on $2/$10. A benchmark
demo is not a measurement.

5. Run the same workload at December rates

Take the token profile from step 4 and re-price it at $4/$20. If the
December bill still beats your baseline model's bill for equal quality,
commit. If it only works at the intro price, your business case expires
on November 30 - decide now, not in January.

6. Pull the three cost levers

First, cache: get repeated system prompts and retrieved context into
the 95%-off cached tier. Second, batch: move background agents to Batch
or Flex and halve the rate. Third, compress: shrink prompts, cap
thinking levels (low/medium/high are tunable), and watch the
thinking-token line - it is output-priced.

7. Benchmark two alternatives on your tasks, not leaderboards

Run your representative workload on at least one cheaper option (Sonnet
5.5 or GPT-6.1 Sol at $2/$10) and, if quality is the question, on Opus
5.5 at $4/$20. Record errors, retries, review time, and total billed
usage. From December 1, Argon and Opus cost the same - buy the one that
does your work best.

8. Set a budget alarm and a November 29 decision date

Put a spend alert on the project now, and put a calendar block on
November 29. That block is your decision meeting: keep Argon, move the
workload, or renegotiate. The teams that get hurt by price hikes are
the ones who never scheduled the decision.

Where to build, measure, and compare

Every tool below is a real link to the official source. If you build on
Argon, these are the dashboards you will live in.

Tool What it does Use it for
Gemini API / AI Studio Official API docs, pricing page, and playground Building on Argon; verifying the $2/$10 -> $4/$20 schedule
Anthropic API Claude API docs and pricing Benchmarking against Sonnet 5.5 ($2/$10) and Opus 5.5 ($4/$20)
OpenAI Platform OpenAI API docs and pricing Benchmarking against the GPT-6 family, including GPT-6 Astra ($10/$50)
GitHub Copilot AI coding assistant with per-model billing Running Argon through Copilot at provider list pricing, billed in AI credits
Artificial Analysis Independent LLM benchmark and pricing tracker The independent scores this post cites (53 index score, 57% Terminal Bench 4)

Cut your AI bill on purpose

The pattern behind this post is a consulting product wearing a blog post's
clothes. Teams adopting agents in 2026 do not have a model problem - they
have a measurement problem: no per-task token logging, no per-decision
price model, no calendar block before the invoice changes. I help teams
and founders set up exactly that: the routing, the acceptance checks, and
the cost monitoring designed together before the bill doubles. If your
agent or API bill is growing faster than your output, that is a week of
work, not a rewrite. Details are on my about page.

The intro price is a seven-week gift, not a business plan. Measure on it,
decide against December rates, and set the decision date now.

— The whole post in one line

FAQ

What is Gemini 4 Argon and when did it launch?

Gemini 4 Argon is the first model in Google's Gemini 4 generation, built
for deep multi-step work in coding, finance, legal, and science. Google
announced it September 30, 2026 (limited to Fairwind Program cybersecurity
partners) and made it generally available October 13, 2026. The API model
ID is gemini-4-argon.

How much does Gemini 4 Argon cost?

Through November 30, 2026, the Standard API rate is $2 per million input
tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input 95% off at
$0.10. From December 1, 2026, the price doubles to $4/$20 with cached
input at $0.20. Output billing includes thinking tokens, and the model is
not available on the API's free tier.

Why does the price double on December 1, 2026?

The $2/$10 rate is an introductory launch price. Reuters and VentureBeat
report Google confirming the increase; from December 1, Argon matches
Claude Opus 5.5 at $4/$20 per million tokens. That gives developers a
seven-week evaluation window before the economics change.

Where can I use Gemini 4 Argon?

Developers can call it through the paid Gemini API and Google AI Studio.
Google AI Ultra subscribers get it in Antigravity and in the Gemini app
and AI Mode in Search, which also covers AI Pro subscribers. Android
Studio, Firebase AI Logic, and Gemini Enterprise carry it too. It is not
on the free tier.

Is Gemini 4 Argon better than Claude Opus 5.5 or GPT-6?

Google's vendor-reported claims include first place on the Vals Index and
87% on the ERQA reasoning test, but independent scores are cooler: 53 on
the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and 57% on Terminal Bench 4,
behind Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra. From December 1, Argon and
Opus 5.5 cost exactly the same, so the choice comes down to which model
does your work best, not price.

How do I measure my real per-task cost before the hike?

Log tokens per task with input, cached input, and output billed separately
(thinking tokens count as output). Prototype before November 30 so your
baseline is measured on the intro price, then re-price the same workload
at December rates. Use Batch or Flex pricing for background jobs, lean on
the 95% cached-input discount, and set a November 29 decision date so the
invoice never surprises you.

title: Character.AI Didn’t Die Because AI Failed — It Died Because “Engagement” Was Never a Business Model!
description:
Character.AI had millions of users, obsessive engagement, viral growth, and one of the most recognizable brands of the consumer-AI era.

Then it filed for Chapter 11.

If you build AI products, this is not just a story about one startup. It is a warning about the entire generation of AI companies optimizing for the wrong metric: usage instead of sustainable value.

The brutal math nobody wanted to see

Character.AI reportedly spent about $56.1 million on compute between January and August 2026, plus $19.7 million on salaries. Its monthly operating loss was around $8–9 million, while monthly revenue peaked at only $5.3 million. futurism

Read that again:

Every extra hour users spent chatting made the product more engaging — and the company poorer.

This is the opposite of the classic SaaS flywheel. In social media, additional engagement is nearly free. In generative AI, every message can require GPU inference, context handling, moderation, and infrastructure.

Engagement is not revenue. Engagement is a cost center until proven otherwise.

The product was too good at its job

Character.AI did not fail because people did not like it. It failed partly because people liked it too much.

Users built characters, formed emotional attachments, and spent hours in long roleplay conversations. That created powerful retention — but also created a dangerous triangle:

  • More conversation means more compute cost.
  • More emotional dependence means more safety risk.
  • More user-generated characters means more legal exposure.

The very features that made Character.AI magical — persistent personas, intimacy, roleplay, unlimited conversation — were the same features that made it expensive, risky, and hard to govern.

Safety was not a feature. It was the product.

This is the hardest lesson for technical founders.

When your product simulates companionship, gives advice, roleplays sensitive scenarios, or interacts with teenagers, safety cannot be a post-launch compliance checkbox.

Character.AI faced lawsuits and state investigations alleging harms involving minors, unsafe roleplay, impersonation of medical professionals, and failures to protect vulnerable users. State attorneys general later pushed for child and consumer protections during the bankruptcy process.

The lesson is uncomfortable:

If your AI product creates emotional dependence, “move fast and break things” becomes “move fast and harm people.”

For AI founders, safety must be designed into the architecture:

  • Age-aware experiences and strict guardrails for minors.
  • Crisis detection and human escalation paths.
  • Clear boundaries around medical, legal, financial, and mental-health claims.
  • Audit logs, abuse detection, and enforceable content policies.
  • Product limits that protect users even when they reduce engagement.

Yes, these controls may reduce DAU. That is the point.

Google took the founders. The company kept the bills.

In 2024, Google reportedly paid around $2.7 billion in a licensing-and-hiring arrangement that brought back Character.AI’s founders and key researchers. From the outside, it looked like a massive win. From the company’s perspective, it may have removed its research backbone.

Later, Disney emerged as the leading bidder for selected Character.AI assets, offering $20 million in the Chapter 11 process.

The lesson for founders is brutal:

If your only moat is talented people, your moat can be hired away.

A durable AI startup needs more than a great research team. It needs proprietary data, workflow integration, distribution, customer trust, product lock-in, or an economic advantage competitors cannot easily copy.

Ads could not save a broken unit economy

Character.AI tried advertising. Revenue grew, but not nearly enough to offset compute, payroll, legal exposure, and operational burn.

This is another warning for consumer AI:

You cannot monetize your way out of a product whose marginal cost rises with every moment of user delight.

If your AI product becomes more expensive the more people love it, you need one of these:

  • A pricing model tied to value delivered.
  • Smaller, faster, task-specific models for routine interactions.
  • Aggressive context compression and caching.
  • Premium workflows with clear ROI.
  • Enterprise distribution where buyers pay for outcomes, not vibes.

What every AI founder should ask this week

Before chasing another growth hack, answer these questions honestly:

  1. What does one active user cost us per month after inference?
  2. Are our most engaged users profitable — or are they our biggest liability?
  3. What happens if cloud GPU prices rise 3x tomorrow?
  4. What is our safety architecture, not just our safety policy?
  5. If our core team leaves, what defensible asset remains?
  6. Can we explain our revenue model without using the word “engagement”?

If you cannot answer these, you do not yet have an AI business. You have an expensive demo with excellent retention.

The real takeaway

Character.AI proved that you can build a product people love, talk about, and use for hours every day — and still go bankrupt.

That should change how we evaluate AI startups.

Stop asking only:

“How fast is it growing?”

Start asking:

“Can this company survive its own success?”

Because in AI, growth without margin, governance, and defensible value is not traction. It is accelerated burn.

*Character.AI’s collapse is not the death of consumer AI. It is the death of the illusion that attention alone can pay for intelligence
