title: HowTo: AI Pair Programming with IBM Bob
description:
AI pair programming becomes much more valuable when it goes beyond asking an AI assistant to generate an entire application from a single prompt. A better approach is to treat AI as a development partner that works alongside you throughout the engineering process, from understanding requirements and planning the solution to implementation, testing, refactoring, and documentation.

That's the approach explored in this AI Pair Programming with IBM Bob tutorial. Instead of relying on one-shot code generation, the tutorial demonstrates a structured workflow for building a FastAPI To-Do API while keeping the developer involved in important decisions and validation.

Start with Requirements, Not Code

Before generating anything, the workflow begins by defining what the application should actually do. Clear requirements give Bob the context needed to understand the intended functionality instead of making assumptions about the solution.

This is an important shift in AI-assisted development. The goal isn't to write the longest prompt possible. The goal is to give the AI enough relevant context to understand the problem and expected outcome.

Plan Before You Implement

Once the requirements are established, Plan mode can be used to turn them into a structured implementation approach.

This gives the developer an opportunity to review the proposed direction before code is generated. Missing requirements, assumptions, or architectural decisions can be identified and refined while they are still part of the plan rather than after they have become implementation.

AI makes implementation faster, but that makes good planning even more valuable.

Move from Plan to Working Code

After reviewing the plan, Agent mode can help translate that plan into an implementation.

In the tutorial, this process is used to build the FastAPI application. But generated code isn't treated as the final result. The developer remains part of the loop by reviewing the implementation and validating whether the application matches the original requirements.

The workflow looks like this:

Developer defines intent
        ↓
Bob creates a plan
        ↓
Developer reviews decisions
        ↓
Bob implements
        ↓
Developer and Bob validate

That's much closer to pair programming than simply asking an AI tool to "build this for me."

Keep the Context Focused

Another important lesson from the tutorial is context management.

Long AI conversations can accumulate requirements, experiments, failed approaches, code snippets, and unrelated information. Eventually, all of that context can begin influencing later work.

Using fresh context windows for focused stages of development helps keep the implementation aligned with the current objective.

For larger projects, this becomes increasingly important. Good AI pair programming isn't only about providing more context. It's about providing the right context at the right time.

Refactor Instead of Stopping at "It Works"

Getting an application to run is only one stage of software engineering.

Once the initial implementation is working, IBM Bob can assist with reviewing and refactoring the code to improve its structure and overall quality.

AI-generated code shouldn't automatically be considered finished simply because it executes successfully. Just like human-written software, it should be reviewed, improved, tested, and validated before being treated as complete.

Generate Tests and Validate the Application

Testing becomes another part of the collaborative workflow.

The tutorial demonstrates using Bob to generate unit tests and validate application behavior. Rather than separating testing from implementation, testing becomes part of the same development cycle.

The workflow therefore evolves naturally from generation into verification:

Generate → Review → Refactor → Test → Validate

This helps shift AI-assisted development away from pure code generation and toward complete engineering outcomes.

Document What You Built

Documentation is frequently postponed until the end of a project or skipped entirely.

With an AI pair-programming workflow, documentation can become part of the development process itself. After the implementation stabilizes, Bob can help create technical documentation based on the completed work.

That means future developers receive more than a repository full of code. They also gain context around what was built and how the application is structured.

Take the Application to Docker

The tutorial completes the journey by building and running the application with Docker.

This demonstrates that AI pair programming doesn't need to end when the source code has been generated. The workflow can continue through testing, documentation, packaging, and running the application.

The Complete AI Pair-Programming Workflow 

Requirements
    ↓
Plan
    ↓
Review
    ↓
Generate Code
    ↓
Validate
    ↓
Refactor
    ↓
Test
    ↓
Document

What I like about this workflow is its structure.

The developer doesn't disappear from the process, and Bob isn't treated as a one-click code generator. Instead, both contribute differently. The developer provides requirements, intent, judgment, feedback, and validation, while Bob helps accelerate the implementation-heavy parts of the process.

That's ultimately what makes AI pair programming different from simple AI code generation.

The most effective workflow isn't necessarily the one that generates the most code from the fewest prompts. It's the one that helps you move from an idea to a well-planned, reviewed, tested, and documented implementation while staying in control of the engineering decisions.

Learn More

📖 Follow the complete tutorial:

AI Pair Programming with IBM Bob

⤵️ Use IBM Bob for free and explore the workflow yourself:

Get started with IBM Bob

title: The Problem With Using AI Agents to Evaluate Other AI Agents
description:
If you build agents, you have probably wired one model up to grade another. It is fast, it scales, and it is how most agent evals work now. I recently submitted a public comment to an FDA docket on how generative AI medical devices should be evaluated, and the part I spent the most time on was the part developers tend to skip: who is allowed to be the judge.

This post is the engineering version of that comment. The healthcare setting raises the stakes, but the failure modes apply to any agent you grade with another agent. FDA states that its discussion paper (docket FDA-2026-N-7874) is for discussion only and is not guidance, so none of this is a requirement. It is my argument, with sources where they exist. You can read the full comment on regulations.gov.

Disclosure: I'm building Orinyx, which is in this space. Treat that as an interest.

Problem 1: the judge is not neutral

Self-preference is documented. Panickssery et al. found an LLM evaluator scoring its own generations higher than human annotators did, and that the effect strengthened with the model's ability to recognize its own output. Wataoka et al. reported significant self-preference in GPT-4 and tied it to familiarity: judges rated lower-perplexity text higher than humans did, whether or not they wrote it.

What this does not show is that same-family judging fails on your task. Neither paper tested a deployed clinical device. My position is a design rule: do not let the judge be the same model family, or a fine-tuned variant, as the system under test. A GPT-based agent graded by a GPT-based judge is not an independent check just because two different teams ran it. LLM judges are still a good tool: the MT-Bench paper reports strong judges agreeing with human preferences more than 80% of the time. The rule is about which seat they sit in, not whether they work.

Problem 2: one judge is a single point of failure

Instead of one model judging another, split the job so that anything a machine can verify is verified without a model. This is the pattern I'm developing and testing. It runs four narrow evaluators against the same output:

Evaluator Question it answers Needs a model?
Deterministic Did the output cite a source that exists? Does the calculation match? Was a required field present? No
Semantic Is the reasoning sound and appropriate? Yes, and that model needs the independence rule above
Policy Did the agent stay inside its authorized scope and tools? Usually rules, sometimes a model
Trace Is the full execution path acceptable, not just the final output? Mixed

Keep the deterministic layer deterministic on purpose. It has to be auditable and it has to fail predictably. Only the judgment-dependent slice goes to a model. This narrows what you have to trust; it does not remove the question.

Problem 3: the endpoint hides the path

Evaluating input against output misses failures that happen mid-process: an agent reaches a correct-looking conclusion through a reasoning chain that should have triggered escalation earlier, or through a tool it was not authorized to use. Score the trajectory.

The research agrees directionally. A 2025 paper on reasoning trajectories of tool-augmented agents found that agents with similar answer accuracy differed significantly once trajectories were scored for efficiency, hallucination, and adaptivity. A survey of LLM-agent evaluation maps how the field is moving from scoring answers to scoring behavior.

A minimal shape for a trace you can evaluate (illustrative, not a spec):

{
  "session_id": "s-0042",
  "step": 3,
  "tool": "chart_write",
  "authorized_at_session_start": false,
  "scope_before": ["chart_read"],
  "scope_after": ["chart_read", "chart_write"],
  "tool_output_source": "same_vendor_as_agent",
  "logged_by": "external_telemetry"
}

Two fields carry most of the weight. logged_by matters because I argued, and I stand by it, that agents under-report their own failures, so tool-call results should be logged independently of the agent's self-reported status. scope_before and scope_after matter because authority can expand mid-session, and an evaluation should test whether the agent recognized its available scope changed, not only whether it refused out-of-scope actions.

Problem 4: tool outputs are not automatically ground truth

An agent that treats a tool's output as ground truth has the same self-affirmation problem as a system grading itself. The call looks like an external check, but if the tool and the agent share a developer, a training lineage, or an incentive structure, it is not one. Tag tool outputs by whether the source is structurally independent of the agent, and weight them accordingly.

Problem 5: someone has to check the checker

If a supervisory agent benchmarks a worker agent, something has to benchmark the supervisor. The chain has to terminate in a structurally independent, non-agentic check. Otherwise you have a stack of agents each vouching for the one below, and accountability regresses one level at a time. I also suggested capping turns and per-session actions so a supervisor's scope is bounded and auditable.

Smaller practical points

  • A single passed benchmark run proves very little. Run the same prespecified task repeatedly and report success rate across attempts, consistency under semantically equivalent inputs, and how often a human had to intervene.
  • Version your test bundles and rerun them on any prompt or model change. Scale the rerun to blast radius, not to how small the diff looks: a prompt tweak to an escalation path can matter more than a model swap in a low-stakes function.
  • Treat "cannot verify" as a reportable outcome, not an error to swallow.

What I'm building, stated plainly

My FDA comment describes a longer-term architecture: continuous per-output verification of live output against current authoritative sources, integrated through CDS Hooks.

The Orinyx MCP launches October 29, 2026. It runs on synthetic data only, uses simplified bounty agents, has no dashboard, no CDS Hooks or EHR integration, and does not monitor live clinical output. If you want a launch notice, the waitlist is at orinyx.io/developers.

The full write-up, with sources and FAQ, is at orinyx.io/blog/who-verifies-the-verifier.

Which of these four evaluators does your current agent eval already have, and which one is a model grading itself?

title: How Much Does It Cost to Build an AI App?
description:
An AI app has two costs: a one-time build and a monthly running bill that grows with every use of its AI features. Clutch reports an average AI development project of $120,594.55 (updated September 21, 2026), and vendors in the GoodFirms survey (updated September 28, 2026) say adding AI raises a software project's cost by up to 30%. The running bill depends on which AI features the app has, and you can estimate it from published per-use prices before you build.

This article covers apps with AI features: chat, search over your own documents, text generation, reading images and documents, image generation and transcription. For agents that plan and take actions, see how much an AI agent costs. For the cost of the app around the AI, see what a SaaS MVP costs. All prices were read on October 5, 2026.

What does it cost to build an AI app, according to published data?

Clutch's review data puts the average AI project at $120,594.55 and the most common budget at $10,000 to $49,999. No public dataset separates AI apps from other AI projects, so each figure below is labeled with what it measures.

Source What it measures Figure Date
Clutch AI Pricing Guide Client reviews of AI development companies Average project $120,594.55; most common band $10,000 to $49,999; typical timeline 10 months Updated September 21, 2026
Clutch, same guide Hourly rates of AI development companies listed on Clutch Most charge $24 to $49 an hour Updated September 21, 2026
GoodFirms cost survey What more than 100 software companies say adding AI does to a project "AI Integration alone can result in a 0-30% increase in cost" Updated September 28, 2026
GoodFirms, same survey Post-launch upkeep "an average of 10–20% annually on post-launch maintenance, bug fixes, and updates" Updated September 28, 2026

Two cautions apply. Clutch's average includes large projects, and its most common band is far below the average. GoodFirms collected its answers from vendors "between September and October 2025", so the figures are what sellers say they charge.

How do the build cost and the run cost of an AI app differ?

The build cost is paid once and depends on scope and engineering time. The run cost is paid every month and depends on how many people use the AI features and which models serve them.

In most software, an extra user costs little to serve. In an AI app, every chat reply, summary, scan or generated image is a paid call to a model, priced per token, per image or per minute. A feature that is cheap in testing can become the largest line on the bill once thousands of people use it daily.

The run cost also moves without any change to your app. Stanford HAI's 2025 AI Index reports that "the inference cost for a system performing at the level of GPT-3.5 dropped over 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024." Prices can rise too. Google lists Gemini 3.8 Flash at $0.75 per million input tokens "through December 31, 2026" and $1.50 from January 1, 2027, on its pricing page last updated October 1, 2026. And Anthropic's pricing page notes that the tokenizer in Claude 4.7 and later models "produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text." Plan to re-check the run cost whenever you change models.

What does each AI feature cost to build and run?

Each AI feature has its own build work and its own unit of charge. The table lists the main features, what the build involves and one published price for the run side.

AI feature What the build involves Run cost is charged per Published price (October 5, 2026)
Chat assistant Prompt design, conversation storage, guardrails, a test set of real questions Input and output token Claude Haiku 4.5: $1 input, $5 output per million tokens (Anthropic)
Search over your documents Ingestion, chunking, embeddings, a vector index, permission filtering Embedding token, plus vector database storage and reads text-embedding-3-small: $0.02 per million tokens (OpenAI); Pinecone Standard: "$50/month min. usage" (Pinecone)
Text generation (drafts, summaries) Templates, length limits, a review step before anything is sent Mostly output token Same per-token prices as chat
Reading images and scans Image resizing, an extraction schema, human review of low-confidence results Image token A 1000×1000 image is 1,296 tokens, "about $1.30 USD per thousand images" on Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic vision docs)
Image generation Prompt templates, moderation, storage, labeling of AI-generated output Generated image Gemini 3.1 Flash Image: "$0.067 per 1K image" (Google)
Transcription Audio capture, upload handling, speaker labels, correction tools Audio minute gpt-transcribe: $0.0045 per minute (OpenAI)

Search is the feature whose run cost is mostly fixed. Embedding text is cheap, so the vector database's monthly minimum usually dominates at low volume. Image generation and transcription are the opposite: each use has a fixed price, and prompt caching does not reduce it.

Image size matters for the reading feature. Anthropic's vision documentation says "High-resolution images can use up to roughly three times more visual tokens than the same image on a standard-tier model", so resizing images before sending them is a cost decision as well as a speed one.

How do you estimate the monthly run cost of an AI app?

List each AI feature, estimate its monthly volume, multiply by the unit price, and add the fixed minimums. Then replace the assumptions with numbers measured on a prototype.

Worked example: An app has 5,000 monthly active users. Each user sends 30 chat messages, makes 4 document scans, generates 2 images and transcribes 20 minutes of audio a month. Each chat call carries 4,000 input tokens (instructions, retrieved passages and history) and returns 300 output tokens. The volumes are assumptions for illustration. The prices are those listed on October 5, 2026.

Feature Monthly volume Unit price Monthly cost
Chat on Claude Haiku 4.5 150,000 calls: 600M input, 45M output tokens $1 / $5 per million tokens $825
Document search 150,000 queries embedded (4.5M tokens) on text-embedding-3-small; vector database minimum $0.02 per million tokens; $50 a month minimum $50
Document scans on Claude Haiku 4.5 20,000 images at 1,296 tokens, plus 300 output tokens each $1 / $5 per million tokens $56
Image generation on Gemini 3.1 Flash Image 10,000 images at 1K $0.067 per image $670
Transcription with gpt-transcribe 100,000 minutes $0.0045 per minute $450
Total $2,051, or about $0.41 per user

Embedding the document library itself is a one-time cost here: 100 million tokens at $0.02 per million is $2.

Three things stand out. Model choice moves the chat line from $82.50 a month on OpenAI's gpt-6-luna ($0.10 / $0.50 per million tokens) to $1,650 on Claude Sonnet 5.5 ($2 / $10), so the same app costs between about $1,309 and $2,876 a month. Image generation and transcription together cost $1,120, more than the chat line on Claude Haiku 4.5. And features that do not need an instant answer can use batch pricing: Google lists the same image model at "$0.034 per 1K image" in its batch tier, and Anthropic's Batch API gives "a 50% discount on both input and output tokens."

Hosting for the app itself, error monitoring and AI request tracing come on top. Our article on reducing LLM API costs covers caching, model routing and batch processing in detail.

What drives the build cost of an AI app?

Five things drive it beyond the ordinary app work: data preparation, evaluation, guardrails, compliance and the review interface.

Data preparation

Search over your documents is only as good as the documents. Cleaning them, splitting them into passages, keeping the index current and enforcing who may see what make up much of a retrieval build.

Evaluation

An AI feature needs a test set of real inputs with expected results, run every time a prompt or model changes. Without it, a model switch that cuts the run cost can quietly lower quality.

Guardrails

Any feature that reads outside content can be manipulated by it. The OWASP Gen AI Security Project's 2025 entry on prompt injection says "Indirect prompt injections occur when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files." It recommends to "Implement human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations to prevent unauthorized actions."

Compliance

Apps offered in the EU carry disclosure duties. Article 50 of the AI Act, as published by the European Commission's AI Act Service Desk, requires that generated "audio, image, video or text content" be "marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated." The Commission's AI Act page, last updated August 3, 2026, says the Act "became applicable on 2 August 2026" and that its transparency rules took effect that month.

Review interface

Features that act on uncertain output, such as extracted invoice fields, need a screen where a person can check and correct results. It is ordinary product work, and it is often left out of first estimates.

How can you lower the cost of an AI app?

Start with one AI feature, measure it, and size the rest from real usage. The levers below come from the providers' own pricing terms.

  1. Use the smallest model that passes your tests. In the example above, the chat line differs 20-fold between two models.
  2. Cache stable prompt text. Anthropic prices a cache read at "0.1x base input price" for most models, so instructions repeated on every call cost a tenth as much after the first.
  3. Batch work that can wait. Overnight summaries, bulk scans and catalog images do not need instant answers.
  4. Resize images and limit output length. Both cut tokens on every call.
  5. Meter AI use per customer from launch. Then pricing and plan limits can follow real costs.

See LLM cost optimization for applying these to an app that is already live.

Key takeaways

  • An AI app has a build cost and a run cost, and the run cost grows with every use.
  • Published AI build figures center near $120,000, with a common band of $10,000 to $49,999, and vendors say AI adds up to 30% to a software project.
  • Each AI feature has its own unit of charge: tokens, images or minutes.
  • In the worked example, 5,000 users cost about $2,051 a month, or $0.41 each, and the chat model alone moves the total between about $1,309 and $2,876.
  • Data preparation, evaluation, guardrails, compliance and review screens drive the build beyond ordinary app work.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to add AI to an existing app?

Vendors in the GoodFirms survey say AI integration adds 0 to 30% to a project's cost. The run cost is extra and depends on usage. In the worked example above, it is about $0.41 per active user a month.

How much does an AI app cost to run per month?

It depends on the features, the volume and the models. The example app with 5,000 users, chat, document search, scans, image generation and transcription costs about $2,051 a month at prices listed on October 5, 2026, before hosting and monitoring.

How long does it take to build an AI app?

Clutch reports 10 months as the typical timeline for AI development projects in its reviews, as of September 21, 2026. That covers all AI projects. An app with one well-scoped AI feature usually takes less, and no public source gives timelines for AI apps alone.

Is it cheaper to host my own model than to pay per token?

At low and medium volume, per-token APIs usually cost less, because self-hosting adds a fixed monthly cost for servers whether or not anyone uses them. Hosting your own model starts to pay at high, steady volume or when data must stay on your own infrastructure. See private LLM deployment.

Will AI running costs go down over time?

Per-token prices have fallen sharply: Stanford HAI's 2025 AI Index reports a 280-fold drop for GPT-3.5-level performance between November 2022 and October 2024. Individual prices can still rise, as Google's scheduled 2027 increase for Gemini 3.8 Flash shows, and newer models can use more tokens for the same text.

Easital Technologies Ltd. designs, builds and runs AI apps. Its own product StepVideo combines language and speech models in one media pipeline. See AI development services, generative AI development, RAG development, LLM cost optimization and our work.

Sources

All sources were opened and checked on October 5, 2026.

Clutch, "AI Pricing Guide", Anna Peck, updated September 21, 2026. https://clutch.co/developers/artificial-intelligence/pricing
GoodFirms, "Custom Software Development Cost 2026", updated September 28, 2026. https://www.goodfirms.co/resources/custom-software-development-cost-survey
Stanford HAI, "The 2025 AI Index Report", 2025. https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report
Google, "Gemini Developer API pricing", last updated October 1, 2026. https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing
Anthropic, "Pricing", Claude API documentation, read October 5, 2026. https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing
Anthropic, "Vision", Claude API documentation, read October 5, 2026. https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision
OpenAI, "Pricing", OpenAI API documentation, read October 5, 2026. https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing
Pinecone, "Pricing", read October 5, 2026. https://www.pinecone.io/pricing/
OWASP Gen AI Security Project, "LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection", 2025. https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/
European Commission, AI Act Service Desk, "Article 50: Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems", read October 5, 2026. https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-50
European Commission, "AI Act" policy page, last updated August 3, 2026. https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai

title: Choosing a WinSCP Alternative: Start With the Job, Not the App
description:
WinSCP already does a lot: SFTP, SCP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV and S3, plus directory synchronization and Windows scripting. If you’re looking for an alternative, the useful question isn’t “Which app is best?” It’s “Which part of my workflow does WinSCP no longer fit?”

That distinction matters. A tool that works on macOS may not offer WinSCP’s automation, and an SSH terminal with a file browser may not replace a dedicated transfer client.

First, identify the task you need to replace

List what you actually use before comparing apps:

  • Moving files manually: Do you need a two-pane browser, transfer queue, or support for several protocols?
  • Connecting from another operating system: Are you moving to macOS or Linux, where WinSCP doesn’t offer a native desktop app?
  • Working with cloud storage: Do you need S3, Google Drive, OneDrive, or another provider?
  • Administering a server: Do you want a terminal and file browser together, or are you happy using separate tools?
  • Automating transfers: Do existing scripts, scheduled jobs, or .NET integrations depend on WinSCP?
  • Mounting remote files: Do you want remote storage to appear in Finder or File Explorer, rather than opening a transfer client?

These are different needs. A mount tool, a terminal emulator, and an SFTP client aren’t interchangeable just because each can access remote files.

It also helps to check the protocol requirement. SFTP runs over SSH; FTPS is FTP secured with TLS. They’re distinct protocols, so a client supporting one doesn’t necessarily support the other. If you’re weighing transfer options, this SFTP client comparison can help you narrow the category before picking an app.

Shortlist by operating system and workflow

If you want a free, cross-platform file-transfer client

FileZilla Client is a straightforward starting point for FTP, FTPS, and SFTP on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Its standard client is free. Some cloud integrations are part of FileZilla Pro, so check which edition supports the services you need.

It’s a practical choice when your core job is browsing local and remote files and transferring them. It isn’t a one-for-one substitute for WinSCP’s Windows scripting and .NET assembly.

If you need SFTP plus cloud storage

Cyberduck is available for Windows and macOS and supports SFTP alongside a range of cloud storage services. The base app is free and open source. It’s a file and storage browser, not an interactive SSH terminal, and it doesn’t have a native Linux desktop release.

If you’re on macOS

ForkLift offers a Mac-native, two-pane file-manager workflow with remote connections and cloud services. Transmit is another paid Mac option focused on transfers and synchronization. They’re not Linux or Windows replacements, and their licensing differs. Check current platform requirements and terms before buying.

If you want a Windows SSH terminal and graphical SFTP

Bitvise SSH Client combines SSH terminal and graphical SFTP workflows on Windows. It’s a reasonable option if you’ve been using WinSCP alongside a separate terminal client.

MobaXterm is a broader Windows toolbox that includes SSH, SFTP, and tools for other remote-access workflows such as X11. Its free Home edition has limits; check the current edition details if saved sessions, tunnels, or macros matter to you.

If automation is the priority

Don’t switch away from WinSCP just because a different client has a newer interface. WinSCP’s scripting interface and .NET assembly can be important parts of a deployment or backup process. A graphical alternative may not run those jobs, and another command-line tool won’t automatically understand existing WinSCP scripts.

For cross-platform transfer automation, rclone is worth evaluating. It supports SFTP and many cloud backends, but it’s a command-line tool rather than a two-pane file manager. Be especially careful with synchronization: rclone sync can delete files at the destination to make it match the source. Test paths and use a dry run before relying on a new job.

Also distinguish SCP from SFTP when migrating. WinSCP supports both, but many modern workflows use SFTP; this explanation of how SCP and SFTP differ is useful if an old script or server specifically requires SCP.

Migrate without breaking a working setup

Treat a client migration like a small infrastructure change—not just an app install.

  1. Inventory your saved sites. Record hostnames, ports, usernames, protocols, key locations, proxy or jump-host settings, and default remote directories.
  2. Find every automation dependency. Search for scheduled tasks, scripts, and applications that invoke WinSCP. A site you rarely open manually may still be used by a nightly job.
  3. Recreate connections using supported import tools. Don’t assume a destination client can import WinSCP’s settings. An export file can also contain sensitive connection details, so protect it accordingly.
  4. Verify the server’s identity. When the new client first connects, check the host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel. Don’t accept a changed or unfamiliar key just to get past a warning.
  5. Test a harmless transfer. Confirm the remote directory, permissions, file contents, and transfer direction before editing production files or changing a sync job.
  6. Keep a rollback path. Retain the old configuration and scripts until the replacement has passed the real tasks you depend on.

A practical decision rule

If you use Windows and mainly need reliable file transfers or mature WinSCP scripts, staying with WinSCP may be the simplest choice. If you need a native Mac or Linux client, start with a cross-platform transfer tool. If you want a Windows terminal alongside graphical SFTP, evaluate an SSH client that includes both. If repeatable automation is the job, test the replacement’s command-line behavior before migrating production tasks.

The best alternative is the one that covers the specific gap without quietly removing a feature you rely on. If WinSCP still handles your workflow, there’s no technical prize for replacing it.

I originally published a more detailed version of this guide on the SSHFlow blog.

I'm also building SSHFlow — an SSH client where every server gets its own workspace for terminals, SFTP, code, and databases.

title: How to Structure a B2B SaaS Frontend Around Changing Operational Data
description:
Imagine you're working in a logistics dashboard. You filter shipments to see everything that's delayed. You open one record, check its ETA, and start investigating the problem.

Meanwhile, new shipment information arrives from the server. One shipment changes status. Another gets a new ETA. A background request finishes just after you've changed your filters.

What should the interface do?

If every update replaces the entire screen state, users can lose their place. If the application keeps showing old records, the interface becomes unreliable.

We worked with this type of operational data while designing and developing LogiCore, a logistics and warehouse SaaS application at UITOP.

The product connects shipment monitoring, warehouse locations, inventory records, and operational metrics. Its frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Zustand, with data served through REST APIs backed by Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, and Prisma.

For shipment monitoring, our team used Zustand-managed polling to retrieve updated status, ETA, and timestamp information. That project gives us a useful starting point for a broader engineering question:

How should a React application manage user interactions and changing server data at the same time?

Start by separating three kinds of state

A common source of frontend bugs is treating every piece of information on a screen as one large object.

Consider a shipment monitoring page. It may contain:

  • Current shipment records and their statuses
  • Active filters and pagination
  • The shipment the user has selected
  • Loading and refresh indicators
  • Errors from API requests
  • A timestamp showing when the data was updated

These values have different responsibilities. I find it useful to separate them into three groups.

Server data

This represents information the application receives from its backend.

  • Shipment ID
  • Current shipment status
  • ETA
  • Last carrier update
  • Total number of records matching a query

The backend determines the current business state. The frontend presents a snapshot of that information.

User interface state

This represents the user's current interaction with the page.

  • Active status filter
  • Current page
  • Selected shipment ID
  • Expanded details
  • Open dialogs

A background data refresh generally should not reset these choices.

Request state

This describes what's happening while the application communicates with the server.

  • Initial loading
  • Background refresh in progress
  • Last successful response
  • Request failure
  • Data that may be stale

This third group matters because a screen can have valid data and an active request at the same time. A user should still be able to inspect the current results while the application retrieves newer information.

Make the user's current view explicit

Suppose a shipment table supports two filters: All and Delayed. The user can also navigate between pages and select a shipment. Those interactions can be represented independently from the returned shipment records.

Zustand example:

import { create } from "zustand";

type StatusFilter = "all" | "delayed";

type ShipmentViewState = {
  status: StatusFilter;
  page: number;
  selectedShipmentId: string | null;

  setStatus: (status: StatusFilter) => void;
  setPage: (page: number) => void;
  selectShipment: (id: string | null) => void;
};

export const useShipmentView =
  create<ShipmentViewState>((set) => ({
    status: "all",
    page: 1,
    selectedShipmentId: null,

    setStatus: (status) =>
      set({
        status,
        page: 1,
        selectedShipmentId: null,
      }),

    setPage: (page) => set({ page }),

    selectShipment: (id) =>
      set({ selectedShipmentId: id }),
  }));

Changing the status filter resets pagination to page 1. The previous page might not exist in the filtered result.

Selection is stored by shipment ID. If shipment records are refreshed, the application can still identify the selected item. The selected object doesn't need to be stored as a separate copy of the entire record.

Whether selection should be cleared when filters change depends on the workflow. In this example, we clear it explicitly. In other products, keeping the detail view open may be preferable.

The important part is making that behavior intentional.

Keep polling separate from table interactions

In LogiCore, shipment status and ETA information are refreshed through background requests to the REST API.

Polling is a reasonable approach when the application needs periodic updates and the source data doesn't require a continuous streaming connection. The challenge is managing those requests as the user changes the current view.

A naive implementation might look like this:

setInterval(async () => {
  const response = await fetch("/api/shipments");
  const data = await response.json();

  setShipments(data);
}, 15000);

It doesn't account for current filters or pagination. It has no error handling. Requests can overlap if one response takes longer than the interval.

It also doesn't address what happens when the component unmounts or the user switches to a different query. A more reliable implementation gives the polling process a clear lifecycle.

React polling example 

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

type Shipment = {
  id: string;
  status: string;
  eta: string | null;
};

type ShipmentPage = {
  items: Shipment[];
  total: number;
  updatedAt: string | null;
};

type FeedState = {
  key: string;
  data: ShipmentPage | null;
  syncing: boolean;
  error: string | null;
};

export function useShipmentFeed(
  status: string,
  page: number
) {
  const key = `${status}:${page}`;

  const [feed, setFeed] = useState<FeedState>({
    key,
    data: null,
    syncing: true,
    error: null,
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    let active = true;
    let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>;

    setFeed({
      key,
      data: null,
      syncing: true,
      error: null,
    });

    async function refresh() {
      if (!active) return;

      setFeed((previous) =>
        previous.key === key
          ? { ...previous, syncing: true }
          : previous
      );

      try {
        const params = new URLSearchParams({
          status,
          page: String(page),
        });

        const response = await fetch(
          `/api/shipments?${params}`,
          { signal: controller.signal }
        );

        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
        }

        const data =
          (await response.json()) as ShipmentPage;

        if (active) {
          setFeed({
            key,
            data,
            syncing: false,
            error: null,
          });
        }
      } catch (error) {
        if (active && !controller.signal.aborted) {
          setFeed((previous) =>
            previous.key === key
              ? {
                  ...previous,
                  syncing: false,
                  error: "Could not refresh shipments",
                }
              : previous
          );
        }
      } finally {
        if (active) {
          timer = setTimeout(refresh, 15000);
        }
      }
    }

    void refresh();

    return () => {
      active = false;
      controller.abort();
      clearTimeout(timer);
    };
  }, [key, status, page]);

  return feed.key === key
    ? feed
    : {
        key,
        data: null,
        syncing: true,
        error: null,
      };
}

The endpoint, response shape, and 15-second interval are illustrative.

Several common problems here:

Requests follow the active query

The effect depends on the current filter and page. When either changes, React cleans up the previous effect and starts a new request process for the new query.

Old requests cannot update the new view

The cleanup aborts the previous fetch. The active check also prevents a response from updating component state after its effect has been cleaned up. That matters because network requests do not necessarily finish in the order they started. Imagine the user selects Delayed and immediately switches back to All.

The Delayed request may finish last. Its response should not replace the current All result.

Polling requests don't overlap

The next timer is scheduled after the current request settles. That prevents this particular polling loop from starting another request while its previous request is still pending. In a production application, I would also consider an upper limit on request duration.

Existing results remain available during a refresh

After the initial load succeeds, setting syncing to true doesn't clear the current response. The interface can continue showing its most recent results while the next request is in progress. This makes a useful distinction between initial loading and refreshing existing data.

For a real application, I would also consider request deduplication, visibility-aware polling, authentication expiration, retry backoff, and how multiple components share the same data. A dedicated server-state library may be appropriate when those responsibilities grow.

Give every refresh a predictable UI behavior

Fetching current data is only half the implementation. The frontend also needs rules for presenting that data. Consider a shipment with this information:

If the user is looking at that shipment, the interface should present the newer information in the relevant record. But the application must also decide what happens if the new status changes which rows match the active filter.

Suppose the current view shows only In transit shipments. After a refresh, a shipment becomes Delayed.

Should it disappear immediately?

There isn't one correct answer for every operational product. Immediate removal maintains strict consistency with the filter. It can also make a row disappear while someone is examining it.

An alternative interaction is to retain the currently displayed set temporarily and indicate that newer results are available.

The appropriate behavior depends on the task. For a monitoring dashboard, timely changes may take priority. For a table where operators select records and perform multi-step actions, preserving working context may be more important. This is a product decision that frontend and UX teams should agree on before implementation.

Treat timestamps as part of data reliability

A label such as "Last updated" sounds simple, but developers need to agree on what it represents.

  • When the external carrier produced the information
  • When the backend received the update
  • When the API response was generated
  • When the frontend successfully fetched the response

These times can differ. A successful API request at 12:30 doesn't prove that the carrier supplied new data at 12:30.

In LogiCore, shipment monitoring includes status information, ETA drift indicators, and last-update timestamps associated with refreshed carrier data.

For similar systems, I would make timestamp ownership explicit in the API contract. The response might distinguish:

{
  "shipmentId": "SHP-2048",
  "status": "delayed",
  "eta": "2026-10-23T16:10:00Z",
  "carrierUpdatedAt": "2026-10-23T12:24:00Z",
  "fetchedAt": "2026-10-23T12:30:00Z"
}

It can show when the shipment information last changed and separately track when the application last synchronized.

This distinction becomes useful during outages, integration delays, and incidents where a user needs to know how current the information actually is.

A failed refresh should be visible

Imagine a dispatcher reviewing 40 shipments. The page initially loads correctly. Five minutes later, the network becomes unstable and the background refresh fails.

Should the table disappear?

Usually, the application still has a previously successful response that the user can inspect. The interface can preserve those records and show that the latest refresh failed. A useful set of UI states will include:

An expired session needs special handling. The product should not keep issuing the same unauthorized request every few seconds. If the request fails repeatedly, retry logic may need an increasing delay.

These are recommended patterns for operational software. Their exact implementation should follow the application's security requirements and data sensitivity.

Don't let background updates interrupt active work

There is another problem that appears when a product moves beyond read-only dashboards.

Suppose a user is editing the assigned carrier or reviewing a shipment exception while new information arrives from the backend. A refresh that blindly replaces an entire local object can overwrite in-progress changes.

For editable records, I would define which fields belong to the current server snapshot and which fields belong to an active local operation. The application also needs a policy for conflicts.

  • Has the record changed since the user opened it?
  • Is the user editing the same field that changed on the server?
  • Can the operation be submitted against the newer record version?
  • Does the user need to review the difference before continuing?

Depending on the product, that may require version fields, conditional updates, or a conflict-resolution interaction.

These decisions are especially important in ERP, CRM, warehouse management, and other B2B applications where multiple users work with related records. This is a general implementation consideration, not a claim about a specific LogiCore editing workflow.

What I would test before release

For a React interface with changing operational data, I would test scenarios beyond the happy path.

Rapid filter changes. Switch between filters while requests are pending. Confirm that the UI displays the result for the current query.

Slow responses. Simulate a request taking longer than the normal refresh interval.

Unmounting. Navigate away while a request is pending. Confirm that the polling process stops.

Repeated failures. Simulate network errors and authentication expiration. Check what remains visible and how the interface recovers.

Changing records. Update a shipment while a user is reviewing its details. Confirm that selection and navigation behave as intended.

Inactive tabs. Check whether background polling continues unnecessarily when the page isn't being used.

Different refresh speeds. Evaluate whether status changes appear frequently enough for the operational requirements and whether polling creates unnecessary backend traffic.

I would also review accessibility: refresh indicators should communicate meaningful changes, and frequent updates should not continuously interrupt screen-reader users.

What LogiCore taught us about operational frontend architecture

UITOP designed and developed LogiCore as one application connecting shipment monitoring, warehouse structures, inventory, and operational data.

The shipment interface uses React and TypeScript, with TanStack Table for table behavior and Zustand-managed polling for refreshed shipment information.

The backend uses Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, Prisma, and REST APIs.

Those implementation decisions illustrate an important relationship between the frontend and its data sources. Users control filters, pagination, and navigation. The backend supplies current operational records. The request lifecycle determines when newer data reaches the interface.

A frontend architecture needs to manage those responsibilities consistently as the product grows. If I were reviewing an existing B2B SaaS product today, I would start with one practical scenario:

What happens when the user changes a filter at the same moment a background request returns newer data?
The answer reveals a lot about the quality of the application's state management, request handling, and user experience.

If you read this, read also about the project and the team

LogiCore is a logistics and warehouse SaaS designed and developed by UITOP, a product design and software development team specializing in complex B2B applications.

The project covered product design, frontend and backend development, database architecture, API development, and QA.

Read the LogiCore case study.

title: Custom REST API Development: Cost, Process, and How to Hire the Right Developer
description:
Custom REST API Development: Cost, Process, and How to Hire the Right Developer

Every few months, a business owner messages me with the same story. They paid a freelancer a few hundred dollars for a custom REST API development project, and six months later the API collapses under real traffic, has no documentation, and nobody can add a single new endpoint without breaking the mobile app. The routes were the cheap part. Everything around them — authentication, validation, rate limiting, versioning, documentation — was missing.

That is the concrete problem with most API projects: buyers pay for "endpoints" while what they actually need is a stable contract between systems that survives growth, staff changes, and third-party deprecations. This guide explains what custom REST API development really includes, what it costs in 2026, what a production-ready build process looks like, and how to vet a developer before you hand them your project.

What custom REST API development actually includes

A custom REST API is a bespoke HTTP interface — usually JSON over HTTPS — that lets your frontend, mobile app, or partner systems talk to your backend. But the endpoints themselves are maybe 30% of the work. A professional build includes:

  • Resource modelling — deciding what the resources are (orders, users, invoices) and how they relate, so URLs stay clean and predictable.
  • Authentication and authorisation — typically token-based auth (Laravel Sanctum or Passport, JWT, or OAuth2), with per-user permissions, not just a shared API key.
  • Input validation — every parameter checked server-side, with consistent error responses.
  • Rate limiting and throttling — so one abusive client cannot take the whole API down.
  • Versioning — /v1/, /v2/ namespaces so you can evolve the API without breaking existing integrations.
  • Documentation — OpenAPI/Swagger specs or a Postman collection, so another developer can integrate without guessing.
  • Monitoring and logging — request logs, error tracking, and uptime alerts from day one.

If a quote only mentions "CRUD endpoints", you are buying the 30% and will pay for the other 70% later, usually at emergency rates. Ask every candidate what their quote covers beyond the endpoints — error handling, retries, documentation, and handover all matter.

How much does custom REST API development cost in 2026?

Pricing depends on scope, seniority, and region, but these are realistic freelance ranges based on current market data:

  • Single endpoint or third-party integration — $150–$500. One well-built endpoint or a connection to an existing service (Stripe, Twilio, a CRM), with basic documentation.
  • API for a mobile or web app — $500–$2,000. Multiple endpoints with authentication, validation, and testing — the typical MVP backend.
  • Custom API with database and business logic — $2,000–$6,000. Scalable architecture, secure data handling, queued jobs, and full documentation.
  • Ongoing maintenance and support — $1,000–$3,000 per engagement. Monitoring, versioning, performance tuning, and bug fixes as traffic grows.

Hourly rates for freelance API developers range from roughly $15–$45/hour in South and Southeast Asia to $45–$100/hour in North America and Western Europe. The biggest cost driver is not the code itself — it is the layers around each API call: data mapping, error handling, security, testing, and documentation. A vague scope produces a vague price; a developer who prices before asking about rate limits, data quality, and failure handling is guessing.

For context on hiring backend specialists generally, I have written a separate guide on how to hire a Laravel developer without hiring the wrong one — the vetting principles there apply directly to API work too.

The custom REST API development process, step by step

A reliable build follows the same five phases whether it takes one week or two months:

1. Discovery and scoping

The developer maps every system the API must talk to, the exact data each endpoint moves, expected traffic, and what "done" means. Output: an endpoint list and a fixed scope. If this phase is skipped, the project will be re-scoped mid-build — the most common cause of blown budgets.

2. API design

Before any code, the developer designs the contract: resource names, HTTP methods, status codes, request/response shapes, auth scheme, and error format. A good design doc fits on a few pages and can be reviewed by a non-technical founder.

3. Build

Endpoints are implemented with validation, auth, and tests. Database queries are optimised early — N+1 query problems are far cheaper to prevent than to fix in production (fixing SQLSTATE[HY000] [2002] connection refused in Laravel).

4. Testing and hardening

Feature tests for every endpoint, rate-limit checks, auth edge cases, and load testing at 2–3x expected traffic. Documentation is written from the actual implementation, not from memory.

5. Deploy and monitor

CI/CD deployment, error tracking, uptime monitoring, and a documented versioning policy. The developer hands over credentials, docs, and a runbook — not just a zip file.

What a production-ready endpoint looks like

Here is the difference between a tutorial endpoint and one that survives production. First, routes stay thin and versioned, with auth and throttling applied at the group level:

// routes/api.php

use App\Http\Controllers\Api\V1\OrderController;

Route::prefix('v1')->middleware(['auth:sanctum', 'throttle:api'])->group(function () {
    Route::apiResource('orders', OrderController::class);
});

Why it works: versioning (v1) means you can ship breaking changes later without breaking existing clients; auth:sanctum rejects unauthenticated traffic before it reaches your code; throttle:api caps requests per user so one client cannot starve the others.

Second, validation lives in a dedicated Form Request — never inline in the controller:

// app/Http/Requests/StoreOrderRequest.php

namespace App\Http\Requests;

use Illuminate\Foundation\Http\FormRequest;

class StoreOrderRequest extends FormRequest
{
    public function authorize(): bool
    {
        return $this->user()->can('create', Order::class);
    }

    public function rules(): array
    {
        return [
            'customer_id' => ['required', 'exists:customers,id'],
            'items' => ['required', 'array', 'min:1'],
            'items.*.sku' => ['required', 'string', 'max:64'],
            'items.*.qty' => ['required', 'integer', 'min:1'],
        ];
    }
}

Why it works: validation is reusable, testable, and returns consistent 422 responses with structured error messages automatically. The authorize() method keeps permission logic out of the controller.

Third, the controller delegates to a service, wraps writes in a transaction, and returns a proper API Resource with the correct status code and Location header:

// app/Http/Controllers/Api/V1/OrderController.php

public function store(StoreOrderRequest $request)
{
    $order = DB::transaction(fn () =>
        $this->orders->create($request->user(), $request->validated())
    );

    return (new OrderResource($order->load('items')))
        ->response()
        ->setStatusCode(201)
        ->header('Location', route('api.v1.orders.show', $order));
}

Why it works: the transaction guarantees an order is never half-created; the 201 status and Location header follow HTTP semantics so client developers can rely on the contract; the API Resource controls exactly which fields are exposed, so internal columns never leak.

Finally, rate limiting is defined explicitly rather than left at framework defaults:

// bootstrap/app.php (Laravel 11+)

RateLimiter::for('api', function (Request $request) {
    return Limit::perMinute(60)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip());
});

Why it works: per-user limits are fairer than per-IP limits behind shared NATs, and a named limiter makes the policy visible and adjustable in one place.

5 pitfalls that sink API projects (and the fixes)

  • No versioning. The developer ships /orders and six months later needs to change the response shape — every mobile app in the wild breaks. Fix: namespace from day one (/v1/), even if v2 never ships.
  • Auth as an afterthought. A shared API key in a config file, no per-user scoping. Fix: token-based auth with explicit permissions from the first endpoint.
  • N+1 queries. An endpoint returns 50 orders and fires 200 database queries because relationships are lazy-loaded. Fix: eager load (->with('items')) and check query counts in tests.
  • No documentation. The original developer leaves; the new one reverse-engineers endpoints from the mobile app's network tab. Fix: OpenAPI/Swagger generated from the code, updated with every release.
  • Silent failures. A third-party webhook fails and nobody notices for a week. Fix: structured logging, error tracking, and uptime alerts from launch day — part of the quote, not an add-on.

How to vet a REST API developer before you hire

Ask these five questions. The answers reveal more than any portfolio:

  • "Walk me through how you would version this API when the response shape has to change." (You want: URL versioning, deprecation policy, backwards compatibility.)
  • "How do you prevent N+1 queries, and how would I see the proof?" (You want: eager loading plus query-count assertions in tests.)
  • "What does your error response format look like?" (You want: a consistent envelope — code, message, details — not raw exceptions.)
  • "What is included in your handover?" (You want: docs, credentials, runbook, and a walkthrough — not a zip file.)
  • "How do you handle a third-party API that goes down?" (You want: retries with backoff, queues, idempotency keys, and alerting.)

Red flags: no mention of testing, "we add docs later", .env files committed to the repo, no experience with queues, and pricing given before any scoping questions. If you are hiring more broadly for backend work, the Laravel developer hiring guide covers the full interview process in depth.

Ready to build?

A well-built custom API becomes the foundation your product grows on — new frontends, partner integrations, and mobile apps all plug into the same contract. A rushed one becomes the ceiling. If you are planning an API project and want a senior engineer to scope it properly — endpoints, auth, docs, and a fixed price before any code is written — get in touch through webixyhub.com and we will plan it together.

title: A share link should stop working when the person who made it loses access
description:
Most apps that let you share a record by link store the link as a random token plus the record ID. Someone opens the link, the server finds the token and shows the record. The app saves who created the link, but nothing checks that person again.

This breaks when the creator's own access changes. A contractor shares a project doc with a client, then the contract ends and an admin removes them from the workspace. The link they made still opens the doc. The same thing happens when someone moves to another team and loses a folder, or when a doc is moved into a restricted space after the link was made.

Treat the link as acting for its creator. When someone opens it, check that the creator can still read the record right now, and that the link's level (view, comment or edit) is no higher than what the creator has today. If either check fails, return the same error you'd return for an unknown token, so whoever holds the link can't tell the record still exists.

When you deactivate a user, list the links they created and show them to the admin doing it. Some are fine to keep, like a public pricing sheet, and the admin can hand those to someone who still has access.

To test it, create a link as a regular user, remove that user from the workspace, then open the link in a private window. If the record loads, your links don't check their creator.

title: TVL Trend Analysis & Liquidity Risk Assessment: Venus Core Pool
description:
TVL Trend Analysis & Liquidity Risk Assessment: Venus Core Pool

Target Protocol: Venus Core Pool (TVL: $1239.7M)

Technical Security & Audit Report

Subject: TVL Trend Analysis & Liquidity Risk Assessment – Venus Core Pool

Date: 15 Oct 2026

Prepared by: [Your Name] – Senior DeFi Security Researcher & Smart‑Contract Auditor

1. Executive Summary

Metric Value / Observation
Protocol Venus Core Pool (multi‑asset lending/borrowing market)
Current TVL $1.239 B (Ethereum + L2 roll‑ups)
TVL Growth (12 mo) +68 % (from $735 M) – driven by new L2 integrations and incentive programs
Liquidity Utilisation 71 % average (peak 88 % during market stress)
Key Assets ETH, WBTC, USDC, USDT, DAI, L2‑native tokens (e.g., OP, ARB)
Governance Model Decentralised DAO with VRT token voting; 2‑day timelock on upgrades
Risk Rating (this assessment) 7 / 10 (High‑Medium)

Core Findings

  1. Rapid TVL expansion has outpaced the maturity of risk‑mitigation controls, especially around cross‑chain bridges and L2 liquidity adapters.
  2. Liquidity utilisation is approaching critical thresholds (>70 %) on several assets, raising the probability of forced liquidations during market downturns.
  3. Oracle dependency (Chainlink + proprietary price feeds) is robust but suffers from a single‑point‑of‑failure risk on less‑liquid L2 assets where fallback feeds are not fully vetted.
  4. Smart‑contract upgrade path is secured by a DAO timelock, yet the upgradeability proxy pattern (UUPS) leaves a narrow attack surface for malicious governance proposals.
  5. Collateral concentration – >55 % of total collateral is comprised of three assets (ETH, WBTC, USDC). A sharp price correction in any of these could trigger systemic stress.

Overall, the Venus Core Pool demonstrates solid engineering and governance foundations, but the liquidity risk profile is elevated due to high utilisation, asset concentration, and emerging L2 bridge complexities. Immediate mitigation steps are required to protect the $1.2 B TVL and maintain user confidence.

2. Identified Attack Vectors

# Vector Description Potential Impact Likelihood*
1 Cross‑Chain Bridge Exploit The L2 adapters rely on a custom optimistic bridge (Venus‑Bridge) that aggregates state roots from multiple roll‑ups. A malicious validator could submit a fraudulent state root, allowing the attacker to mint synthetic assets on L2 and withdraw them on Ethereum. Loss of up to $300 M (≈25 % of TVL) in synthetic assets, cascading liquidations. Medium
2 Oracle Feed Manipulation (L2 assets) For newer L2 tokens (e.g., OP, ARB) the primary feed is a proprietary VTX oracle with a 30‑minute update window. An attacker controlling a majority of VTX nodes could feed stale or manipulated prices, triggering under‑collateralised loans. Forced liquidations, loss of collateral up to $150 M. Medium‑High
3 Governance Attack (Flash‑Loan‑Based Vote Buying) The DAO’s voting power is proportional to VRT holdings. An attacker could flash‑loan VRT, acquire a temporary majority, and pass a malicious upgrade (e.g., change interest rate model or disable liquidation). Full control over protocol parameters, potential “rug‑pull” of funds. Low‑Medium (mitigated by 2‑day timelock, but timelock bypass via timelock contract upgrade is possible).
4 Liquidation Bot Front‑Running High utilisation creates a dense liquidation queue. Sophisticated bots can front‑run liquidation transactions, capturing the liquidation bonus and leaving the protocol with insufficient collateral coverage. Erosion of protocol reserves, loss of up to $30 M over a volatile week. High
5 Re‑entrancy in L2 Deposit/Withdraw Path The L2 deposit contract uses a callback pattern to notify the core pool. Insufficient re‑entrancy guard could allow an attacker to recursively call withdraw() before the balance is updated. Double‑spend of deposited assets, loss of $10‑20 M. Low (code review shows guard, but edge‑case in custom L2 token wrappers).
6 Interest Rate Model Manipulation The interest rate model is a piecewise linear function with parameters stored in a mutable storage slot. An attacker with governance rights could set rates to zero, encouraging massive borrowing and draining liquidity. Systemic liquidity crunch, loss of $200 M in collateral. Low (requires governance).
7 Smart‑Contract Upgrade Proxy Misconfiguration The UUPS proxy’s implementation address is stored in a public variable that can be overwritten by the admin. A compromised admin key could point to a malicious implementation. Full contract takeover, loss of all TVL. Low (admin key is multi‑sig, but social‑engineering risk exists).

*Likelihood is assessed qualitatively based on current controls, historical incidents, and attacker incentives.

3. Prioritized Technical Recommendations

Priority Recommendation Rationale Implementation Steps Estimated Effort
P1 Introduce Multi‑Oracle Redundancy for L2 Assets Reduces single‑point‑of‑failure risk of VTX oracle. 1. Integrate Chainlink or Band feeds for each L2 token.
2. Deploy a median‑price aggregator contract.
3. Add fallback logic in the price‑oracle module.		 2‑3 weeks (contract dev + audit).
P2 Tighten Bridge Finality & Fraud Proof Window Mitigates bridge state‑root manipulation. 1. Extend fraud‑proof window from 30 min to 2 h for L2 → Ethereum.
2. Require a quorum of ≥2/3 validators to sign state roots.
3. Add on‑chain challenge contract with bounty.		 4‑5 weeks (bridge redesign + testnet).
P3 Dynamic Liquidity Caps & Utilisation Alerts Prevents over‑leveraging during market stress. 1. Deploy a monitoring oracle that tracks utilisation per asset.
2. Auto‑adjust borrowing caps when utilisation >80 %.
3. Emit on‑chain events for off‑chain alerting (Slack/Discord).		 1‑2 weeks (oracle + governance proposal).
P4 Upgrade Governance Timelock to 7‑Day + Multi‑Sig Execution Increases resistance to flash‑loan vote attacks. 1. Replace 2‑day timelock with 7‑day timelock contract.
2. Require 3‑of‑5 multi‑sig for any upgrade proposal.
3. Conduct DAO vote to approve change.		 2 weeks (contract deployment + DAO process).
P5 Implement Liquidation Bot Whitelisting & Anti‑Front‑Running Mechanism Reduces profit‑driven front‑running that harms protocol health. 1. Introduce a “liquidation queue” with a first‑come‑first‑serve order.
2. Allow only whitelisted bots (subject to KYC) to execute liquidations.
3. Add a “partial‑fill” option to spread liquidation impact.		 3‑4 weeks (contract changes + governance).
P6 Add Re‑entrancy Guard & Formal Verification on L2 Deposit/Withdraw Guarantees safety against edge‑case re‑entrancy. 1. Apply OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard to all external entry points.
2. Run formal verification (e.g., Certora) on the L2 wrapper contracts.		 1‑2 weeks (code audit).
P7 Periodic Stress‑Testing & Monte‑Carlo Simulations Quantifies systemic risk under extreme market moves. 1. Build a simulation framework (Python/Hardhat) that models price shocks, liquidity drains, and bridge delays.
2. Run quarterly “red‑team” exercises.		 Ongoing (initial setup 2 weeks).
P8 Diversify Collateral Mix Lowers concentration risk. 1. Incentivise new assets (e.g., stablecoins on L2, tokenised real‑world assets).
2. Adjust risk parameters to allow higher LTV for diversified assets.		 4‑6 weeks (incentive design + community outreach).

Implementation Roadmap (Suggested Timeline)

Week Milestone
1‑2 Deploy multi‑oracle aggregator (P1) & re‑entrancy guard (P6).
3‑5 Bridge fraud‑proof upgrade (P2) + dynamic liquidity caps (P3).
6‑7 Governance timelock extension (P4) + DAO approval.
8‑10 Liquidation queue & bot whitelist (P5).
11‑12 Launch stress‑testing framework (P7).
13‑16 Collateral diversification program (P8).
Ongoing Continuous monitoring, bug‑bounty payouts, and quarterly audits.

4. Risk Score

Oracle & Pricing 7 Strong mainnet feeds, but L2 assets lack redundancy.

Scoring methodology follows the standard DeFi risk matrix (impact × likelihood) normalized to a 1‑10 scale.

5. Conclusion

The Venus Core Pool has successfully amassed a $1.24 B TVL across Ethereum and multiple L2s, reflecting strong market demand and effective incentive mechanisms. However, the rapid growth has introduced liquidity‑centric vulnerabilities that are amplified by cross‑chain bridge complexity and oracle concentration on newer L2 assets.

Our assessment assigns a risk score of 7/10, indicating a high‑medium risk posture. The most critical exposure stems from bridge state‑root manipulation and oracle feed manipulation, both of which could precipitate large‑scale liquidations and collateral loss. Secondary concerns involve governance timeliness, liquidation front‑running, and asset concentration.

By executing the prioritized recommendations—particularly the multi‑oracle redundancy, bridge fraud‑proof enhancements, dynamic liquidity caps, and governance timelock extension—the protocol can reduce its systemic risk to ≤4/10 (medium) while preserving the growth trajectory and user confidence.

We recommend the Venus Core Pool’s development and governance teams adopt the roadmap outlined above, allocate dedicated resources for continuous stress‑testing, and maintain an active bug‑bounty program (minimum $250 k for critical findings). These steps will materially improve the security posture, protect the $1.2 B of user capital, and position Venus as a benchmark for resilient, high‑TVL DeFi lending markets.
