title: Ephemeral credentials for databases: moving past the shared application account
description:
Ephemeral credentials for databases: moving past the shared application account

A shared database account is a familiar design. An application reads its connection string from configuration, all replicas use the same username and password, and rotation means a coordinated restart across every service that depends on it. Rotation therefore happens rarely or not at all.

Why the static credential persists

The convenience is real. Connection pools assume a stable identity. Database proxies, failover, and read replicas all inherit the same secret. Introducing per-instance credentials appears to add operational risk rather than remove it.

What short-lived credentials change

Dynamic secrets are issued on request and expire on a schedule. Each application instance receives its own credential, so revocation affects one instance instead of the fleet. Auditing becomes concrete: the database log shows which instance connected when.

The lifetime should match the workload. A batch job that runs for two hours needs a credential that outlives the job. A web service that can re-authenticate on each connection can use a much shorter window.

Handling the transition

Connection pools are the practical obstacle. Pools must be configured to refresh credentials before expiry, and the refresh must be tested against database failover. Applications should handle a rejected connection by requesting a new credential rather than retrying the old one indefinitely.

Emergency access needs its own path. If the issuing service is unavailable, operators need a documented break-glass procedure, with the use of that path logged and reviewed.

Verifying the control

A credential system is only as good as what it prevents. Confirm that a revoked credential is rejected within the expected window, that a leaked credential from one instance cannot be used by another, and that the audit trail records the subject rather than a shared account.

References

  • NIST SP 800-53, Security and Privacy Controls: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final
  • NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final

title: A Guide to 4 Sequence Guarantees for Accepted High Bid Broadcasts
description:
The page says students in a live classroom auction have seen different winning bids after reconnecting. An instructor's screen shows the latest accepted bid, while a student's chat still shows the previous one. Short answer: commit the accepted bid and its room-local sequence number in one authoritative transaction, then broadcast that committed event; on reconnect, fetch the missing sequence range before showing the room as caught up. An Express handler can accept the request, but an HTTP 200 or a successful socket write cannot establish that every student received it.

This is a delivery problem, not a faster-socket problem. A WebSocket connection gives a channel for messages, while application-level recovery still needs an event identifier and a way to read events missed while disconnected. The WebSocket protocol defines framing and connection behavior, not durable room history or exactly-once application processing. See RFC 6455 in Further reading.

No receipt, no certainty.

What should have paged before the classroom diverged?

An alert on disconnected sockets comes late and can miss the actual failure: a connected client may also skip an event after a server restart or a failed fan-out. Measure the age of the oldest committed room event that has not reached the delivery worker, and count detected sequence gaps during client catch-up. Page on sustained backlog age against the room's delivery SLO; use a separate, lower-severity signal for a rising gap-recovery rate. The SLO and alert window need to come from measured classroom requirements, not a copied threshold.

First distinguish three positions: the room's committed sequence, the last sequence a fan-out worker has attempted, and the last contiguous sequence each client has applied. Those counters answer different questions. A broadcast counter that increments before the database transaction commits can advance even when the bid is rejected, leaving a gap that no reconnect can fill. Conversely, a committed event with no delivery attempt is a useful early warning while clients may still appear healthy.

For a live auction inside a course room, a bid request should carry an idempotency key, room ID, bidder identity, and offered amount. The server checks authorization and the current high bid inside the transaction, assigns the next room-local sequence only to an accepted bid, and persists an event with that accepted amount. The acceptance response returns the committed sequence. Other bidders learn the result from the room stream, not from trusting their own submitted amount. Two concurrent requests must serialize around the room's authoritative bid state; otherwise both can claim the same predecessor.

How should an accepted high bid broadcast carry its sequence number?

At the commit boundary. Publishing before commit lets students see a winning bid that later rolls back. Publishing only from the request handler after commit creates the opposite hole: the handler can die between commit and broadcast. A transactional outbox closes that hole by storing the accepted-bid event and the state update in the same transaction; a worker retries delivery afterward. The outbox does not make client delivery exactly once. A worker may send and then crash before recording progress, so consumers must tolerate duplicates. The transactional outbox pattern and its duplicate-delivery consequence are documented in Further reading.

For an Express implementation, keep the route thin: authenticate, pass the command and idempotency key to the transactional bid service, and return the committed sequence; a separate broadcaster drains the outbox. Here is the smaller, transport-independent piece of client-side recovery logic in Go. It never assumes a WebSocket callback represents a durable acknowledgment:

package room

import "errors"

var ErrGap = errors.New("fetch missing room events")

type Event struct {
    RoomID   string
    Sequence uint64
    Kind     string
    Amount   int64 // Minor currency units, as stored by the server.
}

type Cursor struct {
    RoomID   string
    Sequence uint64
}

func Apply(cursor *Cursor, event Event) error {
    if event.RoomID != cursor.RoomID {
        return errors.New("event belongs to another room")
    }
    if event.Sequence <= cursor.Sequence {
        return nil // Retried delivery or replay overlap.
    }
    if event.Sequence != cursor.Sequence+1 {
        return ErrGap
    }
    cursor.Sequence = event.Sequence
    return nil
}

Persist the cursor only after applying the corresponding event to the local view. If the client sees a gap, pause live application, request events after its last contiguous sequence, and replay them in order before resuming the stream. During that handoff, buffer later live events or open the stream first and deduplicate replay overlap by sequence; otherwise an event committed between the history query and subscription can disappear from the view. Consider a student whose cursor is 41 while the worker has committed 42 and 43: if the client queries history through 42, then subscribes after 43 was broadcast, neither the replay nor the live stream contains 43. Opening the stream first and holding its events during replay removes that specific handoff window, provided duplicates are collapsed by sequence. Reconnection needs a bounded retention policy too: if the cursor predates available history, return an authoritative snapshot plus its sequence, then resume from there. A snapshot without its sequence cannot establish a clean handoff.

Replay can get expensive.

Which guarantee is worth carrying on call?

The table is a capacity-planning question as much as a correctness question. A larger room multiplies simultaneous connections and replay demand, while a slow client can retain an unbounded send queue unless the server caps it and forces a clean reconnect.

Choice What it establishes Operational cost
Fire-and-forget fan-out Best-effort live display Small state footprint; disconnected learners miss events.
Persisted room log with replay At-least-once delivery opportunity while events remain retained Storage, replay reads, retention policy, and duplicate handling.
Client acknowledgment of contiguous sequence Evidence of application progress per client Ack storage and extra traffic; acks can also be lost.
Exactly-once display effect One visible application of each room sequence Requires idempotent client state transitions; transport alone cannot provide it.

I would choose a retained log and idempotent application for accepted bids because a duplicated chat bubble is repairable, but a missing high bid changes the apparent outcome. Ordinary typing indicators warrant a different choice: replaying stale presence is more misleading than dropping it. Keep these message classes separate even if they share a connection.

The limitation of a retained log is that it cannot replay forever without a retention and storage budget, and it cannot establish what a client actually displayed unless that client acknowledges application. For a course that does not need recoverable bid history, best-effort broadcasts avoid much of that persistent-state burden; for an auction where the displayed winner matters, that trade-off is unacceptable. Choose the guarantee by event class, not by transport branding.

The buy-versus-build decision follows the same boundary. A managed transport can reduce connection operations, but the team still owns acceptance rules, sequence assignment, retention requirements, and the definition of a caught-up room; self-hosting the transport adds capacity limits, deployment drains, and on-call work. Neither option turns an acknowledgment of network delivery into proof that a student rendered the accepted bid. Test both with a forced disconnect after commit, a duplicate outbox dispatch, two concurrent higher bids, and a reconnect during replay. Track rejected bids separately from accepted-event delivery latency so a legitimate rejection does not appear as lost fan-out.

When does the alert do more harm than good?

Do not page on every reconnect or each transient replay gap. Wireless classroom networks make both common, and a gap that closes within the delivery SLO has not yet violated the user-facing objective. Alert on sustained oldest-undelivered age and on rooms that remain behind after recovery; annotate those signals with room size, replay rate, and outbox backlog so on-call can distinguish a single slow client from a worker-wide stall.

The cost of an aggressive threshold is real: noisy pages train the team to disregard the one backlog that will leave an instructor and students looking at different accepted bids. The cost of a permissive one is a silent, durable disagreement. Set the threshold from observed delivery latency and the classroom's recovery target, then exercise it during controlled worker restarts and client disconnects. The alert should tell on-call which committed sequence is waiting, not merely that a socket closed.

Further reading

  • WebSocket Protocol, RFC 6455: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • Transactional Outbox pattern and duplicate delivery: https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html
  • WebRTC 1.0 specification, for the separate peer-connection transport boundary: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: PCAD-31-02 in Code: Validation Checks and Safe sqlite3 Queries Behind 30 of the 48 Items
description:
The Python Institute PCAD-31-02 exam has 48 items, and 30 of them come from two syllabus blocks: Data Acquisition and Pre-Processing (14) and Programming and Database Skills (16). If you can clean a messy file, validate it, move it into a database with safe queries and read the result back into pandas, you have practised the skills behind 62.5% of the exam.

This post does all of that in one small script you can run. Every output shown below was produced by running it with Python 3.12 and pandas 3.0.6, using only sqlite3 from the standard library for the database part.

What does the PCAD-31-02 exam look like?

PCAD (Certified Associate Data Analyst with Python) is the associate-level data exam of the OpenEDG Python Institute. The figures below come from the official PCAD certification page, read on 15 October 2026.

Item Value
Exam code PCAD-31-02, active since July 15, 2025 (PCAD-31-01 retired July 14, 2025)
Questions 48 single-select and multiple-select items, some scenario-based
Time 60 minutes, plus the NDA screen
Passing score 75%
Price Exam from $195; exam with retake from $225; practice test $49
Delivery Online through OpenEDG Testing Service (TestNow)
Prerequisites None formal; PCAP and PCED (or equivalent) recommended
Validity 6 years

How are the 48 items split across the five blocks?

The Python Institute publishes the split in the PCAD-31-02 exam syllabus, last updated July 15, 2025. Each item is worth up to one point, and the raw score is normalized to a percentage.

Block Items Weight
1. Data Acquisition and Pre-Processing 14 29.2%
2. Programming and Database Skills 16 33.3%
3. Statistical Analysis 4 8.3%
4. Data Analysis and Modeling 9 18.8%
5. Data Communication and Visualization 5 10.4%

Note what that means for your study plan. Blocks 1 and 2 are the bulk, but 30 of 48 is still below the 75% pass mark, so the statistics, pandas and charting blocks cannot be skipped. The script below covers the large blocks; it also touches objective 4.1.1 (cleaning with pandas) on the way.

Why load every column as text first?

Objective 1.2.2 asks you to identify erroneous data before you fix it. If pandas guesses types on load, a bad value can silently change a whole column's type, and you lose the chance to see which rows were wrong. Loading with dtype=str keeps the raw values so the cleaning step decides what each one means.

Here is a small order file with the problems the syllabus lists by name: stray spaces, mixed case, a thousands separator, a missing value written as text, a negative amount, a duplicate row, a date in the wrong format and five spellings of yes and no.

import io
import sqlite3

import pandas as pd

pd.set_option("display.width", 120, "display.max_columns", 10)   # print tables in full

RAW = """order_id,customer,country,amount,paid,order_date,ship_date
1001,  Ana Lima ,BR,120.50,yes,2026-09-01,2026-09-03
1002,ben okafor,NG,"1,080.00",Y,2026-09-02,2026-09-01
1003,Chen Wei,CN,n/a,no,2026-09-02,2026-09-05
1004,Ana Lima,br,-15,TRUE,2026-09-03,2026-09-04
1004,Ana Lima,br,-15,TRUE,2026-09-03,2026-09-04
1005,Dara Singh,IN,64.00,0,03/09/2026,2026-09-06
1006,Ben Okafor,NG,310.00,1,2026-09-04,2026-09-07
1007,Chen Wei,cn,89.90,yes,2026-09-05,2026-09-05
1008,Dara Singh,IN,455.00,N,2026-09-06,2026-09-09
1009,ana lima,BR,72.25,y,2026-09-07,2026-09-08
"""
df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(RAW), dtype=str)
print(len(df), "rows")   # 10 rows

Which cleaning steps does Block 1 name, and what do they look like?

Objective 1.2.4 lists them in one sentence: string manipulation, format standardization, boolean normalization, case normalization and string-to-number conversion. Each one is a single line in pandas.

BOOL = {"yes": True, "y": True, "true": True, "1": True,
        "no": False, "n": False, "false": False, "0": False}

df = df.drop_duplicates()
df["customer"] = df["customer"].str.strip().str.title()
df["country"] = df["country"].str.strip().str.upper()
df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["amount"].str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")
df["paid"] = df["paid"].str.strip().str.lower().map(BOOL)
for col in ("order_date", "ship_date"):
    df[col] = pd.to_datetime(df[col], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
df["order_id"] = df["order_id"].astype(int)
print(df.dtypes)

order_id               int64
customer                 str
country                  str
amount               float64
paid                    bool
order_date    datetime64[us]
ship_date     datetime64[us]
dtype: object

The key argument is errors="coerce". As the pandas.to_numeric reference explains, it turns a value that cannot be parsed into NaN instead of raising an exception. That is what you want during cleaning: the bad value becomes a marker you can count and report, not a crash halfway through a file.

The same idea applies to dates. Passing an explicit format means 03/09/2026 becomes NaT rather than being guessed as March 9 or September 3. Whether that date was day-first or month-first is a question for the data owner, not for the parser.

What do type, range and cross-field checks look like in pandas?

Objective 1.3.1 names three kinds of validation: type, range and cross-field. Build each check as a boolean column, then keep the rows where no check fired. A table of named checks is easier to report to a stakeholder than a chain of filters.

checks = pd.DataFrame({
    "amount_not_numeric": df["amount"].isna(),            # type
    "order_date_unparsed": df["order_date"].isna(),       # type
    "amount_not_positive": df["amount"] <= 0,             # range
    "shipped_before_order": df["ship_date"] < df["order_date"],  # cross-field
})
bad = checks.any(axis=1)
print(checks[bad].set_axis(df.loc[bad, "order_id"]))
clean = df[~bad]
print(len(clean), "rows pass")

          amount_not_numeric  order_date_unparsed  amount_not_positive  shipped_before_order
order_id
1002                   False                False                False                  True
1003                    True                False                False                 False
1004                   False                False                 True                 False
1005                   False                 True                False                 False
5 rows pass

Two details are worth knowing for the exam. First, a comparison with NaN or NaT is always False, so a missing amount does not trip the range check; that is why the type check exists separately. Second, the duplicate of order 1004 was already gone, because drop_duplicates() ran before validation. Removing or imputing a row is a decision with consequences, and objective 1.2.4 asks you to discuss imputation against exclusion. Here exclusion is the honest choice: there is no sensible value to invent for a missing order amount.

How do Python types map to SQLite columns?

Objective 2.4.5 is about converting data types between SQL and Python. The sqlite3 module documentation lists exactly five Python types that go into SQLite without help: None, int, float, str and bytes.

Python value SQLite storage What to do
None NULL Nothing
int INTEGER Nothing
float REAL Nothing
str TEXT Nothing
bool INTEGER (0 or 1) Store as int(value)
datetime or pandas Timestamp No date type Store as ISO 8601 text

SQLite has no boolean and no date storage class. The SQLite page on datatypes and type affinity says booleans are stored as the integers 0 and 1, and dates as ISO 8601 text, a real number or an integer. Here is what happens if you skip the conversion:

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("""
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer   TEXT    NOT NULL,
    country    TEXT    NOT NULL,
    amount     REAL    CHECK (amount > 0),
    paid       INTEGER NOT NULL,
    order_date TEXT    NOT NULL
)""")
first = clean.iloc[0]
try:
    con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                (first["order_id"], first["customer"], first["country"],
                 first["amount"], first["paid"], first["order_date"]))
except sqlite3.ProgrammingError as e:
    print("ProgrammingError:", e)

ProgrammingError: Error binding parameter 6: type 'Timestamp' is not supported

So convert each row explicitly and insert the batch with executemany. The with con: block commits on success and rolls back on an exception, and the CHECK constraint in the table is a second line of defence for the range rule:

rows = [
    (int(r.order_id), r.customer, r.country, float(r.amount),
     int(r.paid), r.order_date.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
    for r in clean.itertuples(index=False)
]
with con:
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders").fetchone())   # (5,)

try:
    with con:
        con.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                    (1010, "Eve Park", "KR", -5.0, 1, "2026-09-08"))
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("IntegrityError:", e)   # CHECK constraint failed: amount > 0

Why does the exam keep asking about parameterized queries?

Two Block 2 objectives, 2.4.4 and 2.4.6, come back to the same point: never build SQL by pasting values into a string. The demonstration takes four lines.

name = "x' OR '1'='1"
unsafe = f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = '{name}'"
print(con.execute(unsafe).fetchone())        # (5,)  every row matched
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = ?", (name,)).fetchone())   # (0,)
print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer = :who",
                  {"who": "Ana Lima"}).fetchone())   # (2,)

The f-string version closes the quote early and turns the filter into a condition that is always true. With a ? placeholder the driver sends the value separately from the SQL text, so the quote characters are just part of a name that matches nobody. The third line shows the named style, :who with a dictionary, which reads better once a query has several parameters.

How do you get query results back into pandas?

Objective 2.4.1 lists the clauses the exam expects you to combine: SELECT, FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY and LIMIT. The query below uses all of them, with a LEFT JOIN so that an order from a country missing in the lookup table is kept and labelled rather than dropped.

con.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE countries (code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO countries VALUES ('BR', 'Americas'), ('NG', 'Africa'), ('IN', 'Asia');
""")
QUERY = """
SELECT COALESCE(c.region, 'Unmapped') AS region,
       COUNT(*)                       AS orders,
       ROUND(SUM(o.amount), 2)        AS revenue,
       MIN(o.order_date)              AS first_order
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN countries AS c ON c.code = o.country
WHERE o.paid = :paid
GROUP BY region
HAVING COUNT(*) >= :min_orders
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5
"""
summary = pd.read_sql_query(QUERY, con, params={"paid": 1, "min_orders": 1})
print(summary)
print(summary.dtypes)

     region  orders  revenue first_order
0    Africa       1   310.00  2026-09-04
1  Americas       2   192.75  2026-09-01
2  Unmapped       1    89.90  2026-09-05
region             str
orders           int64
revenue        float64
first_order        str
dtype: object

The params argument of pandas.read_sql_query passes values to the driver, so the placeholder rule still holds. Look at the last dtype, though: first_order came back as text, because that is how SQLite stored it. Add parse_dates=["first_order"] to the call and the column comes back as datetime64. The round trip from Timestamp to text and back is exactly the kind of conversion objective 2.4.5 has in mind.

The Chen Wei order lands in "Unmapped" because CN is not in the lookup table. With an INNER JOIN that paid order would vanish from the revenue total without any warning, which is a classic scenario question.

Is there a short video on preparing for PCAD?

This three-minute video from the EduSum channel gives preparation tips for the PCAD exam. It is about study habits rather than code, so it pairs well with the hands-on script above.

What should you practise after this script?

Run the script, then break it on purpose. Add a row whose paid value is maybe and see what map() produces; it gives NaN, and the column is no longer boolean. Then write a validation check for it. That loop of breaking the data and then catching the break is a fast way to learn Blocks 1 and 2.

To track the rest of the syllabus objective by objective, this PCAD-31-02 syllabus breakdown with exam details lists every block and topic on one page.

For Blocks 3 to 5, write small scripts of the same kind: a bootstrap of the mean with NumPy, a linear and a logistic regression with a train and test split, and one Matplotlib chart with labelled axes, a title and a legend.

When you want to see how the scenario items are phrased, work through these PCAD sample questions with answers and note which block each one belongs to.

Frequently asked questions

1. How many questions are on the PCAD-31-02 exam, and what score do I need to pass?

The exam has 48 single-select and multiple-select items, and you have 60 minutes plus the NDA screen. You pass with a cumulative score of at least 75%.

2. How much does the PCAD exam cost?

The Python Institute lists the exam from $195, the exam with a retake from $225, the exam with a practice test from $215 and all three from $245. The practice test alone is $49.

3. Is PCAD-31-01 still available?

No. PCAD-31-01 was retired on July 14, 2025, and PCAD-31-02 has been the active version since July 15, 2025. Use the PCAD-31-02 syllabus when you study.

4. Do I need PCAP or PCED before taking PCAD?

There are no formal prerequisites. The Python Institute recommends PCAP and PCED, or equivalent knowledge, plus field-specific skills.

5. How long is the PCAD certification valid, and when can I retake a failed exam?

The certification is valid for 6 years. After a failed attempt you must wait 15 days before you can take the exam again.

title: Optimistic Locking vs. Pessimistic Locking — Handling Concurrent Updates in SQL Databases
description:
What happens when two users try to update the same database row at exactly the same time? Without proper concurrency control, one update can silently overwrite the other, leading to inconsistent or incorrect data (the classic lost update problem). SQL databases solve this with two main concurrency control strategies: Optimistic Locking and Pessimistic Locking.

✅ Optimistic Locking (Version-Based)

Instead of locking the row up front, each transaction reads the current version number along with the data. When updating, the database verifies the version hasn't changed since it was read:

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = ?, version = version + 1
WHERE id = ? AND version = 5;

If another transaction already modified the row (and bumped the version), this UPDATE affects zero rows — the version check fails immediately, and the application detects the conflict via the affected-row count and can retry.

Key characteristics:

  • ✔ No row-level lock held while "thinking" — the row stays fully available to others.
  • ✔ Better throughput for read-heavy systems, since nothing blocks concurrent readers/writers.
  • ✔ Conflicts are detected at UPDATE time, not up front.
  • ✔ The application is responsible for retrying on failure (re-read the row, reapply the change, try again).

Mental model: "Try first. If someone already changed the data, fail fast and retry."

🔒 Pessimistic Locking (Row-Level Lock)

Before modifying data, the transaction explicitly locks the row so no one else can touch it:

SELECT * FROM accounts
WHERE id = 101
FOR UPDATE;

While one transaction holds the lock:

  • Other transactions requesting the same row wait in a queue rather than failing.
  • They execute only after the lock is released (commit/rollback).
  • No version conflict ever occurs, because updates to that row are forced to happen sequentially.

Key characteristics:

  • ✔ Row locked immediately — guarantees exclusive access for the duration of the transaction.
  • ✔ Other requests wait instead of failing outright.
  • ✔ Strong consistency, even under heavy contention on the same rows.
  • ✔ Lower concurrency (more waiting/blocking) but highly predictable execution order.

Mental model: "Wait your turn before making changes."

📌 When Should You Use Each?

Choose Optimistic Locking when:

  • Conflicts are rare.
  • The application is read-heavy.
  • High throughput matters more than avoiding occasional retries.
  • Retries are acceptable at the application layer.

Examples: e-commerce product catalogs, user profiles, content management systems.

Choose Pessimistic Locking when:

  • Data integrity is critical and lost updates are unacceptable.
  • Many users frequently update the same records (high contention).
  • Predictable, sequential execution is more valuable than raw throughput.

Examples: banking transactions, digital wallets, inventory management, ticket booking systems.

💡 Key Takeaway

There isn't a universally "better" approach. The right choice depends on your application's contention level, consistency requirements, throughput goals, and user experience. Understanding this trade-off is essential for designing scalable, reliable, high-performance backend systems — it's a decision made per use case (or even per table/operation), not a single global choice for the whole system.

In practice, each strategy carries a distinct failure mode worth watching for in production:
retry storms under optimistic locking when contention is higher than expected, and lock contention or deadlocks under pessimistic locking when transactions hold locks longer than intended.

title: UsersTable — the dumb component I copy into every admin panel
description:
Every admin panel I've ever built has a users table. Or a products table. Or an orders table. They're all the same shape: rows of records, a couple of status pills, edit and delete actions on the right. And every time, there's a temptation to build the clever version — sorting, filtering, pagination, inline editing — before the panel even works.

In my starter kit, the users table is deliberately dumb. Here's the entire contract:

export default function UsersTable({ users, onEdit, onDelete }) {

Three props. Data in, callbacks out. The component fetches nothing, authenticates nothing, routes nowhere. It renders a table with name, email, a role pill (indigo for admin, gray for everyone else), a formatted creation date, and Edit/Delete buttons that call the callbacks with the user object.

That's it. And that restraint is the feature.

Because the component knows nothing about where the data comes from, the parent page owns all the interesting decisions: how users are fetched, what the edit modal looks like, what happens after a delete (refetch? optimistic removal? confirmation dialog?). I can reuse this exact component in a demo build that runs against an in-memory mock API — the kit has a demoMock seam for exactly that — and in production against the real Laravel API, without changing a line of it. Props in, actions out. The component doesn't care.

This is also how I keep admin features cheap to add later. When a client asks for a products table next month, I don't build a new abstraction; I copy this file, change the columns, and wire new callbacks. Ninety percent of the code is identical. People call this boring. Boring is what lets me ship an admin panel in an afternoon.

A few small details I do keep in the "dumb" version: overflow-x-auto on the wrapper so the table scrolls horizontally on mobile instead of breaking the layout; whitespace-nowrap on cells so dates don't wrap weirdly; hover:bg-gray-50 on rows because affordance matters even in internal tools. And the role pill — a tiny inline conditional — because the person staring at this table is an admin, and the fastest thing their eyes need is "who here is an admin."

The lesson I keep re-learning: the smartest component in your admin panel is the one that knows the least. Push the knowledge up to the page, keep the table stupid, and you'll thank yourself on every project after this one.

The full admin loop — this table, the Users page that drives it, the API behind it, and the tests proving it — ships in my Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit, $19 one-time. The admin panel is done; go build the product.

title: The 8 tests I ship in a starter kit (and why I stop at 8)
description:
Most starter kits ship with one test: test_that_true_is_true. It's the Laravel default, and almost nobody replaces it. When I started packing my SaaS kit for other developers, I decided the test suite had to earn its place — a buyer should be able to run php artisan test, watch green, and trust that the auth layer they just bought actually works.

So the kit ships tests/Feature/AuthTest.php with eight real tests. Here's what they cover and why each one exists.

The register tests. test_register_returns_token_and_user posts to /api/auth/register and asserts a 201 with a user object (shaped through the API resource) and a token. It also asserts the database row was created with role => 'user' — because the register endpoint hardcodes the role. Which leads to the second test: test_register_cannot_self_assign_admin_role. You can POST role: admin all day; you still get created as a user. That's a security property, and security properties are exactly the things that deserve tests — they're the ones that silently regress when someone "refactors" the controller six months later.

The login tests. test_login_returns_token_and_user creates a user via the factory and asserts a 200 with the token and user. test_login_with_wrong_password_returns_401 asserts the failure shape: 401, message Invalid credentials. Testing the sad path matters more than the happy path here — frontend devs build their error UI against the exact status code this endpoint returns.

The contract tests. test_me_requires_authentication hits /api/auth/me with no token and expects a 401. test_me_without_accept_header_returns_json_401 is the sneaky one: it checks that even without an Accept: application/json header, you get JSON back, not a redirect to a login page that doesn't exist. If you've ever debugged a SPA that got HTML back from an API and choked, you know why this test exists. It's a one-line regression test for a bug I hit on a real client project.

The authorization tests. test_non_admin_cannot_list_users and test_admin_can_list_users — a regular user gets 403 on the user index, an admin gets 200. Two tests, the entire role system proven end to end.

And here's the deliberate part: I stop at 8. There is no test for password reset, no test for email verification, no test for Stripe webhooks — because the kit doesn't ship those features. I won't write tests for code that doesn't exist to make the suite look bigger. A starter kit is a foundation, not a framework, and its tests should mirror its actual scope. What it does ship, it proves.

All eight run against a fresh database (RefreshDatabase), take a couple of seconds, and are written against the public API of the app — routes and JSON — not internals. That means a buyer can refactor my controllers freely and the tests still guard the contract their frontend depends on.

If you want the whole thing — Sanctum auth, role middleware, the admin user management loop, and these 8 tests proving it all works — I packed it into the Laravel + React SaaS Starter Kit, $19 one-time. Skip the three days of wiring and start on the part that's actually yours.

title: Two new x402 APIs for AI agents: x402 payment receipt parser + on-chain verifier + OWASP API Top 10 (2023) one-call audit (2026-10-15, cycle 151)
description:
We just shipped 2 new paid x402 endpoints on our URL metadata API — both $0.0005/call, USDC on Base, x402 settlement via pay.openfacilitator.io.

Endpoints:

  1. GET /api/x402-receipt-parse?receipt_b64=<BASE64> OR ?tx_hash=0x... OR POST JSON — x402 payment receipt parser + on-chain tx verifier
  2. GET /api/owasp-api-top10-audit?url=<TARGET> — OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) one-call composite audit

Why these matter for AI agents

1. /api/x402-receipt-parse is the post-settlement companion to /api/x402-payment-trace (c142, pre-send decoder). When an x402 server returns an X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE base64, the AI agent needs to verify on-chain that the payment actually went to the right address, for the right amount, with enough confirmations. The endpoint accepts either the base64 receipt OR a raw tx hash (0x + 64 hex) and fetches it via the Base public RPC (base.gateway.tenderly.co with 1rpc.io/base + base.drpc.org fallbacks), then decodes the USDC Transfer event from the receipt logs (USDC on Base = 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913).

The function-selector decode distinguishes transfer vs transferWithAuthorization (EIP-3009) vs approve — so the agent knows whether the payment was a settled transfer (good) or just an approval (not a payment). It also computes confirmations = latest_block - block_number and warns if <12.

Returns receipt_summary (tx_hash + block_number + from + to + value_atomic + value_usdc + asset + status_is_success + confirmations + function_selector + function_name) + verification (to_matches_our_wallet [0xCa0a6c6Aa7A8F0D5893636CF166Ea2b44fb6500c] + value_matches_amount + transfers_to_our_wallet_count + total_received_usdc) + findings + x402_receipt_score 0-100 A-F.

2. /api/owasp-api-top10-audit is the one-call composite that answers the single most-asked question by an AI agent deciding whether to use a paid API: "is this API safe to call?". Fetches the target + probes 24 conventional API paths in parallel via ThreadPoolExecutor, then runs all 10 OWASP 2023 category checks:

  • API1 BOLA: compare /api/users/1 vs /api/users/2 response equality (identical = no per-object authz)
  • API2 Broken Auth: no-auth + no-bearer on /api/me + /api/users/1
  • API3 BOPLA: PII keywords in unauth response (password/ssn/credit_card/secret/token/api_key) + over-exposure >=15 top-level fields
  • API4 Unrestricted Consumption: no RateLimit-* headers + huge response >5MB
  • API5 BFLA: /admin returns 200 + dangerous methods PUT/DELETE/PATCH open on /api/users/1
  • API6 Sensitive Business Flow: /api/checkout /api/payment/api/cart open without CAPTCHA
  • API7 SSRF: live test /api/fetch/api/proxy/api/avatar with internal URL http://127.0.0.1/ + http://169.254.169.254/ (AWS metadata) + http://localhost:8080/
  • API8 Security Misconfiguration: X-Debug + X-Powered-By + X-AspNet-Version disclosure + ACAO=* wildcard + stack trace in 404 body
  • API9 Improper Inventory: multiple /api/v1+/v2`+ /openapi.json publicly exposed + staging subdomain returns 200
  • API10 Unsafe Consumption: 3p scripts from risky TLDs .tk/.ml/.ga + http:// subresources on https:// page

Returns per_category[10] {id, name, status pass/warn/fail, score, findings[]} + summary {fail_count, warn_count, pass_count} + composite api_top10_score 0-100 A-F + verdict (production_hardened / standard / weak / vulnerable).

The full catalog is now at 217 paid x402 routes

The service runs at https://mins-alternatively-meanwhile-lauderdale.trycloudflare.com and accepts USDC on Base via the standard x402 flow (payTo: 0xCa0a6c6Aa7A8F0D5893636CF166Ea2b44fb6500c, asset: 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913, network: eip155:8453). Discovery at /.well-known/x402 (217 endpoints), GET /openapi.json (213 paths), GET /llms.txt (116KB), GET / (landing HTML 119KB).

The first 2 endpoints are free (just GET /api?url=... returns JSON metadata). Everything else is $0.0005–$0.005 per call.

Test self-settle still works: a buying agent signs a real EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization envelope, the Flask server POSTs to pay.openfacilitator.io/verify + /settle, and the wallet 0xCa0a6c... receives real USDC on Base.

Categories: 24 API path probes, 10 OWASP checks, 2 base JSON-RPC endpoints (tenderly + 1rpc + drpc fallback chain).

Designed for AI agents that need to make trust decisions before paying for a tool.

title: Building Retrieval Architecture for Developer Changelog Tracker — 5 Python Ranking Signals
description:
When a changelog bot cites the wrong release, the root cause is usually a trust-boundary mistake, not a weak language model. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context, then choose ranking signals you can evaluate. Keep region, retention, and deletion policy beside the index design; an AI runtime cannot grant contractual residency for a specialist data store.

The retrieval contract comes before ranking

For a B2B SaaS developer changelog tracker, write the user-visible answer first: “What changed in package X, and when?” Turn that sentence into a contract with required fields: canonical URL, release timestamp, package, version, source region, and a citation span. A result that matches the words but lacks a timestamp is not a valid answer.

I model each chunk with immutable source_id, published_at, updated_at, and deleted_at metadata. The collection is private to the application tenant. Deletions are events, not a cleanup task: remove the record from the collection when the upstream page disappears, and re-index changed content deliberately so an old chunk cannot outrank the current release.

The first stage gathers candidates from lexical web search or a vector collection. The second stage scores them with signals that mirror the contract:

  • lexical overlap for package and version tokens;
  • semantic similarity for paraphrased release notes;
  • recency, with a bounded decay rather than an unreviewed “newer is always better” rule;
  • source authority, such as the maintainer’s canonical feed;
  • metadata completeness and citation-span availability.

That is the trap.

For the orchestration layer, Infrai is worth testing when a team wants a self-describing REST surface: its public discovery endpoint exposes capability schemas and runnable examples, so a Python service can inspect a new retrieval capability without installing another SDK. Keep the tenant's durable records in the system that owns your residency and deletion agreement; the routing layer does not replace that boundary.

How should a Python changelog tracker rank retrieval signals?

Start with a small labeled set: 50–100 real questions, two acceptable citations per question, and a reviewer decision for “stale but relevant.” Measure recall@k for candidate generation and citation precision for the final answer. I would not ship a new weighting because it feels right; I would ship it when the eval harness shows fewer unsupported citations without pushing latency past the product budget. Your mileage may vary because release cadence and tenant vocabulary change the labels.

A simple, inspectable score is often enough for the first iteration:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from math import exp


@dataclass
class Candidate:
    text: str
    lexical: float
    semantic: float
    authority: float
    published_at: datetime
    has_citation_span: bool


def rank(candidates: list[Candidate], now: datetime | None = None) -> list[Candidate]:
    now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    def score(item: Candidate) -> float:
        age_days = max((now - item.published_at).total_seconds() / 86400, 0)
        recency = exp(-age_days / 180)
        citation = 1.0 if item.has_citation_span else 0.0
        return (
            0.30 * item.lexical
            + 0.30 * item.semantic
            + 0.20 * recency
            + 0.15 * item.authority
            + 0.05 * citation
        )

    return sorted(candidates, key=score, reverse=True)

The exact weights are provisional. Log every component, the selected source_id, and the final citation so a failed answer can be replayed. A 429 from a provider is a control-flow event: back off, honor Retry-After, and keep the user request bounded by a deadline.

A bounded two-stage request in Python

The following example keeps discovery and retrieval separate. It searches the public web for candidate release notes, then queries a named vector collection for internal copies. It uses one timeout budget and exponential backoff; no provider key is embedded in the source.

import os
import time
from typing import Any

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def post_json(path: str, payload: dict[str, Any], deadline: float) -> dict[str, Any]:
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}
    delay = 0.5
    while True:
        remaining = deadline - time.monotonic()
        if remaining <= 0:
            raise TimeoutError("retrieval deadline exceeded")
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1{path}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=min(remaining, 8.0),
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            wait = float(retry_after) if retry_after else delay
            time.sleep(min(wait, max(remaining, 0)))
            delay = min(delay * 2, 8.0)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"retrieval failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()


def retrieve(question: str) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], dict[str, Any]]:
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 10.0
    web = post_json("/web/search", {"query": question}, deadline)
    vector = post_json(
        "/vector/query",
        {"collection": "tenant-changelog", "query": question, "limit": 20},
        deadline,
    )
    return web, vector


if __name__ == "__main__":
    web_results, vector_results = retrieve("Python 3.13 deprecation in package acme-sdk")
    print({"web": web_results, "vector": vector_results})

The payload fields should be checked against the current discovery schema before production rollout. The important architectural property is the boundary: web results are candidates, while the tenant collection supplies durable metadata and citation context. Keep raw documents in a storage system whose region, retention, deletion API, and processor terms meet your contract; route only the minimum text needed for ranking.

Infrai is a practical fit when a team wants this wiring behind one plain REST API and a self-describing discovery surface: GET /v1/discovery exposes capabilities, schemas, and runnable examples, so adding a retrieval stage does not require installing another SDK. The same key and consistent interface across backend capabilities also reduce integration bookkeeping. That is an operational benefit, not proof that the service is your data processor of record.

Where the alternatives fit

No single backend wins every trust review. Here is the decision I would put in an architecture record:

Option Strength for changelog retrieval Boundary or trade-off
Elasticsearch Mature lexical ranking, filters, and self-managed deployment choices You own cluster operations, patching, and residency configuration
OpenSearch Open-source distribution with familiar inverted-index and vector features Compatibility and managed-service terms vary by provider
Pinecone Managed vector index with a focused operational surface Confirm region, retention, and deletion guarantees for your tenant contract
Weaviate Hybrid search and schema-oriented objects More platform concepts to govern when the bot needs only a narrow index
Infrai Self-describing REST discovery plus a single integration surface for web and vector stages A specialist search or storage provider may be better for contractual residency controls

The catch is important: stick with a regional Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Pinecone, or Weaviate deployment when legal or procurement requires a processor agreement and deletion evidence that your chosen runtime does not provide. Infrai should be the option to try for the retrieval orchestration layer when transparent discovery and a consistent HTTP integration matter; it should not be used as a substitute for a specialist provider's residency contract.

Ship the eval gate with the index

Before rollout, replay the labeled questions after every re-index. Check that deleted release notes no longer appear, that an updated page has one canonical chunk, and that each answer can point to a source span. Set hard limits for candidate count, query time, and retries; a slow upstream source must not block the user flow.

The eval set should include awkward cases: a package with two releases on the same day, a changelog edited after publication, a superseded security notice, and a question whose answer is “no matching release.” Record the query, candidate IDs, score components, selected span, and policy version. That trace lets a reviewer distinguish a ranking error from a missing document, and it gives you a concrete regression test when the ingestion job changes.

I have found the most useful dashboard is small: recall@20, citation precision, stale-result rate, deletion lag, and p95 retrieval time. Do not collapse those into one vanity score. A bot can improve recall while quietly returning older citations, which is a trust regression even if the language model sounds fluent.

I'm not sure a single global recency half-life will survive every ecosystem. Keep it configurable, record the version of the ranking policy, and inspect misses by package and release age. I've seen enough retrieval reviews to know that a tidy score can hide a messy contract. The useful artifact is a trace, not a confidence adjective; don't ship on confidence wording alone.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the vector discovery and retrieval guidance and verify the live schema before wiring it into production.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/vector/answers/my-rag-chatbot-s-vector-search-keeps-letting-irrelevant/
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/query-dsl.html
  • https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/vector-search/
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/indexes/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate/search/hybrid

title: Cheap Webhook Task Processing Explained — Node.js SaaS Rate-Limit Retry Backoff
description:
Short answer: for a nightly fintech reconciliation, put the delayed webhook work in a queue and make the worker idempotent. A cron trigger should enqueue a bounded batch, while retries and rate limits live at the worker boundary. That shape is cheap to reason about because the provider's rate limit cannot turn one long cron invocation into a hidden scheduler.

The bill is mostly downstream work, not the timer. Every payment lookup, webhook delivery attempt, and retained message costs attention; a cron job that fires 10,000 calls at once creates a burst of throttled retries. Controlling worker concurrency changes that dominant term. It also gives the team one place to record an idempotency key such as reconcile:2026-09-10:merchant-42:payment-981, so a duplicate delivery cannot post the same ledger adjustment twice.

Bursts hurt.

Suppose the provider allows 20 requests per second and the nightly window contains 2,400 merchants. A cron loop that launches every request immediately will spend its first minutes collecting 429 responses, then create a retry wave that is larger than the original wave. With a queue, the trigger publishes the merchant windows quickly, while workers take 20 tokens per second and attach the same reconciliation key to every attempt. Merchant 17 may fail once and return after a 30-second delay; merchant 18 may succeed on its first call. Those paths do not interfere. The audit row records the provider cursor, attempt count, and final comparison before the message is acknowledged. If the worker dies after the provider accepts the adjustment but before ack, the next delivery still carries the same key, so the database uniqueness check and provider idempotency guard converge on one ledger result. This is the operational reason I care about queue shape more than the timer brand.

There is a retention trade-off. An acknowledged queue message is deleted, and retention tops out at 30 days. I keep the reconciliation result and provider response hash in an audit table before acking; I do not pretend the queue is a replay log. When an auditor asks for a six-month trail, the table is what we query, and the queue's short retention is the deliberate cost of keeping the operational path small.

That boundary is where Infrai can fit: its queue is reachable through a plain REST API, so the nightly trigger and a Python or Node.js worker can share one HTTP contract without an SDK. I would test it for the low-complexity path below, not for workflow orchestration.

Two viable shapes for delayed webhook work

The simple shape is cron plus queue: a nightly trigger finds the reconciliation window, publishes one message per merchant or bounded page, and workers consume at a controlled concurrency. Cron executions are capped at 900 seconds, so long work belongs behind the trigger. The queue's standard delivery is at-least-once; the invariant is that the consumer can safely run the same message twice.

The second shape is a durable workflow engine. Temporal or Airflow can model a multi-step reconciliation with joins, compensations, and a long-lived history. That is the right invariant when a payment run is a graph whose later steps depend on several earlier results. It is more machinery than a single provider sweep needs.

For a small SaaS, I would choose the first shape when the job is “fetch, compare, emit, retry.” Its broader backend surface can also keep storage and scheduling behind the same key, which removes a little integration bookkeeping without changing the queue invariant.

How should Node.js teams model rate limits, retries, and backoff?

Treat a rate limit as state, not as a sleep sprinkled through a cron loop. A worker should reserve a provider token, perform one idempotent operation, and requeue a failed attempt with a bounded delay. Exponential backoff with jitter prevents every merchant from retrying on the same second; Retry-After wins when the provider sends it.

Here is the core decision in Python, kept independent of a vendor client so the behavior is testable:

import requests
import json
import os
import random
import time


def retry_delay(attempt, retry_after=None):
    if retry_after is not None:
        return min(float(retry_after), 604800)
    cap = min(2 ** attempt, 3600)
    return random.uniform(cap / 2, cap)


def reconciliation_key(merchant_id, window_start):
    return f"reconcile:{merchant_id}:{window_start}"


def publish_reconciliation(queue, payload, delay_seconds=0):
    body = {"queue": queue, "message": payload,
            "delay_seconds": delay_seconds}
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
               "Idempotency-Key": payload["reconciliation_key"]}
    for attempt in range(5):
        response = requests.request(
            "POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/publish",
            json=body, headers=headers, timeout=20)
        if response.status_code < 400:
            return response.json()
        if response.status_code != 429:
            raise RuntimeError(response.text)
        time.sleep(retry_delay(attempt, response.headers.get("Retry-After")))
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit persisted after five attempts")

Keep delayed messages at or below 604800 seconds, and attach the reconciliation key to the payload. If a write is retried, send the same client id or idempotency key. The platform convention uses an Idempotency-Key header for operations that support it; your application still owns the provider-side idempotency check.

There is no native debounce or throttle primitive, and FIFO deduplication lasts only five minutes. That is a capability boundary, not a failure mode: use a database uniqueness constraint for a longer business window. For one-to-many delivery, publish to separate queues because there is no built-in topic fan-out.

What do queue, cron, and workflow products actually trade?

Option Best fit Retry and rate-limit shape Retention or orchestration caveat
Queue plus cron trigger Delayed webhook batches and ordinary SaaS reconciliation Worker concurrency, requeue, exponential backoff At-least-once; finite retention; no joins
Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers Short, publicly reachable HTTP trigger You build the queue and retry state A single invocation is capped at 900 seconds
Inngest Event-driven functions with managed retry history Function-level retry and step state More orchestration semantics than a basic queue
Temporal Long-running, branching reconciliation workflows Durable workflow timers and activities Operational and modeling overhead is substantial

The comparison is not a price contest. Cloudflare is compelling when the timer and edge execution are already your platform. Inngest is a better choice when each reconciliation has explicit steps and you want their history attached to the run. Stick with Temporal when you need DAG-like joins or compensation logic. A queue is not suitable when replay across multiple consumer groups is a hard requirement; persist an event log or select a stream system instead.

The small implementation I would ship

Create one queue per independent consumer, publish a bounded batch from the nightly trigger, then let workers claim and ack messages only after the audit row is durable. A failed provider call becomes a delayed republish, with the attempt count and next-attempt timestamp in the message. Keep payloads below 256 KB and delayed work within seven days; a later reconciliation window can be scheduled by the next cron run.

I initially thought a FIFO queue would solve duplicate payments by itself. It does not: the five-minute deduplication window is shorter than a nightly business key, and standard queues can deliver at least once. The invariant belongs in the database and in the provider request, where the same reconciliation_key produces the same result.

One operational wrinkle matters in fintech: cron does not backfill triggers missed while paused, and run output is limited to the first 4 KB. Write a run record as soon as the trigger starts, then store detailed diagnostics in your audit system. Your mileage may vary around provider-specific quotas; confirm the live quota contract before choosing worker concurrency.

Infrai is worth trying for teams that want this queue-centered shape and a plain HTTP integration, especially when the same service already needs several backend capabilities under one key. It is not the right choice for a workflow graph, Kafka-style replay, private push endpoints, or native fan-out. In those cases, use Temporal, Airflow, a stream platform, or a specialist queue that states those guarantees directly.

If this boundary matches your reconciliation job, the queue capability details and runnable examples are at docs.infrai.cc.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/queue.push_subscribe
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs
  • https://docs.temporal.io/workflows
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/retrying-failing-jobs
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: Big Tech Is on Track to Spend $800B on AI in 2026. Can the Economics Hold?
description:
One hot inflation report. A sell-off in AI infrastructure stocks. And a question the whole industry can no longer dodge.

For the last few years, the AI conversation has mostly been about capability.

Can a model write code? Can it answer questions? Can it generate images? Can it browse the web? Can it act like an agent?

Those are important questions. But in October 2026, another question has become impossible to ignore:

Can the AI industry turn massive spending into sustainable, measurable value?

This is no longer only a technology question. It is now a business, energy, infrastructure, policy, and investment question. And the answer will shape which companies lead the next decade.

⚡ TL;DR (save this)

  • Markets wobbled. AI and AI-infrastructure stocks fell after hotter-than-expected US inflation data.
  • The spending is enormous. The largest US hyperscalers are on track for about $800B of capex in 2026 and around $1.1T in 2027.
  • There is a gap. An Axios-reported analysis found a ~$1T gap between AI-related spending since 2024 and AI revenue so far.
  • Power is a hard limit. Data-center electricity demand grew 17% in 2025 versus about 3% for overall demand.
  • The next winners will not simply spend the most. They will deliver trustworthy execution.

📉 The Market Just Sent a Warning

This week, major AI and AI-infrastructure stocks fell after the United States released hotter-than-expected inflation data.

Why does inflation matter to AI? Because AI at scale is capital-intensive.

Building and running AI systems requires:

  • Advanced GPUs and specialized chips
  • Large data centers
  • High-speed networking
  • Massive storage systems
  • Reliable electricity
  • Cooling infrastructure
  • Skilled engineering teams
  • Continuous model training and inference capacity

Many companies fund this buildout through debt, future revenue expectations, and investor confidence.

When inflation rises, markets begin to expect higher interest rates. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive. When borrowing becomes more expensive, every large infrastructure project becomes harder to justify.

That is why AI stocks reacted sharply.

Reuters reported that shares of debt-heavy AI infrastructure companies fell as investors became more concerned about the financing of the industry's massive buildout. CoreWeave, Nebius, Oracle, and Dell were among the companies affected.

This does not mean AI is failing. It means the market is asking a fair question:

Is the spending producing enough real value to justify the cost?

💰 The Scale of AI Spending Is Enormous

To understand why this matters, look at the numbers.

Goldman Sachs has estimated that the largest US hyperscalers are on track to spend about $800 billion on capital expenditure in 2026. Consensus expectations suggest this could rise to around $1.1 trillion in 2027.

Capital expenditure, or capex, means money spent on long-term assets such as:

  • Data centers
  • Servers
  • GPUs
  • Networking equipment
  • Land and buildings
  • Power infrastructure
  • Cooling systems

This is not ordinary software spending. This is industrial-scale investment.

Alphabet, for example, reported $80.6 billion in capital expenditures during the first half of 2026 and guided to $195-205 billion for the full year.

That is an extraordinary amount of money being committed to compute, data centers, and AI infrastructure.

At the same time, an analysis reported by Axios found a gap of nearly $1 trillion between hyperscaler AI-related spending since 2024 and the AI revenue generated so far.

This does not mean AI companies have "lost" $1 trillion. It means there is a difference between:

  • Money invested in AI infrastructure
  • Money earned from AI products and services

That difference matters. Investors can support long-term investment when they believe future revenue will arrive. But if spending keeps rising faster than revenue, confidence can weaken.

🏗️ AI Is Becoming an Infrastructure Industry

AI used to feel like a software industry. Now, it increasingly looks like an infrastructure industry.

Why? Because modern AI depends on physical resources: electricity, land, water, fiber networks, chips, cooling systems, data centers, and power grids.

A powerful model is not just an algorithm. It is an algorithm running on expensive hardware, inside a data center, connected to a power grid, supported by supply chains, and maintained by engineers.

This changes the conversation. The question is no longer only:

"How smart can the model become?"

It is also:

  • "Can we power it?"
  • "Can we cool it?"
  • "Can we afford it?"
  • "Can we deploy it responsibly?"
  • "Can it create value for customers?"

AI is becoming similar to railways, electricity grids, telecom networks, and cloud computing. Infrastructure industries create enormous value, but they also require enormous capital, planning, and discipline.

🔌 Electricity Is Becoming a Core AI Constraint

One of the most important facts in this debate is energy.

According to IEA data cited in recent reporting, data-center electricity demand grew by 17% in 2025, while overall electricity demand grew by around 3%.

That is a major difference.

AI data centers need continuous power. They cannot simply switch off during peak hours. Training large models and serving millions of users requires stable, high-capacity electricity around the clock.

This creates several challenges:

1. Power availability

Many regions already face grid constraints. Adding a large data center is not as simple as buying land and installing servers. It requires access to sufficient electricity capacity.

2. Grid upgrades

New data centers may require new transmission lines, substations, and grid upgrades. These projects can take years to approve and build.

3. Energy costs

If data centers increase demand faster than supply, electricity prices can rise for nearby communities and businesses.

4. Environmental impact

AI infrastructure affects carbon emissions, water usage, land use, and local communities.

5. Public policy

Governments are beginning to ask who should pay for the infrastructure required to support AI growth.

In the United States, the House passed a bipartisan bill designed to encourage state utility regulators to protect consumers from rising energy costs linked to large data centers. The bill still needs further approval to become law, but the direction is clear.

In Europe, regulators are preparing stricter disclosure requirements for data centers, including water use, clean-power adoption, and energy efficiency.

The message is simple:

AI growth must be matched by responsible energy planning.

🎯 The Shift From Demos to Business Outcomes

The first phase of enterprise AI was about experimentation.

Companies asked:

  • Can we build a chatbot?
  • Can we connect an LLM to our documents?
  • Can we create a proof of concept?
  • Can we show leadership an AI demo?

That phase was necessary. But demos do not pay for data centers. Business outcomes do.

The next phase is about production AI:

  • AI that reduces manual work
  • AI that improves decision-making
  • AI that accelerates customer response
  • AI that automates repeatable workflows
  • AI that improves quality and compliance
  • AI that creates measurable ROI

This is where agentic AI becomes important.

An AI agent is not just a chatbot. It is a system that can understand a goal, plan steps, use tools, interact with systems, and complete a task.

For example, instead of asking:

"What is our leave policy?"

An employee may ask:

"Apply for two days of leave and confirm my balance has updated."

An agent may need to:

  1. Understand the request
  2. Find the correct application screen
  3. Fill in the required details
  4. Submit the request
  5. Verify the outcome
  6. Report success or failure with evidence

This is much more valuable than a simple question-and-answer system. But it is also more demanding. An agent that takes action must be accurate, safe, observable, and accountable.

🛡️ Why Agentic AI Needs Governance

As AI agents become more autonomous, governance becomes essential.

A chatbot that gives a wrong answer is frustrating. An AI agent that submits the wrong form, sends the wrong email, updates the wrong record, or triggers the wrong workflow can create real business damage.

That is why enterprises need:

Human approval for high-risk actions

Not every action should be automatic. Deleting records, making payments, changing production configurations, or sending external communications may require human confirmation.

Least-privilege access

An agent should only have the permissions required for its task. It should not automatically receive broad access to every system.

Audit trails

Every important action should be logged: what the agent saw, what it decided, what it did, and what evidence supports the result.

Clear success and failure states

A good AI system should say:

  • "Task completed successfully."
  • "Task failed because of a product defect."
  • "Task could not be completed because a required screen or precondition was unavailable."

It should not pretend everything is fine when it could not verify the outcome.

Monitoring and observability

Teams need to monitor agent behavior in real time, detect unusual actions, and stop an agent if needed.

This is especially important as agents move from answering questions to operating inside business systems.

🏆 The Real Competitive Advantage: Trustworthy Execution

Many people think AI competition is only about who has the biggest model. That is no longer the full picture.

The next competitive advantage will come from trustworthy execution.

A company may have access to a powerful model, but if it cannot connect that model safely to its data, workflows, permissions, and business processes, the value remains limited.

The companies that win will be those that can deliver:

  • Reliable AI systems. The system should work consistently, not only in a demo.
  • Measurable ROI. Every AI initiative should answer: What time, cost, risk, or quality improvement did we create?
  • Safe automation. AI should automate the right tasks, with the right controls, in the right environments.
  • Evidence-based results. Users should be able to see why the AI reached a conclusion or completed an action.
  • Responsible infrastructure. AI growth should consider power, water, emissions, and community impact.
  • Human-centered design. AI should assist people, not confuse them or remove accountability.

🏢 What This Means for Businesses

For business leaders, the message is clear: do not evaluate AI only by model benchmarks. Evaluate it by business impact.

Ask questions like:

  • Which workflow are we improving?
  • How much time or cost are we saving?
  • How are we measuring quality?
  • What happens when the AI is wrong?
  • Who approves high-risk actions?
  • How do we audit decisions?
  • What data does the AI access?
  • How do we protect customer information?
  • What is the total cost of ownership?
  • How does this affect our energy and infrastructure needs?

AI strategy should not be "adopt AI everywhere." AI strategy should be:

Adopt AI where it creates clear, measurable, responsible value.

👩‍💻 What This Means for Engineers

For AI engineers, developers, and architects, the skills that matter are changing.

It is no longer enough to know how to call an LLM API.

The most valuable engineers will understand:

  • System design
  • Retrieval and context management
  • Tool use and function calling
  • Agent orchestration
  • Evaluation and testing
  • Observability
  • Security and permissions
  • Cost optimization
  • Human-in-the-loop workflows
  • Production deployment

The best AI systems will not be built by prompt engineering alone. They will be built by combining models, data, tools, policies, tests, monitoring, user experience, and business understanding.

That is where real engineering value lies.

🚀 What This Means for Startups

For startups, this is actually good news.

When AI becomes expensive, companies cannot afford vague experiments. They need focused solutions that solve specific problems.

The best startup opportunities will be in areas such as:

  • AI quality assurance and testing
  • Agent governance and auditing
  • AI cost optimization
  • Enterprise workflow automation
  • Domain-specific AI assistants
  • Data readiness and governance
  • AI security
  • Model evaluation
  • Human-in-the-loop review tools
  • Industry-specific automation

A startup does not need to build a foundation model to create value. It can build the layer that makes AI usable, safe, measurable, and trustworthy inside real organizations.

🔭 The Bigger Picture

AI is not disappearing. It is maturing.

The first phase was about possibility. The next phase is about responsibility.

The first phase asked: "What can AI do?"

The next phase asks: "What should AI do, at what cost, with what safeguards, and for whose benefit?"

That is a healthier phase. Because real transformation does not come from hype. It comes from systems that work reliably in the real world.

AI will create enormous value, but only when companies treat it as more than a trend. They must treat it as:

  • A product
  • A system
  • An infrastructure investment
  • A business process
  • A governance responsibility
  • A long-term commitment

The companies that understand this will build durable advantage. The companies that only chase demos may find that the cost of AI is much easier to measure than its value.

💡 Final Thought

The AI race is no longer only about who can build the most powerful model. It is about who can build the most useful, efficient, safe, and economically sustainable AI systems.

The next winners will not simply spend the most.

They will convert compute into clarity.

They will convert automation into accountability.

They will convert data into decisions.

And they will convert AI into measurable business value.

The future of AI belongs to those who can make it work in the real world.

💬 Your turn

What will matter more in the next phase of AI: model capability or practical, trustworthy execution?

Tell me in the comments. If this helped you think about AI beyond the hype, a reaction and a share help other engineers and leaders find it. Follow for more on AI systems, agents and the economics behind them.

title: Turn a YouTube playlist into RAG-ready chunks with timestamp links
description:
If you build a RAG app, chatbot or search over video content, the first problem is getting clean text with timestamps so answers can link back to the exact moment. Here is a small recipe using the YouTube Transcript Extractor Actor on Apify. It costs $0.004 per transcript, and videos without captions are not charged.

Actor: https://apify.com/xargaar_tools/youtube-transcript-extractor-batch

What comes back

For each video you get the title, channel, duration, view count, language, whether the captions are auto-generated, the full text, and optionally timestamped segments. With chunkWords set, you also get chunks: pieces of roughly that many words, each with a start time. That is the part you want for embedding.

Fetch a playlist and write chunks with deep links 

import json
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("xargaar_tools/youtube-transcript-extractor-batch").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": ["https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=YOUR_PLAYLIST_ID"],
    "maxVideosPerUrl": 20,
    "chunkWords": 200,
    "includeAutoGenerated": True,
})

with open("chunks.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for v in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
        if v.get("status") != "OK":
            continue
        for c in v["chunks"]:
            f.write(json.dumps({
                "text": c["text"],
                "title": v["title"],
                "link": f'{v["url"]}&t={int(c["start"])}s',
            }) + "\n")

Each line of chunks.jsonl is ready to embed, and the link field opens the video at the start of that chunk, so your app can cite the exact spot.

Things worth knowing

  • status tells you why a video has no transcript (private video, captions disabled), so you can skip or retry those without the whole run failing.
  • languages lets you set preferred caption languages, and availableLanguages shows what else exists.
  • YouTube blocks datacenter IPs, so the Actor uses a residential proxy by default. My cost in tests was about $0.0009 per video, which is why it can be priced this low.
  • In my test batch, 11 of 12 videos returned a transcript. The one that did not was reported with a clear status.

If a video you care about fails, open an issue on the Actor page with the URL.
