title: Apple's on-device model called our iPhone 17 "not eligible", so we tested everything except the model
description:
The first time I asked the on-device model whether it could run on a real phone, SystemLanguageModel.default.availability answered .unavailable(.deviceNotEligible). The device was an iPhone 17 on iOS 26.6, which is new enough for Apple Intelligence. It was also bought in mainland China, where Apple Intelligence isn't offered, and as far as I can tell that is the whole reason.

That was a problem. It was the night before I submitted an AI menu for CapScribe, my caption app: keyword emphasis, title suggestions and emoji, all generated on device. The one phone I own will never run it. The simulator can't run it either.

So the honest version of this post is: here is how we shipped a Foundation Models feature we could not run, and what we tested instead.

The gate has more than two states

availability isn't a Bool. When it's unavailable you get a reason, and the reasons deserve different copy:

switch SystemLanguageModel.default.availability {
case .available:
    return .available
case .unavailable(let reason):
    switch reason {
    case .deviceNotEligible:
        return .unavailable("Device not eligible for Apple Intelligence")
    case .appleIntelligenceNotEnabled:
        return .unavailable("Apple Intelligence not enabled in Settings")
    case .modelNotReady:
        return .unavailable("Model is downloading or not ready")
    @unknown default:
        return .unavailable("Model unavailable")
    }
}

Only one of those is permanent. "Not enabled" is a trip to Settings. "Not ready" usually means the model is still downloading and will sort itself out. Collapse them into a single "AI unavailable" string and you tell the user with a fixable problem that they're stuck, while the user with an ineligible phone learns nothing.

My first instinct was to hide the menu whenever the model isn't there. I didn't. A missing button looks like a bug to anyone who read the release notes, and a hidden menu can't explain itself. What shipped: the menu always appears, the three actions are disabled, and a disabled row at the bottom says which case you're in.

A seam so the fallback can be tested

The service takes an optional model behind a one-method protocol:

public protocol AssistantModel: Sendable {
    func respond(to prompt: String) async throws -> String
}

If a model is injected, the service sends it the prompt and decodes the JSON it returns. If not, it checks availability and either opens a LanguageModelSession with a @Generable output type or throws .unavailable(reason). The real path is short on purpose. The less code that only runs on hardware I don't have, the better.

Unit tests inject a mock that records the prompt. That's where the input cap gets checked: transcripts are cut to 3,000 characters before they reach the model, and a test feeds a much longer string and asserts nothing past the cap made it into the prompt.

UI tests can't inject anything, so there's a DEBUG-only launch argument:

#if DEBUG
public static func makeFakeIfNeeded() -> OnDeviceAssistant? {
    guard ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments.contains("-uitest-fake-assistant") else { return nil }
    return OnDeviceAssistant(model: FakeAssistantModel())
}
#endif

The fake returns fixed JSON: a couple of keywords, three titles, one 🎬. With the flag set, a UI test runs all three actions in the editor. It checks that keyword emphasis gets switched on in the style panel, that three title rows appear, and that the emoji really lands at the end of the caption text. Without the flag, a second UI test opens the same menu in the simulator, where Foundation Models reports unavailable, and asserts the actions are disabled and the reason row exists and isn't empty.

That second test is the one I care about most. On my own phone the unavailable path is the only path, and for plenty of users it will be too.

What this doesn't cover

The real model. Prompt quality, latency, whether @Guide(.count(3)) really yields three titles every time on a real device: none of that has run on hardware we own. The App Review notes spell out the device requirement, and real-model verification sits on our roadmap as blocked until we get an eligible phone.

I went back and forth on shipping like that. What tipped it was proportion. The code that only runs on eligible hardware is a handful of lines handed straight to Apple's framework. The code that decides what everyone else sees runs on every build.

If you're adding Foundation Models to an app, two things are worth doing on day one. Give each unavailability reason its own message, and put a protocol between your feature and LanguageModelSession, so the fallback path gets tested in the simulator, where it's the default anyway.

I build CapScribe, an on-device caption app for iOS. The menu in question is in the editor: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6801041856?utm_source=devto

title: React and TypeScript Best Practices: Build Reliable Applications
description:
React and TypeScript are a powerful combination for building maintainable, scalable frontend applications. React makes it easier to create reusable user interfaces, while TypeScript catches many common mistakes before your code reaches production.

However, simply adding TypeScript to a React project does not automatically make the codebase reliable. The real benefits come from defining precise types, designing reusable components, handling asynchronous states correctly, and avoiding unnecessary complexity.

In this guide, we will explore practical best practices for React and TypeScript, using JavaScript examples to demonstrate the underlying patterns. These concepts help developers write more predictable components, simplify debugging, and build applications that remain manageable as requirements evolve.

1. Practical Best Practices for React and TypeScript

Define Explicit Types for Component Props

Well-defined component props make component contracts easier to understand and maintain. Instead of passing loosely structured objects, describe the required properties, optional values, and callback signatures using TypeScript interfaces or type aliases.

For example, a reusable button component might accept a label, a disabled state, and an event handler. Explicit types help prevent missing properties and incompatible callback arguments during development, while keeping the component's public API clear.

Avoid Using Any and Prefer Unknown for Untrusted Data

The any type disables most useful type checking, allowing mistakes to spread throughout a codebase. Prefer unknown when handling values from APIs, external libraries, or other untrusted sources, and validate those values before using them.

TypeScript types disappear at runtime, so declaring an API response as a particular interface does not verify that the server actually returned the expected structure. Runtime validation is important whenever data crosses an application boundary, especially when dealing with user input or third-party services.

Model UI States Explicitly

React applications frequently handle loading, success, empty, and error states. Representing these states explicitly prevents contradictory combinations, such as showing an error and a successful result simultaneously.

Discriminated unions are particularly useful because TypeScript can narrow the available properties based on a shared literal field. This approach makes state transitions easier to reason about and helps ensure that each UI state contains the information it actually needs.

Keep Components Small and Focused

A component should have a clear responsibility, whether that means displaying a product, handling a form, or presenting an error message. Extracting repeated behavior into custom hooks can reduce duplication without forcing every small piece of logic into a separate abstraction.

Keep business logic separate from presentation when doing so improves clarity or makes behavior easier to test. Avoid excessive abstraction, however, because a simple component does not need multiple layers of indirection to become maintainable.

Use Type-Safe Event Handlers and Immutable State Updates

React event handlers should use appropriate event types when working with inputs, forms, and other interactive elements. Functional state updates are especially useful when the next state depends on the previous state, because React can apply the update against the latest queued value.

Treat arrays and objects in state as immutable values. Create updated copies with methods such as map, filter, and object spread instead of modifying existing state directly, so React can reliably detect changes and render the correct UI.

Understand What TypeScript Cannot Guarantee

TypeScript provides compile-time checks, but it does not replace runtime validation, application testing, or accessibility checks. A correctly typed component can still contain a logic bug, render an inaccessible interface, or mishandle a failed network request.

Combine static typing with focused tests, linting, strict compiler settings, and clear error handling. A strong React and TypeScript codebase uses these tools together rather than relying on a single layer of protection.

const assert = require('node:assert/strict');

// This runnable JavaScript example demonstrates patterns that can be
// modeled with TypeScript in a real React application.
// JavaScript itself does not enforce TypeScript interfaces or unions.

console.log('Step 1: Define the application's data contract');

// In TypeScript, define this with an interface or type alias.
// interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string; }
function createUser(id, name, email) {
  return { id, name, email };
}

const initialUser = createUser(1, 'Ansh', 'ansh@example.com');
console.log('User created:', initialUser);
assert.equal(initialUser.id, 1);

console.log('\nStep 2: Validate untrusted API data at runtime');

// TypeScript annotations alone cannot validate a JSON response.
function parseUser(value) {
  if (typeof value !== 'object' || value === null) {
    throw new TypeError('User must be an object');
  }

  if (!Number.isInteger(value.id) || value.id <= 0) {
    throw new TypeError('User id must be a positive integer');
  }

  if (typeof value.name !== 'string' || value.name.trim() === '') {
    throw new TypeError('User name must be a non-empty string');
  }

  if (typeof value.email !== 'string' || !value.email.includes('@')) {
    throw new TypeError('User email must be valid');
  }

  return {
    id: value.id,
    name: value.name.trim(),
    email: value.email.trim(),
  };
}

const apiResponse = {
  id: 2,
  name: '  Priya  ',
  email: 'priya@example.com',
};

const validatedUser = parseUser(apiResponse);
console.log('Validated API user:', validatedUser);
assert.equal(validatedUser.name, 'Priya');

console.log('\nStep 3: Model UI states with a discriminated union pattern');

// A TypeScript version can use a union of loading, success, and error types.
// This JavaScript function demonstrates the same runtime branching.
function describeRequestState(state) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'loading':
      return 'Loading users...';
    case 'success':
      return `Loaded ${state.users.length} users.`;
    case 'error':
      return `Request failed: ${state.message}`;
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unknown status: ${state.status}`);
  }
}

const loadingState = { status: 'loading' };
const successState = {
  status: 'success',
  users: [validatedUser],
};
const errorState = {
  status: 'error',
  message: 'Unable to reach the server',
};

console.log(describeRequestState(loadingState));
console.log(describeRequestState(successState));
console.log(describeRequestState(errorState));
assert.match(describeRequestState(successState), /Loaded 1 users/);

console.log('\nStep 4: Update collections immutably');

const products = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Soap', price: 99, active: true },
  { id: 2, name: 'Shampoo', price: 199, active: true },
  { id: 3, name: 'Oil', price: 149, active: false },
];

// Never modify an existing React state array directly.
// map creates a new array and spread creates a new product object.
const updatedProducts = products.map((product) =>
  product.id === 2
    ? { ...product, price: 179 }
    : product
);

const activeProducts = updatedProducts.filter(
  (product) => product.active
);

console.log('Original shampoo price:', products[1].price);
console.log('Updated shampoo price:', updatedProducts[1].price);
console.log('Active products:', activeProducts);
assert.equal(products[1].price, 199);
assert.equal(updatedProducts[1].price, 179);

console.log('\nStep 5: Use predictable state transitions');

// This reducer can be shared by UI logic and unit tests.
function cartReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add':
      return {
        ...state,
        items: [...state.items, action.product],
      };
    case 'remove':
      return {
        ...state,
        items: state.items.filter(
          (item) => item.id !== action.id
        ),
      };
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unsupported action: ${action.type}`);
  }
}

const emptyCart = { items: [] };
const cartWithProduct = cartReducer(emptyCart, {
  type: 'add',
  product: { id: 10, name: 'Neem Soap', price: 99 },
});

console.log('Cart after adding product:', cartWithProduct);
console.log('Original cart remains unchanged:', emptyCart);
assert.equal(cartWithProduct.items.length, 1);
assert.equal(emptyCart.items.length, 0);

const emptyCartAgain = cartReducer(cartWithProduct, {
  type: 'remove',
  id: 10,
});

console.log('Cart after removing product:', emptyCartAgain);
assert.equal(emptyCartAgain.items.length, 0);

console.log('\nStep 6: Handle asynchronous operations safely');

// In React, manage loading and error states explicitly and consider
// AbortController or effect cleanup when a component unmounts.
async function loadUsers(fetchImplementation) {
  try {
    const response = await fetchImplementation();

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP error: ${response.status}`);
    }

    const payload = await response.json();

    if (!Array.isArray(payload)) {
      throw new TypeError('Expected an array of users');
    }

    return {
      status: 'success',
      users: payload.map(parseUser),
    };
  } catch (error) {
    return {
      status: 'error',
      message: error instanceof Error
        ? error.message
        : 'Unexpected error',
    };
  }
}

async function main() {
  const result = await loadUsers(async () => ({
    ok: true,
    status: 200,
    json: async () => [
      { id: 4, name: 'Riya', email: 'riya@example.com' },
    ],
  }));

  console.log('API operation result:', result);
  assert.equal(result.status, 'success');
  assert.equal(result.users.length, 1);

  const failedResult = await loadUsers(async () => ({
    ok: false,
    status: 503,
    json: async () => ({}),
  }));

  console.log('Handled API failure:', failedResult);
  assert.equal(failedResult.status, 'error');

  console.log('\nAll examples completed successfully.');
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error('Unexpected example failure:', error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

Conclusion

React and TypeScript work best when types communicate clear contracts, components have focused responsibilities, and state transitions remain predictable. Runtime validation is equally important because external data can violate the assumptions expressed by your TypeScript definitions.

Start by enabling strict TypeScript checks, typing component props and event handlers, avoiding unnecessary any types, and modeling asynchronous states explicitly. Add runtime validation where data enters the application, and test business logic independently from component rendering whenever practical.

The goal is not to add types everywhere simply to satisfy the compiler. It is to make incorrect states harder to represent, make component behavior easier to understand, and help your team deliver changes with confidence as the application grows.

title: Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters
description:
title: "Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters"
published: true
published_at: "2026-12-24T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [systemdesign, backend, redis, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of system design architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Comparing Rate Limiting Algorithms: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Implementing Atomic Sliding Window With Redis Sorted Sets (Zadd: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Zremrangebyscore): Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Memory Footprints: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Designing a Distributed Rate Limiter: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Counters functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: System design Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Comparing rate limiting algorithms, implementing atomic sliding window with Redis Sorted Sets (ZADD, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), and memory footprints."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Designing an Audit Trail for Attendance Edits Without Overwriting Source Events
description:
An attendance correction looks like a simple update:

UPDATE attendance_records
SET clock_out_at = '2026-10-15T18:04:00+09:00'
WHERE id = 8412;

That query fixes the current row, but it also destroys the answer to several questions: What was recorded first? Who requested the correction? What evidence supported it? Who approved it? Which value was used for payroll before the change?

For systems that affect pay, deleting that context is a design problem. A safer model treats the original clock event as immutable and records corrections as a separate, reviewable trail.

Start with two different kinds of truth

Attendance software usually contains at least two truths:

  1. Observed truth: the raw event produced by a device, browser, QR scan, or administrator import.
  2. Operational truth: the approved interpretation used for schedules, overtime, and payroll.

Those values can disagree without either being useless. A raw 18:47 clock-out may be genuine, while an approved 18:00 work end may reflect an employee who forgot to clock out after changing clothes. The system should preserve both facts instead of rewriting one into the other.

In Korean workplaces, teams often search for these tools as 출퇴근기록기 (clock-in recorder) or 근태관리기 (attendance management tool). Whatever label the product uses, the important architectural question is the same: does a correction replace evidence, or does it add a decision to the evidence?

Model source events as append-only data

A source event should identify where it came from and when the server received it. Device time alone is not enough because a phone clock can be wrong or an offline client may synchronize later.

CREATE TABLE attendance_events (
  id                BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  event_type        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (event_type IN ('clock_in', 'clock_out')),
  occurred_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  received_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  source_type       TEXT NOT NULL,
  source_reference  TEXT,
  payload_hash      TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The application role that inserts these rows should not have permission to update or delete them. Retention and privacy rules may eventually require controlled deletion, but that should be a separate administrative process rather than an ordinary edit endpoint.

Put corrections in their own workflow

A correction request is not another clock event. It is a proposal to interpret one or more source events differently.

CREATE TABLE attendance_corrections (
  id                  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_id         BIGINT NOT NULL,
  work_date           DATE NOT NULL,
  requested_clock_in  TIMESTAMPTZ,
  requested_clock_out TIMESTAMPTZ,
  reason_code         TEXT NOT NULL,
  reason_detail       TEXT,
  requested_by        BIGINT NOT NULL,
  requested_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  status              TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'approved', 'rejected', 'cancelled')),
  decided_by          BIGINT,
  decided_at          TIMESTAMPTZ,
  decision_note       TEXT
);

The correction should reference the affected source events through a join table. This matters when one workday has duplicate scans, a missing clock-out, or a shift that crosses midnight.

Build the effective record instead of mutating it

Read models can combine raw events with the latest approved correction. The calculation can live in a database view, a materialized projection, or an application service.

effective attendance
  = original source events
  + latest approved correction
  + policy version used for interpretation

Keeping the policy version is important. A record calculated under a 30-minute break rule should not silently change when the company later adopts a 45-minute rule.

For a practical example of the employee-facing recording flow, this attendance record management guide is useful context. The implementation detail to preserve is the boundary between captured events and later administrative decisions.

Make state transitions explicit

Do not let clients set any status they want. Define legal transitions in one domain function:

type Status = "pending" | "approved" | "rejected" | "cancelled";

const allowed: Record<Status, Status[]> = {
  pending: ["approved", "rejected", "cancelled"],
  approved: [],
  rejected: [],
  cancelled: [],
};

export function canTransition(from: Status, to: Status): boolean {
  return allowed[from].includes(to);
}

If an approved correction is wrong, create a new correction that supersedes it. Reopening and editing the old decision makes the audit trail ambiguous.

Protect the workflow from concurrency bugs

Two managers can open the same pending request and approve different values. Use optimistic locking or a conditional update:

UPDATE attendance_corrections
SET status = 'approved',
    decided_by = $1,
    decided_at = now()
WHERE id = $2
  AND status = 'pending';

The update must affect exactly one row. A zero-row result means the request was already handled and the client should refresh instead of pretending the approval succeeded.

For payroll export, store a snapshot identifier or cutoff time. Otherwise, an approval that arrives during export can create a file that cannot be reproduced later.

Log business meaning, not just HTTP requests

An infrastructure log saying PATCH /attendance/8412 200 is not enough. Emit a domain event with the decision context:

{
  "event": "attendance_correction_approved",
  "correction_id": 392,
  "employee_id": 117,
  "work_date": "2026-10-15",
  "previous_effective_clock_out": "2026-10-15T18:47:12+09:00",
  "new_effective_clock_out": "2026-10-15T18:00:00+09:00",
  "reason_code": "forgot_to_clock_out",
  "decided_by": 42,
  "policy_version": "attendance-policy-2026-09"
}

Avoid copying free-form notes, precise location data, or device identifiers into every analytics system. The audit store can retain necessary evidence with stricter access controls, while downstream events carry only the fields needed for operations.

Test invariants, not only endpoints

The most valuable tests assert properties that must remain true across refactors:

  • A source event cannot be updated through the normal application role.
  • A pending correction can be decided only once.
  • A rejected correction never changes the effective attendance record.
  • An approved correction does not erase the referenced source events.
  • Payroll export can be reproduced from a recorded cutoff and policy version.
  • A manager cannot approve a correction outside the manager's authorized team.

Property-based tests are particularly useful around overnight shifts, duplicate events, daylight-saving transitions, and late offline synchronization.

A small implementation checklist

Before shipping an attendance correction feature, verify that the system can answer these questions without reading application logs by hand:

  1. What did the employee or device originally submit?
  2. When did the server receive it?
  3. What replacement value was requested, and why?
  4. Who approved or rejected the request?
  5. Which policy version produced the payable result?
  6. Which version was included in a specific payroll export?

If any answer disappears after an edit, the design is still overwriting history.

The goal is not to implement event sourcing everywhere. It is to preserve the few boundaries that matter: observations remain observations, decisions remain decisions, and payroll results remain reproducible. That separation makes corrections easier to explain, safer to authorize, and much less painful to debug.

title: No Bootstrap, No Principal: The Day My Audit Log Became Fiction
description:
My v0.1.0 series couldn't talk about authorization, because there wasn't any. v0.2.0 shipped RBAC-lite, scoped API keys, and an encrypted secret vault on HivePlane — and the first thing the field test taught me is that attribution has a cold-start problem.

I shipped a control plane with roles, permissions, and an audit trail — and for an hour, none of it was reachable, because there was no way to mint the first API key.

This is the article about the prerequisite for every governance claim I made in the earlier series: a principal. Without one, your audit log is fiction.

The cold start

The finding was D-10. RBAC was wired. /auth/login existed. Scoped keys were implemented. And the entire model was unreachable end-to-end, because there was no HTTP bootstrap to mint the first admin key. The roles existed; nobody could assume one.

The fix was a dev-grade env admin key — boot the first principal from the environment, then issue scoped keys from there:

# the first principal has to come from outside the API
export HIVEPLANE_AUTH__ENABLED=true
export HIVEPLANE_AUTH__ADMIN_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
# now you can POST /keys to issue scoped, tenant-bound keys

The lesson is that authn is the admission gate for the operators. Until there's a principal, every "who did this" question is unanswerable, and every other governance feature is theater.

The audit log that named the wrong person

Then I found the worse one. Pause, resume, stop, kill-switch, quarantine — every privileged operator action — was attributed to a client-supplied actor field. The caller put --operator alice in the request. The audit log recorded alice. Any caller could sign an action as anyone.

tip: A who column populated by the request body is a confession that you don't know. The actor must come from the authenticated principal, not the payload. A client-supplied actor is repudiation by construction.

Findings #560, #561, and #541 were all the same shape: the action was real, the attribution was a string the caller chose. The fix is that the principal resolves the actor; the field is read-only. You can attribute an action to yourself. You cannot attribute it to someone else.

The endpoints that had no permission at all

Then the field test found the gaps RBAC was supposed to cover and didn't:

  • #537 — registry mutation endpoints had no permission checks. A viewer could DELETE /workloads.
  • #526 — destructive immune-system endpoints (quarantine, kill-switch) were ungated.
  • #563 — pause/resume/stop had no permission gate; a viewer could stop any run.
  • #566 — the UI session secret shipped a hardcoded public default.

A role system that doesn't gate the destructive verbs is a role system in name only. The fix is server-side authorization on every privileged action: approve, promote, kill-switch. A viewer cannot approve. A viewer cannot stop. A viewer cannot delete a workload. The 401/403 is the product.

HMAC-first, not bearer-first

The one I didn't see coming was #515. With auth enabled, GitHub and Alertmanager webhooks got 401 before the HMAC signature was verified. The bearer-first model broke event ingest from ≥3 sources — which is a release gate. Triggers are the autonomy layer; if they can't authenticate, the fleet doesn't run itself.

The fix is that webhook ingest is HMAC-first, not bearer-first. The signature is verified before any bearer token is required; the trigger source is trusted by its HMAC, not by a login. Autonomy and authorization have to coexist, or you've secured the plane against its own purpose.

What I learned

Bootstrap the first principal, or none of it exists — the env admin key is the admission gate for operators. Attribution comes from the principal, never the payload: a client-supplied actor is repudiation by construction. Gate the destructive verbs — a viewer who can delete a workload doesn't have a role, they have root. And webhooks are HMAC-first: bearer-first auth breaks event ingest, and autonomy and authorization have to coexist or you've secured the plane against its own purpose.

The v0.2.0 field test asserts per-tenant budget/policy/key isolation with a viewer who cannot approve, and a secret that never appears in logs/traces/agent context (verified by test). Full evidence in the field-test report; the auth bootstrap and key-rotation runbook is at docs/runbooks/auth-bootstrap-and-key-rotation.md.

References

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36)
  • Auth bootstrap & key rotation runbook
  • Secrets, RBAC & access audit design
  • Secrets, RBAC & access audit (User Guide)

Open your audit log. Pick one privileged action. Is the who populated by the authenticated principal — or by a field the caller wrote? If it's the second, your audit log is a story someone else is telling you.

title: Deconstructing Roles with Hiring Managers: A Workshop Guide
description:
• Start with the Outcome, Not the Title
  • Run a Focused Hiring Manager Workshop — 60–90 minutes that produces clarity
  • From Workshop Notes to a Lean Job Description and Interview Scorecard
  • Tie Job Scope Directly to Onboarding, KPIs, and Performance Reviews
  • Workshop Playbook: A 90-minute Hiring Manager Discovery Session
  • Sources

Most hiring failures begin before an interview: a vague role brief. When a hiring manager can’t clearly describe the outcomes they expect, recruiters default to keyword matches, interviewers default to gut checks, and new hires default to guesswork — which erodes time-to-productivity, retention, and team morale.

Hiring symptoms are familiar: job postings rewritten three times, repeated candidate ghosting at late stages, offers accepted then rescinded, new hires whose day‑to‑day tasks don't match the posted responsibilities, and managers surprised at what the hire can't do. Those operational symptoms trace to one root cause: unclear scope and undefined measures of success for the role. You need a repeatable process to deconstruct the work, surface the real success metrics, and translate those decisions into recruitment artifacts the team can act on.

Start with the Outcome, Not the Title

If you want faster hires that stick, stop describing tasks and start describing results. Role deconstruction begins by converting nebulous responsibilities into the handful of outcomes that move the business needle.

  • Define outcomes first: Replace task lists with 3–5 outcome statements (e.g., increase trial-to-paid conversion by 12% in 12 months). Outcomes make job scoping measurable and negotiable.
  • Capture context: team mission, reporting line, key stakeholders, systems the hire must own, and constraints (budget, travel, time zone).
  • Separate must-have from nice-to-have: use a strict two-column rule — if you would cancel the hire without it, it’s a must-have.
  • Use job analysis methods: a short, structured job analysis is not academic fluff — it’s how you map tasks to critical competencies and reduce downstream guesswork.

Contrarian insight: titles rarely predict performance; outcomes do. A “Senior X” that cannot deliver the target outcome is a title, not value. When your job ads and intake briefs prioritize outcomes, your sourcing, screening, and interviewing all get sharply more efficient.

Run a Focused Hiring Manager Workshop — 60–90 minutes that produces clarity

A hiring manager workshop is the fastest way to convert tacit manager expectations into documented hiring artifacts. Keep it compact, focused, and output-driven.

What to invite: the hiring manager (owner), the recruiter (facilitator), one peer from the team, and the HRBP or hiring panel lead (calibrator). No executive committees. Pre-work: hiring manager submits a brief context note (one page) and current team org chart.

Core agenda (timeboxed to 60–90 minutes):

  1. Quick context and priority alignment (5–10 min): business reason for hire and how success maps to the next 6–12 months.
  2. Role deconstruction workshop (20–30 min): identify top 3–5 responsibilities and translate each into a measurable outcome.
  3. Defining success metrics (15–20 min): agree on a 30/60/90 framework and 1–2 KPIs per responsibility (defining success metrics is the deliverable).
  4. Skills & constraints mapping (10–15 min): must-haves, nice-to-haves, blockers, budget, location/remote requirements.
  5. Interview plan & scorecard mapping (10–15 min): choose 3 competencies to score, assign weights, and set debrief rules.
  6. Decisions and next steps (5 min): who writes the job brief, deadline, and interview panel assignments.

Why this works: structured job analysis and consistent interview rubrics increase predictive validity and reduce legal and fairness risk. Use research-backed structure rather than free-form conversation.

Practical facilitation tips:

  • Use a shared whiteboard or live doc and capture evidence-of-success language (exact phrases a manager would say in a 6‑month review).
  • Force decisions: label anything uncertain as hypothesis and assign an owner to validate in hiring.
  • Keep the session to only necessary people to avoid scope dilution.

From Workshop Notes to a Lean Job Description and Interview Scorecard

Translate workshop outputs into two operational artifacts that drive hiring alignment: a lean job description and a calibrated interview scorecard.

Job description skeleton (lean, outcome-first):

  • Role summary: 2–3 sentences emphasizing the team mission and top outcome.
  • Top responsibilities (outcome-based bullets): each bullet begins with the expected outcome and includes the measure and timeframe.
  • Success metrics: explicit 30/60/90 targets and the KPIs you’ll use in hiring and onboarding.
  • Must-have skills vs preferred: list only essentials in the must column.
  • Team & manager profile: who the hire reports to, direct reports, and key stakeholders.
  • Logistics: location, compensation band, required clearances.

Example responsibilities table:

Responsibility (Outcome) Success metric (how measured) 30 / 60 / 90 milestone
Reduce support SLA breaches SLA breaches ≤ 5% month-over-month 30: identify top 3 failure modes; 60: deliver 2 process fixes; 90: SLA ≤ 8%
Increase feature adoption Adoption rate +10% in 6 months 30: baseline adoption; 60: ship onboarding flow; 90: +6% adoption

Convert those bullets directly into interview scorecards. A good interview scorecard contains:

  • Competency name (e.g., Delivery Ownership)
  • Weight (scorecard.weight) as a percentage of final score
  • Behavioral anchors (what a 1/3/5 looks like)
  • Sample evidence you expect (past projects, metrics, artifacts)

Sample interview scorecard in YAML:

role: Product Manager - Growth
competencies:
  - name: Delivery Ownership
    weight: 30
    anchors:
      1: "No clear ownership; missed deadlines without mitigation"
      3: "Delivered with supervision; incremental impact"
      5: "Led cross-functional effort and exceeded targets with measurable outcomes"
  - name: Analytical Rigor
    weight: 25
    anchors:
      1: "No data used in decisions"
      3: "Used basic analysis; needed coaching"
      5: "Built models and demonstrated causal impact"
  - name: Stakeholder Influence
    weight: 20
    anchors:
      1: "Struggles to persuade peers"
      3: "Manages stakeholders with support"
      5: "Built alignment and changed roadmaps through influence"

Evidence basis matters: structured interviews plus behaviorally-anchored rating scales improve selection decisions and fairness. Pair these scorecards with a short work sample or case for mid-senior roles for the best predictive value.

Important: The scorecard is not a feedback form — it’s a decision tool. Score independently, then calibrate evidence in a short debrief.

Tie Job Scope Directly to Onboarding, KPIs, and Performance Reviews

Hiring alignment doesn’t stop at offer acceptance. The same outcomes and metrics you defined during role deconstruction must drive onboarding and early performance conversations.

  • Convert success metrics into a 30/60/90 onboarding plan for the new hire (day 1 deliverables, 30-day learning goals, 90-day outcome targets).
  • Map onboarding tasks to interview evidence: if you weighted stakeholder influence at hire, plan early stakeholder introductions and paired activities to solidify that skill.
  • Feed hiring artifacts into HRIS/ATS and the new-hire checklist so managers have a runbook for ramp. SHRM recommends treating onboarding as an ongoing process (not a single orientation) and aligning it to role outcomes.

Sample 30/60/90 (brief):

  • 30 days: 1) Complete system access + shadowing; 2) Deliver gap analysis of current process.
  • 60 days: Implement one improvement and show metric baseline movement.
  • 90 days: Own a cross-functional deliverable and meet agreed KPI thresholds.

Why this reduces mis-hires: clarity during hiring translates to clarity at Day 1 — managers and new hires know what success looks like, reducing the common "what did I actually hire them for?" problem that drives early attrition. Gallup links declines in role clarity to drops in engagement and retention; making expectations explicit at hire and onboarding is a high-leverage fix.

Workshop Playbook: A 90-minute Hiring Manager Discovery Session

Use this playbook as a repeatable template for role deconstruction and job scoping.

Pre-work (sent 3 business days before):

  • Hiring manager: 1-page context note (team mission, why now, top 3 expected outcomes).
  • Recruiter: current job posting, sample resumes, org chart.
  • Participants: review pre-work and come prepared with one concrete success example for the role.

90‑minute facilitator playbook (timeboxes and scripts):

  1. 0–10 min — Kickoff & framing
    • Script: “We’ll align on one crisp outcome set and leave with a job brief, scorecard, and 30/60/90 plan.”
  2. 10–35 min — Top outcomes & stakeholder map
    • Activity: Whiteboard Top 5 responsibilities; write outcome first.
  3. 35–55 min — Define success metrics
    • Activity: For each top responsibility, list 1 KPI and a 30/60/90 milestone.
  4. 55–70 min — Skills vs. experience & constraints
    • Activity: Move sticky notes into must / nice-to-have columns.
  5. 70–85 min — Scorecard mapping and interview plan
    • Decide 3 competencies to interview against; set weights; list 2 behavioral prompts per competency.
  6. 85–90 min — Decisions & next steps (assign authorship of artifacts)

Deliverables (output within 48 hours):

  • One-page role brief (outcome-first)
  • Job description draft (2–3 sentence summary + outcome bullets)
  • Interview scorecard (YAML/CSV to upload to ATS)
  • 30/60/90 onboarding plan
  • Panel assignments and interview scheduling windows

Calibration protocol (post-interview):

  1. Each interviewer scores independently within 24 hours.
  2. Convene a 30-minute debrief limited to evidence, not opinions.
  3. Tally weights and use a simple threshold (e.g., weighted score ≥ 75) for automatic hiring recommendation or move to reference checks.
  4. If variance > 20 points between interviewers, flag for a calibration retrain.

Quick checklist to attach to the requisition:

  • [ ] Role brief attached to requisition
  • [ ] Scorecard uploaded into ATS
  • [ ] Panel trained on scorecard (5–10 min read)
  • [ ] Offer approval and comp band confirmed
  • [ ] Onboarding owner assigned

A short calibration note: structured, evidence-based interviews and scoring reduce unconscious bias and help panels compare apples to apples. Google’s re:Work guidance and the industrial-organizational research base both recommend this approach for reliability and fairness.

Sources

U.S. Employee Engagement Sinks to 10-Year Low — Gallup - Gallup’s reporting on role clarity and employee engagement; used to support the central role-clarity claim and onboarding alignment rationale.

SIOP: Structured Interviewing and Job Analysis — Society for Industrial and Organizational Psychology - SIOP resources and practitioner guidance on job analysis, structured interviewing, and reducing rating errors; used to justify job analysis and structured interview practices.

The Validity and Utility of Selection Methods in Personnel Psychology — Frank L. Schmidt & John E. Hunter (1998) (summary) - Academic meta-analysis establishing the predictive value of structured interviews plus other assessment tools; cited for the evidence base behind scorecards and selection method validity.

SHRM — New Employee Onboarding Guide - SHRM guidance on treating onboarding as a strategic, ongoing process aligned to role expectations; cited for onboarding alignment and operational recommendations.

Use Structured Interviewing — Google re:Work - Practical guidance and examples from Google on structured interview design, rubrics, and scoring; used to support interview-scorecard design and calibration protocols.

title: When POST becomes GET: a redirect bug in a Node.js fetch wrapper
description:
A POST followed a 302 redirect and became a GET. Its body disappeared, but its Content-Type header stayed behind.

That showed up while extending the client comparisons in ssrf-lab, a testing harness I maintain. The affected package was @tak-ps/node-safeurl@1.8.0, a Node.js fetch wrapper that checks URLs and redirect destinations.

This is a functional redirect-conformance bug. The proposed fix is upstream PR #4, submitted and awaiting review as of October 14, 2026. These tests do not demonstrate an SSRF bypass.

The response looked fine. The request told the story.

The comparison uses a small HTTP server on 127.0.0.1. One route returns a redirect; the destination echoes the method, body, and headers it actually receives. That exact local origin is explicitly allowed in the wrapper's configuration.

Both native fetch and the wrapper successfully completed this request:

{
  method: 'POST',
  body: 'hello',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'text/plain' }
}

After a 302 redirect, the destination observed:

Client Method Body Content-Type
Native fetch GET empty absent
node-safeurl 1.8.0 GET empty text/plain

The same difference appeared for 301 POST and 303 PUT. Checking only the final status or whether the fetch promise resolved would miss it.

The Fetch redirect algorithm changes POST to GET for 301/302, and changes methods other than GET/HEAD to GET for 303. When it discards the body, it also removes the request-body headers: Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Content-Location, and Content-Type.

The wrapper already handled the method and body changes. It was missing the corresponding header cleanup.

The fix belongs in the method-rewrite branch

The patch adds Headers to the existing Undici import, then extends the existing switchToGet branch:

if (switchToGet) {
  fetchInit.method = 'GET';
  fetchInit.body = undefined;

  const headers = new Headers(fetchInit.headers);
  for (const name of [
    'content-encoding',
    'content-language',
    'content-location',
    'content-type',
    'content-length',
  ]) {
    headers.delete(name);
  }
  fetchInit.headers = headers;
}

Content-Length is removed as well, because caller-supplied framing for the discarded body should not carry into the GET. It is separate from the standard's four named request-body headers.

Copying through Headers supports object, tuple-array, and Headers inputs without changing the caller's original headers. Unrelated headers survive. The URL validation logic is unchanged.

The condition matters: a 307 or 308 should preserve the method and body, so stripping these headers on every redirect would introduce another bug.

Prove both the fix and the unchanged cases

The upstream regression test records actual incoming requests and checks seven cases:

Redirect cases Before patch After patch
301 POST, 302 POST, 303 PUT All three fail All three pass
307 POST, 308 POST, 301 PUT, 302 PUT All four pass All four pass

It also checks that an unrelated header is preserved and the caller's headers are not mutated. The full patched upstream suite passes 198 tests on each of Node 22.23.3 and 24.21.0, alongside lint and build.

The recorded evidence includes the original failures, fixed tests, full-suite logs, and published-package comparison.

Run the comparison

With Node 22.19 or newer and npm:

git clone https://github.com/roshan-amble/ssrf-lab.git
cd ssrf-lab
git checkout 41659cda6825b2f7e324294d7242ef1b076b6cce
npm ci --ignore-scripts --prefix integrations/community
node integrations/community/check-redirects.mjs

This prints JSON for native fetch and the unmodified published package across five redirect cases. The HTTP comparison stays on the explicitly allowed loopback origin. The broader SSRF suite has separate network-isolation requirements.

The practical testing lesson is to assert what reached the destination: method, body, and headers. A successful response alone cannot establish that a wrapper preserved fetch semantics.

The harness, adapters, and reproduction are in ssrf-lab. Which redirect or URL-handling edge case would you add to this coverage?

AI disclosure: Codex assisted with the investigation, implementation, and test execution, and drafted this article from the linked code and recorded results.

title: Launching EyeZen v1.0.0: A Local-First Desktop App Built with Rust, Tauri and React
description:
Launching EyeZen v1.0.0: A Local-First Desktop App Built with Rust, Tauri and React

EyeZen v1.0.0 is now available. It's an open-source desktop workspace-personalization application built with Rust, Tauri 2, React and TypeScript.

The guiding idea is simple: the preferences you want while coding may not be the ones you want while reading, editing a video, or working late.

I wanted to build a desktop app that treats those different contexts as configurable workspaces while keeping core configuration local.

What ships in v1.0.0?

The first release includes ten interface themes:

  • Light
  • Dark
  • System
  • Warm Dark
  • Warm Light
  • Sepia Reading
  • Midnight
  • AMOLED-Inspired
  • High Contrast
  • Grayscale

Users can change accent colors, text scale and motion preferences.

EyeZen includes nine starting workspace profiles covering activities such as coding, reading, office work, productivity, gaming, editing and accessibility.

Profiles can be created, edited, applied, imported and exported as JSON.

A scheduling system supports weekday and overnight time windows, priorities for overlapping rules, and a visible manual override.

The optional Break Assistant provides configurable reminder intervals and quiet hours. Notifications depend on OS permissions and environment support.

Settings are stored locally with validation, export/import, and recovery behavior for corrupted files.

The first-run setup introduces the key choices, while an explicit capability report explains which platform integrations are implemented.

Why use Rust, Tauri 2 and React?

Rust provides a foundation for the desktop command layer, validation, persistence and scheduling utilities.

Tauri 2 bridges the application and its native platform features.

React and TypeScript provide the customizable interface, feature views and tests.

The codebase separates the UI, scheduling logic, imports and platform-support boundaries.

Automated frontend and Rust checks run through GitHub Actions across desktop build targets.

Passing CI is useful, but it isn't a replacement for installing and testing the app on real hardware.

Local-first by design

EyeZen's core functionality doesn't require an account, location permission, telemetry service or cloud backend.

Profiles and settings remain on the device, with manual backup/export options.

That is useful both for privacy and for keeping basic workspace personalization independent of an internet connection.

Honest limits in v1.0.0

An important distinction: EyeZen v1.0.0 does not adjust physical monitor brightness or operating-system color temperature.

Warmth and intensity controls save preferences but do not control Night Light, Night Shift, HDR or an external monitor. There is no color overlay or monitor enumeration in this version.

Scheduling and reminders currently run while the application webview is active, so their operation after closing or suspending the app is not guaranteed.

Release installers are CI-built and unsigned, and OS-specific manual acceptance tests are still needed.

EyeZen is a customization tool, not a medical device, and I don't want to make unsupported claims about eye-health outcomes.

Where the project goes next

The roadmap includes more robust background scheduling, broader tray and shortcut controls, improved theme/profile creation, and eventually carefully validated platform-specific display integrations.

Those are future goals, not features in today's release.

Try EyeZen and contribute

I would love feedback on the onboarding experience, theme choices, scheduling logic, keyboard navigation, package installation, and how EyeZen behaves on different desktops.

  • Source code
  • EyeZen v1.0.0 release and downloads
  • Platform support and known limitations

Your screen. Your comfort. Your environment.

title: Verify authentication recovery before treating Configuration as the root cause
description:
A return URL containing error=Configuration suggests a configuration mistake. Yet the inspected Auth.js version also produces that destination when a PKCE cookie is missing. The user-facing classification does not identify the cause by itself.

This investigation read SquadNote's recovery implementation and reran tests against its actual Auth.js dependency. It examines rejection, retry navigation, and diagnostic evidence before drawing a causal conclusion.

The source is circle-hub at d116e8a, checked on September 11, 2026. No production authentication logs or user histories were collected. This is an account of recovery code and rerun verification, not proof of a production incident's cause or resolution.

Distinguish the internal error from Configuration

Auth.js's InvalidCheck reference covers PKCE, state, or nonce checks that cannot be performed. Unavailable cookies can produce it, as can configuration issues.

The repository regression test resolves @auth/core through the application's next-auth dependency. It does not substitute a separately installed latest release.

A synthetic callback without its PKCE cookie produced:

Observation Result
HTTP status 302
Redirect destination /sign-in/error?error=Configuration
Internal type passed to the logger InvalidCheck

The fixture deliberately omitted the cookie, so its cause is known. Seeing the same internal type in production would still require investigating why the cookie did not arrive. Expiration, another initiation, and browser behavior cannot be distinguished from that display alone.

First restore a path from failure to a fresh start

The recovery design record and history show the recovery screen in 061a5f2, repeated-submission protection in 2b88c31, and diagnostics in 7f180ad.

The recovery screen presents sign-in and public help without depending on auth() or the database. Displaying an authentication failure does not require successfully repeating the same authentication dependency.

Return destinations are restricted to safe paths on the same origin. Tests preserve invitation-page returns while rejecting external redirection and authentication-page loops. The original callback URL is not reused unconditionally.

Two new initiation requests sent to the actual Auth.js implementation produced different PKCE challenges, S256, and fresh PKCE cookies. However, the initiation fixture uses the internal CSRF-skip option. It does not verify browser CSRF protection or a round trip through the OAuth provider, and no production setting was changed to disable CSRF checks.

Reject a second start before React rerenders

Disabling a button visually can leave a window before React rerenders in which another button can be pressed. The implementation uses a synchronous guard shared by Google and Apple initiation on the same screen:

export function createSubmissionGuard() {
  let submitting = false;
  return {
    acquire() {
      if (submitting) return false;
      submitting = true;
      return true;
    },
    reset() { submitting = false; },
  };
}

Tests against the actual guard reject immediate reacquisition, allow acquisition after the reset used for failure or history restoration, and keep separate instances independent.

Its scope is repeated submission from one screen. It does not serialize initiation across tabs or browsers, nor remove every possible cause of missing cookies.

Correlate how far the flow progressed

The diagnostics investigate initiation and callback boundaries without storing authentication values. The principal events mean:

Event What it establishes
auth.sign_in_started A start request occurred
auth.authorization_redirect Initiation generated a destination
auth.callback_received A callback arrived
auth.sign_in_succeeded Auth.js emitted its signIn event
auth.server_error Failure and diagnostic information were recorded

Initiation and destination generation do not mean authentication succeeded. In particular, the server action's cookiesAfterStart observes the cookie jar at that time. Existing cookies can be present, so presence alone does not establish fresh issuance.

requestId identifies a failing request; attemptId supports correlation with initiation. The latter marker is client-originated diagnostic information and does not authorize authentication. It represents the browser's most recent initiation, so it does not prove the same OAuth transaction across multiple tabs.

Absent, expired, or provider-mismatched markers can prevent correlation. Record why correlation failed instead of rephrasing that as “no initiation happened.”

Add diagnostics without weakening authentication checks

Diagnostic tests verify that synthetic sensitive values, including cookie values, authorization codes, tokens, raw User-Agent strings, and IPs, do not appear in logs. Cookie observations retain only presence for specific names, and paths are restricted to authentication routes.

Tests also check isolation between concurrent requests, preservation of authentication responses when diagnostics or notifications fail, and preservation of the original Auth.js response cookies. The change does not obtain successful logins by relaxing PKCE, state, or nonce requirements.

Alert suppression operates within a Worker instance; it is not a delivery guarantee across all distributed instances. The diagnostic cookie is not a session replacement either. Neither mechanism belongs in the decision that authentication has succeeded.

The 47 tests and the remaining environment checks

The run passed 47 tests across 8 files copied from the fixed commit. It used Node.js v24.15.0, Vitest 4.1.4, Next.js 15.5.15, next-auth 5.0.0-beta.25, and its Auth.js core dependency 0.37.2. The runner and results are preserved.

Some tests invoke the actual Auth.js implementation; others mock route or notification dependencies. Real Google or Apple accounts, Safari or embedded browsers, multiple tabs, and manual browser-cookie deletion were not tested in this run. Historical UI verification documented in the repository is also separate from these rerun results.

Verify the failure classification, fresh initiation, safe return destination, same-screen repeat protection, and the limits of log correlation in order. While the cause remains uncertain, record the conditions for retry and the questions requiring further investigation.
