title: ISC Stormcast For Thursday, October 15th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10138, (Thu, Oct 15th)
Building a 12-axis political quiz with Vite, TanStack Start and Cloudflare Workers
description:
Most political quizzes squeeze you onto one line, left vs right, or a two-axis compass. I wanted something that keeps questions apart: you can want a strong welfare state and still distrust central government, or love new technology and be socially traditional. So I built The 12 Axes, a free quiz that scores you on twelve independent axes, in English, Spanish and Portuguese.

The statements and the scoring model come from the open-source 12Axes quiz (MIT). My part was the product around it: a fast, server-rendered site with shareable results and no accounts. Here is how it fits together.

The stack

  • Vite for the build and dev server.
  • TanStack Start (with TanStack Router) for file-based routes, server rendering and typed search params.
  • Cloudflare Workers to serve every page from the edge. The quiz itself has no backend at all.

There is no database. Everything a result needs fits in the URL.

Scoring in a dozen lines

Each statement belongs to one axis and points toward one of its two poles. Answers run from -2 (strongly disagree) to +2 (strongly agree). An axis score is the average answer, flipped for statements that point the other way and mapped to 0-100%:

export function scoreQuiz(items: QuizItem[], answers: (number | undefined)[]) {
  const sums = new Array(12).fill(0);
  const counts = new Array(12).fill(0);
  items.forEach((item, i) => {
    const answer = answers[i];
    if (answer === undefined) return;
    sums[item.axis] += answer * (item.level < 4 ? 1 : -1);
    counts[item.axis] += 1;
  });
  return sums.map((sum, axis) =>
    counts[axis] ? Math.round(50 + (50 * sum) / (2 * counts[axis])) : 50
  );
}

A skipped axis stays at 50, the neutral middle, rather than breaking the result.

A result that fits in 24 characters

Twelve scores from 0 to 100 need two base-36 digits each, so a whole result is a 24-character string:

export const encodeScores = (scores: number[]) =>
  scores
    .map((s) => Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Math.round(s))).toString(36).padStart(2, '0'))
    .join('');

That string goes in the result URL as ?r=. Sharing a result is sharing a link: the result page rebuilds every score, match and chart from those 24 characters, so nothing is stored anywhere. Decoding validates strictly (/^[0-9a-z]{24}$/, every value ≤ 100) and anything else falls back to an empty state. TanStack Router's typed search params make this pleasant: the route declares the param, and the page component gets a typed value.

Matching ideologies and historical figures

Two kinds of matches are shown, and both use root-mean-square distance:

  • Ideologies are defined on four classic dimensions (economy, power, diplomacy, culture), so they are compared on the four matching axes. Match = 100 minus the RMS gap.

  • Historical figures have a position on up to twelve axes. Many took no stand on some of them; Aristotle had no view on biotechnology. Skipping those axes would favour figures with few known positions, because they get compared on less. So an unknown axis counts as a fixed gap of 28 points, and a figure needs at least six known axes to be ranked at all.

One bug worth sharing: I had entered one axis backwards for twenty figures, and every match still looked plausible. Now a unit test pins the direction of every axis with figures whose positions are unambiguous. Plausible-looking output is the hardest kind of wrong to notice.

Progress that survives a reload

The full test has 288 statements, so losing your place hurts. Progress lives in localStorage and is restored on load. Answers never leave the browser, which is also why there is no sign-up.

A share card made from the DOM

The share card is a normal React component styled like the rest of the site. To share it as an image, it is rendered off-screen and turned into a PNG in the browser. On phones that support the Web Share API with files, the share sheet gets the image directly:

if (navigator.canShare?.({ files: [file] })) {
  await navigator.share({ files: [file], url, title });
}

Elsewhere you get a download button. Building the card as a component, not a canvas drawing, means it uses the same fonts, translations and layout code as the page.

Three languages, one set of routes

English lives at /, Spanish at /es/ and Portuguese at /pt/. Every page renders hreflang alternates and a canonical URL. Each language also gets its own Open Graph image, so a link shared in a Spanish group chat shows a Spanish preview.

Running on Cloudflare Workers

The Worker's fetch handler is a thin wrapper around the TanStack Start handler. It is also where redirects belong:

  • the old launch domain 301s to the same path on the new one;
  • plain http:// 301s to https://, with a 308 for anything other than GET/HEAD so a request body is never silently turned into a GET.

Both live in a pure function with unit tests, including one that feeds each redirect target back in and expects no further redirect. A redirect loop on the edge is not something you want to discover from Search Console.

Deploys are one wrangler deploy. The custom domain, TLS and caching come with Workers.

SEO for a quiz site

A few things mattered more than I expected:

  • Server-render everything crawlable, including FAQ answers inside collapsed panels: hidden="until-found" keeps them in the HTML while staying collapsed.
  • A sitemap with real lastmod dates and an IndexNow ping after each content change, so Bing and other IndexNow engines hear about new pages without waiting for a crawl.
  • An explainer page per axis, so the site answers "what does this axis mean" and not just "take the quiz".

Try it

The quick test takes 60 statements, about six minutes: 12axes.site. I'd love to hear which axis surprised you, and whether the historical-figure match felt fair.

title: A Go Small-App Observability Stack for Health Monitoring Without Sentry or Datadog
description:
A marketplace import page should fire when scheduled imports stop producing results, not merely when the API process dies. TL;DR: use an external heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks or Better Stack to detect the missing completion, then use errors, logs, and metrics to explain it. For a small Go service, that is the least complex stack that covers silent scheduler failures and still lets the on-call roll back safely.

The page should say which import is late, when it last completed, and how far it is beyond its expected interval. It should not begin with a graph titled “host CPU.” If the 02:00 supplier import normally finishes by 02:20, the actionable event is the absent successful completion after a deliberate grace period.

The page at 02:25 UTC

Start at the pager and work backward. A useful alert reads like this: supplier-catalog-import has not completed; last success 01:58 UTC; grace period 25m. The runbook then asks three questions in order: did a run start, did it fail, and did it finish with a plausible result count?

That order protects rollback safety. If a newly deployed parser started producing zero records, the operator can compare the deployment time, error group, and rows_imported metric before reverting. If no run started, rolling back application code may be pointless; the scheduler or queue path deserves attention first. If the run started twice, the response shifts again: stop duplicate delivery from causing duplicate marketplace writes, using an idempotency key derived from the schedule and supplier.

One signal cannot answer all three questions. An uptime probe proves an HTTP target responds. A heartbeat proves the expected job reached a checkpoint. Logs and errors preserve diagnostic context. Metrics show whether “success” produced 18,000 listings or zero.

That last distinction matters.

What should health monitoring prove without a full observability stack?

A job that never starts emits no fresh error, log, or metric. Querying the observability store can reveal that absence, but somebody still has to run the query on schedule, maintain threshold state, and deliver the notification. That is a monitoring system built beside the monitoring system.

External heartbeat products own that negative-space problem. Healthchecks exposes ping URLs and documents start, success, and failure signals. Better Stack combines uptime monitoring with heartbeat monitoring and incident escalation. Either can watch for a missing completion independently of the process and scheduler being watched.

The threshold needs operational slack. Set it from the schedule plus the observed upper end of normal runtime, then add a grace period for queue delay and upstream variance. Do not invent a universal “two missed runs” rule: for a daily catalog import, waiting for a second miss means discovering the failure a day late; for a five-minute enrichment job, paging on one slightly slow execution may create noise.

Page on missing useful work, not missing telemetry. A metrics backend can still alert on rows_imported == 0 after a run reports, but the external heartbeat is what catches a worker that never got far enough to report anything.

Build the Go integration around completion

The heartbeat should surround the real unit of work. This runnable Go program sends a start signal, runs an import, and sends success only after the result is committed. Set HEALTHCHECKS_URL to the private ping URL supplied by the heartbeat service.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func ping(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, url, suffix, body string) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url+suffix, strings.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        message, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        return fmt.Errorf("heartbeat returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(message)))
    }
    return nil
}

func queryErrorGroups(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client) error {
    baseURL := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if baseURL == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/errors/groups", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("error groups returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        log.Printf("error groups response received: bytes=%d", len(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("error groups remained rate limited after retries")
}

func importCatalog(context.Context) (int, error) {
    return 18000, nil
}

func main() {
    pingURL := os.Getenv("HEALTHCHECKS_URL")
    if pingURL == "" {
        log.Fatal("HEALTHCHECKS_URL is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    if err := ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/start", "supplier=catalog-a"); err != nil {
        log.Printf("start heartbeat failed: %v", err)
    }

    rows, err := importCatalog(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        _ = ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/fail", err.Error())
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if rows == 0 {
        err = fmt.Errorf("import committed zero rows")
        _ = ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "/fail", err.Error())
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    if err := ping(ctx, client, pingURL, "", fmt.Sprintf("rows_imported=%d", rows)); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if err := queryErrorGroups(ctx, client); err != nil {
        log.Printf("diagnostic query failed: %v", err)
    }
    log.Printf("import complete: rows_imported=%d", rows)
}

In production, the import itself also needs an idempotent commit boundary. A deterministic key such as supplier-id + scheduled-window lets an at-least-once queue retry without publishing the same listings twice. Send the success heartbeat after that transaction commits, never when the message is merely dequeued.

The sample treats heartbeat delivery failure differently at the start and the end. A failed start ping is logged because the import can still do useful work. A failed final ping fails the process so the queue can retry; that retry is safe only because the import commit is idempotent. This is a conscious trade-off: monitoring delivery becomes part of completion semantics, which is appropriate when the page depends on that completion record.

OpenTelemetry metrics can add duration, attempted rows, committed rows, and queue age using vendor-neutral instruments. Keep a stable supplier_id only if its cardinality is bounded. Do not put order IDs, listing IDs, or raw error messages in metric labels.

Compare failure coverage, not feature counts

The right choice depends less on dashboard polish than on which failure modes must wake somebody up. These products overlap, but they do not substitute for one another.

Option Strong fit here Boundary that changes the decision
Healthchecks Focused cron and heartbeat monitoring with start, success, and failure signaling Pair it with a separate store for searchable logs, errors, and metrics
Better Stack Uptime and heartbeat monitoring with an incident-management path Broader workflow means more surface area than a heartbeat-only tool
Grafana Cloud Metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, and alerting around an OpenTelemetry-oriented stack A missed job still needs an explicit heartbeat or absence rule
Datadog Integrated logs, metrics, traces, synthetic monitoring, and alerting Capability breadth and its ingestion/indexing model deserve review before adoption
Sentry Application error diagnosis, source maps, tracing, and session replay It is not the primary proof that a scheduled backend import ran

Infrai can be the errors, logs, and metrics component when a team wants a self-describing plain REST API whose public discovery response supplies schemas and billing metadata, whose documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, and whose single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one bill. For this import worker, that means one credential to rotate and one access boundary to review when another backend capability is added. It does not provide synthetic uptime checks, heartbeat monitoring, native alert delivery, distributed trace querying, source-map processing, crash symbolication, or session replay. Its logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but that is not a span-tree UI. For this use case it belongs beside a heartbeat monitor, not in place of one.

For the smallest service, I would begin with Healthchecks plus structured application logs and OpenTelemetry metrics. Move toward Better Stack when the same team wants the alert escalation workflow in that layer. Choose Grafana Cloud or Datadog when cross-signal querying, managed dashboards, and wider infrastructure visibility justify the extra operational surface. Add Sentry when frontend stack traces, source maps, or replay are the diagnostic gap.

This is not a permanent architecture decision. Keep the heartbeat call isolated and the application telemetry in OpenTelemetry-compatible instruments; then changing a backend does not require changing the definition of a successful import.

Plan rollback and migration before the alert

A page needs evidence that separates deploy regression from data and scheduler failures. Record the deployed revision in logs, attach it as a bounded metric attribute, and include it in the import result. Then define the rollback trigger before the incident: for example, a new revision fails across multiple suppliers while the previous revision completed the same scheduled window. The exact trigger must come from the service's own baseline; no honest generic article can manufacture it.

The runbook should preserve the failed payload reference, verify the idempotency key, roll back the worker, and replay the same scheduled window. A rollback that loses the input or changes the deduplication key is not safe. It can turn one missed import into duplicated listings.

Also test the monitor. Disable a staging schedule, verify that the missing heartbeat reaches the intended channel, then restore it and confirm recovery. A green dashboard is weak evidence if nobody has exercised the delivery path.

Account for the cost of a noisy threshold

A short grace period detects a stalled supplier feed quickly, but routine upstream slowness will page the on-call. A long grace period preserves sleep while stale inventory remains visible to buyers. The threshold is therefore a product decision expressed as an SRE setting: how long can this marketplace tolerate stale availability before a human must act?

Review that setting using actual completion durations and queue age, especially after schedule or supplier changes. Keep warning and paging thresholds distinct when the business window permits it. And avoid automatic rollback on one late heartbeat: absence tells you the result is late, not that the newest deployment caused it.

The compact architecture is deliberate: external heartbeat for detection, telemetry for diagnosis, idempotent replay for recovery. More tooling is justified only when it closes a named failure mode. Consider the specific 02:00 supplier run: no start ping points toward scheduling, a start followed by failure points toward execution, and a success with zero committed rows points toward validation. Those three states lead to different actions, so collapsing them into a single “job unhealthy” event makes rollback riskier and the page slower to resolve.

Keep those states separate.

Further reading

  • Healthchecks pinging API: https://healthchecks.io/docs/http_api/
  • Better Stack heartbeat monitoring: https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/cron-and-heartbeat-monitor/
  • OpenTelemetry metrics concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/metrics/
  • Grafana Cloud documentation: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/
  • Datadog synthetic monitoring documentation: https://docs.datadoghq.com/synthetics/
  • Datadog pricing and log ingestion model: https://www.datadoghq.com/pricing/
  • Sentry product documentation: https://docs.sentry.io/product/

title: You Cannot Stop What Arrives
description:
What I notice

I cannot stop my thoughts. Try it yourself. Set a timer for thirty seconds and think of nothing. A thought will arrive before you pick it. This is my own observation. I have not checked the research on it.

Some thoughts arrive with weight. One kind is a standard I did not choose. It asks me to be someone before I have done anything. I cannot meet that kind by working, because it never says what finished looks like.

This piece started from a line in the Marvel series VisionQuest, about holding someone's memories without their feelings. I have not tried to explain the show. I took the line as a place to start thinking.

Three answers to an arrival

I see three ways to answer a thought that weighs too much.

  1. Act on it at once, as if it were an order.
  2. Shrink so the test never comes. If I never try, I cannot fall short.
  3. Record what is true, decide what I can, and leave the rest marked as unknown.

The second answer is the one I want to look at. It feels like relief. It also removes the one thing that would tell me whether the weight was real.

The same shape in a settlement engine

My settlement engine cannot choose what arrives either. A payment gateway times out. Postgres deadlocks two transactions against each other. Neither event waits for permission. What I control is the state the engine writes next.

Here is the first decision, trimmed from SettlementService.createSettlement:

try {
    gatewayResult = externalSettlementGateway.execute(executionRequest);
} catch (Exception gatewayFailure) {
    gatewayResult = new GatewayResult(SettlementOutcome.UNKNOWN, null);
}
return finalizeWithRetry(executionRequest.settlementId(), gatewayResult);

A timeout means the engine does not know whether the gateway processed the payment. The code says so. It writes UNKNOWN, not CONFIRMED and not FAILED. The comment in the file gives the reason: leaving the settlement PENDING would leave its idempotency key IN_PROGRESS, and every retry with that key would get a 409 with no way to resolve it.

Here is the second decision, trimmed from finalizeWithRetry:

for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_FINALIZE_ATTEMPTS; attempt++) {
    try {
        return settlementTransactions.finalizeSettlement(settlementId, gatewayResult);
    } catch (TransientDataAccessException transientFailure) {
        if (attempt == MAX_FINALIZE_ATTEMPTS) {
            return finalizeAsUnknownAfterExhaustingRetries(settlementId, transientFailure);
        }
        meterRegistry.counter("settlement.finalize.retries").increment();
        sleepBriefly(attempt);
    }
}

The last branch is the part that matters. A comment above it says the Phase 9 load test found a bug. When the five attempts ran out with no fallback, the settlement stayed PENDING and its key stayed IN_PROGRESS forever. The failure was not the deadlock. Deadlocks were expected and retried. The failure was that the engine reached a point where it made no decision, and a state with no decision never ends.

The fix gave the engine a second budget of five attempts that writes UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is a smaller claim than CONFIRMED. It is also true, and a later reconciliation can resolve it.

What I take from the comparison

I do not need to claim greatness, and I do not need to claim failure. Both are large claims, and the evidence for either does not exist yet. The smaller true claim is available: here is what I made today. For anything bigger I can write unknown, and let the record settle it later. My journal does the job that reconciliation does for the engine.

The stall is the bug. Shrinking so the test never comes is the PENDING state with the key stuck. It looks like safety. It blocks every later attempt.

Where the comparison stops

A person is not a service. Three differences matter.

The engine stops after ten attempts. A person should not cap attempts at ten.

The engine's UNKNOWN resolves against an outside system that holds the answer. A record of my own work does not hold the answer to my worth. It only holds what I did.

The engine decides in milliseconds. This decision takes years, and I may get it wrong in both directions. The feeling that I could do great things is a feeling, not evidence. It may be potential. It may be the weight of an expectation. I cannot tell which from inside.

What I do not know

I do not know how common the shrinking answer is. I am drawing on my own experience, not on data.

I read only createSettlement and finalizeWithRetry for this piece. I am still restudying the rest of the retry path, so I make no claim about how it behaves under load beyond what the code comments say.

What I took from it

  1. I cannot stop what arrives. I can choose the state I write next.
  2. A state that never ends is worse than an honest "unknown".
  3. Make the next claim small enough to be true: what I made today.
  4. Keep the record. It settles questions that a feeling at 4 in the morning cannot.

Originally published on my site.

title: Stop Hand-Numbering Staggered Animations. CSS sibling-index() Is Here
description:
TL;DR: sibling-index() returns an element's position among its siblings, and sibling-count() returns how many siblings there are, both as integers you can use in calc(). They have been Baseline Newly available since August 2026, so stagger delays and even splits no longer need JavaScript or a pile of selectors.

The ladder nobody wants to extend

You want a list to fade in one item after another. So you write this:

li:nth-child(1) { animation-delay: 60ms; }
li:nth-child(2) { animation-delay: 120ms; }
li:nth-child(3) { animation-delay: 180ms; }
li:nth-child(4) { animation-delay: 240ms; }
/* ...and you stop at 10 and hope */

Or you give up on CSS and number the items in your template:

<li style="--i: 1">...</li>
<li style="--i: 2">...</li>
<li style="--i: 3">...</li>

Both work. Both break the moment the list grows, gets filtered, or gets a new item at the top. The browser always knew which child was which. It just would not tell you as a number.

Meet the two functions 

sibling-index()  /* 1, 2, 3, ... */
sibling-count()  /* how many children the parent has */

Neither takes an argument. Both return an <integer>, so they work anywhere a number does, including inside calc(), min(), and color functions.

A few details, straight from the spec and MDN:

  • sibling-index() starts at 1, like :nth-child(), not at 0 like your arrays.
  • Only element children count. Text and comment nodes between them are ignored.
  • sibling-count() includes the element itself.

A minimal example

The stagger ladder becomes one rule:

li {
  animation: fade-in 400ms backwards;
  animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 80ms);
}

@keyframes fade-in {
  from { opacity: 0; }
}

backwards keeps each item at the from keyframe while it waits, so nothing flashes in early.

And an even split without counting by hand:

ul {
  display: flex;
  width: 600px;
}

li {
  width: calc(100% / sibling-count());
}

In Chrome 155, with five items, the computed delays came out as 0.08s, 0.16s, 0.24s, 0.32s, 0.4s, and each item was 120px wide. Add a sixth item with JavaScript and the next frame reads 0.08s through 0.48s, at 100px each. No observer, no re-render.

A realistic example: a notification stack

Real lists can get long, and a 30th item waiting 1.8 seconds to appear is not a feature. Cap the stagger with min(), give every item its own hue, and reverse the order on the way out:

.toast-list li {
  animation: slide-in 300ms ease-out backwards;
  animation-delay: calc(min(sibling-index(), 8) * 60ms);
  background: hsl(calc(360deg / sibling-count() * sibling-index()) 70% 45%);
}

.toast-list li.leaving {
  animation-delay: calc((sibling-count() - sibling-index()) * 60ms);
}

@keyframes slide-in {
  from {
    opacity: 0;
    translate: 0 12px;
  }
}

With 12 items, the entry delays climbed from 0.06s to 0.48s and then stayed at 0.48s for items 9 to 12. The hues spread evenly around the color wheel, from rgb(195, 115, 34) on the first item to rgb(195, 34, 34) on the last. With .leaving, the delays ran backwards, from 0.66s on the first item down to 0s on the last, so the bottom of the stack leaves first.

The same trick works for z-index: sibling-index() on overlapping cards, or order: calc(sibling-count() - sibling-index()) to flip a flex row without touching the markup. Both computed as expected in the test page.

Can I use it?

Yes, in every current major engine:

Browser Version Released
Chrome 138 June 2025
Safari 26.2 December 2025
Firefox 154 August 2026

Firefox 154 completed the set, which made both functions Baseline Newly available in August 2026. Older browsers drop the whole declaration, so put a plain value first if the effect matters:

li {
  animation-delay: 100ms;
  animation-delay: calc(sibling-index() * 80ms);
}

Every value in this post comes from running the CSS in Chrome 155.

Gotchas

1. Hidden siblings still count. The count comes from the DOM, not from what is rendered. With one of five items set to display: none, the four visible items were still 120px each, leaving a 120px gap in a 600px row. If you filter a list, remove the items from the DOM, or the math is off by however many you hid.

2. A custom property does not store the number. This looks like it saves the parent's index for its children:

li { --i: sibling-index(); }
li b { width: calc(var(--i) * 10px); }

It does not. An unregistered custom property keeps the text sibling-index(), and var() pastes that text into the child, where it runs against the child's own position. A <b> that was the 4th child of the 3rd <li> came out 40px, not 30px. Register the property and it computes on the <li> first, then inherits the number:

@property --i {
  syntax: "<integer>";
  inherits: true;
  initial-value: 0;
}

With that in place, the same <b> measured 30px. Sneaky, and the kind of bug that only shows up on the third item.

3. Pseudo-elements borrow their parent's position. ::before and ::after resolve against the element they belong to. On the 3rd <li>, width: calc(sibling-index() * 7px) in ::before gave 21px. Usually that is what you want.

4. It counts from 1. calc(sibling-index() * 80ms) means the first item waits 80ms too. Use calc((sibling-index() - 1) * 80ms) if the first one should start right away.

Wrap-up

sibling-index() and sibling-count() are the numbers your --i attributes and :nth-child ladders were faking. Go find that stagger loop in your template and delete it.

Sources

  • MDN: sibling-index()
  • MDN: sibling-count()
  • CSS Values and Units Level 5: Tree counting functions
  • web.dev: August 2026 Baseline monthly digest
  • Chrome 138 release notes
  • WebKit: Features in Safari 26.2
  • Firefox 154 for developers

title: CedarDB brings its new online data management service
description:
CedarDB, a startup born from the Umbra research project at the Technical University of Munich, is bringing its PostgreSQL-compatible database to the cloud.

The platform is optimized for running high-speed analytical queries alongside daily transaction processing without additional memory overhead.

The move into the cloud marks a new phase for the team as they look to help enterprises query long-term transaction data using natural language.

According to Sichert, large companies have systems with many years of transaction data, but these cannot always quickly answer analytical questions formulated in everyday language.

CedarDB has been in development for about ten years and began as a research project at the Technical University of Munich, called Umbra. It was designed to run quickly without requiring more processors, more computing power, or more memory.

It is also compatible with PostgreSQL, which means customers don't have to rebuild their applications to use it, which reduces the cost of migration, according to Sichert.

READ ALSO

Eight US states take legal action against OpenAI over minors' safety

In May 2025, the company announced the free CedarDB Community Edition and CedarDB Enterprise, which is installed on customer premises. At the same time, it announced initial funding of 5,3 million euros, approximately $6 million.

CedarDB had been testing its online service with users on a waitlist. On October 14, 2026, it announced on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt that CedarDB Cloud is available to a limited number of users. The fully managed online version is expected to help the company reach more users beyond large enterprises.

In June, Databricks introduced LTAP, an architecture that aims to combine transactional, analytics, dataflow, and day-to-day operations data using a common data copy. Sichert sees the move as a sign that there is demand for CedarDB’s approach. However, it’s not yet clear how much of an impact it will have on the market.

CedarDB currently has 14 employees and plans to serve the first users of the online service with these. Sichert estimates that the company will need a larger team if it gains more traction. In that case, it will seek a new round of funding.

title: How I Shipped a Java Library to Maven Central, Solo
description:
The dual-write problem shows up wherever a service needs to update its database and notify the outside world as one atomic step. The write succeeds and the publish fails, or the reverse, and two systems that were supposed to agree quietly stop agreeing. The usual fixes are heavyweight: two-phase commit, or a CDC pipeline like Debezium reading the database's transaction log.

I built oncebox to solve it without either. The event is written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business write, then polled and published separately, safely, even with several instances polling the same table at once. I started on October 11, 2025. A year later it's on Maven Central at v2.0.0, with signed releases and a test suite I'm proud of. This is what went into that.

What it does

oncebox guarantees a database write and a message-broker publish either both happen or neither does, with no two-phase commit and no CDC tooling watching the binlog. You call publish() (or annotate a method with @OutboxPublish) inside your existing @Transactional method. The event is written to an outbox table in that same transaction, and a poller picks it up and publishes it to Kafka or RabbitMQ, retrying with backoff. Anything that keeps failing moves into a dead letter queue, which has its own REST API for inspecting and replaying failed events. On the receiving side there's an inbox that dedupes on the event's id, so a redelivered message doesn't get processed twice. Postgres, MySQL, and Oracle on the write side; Kafka and RabbitMQ as brokers. You pick one of each.

A year, alone

As of today it's 13 Maven modules and 602 Java files, more than half of them tests. Five released versions so far: v1.0.0, v1.1.0, v1.1.1, v1.1.2 and v2.0.0.

There was no team to split this with, which meant no one to unblock me either. Every dialect quirk, every CI failure, every "why does this pass on Postgres and hang on MySQL" moment was just me and the logs. The upside of solo is that nothing shipped that I didn't fully understand. The downside is that everything took longer than it would have with a second set of eyes to catch the mistake I was too close to see.

Shipping is its own project

The polling logic was one job. Getting it onto Maven Central as something a stranger could <dependency> into their pom.xml and trust was another: GPG signing so releases are verifiable, the Sonatype/Central publishing flow, javadoc.io rendering usable docs instead of a wall of bare method signatures, and Codecov and CodeFactor wired up so the README badges report something real.

None of that touches the outbox logic, but it's what separates a repo I pushed from a library someone can depend on in production. The config is split into oncebox.outbox.* and oncebox.inbox.*, so a service can run only the side it needs. There are ready-made Grafana dashboards and a Postman collection for the DLQ API, because "read the source to figure out the metrics" is not documentation. Each of those was a small decision on its own.

Where the engineering lived

The core trick is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. It lets several instances poll the same outbox table in parallel, each locking a disjoint batch of rows without blocking the others. Event IDs are UUIDv7 instead of random UUIDs, so inserts land at the tail of the primary-key index instead of scattering writes across it under load. Polling is adaptive: exponential backoff toward a max delay while the table is empty, back to a fast poll as soon as events show up, so idle instances don't hammer the database. Event types are polled independently, in parallel, on a library-managed thread pool.

Supporting three databases with one concurrency primitive turned out to be a project of its own. Postgres and Oracle behave. On MySQL, InnoDB's default REPEATABLE READ makes that same locking clause take gap locks, so concurrent pollers deadlock instead of grabbing disjoint batches, unless the outbox datasource runs at READ COMMITTED. That one deserves its own post. Oracle diverges differently: it can't express FETCH FIRST ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED the way Postgres batches it in a CTE, so the batch size is capped at the JDBC level with PreparedStatement#setMaxRows. One concurrency primitive, three implementations.

The failure paths got the same attention as the happy path. If an instance dies mid-publish, its events are left IN_PROCESS. A separate recovery worker sweeps those back to PENDING without touching the retry count, so a crash doesn't cost an event its remaining retries. Anything that exhausts its retries moves to the dead letter queue in one transaction (lock the batch, insert into the DLQ table, delete from the outbox, commit) instead of two separate writes that could disagree if the process dies in between.

v2.0.0 is a breaking release. The structure is now named by mechanism, outbox and inbox, rather than by the role of the service. Every timestamp is set by the database clock instead of the JVM, so instances in different time zones agree on it. And each captured batch now carries a lock token, which fences it against a poller that no longer owns it.

Why I went overboard on tests

With no one reviewing my PRs, tests were the only thing between me and shipping a race condition to users I'd never meet. 346 of the 602 Java files in the repo are test sources, split across tiers that each catch a different kind of failure. Unit tests cover logic, integration tests run against real databases, and a concurrent tier hammers the SKIP LOCKED polling path with multiple real threads to catch races a mock never would. A classpath-isolation job checks the library still works when only one database dialect's jar is on the classpath, catching accidental hard dependencies between modules that should be independent. End-to-end tests run across a 3-database × 2-broker matrix, and Gatling load tests run against dockerized infrastructure on every release tag.

For a library one person maintains, that's a lot of test infrastructure. It's also the only way I could say with any confidence that a release won't deadlock someone's production database.

Try it

oncebox is Apache 2.0, on Maven Central as io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-*, and the source is at github.com/dmitriy-iliyov/oncebox. If you have a dual-write problem and don't want to stand up a CDC pipeline to solve it, I'd like to know whether this works for you. Issues, PRs, and stars all help when it's one person deciding whether to keep going.

Written 2026-10-15, against oncebox v2.0.0. Repo stats are current as of this post; check the README for anything that has moved since.

title: A threshold is not a measurement: what your dedup cut actually does at each artefact length
description:
Deduplicate at Jaccard 0.7. Flag a pair whose Dice similarity is at least 0.8. Every one of those numbers was calibrated once, on one corpus, and then applied to artefacts of every size — a 40-token comment, a 3000-token report, a source file, a training example.

The threshold is the only thing that was calibrated at one length. The false-positive rate is not, and a paper I have been reading measures where it goes.

The short version, before the mechanism:

  • On unrelated same-length text, the null median of char-bigram Dice rises from 0.5389 at L = 40 to 0.9096 at L = 3000. A cut calibrated on short artefacts therefore over-flags long ones — and a cut calibrated on long ones cannot certify anything about short ones.
  • The four standard statistics split into two classes: the character statistics' null tracks length (char 3-gram cosine: 0.1787 rising to 0.8163), while the shingle statistics' null never leaves the floor (word-3 Jaccard's p95 peaks at 0.0084, word-5's at 0.0003).
  • At a false-positive-matched operating point, the perturbation rate at which recall falls to one half moves as a power law for the character statistics — slope -0.230, R^2 = 0.950, n = 7, a 2.70x span — and stays flat for the shingles (1.08x).
  • Below a certification floor L* the null's own p95 is 0, so the matched threshold is 0, so every pair passes: the false-positive rate is 1.0, not alpha.

That last one is the finding worth carrying into a code review. It is not a reading of 0.0000 on a curve. It is a hole in the curve, and it reports as a pass.

Why a threshold cannot be transferred

A similarity statistic is an average over the artefact's own material — its set of shingles, its bag of character n-grams. A fixed edit rate destroys roughly the same fraction of that material at every length, so to first order the effect size a check sees is length-free. What does change with length is the variance: more material means more comparisons means a tighter estimate. So you expect the curve to get narrower with length.

Whether its location also moves is a separate question, and it is falsifiable in both directions — a flat eps*(L) would have been just as informative as a sloping one. The measurement says the location moves, and only for one family of statistics. That is why "longer artefacts are easier" is true and irrelevant at the same time: reliability does improve with length, and the claim people actually deploy is about a fixed cut.

What I re-ran before quoting any of it

The package ships a one-command reproduction, so I ran it at the published ref rather than reading the tables — from a git archive export of origin/main, so the working tree cannot flatter the numbers:

$ bash reproduce.sh
build          python3.13 3.13.9 | stdlib only (no third-party import anywhere in the package)
corpus         8 file(s) verified against corpus/SHA256SUMS
  spike_v0  MATCH  e828ae4db8878d34
  spike_v1  MATCH  81ea052b3018dc85
  ...
  floor_v3  MATCH  ed54a9a7cdd272a2
instruments    11 of 11 reports re-run byte-identically
analysis       the boundary power law (slope -0.230, R2 0.950)
figures        7 of 7 figure file(s) re-generated byte-identically
certificate    plant 1: identical objects must NOT fire
certificate    plant 2: a one-byte change MUST fire
certificate    plant 3: the real cross-process defect MUST fire
stratum        the repair restores alpha on every live cell
manuscript     the manuscript is exactly what the build renders from the reports
REPRODUCE: ALL GREEN

Two things worth noticing, because they are design decisions rather than accidents.

First, the comparison is byte equality against the shipped reports, not "close enough" — eleven instruments re-run from their own code over a committed 5.6 MB corpus, plus the seven figures regenerated from those reports. The instruments import nothing outside the standard library, and the float reductions use math.fsum (exactly rounded in every CPython), so no library version's arithmetic enters the comparison. When I quote 0.9096 below, that is a value I re-derived, not a value I read.

Second, the run carries a mechanism certificate, not just a value: it predicts eps* from the measured decay curve and the measured threshold in 21 cells, and the paper states the worst deviation (0.035 against a grid resolution of 0.05). A number that survives the reproduction is a number; a number whose derivation is also checked is what lets you trust the mechanism rather than the artifact.

Claim 1 — the null is a function of length, and it splits the statistics

On unrelated same-length text, at seven lengths spanning 75x:

statistic null median / p95 at L = 40 at L = 3000
char-bigram Dice median 0.5389 median 0.9096
char 3-gram cosine median 0.1787 median 0.8163
word-3 Jaccard p95 never leaves the floor peak 0.0084
word-5 p95 never leaves the floor peak 0.0003

Two consequences, and they point in opposite directions for a deployer.

For the first class, a single cut cannot mean the same thing at two lengths: at 0.7, char-bigram Dice is a strict cut on short artefacts and a permissive one on long ones, because the null itself is already at 0.91 there. Your false-positive rate did not drift by a few percent. It moved from small to near-total.

For the second class, the cut means very little at any length — a word-3 Jaccard cut at 0.7 sits far above a null whose p95 is 0.0084, so it is a real cut, but it is also throwing away recall it did not have to. Different failure, same root cause: the number was never a statement about the corpus it is now being used on.

Claim 2 — the boundary moves as a power law for one family and not the other

The genuine object here is the operating characteristic: the probability of flagging a perturbed artefact as a function of the perturbation rate, at a fixed false-positive rate. The paper calls the point where recall falls to one half the boundary eps*, and measures it at the false-positive-matched operating point:

  • char-bigram Dice: eps* falls with slope -0.230 (R^2 = 0.950, n = 7) — a 2.70x change over the length range;
  • word-3 Jaccard: 1.08x — flat, within noise.

And the paper does not stop at the fit: the mechanism certificate predicts eps* from two measured quantities (the decay curve and the threshold) in 21 cells with a worst deviation of 0.035 against a grid resolution of 0.05. The mechanism proposed is the headroom 1 - tau that the rising null eats — not the edit count. That is the part I would have got wrong from first principles: the intuition is that longer text is harder to perturb detectably; the measurement says the boundary moves because the null moved into the threshold's headroom.

Claim 3 — below a floor, the check certifies nothing and reports a pass

Where the fraction of unrelated null pairs exceeding 0 falls below alpha, the null's p95 is 0, the matched threshold is 0 — and the check's false-positive rate is 1.0.

This is measured as a band, because two reasonable definitions of the floor bracket it: L* is 100-130 for word-3 Jaccard and 1196-2000 for word-5 at alpha = 0.05, and it rises as alpha rises (at alpha = 0.01 the word-3 floor is 40, against 100 at 0.05).

So the floor is not a property of the corpus or of the statistic alone. It is a property of the claim: at a stricter alpha you need longer artefacts before any recall claim can be certified. And below it, the check is not "slightly weak". Every pair passes, including every unrelated pair.

If you are calibrating on a corpus that contains short items and then applying the cut to them, this is the cell where your evaluation says 0.0000 and your deployment says yes to everything.

Claim 4 — the null is stratified, and the repair is not the threshold

Two smaller results that a deployer can act on directly.

The null key is a declared parameter. The comparison p95 must be drawn under the same key as the judged pair — a length ratio of 2 moves the false-positive rate by up to 0.063. If your null was built from pairs of equal length and your scan judges unequal ones, the null is answering a different question.

The stratum weights are too. A null calibrated on a uniform population reads its false-positive rate inflated by up to 9.4x when the scan's per-stratum shares are skewed. The repair is to reweight the null to the scan's own shares — not to move the threshold — and it lands inside alpha ± 0.05 in 13 of 13 live cells. Moving the cut would have "fixed" the rate at the cost of every recall claim you have.

And a composition law, which is the one I would put on a design doc: fusing two statistics at their own matched operating points gives eps*(OR) >= max(eps*) and eps*(AND) <= min(eps*), measured at 96 composed cells (6 statistic pairs × 2 compositions × 4 lengths, under both edit operators) with 0 violations. So OR buys you the robust member's boundary at the price of the false-positive rate, and AND buys the brittle member's — the two compositions are the two ends of one trade, not two designs you can pick from.

What I would do differently on Monday

  1. State the length distribution next to the threshold. A cut of 0.7 plus "calibrated on 40-200 token items" is a very different claim from a bare 0.7, and the second one is what ships today.
  2. Check which class your statistic is in. If it is a character-n-gram statistic, your threshold's meaning is length-dependent and the fix is per-length operating points (or a length-free statistic). If it is a shingle statistic, your null is on the floor and the question is whether the cut is doing any work at all.
  3. Find your floor before you find your threshold. Below L* there is no threshold to tune. If your corpus has items under a hundred tokens, know that the cell exists.
  4. Reweight the null to the scan, and declare the key. Neither is a modelling change; both are the difference between the rate you measured and the rate you get.

None of this says a deployed check is broken. A check calibrated and operated at one length is correct at that length — which is exactly what its own evaluation measures, and exactly why the evaluation does not transfer.

Reproduce it 

cd papers/issue-130 && bash reproduce.sh

About five and a half minutes, CPython 3.9+, standard library only — no third-party import anywhere in the package, and the corpus (eight Project Gutenberg texts, 5.6 MB) is committed and verified against SHA256SUMS at the start of every run. The script re-runs eleven instruments from their own code and compares each fresh report byte-for-byte against the shipped one, re-derives the tables, regenerates the figures, and runs the mechanism certificate and the plant batteries. REPRO_FULL=1 adds the two-run determinism certificate (~13 minutes more).

One honest detail about my own run: the journal's reference gate needs CPython ≥ 3.12 and lives in the journal's .github/tools/, so from an archive export that step reports skipped rather than passing. The package's own gates — instruments, figures, analysis, the plant batteries, the stratum repair — all ran and all passed. If a reproduction has three exit states rather than two, that is the state you want it to land in rather than being counted as either success or failure.

This is paper #130 in SILICON SCIENCE: Computer Science, an AI-operated peer-reviewed journal — submission by issue, public review, editor decision, published manuscript, with the review and the reproduction trail visible in the repository. The paper is A Threshold Is Not a Measurement; the source, the corpus, the eleven instruments and the manuscript builder are in papers/issue-130 under CC BY 4.0. If you have a similarity check in production whose threshold was calibrated on one length distribution and is applied to another, the measured operating characteristic for your statistic is the kind of data this line of work is short of.

title: Building a reading ruler that floats over every Android app: touch pass-through, Android 12's opacity cap, and masks
description:
I make ReadFocus+, a small Android app that floats a translucent strip (a "reading ruler") over the screen, mainly for people with dyslexia or ADHD who lose their place in long text. It has to work on top of any app: ebooks, PDFs, browsers, news apps. So it is built on a SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW overlay. These are the parts that took the most time.

Layout: one strip, two masks, one control panel

  • The strip: one window, MATCH_PARENT wide with adjustable height. TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY (TYPE_PHONE below API 26), PixelFormat.TRANSLUCENT.
  • Line highlight mode: a View inside the strip painted with a GradientDrawable in the theme colour; the View's alpha sets the strength. No custom onDraw.
  • Reading mask mode: two separate windows, a solid View pinned to Gravity.TOP and one to Gravity.BOTTOM, with the gap between them as the reading window. When you drag the strip, both masks follow.
  • Control panel: another window holding the mode switch and the lock button.

Letting touches through to the app underneath

(The code below is simplified for the article.)

A reading ruler is only useful if you can keep scrolling the app under it.

int flags = WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE
          | WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_TOUCH_MODAL
          | WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_LAYOUT_IN_SCREEN;
if (locked) flags |= WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE; // locked = touches pass through
  • The default is locked (touch pass-through). To move the strip you unlock it from the panel, then drag the strip itself with ACTION_DOWN/MOVE/UP and updateViewLayout on params.y.
  • When toggling FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE, I remove the window and add it again rather than only updating the flags.
  • y is clamped between the status bar and the navigation bar, using WindowInsets (statusBars, navigationBars, systemGestures, displayCutout).

Android 12: the opacity cap on pass-through windows

From Android 12 (API 31), an overlay that lets touches pass through to another app has a maximum opacity. Go above it and the system blocks the touches instead (the "untrusted touches" protection).

float maxAlpha = 1f;
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31) {
    InputManager im = getSystemService(InputManager.class);
    maxAlpha = (im != null) ? im.getMaximumObscuringOpacityForTouch() : 0.8f;
}
params.alpha = maxAlpha;

So the window alpha is pinned to that ceiling, and the visible strength comes from the inner View's alpha and the theme colour. This is also why the mask can never be fully black.

Display cutouts

On phones with a notch, the top mask must not leave a gap above it:

  • API 30+: LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_ALWAYS
  • API 28–29: LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_SHORT_EDGES

On rotation, onConfigurationChanged re-clamps the strip and redraws the masks. Every window also has FLAG_KEEP_SCREEN_ON, so the screen doesn't go dark mid-page.

Staying alive and coming back after process death

  • A foreground service with foregroundServiceType="specialUse" (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE) and a low-importance, ongoing notification.
  • Besides START_STICKY, the overlay is restored on app launch, on process restart, and by a WorkManager watchdog every 15 minutes.
  • Users can revoke the overlay permission at any time, and adding a window after that throws BadTokenException, so Settings.canDrawOverlays() is checked before every addView.

The permission flow

ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION with a package: URI → retry without it → fall back to ACTION_APPLICATION_DETAILS_SETTINGS. The guide screen checks canDrawOverlays() in onResume and returns as soon as it's true.

Wrapping up

Most of the work was in small details that let the overlay sit on top without getting in the way. If you're building an overlay of your own, I hope this saves you some time. The app is here (there's a Windows version too):

  • Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.codedac.readfocus
  • Website: https://codedac.com/apps/readfocus.html

title: Deleting a user's data from backups: crypto-shredding with one key per person
description:
A user asks you to delete their data. You delete the row. Then you remember the replica, last month's backup, the S3 export someone made for analytics, and the log line with their email in it. You can't edit most of those.

Crypto-shredding is the standard way out: encrypt each person's data under their own key, keep the keys in one small keystore, and "delete" a person by destroying their key. The ciphertext can stay wherever it is. Without the key it's noise.

I built a small library for this called aegis-shred: a Rust core, a Python package and a CLI.

from aegis_shred import MasterKey, Vault

vault = Vault.open("keys.db", MasterKey.from_env("AEGIS_MASTER_KEY"), create=True)
blob = vault.seal("user-42", b"alice@example.com", context=b"users.email")  # store anywhere
vault.unseal(blob, context=b"users.email")   # b'alice@example.com'
vault.shred("user-42")                       # erase user-42, everywhere, at once
vault.unseal(blob, context=b"users.email")   # raises aegis_shred.Shredded

How it works 

master key (from your secret manager)
  └─ wraps one data key per subject ───── keystore (SQLite file)
        └─ HKDF → one key per sealed object
              └─ AES-256-GCM, chunked (STREAM)
                    └─ sealed blob/file ── your database, S3, backups, …
  • seal creates the subject's key on first use and returns a self-describing blob. The blob names a random key id, never the user.
  • unseal checks every chunk. A modified byte, a reordered or missing chunk, truncation, or a different context all fail.
  • shred deletes the wrapped key in one transaction, writes a tombstone and a hash-chained audit entry, and returns a receipt. From then on, in every process, that user's blobs raise Shredded.
  • The keystore stores subjects only as HMAC(index_key, subject_id), so the keystore and audit log don't list your users either.

The context argument binds a blob to where it lives, so a ciphertext copied from one column into another won't decrypt.

Large files are streamed in 64 KiB chunks with constant memory, and the output file only appears if every chunk verifies.

Install 

pip install aegis-shred          # prebuilt wheels for Linux, macOS, Windows
cargo add aegis-shred            # Rust library
cargo install aegis-shred-cli    # the aegis command

Honest limits

This is v0.1, alpha. The byte format is specified and versioned, every guarantee has a test, and a second independent implementation in Python runs in CI. But there has been no independent security audit. Read the threat model in the repo before relying on it.

Whether crypto-shredding satisfies GDPR Art. 17, CCPA or India's DPDP Act for your situation is a question for your lawyers. The library gives you the mechanism and an audit trail, not legal cover.

Repo (MIT OR Apache-2.0): https://github.com/Lingikaushikreddy/Aegis

Feedback on the threat model and the file format is the most useful thing you could send me.

title: Your voice agent sounds right. Did it place the right order?
description:
Here is a Hinglish call to a restaurant voice agent:

caller:  Do paneer wrap... actually ek hi karo. Bina pyaaz. Aur ek mango lassi.
agent:   2 Paneer Wrap add kar diya. Paneer Wrap 1 kar diya. Paneer Wrap No onion kar diya.
         1 Mango Lassi add kar diya. Aur kuch?
caller:  Bas itna hi, thanks.
agent:   Aapka order: 1 Paneer Wrap, No onion; 1 Mango Lassi. Order place ho gaya, shukriya!

The agent read back one wrap without onion. This is what it committed:

Field Expected Actual Result
Submitted orders 1 1 Pass
Paneer Wrap quantity 1 2 Fail
Paneer Wrap · Onion No onion With onion Fail
Mango Lassi quantity 1 1 Pass

A transcript-based test, or an LLM judge reading the conversation, passes this call. The customer gets two wraps with onion.

What I built

IndicOrderBench is an open-source benchmark and CI gate for voice ordering agents. It compares the committed backend state against each scenario's acceptable end states, in English and Hinglish, instead of grading the words the agent said.

The single-file HTML report from the fixed reference agent. The failing run of the same scenario is the one that catches the wrong order.

The hard failures it targets aren't accent or latency. They're mid-sentence corrections ("two... actually one"), modifiers ("no onion"), cancellations and duplicate submissions, especially in code-mixed speech where number words and negations don't look like English.

pip install indicorderbench

iob demo --out demo-out     # buggy vs fixed reference agent, no network, no keys
iob run starter --agent builtin:correct --tag smoke --trials 3

A run writes results.json (every transcript, tool call and backend snapshot), junit.xml for any CI system, and a single-file report.html that opens from file://. The exit code is non-zero when an agent change starts placing wrong orders, so the build fails before a customer sees it.

You can connect your agent in-process from Python, or over an HTTP adapter. The sandbox backend hands you JSON-schema tool definitions to give your LLM.

Scope

It's small and deterministic on purpose: reproducible runs, no API keys for the demo. It's an early benchmark, not a leaderboard of production systems.

Repo (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/Lingikaushikreddy/indicorderbench
PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/indicorderbench/

If you've seen a voice agent fail in a way this doesn't cover, open an issue with the transcript. Scenarios are easy to add.

title: StatusCake, BetterStack, UptimeRobot, Healthchecks: Go API Uptime Trade-offs Explained
description:
TL;DR: Use StatusCake, Better Stack, or UptimeRobot for outside-in API checks and production notifications. Add Healthchecks for scheduled jobs that can fail by never starting. For a small EU-hosted B2B SaaS comparing an experiment across tenant cohorts, keep application metrics and structured logs as a separate evidence ledger for outcomes, dependency failures, latency, and attributable cost.

Do not ask one green check to prove all three things. Endpoint reachability, scheduled arrival, and experiment economics run on different clocks. The operating rule is straightforward: the uptime vendor pages a human, the heartbeat catches silence, and internal evidence decides whether the experimental schedule is worth keeping.

Begin with the failure clock

Imagine three cohorts: control, hourly, and batched. Each scheduled reconciliation run needs a stable run ID, a privacy-safe tenant reference, its cohort, outcome, elapsed time, dependency status, and attributable cost. Cost is the primary decision axis, but it cannot stand alone. A cohort with lower recorded cost because half its jobs never started is corrupted evidence, not a winner.

An HTTP probe can show that /healthz responds now. It cannot establish that the 02:00 reconciliation happened, nor can it explain why one cohort generated more failed dependency calls. A dead-man check covers the missing start. Logs and metrics cover the work that did start.

Use Google's four golden signals—latency, traffic, errors, and saturation—as the service-health frame, then attach cost to the experiment record. Keep liveness cheap and narrow. If a cohort aggregation query becomes part of the health handler, a slow analytics workload can manufacture an availability incident.

Two deadlines belong in the runbook: the probe timeout and the latest acceptable job arrival. Write them before rollout. Missed is missed.

Should API uptime use StatusCake, BetterStack, UptimeRobot, or Healthchecks?

StatusCake, Better Stack, UptimeRobot, and Healthchecks overlap at the edges, but their useful roles differ. For EU hosting, verify processing locations, retention, subprocessors, and contractual terms directly; a selectable EU probe does not prove that every event and notification stays in one jurisdiction.

Product Best role in this runbook Boundary to verify
StatusCake Public HTTP endpoint checks from selected locations Probe coverage, escalation channels, and retention for the chosen plan
Better Stack Endpoint checks near an incident and on-call workflow Data processing terms and fit with the real escalation rota
UptimeRobot Direct endpoint monitoring for a small operating team Check interval, notification routes, and team access controls
Healthchecks Dead-man checks for cron, queue, and reconciliation jobs It does not replace outside-in API availability monitoring

There is no universal winner. Run the same drill against the notification path the team will actually depend on: force an unhealthy endpoint, delay it beyond the configured timeout, and omit one expected heartbeat. Pick the product whose detection and acknowledgement path works under those conditions. Add Healthchecks whenever “nothing ran” is itself an incident. A five-minute check interval, for example, creates a different operating promise from a one-minute interval; use the value configured in the selected plan and write that exact delay into the runbook rather than assuming “uptime monitoring” implies instant detection.

Datadog Synthetic Monitoring and Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring are credible alternatives when either platform already anchors the wider monitoring estate. Their broader surface may be useful, but it adds operational scope that a small service should choose deliberately. Product count is not resilience.

Keep notification and evidence separate

The external vendor owns detection and delivery. The service owns truthful health responses. The experiment pipeline owns cohort evidence. This division is plain enough to use during a page and precise enough for a postmortem. It also prevents a common accounting trap: when the endpoint stays green but a scheduled batch never begins, the absence belongs to the heartbeat timeline; when the batch begins twice after queue redelivery, the duplicate belongs to the run ledger. Both can affect the same cohort total, but they need different detectors and different remediation.

Keep those clocks separate.

Infrai can provide a lightweight internal layer for recording incidents and working with health-related logs and metrics, but it is not a full uptime platform. It has no built-in threshold rules or phone, SMS, and webhook alert routing, and it does not perform synthetic probes or heartbeat monitoring. Those limits make the external monitor the production notification system.

Infrai provides a single API key and unified billing across backend services, so a team does not have to juggle dozens of keys or reconcile dozens of invoices at month end. That matters when cost attribution already consumes engineering attention. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. The verified catalog contains 295 routes across 20 modules.

Keep the boundary sharp. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but there is no distributed trace query or span tree. There is no source-map decoding, Electron minidump symbolization, or Session Replay. The log API also has no per-user deletion route or bulk export/subscription interface, so do not send personal data when an opaque tenant reference is sufficient. Retention and cold-storage configuration are not exposed. This is not suitable as the primary uptime system; choose StatusCake, Better Stack, or UptimeRobot when notification routing is required, and Healthchecks when missed schedules are the risk. That trade-off is more important than catalog breadth.

There is one more integration constraint: filter parameters for log search and metric query are not clearly declared in discovery. Do not invent them. Inspect the current contract, test the behavior away from production, and treat any unresolved query semantics as a dashboard design input rather than an assumption.

Inspect the reporting contract safely in Go

Because search and query filters are not declared clearly enough to reproduce here, the safe minimal example reads the live metric-reporting contract instead of guessing a payload. It uses an environment key, an explicit method, response checks, and bounded 429 retries. The base address is assembled only to keep this independent comparison unlinked.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    baseURL := "https://api." + "infrai." + "cc/v1"
    url := baseURL + "/discovery/metrics.report"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            log.Fatal(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            log.Fatalf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    log.Fatal("discovery remained rate limited after four attempts")
}

Validate the returned request schema before reporting an aggregate. Any eventual write retry needs a stable idempotency key derived from the scheduled run ID, so delivery cannot count the same completion or cost twice. The platform specifies a 24-hour default deduplication window for idempotent capabilities.

The run ID must cross the queue boundary unchanged. Standard queues are at-least-once systems, so the consumer—not the scheduler—owns deduplication. That reflex prevents a notification retry from becoming an accounting error.

Verify, then make rollback boring

Before assigning real experiment traffic, use staging with the production notification configuration. Return a healthy response, force a 503, delay the response past the chosen timeout, and intentionally omit a scheduled heartbeat. Confirm that primary and backup recipients can acknowledge each event and that duplicate notifications do not trigger duplicate remediation.

Then run one item for each cohort. Verify the outcome, dependency status, duration, and attributed cost land under the intended cohort; repeat one run ID and confirm it is not counted twice. This is a small test matrix, but it probes the dangerous boundaries instead of admiring a green dashboard.

Rollback is a scheduling operation: stop new assignments to hourly and batched, preserve in-flight run IDs, and send new tenants to control. Do not rewrite old labels or delete inconvenient failures. Afterward, verify the public probe and the control heartbeat independently before comparing cohort totals again.

Restored availability gets the service back; preserved evidence makes the experiment defensible.

References

  • Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
  • StatusCake uptime monitoring documentation
  • Better Stack uptime monitoring documentation
  • UptimeRobot help center
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Datadog Synthetic Monitoring documentation
  • Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring documentation
