title: Architectural Breakdown: We Rendered a HQ Demo Video on a Free Farm Run by Strangers
description:
![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+We+Rendered+a+HQ+Demo+Video+on+round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

# We Rendered a 4K Demo Video on a Free Farm Run by Strangers. Here's the Architecture That Stopped It from Melting Down at 3 AM

The ticket hit at 2:17 AM on a Tuesday. Client wanted a 90‑second 4K demo video. We had a GitHub repo, three unused API keys, and thirty‑seven stranger nodes with 8 GB RAM and zero SLA. I still see the stack trace when I close my eyes.

Here is what happens when you try to render a film on infrastructure you don’t own, don’t control, and absolutely should not trust, and how we patched the holes that nearly cost us the deliverable.

---

## The Night Everything Broke

By hour three, three catastrophes collided: OOM kills on edge nodes, event‑loop stalls hitting twelve seconds during synchronous disk writes, and a lock‑contention storm on the shared output file that dropped throughput to four frames per minute. The coordinator thought we were fine because the chunk tracker was counting optimistic ACKs that never touched durable storage.

Node 12 dropped mid‑chunk. We lost frames 1,847 through 2,103. No checkpoint. No retry. The dispatcher was measuring success flags, not actual bytes written.

That is when I learned the hard way: a distributed render farm without backpressure is just a more expensive way to crash your laptop.

---

## Root‑Cause Breakdown

| Symptom | Root Cause |
|---------|-----------|
| Random OOM kills on nodes | Unbounded per‑frame texture cache, no memory semaphore |
| Event‑loop stalls over 5 seconds | Synchronous I/O blocking the asyncio event loop |
| Lock contention on output files | Global threading.Lock serializing all worker writes |
| Missing frames after node dropout | No idempotent chunk tracking or resumable uploads |
| Rate‑limit errors from cloud storage | Unthrottled multipart uploads from dozens of parallel workers |
| CPU starvation on weak nodes | Hardcoded 4‑core assumption on 2‑core machines |

Every assumption about the free farm was a liability. We fixed them all.

---

## The Architecture: Back‑Pressure‑Driven, Not Hope‑Driven

+-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+
| Coordinator |<-------> | Dispatcher |<-------> | Worker Pool |
| (SQLite WAL) | HTTP | (RingBuffer) | HTTP | (FFmpeg/Blender) |
+-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+
^ ^ ^
| | |
Chunk bookkeeping Backpressure enforcement Memory semaphore gating
Checksum verification Rate limiter Multipart uploader
Watchdog timer Chunk reassignment Status reporting


### Coordinator: Single Source of Truth

SQLite with WAL mode. Every chunk gets a UUID, a status transition log, and a checksum. Nothing lives in memory that is not also on disk. If the coordinator dies, the next restart replays the WAL and picks up exactly where it left off.

The dispatcher pulls from a `collections.deque(maxlen=512)`. Queue fills → new chunks wait. No memory spikes. No queue explosions. This is the kind of boring, deterministic design that ShipMVP’s rapid development stack ships in production builds, no magic, just plumbing that works.

### Dispatcher: The Traffic Cop

Rate limiting via `asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS=12)`. Our S3 bucket started choking at ~15 simultaneous multipart uploads. Each dispatch triggers a checksum verification before handing off to a worker.

Workers heartbeat every 30 seconds. Three missed heartbeats → chunks marked `PENDING_RETRY` and re‑dispatched. Lost nothing.

---

## Production Code: The Critical Path


python
import asyncio
import hashlib
import os
import sqlite3
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional
import aiohttp

MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH = 512
HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT = 90
MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS = 12
CHUNK_SIZE_FRAMES = 30
MEM_PER_CHUNK_MB = 256
NODE_RAM_MB = 8192

max_chunks_per_node = (NODE_RAM_MB * 0.7) // MEM_PER_CHUNK_MB # 22 max
MEMORY_SEMAPHORE = asyncio.Semaphore(max_chunks_per_node)

chunk_queue: deque = deque(maxlen=MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH)
worker_semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_CONCURRENT_UPLOADS)
active_workers: dict = {}
retry_backoff = 0.5

class ChunkTracker:
"""Idempotent chunk state with checksum verification and WAL durability."""

def _init_db(self):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(self.db_path, check_same_thread=False)
    conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
    conn.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS chunk_status (
            chunk_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            worker_id TEXT,
            status TEXT DEFAULT 'PENDING',
            frame_start INTEGER,
            frame_end INTEGER,
            checksum TEXT,
            started_at REAL,
            completed_at REAL,
            failed_at REAL,
            retry_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0
        )
    """)
    conn.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS heartbeats (
            worker_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            last_seen REAL
        )
    """)
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

async def _db_execute(self, sql: str, params: tuple = ()) -> list:
    async with self._lock:
        loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
        return await loop.run_in_executor(
            None,
            lambda: sqlite3.connect(self.db_path).execute(sql, params).fetchall()
        )

async def mark_started(self, chunk_id: str, worker_id: str) -> None:
    async with self._lock:
        await self._db_execute(
            "INSERT INTO chunk_status (chunk_id, worker_id, status, started_at, retry_count) "
            "VALUES (?, ?, 'IN_FLIGHT', strftime('%s','now'), "
            "COALESCE((SELECT retry_count FROM chunk_status WHERE chunk_id=?), 0)) "
            "ON CONFLICT(chunk_id) DO UPDATE SET status='IN_FLIGHT', worker_id=?, "
            "started_at=strftime('%s','now') WHERE chunk_id=?",
            (chunk_id, worker_id, chunk_id, worker_id, chunk_id)
        )

async def mark_completed(self, chunk_id: str, checksum: str) -> bool:
    async with self._lock:
        row = await self._db_execute(
            "SELECT status FROM chunk_status WHERE chunk_id=?", (chunk_id,)
        )
        if row and row[0][0] == "COMPLETED":
            return False
        await self._db_execute(
            "UPDATE chunk_status SET status='COMPLETED', checksum=?, "
            "completed_at=strftime('%s','now') WHERE chunk_id=?",
            (checksum, chunk_id)
        )
        return True

async def mark_failed(self, chunk_id: str) -> None:
    async with self._lock:
        await self._db_execute(
            "UPDATE chunk_status SET status='PENDING_RETRY', failed_at=strftime('%s','now'), "
            "retry_count=retry_count+1 WHERE chunk_id=? AND status='IN_FLIGHT'",
            (chunk_id,)
        )

async def get_pending_chunks(self, limit: int = 50) -> list:
    async with self._lock:
        return await self._db_execute(
            "SELECT chunk_id, frame_start, frame_end FROM chunk_status "
            "WHERE status IN ('PENDING','PENDING_RETRY') ORDER BY created_at LIMIT ?",
            (limit,)
        )

async def escalate_if_over_retry(self, chunk_id: str) -> bool:
    row = await self._db_execute(
        "SELECT retry_count FROM chunk_status WHERE chunk_id=?", (chunk_id,)
    )
    return row and row[0][0] >= 3


### Watchdog: Detecting Dead Nodes Before Data Loss


python
async def watchdog(task_queue: asyncio.Queue, tracker: ChunkTracker):
while True:
await asyncio.sleep(15)
now = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()
dead_workers = [
wid for wid, last in active_workers.items()
if now - last > HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT
]
for wid in dead_workers:
del active_workers[wid]
rows = await tracker._db_execute(
"SELECT chunk_id FROM chunk_status WHERE worker_id=? AND status='IN_FLIGHT'",
(wid,)
)
for (chunk_id,) in rows:
await tracker.mark_failed(chunk_id)
escaped = await tracker.escalate_if_over_retry(chunk_id)
if escaped:
print(f"[ALERT] Chunk {chunk_id} exceeded 3 retries")
task_queue.put_nowait(chunk_id)


### Worker: Bounded, Stateless, Idempotent


python
async def worker_task(worker_id: str, tracker: ChunkTracker, upload_queue: asyncio.Queue):
while True:
chunk_id = await asyncio.to_thread(upload_queue.get)

    async with MEMORY_SEMAPHORE:
        await tracker.mark_started(chunk_id, worker_id)
        active_workers[worker_id] = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()

        env = os.environ.copy()
        env["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "2"
        cmd = [
            "ffmpeg", "-y", "-i", f"frames_{chunk_id}.txt",
            "-frames:v", str(CHUNK_SIZE_FRAMES),
            "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", "-c:v", "libx264",
            "-preset", "fast", "-threads", "2",
            "-movflags", "+faststart", f"chunk_{chunk_id}.mp4"
        ]

        proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
            *cmd, env=env,
            stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
            stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE
        )
        stdout, stderr = await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=120)

        if proc.returncode != 0:
            await tracker.mark_failed(chunk_id)
            continue

        with open(f"chunk_{chunk_id}.mp4", "rb") as f:
            checksum = hashlib.md5(f.read()).hexdigest()

        completed = await tracker.mark_completed(chunk_id, checksum)
        if completed:
            print(f"[OK] {chunk_id} checksum={checksum}")
        else:
            print(f"[SKIP] {chunk_id} already completed (idempotent)")


---

## Hardware Profiling: What 8 GB RAM Actually Gives You

| Node Type | vCPUs | RAM | Measured FPS | Peak Memory | Stall Events |
|-----------|-------|-----|-------------|-------------|--------------|
| t2.micro clone | 1 | 4 GB | 2.1 | 3.8 GB | 47 |
| t3.small clone | 2 | 8 GB | 4.3 | 6.1 GB | 12 |
| c5.large clone | 2 | 4 GB | 3.8 | 3.9 GB | 31 |
| n1‑standard‑2 | 2 | 7.5 GB | 5.1 | 6.8 GB | 8 |
| Custom 4‑core | 4 | 8 GB | 6.2 | 7.4 GB | 3 |

The 2‑core 8 GB nodes were the sweet spot. More cores did not help; FFmpeg’s CPU‑bound rendering hit diminishing returns past 2 threads per chunk, and extra context switching killed tail latency. The 4‑core nodes looked great on paper but aggressive CPU sharing with other tenants caused unpredictable pauses that wrecked frame‑timing consistency.

We locked in `CHUNK_SIZE_FRAMES=30` with `MEM_PER_CHUNK_MB=256`. Stayed under 6 GB peak on the worst node. Render times between 8 and 14 seconds per chunk.

---

## The Multipart Upload That Saved Us

Resumable multipart uploads with per‑part checksums. Every worker streams directly to cloud storage in 5 MB parts. Each part gets an MD5 before upload. If a worker drops mid‑upload, the next one picks up from the last successful part boundary. No re‑rendering. No wasted cycles.

When Node 28 vanished during a 47‑minute upload window, we resumed from part 94 of 127. The client saw a green dot because we reported partial completion percentages, not binary success or failure.

---

## What We Learned the Hard Way

Three uncomfortable truths: the free farm would betray you, your monitoring would always be incomplete, and the first design would fail. We learned to measure actual bytes transferred instead of trusting optimistic progress bars. We learned to treat every node as temporary and stateless. We learned that backpressure is not a performance feature; it is the difference between graceful degradation and silent corruption.

The video rendered. 94 seconds of 4K. Zero missing frames. Two nodes died mid‑job and neither loss showed up. Total cost: $0.00. Engineering effort: ~180 person‑hours.

Worth it.

---

**Question for the comments:** What is the most painful distributed system failure you have debugged at 3 AM, and did you solve it by adding more observability or by removing entire components from the critical path?

title: Free MCP Server Hosting: What Zero Dollars Actually Gets You
description:
We build a cloud whose agents operate it over MCP, so we spend a lot of the week talking to servers we wrote. Every one of those servers is hosted, always-on, and billed by the hour. But before any tool of ours is hosted, it lives on a laptop, behind a tunnel, answering calls from an agent on the same desk. That stage is free, it is where everyone should start, and this post is about how much you can get done there before you pay anything.

The short version for anyone searching this exact question: yes, you can host an MCP server for free. Run it on a machine you already own, use the free tier of a managed platform, or use serverless if your tools keep no state. Each is genuinely free and each breaks in a way you can predict. We have hit all three breaks, from both sides: as the people hosting the tools, and as the platform that inherits them when they grow.

Path What it costs Where it breaks Who it suits
Your machine behind a tunnel $0 The machine sleeps, reboots, loses wifi; the tool is up only while you are Development and solo experiments
The free tier of a managed platform $0, the platform carries the idle hours One instance, a memory ceiling, sometimes a request cap A first real tool, before a teammate depends on it
Serverless, stateless tools only $0 per call and response No state and no held connections; most MCP servers do not qualify Pure call-and-return tools

The rest of this post is about where each of those breaks, because that is the part the table cannot tell you.

The tunnel stage, and why it ends

Your laptop can be an MCP server tonight. Start the process, put a tunnel in front of it, point your agent at the URL, and you have a hosted server for zero dollars. We still develop this way; nothing beats editing a tool and watching the agent pick up the change seconds later.

It ends the first time the tool is useful to someone who is not you. A tunnel only works while the machine is awake, and the machine is yours: it sleeps when you sleep, it reboots when an update lands, it loses the wifi exactly once, at the worst moment. A remote MCP server is only remote if it stays up. The lesson is not that tunnels are bad. It is that shared usefulness and shared uptime are the same requirement, and a laptop cannot provide either.

Free tiers are real, read the edges

The managed path costs nothing on a free tier, and we want to defend free tiers for a moment, because we run one. A free tier that carries one small always-on service costs the platform almost nothing and makes the platform useful enough that you stay. That is the whole trade, and it is a fair one.

What the edges look like, from our side of the fence: one instance, a memory ceiling, sometimes a request cap. One small MCP server is a lightweight process speaking HTTP, and it fits. What does not fit is the day two agents call at once, or the day your tool needs a database next to it and you start gluing vendors together for state that should live on the same platform.

If your tools keep no state at all, a serverless function is another zero-dollar route, and for a pure request-and-response tool it is a good one. Most MCP servers do not qualify: they hold connections open and remember things between calls, which fights the request-and-forget model. We tried the stateless-only shape ourselves and kept running back to a real process.

The math that hides under "free"

An always-on service, however small, is 730 metered hours a month. It answers twice a day and meters around the clock. Free tiers pay that slice for you because it is the cheapest loyalty program ever invented, and honestly, it works.

We wrote before about what an always-on VM actually costs once it is billed by the hour, and the punchline was a customer spending 84% of a real bill on one VM that never slept. Scale-to-zero exists because of stories like that. Free tiers are the same instinct pointing the other direction: the platform carries the idle hours so your first tool costs nothing. Neither model is charity. Both are fine, as long as you know which side of the meter you are standing on.

The day to stop being free

It is not a resource threshold, it is a trust threshold. You will notice one of these three things: you check that the server is up before you check your email, because a teammate's agent depends on it now. A workflow treats its downtime as an incident. Or a second process appears because one instance became a queue.

Any one of those means the tool has outgrown the free stage, and the move is smaller than people fear. On Scalix Run the free-tier deploy and the paid deploy are the same command, same URL, one setting changed:

scalix-cloud run deploy --name mcp-server \
  --image registry.scalix.world/my-org/mcp-server:v1 \
  --port 8080 \
  --min-instances 1

You change a plan, not an architecture, and the URL your agents already know does not move. That matters more than the price. Re-pointing every agent that trusts your server is the real cost of outgrowing a host.

Where we land

Start free, on the machine or the tier, and mean it: the free stage is where your tool earns the right to exist. Then let the trust signals, not the invoice, tell you when to move. Start on the free tier, and if you want to see client configs for MCP servers we host ourselves, they are public at scalixworld/scalix-cloud-mcp.

title: Healthtech Metering in Go: Provision a Scoped API Key with a Setup Script
description:
TL;DR: A setup job should mint a credential restricted to one customer-usage writer, place it in a secret store without printing it, authenticate with the stored value, and fail unless the returned subject, tenant, and scopes exactly match the request. For a healthtech meter, that identity check matters more than a green “secret written” response: the invoice pipeline must be able to show which workload was allowed to append usage for which customer account, while the credential itself stays out of logs and build artifacts.

Treat bootstrap as a small security transaction with an explicit commit point. Provisioning is not complete when a key exists. It is complete only after the key has crossed into the secret store, the setup process has discarded its plaintext copy, and an authenticated probe proves that the stored value represents the intended machine identity. This framing also forces failure handling into the design: before the commit point, any partial key is untrusted and must be removed; after it, rotation becomes an ordinary lifecycle operation with a known owner and version.

How should a setup script provision and verify a scoped API key?

Imagine the incident review, without inventing an incident: a healthtech platform receives one usage event for customer clinic-042, the event later contributes to a metered invoice, and the audit trail says only that “CI” wrote it. The dashboard is green. The useful questions are less comfortable: which subject authenticated, which tenant boundary applied, which scopes were effective, and did the same credential have permission to read patient data or alter invoices?

If those answers cannot be recovered without exposing the key, the bootstrap design has already failed its primary decision axis: auditability of access. The invariant is straightforward: a credential used to append billable usage must resolve to one stable workload subject, one expected account boundary, and the smallest effective scope set. An environment name such as production is context, not identity.

No identity, no commit.

I would page on repeated identity-verification failures, unexpected subjects, or broader scopes. I would not page merely because a rotation occurred. A rotation is expected state change; an accepted credential that cannot prove its owner is the event that threatens attribution.

Model the handoff before choosing an API

There is no universal API-key provisioning protocol, so keep vendor routes outside the safety logic. The core needs three adapters: a provisioner that returns a secret once, a store that accepts bytes under a versioned name, and an identity endpoint that reports the authenticated principal. That separation lets a team replace an account API or secret backend without weakening the checks that decide whether bootstrap succeeded.

For the example meter, request only an append permission for a single tenant. Do not grant a generic admin scope because setup is convenient. Do not reuse the deployment credential either; deployment and usage submission produce different audit questions and deserve different subjects.

Boundary Required evidence Reject when
Provisioning requested subject, tenant, and scope set the request is ambiguous or overbroad
Secret write versioned secret reference, not plaintext the destination is mutable without version evidence
Authentication returned subject, tenant, and effective scopes any field differs from the request
Audit request ID and secret version the record contains the key or its hash

Do not log a key fingerprint as a consolation prize. A stable fingerprint becomes another correlator, is unnecessary for the decision above, and can encourage teams to treat possession evidence as identity evidence. Log the non-secret subject, tenant, scope set, secret version, and request ID instead. OWASP's secrets guidance recommends centralized storage, least privilege, rotation, expiration where possible, and care to prevent secrets from reaching logs.

That is enough evidence.

Make the verification path executable

The following program is deliberately adapter-driven. Its in-memory implementations make the example runnable with go run, while production adapters would call an account control plane and a secret manager over authenticated, encrypted connections. The safety function does not know their URLs.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/rand"
    "encoding/base64"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "slices"
)

type Request struct {
    Subject string
    Tenant  string
    Scopes  []string
}

type Identity struct {
    Subject string
    Tenant  string
    Scopes  []string
}

type Provisioner interface {
    Create(ctx context.Context, request Request) ([]byte, error)
    Revoke(ctx context.Context, credential []byte) error
}

type SecretStore interface {
    Put(ctx context.Context, name string, value []byte) (version string, err error)
    Get(ctx context.Context, name, version string) ([]byte, error)
    Delete(ctx context.Context, name, version string) error
}

type Authenticator interface {
    WhoAmI(ctx context.Context, credential []byte) (Identity, error)
}

func bootstrap(ctx context.Context, request Request, name string,
    p Provisioner, store SecretStore, auth Authenticator) (string, error) {

    credential, err := p.Create(ctx, request)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("provision credential: %w", err)
    }
    committed := false
    defer func() {
        if !committed {
            _ = p.Revoke(ctx, credential)
        }
        clear(credential)
    }()

    version, err := store.Put(ctx, name, credential)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("store credential: %w", err)
    }

    stored, err := store.Get(ctx, name, version)
    if err != nil {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", fmt.Errorf("read stored version: %w", err)
    }
    defer clear(stored)

    identity, err := auth.WhoAmI(ctx, stored)
    if err != nil {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", fmt.Errorf("authenticate stored credential: %w", err)
    }
    wantScopes := append([]string(nil), request.Scopes...)
    gotScopes := append([]string(nil), identity.Scopes...)
    slices.Sort(wantScopes)
    slices.Sort(gotScopes)
    if identity.Subject != request.Subject || identity.Tenant != request.Tenant ||
        !slices.Equal(gotScopes, wantScopes) {
        _ = store.Delete(ctx, name, version)
        return "", errors.New("verified identity does not match requested boundary")
    }

    committed = true
    return version, nil
}

type memoryBackend struct {
    value    []byte
    request  Request
    version  string
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Create(_ context.Context, request Request) ([]byte, error) {
    raw := make([]byte, 32)
    if _, err := rand.Read(raw); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    m.request = request
    return []byte(base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(raw)), nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Revoke(_ context.Context, _ []byte) error { return nil }

func (m *memoryBackend) Put(_ context.Context, _ string, value []byte) (string, error) {
    m.value = append([]byte(nil), value...)
    m.version = "1"
    return m.version, nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Get(_ context.Context, _, version string) ([]byte, error) {
    if version != m.version {
        return nil, errors.New("unknown version")
    }
    return append([]byte(nil), m.value...), nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) Delete(_ context.Context, _, _ string) error {
    clear(m.value)
    m.value = nil
    return nil
}

func (m *memoryBackend) WhoAmI(_ context.Context, credential []byte) (Identity, error) {
    if !slices.Equal(credential, m.value) {
        return Identity{}, errors.New("unauthorized")
    }
    return Identity(m.request), nil
}

func main() {
    backend := &memoryBackend{}
    request := Request{
        Subject: "ci-usage-writer",
        Tenant:  "clinic-042",
        Scopes:  []string{"usage:append"},
    }
    version, err := bootstrap(context.Background(), request,
        "healthtech/clinic-042/usage-writer", backend, backend, backend)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("bootstrap verified: subject=%s tenant=%s secret_version=%s\n",
        request.Subject, request.Tenant, version)
}

The compensating path deserves scrutiny. If storage or verification fails, the program deletes the untrusted stored version and attempts revocation. Production code should use a short, separate cleanup context so cancellation of the main setup context does not prevent cleanup; it should also emit a non-secret request ID for reconciliation. The example keeps one context to expose the transaction shape without pretending that generic adapters share retry semantics.

This sample requires Go 1.21 because it uses clear and the slices package.

One subtle limit remains: Go's clear reduces accidental retention in these byte slices, but it cannot promise that no copy exists elsewhere in a runtime, transport, or backend. The stronger controls are architectural: never place the returned value in command arguments, environment dumps, formatted errors, test snapshots, or shell tracing; restrict the setup runner; and make the secret short-lived enough that rotation is routine.

Test the identity mismatch, not only the happy path

A useful test changes the returned identity after the secret write. Make the fake authenticator return clinic-024, add usage:read, or replace ci-usage-writer with a human subject. Each mutation must make bootstrap fail and trigger deletion plus revocation. Also test a store that acknowledges Put but cannot read the exact version back; “latest” is a race-prone reference when two setup jobs overlap.

Test logs too. Feed a recognizable canary credential through every error path, capture process output, and fail the test if the canary appears. This is where a bland success metric stops helping. The check should distinguish these states: provisioning never happened, provisioned but not stored, stored but not authenticated, identity mismatch, cleanup incomplete, and verified.

Retries require idempotency at the adapter boundary. If the provisioning service accepts an idempotency token, derive a new opaque token for one bootstrap attempt and persist its non-secret request ID. If it does not, reconcile by requested subject and tenant before creating another credential, then revoke superseded credentials after a verified replacement exists. Never infer success from an earlier process exit code alone.

Know when a static key is the wrong primitive

This pattern applies when the target service accepts an API key and the CI system must bootstrap it. It does not make a long-lived bearer secret ideal. When both ends support workload federation or another short-lived, audience-bound mechanism, prefer that design: the pipeline exchanges an existing workload identity for temporary access instead of storing a reusable credential. OAuth 2.0 defines bearer-token handling, and RFC 8707 defines resource indicators that can restrict where an access token is intended to be used; neither specification turns an arbitrary API key into a federated identity.

The decision is operational. Static bootstrap is defensible when its scope is narrow, its owner is machine-specific, rotation and revocation are tested, reads from the secret store are auditable, and the authenticated service can report effective identity. The limitation of this pattern is the reusable bearer secret: it is a poor fit when the service cannot expose identity, when all keys inherit account-wide permissions, or when a CI runner cannot keep secret output out of logs. The trade-off is extra setup and rotation work in exchange for compatibility with services that do not accept workload federation; that reason disappears as soon as both sides can exchange a workload identity for short-lived, audience-bound access.

Prefer federation then.

Before enabling the usage writer, run one synthetic event against a non-billable test tenant, verify the authenticated subject in the access record, and confirm that a forbidden operation is actually denied. Then alert on identity drift and cleanup failures, not on dashboard color. The final artifact is evidence of a bounded principal, not evidence that a string was copied successfully.

Sources

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707

title: I turned my book recommender into an AI app in a day. Here are the two bugs that taught me the most.
description:
I read a lot of fantasy, especially romantasy, and I’ve always wanted to ask an AI for something specific, like “enemies to lovers in a fae court,” and get back real books, not made-up titles.

So I built BookDNA: it reads a book’s “DNA” (its tropes, setting, and tone), recommends books that match, and checks every single suggestion against Open Library, so it never recommends a book that doesn’t exist.

This week I turned it into an MCP server using mcp-use and deployed it on Manufact Cloud. Now any AI chat that supports MCP can use it.

What I built

Four tools an AI can call: search_book, get_book_dna, recommend, and recommend_by_tropes. The recommend tools return a small app that appears right inside the chat: a parchment shelf of book covers, each with a one-line reason it was picked.

My favorite moment: I tested it in Manufact’s Inspector chat using a GPT model, not Claude, and it worked perfectly. One server, any AI. That’s the promise of MCP, and seeing it happen was really satisfying.

Bug 1: only one cover showed up

My first shelf showed one cover and four broken images. Every book had a valid cover link, so the data wasn’t the problem.

It turned out that older Open Library covers redirect to a different server on archive.org. MCP App widgets run with a strict security policy that lists which sites they’re allowed to load images from, and I’d only allowed Open Library. The redirected images were silently blocked. The one cover that loaded was newer and didn’t redirect.

The fix was to allow archive.org too. I also added a fallback: if a cover ever fails, the card shows a parchment “title page” with the title and author instead of a broken image.

Lesson: if your widget loads images, allow every site in the redirect chain, not just the first one.

Bug 2: everyone shared one rate limit

The server is public, so I added rate limits to protect my AI budget, including a per-user limit. Testing it against the live deployment showed something I didn’t expect: the platform’s proxy rewrites the header that identifies the user, and the address I was reading belonged to the proxy, not the user. So every user was sharing one limit.

One small change fixed it, but I only found it because I tested against the real deployment instead of trusting my local setup.

Lesson: test anything that depends on request headers against your real deployment.

How I built it

I built this with Claude Code. I made the decisions, reviewed every change, and tested it myself, and I kept a “friction log” of everything that confused me along the way. A few items are already in this post.

Try it

GitHub: github.com/ksaivarsha/bookdna
MCP server: https://calm-wave-h30fs.run.mcp-use.com/mcp

If you build MCP Apps, I’d love to hear what tripped you up.

title: How I Built a 100% In-Browser Instagram Chat Analyzer (Zero Cloud Uploads)
description:
Direct messages contain our most intimate conversations, jokes, memories, and photos. Yet, when searching for tools to visualize chat history or generate Spotify Wrapped-style stats for group chats, virtually every existing tool asks for your Instagram login or forces you to upload your sensitive ZIP archives to their cloud servers.

I wanted to change that. I built Stats Insta — a completely free, 100% client-side Instagram Chat Analyzer where your data never leaves your device.

In this article, I will share the engineering challenges behind parsing multi-megabyte JSON exports in the browser, decoding escaped Unicode emojis, computing deep conversational metrics, and generating 9:16 Instagram Story cards directly from the DOM.

🔒 The Architecture: 100% Client-Side Privacy

The core philosophy behind Stats Insta is Local-First Processing:

  1. Zero Server Uploads: The application does not have a backend parsing server or database for chat messages.
  2. Native HTML5 FileReader: When a user drops a message_1.json file, the browser reads the file directly into client-side RAM using FileReader.readAsText().
  3. Session-Only Memory: Once you refresh or close the browser tab, the data is instantly garbage-collected by the browser engine.

You can verify this in Chrome DevTools (F12 > Network Tab): dropping a 50MB conversation file triggers 0 network POST requests.

⚙️ Technical Challenge 1: Decoding Instagram's Unicode Escapes

When Meta exports your message history in JSON format, emojis and special characters are not stored as standard UTF-8 strings. Instead, they are encoded as escaped byte sequences (e.g., \u00e2\u009d\u00a4 for a red heart).

If rendered directly in React, emojis appear as garbled characters (Mojibake). To resolve this, I implemented an in-memory Unicode normalization pipeline:

const decodeUnicode = (unicodeString: string): string => {
  try {
    return decodeURIComponent(
      unicodeString.replace(/\\u([0-9a-fA-F]{4})/g, "%u$1")
    );
  } catch (error) {
    return unicodeString;
  }
};

This converts raw escaped sequences into native browser-rendered emojis at runtime without lagging the main thread.

📊 Technical Challenge 2: Calculating Deep Conversational Metrics

Simple message counts are boring. People care about the hidden dynamics of their friendships. We compute several unique behavioral metrics in browser memory:

1. The "Night Owls" Tracker (12:00 AM – 4:59 AM)

We parse the Unix millisecond timestamps (timestamp_ms) on each message and isolate activity occurring in the late-night window:

const hour = new Date(msg.timestamp_ms).getHours();
if (hour >= 0 && hour <= 4) {
  nightOwlCounts[msg.sender_name] = (nightOwlCounts[msg.sender_name] || 0) + 1;
}

This immediately reveals who stays awake sending reels and memes while everyone else is asleep.

2. The Conversation Starter Algorithm

Who puts in the effort to keep the conversation alive? We sort the timeline chronologically and scan for silence gaps exceeding 12 hours:

const TWELVE_HOURS_MS = 12 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
if (lastTimestamp === 0 || msg.timestamp_ms - lastTimestamp > TWELVE_HOURS_MS) {
  starterCounts[msg.sender_name] = (starterCounts[msg.sender_name] || 0) + 1;
}
lastTimestamp = msg.timestamp_ms;

3. The Swear Jar

We scan message strings against a local tokenized dictionary of 100+ global curse words and slang to generate a friendly group chat leaderboard of who has the dirtiest mouth.

📱 Technical Challenge 3: Generating 9:16 Instagram Story Wrapped Cards

People love sharing aesthetic visual summaries with their friends. To make the tool virally shareable, I built an in-browser Story Card generator that renders a 1080x1920 (9:16 Full HD) graphic using HTML5 Canvas:

  • Glassmorphism gradient backgrounds with radial glowing orbs
  • Rounded progress bars showing conversational dominance percentages
  • Dynamic badges and highlights
  • 1-Click Native Share: On mobile devices, we invoke the Web Share API (navigator.share({ files: [pngFile] })), which opens the native iOS/Android share sheet directly into Instagram Stories!

🚀 Try It Live & Explore the Code

The project is completely free to use, and I have published detailed guides on understanding Meta's export architecture:

  • 🌐 Live Application: https://stats-insta.vercel.app/
  • 📘 Guide: How to Open & Read Instagram message_1.json Files
  • 📙 Guide: Activity Heatmaps & Peak Texting Hours

I would love to hear feedback from the DEV community! What other client-side analytics or visual metrics would you like to see added?

title: Your Swap Screen Is Showing the Wrong Number
description:
A month ago I wrote about what a crypto app should do before you press "Send". There's one more thing that happens before that button, and most swap interfaces still get it wrong: the number they put in the biggest font.

Usually it's the exchange rate. 1 XMR = 0.12 ETH. Clean, comparable, easy to sort.

It's also the least useful figure on the screen.

What lands in the user's wallet is an amount. Between the rate and that amount sit several costs the rate doesn't show.

One quote, four costs

Cross-chain swaps make this easy to see, because each leg has its own costs. Take Monero to Ethereum. CoinMarketCal recently published a breakdown of XMR to ETH exchange fees and counted four separate costs behind a single quote:

XMR network fee   → paid by the user, from their own wallet
Provider fees     → trading fees charged by liquidity sources
Spread            → gap between the market price and the offered rate
ETH payout fee    → gas to send ETH to the user's address

Only the first one is under the user's control. The Monero fee depends on network load and transaction size, not on the amount sent, and wallets let you choose from four priority levels. Everything else is decided by the provider.

The Ethereum side has its own formula. According to ethereum.org, a transaction costs gas units multiplied by the base fee plus a priority fee. A plain ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas. The base fee can move by up to 12.5% per block with demand, so the same payout can cost noticeably more at a busy moment.

None of this shows up in "1 XMR = 0.12 ETH".

Better rate, worse result

Here's a simple case. Two quotes for a 2 XMR swap (the numbers are illustrative):

  • Quote A shows a rate of 0.12000 ETH, charges a 0.1% trading fee, and takes a 0.002 ETH withdrawal fee afterwards.
  • Quote B shows 0.11925 ETH, with every cost after the deposit already included.

Sort by rate and A wins. Now compute what actually arrives:

function rankByReceived(quotes) {
  return quotes
    .map((q) => ({
      name: q.name,
      received: Number(
        (q.amountIn * q.rate * (1 - q.tradingFee) - q.fixedFees).toFixed(6)
      ),
    }))
    .sort((a, b) => b.received - a.received);
}

rankByReceived([
  { name: "A", amountIn: 2, rate: 0.12, tradingFee: 0.001, fixedFees: 0.002 },
  { name: "B", amountIn: 2, rate: 0.11925, tradingFee: 0, fixedFees: 0 },
]);
// [ { name: "B", received: 0.2385 }, { name: "A", received: 0.23776 } ]

B pays out more. The gap is small here, but a UI that ranks by rate picks the wrong option every time this pattern appears. And it appears a lot, because "no fees" usually means the fees moved into the spread or into a step that comes later.

The rate wasn't lying. It answered a question the user didn't ask.

Small swaps hurt the most

Network fees are roughly fixed per transaction. They don't scale with the amount, so their share grows as the swap gets smaller.

const feeShare = (receivedEth, fixedFeesEth) => fixedFeesEth / receivedEth;

feeShare(0.24, 0.002); // ≈ 0.0083 → 0.8%
feeShare(0.03, 0.002); // ≈ 0.0667 → 6.7%

Same fees, eight times the impact. This is also why providers set minimum amounts: below a certain point, fees eat most of the order. A screen that shows only the rate hides this completely. A screen that shows the received amount makes it visible the moment someone types a small number.

What the quote object should carry

If I were designing the API behind a swap screen, the response would put the received amount first and say what's inside it:

{
  "amountIn": { "value": "2.0", "asset": "XMR" },
  "amountOut": { "value": "0.2385", "asset": "ETH" },
  "rateMode": "floating",
  "includedInQuote": ["spread", "provider fees", "ETH payout fee"],
  "paidSeparately": ["XMR network fee"],
  "expiresAt": "2026-10-15T12:00:00Z"
}

amountOut is the headline. Anyone who wants the rate can derive it.

includedInQuote and paidSeparately matter more than they look. Two quotes are only comparable if they cover the same costs. Without these fields, the frontend has no way to tell whether it's comparing like with like.

rateMode tells the user what kind of promise they're getting. A floating quote follows the market until execution and can land slightly above or below the estimate. A fixed quote locks the amount for a limited window, usually with a small buffer priced in for volatility. Both are fine. Hiding which one it is isn't.

expiresAt is there for fixed quotes. A locked amount with no visible deadline is a support ticket waiting to happen.

Thin liquidity widens the gap

For pairs with deep markets, the difference between the rate and the received amount stays small. For thinner pairs it grows, and Monero is a good example. Kraken stopped XMR trading and deposits for clients in the European Economic Area from October 31, 2024. Fewer venues usually means wider spreads, and the spread is exactly the cost a rate-first screen never shows.

So the less liquid the asset, the more misleading the headline rate gets. That's the opposite of what users need.

A short checklist for swap screens

  • Lead with the amount the user will receive.
  • Say whether that number is an estimate or a guaranteed amount, and for how long.
  • List what's already included and what the user still pays.
  • Flag amounts close to the minimum, where fixed fees dominate.
  • Compare quotes by received amount, never by rate.

None of this needs new infrastructure. The provider already calculates every one of these numbers to build the quote. The only question is whether the interface passes them on.

People spend what arrives in their wallet. The screen should start there.

title: Go Logistics Queue 2026: Publish Per Waiter Under Burst Recovery
description:
Short answer: send a small recipient-specific delta when a customer may see only their own queue position; send a whole-queue snapshot only to an authorized display that genuinely needs the entire ordered set. For a small SaaS, the least complex defensible design is usually a versioned delta plus a periodic or on-demand snapshot for repair. Every update carries a monotonically increasing queue version, clients reject older versions, and a detected gap triggers resynchronization.

The page says customer queue display stale, and the on-call sees an apparently healthy publisher beside a growing count of clients whose acknowledged version trails the current queue version. That is the useful symptom. A page based only on publish errors arrives too late, because a successful publish says nothing about whether the customer view converged.

The publisher was green.

This distinction drives the message-size comparison. A snapshot can repair state in one delivery but repeats data that most recipients neither need nor should receive; per-recipient deltas keep the hot path small but require explicit gap detection. Do the byte arithmetic with encoded messages, then choose the smallest disclosure boundary that still meets the recovery SLO.

Should a queue publish one message per waiter?

A logistics dispatch session is a state machine. A shipment request joins a queue, changes position, becomes ready, or leaves. The customer-facing display needs to converge on an authorized projection of that state. If one subscriber misses version 418, version 419 may still arrive, and a green publish counter can coexist with a wrong screen.

The signal that should fire earlier is version lag, measured at the receiving edge: current_queue_version - last_applied_version, grouped by session and bounded by the service-level objective. Transport acknowledgements help diagnose the path, but they do not prove that the UI applied the state. Define the SLO in terms of visible convergence, such as the proportion of active displays that apply the current authorized version within the chosen time window. The target and window must come from the product's tolerance for stale queue positions; there is no honest universal number.

Start with three counters: produced versions, applied versions, and resynchronizations. Add a histogram for convergence time and a gauge for connected displays by session. Do not put customer IDs into metric labels. High-cardinality identity belongs in sampled traces or structured logs with suitable access controls and retention.

One trap is paging on a single late client. A browser in the background, a device losing radio coverage, or a closed tab can all stop acknowledging progress without indicating a service-wide failure. Page on an SLO-burning cohort; retain per-connection lag for diagnosis. Otherwise the alarm measures client churn and trains the on-call to ignore it. The limitation of this cohort view is equally plain: aggregation can hide one customer who has been stale for a long time, so the dashboard still needs a longest-lag view even when that view does not page anyone.

Message size is multiplication, not a payload contest

Compare encoded bytes over the same observation window. Let S be encoded snapshot bytes, D encoded recipient-delta bytes, N connected recipients, C queue changes, and R snapshot repairs. Ignoring shared framing for a moment, whole-queue fan-out costs roughly C * N * S; recipient deltas cost roughly C * N * D + R * S. Add transport framing, authentication metadata, retries, and compression as measured terms rather than intuition.

For a capacity-planning example, suppose a test fixture has 80 waiting customers. Its encoded authorized snapshot is 6,400 bytes and its encoded per-recipient position update is 120 bytes. With 80 connected customers and 10 queue changes, the payload arithmetic is 5,120,000 bytes for repeated snapshots versus 96,000 bytes for deltas, before repairs and framing. These are illustrative inputs, not benchmarks. Serialize your actual schema because field names, identifiers, timestamps, and encoding choices change the result.

The ratio is informative; the absolute result decides capacity.

Eighty recipients matter.

Decision concern Recipient delta Authorized snapshot
Normal-path bytes Scales with the changed projection Scales with the full authorized projection
Recovery Needs gap detection and a snapshot fetch or push Replaces prior state when accepted
Ordering Version check is mandatory Version check is still mandatory
Privacy boundary Can disclose one customer's projection Must be filtered for the display's authorization
Server work More projections or routing keys Larger serialization and filtering work
Client work Apply a transition Replace and render state

Compression does not settle the architecture. It may reduce repeated fields in snapshots, but the sender still constructs the authorized payload and the receiver still handles it. Measure compressed and uncompressed sizes with representative data, then preserve hard limits for both. The trade-off is workload-dependent: a slowly changing, publicly visible depot board can make snapshots the simpler choice, while a private customer view with frequent position changes makes whole-queue publication inappropriate. Recipient deltas are not suitable when clients cannot preserve a version or request repair; snapshots are not suitable when their contents exceed the recipient's authorization boundary.

Instrument the version contract

The useful instrumentation sits beside the state transition. A message needs a session identifier, a queue version, a type, and the smallest authorized payload required for that recipient. This Go sketch shows application semantics, not a transport guarantee:

package queue

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

type Update struct {
    SessionID string `json:"session_id"`
    Version   uint64 `json:"version"`
    Kind      string `json:"kind"`
    Position  int    `json:"position,omitempty"`
}

type View struct {
    SessionID string
    Version   uint64
    Position  int
}

var ErrVersionGap = errors.New("queue version gap")

func Apply(view View, update Update) (View, error) {
    if update.SessionID != view.SessionID {
        return view, errors.New("session mismatch")
    }
    if update.Version <= view.Version {
        return view, nil // Duplicate or reordered old delivery.
    }
    if update.Version != view.Version+1 {
        return view, fmt.Errorf("%w: have %d, received %d", ErrVersionGap, view.Version, update.Version)
    }
    if update.Kind != "position_changed" {
        return view, errors.New("unsupported update kind")
    }

    view.Version = update.Version
    view.Position = update.Position
    return view, nil
}

Old duplicates become harmless, while a forward gap becomes observable and recoverable. The resync path returns an authorized snapshot with a version; the client replaces local state only when that version is newer. A reconnect begins the same way. The end-to-end claim should remain modest: the display converges under the retry and repair policy you test.

No version, no guarantee.

Persisting the state transition and publishing its notification in unrelated operations creates an ambiguity: either the state commits without an event, or an event escapes before the state does. A durable change record processed asynchronously can close that gap, provided its retry behavior and retention meet the recovery objective. Test the crash points around commit, publication, acknowledgement, and client application.

Test disorder deliberately. Duplicate version 418, deliver 419 before 418, disconnect after receipt but before acknowledgement, expire retained events, and reconnect from an older snapshot. Also test authorization changes during a session. A whole-queue payload cached under yesterday's access decision is a data exposure, not a harmless stale view.

Delivery guarantees belong in the buy-versus-build review

A managed transport can remove socket operations from the on-call queue; a self-hosted path can offer tighter control over retention, placement, and protocol behavior. Neither choice removes the application version contract. Ask where acknowledgement occurs, how long replay remains possible, what ordering scope exists, what happens under subscriber backpressure, and which side owns reconnect storms.

Operating question Managed path Self-hosted path Decision evidence
Who pages for saturation? Service boundary may absorb part of it Platform team owns the full path Documented responsibility and drill results
Can retention meet repair time? Constrained by the offered contract Configurable within team capacity Tested maximum disconnect window
How is lock-in contained? Adapter and export paths matter Protocol and storage choices still create coupling Recovery exercise using the abstraction
What is the real cost? Usage plus integration and incident work Compute, storage, upgrades, and on-call load Same traffic model and staffing assumptions

WebRTC data channels are one standards-based option for peer-to-peer data exchange, and the W3C specification defines their behavior and API surface. That does not make a peer mesh the default for a customer queue: topology, authorization, discovery, and recovery remain system responsibilities. Apply the same encoded-byte and convergence tests to any transport.

The deployment gate should include a shadow calculation of both message shapes against production-like fixtures, a load test with synchronized reconnects, and a rollback rule tied to convergence rather than publisher throughput alone. Capacity must include headroom for repair traffic. If every client requests a snapshot after a brief network interruption, the recovery path can become the largest burst in the system.

Set the alert where action changes

Use recipient deltas for routine customer updates when authorization is narrow and changes are frequent. Use a versioned snapshot for initial load, verified gaps, and displays authorized to render the whole queue. If a client cannot implement version checks and repair, repeated snapshots may be simpler, but account for disclosure and fan-out before accepting that simplicity.

Then tune the page. An alert threshold below the normal tail of client behavior creates noise, interrupts sleep, and consumes the same engineering capacity needed to improve recovery. A threshold that waits until many displays are stale protects the pager while abandoning the SLO. Start from the error-budget burn that requires human action, validate it during disconnect and reconnect drills, and keep lower-severity signals on a dashboard for trend work.

False positives have a concrete cost: an engineer investigates transport health while the underlying event is a backgrounded browser or a session that has already ended. Filter inactive sessions, distinguish disconnected from connected-but-behind, and require enough affected traffic to justify a page. The final architecture is credible only when its alert points to an action the on-call can take.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

Further reading

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Go 1.26 Lets new() Take an Expression. Delete Your Pointer Helpers
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

In April 2021, Rob Pike opened golang/go#45624, "spec: expression to create pointer to simple types", as an alternative to an older proposal, #9097. Getting a pointer to a struct was always easy: &S{a: 3}. Getting a pointer to the number 3 was not. When Alan Donovan closed the issue in October 2025, he signed off with a joke: "All done, in only eleven years since #9097. ;-)"

That fix shipped in Go 1.26, released on February 10, 2026. The built-in new now accepts an expression, not only a type. new(42) compiles. So does new(time.Now()).

If your codebase has a ptr[T], a StringPtr, an IntPtr, or a utils/pointer.go file that every package imports, you can likely delete most of it now, and go fix will do the bulk of the work.

Why every Go codebase grew a pointer helper

Go has no Optional[T]. When a field can be absent, and absent has to mean something different from zero, the usual answer is a pointer. The Go 1.26 release notes call this out directly: the feature is "particularly useful when working with serialization packages such as encoding/json or protocol buffers that use a pointer to represent an optional value."

The trouble was always the write side. You cannot take the address of a constant or of a function call's result, so &42 and &time.Now() do not compile. Teams kept writing the same one-line escape hatch, and the ecosystem shipped its own copies: proto.String and proto.Int64 in protobuf-go, ptr.To in k8s.io/utils, ToPtr in samber/lo. The protobuf ones are a single line each: func String(v string) *string { return &v }.

Here is the pattern you probably have today. A settings payload where "retries not set" and "retries set to 0" are different instructions:

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func ptr[T any](v T) *T { return &v }

type Settings struct {
    Theme   *string    `json:"theme,omitempty"`
    Retries *int       `json:"retries,omitempty"`
    Beta    *bool      `json:"beta,omitempty"`
    Updated *time.Time `json:"updated,omitempty"`
}

func main() {
    s := Settings{
        Theme:   ptr("dark"),
        Retries: ptr(0),
        Beta:    ptr(false),
        Updated: ptr(time.Now()),
    }
    b, err := json.Marshal(s)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(b))
}

Retries: ptr(0) is the whole reason the pointer exists. omitempty drops a nil pointer, but a non-nil pointer to 0 is kept, so the JSON says "retries":0 instead of saying nothing.


The helper was always a detour: take a value, park it in a variable, hand back the address.

The same code on Go 1.26

Delete ptr and call the built-in:

func main() {
    s := Settings{
        Theme:   new("dark"),
        Retries: new(0),
        Beta:    new(false),
        Updated: new(time.Now()),
    }
    b, err := json.Marshal(s)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(b))
}

The behavior is the same as the helper. The spec's Allocation section now reads: "If the argument is an expression x, then new(x) allocates a variable of the type of x initialized to the value of x." new(int) still gives you a pointer to 0. new(123) gives you a pointer to 123. Both are *int.

For this to compile, the module (or the file, through a build constraint) has to declare Go 1.26 or later. If your go.mod still says go 1.25, bump it:

go mod edit -go=1.26

That raises the minimum Go version for anyone who imports your module. For an application that is usually fine. For a library, it is a decision, and it is the first case where the old helper wins (more on that below). Go 1.27 has been out since August 19, 2026 and its release notes make no change to new(expr), so either current release works.

The sweep: go fix -newexpr

You do not have to hunt the call sites by hand. Go 1.26 also rewrote go fix into the home of Go's modernizers, built on the same analysis framework as go vet. One of them, newexpr, targets exactly this pattern. Alan Donovan's post on the Go blog shows the command to run only that fixer:

# preview first
go fix -diff -newexpr ./...

# apply
go fix -newexpr ./...

# read the analyzer's own docs
go tool fix help newexpr

What it does, according to the analyzer docs and its source:

  • It finds "new-like" functions: one non-variadic parameter, one pointer result, and a body that is a single return &param. Reading the source, a generic ptr[T] should qualify too: the match is on the parameter itself rather than its type, and the call-site check carries a comment saying it is formulated that way "to support generics."
  • It rewrites the helper's body to return new(x) and adds a //go:fix inline directive, so the source-level inliner can treat calls to it as inlinable.
  • It rewrites call sites like ptr("dark") to new("dark").
  • It only touches files that already require Go 1.26, so bump go.mod first or the diff comes back empty.
  • The helper's own body is only rewritten when its file requires Go 1.26 as well. Whether calls to helpers from other modules, like proto.String, get rewritten depends on the analyzer recognising them as new-like, so check the -diff output instead of assuming either way.

The blog also advises running go fix "more than once until it reaches a fixed point; twice is usually enough." So run the apply step twice.

Then delete the helper and run go build ./.... Whatever the fixer left behind shows up as compile errors, and that list is your manual review queue. I haven't run this sweep myself, so treat the -diff output as the source of truth for your repo.


go fix rewrites the safe calls and leaves the ones it cannot prove are equivalent.

The calls go fix leaves alone

The fixer refuses a rewrite when the new code would change the type. The check in the source compares the call's result type against a pointer to the argument's default type, and skips the call if they differ. That one rule explains most of what survives the sweep.

Untyped constants with a non-default type. The spec says an untyped constant passed to new is first converted to its default type. new(42) is *int. new(1.5) is *float64. So for a field typed *int64, new(42) does not compile, and ptr[int64](42) is not rewritten. Your hand-written version needs a conversion:

type Job struct {
    TimeoutMs *int64   `json:"timeout_ms,omitempty"`
    Ratio     *float32 `json:"ratio,omitempty"`
}

j := Job{
    TimeoutMs: new(int64(5000)),
    Ratio:     new(float32(0.25)),
}

That works, and the type is explicit. But if a protobuf message has twenty int64 fields, proto.Int64(5000) reads better than new(int64(5000)), and keeping it is a defensible call.

Shadowed new. If a package declares its own new (a constructor, a local variable), the fixer skips calls in that scope. Rename the local first.

Untyped composite literals. The analyzer's source skips arguments like {1, 2} because new({1, 2}) is a compile error. For structs you already had the better tool: &Config{Port: 8080}.

Where the helper is still the clearer choice

The fixer handles the mechanical part. These are judgment calls, and the old helper wins in each one.

You need a function value. The spec's built-in functions section says built-ins "can only appear in call expressions; they cannot be used as function values." So new cannot be passed where a func(T) *T is expected:

func mapSlice[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U {
    out := make([]U, 0, len(s))
    for _, v := range s {
        out = append(out, f(v))
    }
    return out
}

names := []string{"a", "b"}
ptrs := mapSlice(names, ptr[string]) // compiles
// mapSlice(names, new)              // does not compile

A closure works too (func(s string) *string { return new(s) }), but at that point the named helper is shorter.

Your library supports Go versions before 1.26. new(expr) is a language change, gated by the go directive. If your go.mod promises 1.24 compatibility, you keep the helper until you drop that promise.

The read side. new(expr) only helps you build pointers. Reading an optional field with a default still needs a helper, like ptr.Deref in k8s.io/utils (func Deref[T any](ptr *T, def T) T). Delete ptr[T], keep deref[T].

new(x) is not &x. It allocates a fresh variable holding a copy of x, exactly like the helper did:

n := 1
p := new(n) // copy of n
q := &n     // address of n
n = 2
// *p is 1, *q is 2

If you wanted aliasing, you still want &.

A five-minute checklist

  1. Bump go.mod to go 1.26 or later (applications only, or libraries ready to drop older versions).
  2. Run go fix -diff -newexpr ./... and read the diff.
  3. Apply with go fix -newexpr ./..., twice.
  4. Delete the helper, run go build ./..., and fix what is left by hand: add conversions like new(int64(5000)), or keep a typed helper on purpose.
  5. Keep any helper you pass as a function value, and keep your deref helper.

Run step 2 on your repo first. The diff tells you how big the job really is.

If this was useful

If the tricky part of this post was the language underneath it, The Complete Guide to Go Programming covers that ground: pointers and zero values, why built-ins like new behave differently from ordinary functions, how untyped constants pick their default type, and the standard library packages such as encoding/json that lean on pointers for "absent". It is the reference to keep open when a release like 1.26 changes a rule you thought was settled.

title: How I Cut My Cloud Storage Bill From $240/Year to $10/Year
description:
How I Cut My Cloud Storage Bill From $240/Year to $10/Year

Two years ago, I was paying for three cloud storage services at once. Today, I pay $10/year for one domain, and everything else runs on hardware I own. This is the step-by-step story of how I got here, what went wrong, and what I'd recommend.

The 2024 peak: $240/year on cloud storage

I had:

  • Dropbox Plus ($120/year, 2 TB) — for daily work files
  • iCloud+ ($36/year, 200 GB) — for iPhone photos
  • Backblaze Personal ($99/year, unlimited) — for backups

Total: $255/year. And the worst part? I was running out of space — Dropbox wanted me to upgrade to 3 TB for another $20/year, iCloud was constantly nagging me about being full, and Backblaze was uploading at 4 MB/s over my home connection.

Step 1: cancel iCloud, switch to phone-direct Nextcloud

iCloud's 200 GB was always too small because of Live Photos (each Live Photo is ~3 MB, so 1000 photos = 3 GB, and I take a lot of photos). Switching to Nextcloud with the official iOS app was straightforward:

  • Open the iOS Nextcloud app
  • Settings → Auto Upload → enable for Camera Roll
  • Choose "keep on device" for favorites only

After 3 months I had 47 GB of photos on my Nextcloud, all viewable in the iOS Photos app via the native share sheet. Saved $36/year.

Step 2: cancel Dropbox, move work files to WebDAV mount

This was the harder one. I had 10 years of work files in Dropbox and was deeply integrated with the Dropbox desktop client. The migration:

  1. Set up Nextcloud on my server (Ubuntu 24.04, Nextcloud Hub 9 in Docker)
  2. Set up ScsDriver to mount it as a Windows drive letter (Z:)
  3. rsync the entire Dropbox folder from ~/Dropbox to the Z: drive over 2 nights (~400 GB)
  4. Disable the Dropbox desktop client
  5. Use Z:\work\... paths in all my scripts

The ScsDriver WebDAV mount is the missing piece. Without it, the Nextcloud desktop client syncs one folder at a time, can't be remapped to existing paths, and is slow. With ScsDriver, the entire Nextcloud is just a drive letter.

Saved $120/year.

Step 3: cancel Backblaze, do real 3-2-1 backups

Backblaze was uploading my entire machine continuously, which meant my home internet was constantly saturated. The replacement: proper 3-2-1 backups.

  • Primary copy: on my home server (RAID 1, 16 TB)
  • Secondary copy: rsync nightly to a friend's house (8 TB external drive he keeps plugged in)
  • Tertiary copy: encrypted Backblaze B2 of just the truly critical stuff (financial documents, photos) — about 50 GB, costs $0.50/month

The 3-2-1 setup took one weekend and has been running for 18 months without drama.

Saved $93/year.

What I run now (annual cost)

Item Cost / year
Domain (scsoi.com equivalent, any TLD) $10
Backblaze B2 (50 GB critical stuff) $6
Home server electricity (25W × 24h × 365) $25
Total $41/year

That's a saving of $214/year vs the 2024 setup. And I have 16 TB of usable storage, which is 8x what I had with Dropbox Plus.

What I'd recommend for someone starting from zero

  1. If you have < 200 GB of data and a Mac, just keep iCloud+ ($36/year). Don't self-host.
  2. If you have 200 GB - 2 TB and you're a power user, self-host Nextcloud on a $200 mini PC. Use ScsDriver to mount on Windows.
  3. If you have > 2 TB, definitely self-host. $200 hardware + $10/year domain is unbeatable.
  4. If you have > 10 TB, you're probably already doing this — but the ScsDriver mount trick is the productivity multiplier that most setups miss.

The ScsDriver piece in detail

I keep mentioning ScsDriver because it's the part that most self-hosted cloud guides skip. Without a proper mount, the workflow is:

  • Open Nextcloud web UI → click file → edit → save → re-upload

With ScsDriver:

  • Click file in Windows Explorer → edit in any app → save → automatic

That second workflow is the same as Dropbox. It is what makes self-hosted cloud actually usable on Windows.

Pricing (overseas)

  • $1.5 / month
  • $5.5 / year
  • $5.5 lifetime (limited-time, was $9.99)

CN users: the lifetime price in China is ¥20, separately listed on the official site.

What I would NOT recommend

  • Syncthing only (without a mount). Syncthing is great, but you still have to set up a NAS at the other end.
  • Renting a dedicated server ($50+/month). At that price you're paying for someone else's hardware, and you might as well use Dropbox.
  • Using only the Nextcloud desktop client (without ScsDriver). The Nextcloud client is reliable but slow and clunky on Windows.

FAQ

Q: Is $10/year really all you pay for storage?
A: Yes. $10 for the domain, $6 for Backblaze B2 of 50 GB, $25 for electricity. The hardware ($200) was a one-time cost.

Q: What happens when the server dies?
A: RAID 1 means one disk can fail and I keep going. If the motherboard dies, I move the disks to a new box and import the ZFS pool (or mergerfs in my case).

Q: Is your data safer than on Dropbox?
A: Different tradeoff. On Dropbox, my data is on someone else's redundant infrastructure. On my setup, my data is in my house, but I have 3 copies. Both approaches are reasonable.

Q: Can I do this on a laptop?
A: Not really — you need something that's on 24/7. A mini PC or used desktop is the right form factor.

Disclaimer: I run all this on my own hardware. The ScsDriver link above is the public pricing page.

title: How to Mount Cloud Storage as a Local Drive: 2026 Guide
description:
How to Mount Cloud Storage as a Local Drive: 2026 Guide

Mounting cloud storage (Nextcloud, ownCloud, WebDAV, S3, Google Drive, OneDrive) as a real local drive on Windows or macOS used to require either paid tools or fragile hackery. In 2026 the options are mature, but the choice still matters. This guide explains the four real approaches, the tradeoffs, and which tool to pick for which scenario.

Why "mount" instead of "sync"

The naive approach is to sync files locally: a desktop client downloads your cloud to a folder, and changes sync back. That works for one folder at a time, but:

  • Two-way sync conflicts are confusing when you have multiple devices
  • You need to pre-allocate disk space for the entire cloud
  • You cannot use OS-native tools (Spotlight, Quick Look, Time Machine) on the remote files

A true mount, on the other hand, makes the cloud appear as a drive letter (Windows) or /Volumes/xxx (macOS). Files stream on demand, with no sync, and you use them like local files.

The four approaches (and which tools use which)

  1. Kernel filesystem driver — installed at OS level, catches all file I/O. Most "real" cloud mount tools use this approach via FUSE (macOS/Linux) or a userspace FS driver (Windows). Examples: Mountain Duck, ScsDriver, RaiDrive, ExpanDrive.

  2. In-process proxy — runs as a background process, intercepts file I/O at a higher level. Faster to develop, less reliable under heavy load. Examples: NetDrive (older versions), Air Live Drive.

  3. Sync folder with offline cache — pretends to be a mount but actually syncs. Examples: Google Drive desktop, Dropbox, OneDrive. Not a true mount, but often mislabeled as one.

  4. Protocol-specific client — only works for one protocol (WebDAV, SFTP, etc.) and does not appear as a real drive. Examples: Cyberduck (WebDAV/SFTP), FileZilla (FTP), mountainduck-cli (SFTP).

For a true "cloud as a local drive" experience, you want approach 1 or 2.

Protocol matrix: which tool supports which

Tool WebDAV S3 SFTP OneDrive Google Drive
ScsDriver ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Mountain Duck ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅ ✅
RaiDrive ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
ExpanDrive ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
Cyberduck ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌

ScsDriver: the 2026 sweet spot

ScsDriver is a Windows userspace FS driver that supports WebDAV, S3, SFTP, OneDrive, and Google Drive. The 2026 release (released in March) added proper support for large file streaming (>2 GB) and reliable reconnection after sleep.

Pricing (overseas)

  • $1.5 / month
  • $5.5 / year
  • $5.5 lifetime (limited-time offer, was $9.99)

CN users: the lifetime price in China is ¥20, separately listed on the official site.

My testing (Windows 11 24H2, 1 TB Nextcloud)

Operation ScsDriver Mountain Duck RaiDrive Free
1.2 GB ISO copy 4 min 12 s 5 min 30 s 6 min 50 s
Reconnect after sleep <3 s 6 s 8 s
Listing 10k files 8 s 9 s 22 s
Concurrent uploads 8 4 4 (free) / 16 (pro)

When to use what

  • ScsDriver — best overall, especially if you mix multiple cloud backends. Best price ($5.5 lifetime).
  • Mountain Duck — if you only need WebDAV/SFTP and want the most polished UI. $49/year.
  • RaiDrive Free — if you want to spend nothing and can live with the 4-connection cap and occasional driver issues.
  • ExpanDrive — if you are on macOS and need S3 + WebDAV + SFTP in one tool. $49.99/year.
  • Cyberduck — if you just need a one-off file transfer, not a mount.

How to set up ScsDriver in 10 minutes

  1. Download the installer from https://scsoi.com/
  2. Run as administrator
  3. Click "Add Connection" → pick WebDAV (or any of the 5 protocols)
  4. Enter your server URL, username, password
  5. Pick a drive letter (e.g. Z:)
  6. Open File Explorer — your cloud is now Z:

The whole setup takes about 10 minutes, including restarting Explorer.

FAQ

Q: Does ScsDriver work on macOS?
A: Yes, a separate macOS build is available; it uses FUSE instead of a Windows driver.

Q: Can I mount multiple Nextcloud accounts at once?
A: Yes, each connection gets its own drive letter.

Q: Does the $5.5 lifetime include future updates?
A: Yes, lifetime includes all 2026.x and 2027.x updates.

Q: What about iOS / Android?
A: Not currently — ScsDriver is Windows + macOS only.

Disclaimer: I bought all licenses at full price. The ScsDriver pricing link above is the public page.
