title: I’ve Been Building a Student Hub, and I’d Love Some Feedback
description:
Hey everyone!

This is my first post on DEV.to, so I thought I'd start by sharing something I've been working on.

I'm currently a Psychology student from the Philippines. Before switching programs, I spent three years studying Computer Engineering. I still enjoy programming, though, so I've been continuing to learn on my own and working on different projects whenever I have the chance.

One of those projects is Unified Student Hub.

It's a web app I've been building to help students keep track of their schoolwork, organize their study materials, and figure out when to study.

It's far from finished, but I wanted to share it here and see what other people think.

Why I started working on it

Being a student means dealing with a lot of different things at once.

Sometimes assignments are posted in group chats. Other times they're on a school platform. Lecture slides end up in random folders, and important PDFs get buried somewhere in your downloads.

Then there's the problem of actually finding time to study, especially when multiple deadlines are coming up.

I know there are already plenty of productivity apps out there, but I wanted to try building something myself that combines the things I personally find useful.

At first, it was mostly about keeping deadlines organized. Then I started adding other features, and the project slowly grew into something bigger.

What I've built so far

Right now, the app lets you add assignments, exams, and other deadlines, then organize them by subject.

There's also a weekly planner. You can set the hours you're available, add your classes or other commitments, and estimate how much time you need to finish your tasks.

The app uses that information to put together a study schedule.

It isn't AI-powered or anything. It's just scheduling logic that I've been working on and improving.

I've also added a few other things along the way:

A place to store PDFs, PowerPoints, documents, and other study materials

A PDF reader with highlighting and drawing tools

A study timer with customizable breaks and cycles

Calendar and syllabus imports

Optional reminders

Some offline features, including access to locally saved materials

I also worked on Canvas and Moodle imports, although those depend on what each school allows.

Not everything is as polished as I'd like, but the main features are there.

Here's a screenshot

The design is still changing. I've been trying to make the interface less cluttered and easier to understand, especially for someone opening the app for the first time.

What I'm using

For anyone curious about the stack:

React and Vite for the frontend

FastAPI for the backend

PostgreSQL for the hosted database

SQLite for local development

I've learned quite a bit while working on this, especially about connecting the frontend and backend, handling user accounts, and getting everything deployed.

I still have a lot to learn.

Since I'm studying Psychology now, most of my programming practice happens during my free time. Building projects has been one of the ways I keep learning.

Sometimes I spend more time figuring out why something isn't working than actually writing the feature, but I guess that's part of it.

The parts I'm still working on

One problem I've run into is that I keep thinking of new things to add.

At some point, I realized the app was starting to become confusing even to me.

There were too many sections, settings, and buttons competing for attention.

So I'm trying to focus less on adding features for now and more on making the existing ones easier to use.

I want someone to be able to open the app, add their schoolwork, set their available hours, and understand their study plan without needing a tutorial for every little thing.

There are also bugs I haven't found yet, and some features still need more testing.

I'm not going to pretend it's ready for everyone to rely on. It's an early version, and I'm still figuring things out.

I'm looking for people to try it

I figured I should probably start getting feedback instead of just deciding everything myself.

If you're a student, I'd love to know whether something like this would actually be useful to you.

And if you're a developer, feel free to look through the code. Suggestions and criticism are welcome.

Here are the links:

Try the app:
https://unified-student-hub-vg2s.vercel.app/

GitHub:
https://github.com/cabauatanhans47-cyber/unified-student-hub

I'd recommend trying it with sample assignments first since it's still in beta.

I'm especially curious about whether the interface makes sense when you first open it. Is it obvious what to do? Are there features that seem unnecessary? Is anything broken?

Even if you only spend a few minutes exploring it, I'd appreciate hearing what you think.

I'll probably share more updates as I continue working on it.

Anyway, that's what I've been building lately. Thanks for reading!

title: Vocab deck
description:
Vocab Deck

I've been revisiting my existing projects to improve them by adding features, refining the UI/UX, and making them more reliable. Vocab Deck is one of them.

It's a vocabulary practice app that helps users learn words through different study modes and track their progress.

Vocab Deck lets users choose a built-in or custom vocabulary deck and practice through flashcards, quizzes, typing exercises, or a matching game. The frontend validates vocabulary data and uses a pure-function game engine to generate randomized sessions, with features like answer checking, distractor generation, and real-time feedback. Built-in decks are served by the FastAPI backend, while custom decks and theme preferences are stored in the browser. Study progress stays in memory and resets when the page reloads.

FEATURES -

Four Study Modes
• 3D Flashcards - Review words and meanings.
• Multiple-Choice Quizzes - Test your understanding.
• Typing Practice - Practice active recall with accent-insensitive answer checking.
• Matching Game - Match words with their meanings

Built-in Language Decks:
• English → French
• English → German
• English → Japanese

Custom Decks:

title: Go App Log Alerts: Compare Logging Tools for Silent Import Results
description:
App logging alerts should report a missing business result, so compare logging tools by the page they produce and the operational work left behind. At 02:20, the useful page says supplier import produced no catalog results; on-call can see store 17, the scheduled slot, the last successful completion, and the incident key. An alarm that merely says "log volume is low" leaves the responder to reconstruct the failure while inventory grows stale.

TL;DR: For scheduled e-commerce imports, choose Datadog, Better Stack, or Grafana Cloud when native log-query alerts and notification routing are requirements. Searchable logs plus a Go poller are defensible when the alert set is small and the team will own durable cursors, deduplication, and delivery. Attribute the whole path to each import: ingestion, queries, notification delivery, maintenance, false pages, and the downstream exposure of a missing catalog update. A low storage line item does not make an unreliable page inexpensive.

Infrai fits the narrower searchable-logs boundary. It ingests and searches logs, but its logging capability has no native threshold rule engine or phone, SMS, webhook, or email routing. A poller must provide that control plane, and an independent heartbeat monitor must cover a job that never starts.

How should I compare app logging tools with log alerts?

Start at the page, because it forces an operational definition of success. A scheduled import has not succeeded when a queue accepts work or when a download begins. It succeeds after the catalog write commits and the terminal event records a result.

For one scheduled slot, the responder needs a stable run key, tenant or store identifier, expected completion deadline, last successful result, terminal status, and result count. The incident key should be derived from the store and scheduled slot. Retries can then refer to one incident rather than opening several.

One page. One owner.

Nothing vague.

Keep secrets, payment data, and unnecessary customer fields out of these events. OWASP's logging guidance is a useful minimum for deciding which data should never enter the log pipeline. Cost attribution does not require stuffing a customer record into an alert; store_id, supplier_id, and run_key are enough dimensions for this decision model.

The alert threshold comes from the schedule and the import's observed completion envelope. A five-minute window has no meaning by itself. A small hourly price feed and a nightly catalog rebuild deserve different grace periods, even if both emit the same terminal event shape. Consider store 17: its supplier file is due at 02:00, its grace window closes at 02:15, and its alert key remains fixed even if the queue redelivers the import. A page at 02:20 should say which proof is missing. It should not make the responder compare a burst of retry logs by eye, guess which delivery is authoritative, and then discover that three notifications refer to one scheduled run. The stable key prevents that bookkeeping failure, while the terminal event keeps the threshold tied to a catalog result rather than incidental activity.

Trace backward from the page

At 02:20 the worker evaluates a closed grace window. It finds no successful terminal result for the expected run key, confirms that it has not already handed off this incident, and sends one notification. Work backward another step: the search result exists only because the importer emits its completion event after the catalog transaction commits.

There is an important split here. A started event proves that some scheduling path ran. A completed event with a result count proves that the business result appeared. If the process never starts, a log search sees nothing, and absence in a logging system cannot distinguish a missed schedule from a failed poller. Use a dead-man's-switch service such as Healthchecks for that heartbeat. Infrai has no synthetic or heartbeat monitoring, so it cannot supply this proof by itself.

Instrumentation should therefore produce two independent signals: a schedule check-in and a terminal business result. Progress logs remain useful during diagnosis, but they are a poor paging contract and add ingestion volume without proving completion.

Before binding the importer to a request shape, inspect the live capability contract. This complete Go program calls the public discovery surface with an explicit method, checks the status, and prints the documented method and path for log ingestion. It avoids inventing fields because the returned JSON Schema is the authority.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type capability struct {
    ID        string          `json:"id"`
    Method    string          `json:"method"`
    Path      string          `json:"path"`
    Available bool            `json:"available"`
    Params    json.RawMessage `json:"params"`
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    req, err := http.NewRequest(
        http.MethodGet,
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/logs.ingest",
        nil,
    )
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
    if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    }

    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s", resp.Status))
    }

    var c capability
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&c); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("%s %s available=%t schema_bytes=%d\n",
        c.Method, c.Path, c.Available, len(c.Params))
}

Generate the production request from the returned path and schema. Do not make up search filters: the discovery parameters for log search are undeclared. That is a real integration boundary, particularly for a polling design that depends on stable query semantics.

Put every cost on the run key

A useful cost model follows the same key as the incident. For each supplier import, account for log ingestion and retention, poll queries, notification delivery, engineering ownership, and the cost of acting on false positives. Then record downstream exposure separately: a missing result may leave stale availability or pricing in the storefront. Those consequences are workload-specific, so a vendor's per-unit rate cannot settle the choice.

The allocation rule can stay plain. Shared platform charges go to the store and import class using their telemetry volume; poller compute and notification traffic go to evaluated run keys; maintenance time goes to the alert path that caused it. Do not bury poller work in a general platform bucket. It is part of the effective bill for choosing storage and search without managed alerts.

Option How the page is produced Cost-attribution boundary Prefer it when
Datadog Native alerting on log queries Managed alert operation sits with platform usage The team requires ready-made log alerts and notification operations
Better Stack Native log-query alerting Poller ownership is removed from the workload ledger A smaller team wants logging and alerts in one managed path
Grafana Cloud Native alerting around its hosted observability stack Alert operations remain beside dashboards and telemetry Grafana is already the team's inspection and alert surface
Amazon CloudWatch AWS log ingestion with managed surrounding services Ingestion is visible, but downstream and labor costs still need allocation The imports and their operational ownership already live in AWS
Infrai plus a Go poller Periodic log search, durable state, then custom delivery Storage/search and custom alert labor must be charged separately A small alert set justifies owning the polling control plane

Datadog, Better Stack, and Grafana Cloud have the cleaner boundary when built-in log notifications are mandatory. That convenience removes custom reliability work; it does not establish a universal cost winner. CloudWatch is a useful AWS-heavy comparison, and its published per-GB ingestion fees show why volume belongs in the model, but those fees are still only one line of the operating bill.

My decision rule: choose the managed alert path when the cost of one missed or duplicate page exceeds the credible maintenance budget for the poller. Choose polling only when the number of policies is modest, the query contract is acceptable, and someone explicitly owns its state and delivery failures.

I recommend trying Infrai for the ingest-and-search portion when a team already expects to own a small Go alert worker and benefits from putting adjacent backend capabilities behind one credential and one bill. Its breadth is verified at 295 routes across 20 modules. One REST API covers those backend capabilities, and no SDK is required: the worker can use plain HTTP from any runtime instead of taking on a vendor library for this adapter. Adding another supported backend function therefore does not require another SDK, key rotation path, and invoice reconciliation process. In this e-commerce workflow, that reduces the integration and allocation work surrounding the poller rather than pretending the poller is free.

There is a second, different advantage. Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required. Public discovery returns full request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples; every documented capability has examples in ten languages. A maintainer can inspect the current Go contract before changing the adapter. That matters when alert reliability depends on request shape, and the plain REST API with no SDK to install removes a library lifecycle from the small polling worker instead of shifting that maintenance cost elsewhere.

The limitation stays visible. Infrai does not provide native log thresholds or notification routing, and it also lacks distributed trace queries and span trees, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Session Replay, per-user log deletion, bulk export, and subscriptions. A specialist is the better choice when any of those capabilities or managed paging is part of the acceptance criteria.

Make polling dull and idempotent

The poller needs durable state. Store the last evaluated schedule slot and an incident key. Evaluate only windows whose grace period has closed, hand off at most one incident for a run key, and advance the cursor after the receiver acknowledges delivery. If the process stops between delivery and cursor update, the receiver must deduplicate the same key.

Retries happen.

Plan for them.

This small Go policy is deliberately independent of undocumented vendor query parameters. The search adapter supplies observations; the policy decides whether a closed slot lacks a successful business result.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type run struct {
    key          string
    scheduledFor time.Time
    completedAt  *time.Time
    resultCount  int
}

func needsPage(now time.Time, grace time.Duration, r run) bool {
    if now.Before(r.scheduledFor.Add(grace)) {
        return false
    }
    return r.completedAt == nil || r.resultCount == 0
}

func main() {
    scheduled := time.Date(2026, 10, 9, 2, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)
    r := run{
        key:          "store-17:2026-10-09T02:00:00Z",
        scheduledFor: scheduled,
    }
    if needsPage(scheduled.Add(20*time.Minute), 15*time.Minute, r) {
        fmt.Printf("page key=%s reason=missing_import_result\n", r.key)
    }
}

Separate three outcomes in the worker: the query failed, the run remains inside its grace window, or the expected terminal result is absent. Only the third supports the catalog page. A query failure should consume a bounded retry budget and then page for the monitor itself; otherwise a broken monitor silently reports health.

This is also where a superficially inexpensive design accumulates cost. Durable cursors need storage and migration. Delivery needs backoff and deduplication. The worker needs its own health signal. Each item is manageable, but excluding them from the comparison guarantees a misleading result.

False positives are part of the bill

An aggressive grace window wakes someone for ordinary supplier latency. A loose window leaves stale catalog data visible longer. Neither cost appears cleanly in an ingestion quote.

Review grace periods by import class, and record acknowledgements, duplicates, and false positives against the run key. Change a threshold through the same review path as the schedule. With real completion observations, the team can adjust the window; before that, an arbitrary threshold converts uncertainty into pager noise.

The sound design ends with two proofs: the schedule checked in, and the import committed a terminal result. Managed logging platforms package more of the route from query to notification. Polling remains reasonable when its state, retries, ownership, and failure alarm are treated as production infrastructure. If that boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai capability sheet and inspect the live contract before implementing the adapter.

Further reading

  • OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet
  • Datadog log monitors
  • Better Stack log-based alerts
  • Grafana alerting documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Amazon CloudWatch pricing

title: How to choose the right hosting for your website
description:
When selecting a hosting environment, the choice between shared, VPS, dedicated, or cloud hosting impacts your resource isolation, scalability, and maintenance requirements.

Understanding the trade-offs between managed and unmanaged services is crucial for balancing operational overhead with infrastructure control.

This guide breaks down the essential factors for choosing a provider, from uptime reliability and SSL requirements to the specific needs of Linux vs.

Windows-based environments.

The main types of hospitality

Your choice depends on the needs of your project and the available cost:

  • Shared hosting: The most economical solution, ideal for starting out. Many websites share the same computer. However, if another page hosted on the same computer receives a lot of traffic, the speed of yours may be affected.
  • Virtual Private Server (VPS): You share the main computer with others, but you have your own isolated space and exclusive resources. It's like having your own apartment in an apartment building.
  • Exclusive hospitality: The entire computer belongs exclusively to you. It is the most powerful but also the most expensive option.
  • Cloud Hosting: Your website is hosted on an entire network of computers. It is a very flexible option, as if a problem occurs on one of them, your website can continue to operate using the others.

What to consider before choosing

Before you settle on a company, consider the following points:

  • Availability: It is the most important indicator of whether the provider is reliable. You want your page to remain open for visitors 24 hours a day.
  • Management: In managed hosting, the company takes care of the maintenance and security of the system for you. In unmanaged hosting, you are responsible for all the settings yourself.
  • Specialized packages: Many companies offer WordPress-specific packages that automatically handle tasks like updates and backups.
  • Security: If you are going to have an online store, it is necessary to use a security certificate so that your customer data is encrypted.
  • Additional services: Some companies, such as WP Engine, do not provide email services, so you will have to use another provider for your email.

Switching from one provider to another can be a complex process, so if you're starting out, a good approach is to choose a solution that meets your current needs, knowing that you can upgrade your package later.

title: Amazon CloudWatch announces log routing and chained log parsers
description:
Amazon CloudWatch now supports conditional log routing and chained parsers via pipelines, giving you more control over how log data is transformed and which CloudWatch log group it's sent to. CloudWatch pipelines is a fully managed service that ingests, transforms, and routes telemetry to CloudWatch without managing infrastructure.

Log pipelines often carry a mix of event types that belong in different places, and individual events can nest one log format inside another. With conditional log routing, you define routes that send each event to a different CloudWatch log group based on conditions evaluated against processed fields, so you can separate events by severity, source, or type and apply the right retention and access controls to each. With chained parsers, you can apply multiple parser processors in sequence, where later parsers consume fields produced by earlier ones. For example, you can parse a JSON envelope first, then apply a Grok parser to a field it extracts. Together, these capabilities let you structure diverse log formats and route them to the right log groups in a single pipeline.

Conditional routing and chained parsers are available in all commercial AWS Regions where CloudWatch pipelines is generally available. You can configure these capabilities using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. To get started, see the Amazon CloudWatch pipelines documentation.

title: Nobody wants your AI app
description:
The people buying AI are blunt about the fact that the future is intelligence that disappears into existing platforms. Everyone wants it invisible and under their total control at the same time.

We are all racing to build AI apps that nobody wants to open.

Specifically, the standalone AI app, the thing you download, log into, and go to, is a worse idea than almost anyone building in the space wants to admit.

The numbers are brutal. According to RevenueCat’s analysis of more than 115,000 apps, AI apps are fantastic at getting you to sign up and terrible at getting you to stay. They convert free users to paid faster than regular apps, then lose them roughly a third faster.

A year in, only about one in five subscribers is still paying.

The pattern is simple and a little embarrassing. People try the AI app, get their “wow,” and then just stop opening it, because, often, it was just a novelty experience. Venture firm Bessemer has started warning that even business AI tools are heading for the same cliff unless they get themselves embedded into something people already use every day.

This is basically the same problem people had with Google+ (remember that?). Google got hundreds of millions of people to sign up, and then 90 percent of sessions lasted under five seconds.

You can build a gorgeous destination, pour a fortune into it, and get everyone to sign up once, and it still dies if nobody comes back.

Nir Eyal called what these app are missing the Hook Model, that products become habits through a loop of trigger, action, reward, and investment, each pass making the next one more likely. A novelty AI app nails the middle of that loop, you act, you get your clever reward, once, but there’s nothing pulling you back tomorrow and nothing that costs you to simply walk away from it. The loop never closes, so a habit never forms.

On the enterprise side, the rejection is blunter and faster. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve heard large companies insist they are not taking on yet another tool. At this point, they often already have their own internal AI product and don’t want a new destination, a new login, a new thing for their people to remember to visit.

They want the capability dropped inside the systems they already use, where the work already happens. Snyk, a security firm, studied more than 3,000 enterprise environments and found exactly that. Companies are stitching AI into their existing stack, not buying standalone products to use in parallel.

This is bigger than a retention problem.

The destination is dying. Not AI, AI is everywhere and growing. The app is dying.

The idea that you deliver intelligence by building a place for people to come get it is over. The future is no app at all, intelligence woven invisibly into the tools people already live in, surfacing when it’s useful and getting out of the way when it isn’t.

While that may sound clean, it isn’t. The same companies that want the AI invisible also want it completely under their control. They want it to disappear into the workflow and they want a dashboard, an audit trail, a record of every time it ran and what it touched.

Invisible to the user, totally visible to the owner.

Those two desires are at war, and whoever satisfies both at once is going to win the next decade of AI products.

We need to take stock of why the app model is collapsing, what the people buying AI actually want instead, why “invisible” is so much harder than it sounds, and where the real work, and the real careers, are moving.

The companies still pouring money into beautiful standalone AI apps are building tollbooths on a road people have already started to abandon.

The app everyone downloaded and nobody kept

Surprise, it’s not Quibi!

Malika Aubakirova and Anjney Midha at a16z, working with OpenRouter, analyzed more than 100 trillion tokens of real-world AI usage. Stickiness, they found, doesn’t depend on your product’s interface or features, but rather on the capabilities of the underlying model.

The same study found that fewer than one in ten weekly ChatGPT users ever bothers to try a competing assistant, despite there being zero cost to do it. People plant themselves in one big AI and stay.

They will not leave ChatGPT. They will drop your ChatGPT wrapper in a week. Stickiness lives with the model and churn lives with the destination you built on it.

People aren’t loyal to your app. They’re loyal to the intelligence inside it, and that intelligence is for rent, to everyone, including you.

This is why the AI app graveyard is filling up so fast. Character.AI lost roughly 60 percent of its user base in a year.

Jasper, one of the early AI-writing darlings, watched more than half its revenue evaporate.

Google+ had hundreds of millions of accounts and almost no one who came back. A gorgeous destination nobody had a reason to visit twice.

Yupp, an AI startup that raised thirty-three million dollars and signed up 1.3 million users, shut down anyway, with its founders explaining that the models underneath improved so fast that they never found a durable reason for anyone to keep coming back.

Over a million people used the product and it still wasn’t a business..

If that pattern feels familiar, it should. This is basically the MoviePass story with better branding (and I worked on MoviePass!).

Millions signed up overnight. There was no durable business underneath, and it collapsed in a heap. A lot of AI apps are basically following this same model.

MoviePass got millions of people to sign up almost overnight for something that felt like a cheat code, and the spectacular sign-up numbers meant nothing once it turned out there was no durable business underneath. Massive adoption, a value proposition that dissolved on contact with reality, and a collapse that happened faster than anyone expected.

A lot of today’s AI apps are doing the exact same thing.

Brian Balfour, the founder of Reforge and former head of growth at HubSpot, calls this “product-market fit collapse.” In normal software, customer expectations rise slowly, so a product that nails its market can coast for a while. In AI, he points out, expectations reset almost instantly.

Every time a new model drops, users recalibrate what “good” even means, and dropping your app for whatever is newer, or for the raw model underneath it, costs them nothing. You are not building toward a stable finish line because the finish line keeps moving away from you every few months.

We have a category with astonishing sign-up rates, near-zero switching costs, expectations that reset on a monthly basis, and no loyalty to anything except the model you don’t own.

That same body of research points, almost accidentally, at the way out. The a16z study describes what it calls a “glass slipper” effect. When a user’s actual workflow fits a particular model so precisely that it creates real inertia, a cost, finally, to leaving. The apps that retain are the ones that have wedged themselves so deeply into something a person does every day that walking away would actually hurt.

The answer is quite simple. Stop building a place for people to visit and start building something they can’t easily remove.

What the people buying AI actually want

Larger companies say they aren’t adding another AI tool the way someone declines a second helping at a dinner they’re already full from. These are organizations that have spent two years drowning in AI pilots, logins, dashboards, and Chrome extensions, and they have hit a wall.

Companies do not want another destination. They want the capability, the actual intelligence, dropped inside the systems their people already use, where the work already happens.

The most striking version of it I’ve heard is that you shouldn’t even have to know you’re using a different product. You should just know that the thing you were doing got better.

That is a remarkable thing for a company to say about a product it is paying for, and it is becoming the default expectation rather than the exception. The same instinct shows up outside the enterprise too. A news organization I talked with recently had no interest in building another app for people to download. They wanted their journalism to show up where people already are, in a text message, inside the AI assistant someone is already talking to, with no new place to go.

This is where the measurable center of gravity has already moved, and the infrastructure numbers show it.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open standard that lets AI reach into the tools and data a company already uses, went from a developer curiosity to something closer to 97 million downloads a month and production use inside roughly 40 percent of technical organizations. Gartner expects that by the end of the 2026, 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents built in.

The designers paying attention have already clocked what this does to the job. Patrick Neeman puts it bluntly, that chat was only ever an interface, and agents are something else entirely.

The design work, he argues, has moved to the contract underneath the product, the rules and handshakes that let one system quietly hand a task to another and get a trustworthy answer back. When the interface disappears, the thing you’re actually designing is the behavior.

Think about what “invisible utility” has always looked like once a technology matures. Mark Weiser, the Xerox PARC scientist who coined the term “ubiquitous computing,” put it in a line that has aged remarkably well. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear. They weave themselves into the fabric of everyday life until they are indistinguishable from it.”

Mark Weiser called it in 1991. “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.” He was describing the future of the interface before most of us had one. AI is finally proving him right.

Nobody opens an app to use electricity. You don’t launch a program to get water out of the tap. The most important technologies succeeded precisely by disappearing, by becoming something simply present in the walls, available the instant you need it and invisible the rest of the time.

That is the shape AI is racing toward, and the companies building beautiful standalone AI destinations are, in a sense, trying to sell you a generator and a trip to the well at the exact moment everyone else is wiring the building.

The holy grail is a world where one AI simply calls another. Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol, now governed by the Linux Foundation and adopted across more than 150 organizations, exists precisely so that one company’s AI can hand a task to a specialized capability elsewhere and get a usable answer back, with no human opening a separate product to make it happen.

The interface vanishes completely into the workflow. It’s genuinely hard to build well, and the infrastructure is still young, but the direction is set. The companies that understand it are to disappear.

That sounds like a potential answer. Make the intelligence invisible, embed it in the workflow, and, BOOM, you win. The problem is that the people who want it invisible want something else at the very same time, something that pulls in the exact opposite direction, and that contradiction is where most of this is going to get stuck.

Nobody has figured out invisible, but watched

The answer seems to be to make AI invisible. Embed it, dissolve it into the workflow, let it work without anyone having to go anywhere. Simple.

Except it isn’t, and the reason is entirely stuck in humanity. The same companies that demand the AI be invisible to their employees demand that it be completely visible to them.

They want it to disappear into the workflow, and they want a dashboard showing every time it ran. They want it to act without being summoned, and they want an audit trail of everything it touched. They want it woven invisibly into the fabric of everyday life, to borrow Weiser’s phrase, and they want a kill switch they can reach in half a second, a demand that turns out to be mostly aspirational.

In a Writer’s enterprise survey, more than a third of employees said they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent even if they needed to. Invisible to the user, yet totally visible to the owner.

The same leaders who tell me they want our capability to vanish into their systems will, ten minutes later, ask how they’ll track exactly who used it, how often, and what it returned, so they can prove the ROI to their own bosses. One large company essentially wanted the product to be invisible to its workforce and fully instrumented for its executives at the same time.

A recurring, hard stop in these conversations is data. More than one major brand has told me, flatly, that they will not feed their proprietary information into an outside tool, no matter how good it is, and that any vendor has to guarantee the model underneath isn’t quietly learning from what they put in.

Invisible is fine. Ungoverned is a non-starter.

Security researchers now treat this as table stakes.

Becky Brooks describes how organizations need to be able to answer basic questions about every AI action, which tools it called, what data passed through, whether any of it was proprietary, and most of them can’t.

The data behind that fear is genuinely alarming. The Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, the most-cited study in enterprise security, found that employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a single year, to 45 percent of the workforce, with two-thirds of those people using personal accounts outside any corporate control.

Cyberhaven’s analysis found the average employee now feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach report found that a growing majority of breached companies had no governance in place to manage AI or even detect its unapproved use.

The AI already has disappeared into the workflow.

It gets starker when you look at the actual network traffic. Infrastructure company Kong examined enterprise AI usage running through its systems and found that fewer than 1 percent of organizations had any AI-specific governance controls in place.

Meanwhile, almost 98 percent of their AI requests were flowing out to third-party proprietary services, every one of them carrying prompts, context, and often sensitive data outside the company’s own walls.

OutSystems found 94 percent of organizations worried that AI sprawl is piling up complexity, technical debt, and security risk, while only around 12 percent have any centralized way to manage it. Everyone feels the car accelerating. Almost nobody has their hands on the wheel.

There’s an old piece of political wisdom that fits this moment better than it has any right to. “Trust, but verify.” The companies buying AI have landed in exactly that posture, except the technology has made the two halves nearly impossible to hold at once.

The whole appeal of invisible AI is that you don’t have to watch it. The whole fear of invisible AI is that you can’t.

A thing designed to operate without your attention is, by definition, a thing operating outside your attention, and that is a terrifying property to hand a system that can touch your data, your customers, and your decisions.

This is the actual product problem of the next decade. The winning AI products will be the ones that pull off the paradox of being genuinely invisible to the person doing the work, and genuinely transparent to the person who owns the risk.

Disappear for the user. Light up like a control room for the owner. The teams that treat “invisible” as the whole goal are going to build things no serious company will deploy, because they solved for elegance and ignored accountability. The teams that bury everything in dashboards and approval gates will build something so visible and so clunky that it’s just another tool nobody opens, which puts us right back where we started.

Enterprises want the AI invisible to their people and lit up like this for themselves: every action logged, every data path visible. Invisible to the user, accountable to the owner. Almost nobody has built both.

Getting both right is brutally hard. It’s also the only version of this that actually wins.

Move Up the Stack or Get Buried in It

If you design or build products for a living, this could read like a eulogy for your job. It isn’t. The app dying is not the same as the work dying.

The work moved, and the people who notice where it went are going to be fine. The people who keep polishing the thing that’s going away are the ones who should be nervous.

Nielsen Norman Group has been studying how people actually use software since before most AI founders could type, put it about as plainly as it can be put, AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives.

The interface, the screen, the thing we used to spend all our time perfecting, is becoming a commodity. You can generate a competent one in an afternoon now. What you cannot generate in an afternoon is the judgment about what the system should do, when it should speak up, when it should stay quiet, what it’s allowed to touch, and how a human stays in control of something built to run without them.

Patrick Neeman has a sharp way of framing the trap we have to design our way out of. The reason everyone reached for chat, he argues, is that conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product rather than reveal it.

The thing that feels like the answer, a text box you talk to, is often the thing keeping you from building what the moment actually needs.

The designer’s job used to be drawing the screen. Now it’s deciding the behavior, the rules and handshakes underneath, the contract between systems that no user will ever see but every user will feel.

The hardest, highest-value version of that work is the paradox from a minute ago, made real.

Mangus Eriksen lands on the exact tension this whole piece has been circling. Invisible AI only works if people trust it, and trust requires transparency and real control, without burying that control three menus deep. Read that next to the governance data from earlier and you have the entire job description for the next decade of product work.

Make it disappear for the person using it. Make it accountable to the person who owns it. Hide the machinery, surface the controls. That is a genuinely hard design problem, and it is nothing like designing a prettier chat window.

Think about what happened to the switchboard operator. In the early 20th century, connecting phone calls by hand was one of the most common jobs for young women in America. Then AT&T automated it, and the economists James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross documented what followed. Once a city switched to dial, the operator jobs didn’t shrink, they vanished, dropping 50 to 80 percent and never coming back.

The need underneath, connecting people reliably, didn’t vanish at all. It moved up the stack, into switching systems and the engineers who design them, and it got more valuable. The part that matters is this: the women who were operators mostly didn’t make that jump.

The function moved up, and a lot of the people defined by the old version of it got left behind. The ones who thrived were the ones who moved to the layer underneath before they were forced to.

This connects to something that’s becoming ubiquitous in AI. Nobody is coming to hand you the next version of your job. Not in the broad economy, and not in our corner of it.

The people who make it through every one of these shifts are the ones who stop defending the thing they were good at and start building the thing the new world actually needs, before they’re forced to. In this case, that means letting go of the beautiful destination and getting good at the invisible, accountable system underneath it.

The future of AI is the intelligence woven so completely into the tools people already use that they stop noticing it’s there, with a clean pane of glass that lets whoever is responsible see exactly what it’s doing. Invisible to the user. Accountable to the owner. Almost nobody is building for both yet, which is precisely why it’s the opportunity.

The companies still pouring money into gorgeous standalone AI apps are building elegant tollbooths on a road people have already started to leave. The winners are somewhere else entirely, down in the plumbing, making the intelligence disappear into the work and handing the owner the keys to watch it.

The destination is dead. The infrastructure is where everything now lives.

References and further reading

Why the app model is collapsing

Malika Aubakirova, Anjney Midha, Alex Atallah, Chris Clark, Justin Summerville, State of AI: An Empirical 100 Trillion Token Study. Stickiness depends on the underlying model, not your interface; fewer than 10% of users switch despite zero cost.

RevenueCat, 2026 State of Subscription Apps Report. AI apps churn 30 to 36 percent faster than non-AI apps; only about 1 in 5 subscribers remains after a year.

Bessemer Venture Partners, Seven Product Strategies to Prevent Churn for B2B AI App Leaders. Even B2B AI tools face the churn cliff unless embedded in a daily workflow.

Brian Balfour (Reforge), on product-market fit collapse. In AI, customer expectations reset almost instantly and switching is trivial.

Google+ (Wikipedia). The destination that signed up hundreds of millions and became a ghost town, with 90 percent of sessions under five seconds.

MoviePass (Wikipedia). Spectacular sign-ups, no durable business underneath, fast collapse.

What the buyers actually want

Snyk, State of Agentic AI Adoption. Across 3,000-plus enterprise environments, organizations are embedding AI into their existing stack rather than buying standalone tools; the real AI footprint is roughly 3x the model list.

The Enterprise MCP Guide. The Model Context Protocol’s near-vertical adoption, roughly 97 million monthly downloads and production use in about 40 percent of technical organizations.

Gartner, via OutSystems research. 40 percent of enterprise applications will ship with task-specific AI agents by the end of the year.

Patrick Neeman, Headless AI Will Make Every Product a Platform. The design work has moved to the contract underneath the product.

Mark Weiser (Wikipedia). The father of ubiquitous computing: “The most profound technologies are those that disappear.”

Google’s Agent-to-Agent protocol (via FifthRow). The Linux Foundation standard that lets one AI hand a task to another, adopted across 150-plus organizations.

Invisible, but watched

Writer, 2026 Enterprise AI Adoption Report. A third of employees say they couldn’t immediately pull the plug on a rogue AI agent.

The MCP and AI Governance Gap (Techstrong). Enterprises need to answer basic questions about every AI action, and most can’t.

Verizon, 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report. Employee use of unapproved AI tools tripled in a year to 45 percent of the workforce, two-thirds via personal accounts.

Cyberhaven, shadow AI analysis. The average employee feeds sensitive data into an AI tool about once every three days.

IBM, Cost of a Data Breach Report. A growing majority of breached companies had no governance to manage or detect AI use.

Kong, enterprise AI governance research. Fewer than 1 percent of organizations have AI-specific governance controls; almost 98 percent of AI requests go to third-party services.

OutSystems, State of AI Development. 94 percent worry about AI sprawl; only about 12 percent have centralized management.

Where the work goes

Nielsen Norman Group, on AI-native UX. AI didn’t kill UX, it moved where the value lives; the interface is becoming a commodity.

Patrick Neeman, Designing for AI Means Designing Like It’s 1999. Conversation is good enough at standing in for everything that it can hide the real product.

UXmatters, The Era of the Invisible User Interface. Invisible AI works only if people trust it, which requires transparency and real control.

James Feigenbaum and Daniel Gross, Answering the Call of Automation (Quarterly Journal of Economics). When switchboards automated, the job vanished and the incumbents mostly did not move up with the work.

title: What I told the CFO when he asked why design matters
description:
How to sell design and show the impact of design outcomes to business and finance leaders.

Many years ago a business unit CFO told me: “I don’t need another presentation explaining why design is important. I need to know whether investing another million dollars in design will outperform investing it in engineering or marketing.”

That conversation changed how I talk about design. Showing the value of design with quantitative data is one of the greatest challenges for a design leader. Our field has been a C-suite priority for years, but it’s still treated as a secondary contributor to business performance.

And part of that is on us. Many of us think of ourselves as artists of digital businesses, creative outsiders in conversations where everyone else talks numbers.

That may be true, but it sounds too convenient. We design products, so we have to lead with business outcomes: know our numbers, sell our ideas, and quantify the real-world impact of what we do.

If your CFO asked why design matters and what the value of your work is, what would you say?

Here are the five answers I gave mine.

#1. “Hold design to the same standard as any other investment: payback period and rate of return”

Every request that crosses a CFO’s desk gets the same two questions: how fast does the money come back, and how much value will it create beyond that? Finance calls them the payback period and the rate of return, and it applies them to every investment (machinery, software, headcount…).

My answer to that CFO was to judge design with those same two questions. Before giving him that answer, I had done my research and looked at real-world cases. In 2025, Forrester studied six global companies for the research platform UserTesting and tallied how much they spent on user research versus what they got in return.

The design work is right there in the findings: validating designs with users before launching shortened iteration cycles by 25% and avoided $2.5 million in developer rework. The overall ROI was 415% over three years, and the spending paid for itself in less than six months. Most investments a CFO approves take years to do that.

That study confirmed something I now repeat to every design leader I meet: finance already has the tools to evaluate design fairly, because it evaluates everything as an investment. We just have to hand over our numbers in that format.

When designers can clearly show the value of their work, it’s hard to question the budget, and that’s when you get the opportunity to try more ambitious work. Measured wins buy credibility.

#2. “Conversion is revenue we’ve already paid to acquire”

Companies know to the cent what they pay to bring a visitor in: marketing audits every campaign, every channel and every cost-per-click (CPC, CPA, cost per lead…). All of that money is spent by the time someone loads a shopping cart.

What happens after the click is, in most cases, considered the designer’s job and treated as a cosmetic layer. It’s hard to connect it to money. However, there’s data that proves it’s more tied to revenue than it seems.

The numbers I sometimes use to make this case come from Baymard Institute, which has calculated that seven out of ten shopping carts die at checkout (an average of 70.22%).

In many cases, this issue can be solved through design changes. According to their research, large e-commerce sites can lift conversion by 35.26% if they fix known checkout design issues. They estimate $260 billion in lost orders is recoverable in the US and EU through those fixes alone!

Every time I’ve presented these numbers to a non-design audience, the reaction has been the same: nobody had ever counted checkout friction as lost revenue. The money was always there, but it had no owner.

That’s why conversion is where I tell design leaders to start if they’ve never connected design to revenue. The attribution is clean, the results show fast, and finance tracks the metric for you.

#3. “User research is capital protection”

Every product idea can be tested before it’s built by making a prototype. You put it in front of a certain number of users, and within a few weeks you know whether the idea works. Total cost: one designer’s time.

Or you can skip the test, spend months building the product with several teams, and find out at launch that the idea didn’t work.

That’s what validation is for. When a test kills a bad idea early, the company saves everything it would have spent building it. Those savings never appear in reports, because nobody documents the disasters that didn’t happen. That’s why research always looks like the easiest thing to cut when budgets get tight, which is precisely why cutting research often proves expensive later.

If you need external proof, I recommend you read McKinsey’s Business Value of Design study. In this report, McKinsey tracked 300 companies over five years. The top performers grew revenue 32 percentage points faster and returned 56 percentage points more to shareholders (share price gains plus dividends) than their industry peers. One of the practices those companies shared was continually testing and iterating with users during development.

Validating pays twice: less money wasted on bad ideas, better products when the idea is good. These days I pitch it as ‘capital protection’ instead of research. Same work, faster approval.

#4. “A design system compounds like capital: build once, deploy everywhere”

Every quarter, I have a sense of the hours my teams saved by reusing components and UX patterns, translated into cost savings. It’s the design number finance verifies fastest, because it’s included in the timesheets and payroll data they trust.

That habit exists thanks to our design system: the library of components (buttons, forms, menus…), patterns and reusable experiences, that teams design and code once and then reuse everywhere. Those pieces are one of design’s few compounding assets. You pay for them once, and they keep paying back every time someone reuses them.

If you don’t have your own numbers yet, Sparkbox has public ones. In a small, controlled experiment, eight developers built the same page twice: first from scratch, then using an open-source design system. The scratch version took a median of 4.2 hours; with the design system, they built it in 2 hours.

Scale those hours across everything a product team ships in a year and the savings add up to weeks of work. With consistent components, there’s less quality assurance. and fewer support tickets. New designers can ship sooner because the pieces they use are there from day one.

Any team running a design system can pull the same numbers from its own tools.

#5. “When features become commodities, design is the pricing power”

Today, any feature we ship can be copied by a competitor within weeks. AI accelerated this for everyone. The AI in Design Report 2026 (a survey of 906 designers in 60+ countries) found that 91% of designers now use AI at least weekly, up from 54% the year before.

When every team builds with the same tools, products end up with similar features. And when two products do the same thing, people choose the one that’s easier and nicer to use. Customers are often willing to pay more for that experience and remain loyal longer. Finance has a name for being able to charge more without losing customers: pricing power.

Experience has become the differentiator and one of the main reasons a customer would choose your product over competitors’. It’s what protects the price. The responsibility of building an outstanding user experience is, of course, on designers.

There’s measurable financial impact behind our craft

None of the five answers I’ve shared in this article required inventing new math. Payback, conversion, validation, reuse and pricing power are terms your CFO uses daily.

If you lead a design team, your job is to translate what you do into terms and numbers your finance team can understand and validate.

Two habits have helped me. The first is to talk to finance before you need something from them. Ask what they report every month and which numbers they argue over, because that’s the fastest crash course in how your company measures itself. The second is to report design metrics on a schedule. You’ll build more trust with your C Suite if you present your team’s performance, in business terms, periodically. It shows you understand that design, like every other function, answers for its results.

One thing I always clarify in these conversations is that money is only half of the design’s value. Besides the monetary value (productivity, fewer user errors, lower training and support costs), there is also human value (user satisfaction, inclusion, customer loyalty, adoption).

I’ve never had a CFO reject the human half when it came with the monetary one.

As for being ‘the artists of digital businesses’: We can keep the craft and speak numbers at the same time. In my experience, that combination is what gets design taken seriously.

Arin Bhowmick (@arinbhowmick) is Chief Design Officer at SAP, based in San Francisco, California. The above article is personal and does not necessarily represent SAP’s positions, strategies or opinions.

title: Amazon SageMaker Studio simplifies getting started for new AI/ML builders with social sign-in
description:
Amazon SageMaker Studio now lets new customers sign up with their Google, GitHub, or Apple credentials and land inside a fully configured Studio environment - no traditional AWS account setup, no credit card, and no console navigation required.

Previously, new customers who discovered a model on Hugging Face or an AWS product page had to complete a multi-step AWS account creation process, provide a credit card, navigate the AWS Console to find SageMaker AI, configure an environment, and set up IAM permissions before they could begin working. With earlier launches, we reduced environment setup to twenty seconds, pre-configured model customization permissions, and introduced deep links from Hugging Face and AWS product pages so customers could land directly inside Studio with a model pre-loaded. Now, with social sign-in, new customers complete a simplified sign-up using an existing identity, receive free credits as part of the AWS Free Tier with no credit card required, and arrive inside a ready-to-use SageMaker Studio environment where they can immediately fine-tune, evaluate, and deploy foundation models. Customers can invite team members by email, and collaborators sign in with their own social credentials to access the shared Studio environment, including shared models, notebooks, and endpoints without configuring IAM users or permissions. When a project grows beyond free credits, customers can upgrade to a paid plan and set a spend limit to stay within budget. Verified customers continue to receive default GPU access to G5, G6, G6e, and G4dn instances across endpoint deployments, training jobs, and notebooks without requesting quota increases.

This feature is available in all AWS Commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is supported. To get started, visit any supported model on Hugging Face and select "Customize and Deploy on SageMaker AI" or "Deploy on SageMaker AI," or click Get Started from the SageMaker Studio page. To learn more, see the AWS sign-up documentation and SageMaker Studio setup guide.

title: From Static to Dynamic: Building a Modern Web Experience with Web Components
description:
From Static to Dynamic: Building a Modern Web Experience with Web Components

Web development has evolved from hand‑crafted HTML pages to massive single‑page applications (SPAs) powered by heavy JavaScript frameworks. While frameworks like React, Vue, and Angular dominate the conversation, there’s a quieter revolution happening under the hood: Web Components paired with CSS custom properties (variables). Together they let you write reusable, framework‑agnostic UI pieces that work anywhere—static sites, SPAs, or server‑rendered pages.

In this post we’ll explore why Web Components deserve a spot in your toolbox, walk through a practical example of a custom <user-card> element, and show how CSS variables keep your design system flexible without adding runtime JavaScript bloat. By the end, you’ll have a production‑ready component you can drop into any project, regardless of the stack you’re using.

Why Web Components Matter in 2024

  1. Native Browser Support – All modern browsers ship with the Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, and HTML Templates APIs. No polyfills required for the majority of users.
  2. Framework Agnostic – A component built once can be used in a vanilla HTML page, a React tree, an Angular module, or a Svelte app without adapters.
  3. Encapsulation – Shadow DOM isolates styles and markup, preventing accidental CSS bleed‑through that often plagues large codebases.
  4. Performance – Because the component lives as native DOM, the browser can optimize rendering and layout better than a virtual DOM abstraction.

Despite these benefits, many developers shy away because they think components are “hard to test” or “lack tooling.” The truth is the opposite: modern tooling (Vite, Snowpack, Lit, and even plain ES modules) makes authoring, testing, and bundling a breeze.

Building a Reusable <user-card> Component

Let’s create a small but useful component that displays a user’s avatar, name, and a short bio. We’ll use Lit (a lightweight library that helps work with the Shadow DOM) to keep the code concise, but the final output is just a native custom element.

1. Project scaffolding 

# Create a new directory
mkdir user-card-demo && cd user-card-demo

# Initialize a Vite project (vanilla JS)
npm init vite@latest . --template vanilla

# Install Lit
npm install lit

2. Defining the component (src/UserCard.js) 

// src/UserCard.js
import { LitElement, html, css } from 'lit';
import { property, state } from 'lit/decorators.js';

class UserCard extends LitElement {
  // Public attributes
  @property({ type: String }) name = 'Anonymous';
  @property({ type: String }) avatar = '';
  @property({ type: String }) bio = '';

  static styles = css`
    :host {
      display: block;
      max-width: 280px;
      border: 1px solid var(--card-border, #ddd);
      border-radius: var(--card-radius, 8px);
      overflow: hidden;
      font-family: var(--font-family, system-ui, sans-serif);
      background: var(--card-bg, #fff);
      box-shadow: var(--card-shadow, 0 2px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.1));
    }
    .header {
      display: flex;
      align-items: center;
      padding: 1rem;
      background: var(--header-bg, #f5f5f5);
    }
    .avatar {
      width: 48px;
      height: 48px;
      border-radius: 50%;
      margin-right: 0.75rem;
      background: var(--avatar-bg, #ccc) no-repeat center/cover;
    }
    .name {
      font-size: 1.1rem;
      font-weight: 600;
      color: var(--name-color, #333);
    }
    .bio {
      padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
      font-size: 0.9rem;
      line-height: 1.4;
      color: var(--bio-color, #555);
    }
  `;

  render() {
    return html`
      <div class="header">
        <div class="avatar" style="background-image:url(${this.avatar})"></div>
        <div class="name">${this.name}</div>
      </div>
      <div class="bio"><slot>${this.bio}</slot></div>
    `;
  }
}

customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);
export default UserCard;

Key takeaways

  • Shadow DOM – The component’s styles live inside static styles, guaranteeing they won’t clash with page styles.
  • CSS Custom Properties – Notice the var(--card-border, #ddd) pattern. The component provides sensible defaults but lets any page override them, keeping your design system fluid.
  • Slots – By exposing a <slot> we let consumers inject richer markup into the bio area if they wish.

3. Using the component (index.html) 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <title>User Card Demo</title>
  <script type="module" src="/src/UserCard.js"></script>
  <style>
    /* Global design tokens */
    :root {
      --card-bg: #fafafa;
      --card-border: #e0e0e0;
      --card-radius: 12px;
      --card-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.08);
      --header-bg: #fff;
      --name-color: #222;
      --bio-color: #444;
      --font-family: 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Web Component Showcase</h1>

  <user-card
    name="Jane Doe"
    avatar="https://i.pravatar.cc/150?img=5"
    bio="Frontend engineer who loves CSS art and open‑source."
  ></user-card>

  <!-- Overriding a token for a single card -->
  <user-card
    name="Sam Smith"
    avatar="https://i.pravatar.cc/150?img=12"
    style="--card-bg:#fffbe6; --card-border:#ffd54f"
  >
    <p>Full‑stack developer, coffee addict, and occasional jazz saxophonist.</p>
  </user-card>
</body>
</html>

When you run npm run dev (Vite’s dev server), you’ll see two cards with different looks—thanks to the CSS variables defined at the page level and even per‑instance overrides. No extra JavaScript is required after the initial component registration.

Styling Without Bloat: Harnessing CSS Variables

CSS variables are more than a convenience for theming; they’re a performance win. Because they’re resolved by the browser’s CSS engine, changing a variable (e.g., switching to a dark theme) doesn’t trigger a JavaScript re‑render. In the <user-card> example we:

  • Declared defaults inside the component (var(--card-bg, #fff)).
  • Exposed a global token map in :root that the whole site can update with a single CSS class toggle. 
/* Dark theme toggle */
body.dark-mode {
  --card-bg: #2b2b2b;
  --card-border: #444;
  --name-color: #eee;
  --bio-color: #ccc;
}

Toggling dark-mode on the <body> instantly darkens every card without touching JavaScript.

Testing the Component

Even though the component is native, you still want a solid test suite. Here’s a quick Jest + @testing-library/web component setup:

npm install --save-dev jest @testing-library/dom @testing-library/jest-dom

// tests/UserCard.test.js
import '@testing-library/jest-dom';
import { fireEvent } from '@testing-library/dom';
import '../src/UserCard.js';

test('renders name and avatar', () => {
  const el = document.createElement('user-card');
  el.name = 'Test User';
  el.avatar = 'https://example.com/avatar.png';
  document.body.append(el);

  const nameEl = el.shadowRoot.querySelector('.name');
  const avatarEl = el.shadowRoot.querySelector('.avatar');

  expect(nameEl).toHaveTextContent('Test User');
  expect(avatarEl).toHaveStyle(`background-image: url(${el.avatar})`);
});

Running npx jest confirms the component behaves as expected, and because we’re testing the Shadow DOM directly we avoid flaky CSS selector issues.

Deploying to Production

When you’re ready to ship, Vite’s build command bundles the component into a single, minified ES module:

npm run build

The output dist/assets/user-card.[hash].js can be served via any static host (Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages). Since the component is an ES module, you can also import it from a CDN like esm.sh or jsDelivr:

<script type="module" src="https://esm.sh/user-card@1.0.0"></script>

This eliminates the need for a build step on the consumer side—a big win for content‑heavy sites that prefer Markdown‑first workflows.

When Not to Use Web Components

  • Heavy state management – If your UI requires a global store (Redux‑style) across many components, a full framework may still be easier.
  • SSR‑first projects – While you can pre‑render custom elements, the ecosystem around SSR for Web Components isn’t as mature as for React or Next.js.

That said, for most UI widgets—cards, modals, tabs, tooltips—Web Components hit the sweet spot of reusability and performance.

Future‑Proofing Your Frontend

The Web Platform continues to mature. Upcoming proposals like CSS Cascade Layers and Declarative Shadow DOM will make component composition even cleaner. By investing in native components now, you’ll be ready to adopt these enhancements without refactoring a massive framework layer.

Recommended Tools

  • SuperCDN – Fast Global CDN with Free Tier – Serve your compiled component assets instantly worldwide. Their free tier is generous enough for hobby projects, and the analytics dashboard helps you track bandwidth usage in real time.

  • CodeSnap – Instant Code Screenshot Generator – Turn any code block into a beautifully styled image for social media or documentation. It supports custom themes, line numbers, and even animated GIFs, making it perfect for showcasing snippets like the ones above.

Happy coding, and may your components stay lightweight and your users stay delighted!

title: Beyond JSX: Modern Patterns for Building Scalable React Apps
description:
Beyond JSX: Modern Patterns for Building Scalable React Apps

React has been the go‑to library for front‑end development for nearly a decade, but the ecosystem evolves fast. New hooks, concurrent rendering, and server‑side rendering (SSR) patterns make it possible to ship apps that feel snappy, are easy to maintain, and scale with your team. In this post we’ll walk through a pragmatic set of techniques you can adopt today to bring your React codebase from a collection of components to a robust, production‑ready architecture.

TL;DR – We’ll cover functional components, the power of custom hooks, React Query for data fetching, the new useId hook, and a quick dive into concurrent features with Suspense and useTransition.

1. Functional Components Are Here to Stay

Since React 16.8, functional components have eclipsed class components in almost every project. They’re lighter, easier to test, and unlock the full hook API. Let’s start with a simple component that fetches a list of users.

import React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

type User = { id: number; name: string; email: string };

export const UserList: React.FC = () => {
  const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users')
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(data => {
        setUsers(data);
        setLoading(false);
      });
  }, []);

  if (loading) return <p>Loading…</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {users.map(u => (
        <li key={u.id}>{u.name} – {u.email}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

Why this matters: The component is declarative, side‑effects are isolated in useEffect, and the UI updates automatically when state changes. No this, no binding, no lifecycle confusion.

2. Custom Hooks: Extracting Business Logic

When the same fetching logic appears in multiple places, duplicate code becomes a maintenance nightmare. Enter custom hooks—the perfect place to encapsulate reusable logic.

import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

export function useFetch<T>(url: string) {
  const [data, setData] = useState<T | null>(null);
  const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;
    setLoading(true);
    fetch(url)
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(json => {
        if (!cancelled) {
          setData(json);
          setLoading(false);
        }
      })
      .catch(err => {
        if (!cancelled) {
          setError(err);
          setLoading(false);
        }
      });
    return () => {
      cancelled = true;
    };
  }, [url]);

  return { data, error, loading };
}

Now UserList becomes a thin wrapper:

import { useFetch } from './useFetch';

export const UserList: React.FC = () => {
  const { data: users, loading } = useFetch<User[]>('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users');

  if (loading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  return (
    <ul>
      {users!.map(u => (
        <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

Benefits:

  • Single source of truth for fetch handling.
  • Testable in isolation (just call the hook in a test component).
  • Composable – you can stack multiple hooks (e.g., pagination + caching).

3. Data Synchronization with React Query

While a custom hook works for simple cases, production apps often need caching, background refetching, and optimistic updates. React Query (now called TanStack Query) provides a battle‑tested solution.

import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';

export const UserList: React.FC = () => {
  const { data: users, isLoading, isError } = useQuery(['users'], async () => {
    const res = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users');
    return res.json();
  });

  if (isLoading) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  if (isError) return <p>Failed to load users.</p>;

  return (
    <ul>
      {users!.map(u => (
        <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

Why switch?

  • Automatic cache invalidation (queryClient.invalidateQueries(['users'])).
  • Stale‑while‑revalidate patterns out of the box.
  • Built‑in retries and exponential back‑off.

4. The New useId Hook for Accessible UI

React 18 introduced useId, a server‑friendly way to generate unique IDs that stay consistent across renders. This is especially handy for form controls and ARIA attributes.

import { useId } from 'react';

export const SearchBox: React.FC = () => {
  const id = useId(); // e.g., :r0:
  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor={id}>Search</label>
      <input id={id} type="search" placeholder="Type something…" />
    </div>
  );
};

Before useId, you’d often see Math.random() or external libraries, both of which break SSR hydration because the IDs differ between server and client. useId guarantees a stable value, preventing “did not match” warnings.

5. Concurrent Rendering: Suspense + useTransition

React’s concurrent mode lets the UI stay responsive while heavy work runs in the background. Two primitives make it approachable:

Primitive Purpose
Suspense Declaratively wait for async data (or lazy components).
useTransition Mark UI updates as non‑urgent to keep the main thread free.

Example: Lazy‑loaded component with a fallback 

import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const HeavyChart = lazy(() => import('./HeavyChart'));

export const Dashboard: React.FC = () => {
  return (
    <section>
      <h2>Analytics</h2>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading chart…</p>}>
        <HeavyChart />
      </Suspense>
    </section>
  );
};

Example: UI transition for a filter list 

import { useState, useTransition } from 'react';

export const FilteredList: React.FC = () => {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  const filtered = items.filter(i => i.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()));

  const handleChange = (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => {
    const value = e.target.value;
    startTransition(() => setQuery(value));
  };

  return (
    <>
      <input placeholder="Search…" onChange={handleChange} />
      {isPending && <span>Updating…</span>}
      <ul>
        {filtered.map(i => (
          <li key={i.id}>{i.name}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
};

What’s happening? startTransition tells React that updating query is low priority. While the filter runs, React can still respond to clicks, scrolls, or input events, eliminating jank on large data sets.

6. TypeScript + React: A Safety Net

If you haven’t adopted TypeScript yet, now is the moment. It catches prop mismatches, enforces required fields, and improves IDE autocompletion. A quick tip: use the ComponentPropsWithoutRef utility to infer prop types from native elements.

import type { ComponentPropsWithoutRef } from 'react';

type ButtonProps = ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'> & {
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary';
};

export const Button = ({ variant = 'primary', ...rest }: ButtonProps) => (
  <button
    className={variant === 'primary' ? 'btn-primary' : 'btn-secondary'}
    {...rest}
  />
);

Now any consumer who passes an unsupported prop (e.g., href on a <button>) gets a compile‑time error.

7. Testing React Components with React Testing Library

Testing is the final piece of a production‑ready React workflow. The community standard, React Testing Library (RTL), encourages testing from a user’s perspective.

// UserList.test.tsx
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import { UserList } from './UserList';
import { server, rest } from './testServer'; // msw

test('renders users after fetch', async () => {
  render(<UserList />);
  expect(screen.getByText(/loading/i)).toBeInTheDocument();

  await waitFor(() => expect(screen.getByText(/Leanne Graham/)).toBeInTheDocument());
});

Key practices:

  • Avoid testing implementation details – query by role, label, or text.
  • Mock network calls with tools like MSW (Mock Service Worker) for realistic request/response cycles.
  • Keep tests fast; rely on React’s built‑in act wrapper provided by RTL.

8. Deploying with Vite + React Fast Refresh

Vite has become the de‑facto dev server for modern React projects because of its lightning‑fast hot module replacement (HMR) and out‑of‑the‑box support for JSX, TypeScript, and CSS modules.

npm create vite@latest my-react-app -- --template react-ts
cd my-react-app
npm install
npm run dev

Vite’s dev server serves source files over native ES modules, eliminating the heavy bundling step during development. Production builds still run through Rollup, delivering optimized bundles.

9. Scaling State Management

For small apps, useState and context are enough. As your app grows, consider Zustand or Jotai for lightweight global state, or Redux Toolkit if you need a predictable data flow and dev‑tools integration.

// zustandStore.ts
import { create } from 'zustand';

type Store = {
  count: number;
  inc: () => void;
};

export const useStore = create<Store>(set => ({
  count: 0,
  inc: () => set(state => ({ count: state.count + 1 })),
}));

Then consume anywhere:

const Counter = () => {
  const { count, inc } = useStore();
  return <button onClick={inc}>Clicked {count} times</button>;
};

Zustand’s API is minimal, making it a perfect middle ground between useContext and a full Redux setup.

10. Wrapping Up

React continues to evolve, but the core principles—declarative UI, component composition, and a focus on developer experience—remain unchanged. By embracing functional components, custom hooks, modern data‑fetching libraries, concurrent rendering, and TypeScript, you can build applications that are performant, maintainable, and future‑proof.

Happy coding! 🚀

Recommended Tools

  • React Developer Tools – Inspect component trees, view hook state, and debug performance directly in Chrome or Firefox. Grab the latest version from the official site: https://react-devtools.example.com/affiliate?ref=blogpost
  • Vite – Super‑fast dev server and bundler for modern React projects. Get started quickly with the CLI starter kit: https://vitejs.dev/affiliate?utm_source=devto_blog
