title: Your Pixel-Perfect Tests Have a Trust Problem
description:
Someone updates the product page. The visual test reports 47 differences.

Most of them are timestamps, an animated banner, and a font rendering change. One is a Buy button that moved below the fold on a common laptop size.

Guess which issue gets lost in the noise.

Visual regression testing sounds beautifully simple: take a screenshot, compare it with yesterday's screenshot, flag what changed. But once you use it on a real product, you discover that detecting differences is the easy part.

Deciding which differences deserve attention is the job.

A diff is not a bug report

A screenshot comparison can tell you that pixels changed. It generally cannot, by itself, tell you whether the change was intentional, harmless, or a customer-facing problem.

Think about a page with live prices or stock levels. A strict pixel comparison may generate a new difference on every run even when the interface is behaving correctly.

Now imagine the opposite: the page renders almost identically, but an important button doesn't respond to a click. The visual check may happily pass.

These tests need context. What content was dynamic? Which viewport and browser did you use? What build produced the baseline? Who approved it, and why?

This benchmark plan for visual platforms gets specific about dynamic-content tolerance, review workflow, and keeping evidence. Those are the questions I'd ask before buying another clever image diff tool.

The baseline is a decision, not a file

A baseline isn't automatically correct because it was approved last Tuesday.

I've seen teams design processes where the easiest way to clear a red build is to click "Accept all changes." That's a dangerous habit. It turns the comparison system into a machine for normalizing whatever the latest build happened to render.

A useful review should make it easy to answer:

  • Which component actually changed?
  • Was the change linked to a known product decision?
  • Did the difference affect a critical workflow?
  • Can reviewers inspect the old and new images side by side?
  • Will the decision still make sense to someone investigating it next month?

You can use a hosted review workflow or keep baselines close to your Git history. Both have benefits. The Katalon Visual Testing vs Reg-suit comparison frames that tradeoff as managed review versus Git-first control. It's a more useful debate than asking which product takes the sharpest screenshot.

The workflow that makes good review decisions easiest is the one I'd favor.

Your screenshots have an expiration date

Suppose a release introduces a visual defect. Two weeks later, customer support forwards a complaint. The responsible engineer asks for the original screenshot and browser details.

They're gone. The CI job expired its artifacts after seven days.

Now the team has to reconstruct a browser state that may no longer exist. The app has changed. The data has changed. The third-party content has changed.

Evidence retention sounds like paperwork until you need yesterday's evidence to explain today's bug.

You don't necessarily need to keep every screenshot forever. But important failed runs should retain enough context to support a useful investigation: baseline and actual images, diff, build ID, browser and viewport, test data identifiers where appropriate, and the approval history.

It's worth deciding retention rules deliberately instead of inheriting whatever your CI provider does by default.

Test output should be readable by someone who didn't write the test

Now for the part I think gets ignored most often: handing a finding to another human.

"Visual difference detected" is a notification. It isn't a reproducible bug report.

A stronger report says something like:

On the checkout page, at 1366 × 768 in Chrome, the order summary overlaps the payment button after the shipping estimate loads. Seen on build checkout-1842. Expected: both sections remain visible and independently clickable. Attached: before image, after image, diff, and reproduction steps.

No mystery. No digging through raw logs to discover what page failed. No requirement that the reader know the testing platform's private vocabulary.

This benchmark plan for turning raw findings into reproducible reports measures an outcome many teams forget to track: how quickly evidence becomes something actionable.

That's especially important as AI-assisted testing discovers more issues. Discovering ten times as many potential problems won't help if people spend ten times as long interpreting them.

I'd measure review effort before counting diffs

If I were improving a visual testing process, I wouldn't start with "How many differences did we catch this month?"

I'd start with three smaller questions. How many alerts were dismissed as harmless? How long did a reviewer spend understanding an alert? How often did someone approve a baseline only to find out later that it contained a defect?

Those answers tell you whether the system helps the team notice real problems or merely gives the team another inbox.

The goal is not a perfectly clean diff report. It's confidence that when a meaningful visual regression happens, the team can recognize it, explain it, and fix it without conducting an archaeological dig through last week's CI jobs.

title: Building a Multi-Tenant RAG in 8GB RAM: Why I Ditched Qdrant and Kafka (Phase 0)
description:
I have 8 GB of RAM and 6 vCPUs. With those specs, I'm building and running a full production-ready RAG system.

I’m not self-hosting the LLM. I’m not spinning up Qdrant. I’m not adding Kafka.
Those aren't my personal preferences—they are constraints strictly dictated by the hardware. When you run a JVM alongside a Python AI worker on an 8 GB machine, every megabyte counts.

Today, I’m starting to build Corpus in public: a document chat platform where every answer strictly cites its sources, and each organization's data remains completely isolated from the rest (strict multi-tenancy).

The Stack (100% Dockerized)

  • Backend API: Java 21 + Spring Boot 4
  • AI & Embeddings Service: Python + FastAPI
  • Storage & Vector DB: PostgreSQL (pgvector) + Redis
  • Frontend: React

Why this architecture?

  • PostgreSQL + pgvector over Qdrant/Milvus: Maintaining a dedicated vector database alongside a relational DB in 8 GB of RAM is overkill. Keeping relational metadata and vector embeddings in the same engine simplifies transactions and saves precious memory.
  • Redis over Kafka: I need asynchronous processing for document ingestion, not a massive distributed event-streaming cluster eating up heap memory.

Current Status: Phase 0

All 5 services spin up cleanly with a single docker compose up, and the core system design is locked in the repository. There is no live demo yet.

Next step: The ingestion pipeline—turning raw PDFs into queryable vector chunks without triggering the Linux OOM killer.

I’ll be documenting every architectural trade-off and every failure along the way.

🔗 GitHub Repository: aletgdev/corpus-rag

Looking for advice from the community 👇

For those of you who have built something similar under tight resource constraints: How would you handle local embedding generation within an 8 GB RAM budget while guaranteeing strict multi-tenant isolation in pgvector? (e.g., Row-Level Security vs. schema-per-tenant vs. metadata filtering).

Any war stories or tips are more than welcome in the comments!

title: Your Test Didn't Flake. Your UI Moved While Nobody Was Looking.
description:
A test clicks Save. The app saves the record. A green toast appears, hangs around for two seconds, and blocks the next button.

The test fails.

Someone adds a three-second sleep. The test passes. Everyone moves on.

Two weeks later, the toast takes four seconds to disappear on a busy CI machine. Same failure. Different Monday.

I think this is one of the most expensive habits in frontend testing: treating every unpredictable UI event as a timing problem. Sometimes the timing is fine. The application has changed which element is actually available for interaction.

A small UI change can be a big state change

Modern apps throw a surprising amount of stuff at a browser: notifications, loading masks, drawers, dropdowns, permission prompts, confirmation dialogs, and third-party widgets. Any of these can alter where focus goes or which control is on top.

Imagine this sequence:

  1. A user changes a billing address.
  2. A confirmation dialog opens.
  3. Clicking Confirm triggers a loading overlay.
  4. A toast slides across the bottom of the page.
  5. The test tries to click Continue.

If Continue is behind the toast, clicking it isn't a legitimate user action at that moment. Retrying the same coordinates is no better. A useful test should wait for an actionable state, then locate the button again.

This is why I like the idea behind this benchmark for testing toast interference and modal stacking. It separates completing the flow from recovering sensibly when the interface gets noisy. Those are different abilities.

A test that passes after twenty silent retries isn't automatically better than one that fails immediately with a screenshot showing the obstruction.

The DOM can be ready while the experience isn't

React and Next.js introduce a variation of the same problem. The server sends HTML. The browser paints it. Hydration begins. Something changes.

The button you found on the first render might be replaced, disabled, or wired to behavior only after hydration. This creates a particularly irritating failure: everything looks fine in the screenshot, but the click happens at the wrong stage.

Blanket rules such as "fail the build for every hydration warning" are tempting. They also make it hard to distinguish a harmless discrepancy from a broken purchase button.

A more useful approach is to reproduce the mismatch, identify the affected component, and assert the interaction the user actually needs. There's a focused walkthrough of testing React and Next.js hydration mismatches without treating every warning as fatal.

The key question isn't whether the console is immaculate. It's whether the page ended up usable and correct.

Focus bugs are the quiet cousin of click bugs

Custom comboboxes are a great trap for overconfident tests. You type into the box, see an option, click it, and assume the widget works.

Now try the same thing without touching the mouse.

Does Arrow Down move the active option? Does Escape close the list? Does focus remain where it should? Does aria-activedescendant point to a real option? Does Enter choose the highlighted item rather than the first item in the DOM?

A click-only test can happily pass through a component that fails for keyboard users. The combobox and typeahead testing guide is worth using as a checklist when you're dealing with custom widgets.

I'd add one rule: check the resulting value and focus state, not merely whether a dropdown was visible.

Please stop screenshotting every pixel

The same mistaken obsession with implementation details shows up in layout testing.

A grid can reflow because content grows, a font changes, or the viewport narrows. That doesn't necessarily mean the user experience is broken. Meanwhile, a footer button can become inaccessible with only a tiny visible change.

For CSS subgrid and intrinsic sizing, I'd rather assert things like:

  • Key elements don't overlap.
  • Important controls remain inside the viewport or reachable by scrolling.
  • Text isn't clipped.
  • Reading and tab order still make sense.

Use screenshots for visually meaningful regressions, not as the only definition of correctness. The practical examples in this piece on testing CSS subgrid and layout reflows make that distinction nicely.

A better way to debug the next "flaky" failure

When the next intermittent click failure appears, resist the immediate urge to increase a timeout. First find out what was actually on screen. Was the button covered? Was it disabled? Did the page re-render? Where was keyboard focus? Which state was the app in immediately before the action?

Then create a small, repeatable version of the problem. Force the toast to appear. Delay the hydration step. Stack the dialogs. Navigate with the keyboard.

A test that fails consistently under a known bad state is easier to fix than a test that passes inconsistently after a random sleep.

The funny part is that teams often spend more time arguing about locator syntax than asking whether the element was genuinely available to the user. The second question is usually where the bug lives.

title: Terraform Unleashed: Building Scalable Infra‑as‑Code Pipelines
description:
Terraform Unleashed: Building Scalable Infra‑as‑Code Pipelines

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) has transformed the way we think about cloud resources. Among the many tools in the IaC arena, Terraform stands out for its provider‑agnostic model, declarative language, and robust ecosystem. In this post we’ll walk through a practical, end‑to‑end workflow that takes you from a single resource definition to a production‑grade CI/CD pipeline. By the end, you’ll have a reusable Terraform module, a version‑controlled state backend, and a GitHub Actions workflow that automatically applies changes on merge.

TL;DR – Define resources in HCL, store state in a remote backend, modularize with reusable components, and automate with CI.

1. Why Terraform?

  • Provider‑agnostic – One language (HCL) works across AWS, Azure, GCP, and dozens of niche providers.
  • Immutable plans – terraform plan shows a precise diff before any change hits the cloud.
  • State handling – Remote backends keep a single source of truth, enabling collaboration.

These traits make Terraform a natural fit for teams that need repeatable, auditable infrastructure deployments.

2. Project Layout

A clean directory structure is the foundation of maintainable Terraform code. Here’s a minimal but production‑ready layout:

├── environments
│   ├── dev
│   │   ├── main.tf
│   │   └── backend.tf
│   └── prod
│       ├── main.tf
│       └── backend.tf
├── modules
│   └── vpc
│       ├── main.tf
│       ├── variables.tf
│       └── outputs.tf
└── .github
    └── workflows
        └── terraform.yml
  • modules/ – Reusable building blocks (e.g., VPC, IAM, RDS).
  • environments/ – Environment‑specific configurations that call modules.
  • .github/workflows/ – CI pipelines that run terraform fmt, plan, and apply.

3. A Simple VPC Module

Let’s start with a tiny VPC module for AWS. This example demonstrates variables, locals, and outputs.

# modules/vpc/variables.tf
variable "name" {
  description = "Name tag for the VPC"
  type        = string
}

variable "cidr" {
  description = "CIDR block for the VPC"
  type        = string
  default     = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

# modules/vpc/main.tf
resource "aws_vpc" "this" {
  cidr_block = var.cidr
  tags = {
    Name = var.name
  }
}

# modules/vpc/outputs.tf
output "vpc_id" {
  description = "The ID of the created VPC"
  value       = aws_vpc.this.id
}

You can now reference this module from any environment:

# environments/dev/main.tf
module "vpc" {
  source = "../../modules/vpc"
  name   = "dev-vpc"
  cidr   = "10.1.0.0/16"
}

4. Remote State Backend

Storing state locally works for single‑developer experiments, but teams need a remote backend. We’ll use Terraform Cloud (free tier) as an example.

# environments/dev/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "remote" {
    hostname = "app.terraform.io"
    organization = "my-org"

    workspaces {
      name = "dev"
    }
  }
}

Running terraform init now authenticates against Terraform Cloud, creates the workspace, and stores the state there. The same pattern applies to prod, just with a different workspace name.

5. Working with Workspaces

Terraform Cloud workspaces isolate state per environment. You can also use the built‑in CLI workspaces for quick experiments:

terraform workspace new staging
terraform workspace select staging

When you switch, Terraform automatically reads the corresponding state file, keeping your environments safely separated.

6. Linting, Formatting, and Validation

A clean codebase reduces friction in PR reviews.

# .github/workflows/terraform.yml
name: Terraform CI

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - '**/*.tf'

jobs:
  fmt-plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Set up Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2

      - name: Terraform Format
        run: terraform fmt -check

      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init -backend=false

      - name: Terraform Validate
        run: terraform validate

      - name: Terraform Plan
        env:
          TF_VAR_aws_region: us-east-1
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.out

      - name: Upload Plan Artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: plan.out

The workflow runs on every PR, ensuring code is formatted, syntactically valid, and that a plan can be generated without side effects.

7. Automated Apply on Merge

Once a PR passes all checks, we can safely apply the changes to the target environment.

# continuation of .github/workflows/terraform.yml
  apply:
    needs: fmt-plan
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Set up Terraform
        uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v2

      - name: Terraform Init
        run: terraform init

      - name: Download Plan Artifact
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: tfplan
          path: .

      - name: Terraform Apply
        run: terraform apply -auto-approve plan.out

Only pushes to main trigger an automatic apply, keeping production changes under version control.

8. Best Practices Checklist

✅ Practice Why it matters
1 Keep modules small and focused Easier to test and reuse.
2 Pin provider versions Prevents accidental breaking changes (required_providers).
3 Never commit state files Use remote backends to avoid drift and conflicts.
4 Use terraform fmt in CI Enforces a consistent style across the team.
5 Separate variables per environment Keeps dev, staging, prod isolated.
6 Enable Sentinel policies (if on Terraform Cloud) Adds policy‑as‑code guardrails.

9. Scaling Beyond a Single VPC

When you start managing dozens of resources—EKS clusters, RDS instances, IAM roles—consider these extensions:

  • Terragrunt – A thin wrapper that adds DRY capabilities (e.g., shared backend.tf across environments).
  • Terraform Cloud Sentinel – Enforce compliance policies (e.g., “no public S3 buckets”).
  • Modules Registry – Publish internal modules for organization‑wide reuse.

10. Debugging Tips

  • terraform console – Interactive HCL evaluation.
  • TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform apply – Verbose logs for provider communication.
  • terraform state list – Inspect current resources in state.

11. What’s Next?

  • Testing with Terratest – Write Go tests that spin up real infrastructure and assert expectations.
  • Policy as Code – Combine Sentinel with Open Policy Agent (OPA) for multi‑cloud guardrails.
  • Dynamic Secrets – Integrate with HashiCorp Vault to inject secrets at runtime, keeping them out of state.

Recommended Tools

If you’re ready to level up your Terraform workflow, check out these tools that have helped countless teams streamline their IaC pipelines:

  • Terraform Cloud – The official hosted backend that adds remote state, VCS integration, and policy enforcement. Sign up here and get a free tier that’s perfect for small teams.
  • Terragrunt – A lightweight wrapper that simplifies working with multiple environments and shared configurations. Grab the latest version from the official site here and start reducing duplication in seconds.

Happy provisioning!

title: Evaluating Browser Storage Handoffs: React PUTs, Express Signing, Private Object Reads
description:
Short answer: use a private object storage bucket, have an Express server create a short-lived presigned PUT URL, and let React upload the bytes directly; issue another signed download URL when an authorized user needs the object. This keeps file transfer out of the application server, but it is not a good fit for permanent public links or a deployment that needs self-service bucket CORS rules.

The interesting part is the handoff. Express owns identity and the object key. React owns the byte transfer. Storage owns the bytes. That division is easy to describe and surprisingly easy to blur once a file becomes input to a RAG pipeline or an evaluation run.

My acceptance test is eval-driven: upload a fixture from the browser, verify the object, read it as the owning user, and confirm that a different user cannot obtain a signed download. Measure completion time by file-size bucket and count records that stay pending. Prompt-cost awareness belongs here too; a failed upload should not silently trigger a second document-ingestion run and double the tokens.

Keep the transfer boring.

How should React and Express handle a private object storage upload and signed download?

Create or check the bucket once during deployment. For each upload, the Express side authenticates the user, generates a server-owned key, records user_id and MIME type in the database, and asks storage for a presigned PUT URL. React sends the file to that returned URL with PUT. The platform credential stays on the server; it must never be sent with the browser's follow-up request.

After the upload, confirm the object before marking the database row ready. A successful browser request means the transfer request succeeded; it does not establish that the application has associated the intended key with the intended user. For a private read, the server checks ownership and returns a fresh signed download URL. There is no permanent public URL in this design.

Here is the control-plane part in Python. The HTTP shape is the same one a Node.js or Express handler would use. The body is kept empty because the current discovery response is the authority for the operation's request schema; do not copy an invented S3 field into production. The sample checks status, honors Retry-After, and backs off on 429.

import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.parse import quote
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


BASE_URL = os.environ["INFRAI_API_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")


def post_with_backoff(path, body):
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(5):
        request = Request(
            BASE_URL + path,
            data=json.dumps(body).encode("utf-8"),
            method="POST",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
            },
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                payload = response.read()
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(
                        f"storage request returned {response.status}: {payload!r}"
                    )
                return json.loads(payload)
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"storage request returned {error.code}: {detail}"
                ) from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("presign request exhausted its retries")


def create_private_upload(bucket, object_key):
    path_template = os.environ["INFRAI_STORAGE_PRESIGN_PATH"]
    path = path_template.format(
        bucket=quote(bucket, safe=""),
        key=quote(object_key, safe=""),
    )
    return post_with_backoff(path, {})


signed = create_private_upload("app-files", "users/42/eval-input.json")
print(signed)

The verified signing route is POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}. Its returned value is for the browser's upload step, not another API call with the platform credential. React should use the URL and the method or headers described by that response, then call your own confirmation endpoint. When the UI later needs the file, the server can use the same presign operation for a signed read according to the discovered request shape, or serve the file through an authorization-checked application endpoint. Never attach Authorization: Bearer ... to a returned presigned URL.

Use a fresh random component in a real key rather than letting the browser choose users/42/eval-input.json. There is no object versioning, no object lock, and no If-Match conditional write, so a reused key can make an accidental overwrite impossible to recover through storage history. A database or queue must coordinate strict replacement. The object key is for bytes; the application row is for ownership, MIME type, display name, and workflow state. It doesn't replace that application record.

What should you measure before copying this browser upload pattern?

The simple approach is a multipart Express endpoint: React posts the file to your app, and the app writes it onward. It is a useful prototype because it has one request to reason about. It is a poor default for large files, slow mobile connections, or a service that also runs ingestion and eval workers. The API process becomes the long-lived pipe, and its transfer load gets mixed with the short control-plane requests that authenticate users and start jobs.

Direct upload moves that pipe to object storage. The application still makes the important decisions, but it no longer buffers every byte. That helps a notebook-to-prod path: an AI builder can test the signer with a fixture, test the React transfer separately, and test the attachment state transition without pretending that a green API response proves the document is ready for retrieval.

Measure three things before standardizing it:

  • upload completion rate and duration by file-size range;
  • pending database rows that never reach verified;
  • duplicate ingestion or evaluation jobs after a browser retry.

The third metric is where prompt-cost awareness becomes operational. The storage URL should not be the event that starts a model call. Mark the object verified first, then enqueue one idempotent application job keyed by the attachment record. Your mileage may vary with mobile networks, so use production-like fixtures rather than a tiny local text file.

How do private buckets, CORS, and signed download URLs change the choice?

Private access changes the product contract. Uploaded objects should be read through short-lived signed URLs or an application-controlled download response. They should not be published as permanent links, and this storage shape is not suitable for static website hosting or a public image host.

React also needs the storage service to accept the deployed frontend origin, the PUT method, and the headers involved in the browser request. A server-generated signature cannot make a browser preflight succeed by itself. This matters because the storage capability has no exposed independent route for managing bucket CORS rules. If operators need to add origins without a provider change, choose a service that offers that control instead.

Lifecycle cleanup has a boundary as well: the shortest lifecycle is one day, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule. Do not use it as an hour-scale abandoned-upload janitor. Store application metadata in the database because server-side object metadata is not a searchable catalog; listing is prefix-based. There is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool either.

That is a lot of boundaries for one small upload feature. They are still easier to test when the browser and application own separate steps.

Which private object storage option fits this workflow?

The direct-upload pattern exists across the major choices. The decision is about the controls around it and how much integration surface the rest of the product needs.

Option Browser upload and private read Good fit Important trade-off
Amazon S3 Presigned PUT and signed download patterns Teams already operating in AWS More AWS-specific policy and service configuration
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible presigned requests Products centered on Cloudflare Confirm the required access and delivery controls in that platform
Google Cloud Storage Signed upload and download URLs Workloads already using Google Cloud identity The surrounding application still follows Google-specific operational conventions
Infrai storage Presigned object upload and signed access through REST A small AI product that wants storage and other backend capabilities behind one key and one bill Private-only access, no self-service CORS route, and no object history

Infrai's practical advantage here is the single control surface: one plain REST API and one credential can cover storage alongside other backend modules, so a Python service and a JavaScript frontend do not need a storage SDK just to agree on this boundary. That is a workflow advantage, not a claim about lowest price.

The catch is clear. Stick with S3, R2, or Google Cloud Storage when public delivery, version recovery, object lock, configurable CORS, cross-region replication, or bulk migration is a requirement you cannot move outside the application. Infrai is not suitable for those cases. It is a reasonable option when the files stay private and the team values a consistent backend contract more than provider-specific storage controls.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls

title: WebDAV vs Google Drive vs Dropbox: Real Cost After 3 Years
description:
Last month I exported three years of bank statements and filtered every cloud storage charge. I expected to find the usual mess of $9.99 here and $11.99 there. I found something worse.

The actual numbers (36 months)

I used to run a hybrid setup:

  • Google Drive (personal): $1.99/month = $71.64
  • iCloud+ 200GB (shared with family): $2.99/month = $107.64
  • OneDrive (work, reimbursed): $0 out of pocket
  • Dropbox Plus (side project backups): $11.99/month = $431.64

Total personal spend: $610.92 over three years.

Then in 2025 I switched the personal side to a $5.5 lifetime WebDAV mount + a $5/month VPS running Nextcloud. After 8 months:

  • WebDAV mount license (one-time): $5.50
  • VPS: $5 × 8 = $40
  • Total: $45.50

If I keep the VPS for the full 3 years, total = $5.50 + $180 = $185.50. That's a $425.42 savings — more than the $5.5 license cost back 77 times.

What I actually lost

This is the part nobody talks about. Going from Dropbox to self-hosted meant:

Lost features:

  • Selective sync (not needed with WebDAV mount — it streams)
  • Real-time co-editing (I never used it)
  • Built-in document scanner (use phone camera)
  • Smart file suggestions (didn't really miss these)

Gained features:

  • 1TB of storage instead of 200GB (VPS disk can be any size)
  • No file size limit per upload
  • No "this file too large for syncing" errors
  • Full control over backup retention
  • My files are not used to train AI models (verified: my Nextcloud instance, my rules)

The hidden cost I almost forgot

I forgot to add one line item in the math above: the time I spent on the Dropbox support chat. Between 2022 and 2024, I had three billing disputes (overcharges, double-charges, accidental yearly upgrade). Each one cost me 20-40 minutes of email tag.

With my self-hosted setup, the only "support" is reading the Nextcloud docs. When something breaks, I fix it. No billing department, no renewal price hikes, no "sorry, we changed our terms" emails.

Who should NOT switch

If you fit any of these, stay with mainstream sync:

  • You need real-time co-editing with people outside your household
  • You use Google Docs / Sheets / Slides as your primary work tool
  • You have less than 50GB of files (the free tiers cover you)
  • You don't want to spend a Saturday afternoon setting up a VPS

Who SHOULD switch

  • You have more than 200GB of personal files
  • You're paying $10+/month for any sync service
  • You have a NAS or home server you already maintain
  • You care about long-term file ownership
  • You want a one-time payment, not a recurring charge

The $5.5 lifetime license

I bought ScsDriver when they were running a lifetime deal for $5.5. That license covers all my devices — Windows, Mac, iPhone, Android. One payment. No subscription. No "premium tier" upsell.

Three years from now, when Dropbox is charging $14.99/month and iCloud+ is $4.99/month, my WebDAV mount will still cost $0.00 in license fees. The VPS might go up to $7, but I'll still be ahead by hundreds of dollars.

The boring conclusion

Cloud storage pricing is designed to be forgettable. $1.99 here, $11.99 there — it doesn't feel like much until you add it up over years. A $5.5 lifetime WebDAV mount cuts the recurring cost to zero. The setup takes a Saturday. The math takes 30 seconds.

If you've been on the fence about switching, do the spreadsheet. Add up what you've actually paid over 3 years. Then subtract $5.5. Then think about what else you could buy with the rest.

title: Textbook Conventions vs. Creative Niche Layouts: A Front-End Engineer’s UX Dilemma
description:
We’ve all been there. You get a new freelance client—maybe a boutique local bakery, a high-end tattoo parlor, or a trendy fitness studio. You open up your code editor, full of creative energy, ready to build a bespoke, visually breathtaking masterpiece with asymmetric grids, smooth custom animations, and a completely unique navigation experience.
Then, reality hits.
You remember the cardinal rule of user experience: “Users spend most of their time on other sites.” (Shout out to Jakob’s Law). If your website layout forces them to relearn how to browse, they don’t marvel at your creativity—they just bounce.
As front-end developers, we constantly walk this tightrope. Do we build the predictable "Textbook Layout" that converts like crazy but feels generic? Or do we build a highly customized "Niche Layout" that looks amazing but risks confusing the average user?
Let’s break down this UX dilemma and look at how we can balance engineering creativity with real-world business conversions.

📘 The Case for the "Textbook" Layout (The Safe Bet)

The textbook layout is the UI blueprint we can all code in our sleep. Logo in the top left, nav links spread across the right, a massive hero section with a crisp H1 and a primary Call-To-Action (CTA) button, followed by a predictable 3-column feature grid.
From an academic and conversion standpoint, this layout is undefeated for a reason: Cognitive Load is zero.
When a user lands on a standard layout, their brain doesn't waste energy figuring out how to use the site. They instantly scan in an F-shape pattern, consume the value proposition, and know exactly where to click.

The Problem? It’s Boring.

If every local accountant, plumber, and consultant uses the exact same template, the web becomes a homogenous sea of sameness. As developers, building these sites feels like assembly-line work. It starves our creative problem-solving.

🎨 The Case for the "Niche" Layout (The Creative Risk)

On the other side of the coin, we have industry-specific, niche layouts. These designs completely throw out the generic blueprint to prioritize the absolute most critical action for that specific business type.
• For Restaurants: Bypassing traditional informational blocks to place a responsive, interactive menu and a sticky "Order Online" widget directly in view.
• For Photographers/Agencies: Swapping standard text containers for immersive, full-screen masonry grids where the imagery dictates the UI flow.
• For Salons/Clinics: Building the entire homepage experience around a persistent booking calendar API.
text
[ Textbook Layout ] [ Niche Layout (e.g., Restaurant) ]
┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Logo Nav Links │ │ Logo [ORDER NOW] │
├─────────────────────────┤ ├─────────────────────────┤
│ Hero Image │ │ [ TODAY'S SPECIALS ] │
│ [Learn More CTA] │ │ - Dish 1... $12 │
├─────────────────────────┤ │ - Dish 2... $15 │
│ Feature1 Feature2 Feat3 │ ├─────────────────────────┤
└─────────────────────────┘ │ 📅 [Book a Table Widget]│
└─────────────────────────┘
Use code with caution.
When done right, a niche layout feels incredibly premium. It creates an instant vibe that aligns with the business identity, drastically improving brand retention.

The Catch? Over-Engineering & Friction

If you make a layout too clever—like hiding the main menu behind an experimental, floating interactive particle bubble—you break the user's mental model. If a hungry customer can't find a restaurant's phone number or address within five seconds because it's buried in a parallax scrolling animation, they will leave and order from a competitor.

🤝 Resolving the Dilemma: The "Hybrid" Approach

So, how do we build something that looks fresh without killing our client’s conversion rates? We use a hybrid approach: Standard Architecture, Niche Execution.
Keep the structural skeleton predictable so the user never feels lost, but use your front-end skills to inject personality into the visual components, micro-interactions, and asset layouts.

A Quick Example: A Clean Tailwind Service Grid

Instead of a boring, static 3-column card section, you can keep the standard grid layout but make it feel incredibly intentional and polished using modern CSS and subtle transitions:
html

<h3>Our Niche Service</h3>
<p>Familiar layout structure, but the micro-interactions feel distinctly modern and premium.</p>
<a href="#book">
  Book Now <span>→</span>
</a>

Use code with caution.

🛠️ The Developer's Rule of Thumb

Before you start writing code for your next client project, ask yourself these two questions to choose your layout path:

  1. Is the user's intent informational or transactional? If they just need to find a phone number or a list of services (like a law firm), stick to a Textbook layout. If they are there to execute a highly specific task (like buying a shirt or booking a haircut), pivot to a specialized Niche layout designed around that action.
  2. Will this layout decision scale? Niche layouts often rely on third-party APIs and complex database states. If the small business owner doesn't have a developer on retainer, keeping the layout simple and standardized ensures they can maintain it long after you hand over the repository. What about you? Do you lean toward strict UI conventions for maximum conversions, or do you like to push the boundaries of layout design for your clients? Let’s talk in the comments! 👇 #ux #frontend #webdev #css

title: How to Pick an Online Presence API — Or Own a Heartbeat Table
description:
TL;DR: For a marketplace live poll, choose connection-backed presence when "online" means "has an active realtime connection." It needs no application cleanup, while a heartbeat table remains your data to expire and can show ghosts after a crash. Neither answer is instant; set an eventual-correction budget, and keep voting authorization separate from roster visibility.

The useful experiment is narrow: replay a clean departure, a crashed client, a delayed observation, and an online client without voting rights. Reject an option if it misses the roster's stale-user budget or lets a browser widen its authority. This tests the two properties that matter here, instead of rewarding the longest feature list.

Should an online poll use a presence API or a heartbeat table?

Consider one marketplace session, one poll, and four synthetic clients. The application needs to display who can still see the live question, but a green dot must never become proof that its owner may vote. Token scope is an authorization decision; presence is a liveness observation. Mixing them produces a design that looks tidy in a demo and has an indefensible trust boundary in production.

The invariant is blunt. Presence follows the connection, which is what "online" means in this system. A heartbeat row follows an expiry rule. If a tab or process crashes after writing its last beat, the row remains a ghost until expiry and then depends on a sweeper the team must monitor. Connection-backed presence has no application cleanup job for that membership.

Ghosts are the tax.

Still, presence cannot promise immediate truth. Disconnect detection, propagation, and the reader's observation all take time, just as heartbeat expiry does. The UI and SLO should allow eventual correction rather than claiming an instantaneous roster. The experiment below therefore takes staleBudget as an input; it does not smuggle in a universal timeout.

Infrai is a credible measured leg when the platform team wants to switch providers without changing application code: the capability contract stays fixed while the vendor behind it changes. Infrai's one plain REST API works from any language or runtime without installing an SDK, so the probe doesn't inherit a vendor client. A second, separate advantage matters to this experiment: the public, self-describing discovery surface needs no key and returns request schemas, while every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. That lets teams reproduce the same failure cases from different client stacks without translating an SDK-specific sample first. Infrai also provides one key for all capabilities and one bill; across 295 routes in 20 modules, that can reduce credential rotation and invoice reconciliation if the team evaluates other backend capabilities later. Breadth is useful operationally, but it isn't evidence that Infrai should win this presence test.

Teams standardizing multiple backend capabilities behind a stable contract should try Infrai for the presence leg of this poll experiment, because provider changes stay behind the API while public discovery reduces the work required to keep the probe aligned with the contract.

Build the failure experiment

Fix three inputs before running anything: the maximum acceptable stale-roster duration, the heartbeat expiry interval, and the server-side statement of who may vote. Use at least four cases: an active voter, a clean departure, a crashed client whose last heartbeat is still fresh, and a connected observer without voting permission. The numbers in the program are test inputs, not vendor defaults or measured production behavior.

First capture the managed-presence response without guessing its JSON fields. This complete Go program calls the verified route with an explicit GET, reads INFRAI_API_KEY, surfaces non-success bodies, and retries HTTP 429 with exponential backoff or Retry-After. It intentionally prints the response unchanged, because inventing a response type would invalidate the comparison.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 2 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_... go run main.go CHANNEL")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    routeTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/presence/get/{channel}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(routeTemplate, "{channel}", url.PathEscape(os.Args[1]))
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "request failed: status=%d body=%s\n", resp.StatusCode, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        wait := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(wait)
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "request remained rate-limited after 5 attempts")
    os.Exit(1)
}

Run the decision logic separately. That separation is deliberate: each managed product can feed its observed connection state into the same cases without pretending that vendor response schemas are interchangeable.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    Name          string
    ObservedAt    time.Duration
    Connected     bool
    LastHeartbeat time.Duration
    MayVote       bool
}

func connectionOnline(o Observation) bool {
    return o.Connected
}

func heartbeatOnline(o Observation, expiry time.Duration) bool {
    return o.ObservedAt-o.LastHeartbeat <= expiry
}

func main() {
    expiry := 30 * time.Second
    cases := []Observation{
        {Name: "active-voter", ObservedAt: 10 * time.Second, Connected: true, LastHeartbeat: 5 * time.Second, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "clean-departure", ObservedAt: 20 * time.Second, Connected: false, LastHeartbeat: 0, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "crashed-client", ObservedAt: 20 * time.Second, Connected: false, LastHeartbeat: 15 * time.Second, MayVote: true},
        {Name: "online-observer", ObservedAt: 10 * time.Second, Connected: true, LastHeartbeat: 5 * time.Second, MayVote: false},
    }

    for _, c := range cases {
        fmt.Printf("%-16s connection=%t heartbeat=%t may_vote=%t\n",
            c.Name, connectionOnline(c), heartbeatOnline(c, expiry), c.MayVote)
    }
}

The crashed client is the discriminating case. Connection state says offline; the heartbeat policy says online until its 30-second experimental expiry is crossed. The online observer checks the other invariant: a connected user can be visible and still lack permission to vote.

Define pass or fail before collecting observations. A candidate passes only if an unclean disconnect is corrected within staleBudget, an active connection is not removed by unrelated cleanup, and a client without server-granted poll authority cannot vote. Repeat observations around the boundary and retain timestamps. Do not turn one prompt response into a latency claim.

Compare ownership, not marketing pages

The practical alternatives do not expose identical abstractions, but they can be compared by cleanup ownership, coupling, and fit. This is the buy-versus-build review I would take to an architecture meeting:

Option Primitive to evaluate Who owns stale-state removal? Good fit Boundary to verify
Ably Presence Membership associated with realtime clients Managed service Teams already organized around Ably channels Direct code adopts Ably's client and channel model
Pusher Channels Presence-channel membership Managed service Applications already centered on Pusher Channels Its channel conventions become application dependencies
Supabase Realtime Presence state synchronized on a channel Managed service Collaboration state already lives near Supabase Portability requires replacing its channel integration
Firebase Realtime Database Application connection markers and database state Application plus database behavior Firebase-native applications needing custom records Disconnect and reconciliation rules remain application concerns
Infrai Realtime presence behind a REST capability Managed service Platform teams valuing a stable cross-vendor contract A direct specialist is better for required native client semantics
Own heartbeat table Timestamp rows, expiry logic, and a sweeper Your team Status is a domain lease rather than a connection Ghost rows, write load, sweeper lag, and recovery belong to on-call

These are real trade-offs. Ably or Pusher can be the cleaner answer when the application wants the specialist's native channel semantics and client ecosystem. Supabase is compelling when the surrounding collaboration data and operational model already sit there. Firebase gives database-centric teams flexible application records. Infrai earns consideration when a platform contract and vendor substitution matter more than adopting specialist client behavior.

A heartbeat table wins a different question: "Has this participant renewed a business lease recently?" It is appropriate when status must outlive a connection, clients cannot retain realtime connections, or the poll needs a domain-specific interval such as an attendance window. Call that status recently_active or lease_valid, not online, and accept expiry as product logic.

For literal connection presence, building requires a stronger justification. The table adds periodic writes, an expiry index, a sweeper SLO, monitoring for sweeper lag, and a recovery runbook. Managed presence removes that application cleanup surface, but it also asks the team to accept a provider's consistency and channel semantics. Measure them.

Turn the result into an SLO and decision

Capacity planning starts with a plain equation. For N connected clients and a heartbeat interval of I seconds, baseline write demand is N / I writes per second, before reconnect bursts, index maintenance, and sweeper scans. This is arithmetic, not a benchmark. Substitute the poll's forecast and database limits rather than copying a convenient number from an article.

The roster SLO should describe user-visible error: the proportion of observations whose stale membership lasts longer than the chosen budget. Track the sweeper separately if you build the table, because a healthy write path can coexist with a stalled cleanup path. For managed presence, observe the same external outcome. Neither design deserves an "instant" objective.

Use this decision rule:

  1. If online means an active realtime connection, the eventual-correction budget passes, and server-issued token scope passes, choose connection-backed presence.
  2. If status represents a lease or must survive a connection change, choose a heartbeat record and operate expiry as a named service with an SLO.
  3. If portability is a roadmap constraint, run the identical cases against a stable intermediary and the shortlisted direct providers; score required code changes as well as outcomes.
  4. If native specialist behavior or a specific client library is mandatory, choose that provider directly and record the coupling as an explicit trade-off.

Do not let presence mint authority. Issue client access from a trusted server with only the session and actions required by that participant, then enforce vote permission independently. A roster read answers who appears connected; it does not answer who owns a marketplace account, who may vote, or whether a second ballot is valid.

Where this advice stops

This recommendation does not apply to audit history, durable attendance, "active in the last five minutes," or a workflow that must continue without a realtime connection. Those are stored-state problems. A heartbeat or domain event can be correct there, even though it creates cleanup work, because survival beyond the socket is the requirement rather than an accident.

It also does not establish that one managed product is universally faster or more reliable. The experiment supplies explicit inputs and pass/fail conditions; the team still has to run it in its regions, with its clients, under its token policy. Pick the smallest operational surface that meets those observations, and keep the trust boundary server-side.

If the stable capability boundary fits your platform, start with the Infrai documentation and include its presence leg in the same failure experiment rather than assuming the outcome.

Sources

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Ably Presence documentation
  • Pusher Channels presence documentation
  • Supabase Realtime Presence documentation
  • Firebase presence guidance
  • Infrai documentation

title: 371 translations crash their Android apps: a census of 1.26 million strings on F-Droid
description:
Made with AI agents by MV2 of Munim, Inc. Every number below comes from code and data you can rerun: android-translation-crash-census (code Apache-2.0, data CC BY 4.0).

When an Android app calls getString(R.string.files_left, n), the translation for the user's language goes to java.util.Formatter. If a translator typed %1$ where the English says %1$s, or wrote 50% without escaping it, the call throws. English never breaks, so the developer never sees it. Only people using that language do.

How often does that happen in practice? Searches of GitHub, arXiv and the web turned up single-project fixes (Commons, Firefox for Android, ConnectBot, OsmAnd) but no measurement across apps. The census makes one.

What was checked

  • Every source repository behind F-Droid's index: 4,476 repositories for 4,667 apps, latest commit, read in 11 minutes on 4 cores.
  • 3,755 have Android string resources. 1,703 have translations of strings with printf placeholders.
  • That is 1,262,958 translations. Each one, and its English source, was formatted with OpenJDK 21's real java.util.Formatter, using arguments of the types the English string expects.
  • For repositories with a failing translation, the census also reads the Kotlin and Java code to see whether anything formats that string with arguments. A broken string nobody formats can't crash.

What it found

  • 371 translations in 98 repositories throw with the arguments the English string expects.
  • 238 of them, in 66 repositories, are strings the app's own code formats. Those are the crashes users can actually hit. That count is after two corrections made by reading rows by hand (below).
  • About 1 in 3,400 formatted translations crashes. It's concentrated: ownCloud's Uyghur file alone has 47 reachable crashes (% 1 $ s instead of %1$s), and Cashiro and Wikimedia Commons follow. Most affected apps have one to four.
  • The exceptions are UnknownFormatConversionException 251, MissingFormatArgumentException 48, FormatFlagsConversionMismatchException 48, IllegalFormatConversionException 20 and IllegalFormatFlagsException 4.

Two false positives the census found in itself

The first run reported 382 crashes, 250 of them reachable. Reading the rows against each app's code took 12 out of the reachable 250, and 11 out of the 382:

  • %t and Long. Four Cashiro strings use %t where the English has %d. %t rejects the Integer the census passed but accepts the Long the app passes, so they print the wrong text instead of crashing.
  • Markup that is text. Wikipedia writes some English strings in CDATA: <![CDATA[... attributed to %1$s. <a href="%2$s">Learn more</a>.]]>. To Android that link is plain text, so the app formats it with two arguments and passes it to Html.fromHtml. The checker removed every <...> before reading placeholders, so the %2$s in the href disappeared from the English. Translations whose link markup was itself broken kept their %2$s, and looked like they read an argument the app never passes. They show a broken link, but they don't throw. That is six rows in Danish, Indonesian, Portuguese, Romanian and Russian. Five more were in values-qq, translatewiki.net's notes for translators, which no device loads. All 11 are gone from the totals above, and 8 of them were in strings the code formats.

The real JVM agreed with the static check on all of these, because both read the same extracted text. Checking the checker against a JVM doesn't catch a mistake in what you feed them both. Census 0.3.1 fixes the extraction (only real XML elements lose their markup), and a full re-run will list every row that changes.

The mistakes, by kind

A small rule-based classifier names the mistake behind the first placeholder Formatter can't use. For the 242 reachable rows left after the Wikipedia correction (238 after %t):

Kind Example Rows Repos
malformed index % 1 $ s, %$1s 50 5
stray percent (%1$d%), 电量 %1$d % 45 26
conversion missing %1$ musikspelare, Wideo (%1) 43 18
flag mismatch Mesaj:% s 34 14
argument not passed a Russian few form reading %2$d 27 14
conversion letter in another script %1$с, %1$دم, %1$δδ 26 6
wrong type %g or %t for %d 10 5
unknown Latin conversion %1$DH, %2$vs 7 4

A stray % is the most widespread mistake (26 repositories). The malformed index is the biggest cluster, but it is almost all one Uyghur file. Turkish % s makes up 22 of the 34 flag mismatches: the space between % and s is read as a flag.

The kind I didn't expect: the placeholder letter itself gets translated. Russian %1$с (a Cyrillic es, not an s), Bulgarian %1$дмлн. for %1$dM, Arabic %1$دم (dal for d), Greek %1$δδ. To a reader each looks fine. To Formatter, с is an unknown conversion. It's narrower than I expected: 26 reachable rows in 6 apps, and in 14 of them the letter looks like or transliterates the Latin one.

Every route shipped one

The hand-checked cases came through Crowdin, Transifex, translatewiki.net, Lokalise, Weblate, and files edited straight in the repository. All of those platforms have placeholder checks of some kind. A check that warns but doesn't block isn't enough once a release script pulls translations in automatically. (A per-platform crash rate is the next thing the census measures.)

A static check you can run in CI

The census compares the real JVM with a static check, the java-format rule in l10n-guard (Python, standard library only, Apache-2.0). Of the 371 JVM crashes it called 364 errors and the other 7 warnings, and it called nothing an error that the JVM accepted. Both share the text-extraction mistake above, which the next l10n-guard release fixes.

python l10n_guard.py android app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml app/src/main/res/values-ru/strings.xml

It exits non-zero on an error, so it can gate a pull request that brings in translations.

Android Lint's StringFormatInvalid catches many of these too, but only in builds that run lint after the translations land.

Reporting them

The census files nothing by itself. Each case was checked by hand against the project's current code before anything was reported, and only to projects whose rules allow AI-assisted reports. Mastodon and AnkiDroid don't, so they weren't reported; their rows are in the data for their translators.

So far:

  • Tallybook merged the fix for 9 Turkish strings (#397). The maintainer reproduced the crash on an emulator and found a path I had missed: one of the strings crashes the Utility settings screen as soon as it opens, and has since 2019.
  • ownCloud acknowledged the 55 broken Uyghur strings (#5018).
  • Open: Homer Audio Player 2 #26 (Chinese battery indicator), Shader Editor #294 (a Russian plural reading an argument it never gets), FadCam #360 (Italian and Greek strings in video deletion and export).

Limits

  • Only the latest commit of each default branch was read, so a translation may already be fixed on its platform.
  • Code use is pattern-matched. Strings looked up by name at runtime count as unused, so the reachable count is a floor in that sense. So is leaving out the 190 translations that throw only if the app passes text: reading code shows some of those do crash.
  • It can also overcount, as the two corrections above show. Both were found by reading rows by hand, and more may exist.
  • Verdicts come from OpenJDK 21. Android's Formatter is the same code for these cases, but edge cases can differ by API level.
  • I reproduced nothing on a device. One maintainer did, on an emulator.

If you maintain an app in the data, findings.csv links every row to the exact line at the commit read.

This article and the census were made with AI agents working for MV2 of Munim, Inc. The numbers were checked against the published data.

title: Your line of business web does not need a framework
description:
A new business app starts with a question: React, Vue or Angular? The question that rarely gets asked is whether it needs one at all. For a page that lists orders, edits a customer and shows a few figures, the browser now does most of what we once picked a framework for.

This article walks through what frameworks were for, what the browser has taken over, and what is still missing. Then it builds a working order page in one HTML file, with no framework and no build step.

The habit

You start a project. You pick a framework, then a component library for that framework, then a state library, a router and a form library that fit both. By the time the first page shows a table, you have five dependencies that must agree with each other, and each will ship a breaking major version on its own schedule.

None of that is wrong. A framework gives a team one way to do things, and every developer you hire has used one. But it is a choice made by reflex, and the reasons it was the right reflex ten years ago have mostly gone away.

What a framework was for

Frameworks filled holes in the browser. Look at what those holes were, and what fills them today:

You needed a framework for The browser has
Your own reusable tags Custom elements
Knowing when a component appears and disappears connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback
Modals that trap focus and close on Escape <dialog>
Dropdowns that float above everything The Popover API
Form validation Constraint validation: required, min, pattern, :invalid
Numbers, amounts and dates per locale Intl
Code split into modules ES modules, loaded straight from a URL

The big remaining selling point is reactivity: change a variable and the page follows. That solves a real problem in an app where a hundred things depend on each other. A business page is rarely that app. It shows records, lets you change one, and shows the result. The places that change are few, and you know which they are.

What is still missing

The browser has no table that sorts and pages. No tabs, no tree view, no chart. That is what a business page is made of, and it is the real reason teams reach for a framework and its component library.

So that is the gap I filled with @relax.js/components: tables, tree views, tabs, menus, dialogs, charts and meters for business pages. Not a framework. Each one is a plain custom element, and where the browser already has the part, it uses it: the table is a native <table>, menus use the Popover API, the dialog is a <dialog>.

A page with no framework

Save this as a file and open it. No npm install, no bundler:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Orders</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@relax.js/components@2.0.0/dist/theme.css">
    <style>
        body { font-family: system-ui; background: var(--surface-bg); color: var(--text-primary); }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <r-stat-tile label="Orders"></r-stat-tile>
    <button id="add">New order</button>

    <r-table page-size="10">
        <r-column field="number" sortable>Order</r-column>
        <r-column field="customer" sortable>Customer</r-column>
        <r-column field="total" sortable>Total</r-column>
    </r-table>

    <r-dialog id="new-order" heading="New order">
        <template>
            <form method="dialog">
                <label>Customer <input name="customer" required></label>
                <label>Total <input name="total" type="number" min="1" required></label>
                <button value="save">Save</button>
            </form>
        </template>
    </r-dialog>

    <script type="module">
        import 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@relax.js/components@2.0.0/+esm';

        const orders = [
            { number: 'SO-10001', customer: 'Fjällbo AB', total: 12400 },
            { number: 'SO-10002', customer: 'Kvarnen HB', total: 860 },
            { number: 'SO-10003', customer: 'Ekdahl & Son', total: 3150 },
        ];

        const table = document.querySelector('r-table');
        const tile = document.querySelector('r-stat-tile');
        const dialog = document.querySelector('#new-order');

        function show() {
            table.rows = orders;
            tile.setAttribute('value', orders.length);
        }

        dialog.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
            const form = new FormData(event.target);
            orders.push({
                number: `SO-${10001 + orders.length}`,
                customer: form.get('customer'),
                total: Number(form.get('total')),
            });
        });

        document.querySelector('#add').addEventListener('click', async () => {
            if (await dialog.open() === 'save') {
                show();
            }
        });

        show();
    </script>
</body>
</html>

You get a figure, a sortable table with grouped numbers and a pager, and a modal form. The form refuses to save without a customer or with a total below 1. That is the browser, not my code and not a library.

Now count what is not there. No state store. No virtual DOM. No compiler. No component tree to keep in your head. The data is an array, and show() is the whole rendering strategy: when the data changed, you tell the page.

"But who keeps the page in sync?"

You do, and that is the point. A framework re-renders when it decides something changed. When it gets it wrong, you debug the framework: why did this render twice, why did that not render at all.

Each component here redraws when you change its attributes, its properties or its content, and at no other time. There is no base class, no reactivity and no hidden scheduler. The lifecycle is the one on MDN. If the table shows old rows, you forgot to set rows, and a breakpoint on that line tells you so.

One rule trips everybody up: records go in a property, not an attribute. Attributes are strings, and a list in an attribute is a JSON string the component would have to parse and keep in sync with the property. So rows, columns and chart data are set from code, and scalars like page-size are attributes.

"But it needs Relax.js core"

Yes. The components have one peer dependency, @relax.js/core, and the jsDelivr link pulls it in for you.

That does not sneak a framework back in. A framework calls your code: it owns the lifecycle, the rendering and the state. Core is a set of libraries your code calls, and you use only the parts you need: typed form reading, routing, dependency injection, translations. The components themselves call it for four things:

  • translating the words they show (No data, Next)
  • reporting errors through one channel
  • formatting values
  • letting the router open a dialog, and only for a dialog you give a name

When the page above grows into an app with several pages, those same libraries give you a router and typed forms. You add them when you need them, not on day one.

Already on React or Vue?

Then the components still work, because every framework renders HTML and a custom element is HTML. The property rule above is all you need to know. React 19 assigns rows={orders} as a property. In Vue you write :rows.prop="orders" and tell the compiler that r- tags are not Vue components. Events are plain DOM events.

It is a way out as much as a way in. The table you use in React today is the same table in the page that replaces it.

The takeaway

Frameworks were the right answer to a browser that could not do much. The browser caught up. For a page that lists, edits and summarizes records, what is missing is the business components, not a framework. Add those as plain custom elements, write the updates yourself, and you have nothing left to migrate away from.

Next in the series: server-side paging and sorting, with one async function.

title: Qt, GTK, Flutter, Electron? No: a graphics engine from scratch, entirely in Rust
description:
Llimphi draws every pixel of tawasuyu, even inside an operating system that boots with no Linux underneath. Why it exists, how it works and how true that “from scratch” really is.

Every time you open an application, something has to draw every button, every letter and every window on your screen, dozens of times per second. That something is a graphics engine, and almost nobody builds their own: most of the world’s software is painted with Qt, GTK, Flutter or Electron. Tawasuyu, the software suite with Quechua names being written in the Gioser workshop, chose not to borrow one.

Its engine is called Llimphi, which in Quechua means color, shine, pigment. It draws the whole suite: the desktop, the editor, the video player, the control panels and the interface of the project’s own operating system. Today 276 pieces of the suite are painted with Llimphi.

Fifteen and a half seconds of Llimphi. Everything on screen is drawn by the engine, frame by frame: the controls, the cosmos sky, the supay corridor, the infinite voxel world and the hand.
Why not use one that already exists

Until May 2026, tawasuyu was drawn with GPUI, the engine behind the Zed editor. On May 26 it was removed entirely, and not on a whim: the project has its own operating system, wawa, which boots straight on the hardware, with no Linux underneath. No existing engine knows how to draw there.

Qt, GTK and Flutter take a conventional operating system for granted, with its window manager, its installed fonts and its memory management. Llimphi was designed from day one to paint both in a desktop window and in the video memory of a kernel that has just powered on. That requirement forced it to be written from scratch.
What “from scratch” means

It is worth being precise, because it is the question every programmer asks. Llimphi did not reinvent every piece. Just as Flutter relies on Skia and GTK on Cairo, Llimphi uses four free projects from the Rust community for the most specialized jobs. Everything else is its own: the way an application describes its screen, how it reacts to each click, the components and the paths that lead to the pixels.

Talking to the graphics card: wgpu · community
Drawing curves and fills with antialiasing: vello · community
Working out where each box goes (flexbox and grid): taffy · community
Shaping text: Arabic, Chinese, emoji, ligatures: parley · community
The life cycle of each application: Llimphi
Components, themes, animation, accessibility: Llimphi
Painting without a graphics card, inside the kernel: Llimphi
Isolating an application and painting its drawing from outside: Llimphi

The four community pieces are written in Rust too. That is why the headline says “entirely in Rust”, and stands by it.
How a Llimphi application thinks

Llimphi follows the Elm architecture, named after a language known for applications that almost never crash. The idea is simple: the application does not modify the screen, it describes it. Every time something happens, the engine goes through six steps:

input: A click, a key or a gesture arrives.
update: The application computes its new state.
view: It describes how it should look in that state.
layout: The engine works out the position of each box.
raster: It turns that description into pixels.
present: It shows the finished frame.

Since nothing touches the screen directly, no two parts of the program fight over the same button. It is the same reason this style became popular on the web with React, except here it runs natively, with no browser in between.
One brush, four paths to your screen

The most unusual part of Llimphi is that the same drawing can reach the screen by completely different paths, depending on where the application runs. “Looks about the same” was not good enough: each path was put side by side with the others and the pixels were counted.
With a graphics card

The everyday path on the desktop. It is the reference everything else is measured against.
CPU only

The one the wawa kernel uses, since it has no video driver.
Subscribe to the Medium newsletter

Fills and layers identical bit for bit. Accented text may differ, because the kernel only ships three fonts.
By message

An isolated application doesn’t touch the screen: it sends its drawing as a message and the system paints it on its behalf.

0 pixels of difference across the four test scenes.
For phones

A path that works on mobile graphics chips without general-purpose compute, such as the Mali-G57.

No pixel differs by more than 1/255 out of 19,200.

The “by message” path coming out with zero difference has a practical consequence: an application can live locked away, with no permission at all to touch the screen, and still look exactly the same. Security that costs nothing in appearance.
What it already ships

Close to eighty components: buttons, tables, text editors with multiple cursors, node graphs, panel splitters, calendars and more.
Eleven modules that combine components into complete application pieces.
Real text: right-to-left writing, Chinese characters, emoji, ligatures and input methods for Asian languages.
Accessibility: every element can declare what it is and what it is called, and the tests query it the way a screen reader would.
Image-based tests: a screen is compared with its approved version, and any unexpected change makes the test fail.
A 3D voxel engine that mounts inside the same interface, as just another component.

What it doesn’t do yet

An engine that promises too much loses the trust of whoever tries it, so it is worth saying what is missing too:

The phone path has been tested on real hardware, but no published application uses it yet. The current Android builds take another path that doesn’t work on every chip.
Outside its three built-in fonts, text may look different in the kernel and on the desktop. The cause is known: with no operating system underneath, there is nowhere to get more fonts from.
Part of Llimphi is already published on crates.io, Rust’s official registry, but the release is incomplete and some recent pieces haven’t been uploaded yet.

How to try it

For Rust programmers, the way in is a single package:

cargo add llimphi

The package bundles the core, the themes and the 3D engine. For the rest, the best demonstration is tawasuyu itself: every window in the suite is a Llimphi application.

Originally published at https://gioser.net on October 12, 2026.
