title: Postgres SMS Alert Service Alternative — Startup App Receipts for Property Viewings
description:
Keep property-viewing message templates in the application, put suppression and send intent in Postgres, and treat the SMS provider as a replaceable delivery adapter. TL;DR: for a healthtech startup coordinating property viewings, the simplest defensible design is an app-owned template rendered into an immutable message snapshot, an idempotent send command, and a polling worker that records delivery evidence. Choose a polling-oriented API when uncomplicated wiring matters more than live event streams or multi-channel journeys.

This decision keeps the business contract stable while the vendor behind delivery changes. It also draws a hard line around what a delivery receipt proves: transport state, not that a patient, caregiver, or agent read the message.

Which SMS alert service alternative should a startup app choose?

The first invariant is suppression before dispatch. A recipient who has opted out, or whose number has been classified as invalid, must not receive another viewing confirmation merely because a job was retried. Maintain the provider suppression state, but mirror the decision in an application ledger so that the send path has a local, auditable gate.

The second invariant is that one business event creates one send intent. Use a stable key such as viewing-confirmation:{viewing_id}:{recipient_id}:{template_version}; store it under a unique constraint before making the network call, and carry an idempotency key through any provider adapter that supports one. Exactly-once delivery over a network is not a credible promise. Exactly-once intent plus deduplicated side effects is the useful target.

The third invariant is evidence preservation. Store the rendered body, template version, consent basis, destination in the minimum form your retention policy permits, provider message identifier, state transitions, and timestamps. Do not overwrite sent with delivered; append a transition. Compliance limits still apply: delivery logs can contain personal data, so retention, access, redaction, and regional handling need explicit policy rather than an indefinite debug table.

Failure boundaries follow from those invariants. The database owns eligibility and intent; the adapter owns submission; the receipt worker owns observations. A timeout after submission is ambiguous, so a blind second send is unsafe. A missing receipt is unknown, not failed. Keep it that way.

No guesswork.

Template ownership decides the architecture

The central choice is not the smallest advertised per-message rate. It is who owns the template contract and therefore controls versioning, review, localization, evidence, and migration.

Option Template ownership Receipt model Best fit Boundary to accept
Twilio Messaging Application or provider-managed content, depending on the product selected Status callbacks are documented Teams wanting a mature messaging-specific surface and push-style status handling The application still needs its own consent, suppression, and audit model
AWS End User Messaging SMS Application-centered message construction with AWS-managed origination resources Delivery event destinations are documented AWS-centered systems that already operate IAM, CloudWatch, or event destinations More cloud resource configuration enters the delivery path
Vonage SMS API Application-owned message content Delivery receipts are documented Teams wanting a focused SMS API with asynchronous receipt handling Vendor-specific receipt semantics belong behind an adapter
Infobip SMS Application content plus platform messaging features Delivery reports are documented Programs likely to grow into broader communications workflows The larger platform surface may exceed a small alert service's needs
Infrai Application-owned template snapshot behind one REST API Polling, with no webhook event push A startup prioritizing one credential, explicit sender setup, suppression APIs, and a stable contract when the underlying vendor changes It is a poor fit when webhook receipts, voice, WhatsApp, RCS, SMTP relay, or provider-hosted journeys are required; receipt latency is polling-bound and cost attribution stays local

Sender setup is part of the system, not an onboarding footnote. Registration rules differ by destination and use case, so model a sender as a deployable dependency with states such as requested, active, and retired; never let production choose an arbitrary sender string. Geographic anti-abuse limits and country-level spend circuit breakers also belong in the application layer. That is particularly important when US and EU traffic share one product workflow but do not share one regulatory regime.

The comparison favors different answers under different constraints. Twilio or Vonage is a natural fit when callback-driven receipts are a firm requirement. AWS is coherent when operational ownership is already concentrated there. Infobip earns consideration when SMS is likely to become a wider engagement program. SendGrid, Postmark, Resend, Mailgun, and Amazon SES solve email delivery, so they are not substitutes for an SMS alert service; they belong in a separately owned fallback path if email is required. A polling-first unified API is reasonable when a small team values a stable backend contract and accepts delayed state convergence, but its limitations rule it out when immediate event push is a product requirement.

The critical path in Go

The first runnable program below makes the actual SMS request without inventing a vendor request schema. Set INFRAI_SMS_JSON to a JSON object produced against the current public discovery schema; the program verifies that it is an object, submits it with Bearer authentication and an idempotency key, checks every response, and backs off on HTTP 429. INFRAI_BASE_URL is explicit because this independent article does not link to the service. The response is retained as raw evidence rather than decoded into fields that were not specified here.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    body := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_SMS_JSON"))
    if baseURL == "" || key == "" || len(body) == 0 {
        panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_API_KEY, and INFRAI_SMS_JSON are required")
    }
    var object map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &object); err != nil || object == nil {
        panic("INFRAI_SMS_JSON must be a JSON object matching the current discovery schema")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, baseURL+"/v1/sms/send", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "viewing-confirmation-viewing-482-recipient-19-v3")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("send failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, responseBody))
        }
        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            panic(ctx.Err())
        }
    }
    panic("send remained rate limited after five attempts")
}

The next program demonstrates the application contract boundary. The in-memory maps stand in for Postgres unique constraints and append-only tables, making the ordering visible without hiding it in framework code. Swap MockAdapter for the HTTP adapter above; the domain service remains unchanged.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type State string

const (
    Accepted  State = "accepted"
    Delivered State = "delivered"
    Bounced   State = "bounced"
)

type SendCommand struct {
    IntentKey       string
    Recipient       string
    RenderedBody    string
    TemplateVersion string
}

type Receipt struct {
    ProviderID string
    State      State
    ObservedAt time.Time
}

type SMSAdapter interface {
    Send(context.Context, SendCommand) (string, error)
    Receipt(context.Context, string) (Receipt, error)
}

type Ledger struct {
    mu          sync.Mutex
    suppressed  map[string]bool
    providerIDs map[string]string
    transitions map[string][]Receipt
}

func (l *Ledger) reserve(cmd SendCommand) (string, bool, error) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    if l.suppressed[cmd.Recipient] {
        return "", false, errors.New("recipient suppressed")
    }
    if id, exists := l.providerIDs[cmd.IntentKey]; exists {
        return id, false, nil
    }
    l.providerIDs[cmd.IntentKey] = "pending"
    return "", true, nil
}

func (l *Ledger) recordID(intentKey, providerID string) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.providerIDs[intentKey] = providerID
}

func (l *Ledger) appendReceipt(r Receipt) {
    l.mu.Lock()
    defer l.mu.Unlock()
    l.transitions[r.ProviderID] = append(l.transitions[r.ProviderID], r)
}

type MockAdapter struct{}

func (MockAdapter) Send(_ context.Context, cmd SendCommand) (string, error) {
    return "msg-" + cmd.IntentKey, nil
}

func (MockAdapter) Receipt(_ context.Context, id string) (Receipt, error) {
    return Receipt{ProviderID: id, State: Delivered, ObservedAt: time.Now().UTC()}, nil
}

func dispatch(ctx context.Context, ledger *Ledger, sms SMSAdapter, cmd SendCommand) (string, error) {
    id, reserved, err := ledger.reserve(cmd)
    if err != nil || !reserved {
        return id, err
    }
    id, err = sms.Send(ctx, cmd)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    ledger.recordID(cmd.IntentKey, id)
    return id, nil
}

func main() {
    ledger := &Ledger{
        suppressed:  map[string]bool{},
        providerIDs: map[string]string{},
        transitions: map[string][]Receipt{},
    }
    cmd := SendCommand{
        IntentKey:       "viewing-confirmation:viewing-482:recipient-19:v3",
        Recipient:       "+15555550199",
        RenderedBody:    "Your property viewing is confirmed for 10:30 AM.",
        TemplateVersion: "v3",
    }
    id, err := dispatch(context.Background(), ledger, MockAdapter{}, cmd)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    receipt, err := (MockAdapter{}).Receipt(context.Background(), id)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    ledger.appendReceipt(receipt)
    fmt.Printf("%s %s\n", receipt.ProviderID, receipt.State)
}

Production Postgres changes two details. Reserve the intent with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, and use an outbox worker so a committed intent cannot be stranded between the transaction and the network call. Encrypt or tokenize recipient identifiers according to the threat model; a hash alone may still be personal data when the input space is enumerable.

That ordering is the design.

Polling needs restraint. Schedule the next check with backoff and jitter, stop at a documented terminal state, and cap the observation window. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present; otherwise back off exponentially. The worker must persist each raw observation before advancing its cursor, because audit trails assembled after the fact are usually incomplete.

Bounces, invalid numbers, and cost attribution

“Bounce” is email vocabulary, but the operational response maps cleanly to SMS: normalize a terminal invalid-recipient result into a suppression reason, record its source, and block future sends before dispatch. Keep provider-specific status strings in the evidence record while exposing a small internal state machine to product code. That preserves detail for reconciliation without coupling every caller to a vendor taxonomy.

Do not suppress on every non-delivery. Temporary carrier conditions and an invalid destination have different consequences, and the adapter must translate only documented terminal outcomes. Likewise, an opt-out suppression should not be silently removed by a later profile edit. Require a new, auditable consent event.

Cost attribution needs its own ledger because the unified option does not expose tag-level aggregated cost reporting. Record tenant, campaign, intent key, and the returned per-call cost metadata in the same reconciliation stream; aggregate locally. Finance can then reconcile totals against the provider bill without making mutable message tags the accounting system of record.

Why reject provider-owned templates here?

Provider-owned templates can be valid. They reduce application rendering code, and they are attractive when non-engineering teams must edit copy inside an established communications platform, especially for multi-step journeys with provider-side approval workflows.

I would reject them for this confirmation path because a property-viewing event already originates in the application, while the audit record must preserve the exact content and consent decision associated with that event. Splitting template history between the database and a provider console complicates replay analysis and vendor migration. It also makes the adapter contract larger than Send(rendered message).

There is a limit to this decision. If a jurisdiction or message class requires provider-hosted, pre-approved content, compliance wins; store the provider template identifier and immutable version evidence beside the intent. Application ownership is an architectural preference, not permission to bypass sender registration or local messaging rules.

The final rule is compact: own eligibility, content snapshots, idempotency, and audit history; rent transport. Select the transport whose receipt model and sender-registration workflow match the operational team. For this startup-shaped alert path, polling is an acceptable trade when it buys a smaller integration surface and the product does not promise real-time delivery state.

References

  • Twilio, “Outbound Message Status in Status Callbacks”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging/guides/outbound-message-status-in-status-callbacks
  • Twilio, “What is the SMS character limit?”: https://www.twilio.com/docs/glossary/what-sms-character-limit
  • AWS, “Amazon SNS SMS delivery status”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sms_stats.html
  • AWS, “AWS End User Messaging SMS User Guide”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sms-voice/latest/userguide/what-is-service.html
  • Vonage, “SMS delivery receipts”: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/guides/delivery-receipts
  • Infobip, “SMS delivery reports”: https://www.infobip.com/docs/sms/delivery-reports
  • PostgreSQL, “INSERT”: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html
  • IETF, “Retry-After” in HTTP Semantics (RFC 9110): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-retry-after

title: The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It
description:
What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

**Uncertain rewards. **Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

**Self-regulation. **In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?

title: Unlocking Go: A Deep Dive into the Language that Powers Modern Cloud Apps
description:
Introduction

If you’ve been watching the cloud-native wave for the past few years, you’ve probably heard the name Go (or Golang) tossed around a lot. From Docker and Kubernetes to HashiCorp’s suite of tools, Go has become the lingua franca of infrastructure software. But what makes Go so compelling for developers building high‑performance, maintainable services? In this post we’ll explore Go’s core philosophy, walk through practical code examples, and highlight best‑practices that will help you write production‑grade Go code.

Why Go?

Go was created at Google in 2007 by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, and Ken Thompson. Their goal was simple: a language that feels like a scripting language but compiles to fast, native binaries. The design principles are:

  • Simplicity – a small standard library, minimal syntax, and a single, opinionated way to do things.
  • Concurrency as a first‑class citizen – goroutines and channels provide lightweight parallelism.
  • Fast compilation – sub‑second build times keep the feedback loop tight.
  • Static typing with type inference – catch bugs early while keeping code readable.

These goals translate into tangible benefits for cloud‑native development: quick iteration, low overhead binaries, and reliable concurrency.

Getting Started: Hello, World! 

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, World!")
}

Compile with go build -o hello . and run ./hello. The binary is self‑contained – no runtime dependencies needed.

Structuring a Go Project

A typical Go module looks like this:

myapp/
├─ go.mod          # module definition
├─ cmd/            # entry points (main packages)
│   └─ server/main.go
├─ internal/       # private packages
│   └─ handler/
│       └─ handler.go
└─ pkg/            # reusable libraries (optional)
    └─ config/
        └─ config.go
  • go.mod declares the module path and dependencies. Run go mod init github.com/yourname/myapp to create it.
  • Keep business logic inside internal/ – this prevents other modules from importing it unintentionally.
  • Use cmd/ for the executable(s) that wire everything together.

Concurrency Made Easy: Goroutines & Channels

Go’s concurrency model is built around goroutines (lightweight threads) and channels (typed pipes). Here’s a classic example that fetches URLs concurrently:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io/ioutil"
    "net/http"
    "sync"
)

func fetch(url string, wg *sync.WaitGroup, ch chan<- string) {
    defer wg.Done()
    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        ch <- fmt.Sprintf("%s: error %v", url, err)
        return
    }
    body, _ := ioutil.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    ch <- fmt.Sprintf("%s: %d bytes", url, len(body))
}

func main() {
    urls := []string{"https://golang.org", "https://dev.to", "https://github.com"}
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    ch := make(chan string, len(urls))

    for _, u := range urls {
        wg.Add(1)
        go fetch(u, &wg, ch)
    }
    wg.Wait()
    close(ch)

    for result := range ch {
        fmt.Println(result)
    }
}

Key takeaways:

  • go fetch(...) launches a goroutine instantly.
  • sync.WaitGroup ensures the main routine waits for all workers.
  • The buffered channel collects results without blocking the workers.

Error Handling – The Go Way

Go eschews exceptions; errors are explicit values. This makes failure paths clear and testable.

func readFile(path string) ([]byte, error) {
    data, err := os.ReadFile(path)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("read %s: %w", path, err)
    }
    return data, nil
}

func main() {
    if _, err := readFile("/nonexistent"); err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Fatal error: %v", err)
    }
}
  • Wrap errors with %w to retain the original cause – errors.Is and errors.As can later inspect it.
  • Use log.Fatalf for unrecoverable errors in simple tools; in libraries, return the error up the stack.

Testing & Benchmarking

Go ships with a built‑in testing framework. A typical test file ends with _test.go:

package math

import "testing"

func Add(a, b int) int { return a + b }

func TestAdd(t *testing.T) {
    got := Add(2, 3)
    if got != 5 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 5, got %d", got)
    }
}

func BenchmarkAdd(b *testing.B) {
    for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {
        Add(i, i)
    }
}

Run go test -v ./... for verbose output, and go test -bench=. ./... to execute benchmarks. The testing package also supports table‑driven tests, subtests, and coverage reporting (go test -cover).

Dependency Management with Modules

Since Go 1.11, modules are the default. Add a third‑party library with:

go get github.com/spf13/viper@v1.15.0

The go.mod file will now contain:

module github.com/yourname/myapp

go 1.22

require (
    github.com/spf13/viper v1.15.0 // indirect
)

Run go mod tidy to prune unused dependencies and ensure reproducible builds.

Deploying Go Binaries – From Docker to Serverless

Because Go produces static binaries, containerization is straightforward:

FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN go build -o server ./cmd/server

FROM alpine:latest
COPY --from=builder /app/server /usr/local/bin/server
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["server"]

The final image is only ~15 MB. For serverless platforms like AWS Lambda, use the aws-lambda-go library and compile with GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64.

Best Practices Checklist

✅ Practice
✅ Keep functions small (ideally < 30 lines)
✅ Prefer composition over inheritance – use interfaces
✅ Use context for cancellation & deadlines
✅ Run go vet, staticcheck, and golint in CI
✅ Document exported symbols with GoDoc comments
✅ Avoid global variables – inject dependencies
✅ Write table‑driven tests for edge cases

Conclusion

Go’s blend of simplicity, performance, and first‑class concurrency makes it a natural fit for modern cloud‑native services. By embracing Go’s idioms – explicit error handling, lightweight goroutines, and a strong standard library – you can ship reliable binaries fast and keep your codebase maintainable.

Ready to give Go a spin? Clone the starter repo, run go test ./..., and watch your first binary fire up in seconds. Happy coding!

title: Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp
description:
You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect.

In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?”

The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort.

This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example.

Before you begin

You need a Kubernetes cluster with Kueue installed, a Headlamp installation, and the 0.1.0-alpha Kueue plugin. Your Kubernetes identity must be allowed to read the Kueue resources used in this article.

The alpha release provides read-only views for Kueue v1beta2 Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues, ResourceFlavors, and Workloads. It does not add its own create, edit, stop, resume, or delete workflows. Headlamp still provides its standard YAML and resource actions where your permissions allow them.

First, separate admission from Pod scheduling

Kueue and the Kubernetes scheduler answer different questions.

  • Kueue admission: Should this Workload start now, considering queue policy, quota, ResourceFlavors, admission checks, and other waiting Workloads?

  • Pod scheduling: After the Workload is admitted and the Job resumes, which nodes can run its Pods?

That boundary changes the investigation. If the Workload is not admitted, stay in the Kueue section of Headlamp. If it is admitted but its Pods are still Pending, move to Headlamp's normal Job and Pod views and inspect scheduler events.

The Headlamp-first troubleshooting path

The quickest investigation starts with the Workload, not with a shell.

Step 1: Open the Workloads view

In Headlamp, open Kueue → Workloads. Select the namespace that contains the Job, then find the Workload created for it.

Kueue creates a Workload to represent the resource request and admission state of a Job. In the alpha plugin, owner references are shown as Kind/name text but are not yet clickable. The Workload name normally contains the Job name, so the namespace filter and table search are the simplest ways to locate it.

Before opening the detail page, the list already gives you a useful first scan:

  • LocalQueue

  • priority and priority class

  • active state

  • admitted state

  • completion state

  • a readable current status such as Admitted, Finished, or Inadmissible

  • age

If there is no matching Workload, check three things before going further: the selected namespace, whether the Job was submitted to a LocalQueue, and whether your Kubernetes account can list Workloads. The plugin performs permission checks and displays an access message when the current identity cannot read a resource.

Step 2: Read status, conditions, and events

Open the Workload. Start with its current status and conditions, not with the full YAML.

For admission troubleshooting, the most important condition types are QuotaReserved and Admitted.

  • Admitted=True means Kueue has admitted the Workload. The Job can resume, so any remaining Pending Pods belong to the scheduling branch of the investigation.

  • QuotaReserved=False with a reason such as Pending means Kueue has not reserved quota. The condition message explains what prevented the reservation.

  • An Inadmissible status means the Workload currently cannot fit the available queue configuration. A missing covered resource, unsuitable ResourceFlavor, stopped queue, or admission check can all lead you here.

For example, a condition message may report that Kueue could not assign a ResourceFlavor because the ClusterQueue has insufficient CPU quota. That message is the first real answer to “Why is my Job still pending?” The rest of the Headlamp journey explains the configuration behind it.

Also check the Events section. Conditions describe the current state; events help show what recently changed or what Kueue attempted.

Step 3: Compare the Workload's request with its assignment

Stay on the Workload detail page and inspect the PodSets and resource requests. The plugin shows the requested Pod count, CPU, memory, and other resources that Kueue evaluates together.

This matters because a Job with parallelism: 3 and a one-CPU request per Pod asks Kueue for three CPUs in total. Looking at only one Pod's template would underestimate the Workload.

If quota has already been reserved, the same page also shows the assigned ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavors, and admitted resource usage. If those admission assignments are absent, the Workload has not reached that point yet.

In our example, the Workload requests:

  • three Pods

  • three CPUs in total

  • 600 MiB of memory in total

The next question is where that request entered Kueue.

Step 4: Follow the linked LocalQueue

Use the LocalQueue link on the Workload detail page. A LocalQueue is the namespace-level entry point used by the Job. It connects namespaced Workloads to a cluster-scoped ClusterQueue.

The LocalQueue page shows:

  • its namespace and connected ClusterQueue

  • stop policy and current status

  • pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts

  • Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events

  • related Workloads in the same namespace

This page answers two practical questions: Did the Job enter the queue you expected, and is it the only Workload waiting there?

If the LocalQueue is inactive or stopped, that may already explain the wait. If it is active, follow the linked ClusterQueue to inspect the capacity behind it.

Step 5: Inspect ClusterQueue capacity and usage

A ClusterQueue represents the cluster-level quota and admission policy available to one or more LocalQueues.

On its Headlamp detail page, compare the Workload request with:

  • covered resources

  • nominal quota for each ResourceFlavor

  • current reservations and usage

  • borrowing and lending limits

  • pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts

  • queueing strategy and stop policy

  • preemption, fair-sharing, flavor-fungibility, and admission-check settings

  • Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events

For the example in this article, the ClusterQueue provides a nominal quota of two CPUs and two Pod slots. The Workload asks for three of each. The condition message and the ClusterQueue page now tell the same story: the Workload does not fit, so Kueue leaves the Job suspended.

This is an admission-capacity problem. It is not evidence that kube-scheduler failed to find a node.

Step 6: Check ResourceFlavor and Cohort when needed

Quota is not always a single pool. A ResourceFlavor can represent a class of compute through node labels, taints, tolerations, or topology settings. Use the ResourceFlavor link from the ClusterQueue when the condition mentions flavor assignment or when the Workload requires a particular hardware class, such as GPU nodes.

If the ClusterQueue belongs to a Cohort, follow that link too. Cohorts let ClusterQueues share unused quota. The Headlamp page shows parent and child Cohorts, member ClusterQueues, referenced ResourceFlavors, resource groups, borrowing and lending limits, and fair-sharing information.

These pages help answer a more subtle question: Is the Workload blocked because the queue has no quota of its own, because it cannot borrow enough, or because no suitable flavor can be assigned?

What we learned without leaving Headlamp

For the sample pending Job, the UI gives us a complete explanation:

  1. The Workload is not admitted.

  2. Its QuotaReserved condition is false and the message points to insufficient quota.

  3. The Workload requests three CPUs and three Pod slots.

  4. Its LocalQueue is active and points to the expected ClusterQueue.

  5. The ClusterQueue provides only two CPUs and two Pod slots.

  6. Kueue therefore keeps the Job suspended until quota becomes available or the queue configuration changes.

The important part is not that Headlamp invents a new status. It reads the same Kubernetes API objects as other clients, then places the related resources and human-readable values in one connected investigation.

If the Workload is admitted, switch views

Suppose the Workload detail page shows Admitted=True, but the application is still not running. Kueue has completed its part of the decision. Continue in Headlamp's standard Kubernetes views:

  1. Open Workloads → Jobs and inspect the Job state and events.

  2. Open Workloads → Pods and filter by the Job name or namespace.

  3. Select a Pending Pod and read its Events section.

At this stage, look for scheduler concerns such as insufficient node capacity, node affinity, taints and tolerations, topology constraints, persistent-volume binding, or image-pull failures.

This handoff is the most useful troubleshooting rule in the article:

  • Not admitted: investigate Kueue resources in Headlamp.

  • Admitted, but Pods are Pending: investigate Job, Pod, node, and scheduler information in Headlamp.

A repeatable Headlamp checklist

When the next Job does not start, use this short path:

  1. Open Kueue → Workloads and select the correct namespace.

  2. Find the Workload associated with the Job.

  3. Check the readable status, Admitted, and QuotaReserved conditions.

  4. Read the condition message and recent events.

  5. Compare PodSet resource requests with any admission assignments.

  6. Follow the LocalQueue link and confirm its status and ClusterQueue.

  7. Follow the ClusterQueue link and compare quota, reservations, usage, and policy.

  8. Inspect ResourceFlavor or Cohort details when the message points to flavor selection or shared quota.

  9. If admitted, move to Headlamp's Job and Pod views.

What Headlamp replaces during this investigation

The plugin does not replace kubectl or kueuectl for scripts, exact object output, or changes. It replaces the repetitive UI-less navigation needed during an interactive investigation.

Question Headlamp path Command-line equivalent
Is the Workload admitted? Kueue → Workloads → status and conditions kubectl describe workload <workload-name> -n <namespace>
Which LocalQueue did it enter? Workload → linked LocalQueue kubectl get localqueue <localqueue-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml
Which ClusterQueue provides quota? LocalQueue → linked ClusterQueue kubectl get clusterqueue <clusterqueue-name> -o yaml
Which flavor or shared quota matters? ClusterQueue → ResourceFlavor or Cohort kubectl get resourceflavor <flavor-name> -o yaml or kubectl get cohort <cohort-name> -o yaml
What happened after admission? Workloads → Jobs and Pods → events kubectl describe job <job-name> -n <namespace> or kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace>

For scripts and GitOps workflows, the command line remains the right tool. For a person asking “why is this waiting?”, the linked Headlamp path is usually faster to read.

Optional: reproduce the pending scenario

The plugin repository includes sample Cohort, ClusterQueue, LocalQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Job manifests for local testing. Apply those examples to a cluster where Kueue is installed, then open the Kueue section in Headlamp.

To reproduce the specific quota mismatch used in this article, configure a ClusterQueue with two CPUs and two Pod slots, then submit a three-Pod Job that requests one CPU per Pod. The Job enters its LocalQueue, Kueue creates a Workload, and the Workload remains pending because the combined request is larger than the available quota.

Keeping this setup separate from the main walkthrough is intentional: once the resources exist, the investigation itself should happen in Headlamp.

Current alpha limitations

The 0.1.0-alpha release is an initial read-only view of the Kueue admission path.

  • The plugin does not add its own create, edit, pause, resume, or delete flows.

  • Workload owner references are displayed as text and are not currently navigable.

  • The UI depends on the Kubernetes permissions of the identity used by Headlamp.

  • Metrics and a visual relationship map are possible follow-up areas rather than features of this release.

These limits are useful to state clearly: the plugin's current purpose is to make admission state and resource relationships easier to inspect.

Developed during LFX Mentorship

The plugin was developed during CNCF LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 2 using TypeScript, React, Kubernetes APIs, and Headlamp's plugin system.

Utkarsh Raj implemented the plugin with guidance and review from René Dudfield (@illume) and Kevin Hannon (@kannon92). Feedback from the Headlamp and Kueue communities shaped the resource views, status presentation, navigation, documentation, tests, and first alpha release.

Try it and share feedback

Explore the plugin source and README, read the 0.1.0-alpha release documentation, or share feedback in the release issue.

If a pending Workload is still difficult to explain after following the Headlamp path, that is exactly the kind of feedback that can improve the plugin.

title: Understanding Aspect Ratios in CSS and Canvas: Formulas, Responsive Rules, and Image Cropping
description:
When building responsive image galleries, hero sections, or interactive media canvases, aspect ratio mismatches are among the common causes of Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) and awkward visual cropping.

A browser may not know an image's intrinsic dimensions early enough to reserve the right space before layout, unless the dimensions or aspect ratio are provided in advance. When the rendered image changes the space occupied by surrounding content, the page can shift unexpectedly.

Here is a practical breakdown of how aspect ratios work, how to reduce them in JavaScript, and how to prevent visual distortion across screens and print frames.

1. The Mathematics of Aspect Ratio Reduction

An aspect ratio represents the proportional relationship between width and height. It is commonly written as width : height, or simply W:H.

For example, an image that is 1920 × 1080 pixels has an aspect ratio of 16:9. To determine the simplest ratio, divide both the width and height by their Greatest Common Divisor (GCD).

The standard method for computing the GCD in software is the Euclidean algorithm:

function getGCD(a: number, b: number): number {
  return b === 0 ? Math.abs(a) : getGCD(b, a % b);
}

function calculateAspectRatio(width: number, height: number): string {
  // This example expects positive integer pixel dimensions.
  if (!Number.isInteger(width) || !Number.isInteger(height) || width <= 0 || height <= 0) {
    throw new Error("Width and height must be positive integers.");
  }

  const divisor = getGCD(width, height);
  return `${width / divisor}:${height / divisor}`;
}

// Example calculations:
console.log(calculateAspectRatio(1920, 1080)); // "16:9"
console.log(calculateAspectRatio(1200, 800));  // "3:2"
console.log(calculateAspectRatio(1000, 800));  // "5:4"

Decimal Multipliers

Aspect ratios can also be expressed as a single decimal number. Divide the width by the height:

Decimal ratio = width ÷ height

Examples:

  • 16:9 = 1.7778 (standard widescreen video)
  • 3:2 = 1.5000 (common DSLR and mirrorless camera sensor ratio)
  • 4:3 = 1.3333 (common for some camera sensors, tablets, and web cards)
  • 5:4 = 1.2500 (traditional 8 × 10-inch photographic print)
  • 1:1 = 1.0000 (square avatars and UI thumbnails)

2. Modern CSS: Reserving Space and Enforcing Proportions

Before CSS introduced the native aspect-ratio property, web developers often relied on the "padding-top hack." With this technique, vertical padding is set as a percentage of the container's width.

Padding-top percentage = (height ÷ width) × 100

For a 16:9 container, the calculation is:

(9 ÷ 16) × 100 = 56.25%

So the older technique required padding-top: 56.25%.

Today, modern browsers support the aspect-ratio property natively:

.media-container {
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 800px;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  overflow: hidden;
  background-color: #f1f5f9;
}

.media-container img {
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
  object-fit: cover;
  object-position: center;
}

By defining aspect-ratio: 16 / 9, the browser can reserve space for the media container before the image loads. This can help reduce unexpected layout shifts when the element's sizing rules and surrounding layout are consistent.

3. The Print-Frame Cropping Conflict

A recurring frustration in digital image handling occurs when transferring photos between cameras, web layouts, and physical print products.

Many digital cameras use a 3:2 aspect ratio, which is equivalent to a decimal ratio of 1.50. Standard print sizes can use different proportions:

  • 4 × 6-inch print: 3:2 ratio (1.50). No cropping is required when the source image is also 3:2.
  • 5 × 7-inch print: 7:5 ratio (1.40). This is narrower than 3:2; a centered crop removes about 6.7% of the original image width in total.
  • 8 × 10-inch print: 5:4 ratio (1.25). This is narrower than 3:2; a centered crop removes about 16.7% of the original image width in total when the full image height is retained.

If you stretch an image to fit these containers, facial proportions and geometric objects can look distorted. If you use object-fit: contain, empty space may appear around the image. A carefully positioned crop can help the image fit the intended frame without distortion.

For an interactive way to calculate proportions, try this free aspect ratio calculator. Before publishing, confirm that any claims about image previews or local processing accurately describe the current implementation.

4. Client-Side Bounding Box Calculation in HTML5 Canvas

When implementing client-side crop tools, calculate the crop rectangle while preserving the target aspect ratio.

Here is core logic for center-cropping a source image to a target ratio:

function calculateCenterCrop(srcWidth, srcHeight, targetRatioWidth, targetRatioHeight) {
  if ([srcWidth, srcHeight, targetRatioWidth, targetRatioHeight].some(value => !Number.isFinite(value) || value <= 0)) {
    throw new Error("Source dimensions and target ratio values must be positive numbers.");
  }

  const targetRatio = targetRatioWidth / targetRatioHeight;
  const srcRatio = srcWidth / srcHeight;

  let cropWidth, cropHeight, cropX, cropY;

  if (srcRatio > targetRatio) {
    // Source is wider than target: crop horizontal edges
    cropHeight = srcHeight;
    cropWidth = srcHeight * targetRatio;
    cropX = (srcWidth - cropWidth) / 2;
    cropY = 0;
  } else {
    // Source is taller than target: crop vertical edges
    cropWidth = srcWidth;
    cropHeight = srcWidth / targetRatio;
    cropX = 0;
    cropY = (srcHeight - cropHeight) / 2;
  }

  return {
    cropX: Math.round(cropX),
    cropY: Math.round(cropY),
    cropWidth: Math.round(cropWidth),
    cropHeight: Math.round(cropHeight)
  };
}

Rendering onto Canvas 

const canvas = document.getElementById('previewCanvas');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');

const crop = calculateCenterCrop(img.naturalWidth, img.naturalHeight, 5, 4);

// Set canvas to target display dimensions
canvas.width = 500;
canvas.height = 400;

ctx.drawImage(
  img,
  crop.cropX, crop.cropY, crop.cropWidth, crop.cropHeight, // Source crop rectangle
  0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height                       // Destination canvas
);

Summary Checklist for Developers

  1. Reserve space early: Use CSS aspect-ratio or explicit image dimensions to help the browser lay out media before it loads.
  2. Avoid distortion: Do not stretch width and height independently. Use object-fit: cover when filling a frame and when cropping is appropriate.
  3. Account for print sizes: When building export tools, remember that 4 × 6, 5 × 7, and 8 × 10-inch prints use different aspect ratios.
  4. Choose the right processing model: Aspect-ratio calculations can run in the browser. Only describe image processing as client-side if the implementation actually keeps that processing local.

title: A/B tests your coding agent can run
description:
Your coding agent can change a headline in seconds. Finding out whether that headline helps people sign up takes an experiment.

I built SplitHub to keep that experiment in the same workflow as the code. You declare variants and a goal in splithub.config.ts, render the assigned value in your app, and read results from the CLI or an MCP client.

Start in your app

SplitHub needs Node.js 22.13 or newer. Run:

npx splithub init

For your own database, use:

npx splithub init --mode self

The React SDK provides SplitHubProvider, useVariant, useValue and useTrack. The Next.js package adds middleware and server component helpers. Assignment uses a local hash, so choosing a variant doesn't require a network request during rendering.

Give your agent the tools

To connect the MCP server in Claude Code:

claude mcp add splithub -- npx -y @splithub/mcp

For another MCP client, the configuration is:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "splithub": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@splithub/mcp"]
    }
  }
}

You can then ask it to create a headline test, start or pause an experiment, push config, or read results. The server uses the same project config and credentials as the CLI.

For example:

Test a shorter headline on the pricing page, using signup as the goal.

Later:

Read the results for the pricing headline test. Is there enough evidence to choose a variant?

The CLI also lets you inspect results directly:

npx splithub status
npx splithub results hero-title

Replace hero-title with your experiment key.

Cloud or your own storage

SplitHub Cloud returns statistical verdicts. Self-hosted storage returns raw visitors, conversions, conversion rates and revenue. The public SDK is MIT licensed; the cloud analysis is separate.

You still need real visitors and a measured goal. An agent can help operate a test, but it can't replace evidence with a confident answer.

The repository includes complete Vite + React and Next.js examples.

Explore the SDK on GitHub · Documentation

Questions or feedback: info@splithub.io

title: Escape Analysis: How Can a Compiler Eliminate a Heap Allocation Without Changing Your Code?
description:
Consider this Java method:

double distanceBetween(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
    Point b = new Point(x2, y2);
    return Math.sqrt(
        Math.pow(b.x - a.x, 2) + Math.pow(b.y - a.y, 2)
    );
}

Two Point objects are created, used in a calculation, and then discarded. The source code calls new, which in Java means heap allocation, object initialization, and eventually garbage collection. But if you look at this from a different angle: both objects are born at the start of the method, used for arithmetic, and are completely useless after the return statement. Nothing outside the method ever sees them. No other thread can observe them. They exist solely to hold two doubles each.

Does the runtime actually need to allocate heap memory for them? That question is what escape analysis is designed to answer.

What It Means for an Object to Escape

Before a compiler can eliminate an allocation, it needs to prove that the allocation can be eliminated. The key concept is whether an object escapes its local scope.

An object escapes when a reference to it can be observed from outside the context in which it was created. There are several ways this happens:

Return. A method that returns a reference to a locally created object immediately causes it to escape. The caller now holds a live reference, so the object must exist somewhere accessible after the method returns. Stack frames are discarded on return, which means the object cannot safely live in one.

Shared state. Storing a reference in a field of an object that outlives the current scope, or in a static field, allows code anywhere in the program to observe the object. The compiler must assume the object could be read at any time.

Opaque callees. When a method passes an object to another function and the compiler cannot fully analyze what that function does with the reference, it must conservatively assume the object might escape. If the callee stores the reference in a field or returns it to its own callers, the assumption would be violated.

Non-escaping objects are those where the compiler can prove that every reference to the object stays within a bounded scope. It is created, used, and the last reference to it disappears, all within a region the compiler can reason about.

The Point objects in the opening example are non-escaping. The references a and b are local variables. They are never returned, never stored in any field, never passed to an opaque method. The compiler can trace every use of them.

How the Compiler Reasons About References

Escape analysis is not a single yes-or-no check. It is a data flow analysis that the compiler runs over the program's intermediate representation, tracking how references to each object propagate through the code.

The classic formulation, and the one underlying HotSpot's C2 compiler, builds a connection graph: a representation of the relationships between object references, the fields through which they flow, and the boundaries across which they might cross. Each object in the graph carries an escape state. HotSpot's C2 uses three states: NoEscape, for objects whose references are entirely contained within the method; ArgEscape, for objects passed as arguments but not observed to escape further; and GlobalEscape, for objects accessible from outside the method or thread.

The analysis is conservative. If the compiler cannot prove that a reference stays local, it assumes it might escape. Conservative analysis is safe: it never eliminates a necessary allocation. But it also means some allocations that a human could see are unnecessary will be retained because the compiler's model of the code is not complete. Inlining is one of the most important enablers of escape analysis. When a callee is inlined into the caller, the compiler gains full visibility into what the callee does with every argument, which allows escape states to be refined. HotSpot's C2 requires inlining to occur before scalar replacement can work. If a method is not inlined because it is too large or was not compiled at the right optimization tier, the analysis may classify its arguments as escaping, even if they do not.

The Optimization: Scalar Replacement

The natural first guess is that escape analysis moves objects from the heap to the stack. For some compilers and runtimes, that is exactly what happens. The Go compiler does this: if it proves that a value will not outlive the current function, it allocates the value in the goroutine's stack frame rather than on the heap. You can observe this directly with go build -gcflags="-m", which annotates each allocation decision.

HotSpot's C2 JIT takes a different path. According to the OpenJDK wiki: "C2 does NOT replace a heap allocation with a stack allocation for non globally escaping objects." Instead, C2 performs scalar replacement.

Scalar replacement decomposes an object into its constituent fields and eliminates the object itself. Rather than allocating a block of memory and storing field values in it, the compiler treats each field as an independent local variable. The object never materializes as a contiguous region of memory. No allocation happens. No garbage collector ever needs to reclaim it.

The transformation for the Point example looks conceptually like this. Before scalar replacement:

// What you wrote
Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
double ax = a.x;
double ay = a.y;

After scalar replacement, the compiler replaces all field accesses with synthetic local values:

// What the compiler works with internally
double a_x = x1;  // scalar substitute for a.x
double a_y = y1;  // scalar substitute for a.y

The Point object never exists. The field reads (a.x, a.y) become references to local values that can be kept in registers. Aleksey Shipilëv's JVM Anatomy Quarks describes this precisely: HotSpot "does not do stack allocations per se, but it does approximate that with Scalar Replacement."

From there, register allocation can place those scalar values in CPU registers for the duration of the computation. The two doubles that would have been heap-allocated objects end up as register values, with no allocation, no initialization overhead, and no GC involvement.

A Concrete Walk-Through

Take the full distance method from the opening:

double distanceBetween(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    Point a = new Point(x1, y1);
    Point b = new Point(x2, y2);
    return Math.sqrt(
        Math.pow(b.x - a.x, 2) + Math.pow(b.y - a.y, 2)
    );
}

For scalar replacement to apply, C2 needs to:

  1. Inline the Point constructor so it can see that no reference to the new object leaks out of the construction.
  2. Determine that a and b have escape state NoEscape: no return of the references, no field stores into external objects, no passing to opaque methods.
  3. Replace new Point(x1, y1) with two scalar variables a_x = x1, a_y = y1.
  4. Rewrite every a.x and a.y access to use those scalars.
  5. Eliminate the allocation instruction entirely. After this transformation, the method compiles to arithmetic on four double values, none of which requires heap memory. The behavior observed by any caller is identical: they receive the same double result. The only change is internal to the representation of the computation.

Lock elimination is a related optimization that escape analysis enables. If an object is non-escaping, no other thread can hold a reference to it, so any synchronized blocks on that object are unnecessary. The compiler can remove them.

Where the Analysis Fails

Escape analysis has hard limits, and understanding them is as important as understanding what it can do.

The most common barrier is an opaque method call. If distanceBetween passed a to any method that C2 has not inlined, the compiler would have to assume the reference might escape. The Point would remain heap-allocated. This is why HotSpot's OpenJDK scalar replacement documentation explicitly lists non-inlined methods as a case where scalar replacement is prevented.

Interface dispatch is a related problem. When a method is called through an interface, the compiler cannot always determine which concrete implementation will run, which makes it impossible to inline the callee. Without inlining, the escape state of the argument is unknown.

Some operations are identity-sensitive. Java's == operator on objects tests reference identity. If the compiler replaces an object with scalars, two allocations that previously produced distinct references might appear identical or might behave incorrectly if the program depends on them being different objects. The compiler must verify that no code in scope depends on the object's identity before it can safely decompose it.

Synchronization presents a harder constraint. If code synchronizes on an object that the compiler is considering for scalar replacement, the semantics of Java's memory model require that the lock be observable. Lock elimination is sound only when the object is genuinely non-escaping, so the compiler must be certain before removing it.

Conservative analysis also means that HotSpot will retain an allocation if any uncertainty exists. The analysis can handle many cases that appear complex in source code, but it cannot analyze beyond what it can observe. Dynamic loading of classes, reflection, and native code are all effectively opaque.

The Performance Picture

Removing allocations reduces pressure on the garbage collector by producing fewer objects that need to be tracked and collected. In throughput-sensitive code that creates many short-lived objects in tight loops, this can meaningfully reduce GC pause frequency and time spent in allocation paths. Keeping data in registers rather than memory also reduces memory traffic.

That said, allocation in modern JVMs is fast. HotSpot's thread-local allocation buffers (TLABs) allow most allocations to complete with a simple pointer bump. The cost of a single allocation is small. The benefit of elimination comes from the aggregate effect over many allocations, particularly in hot loops, and from the downstream reduction in GC work.

Whether scalar replacement improves a specific workload depends on the compiler's ability to apply it, the allocation rate of the relevant code, and the GC configuration. Profiling with allocation-aware tools is the right way to measure this, not inference from source code alone.

The Developer's Relationship With This Optimization

The existence of escape analysis and scalar replacement changes what source-level object creation actually means. Writing new Point(x, y) in Java does not guarantee that a heap allocation will occur at runtime. Whether one does depends on the JIT compiler's escape analysis, whether the relevant methods were inlined, and the escape state the analysis assigned to the object.

This is intentional. The language specification defines what the program must compute and what observable side effects it must produce. It says nothing about whether intermediate objects need physical representation. The JIT compiler is free to choose any implementation that preserves observable behavior.

Several practical points follow from this:

Write code that is clear and correct. Avoiding allocation for its own sake by using awkward data structures or manual field decomposition will not necessarily produce faster code and will make the compiler's job harder if it disrupts inlining.

Measure before concluding. Allocation sampling profilers can show which allocations actually reach the heap at runtime. An allocation that appears in source code may not appear in profiles if scalar replacement has already eliminated it.

Do not assume Java and Go behave identically. Go's escape analysis operates at compile time and makes stack-allocation decisions that are baked into the generated machine code. HotSpot's analysis operates in the JIT compiler and uses scalar replacement rather than stack allocation. The mechanisms, the triggering conditions, and the diagnostics are different.

Check compiler output when it matters. Go's -gcflags="-m" flag reports escape decisions. HotSpot's -XX:+PrintEliminateAllocations flag reports scalar replacement. These are the ground truth; source code is not.

The Deeper Insight

Escape analysis reflects a broader principle in compiler design: a language's specification describes the required observable behavior of a program, not its required internal representation. The compiler is free to transform how data is stored, how operations are sequenced, and how objects are physically represented, as long as anything the program is permitted to observe remains consistent with the specification.

A heap allocation is a mechanism for giving data a lifetime that outlives a function call. When the compiler can prove that a particular datum does not need that extended lifetime, the allocation is unnecessary. The datum can be represented as local values, stored in registers, and discarded the moment the function returns. The program computes the same result. The method's caller observes the same returned value. Nothing that any correct program could observe has changed.

What the compiler has changed is what never needed to exist in the first place.

Sources

  • OpenJDK HotSpot Escape Analysis Wiki — authoritative description of C2's escape analysis algorithm and its explicit statement that C2 does not perform stack allocation.
  • Aleksey Shipilëv: JVM Anatomy Quarks #18 — Scalar Replacement — detailed technical explanation of scalar replacement in HotSpot C2.
  • HotSpot Escape Analysis and Scalar Replacement Status (OpenJDK) — analysis of escape analysis coverage and limitations in C2.
  • Oracle Java Magazine: Escape Analysis in the HotSpot JIT Compiler — accessible explanation with GC log evidence.
  • Segment Engineering: Allocation Efficiency in High-Performance Go Services — practical explanation of Go's stack-allocation-first approach and escape analysis flags.
  • Go compiler escape analysis flags — go build -gcflags="-m" documentation.
