title: Do You Want Your Web App to Feel Like a Native App?
description:
You can give your Codename One web app the same desktop theme family as your users' operating system: Aqua on macOS, Fluent on Windows, or Adwaita on Linux. Menus can sit above the app in HTML, with commands such as File and View visible instead of tucked into a mobile overflow menu.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

That gives you a browser version of your app that fits more comfortably on a desktop. The JavaScript port now supports both choices, and the same theme work reaches the Certificate Wizard you use to sign your apps.

Follow the operating system, or choose a theme

Set these in the Settings app's Build Hints:

nativeTheme=native
javascript.titleBar=html

In codenameone_settings.properties, use codename1.arg.nativeTheme and codename1.arg.javascript.titleBar instead. Desktop browsers select Fluent for Windows, Aqua for macOS, and Adwaita for Linux and the remaining desktop systems. Phones and tablets keep the mobile theme selection. The browser detection treats an iPad as a tablet even when it reports a Mac browser.

These are Codename One themes drawing the controls. They are not the operating system's native widget toolkit embedded in the page.

The Settings app demonstrates the three desktop theme families now available to browser apps. Click to compare the controls at full size.

You can pin a desktop theme when the application's design calls for it:

javascript.desktopTheme=fluent

The other explicit choices are aqua, adwaita and none. none keeps mobile themes on desktop browsers. Leave the value at auto to follow the operating system. The broader nativeTheme=modern setting has different behavior: it selects the modern mobile families, including on desktop browsers. Use native when desktop family selection is what you want.

Put commands above the app

The default javascript.titleBar=toolbar keeps the themed Toolbar inside the app. With html, the page supplies title and menu bars instead. The title follows the current form; commands group into menus using the same Command.setDesktopMenu() hint used on the desktop ports.

For example, inside an initialized app:

com.codename1.ui.Form form = new com.codename1.ui.Form("Notes");
com.codename1.ui.Command refresh = new com.codename1.ui.Command("Refresh") {
    public void actionPerformed(com.codename1.ui.events.ActionEvent event) {
        form.setTitle("Notes refreshed");
    }
};
refresh.setDesktopMenu("View");
form.getToolbar().addCommandToOverflowMenu(refresh);
form.show();

Commands without a menu hint go into a Commands menu. The HTML bars follow the selected appearance and the browser's light or dark preference. They do not have fake minimize, maximize or close buttons: the page does not own the browser window. The browser tab title remains the application's display name.

The source is in JavaScriptDesktopChrome, with build-hint and page behavior documented in the JavaScript guide.

Keep navigation inside your browser app

We do not support additional native Window surfaces in the JavaScript port. Popup blockers and the browser's window ownership make that a different promise from drawing a menu inside the current page. Windows browsers are supported; extra OS windows are the unsupported feature. Dialogs and navigation within the app remain the appropriate model.

There are renderer limits too. For example, the full lifted-lens optics from Sunday's iOS article are not implemented in the browser. Try the actual controls and effects your app uses rather than assuming a theme name proves complete renderer parity.

The build prunes theme resources it can prove the app will not reach. If your code constructs resource names dynamically, set javascript.pruneThemes=false; otherwise a theme loaded only through that constructed name may be missing.

Use the same desktop styling when you sign your app

A gallery of buttons cannot tell us whether an application works comfortably with a desktop theme. The Certificate Wizard has longer forms, tables, dialogs and instructions that people must actually read to finish a task.

PR #5916 adopts the native desktop themes there, continuing the work we did in Settings. Its current source uses @DesktopBuild(themeMode = "native", titleBar = DesktopTitleBar.NATIVE, ...), with interactive scrollbars. Fluent, Aqua and Adwaita now provide the surrounding control styles instead of a separate wizard-specific desktop imitation.

The same change fixes handling of an App ID's team prefix. That is a separate functional repair, not a consequence of adopting a theme. The wizard's current source keeps both changes visible.

Try the browser theme with a form that has real commands and enough content to scroll. Switch appearances, open its menus and check keyboard navigation. That will teach you more than another screenshot of an isolated button.

The weekly overview links the rest of the release. It also includes this week's smaller map-label improvement.

title: The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It
description:
The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It

What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

Uncertain rewards. Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

Self-regulation. In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?

title: EffectCraft: The Open-Source Motion Graphics Powerhouse Built in Rust!
description:
Quick Summary: 📝

EffectCraft is an open-source motion graphics and compositing tool written in Rust, aiming to be a clean-room reimplementation of Adobe After Effects. It offers features like Lottie import/export, scriptability, and a readable project file format, making it suitable for creating animated titles, motion graphics, and visual effects.

Key Takeaways: 💡

  • ✅ EffectCraft is a free, open-source, Rust-based clean-room reimplementation of Adobe After Effects.

  • ✅ It offers a familiar UI with extensive features like 306 effects, 3D support, and cross-platform compatibility (including browser).

  • ✅ Developers benefit from built-in Lottie support for web/app animations and human-readable JSON project files for version control.

  • ✅ The entire application is scriptable, enabling powerful automation and custom workflow integrations.

  • ✅ Its pure Rust video/audio codecs ensure efficiency and minimal external dependencies.

Project Statistics: 📊

  • ⭐ Stars: 6363
  • 🍴 Forks: 3283
  • ❗ Open Issues: 298

Tech Stack: 💻

  • ✅ Rust

Hey fellow developers! Ever felt the pinch of proprietary software when diving into motion graphics or visual effects? Or wished for a more developer-friendly, open-source tool that lets you create stunning animations without breaking the bank or wrestling with opaque file formats? Well, prepare to get excited, because I just stumbled upon a GitHub project that's poised to revolutionize the game: EffectCraft!

Imagine having a tool that mirrors the power and flexibility of industry giants like Adobe After Effects, but is completely free, open-source, and built from the ground up in pure Rust. That's exactly what EffectCraft is aiming to be. It's a clean-room reimplementation, meaning it's not just a clone, but a fresh take on motion graphics, designed with modern development practices in mind. This isn't just a passion project; it's a rapidly evolving, already usable application for creating animated titles, complex compositions, and dazzling visual effects.

EffectCraft embraces the core concepts you'd expect: compositions, layers, keyframes for precise animation control, and a massive library of 306 effects. It even includes layer styles, expressions, and full 3D camera and light support, culminating in a robust render queue. What's truly impressive is its native availability across macOS, Windows, and Linux, and yes, even in the browser! This cross-platform versatility alone is a huge win for any developer or artist.

Now, let's talk about why EffectCraft is a game-changer for us developers. First off, it boasts built-in Lottie import and export. For anyone working on web or mobile applications, this is massive! No more clunky plugins or conversion headaches; your animations go straight from EffectCraft to your apps and websites seamlessly. This feature alone makes it incredibly appealing for front-end and UI/UX developers.

But wait, there's more! EffectCraft's project files are readable JSON (.ecproj). This is a huge deal for collaborative teams and version control. Imagine being able to git diff your animation projects! This level of transparency and integration with standard developer workflows is practically unheard of in this space. Furthermore, every single action within EffectCraft is scriptable. Whether you want to automate tasks via the command line, control it through a JSON channel, or integrate it with an agent-based system, the possibilities for automation and custom workflows are endless. And as a final cherry on top, it uses pure Rust for all video and audio decoding and encoding, ditching FFmpeg for a lean, efficient, and dependency-minimal approach.

EffectCraft is young and moving fast, but it's already incredibly powerful and brimming with potential. It offers a familiar interface for those coming from other tools, but with a foundational architecture that's built for the future. If you're into motion graphics, animation, or just curious about what's possible with Rust in the creative space, you absolutely need to check out EffectCraft. It's truly exciting to see such a robust and developer-friendly tool emerge in this domain. Go give it a star and join the community!

title: ARC Region switch adds four new capabilities
description:
Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) Region switch helps you orchestrate the failover of multi-Region applications to achieve a bounded recovery time during a Regional impairment. Today, Region switch adds four new capabilities: AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block, payloads for custom action Lambda execution block, service quota parity checks, and wait for target group health feature for compute scaling actions.

AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block. During failover, you often need to run commands on managed instances and VMs. This execution block lets you invoke Run Command actions on managed instances during failover, with plan evaluation verifying that command documents target valid instances and that IAM permissions are correctly configured.

Payloads for custom action Lambda execution block. ARC Region switch now lets you pass payloads to your custom action Lambda execution block, allowing reusability of your Lambda functions across recovery plans.

Service quota checks. Service quota limits are a common failure mode during recovery. Region switch now verifies quota parity between your primary and standby Region, and automatically submits quota limit increases, reducing the risk of insufficient service quotas during recovery.

Wait for target group health. Amazon ECS service scaling and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group execution blocks help you provision compute capacity during recovery, but provisioned capacity may not be ready to serve traffic. The optional wait for target group health feature verifies that your provisioned capacity is ready to serve traffic.

To get started, see the documentation for AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block , custom action Lambda execution block , Service quota checks  and the Wait for target group health for Amazon ECS service scaling execution block  and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group execution block .

title: Good Onboarding Starts Before Sign-Up: My Take on AviorSwap
description:
As a developer, I often think about onboarding as something that happens after registration.

There’s a welcome screen, maybe a checklist, and a few tooltips explaining where to click.

But as a user, I start forming my understanding much earlier. The homepage is already teaching me how to think about the product.

That’s what I appreciate about AviorSwap’s presentation: it gives me a straightforward introduction to what the platform is for and how to get started.

Give me a direction first

When I explore a new service, I don’t need to understand every feature immediately. I need a useful starting point.

AviorSwap makes deposit and swap actions visible early in the experience. For me, that establishes a clear direction.

I can identify the main activities without first learning a complicated navigation structure.

This is a design decision I respect because it requires prioritization. Every product has multiple things it could highlight. Choosing the actions that best explain its purpose helps a new visitor get oriented.

Let curiosity be part of the experience

I don’t always arrive at a platform ready to perform a specific action. Sometimes I just want to explore.

AviorSwap’s market sections, including popular assets and daily movers, give that curiosity somewhere to go.

I like this combination: a clear path for task-focused users and an entry point for people who are still getting familiar with the service.

It reminds me of good documentation. Sometimes I need a specific command. Sometimes I need an overview that helps me decide what to investigate next.

Both are valid ways to begin.

Explain the sequence in everyday language

One part of the public website I appreciate is the FAQ’s description of the onboarding process.

It outlines the progression from creating an account to setting up a wallet, depositing cryptocurrency, and exchanging assets.

Knowing the sequence helps me build expectations. I can understand how one step connects to the next before entering the workflow.

As developers, we spend so much time inside our products that we can forget how valuable this basic explanation is.

A new user shouldn’t need to reverse-engineer the journey from button labels.

Make the important topics easy to find

AviorSwap also puts pricing and fees near the center of its messaging.

I see that as a positive presentation choice. Costs are naturally part of how someone evaluates an exchange, so they deserve a visible place in the introduction.

When I design interfaces, I try to ask: what question is the user likely to have at this point?

Putting relevant information near the moment that question appears is one of the most useful things an interface can do.

What I’d bring into my own work

My impressions come from exploring AviorSwap’s public website. The aspect that stands out to me is how its presentation introduces the service through recognizable actions and short explanations.

It’s a useful reminder that onboarding includes everything a user sees while deciding whether a product makes sense to them.

For my own projects, I’d carry forward three ideas:

Make the primary action easy to recognize.

Give curious visitors something meaningful to explore.

Explain the overall process before asking users to navigate it.

That’s why AviorSwap’s approach appeals to me. It brings attention to the early moments when a visitor is becoming a user—and those moments deserve thoughtful design.

What’s the best onboarding decision you’ve borrowed from another product?

title: Why AviorSwap’s Focus on Simplicity Appeals to Me as a Developer
description:
I appreciate products that make their purpose easy to understand.

When I open a new platform, I want to answer three questions quickly: What can I do here? Where should I start? What information will help me take the next step?

Looking through AviorSwap’s public website, I found myself thinking about those questions from both a user’s and a developer’s perspective.

What appeals to me is its focus on making the exchange experience approachable.

Clear actions make a good first impression

AviorSwap gives deposit and swap actions a prominent place in its interface.

That sounds like a small detail, but navigation shapes the entire first impression of a product. When the main actions are easy to identify, I can spend more time understanding the service and less time searching through menus.

As a developer, I appreciate that kind of prioritization.

A homepage has limited attention to work with. Giving the core workflow room to stand out is a design choice I value.

Room to explore before taking action

I also like the combination of market discovery and direct actions.

The homepage includes sections for popular assets and daily market movements. That gives the experience a useful starting point even when I’m simply browsing.

Sometimes I approach a platform with a specific task. Other times, I want to get a sense of what’s available before deciding where to go next.

An interface that supports both approaches feels more welcoming to me.

It’s a principle I’d happily carry into my own projects: make the main action obvious, while leaving space for exploration.

Explaining the workflow helps users get oriented

AviorSwap’s FAQ outlines a sequence involving registration, wallet setup, a deposit, and an exchange.

I appreciate seeing the process described in plain language. It helps me form a basic picture of the workflow before stepping into it.

This is something we can underestimate as developers. Once we understand a system, its sequence starts to feel obvious. A new user doesn’t have that background.

A short explanation can make a product easier to approach without requiring a lengthy tutorial.

Pricing deserves a visible place

Another aspect I like is the attention given to pricing in the website’s messaging.

AviorSwap presents clear fees and competitive rates as priorities. Those are the right topics to put in front of someone evaluating an exchange service.

For me, this is about helping users focus on the information that matters to their decision. I want the discussion of costs to be part of the main experience.

My impressions here come from the public website, so I’m describing its presentation rather than claiming verified execution speeds or trading results.

A useful reminder for my own projects

What I take away from AviorSwap is an appreciation for focused product presentation.

Visible actions, opportunities to explore, and accessible explanations all contribute to how I understand a service. They’re also choices that apply well beyond crypto—to dashboards, developer tools, and everyday web applications.

As a potential user, I find that approach inviting. As a developer, it reminds me to give the basics the attention they deserve.

What’s one interface detail that immediately gives you a positive first impression of a new product?

title: Stop exporting JSON tokens and use CSS variables instead
description:
A designer tagged me in a Figma comment on Tuesday morning. They wanted to know if we could start exporting our brand tokens as deeply nested JSON files. They had just read an article about complex token pipelines. I just stared at my screen for a minute. We are a web team building a React application. We do not need a massive parsing engine just to read a blue hex code.

This happens all the time in our industry. Teams get obsessed with the idea of a universal format. They build massive configurations to transform JSON into something the browser can actually use. It feels like everyone is overcomplicating the simplest part of frontend development.

The pipeline trap

I see this pattern everywhere. A team decides they need a design system. They set up a pipeline that exports something like this from Figma.

{
  "color": {
    "brand": {
      "primary": {
        "value": "#0052cc",
        "type": "color"
      }
    },
    "background": {
      "base": {
        "value": "#ffffff",
        "type": "color"
      }
    }
  }
}

Then the web developers have to write a script to flatten this object. They have to map it to their styling solution. Maybe they are using Tailwind. Maybe they are using styled-components. Either way, it adds a completely unnecessary layer of complexity.

If a colour breaks in production, you cannot just inspect it easily. You have to trace the error back through your build script. You have to figure out if the JSON was malformed or if your parser failed. That is a lot of wasted time for a background colour.

The browser already solved this

CSS variables are the only token format that actually matters for the web. You do not need a build step to use them. You just load the file and the browser understands it immediately.

Look at how much cleaner the CSS approach is.

:root {
  --color-brand-primary: #0052cc;
  --color-background-base: #ffffff;
}

You can inspect this directly in Chrome DevTools. You can change the values on the fly to test new designs. You can scope them to specific components. JSON cannot do any of that natively.

Theming is where CSS variables really show their power. If you want to add a dark mode using JSON, you usually have to output multiple files. Then you have to write JavaScript logic to swap those themes in your application. With CSS variables, the browser does all the heavy lifting for you.

[data-theme="dark"] {
  --color-brand-primary: #4c9aff;
  --color-background-base: #111111;
}

You just toggle a data attribute on your HTML tag. The browser updates every single component instantly. There is no JavaScript required. There is no complex state management. It just works.

What about native apps?

This is always the counter-argument I hear. People say you need JSON so iOS and Android can consume the exact same tokens.

That is technically true if you work at a massive tech company with dedicated mobile teams. But most teams are web-first. Even if you do have mobile developers, forcing the web team to parse JSON just to appease iOS is backwards. Let the mobile teams compile what they need. The web should just get CSS. You should optimise for the platform where your users actually spend their time.

A better workflow

We stopped doing the JSON dance months ago. Now we just push CSS variables straight from Figma to our repository.

The designer updates a colour in Figma. A pull request automatically appears in our GitHub repository with the raw CSS file. The developer reviews the visual diff and merges it. The pipeline is entirely transparent. There are no build scripts to maintain.

This is exactly why I built Design System Sync. I got incredibly tired of writing parsing scripts for different teams. I wanted a tool that respects how the web actually works. It exports your Figma variables directly to GitHub or Bitbucket as ready-to-use CSS variables. It handles the formatting automatically.

You can check it out at https://ds-sync.netlify.app?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot or grab the plugin directly from the Figma Community at https://www.figma.com/community/plugin/1561389071519901700?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=bot.

It also supports W3C formats if you really need them. But honestly, you probably just need CSS.

Are you still maintaining custom build scripts to parse JSON tokens for your web application?

title: Java var, Records and Sealed Classes Explained Simply
description:
Java has a reputation for being wordy, and for a long time it earned it. To store a simple pair of numbers, I had to write a class with two fields, a constructor, two getters, equals, hashCode and toString. That's around forty lines for something that is just "x and y." And a line like this made my eyes tired:

Map<String, List<Integer>> scores = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();

Modern Java fixed a lot of this. In this post, we'll learn three features that make code shorter and safer:

  • var (local variable type inference), so you stop repeating types.
  • record classes, which give you data classes in one line.
  • sealed classes, which let you say exactly which classes may extend yours.

At the end, we'll combine all three in one small program. If you read the post about streams, you'll notice that these features fit with them very well.

A quick note on versions, because each feature arrived at a different time: var came in Java 10, records are final in Java 16, sealed classes in Java 17, and the pattern-matching switch that I use with sealed types is final in Java 21. Any recent LTS version has all of them.

Unless I show a full class, the snippets go inside a main method. Records and other types are declared outside it.

Part 1: var (local variable type inference)

What is var?

var lets the compiler work out the type of a local variable from the value on the right side. This is called LVTI, short for Local Variable Type Inference.

var name = "Asha";
var count = 10;
var prices = new ArrayList<Double>();
var scores = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();

The long line from the start of this post becomes much shorter, because the type was already written on the right side. Why say it twice?

var is NOT dynamic typing

This is the most common misunderstanding. var doesn't make Java behave like JavaScript. The variable still has one fixed type, chosen at compile time:

var name = "Asha";
System.out.println(name.toUpperCase());

name = 5;

Output:

ASHA

and then a compile error on the last line:

incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String

name is a String forever. You can call String methods on it, and you can't put a number in it.

Behind the scenes

The compiler simply replaces var with the real type while compiling. The bytecode is exactly the same as if you had written the type yourself, so var has no cost at run time.

   var count = 10;                       -->   int count = 10;
   var names = new ArrayList<String>();  -->   ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<String>();

   The type is worked out when you COMPILE. Nothing changes when the program RUNS.

Where you can use it

var works for local variables, in several places:

var message = "Hello";                          // normal local variable

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }                 // classic for loop

for (var n : List.of(1, 2, 3)) { }              // enhanced for loop

BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add =
        (var a, var b) -> a + b;                // lambda parameters (Java 11+)

Where you can't 

   var x;                  error: cannot infer type (no initial value)
   var x = null;           error: cannot infer type (the value is 'null')
   var f = () -> 1;        error: cannot infer type (lambda needs a target type)
   var a = {1, 2, 3};      error: cannot infer type (array initializer needs a type)

   Also NOT allowed: fields, method parameters and return types.

The compiler can only infer a type when the right side makes it clear. In all these cases, there's nothing (or not enough) to infer from. Also, var is only for local variables, so it can't be used for class fields or in method signatures.

A gotcha: the diamond 

var list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("a");
list.add(1);

System.out.println(list);

Output:

[a, 1]

With a normal declaration, List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); tells the compiler to use String for the diamond <>. With var, there's no target type, so the compiler picks ArrayList<Object>, and the list accepts anything. Write new ArrayList<String>() when you use var.

Another small thing to know: var list = new ArrayList<String>(); has the type ArrayList<String>, not List<String>. If you want your variable to use the interface type (a good habit), write it out: List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();.

Is var a good idea?

It depends on readability:

  • Good: the type is obvious from the right side. var users = new ArrayList<User>(); and var reader = new BufferedReader(...); need no extra explanation.
  • Not good: the right side hides the type. In var result = process(data);, a reader has to look up process to learn what result is.

A good rule: use var when it removes repetition, and use the explicit type when it adds information. And since the type is no longer visible, choose clear variable names.

Part 2: Records

The problem: so much code for plain data

Here is a simple class that just carries two numbers:

class PointClass {
    private final int x;
    private final int y;

    PointClass(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }

    int getX() { return x; }
    int getY() { return y; }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof PointClass)) return false;
        PointClass other = (PointClass) o;
        return x == other.x && y == other.y;
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(x, y);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "PointClass[x=" + x + ", y=" + y + "]";
    }
}

That's a lot of text, and every line is boilerplate (code you write only because the language requires it). A record does the same in one line:

record Point(int x, int y) { }

Point p = new Point(3, 4);

System.out.println(p);
System.out.println(p.x());
System.out.println(p.equals(new Point(3, 4)));
System.out.println(p.hashCode() == new Point(3, 4).hashCode());

Output:

Point[x=3, y=4]
3
true
true

Two points with the same values are equal, even though they are different objects. Records compare by value, not by identity.

What the compiler writes for you

The list in the parentheses, (int x, int y), is called the record's components. For them, the compiler generates:

   record Point(int x, int y) { }
            |
            |   the compiler expands it into roughly this:
            v
   final class Point extends java.lang.Record {
       private final int x;
       private final int y;

       Point(int x, int y) { ... }         // the "canonical" constructor
       int x() { return x; }               // accessors: note, NO "get" prefix
       int y() { return y; }
       boolean equals(Object o) { ... }    // compares all components
       int hashCode() { ... }
       String toString() { ... }           // Point[x=3, y=4]
   }

You can verify the hidden parts yourself:

System.out.println(Point.class.getSuperclass());
System.out.println(java.lang.reflect.Modifier.isFinal(Point.class.getModifiers()));

Output:

class java.lang.Record
true

So a record is a real class. It's final (nobody can extend it), and its parent is java.lang.Record. (Behind the scenes, the generated equals, hashCode and toString are wired up with the same invokedynamic mechanism we saw with lambdas.)

Validation with a compact constructor

What if you want to reject bad values? Write a compact constructor. It has the record's name but no parentheses. It runs before the fields are set:

record Age(int value) {
    Age {
        if (value < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");
        }
    }
}

System.out.println(new Age(25));

try {
    new Age(-1);
} catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
    System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
}

Output:

Age[value=25]
Error: Age cannot be negative

You can also adjust a value in the compact constructor by reassigning the parameter. And records can have their own methods and static helpers:

record Person(String name, int age) {
    Person {
        name = name.trim();
    }

    String greeting() {
        return "Hi, " + name;
    }

    static Person of(String name) {
        return new Person(name, 0);
    }
}

System.out.println(new Person("  Asha ", 25));
System.out.println(Person.of("Ravi").greeting());

Output:

Person[name=Asha, age=25]
Hi, Ravi

The rules of records

  • A record is implicitly final and can't extend another class (it already extends Record).
  • It can implement interfaces, and it can be generic, like record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second).
  • The component fields are private final. You can't add extra instance fields, and there are no setters.
  • You can add methods, static methods and static fields.
  • Any extra constructor must call the canonical one with this(...).

A trap: records are shallowly immutable

The fields can't be reassigned, but if a field holds a changeable object, that object can still change:

record Team(String name, List<String> members) { }

var members = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Asha"));
var team = new Team("Core", members);

members.add("Ravi");
System.out.println(team);

Output:

Team[name=Core, members=[Asha, Ravi]]

The team changed even though we never touched the record! The fix is a defensive copy in the compact constructor:

record SafeTeam(String name, List<String> members) {
    SafeTeam {
        members = List.copyOf(members);
    }
}

var members = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Asha"));
var team = new SafeTeam("Core", members);

members.add("Ravi");
System.out.println(team);

Output:

SafeTeam[name=Core, members=[Asha]]

Now the record keeps its own unchangeable copy.

Records work nicely with streams

Because the accessors are plain methods, they fit method references:

record Student(String name, int marks) { }

List<Student> students = List.of(
        new Student("Asha", 88),
        new Student("Ravi", 72),
        new Student("Meera", 95));

students.stream()
        .filter(s -> s.marks() > 80)
        .map(Student::name)
        .forEach(System.out::println);

Output:

Asha
Meera

Records are ideal for small data carriers: results that return several values, map keys, DTOs (objects that carry data between layers) and test data.

Part 3: Sealed classes

The problem: inheritance is too open

Normally, if you write interface Shape, anyone can implement it, anywhere, at any time. That's flexible, but sometimes it's a problem. Imagine you want to say "a Shape is only a Circle or a Rectangle, nothing else." With normal inheritance, you can't say that, and the compiler can never be sure it has seen every possible shape.

A sealed class or interface solves this. It lists exactly which classes may extend or implement it, using the permits keyword:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle { }

record Circle(double radius) implements Shape { }
record Rectangle(double width, double height) implements Shape { }

   Normal hierarchy:    Shape  <---  anyone can extend it (unknown subclasses)

   Sealed hierarchy:    Shape  <---  ONLY Circle and Rectangle
                                     the compiler knows ALL the cases

If another class tries to join the family uninvited:

final class Triangle implements Shape { }

class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Shape (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause)

The three choices for a subclass

Every class that is permitted by a sealed class must declare what happens next in the family, with one of three keywords:

  • final: no more subclasses. The family ends here.
  • sealed: it restricts its own subclasses again, with its own permits list.
  • non-sealed: it opens the hierarchy back up, so anyone may extend it. 
sealed class Vehicle permits Car, Truck, Bike { }

final class Car extends Vehicle { }

sealed class Truck extends Vehicle permits Pickup { }
final class Pickup extends Truck { }

non-sealed class Bike extends Vehicle { }

              Vehicle  (sealed)
             /    |     \
          Car   Truck    Bike
        final  sealed   non-sealed
                  |
               Pickup
                final

Records are automatically final, which is why they pair so well with sealed interfaces. A few more rules:

  • A permitted subclass must directly extend the sealed class.
  • It must be in the same module (or the same package, if your project doesn't use modules).
  • If all the subclasses are in the same file as the sealed class, you can leave out permits, and the compiler works it out.

The payoff: exhaustive switch

Because the compiler knows every possible subtype, a switch over a sealed type doesn't need a default:

static double area(Shape shape) {
    return switch (shape) {
        case Circle c    -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
        case Rectangle r -> r.width() * r.height();
    };
}

System.out.println(area(new Circle(1)));
System.out.println(area(new Rectangle(3, 4)));

Output:

3.141592653589793
12.0

(This pattern-matching switch needs Java 21 or newer.) The best part comes later. Imagine you add a Triangle to the permits list but forget to update area. The code stops compiling:

the switch expression does not cover all possible input values

The compiler found the bug for you, long before a user would. That's the real value of sealed types: when the set of cases changes, every place that must handle them is flagged.

In Java 21 and newer, you can even take a record apart inside the case:

case Circle(double radius)             -> Math.PI * radius * radius;
case Rectangle(double width, double height) -> width * height;

A practical example: success or failure

A common use is a result type that is either a success or a failure:

sealed interface Result permits Success, Failure { }
record Success(String data) implements Result { }
record Failure(String error) implements Result { }

static String describe(Result r) {
    return switch (r) {
        case Success s -> "OK: " + s.data();
        case Failure f -> "Error: " + f.error();
    };
}

System.out.println(describe(new Success("saved")));
System.out.println(describe(new Failure("timeout")));

Output:

OK: saved
Error: timeout

Behind the scenes

The permits list is stored inside the .class file. When a class is loaded, the JVM checks it, so the rule is enforced both by the compiler and at run time. You can even read it with reflection:

System.out.println(Shape.class.isSealed());

for (Class<?> c : Shape.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) {
    System.out.println(c.getSimpleName());
}

Output:

true
Circle
Rectangle

Sealed vs enum vs final

These three often get confused:

  • final means no subclasses at all.
  • enum means a fixed set of objects (like MONDAY, TUESDAY), each created once.
  • sealed means a fixed set of types, and each type can have many objects, usually with different data (a Circle has a radius, and a Rectangle has a width and height).

Putting it all together

Let's use everything in one small program: a tiny calculator that models expressions as a sealed hierarchy of records, walks them with a switch, and uses var for the local variables.

sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { }
record Num(int value) implements Expr { }
record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }
record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }

public class Calculator {
    static int eval(Expr e) {
        return switch (e) {
            case Num n -> n.value();
            case Add a -> eval(a.left()) + eval(a.right());
            case Mul m -> eval(m.left()) * eval(m.right());
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        var expr = new Add(new Num(2), new Mul(new Num(3), new Num(4)));

        System.out.println(eval(expr));
        System.out.println(expr);
    }
}

Output:

14
Add[left=Num[value=2], right=Mul[left=Num[value=3], right=Num[value=4]]]

Look at how each feature helped:

  • Records gave us four tiny data types in four lines, and a readable toString for free.
  • Sealed told the compiler that Expr is only Num, Add or Mul, so eval needs no default.
  • switch with patterns unpacked each case without casts.
  • var kept the long type name out of main.

Try adding a Sub record to the permits list, and watch the compiler point at eval.

Which one should I use?

  • var or the explicit type? Use var when the right side already shows the type (new ArrayList<String>(), a constructor call, a clearly named factory). Use the explicit type when it helps the reader, or when you want an interface type like List<String>.
  • Record or class? Use a record for plain, unchangeable data carriers: DTOs, map keys, multiple return values, test data. Use a class when you need changeable state, inheritance, hidden internal data or behavior that doesn't revolve around the data. Many frameworks that need changeable, proxied objects (such as JPA entities) don't fit records.
  • Sealed, enum or open interface? Use an enum for a fixed set of constants. Use a sealed hierarchy for a fixed set of types that carry different data. Use a normal open interface when other people should be able to add their own implementations (a plugin system, for example).
  • Records and sealed together? This is a great combination for modeling "one of several shapes of data," like results, events, commands and expressions.

Common mistakes

  1. Using var when the type becomes unclear. If a reader can't tell what the variable is without hunting, write the type. Also remember var list = new ArrayList<>() gives you ArrayList<Object>.
  2. Thinking var makes Java dynamic. The type is fixed at compile time. You can't assign a different type later, and you can't use var for fields, parameters or return types.
  3. Assuming records are fully immutable. If a component is a list or another changeable object, it can still change. Make a defensive copy in the compact constructor, and remember that you can't add instance fields or setters.
  4. Using the wrong accessor name. A record's accessor is p.x(), not p.getX(). And equality is based on values, so two records with the same data are equals.
  5. Forgetting what a permitted subclass must say. Each one has to be final, sealed or non-sealed, and it must sit in the same module (or package). Otherwise, the code won't compile.
  6. Adding a default branch to a switch over a sealed type. It silences the compiler's exhaustiveness check. When you add a new subtype later, it falls into default without any warning. Leave default out so the compiler can protect you.

Quick recap

  • var lets the compiler infer the type of a local variable. The type is still fixed at compile time, and the bytecode is the same as if you'd written it out.
  • var needs an initial value that shows the type. It can't be used for fields, parameters, return types, null or lambdas without a target type. Use it when it removes repetition, not when it hides the type.
  • A record is a one-line data class. The compiler generates the final fields, canonical constructor, accessors like x(), and equals, hashCode and toString. It's implicitly final, extends java.lang.Record and can't have extra instance fields.
  • Use a compact constructor for validation, and make a defensive copy of changeable components.
  • A sealed class or interface lists its allowed subclasses with permits. Each one must be final, sealed or non-sealed.
  • Sealed types give you an exhaustive switch with no default, so the compiler tells you when you forget a case.
  • Records plus sealed interfaces plus pattern-matching switch is a powerful modern-Java pattern.

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: model a payment system. Create a sealed interface Payment permits Card, Upi, Cash, with a record for each, such as Card(String number, int amount), Upi(String id, int amount) and Cash(int amount). Write a method fee(Payment p) that returns a different fee for each, using a switch with no default. Use var for your local variables in main.

For a bonus experiment, add a new record NetBanking to the permits list, and read the compiler error on your switch. Then handle the new case and see it compile again.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

That wraps up this two-part series on modern Java.

title: AWS HealthOmics introduces resource fallback order for Nextflow workflows
description:
Today, AWS HealthOmics introduces the resource fallback directive for tasks in your Nextflow workflows, enabling you to define an ordered list of preferred accelerator types, including an option to fallback to CPU instances. Researchers and bioinformaticians can use this directive to reduce time spent diagnosing and resubmitting runs due to accelerator constraints and keep production workflows running. AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows. 

With resource fallback for Nextflow workflows, you can prioritize your preferred accelerator for your task. When your preferred accelerator is unavailable, HealthOmics automatically moves through your specified alternatives in the fallback without resubmission. Each accelerator profile has a configurable timeout, giving you control over how long HealthOmics searches for that accelerator before moving to the next. Shorter timeouts help you move quickly through the fallback order, while longer timeouts increase the probability of reserving your preferred accelerator. You can also include a CPU profile as a final fallback to increase the likelihood of your task reserving an instance. 

You can now use resource fallback for Nextflow workflows in all AWS HealthOmics Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Seoul, Singapore, Tokyo). To learn more, visit the advanced resource configuration and Nextflow specifics documentation.

title: DevSecOps in Practice: Securing Java and Spring Boot Delivery Pipelines
description:
DevSecOps is often described as "shifting security left," but in practice many teams still experience security as a gate at the end of the pipeline. A scanner runs, a report lands in a shared folder, and a developer discovers three weeks later that a critical dependency has been waiting to be fixed the whole time. The goal of DevSecOps is not to add more gates. It is to make security a property of the delivery pipeline itself, so that the safe path is also the fastest path.

This article walks through the practices I use when building Java and Spring Boot services in regulated environments. It covers how to automate dependency and secret scanning, how to enforce policy as code, how to harden container images, how to protect the runtime, and how to make the whole system produce evidence that auditors and incident responders can rely on.

What DevSecOps Actually Means

DevSecOps extends DevOps by treating security as a shared responsibility across development, operations, and security teams. Three ideas make it work:

  1. Automate the checks. Manual reviews do not scale to dozens of deployments a day. Every check that can be automated should be.
  2. Fail fast, but with useful feedback. A build that fails with a clear explanation and a suggested fix is far more useful than a report generated next month.
  3. Make the secure path the default. Templates, base images, and shared pipeline stages should be secure out of the box, so that teams do not need to remember every rule.

The rest of this article applies these ideas to concrete stages of the delivery pipeline.

Stage 1: Secure Coding Feedback in the IDE

The earliest feedback comes from the developer's own environment. Static analysis plugins for IntelliJ IDEA or VS Code can flag common issues such as SQL built with string concatenation, unsafe deserialization, or hardcoded credentials as the developer types. These tools are useful, but they only help if the team agrees on a shared rule set. Commit a configuration file to the repository so that everyone runs the same rules.

The most common class of vulnerabilities in Java services is still injection. Compare these two approaches:

// Vulnerable: user input concatenated into SQL
public List<Customer> findByEmail(String email) {
    String sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = '" + email + "'";
    return jdbcTemplate.query(sql, customerRowMapper);
}

// Safe: parameter binding
public List<Customer> findByEmail(String email) {
    return jdbcTemplate.query(
            "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = ?",
            customerRowMapper,
            email);
}

A static analysis rule can detect the first pattern automatically. Make it a blocking check in the pipeline rather than a warning that everyone learns to ignore.

Stage 2: Secret Detection Before the Commit Leaves the Machine

Secrets in source control are one of the most common causes of breaches, and they are expensive to clean up because the history of the repository keeps them alive. Prevent them at three points:

  • Pre-commit hooks that scan staged changes for API keys, tokens, and private keys.
  • Pipeline scanning on every push, using a dedicated secret scanner such as Gitleaks or TruffleHog.
  • Repository-level protection that blocks pushes containing known secret patterns.

A simple pre-commit configuration with Gitleaks looks like this:

# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.18.4
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

When a secret is detected, the response should be rotation first and cleanup second. Assume the credential is compromised, rotate it in the secrets manager, and then remove it from history if needed.

Applications should never read secrets from files in the repository. Load them at runtime from a secrets manager such as AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, OCI Vault, or HashiCorp Vault:

@Configuration
public class DatabaseConfig {

    @Bean
    DataSource dataSource(
            @Value("${db.url}") String url,
            @Value("${db.username}") String username,
            @Value("${db.password}") String password) {
        HikariDataSource ds = new HikariDataSource();
        ds.setJdbcUrl(url);
        ds.setUsername(username);
        ds.setPassword(password);
        return ds;
    }
}

In this example, the password is resolved from the environment or from a secrets integration at startup. The value never appears in a file under version control. Spring Cloud Config, the AWS Secrets Manager integration, or the Vault Spring integration can supply these properties without changing application code.

Stage 3: Dependency and Supply Chain Scanning

Most of the code running in a typical Spring Boot service was written by someone else. That is an advantage, but it also means that a single vulnerable transitive dependency can expose your entire system. Dependency scanning should happen on every build.

The OWASP Dependency-Check Maven plugin is a common choice for Java projects:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.owasp</groupId>
    <artifactId>dependency-check-maven</artifactId>
    <version>10.0.4</version>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>check</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
    <configuration>
        <failBuildOnCVSS>7</failBuildOnCVSS>
        <suppressionFiles>
            <suppressionFile>owasp-suppressions.xml</suppressionFile>
        </suppressionFiles>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

The failBuildOnCVSS setting stops the build when a dependency has a high-severity known vulnerability. Suppressions should be explicit, reviewed, and time-limited. A suppression without an expiration date tends to become permanent.

Beyond scanning, three supply chain practices reduce risk:

  • Pin versions. Use explicit versions in the build file and review updates instead of accepting floating ranges.
  • Generate an SBOM. A Software Bill of Materials, produced with CycloneDX for example, lets you answer quickly whether a newly disclosed vulnerability affects any of your services.
  • Verify artifacts. Sign container images and build artifacts, and verify signatures before deployment.

Stage 4: Static and Dynamic Analysis in the Pipeline

Static Application Security Testing (SAST) analyzes source code for vulnerability patterns. Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) probes a running application from the outside. Both have a role, and both produce noise if they are configured carelessly.

For SAST, focus on rules that map to real risk in your context, such as injection, broken authentication, path traversal, and insecure deserialization. Triage new findings on every pull request, and track the trend over time rather than fixating on the total count.

For DAST, run a baseline scan against a deployed test environment on a schedule, and run a more thorough scan before major releases. Keep the scan credentials limited to test accounts with the minimum necessary permissions.

Stage 5: Container Hardening

Containers package your application together with its operating system libraries, and each layer can carry vulnerabilities. Harden the image in three ways.

Use minimal base images. A distroless or slim Java runtime image contains far fewer packages than a full operating system image, which means fewer vulnerabilities to patch.

FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -B -DskipTests package

FROM gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12:nonroot
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /workspace/target/payments-service.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

This multi-stage build keeps the build tools out of the final image, and the nonroot variant of the distroless base runs the process as a non-root user.

Scan the image. Run Trivy or Grype against the built image in the pipeline, and fail the build on critical vulnerabilities that have a fix available.

Set runtime restrictions. In Kubernetes, configure the pod to run as non-root, drop Linux capabilities, and mount the root filesystem as read-only where possible:

securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  capabilities:
    drop:
      - ALL

Stage 6: Policy as Code

Security rules that live only in a document are difficult to enforce consistently. Policy as code expresses those rules in a form that the pipeline and the cluster can evaluate automatically. Open Policy Agent (OPA) with Rego, or Kyverno for Kubernetes, are common choices.

A simple example is a rule that rejects any deployment without resource limits, which protects other tenants from a runaway service. In Kyverno, a policy might look like this:

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-resource-limits
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: check-limits
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds:
                - Pod
      validate:
        message: "CPU and memory limits are required."
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - resources:
                  limits:
                    memory: "?*"
                    cpu: "?*"

The advantage of policy as code is that it is versioned, reviewed, and tested like any other code. When a policy changes, the change is visible in history, and the same rule applies in every environment.

Stage 7: Runtime Protection and Observability

No pipeline catches everything, so the system needs to detect and respond to suspicious behavior at runtime. Three capabilities matter most.

Structured security logging. Log authentication failures, authorization denials, and sensitive actions in a structured format, with a correlation identifier. Make sure that logs never contain tokens, passwords, or full personal data.

@Component
public class SecurityEventLogger {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger("security");

    public void authorizationDenied(String principal, String resource, String action) {
        log.warn("event=AUTHZ_DENIED principal={} resource={} action={} correlationId={}",
                principal, resource, action, MDC.get("correlationId"));
    }
}

Rate limiting and abuse detection. Limit login attempts and sensitive endpoints, and alert on unusual patterns such as many denials from one client in a short window.

Runtime threat detection. Tools such as Falco can detect unexpected process execution, shell access in containers, or writes to sensitive paths, and send alerts to the security team.

Connect these signals to your incident response process. An alert that nobody reads provides no protection.

Stage 8: Evidence and Compliance

DevSecOps is not complete until you can prove that your controls work. Compliance frameworks such as PCI DSS, SOC 2, and ISO 27001 require evidence, and the most efficient evidence is the kind the pipeline generates automatically:

  • Build logs showing that scans ran and their results
  • Records of who approved each deployment and when
  • Policy evaluation results for each release
  • Access reviews generated from identity provider data
  • Vulnerability management metrics, such as mean time to remediate by severity

Store this evidence in a system that the delivery team cannot silently modify, and retain it according to your regulatory requirements. When an auditor asks how a control works, the answer should be a link to the pipeline definition and a sample of its output, not a meeting to reconstruct what happened.

Measuring DevSecOps Maturity

Metrics keep the program honest. Useful measures include:

  • Mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities, by service
  • Percentage of services with automated scanning in their pipeline
  • Secret detection rate before and after pre-commit hooks were introduced
  • Deployment failure rate caused by security policy, which shows whether the controls are too strict or too loose
  • Exception count and age, to ensure suppressions do not accumulate

Review these metrics regularly with both engineering and security leadership. The goal is to improve the system over time, not to produce a perfect score on day one.

Common Pitfalls

Several patterns undermine DevSecOps programs in practice:

  • Scanning without action. A dashboard full of unresolved findings trains teams to ignore security signals. Set clear ownership and service-level targets for remediation.
  • Too many blocking rules at once. Introducing dozens of strict gates on the first day causes teams to find workarounds. Start with the highest-impact checks and expand gradually.
  • Security as a separate team's pipeline. If developers cannot see or fix the findings themselves, the feedback loop is too slow. Give teams direct access to results and guidance.
  • Ignoring the human path. Developers under deadline pressure will choose the fastest route. Make sure the secure route is also the easiest one.

Key Takeaways

  • DevSecOps makes security a property of the delivery pipeline, not a separate phase at the end.
  • Automate secret detection, dependency scanning, and static analysis, and make the critical checks blocking.
  • Keep secrets out of source control and load them from a secrets manager at runtime.
  • Harden container images with minimal bases, non-root execution, and image scanning.
  • Express security policy as code so it is versioned, reviewed, and enforced consistently.
  • Monitor runtime behavior and connect alerts to a real response process.
  • Generate compliance evidence automatically from the pipeline itself.
  • Measure progress with metrics that reveal both the strength of controls and the friction they create.

DevSecOps works best when it feels like an improvement to the delivery process rather than an obstacle to it. Start with one pipeline, add secret detection and dependency scanning this week, and expand from there. Each automated check removes a class of risk without asking anyone to remember a rule.
