title: Engineering a Modern Vehicle-Rental Marketplace: Architecture, Search, and UX Challenges
description:
Introduction

Vehicle-rental platforms sit at the intersection of e-commerce, geospatial search, and logistics coordination. Unlike standard retail marketplaces where a product sits in a centralized warehouse, a mobility marketplace deals with distributed, heterogeneous assets managed by independent local providers.

The software challenge lies in synchronizing search, listing information, dynamic availability, transparent pricing, and booking workflows into a seamless user experience. For travelers navigating unfamiliar terrain, the system must abstract away provider fragmentation while remaining strictly honest about what data is verified versus what is assumed.

Designing a Useful Vehicle-Discovery Experience

A robust discovery engine must filter vehicles by geographical constraints, vehicle categories, rental durations, and practical requirements. When engineers design the catalog interface, treating motorcycles, scooters, and cars as interchangeable entities leads to poor UX.

Listing components must dynamically render attributes relevant to the chosen category—such as engine displacement and luggage capacity for motorcycles or seating capacity and transmission type for cars. Platforms specializing in motorcycle rental Colombia must ensure that filtering parameters reflect the technical and logistical realities of the region, helping users quickly distinguish between light city commuters and heavy touring rigs.

Building Location-Aware Search

Geospatial queries form the backbone of any travel mobility platform. Travelers searching for transport require location-aware filtering that adapts to different urban and regional contexts.

Consider three distinct operational hubs across Colombia:

  • Bogotá: High-altitude urban commuting, dense traffic patterns, and frequent suburban departures require reliable filtering for city-appropriate scooters and versatile cars.
  • Medellín: Nestled within an Andean valley, the terrain demands precise categorization for riders looking for agile machines suited to steep inclines and winding mountain roads.
  • Cartagena: Coastal conditions and flat coastal highways favor lightweight scooters and comfortable cars for regional exploration.

Engineers must optimize spatial indexes (such as PostGIS extensions or Elasticsearch geo-queries) to ensure fast radius searches around specific pickup points, transit hubs, or neighborhoods. Implementing intuitive search filters for pickup locations, rental dates, and provider details minimizes user friction and reduces bounce rates during the initial discovery phase.

Supporting Different Vehicle Categories

Different vehicle classes serve fundamentally distinct travel intentions. Grouping them incorrectly in the database schema or UI creates confusion.

For instance, urban commuters looking for a scooter rental Colombia require agile, fuel-efficient transport with simple storage solutions. Conversely, travelers planning extended coastal drives or urban commuting in major business centers rely heavily on car rental Medellin or general car rental Colombia listings.

Product teams must design modular database schemas that allow vehicle attributes to scale independently. A motorcycle listing requires fields for helmet inclusion, luggage racks, and engine specs, while a car listing requires details on doors, AC, and transmission. Emphasizing these distinctions prevents booking errors and ensures renters select equipment matching their actual operational needs.

Making Listing Information Transparent

Trust in a rental marketplace is directly proportional to data transparency. Ambiguous pricing, hidden fees, or unclear pickup instructions cause immediate user drop-off and support overhead.

Engineering systems must enforce strict data contracts for listing pages, displaying:

  • Granular vehicle specifications and maintenance notes.
  • Exact rental duration calculations and time-zone-aware pickup/return windows.
  • Transparent total pricing, itemizing base rates, taxes, and applicable deposits.
  • Provider information, verified compliance badges, and required documentation (such as valid driver's licenses and international permits).
  • Clear cancellation policies and insurance terms.

A well-architected marketplace distinguishes confirmed provider-supplied data from assumptions, guiding users directly to official terms without hiding restrictions behind opaque UI patterns.

Trust, Verification, and Booking Workflows

Building a resilient booking workflow requires careful state machine design. A reservation typically moves through distinct states: draft, pending_provider_review, confirmed, active, and completed.

Provider verification should be handled as a data attribute rather than an absolute safety guarantee. Platforms must avoid over-promising; verification simply means identity and documentation checks have met baseline platform standards.

From a frontend perspective, UX principles dictate clear error boundaries, idempotent payment processing steps, immutable confirmation screens, and secure handling of PII (Personally Identifiable Information). If a payment gateway times out or inventory status changes mid-checkout, the state machine must gracefully roll back without leaving orphaned reservations or charging users twice.

Supporting Adventure Travel and Tours

Long-distance journeys and organized excursions introduce unique technical and logistical requirements. Explorers planning extensive itineraries often seek specialized options, such as an adventure motorcycle rental Colombia or curated motorcycle tours Colombia, when organizing a multi-day motorcycle road trip Colombia.

From a product standpoint, supporting adventure travel means integrating rich content blocks, itinerary maps, and explicit pre-trip checklists. Platforms must prompt users to verify their rider eligibility, international licensing credentials, protective gear availability, and regional weather or road restrictions. Encouraging travelers to consult official transport authorities and local providers ensures safety compliance beyond what software can automate.

A Practical Marketplace Engineering Checklist

  1. Define Journeys: Map clear user journeys for both renters and independent local providers.
  2. Modular Schema: Design scalable database schemas for distinct vehicle categories and location filters.
  3. Data Integrity: Keep listing data synchronized and flag unverified fields clearly.
  4. Transparent Pricing: Display itemized totals, deposits, and cancellation terms upfront.
  5. State Management: Implement robust state machines for booking confirmation and payment handling.
  6. Data Privacy: Encrypt and secure personal information and payment tokens.
  7. Mobile Optimization: Test responsive layouts extensively on mobile devices used by on-the-go travelers.
  8. Friction Analytics: Monitor search-to-booking conversion funnels using privacy-conscious analytics tools.
  9. Feedback Loops: Collect structured user feedback to refine confusing checkout or search workflows.

How MotoShare.co Fits Into the Travel-Mobility Landscape

Platforms like MotoShare.co exemplify how localized marketplaces connect travelers with independent vehicle providers across Colombia. By focusing on transparent discovery for motorcycles, scooters, and cars, the platform aligns with core marketplace architecture principles: clear categorization, location-driven search, and straightforward provider coordination without unnecessary booking friction. Keeping listings transparent and decentralized allows local providers to manage their own fleet details while giving users a unified discovery interface.

Conclusion

Building a successful vehicle-rental marketplace requires more than just a searchable database. It demands rigorous data modeling, transparent pricing UX, reliable state management, and clear communication of rental terms. By prioritizing data accuracy and user-centric design, engineering teams can build resilient platforms that simplify mobility for travelers and empower local providers alike.

title: curl Patches HTTP/2 Upload Flaw After PoC Demonstrates Client-Side Code Execution
description:
A flaw in how curl handles HTTP/2 uploads lets a malicious server receiving an upload corrupt the client's memory, and the researcher who reported it turned that into code execution on the uploading machine.

The curl project fixed it on October 14 in curl 8.23.0. Taking over a client needs exact knowledge of its build and memory layout, and curl expects a real attack to end in a crash

title: A CSS mutation test for your Ionify pilot
description:
A shorter rebuild is useful when the page shows your latest change. This Ionify lab checks one visible result—a border changing from 2px to 6px—while keeping local engine state. Use a disposable, supported app and retain your normal styling packages.

Add an unmistakable rule

In a stylesheet already imported by the app:

.build-lab-card {
  border: 2px solid #b77928;
  padding: 1rem;
}

Apply the class to an element you can easily find. Build with pnpm exec ionify build and inspect the production output through your normal static preview server.

Now change only the border width to 6px. Build again without deleting the local engine state. Check the element's computed border width in the browser. Record the result, not just the time.

Which styling path did you try, and did the production border reach 6px?

Exercise the real styling path

If your app uses CSS Modules, repeat with a property in an imported module. If it uses a preprocessor or generated utility CSS, make a change that that pipeline must observe. Do not assume the plain-CSS result covers it.

Ionify's public setup describes CSS/CSS Modules support. Sass and Less still require their compiler packages. Tailwind and PostCSS need their normal packages and configuration. Follow the current configuration reference for the version under test.

Optional: record enough to debug 

Project / report key:
Stylesheet mechanism:
Exact build command:
Starting state / state retained:
Changed source and value:
Expected computed style:
Actual production computed style:
Engine and styling package versions:
Config files involved:
Was a service worker or browser cache active?
Evidence: redacted screenshot or public reproduction URL

If the style is stale, first confirm the browser is serving the output you just built. Preserve the failure before clearing caches so the reproduction still explains what happened.

The purpose is a reliable edit-to-check loop. No style change needs to become a migration argument; it just needs to reach the app correctly.

title: Your AI Agent Is Smart. So Why Shouldn't You Trust It?
description:
Why AI Agents Should Preview Changes Before Executing Them

Because understanding a request and safely executing it are two different things.

Imagine building an AI assistant that manages calendar events.

A user asks:

“Clear my Tuesday and move everything to next week.”

The AI understands the instruction. It identifies the events and proposes new dates. Everything seems fine.

But should the application immediately update the calendar?

Not necessarily.

AI Agents Can Make Real Changes

Modern AI assistants can do much more than answer questions. They can modify records, create tasks, delete information, and trigger workflows.

That makes them powerful. It also means mistakes can have real consequences.

What if the assistant moves an important meeting? What if the user meant only personal tasks? What if the proposed schedule conflicts with another commitment?

Even when an AI generates a reasonable plan, executing it without review can lead to unexpected results.

The Human-in-the-Loop Pattern

At ByDesign, AI scheduling follows a preview-first approach.

Instead of immediately applying generated changes, the application presents a proposed schedule for the user to review.

The workflow looks like this:

User Request → AI Generates a Plan → Preview Changes → User Reviews → Accept and Schedule

The user can inspect the proposed changes before they are applied. This creates a clear separation between generating a plan and committing changes to persistent data.

The AI can suggest what should happen, while the user remains in control of whether those changes should be applied.

Why This Pattern Matters

Human-in-the-loop design provides three important benefits.

1. Transparency

Users can see what the AI intends to change before those changes take effect.

2. Control

Users can review the proposed schedule, identify mistakes, and adjust the plan before accepting it.

3. Trust

Important changes are not silently applied. Users have a clear opportunity to understand and approve the outcome.

ByDesign also includes undo behavior and confirmation for destructive actions, helping users recover from mistakes and make important changes more deliberately.

The Bigger Lesson

Not every AI action needs manual approval. Low-risk actions may be handled automatically when the user has clearly authorized them.

However, when an AI agent can modify important user data, it is worth considering whether an action should be previewable, reversible, or explicitly confirmed.

The right approach depends on the impact of the action, the user's intent, and the consequences of getting it wrong.

A reliable AI agent isn't one that acts without hesitation. It's one that knows when to ask.

Explore ByDesign

title: The 11-year-old premise inside Rust's memory-safety proof
description:
"If it compiles, the memory is safe."

That is Rust's brand — not a slogan, a machine-checked proof: the borrow checker refuses unsafe lifetimes at compile time, host-enforced, the strongest rung any language has claimed. Yesterday, issue #164250 landed on the rust-lang tracker: an unsoundness in the borrow checker, reproducing on current stable, with variants compiling since 1.18.0 (2017) — and one version traced back to 1.4. Eleven years inside the proof.

I ran the reproduction tonight on the official playground — stable channel. The output, verbatim:

read after scope: hello world, this is long enough
the stack slot is freed. the string still printed.

A short-lived reference escaped a T: 'static bound through field assignment after construction, survived a Drop that assumed the bound held, and was read after its stack slot was freed. On stable. Same result on nightly. The receipts are one click away — the playground permalink runs it in seconds.

The mechanics, in three sentences

struct Q<T: 'static + Send> demands its payload outlive the program. Assigning a field after construction (q.0 = Some(&l), where l is stack-local) unifies the types covariantly — and that unification does not re-check the 'static bound. A Drop impl that pushes the value into a static list assumes the bound held; it leaks the reference out; a downcast_ref::<&'static String>() reads freed stack memory. With AddressSanitizer, per the issue, the same program crashes with stack-use-after-scope.

The number that matters is not 11

It is the severity call: P-high, downgraded from P-critical. The pinned note from lcnr is explicit — it would have been P-critical regardless of whether anyone encountered it in the wild, and it is P-high only because it has been latent for eleven years with "very likely that this unsoundness has not caused memory unsafety by accident." The exploit requires, per the issue, "an intentionally malicious Drop implementation."

Read that as an auditor, because it is a premise confession, and it is not Rust-specific. The compiler's proof descends a ladder: borrow check → variance rules → trait bounds → and at the floor, an assumption nobody executes — Drop implementations respect the bounds they inherit. The type system verified everything it could check and rested on the one thing it could not: the honesty of every Drop impl ever written by every hand that touched every crate. Eleven years, that premise held by accident of nobody aiming at it. This week someone aimed.

Sound familiar? It is the QGIS conscience test — "did you in good conscience write the code yourself" — inside a compiler. It is the authority ladder — rung 0, "the caller's argument": a claim the impl author makes, unverifiable by the checker below. Every soundness proof, every security certification, every "guaranteed" has a floor like this. The floor is not a scandal. An unlabeled floor is.

Credits, because the finder's method is the receipts

  • jsnell filed it October 13, with the reproduction that compiles and prints freed memory.
  • theemathas added the I-unsound label, a minimal core repro, and traced a variant compiling "ever since 1.18.0 (2017)" — and asked the question in the thread: "How on earth was this not found before this???"
  • maxdexh contributed a version going back to 1.4, and the generalization: "unification just generally doesn't check lifetime bounds of the type" — including via mem::swap, no field assignment needed.
  • lcnr pinned the severity reasoning and the linkage to the next-gen trait solver and Project Zero rework. PR #164277 is the fix in motion.

Four people, four contributions, each with its own denominator. That is what a healthy process looks like from the outside — and it is also, per the issue, a thread that was briefly locked as too heated before being unlocked and re-locked to collaborators. Soundness conversations run hot.

What to steal

  • Audit the premises under your proofs. Every guarantee you rely on — a type system, a SOC 2 report, a DCO sign-off, a "tested and measured" claim — rests on unlabeled assumptions the guarantee cannot check. Name one. The table is the audit.
  • Label your severity calls with their reasons. P-high because eleven years latent because it needs a malicious Drop — that reasoning is the difference between a decision and an assertion. Rust's team did this in the pinned note; copy the format.
  • Permalinks for reproductions. The playground link makes my claim one click from being your claim. If your repro needs setup, ship the setup.

Two honest limits

The exploit requires a malicious Drop by design, and the team's downgrade is defensible. Eleven years without an accidental hit is evidence of something — either the premise held because nobody aimed, or because honest Drops overwhelmingly dominate. Both readings favor the team's call. My point is narrower: the premise existed, was unlabeled, and now is labeled — by the issue, in public.

And my run is a playground snapshot, not a forensic audit. Stable and nightly, debug profile, no AddressSanitizer in my harness — the stack-use-after-scope confirmation cited in the issue comes from their ASAN run, not mine. One compiler family, one evening. The issue's own denominators are better than mine; use theirs.

Your turn

The reproduction is twenty lines, the playground is free, and here is the whole thing — paste it into the playground, hit Run, and compare your output to mine:

static KEPT: std::sync::Mutex<Vec<Box<dyn std::any::Any + Send>>> =
    std::sync::Mutex::new(Vec::new());

struct Q<T: 'static + Send>(Option<T>);

impl<T: 'static + Send> Drop for Q<T> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        if let Some(v) = self.0.take() {
            KEPT.lock().unwrap().push(Box::new(v));
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let l = String::from("hello world, this is long enough");
    {
        let mut q = Q(None);
        q.0 = Some(&l);
    } // <- Drop here: the short-lived reference escapes as if 'static

    let kept = KEPT.lock().unwrap();
    let s = kept[0].downcast_ref::<&'static String>().unwrap();
    println!("read after scope: {}", s);
    println!("the stack slot is freed. the string still printed.");
}

Run it on your rustc, your channels, your edition, and post your output — the issue's variants reach back to 1.4, and every data point sharpens the map. Then pick one guarantee you ship or rely on, and write down the premise under it that nobody executes. That list is where the next eleven-year bugs live.

title: Our header is 48 pixels tall, every page offsets by 56, and the root layout renders no header at all
description:
notifio.app is the marketing site for a desktop app that watches rental search pages and alerts you when a new listing appears. The site is 38 URLs. Its header is one component, 70 lines, and the three most interesting things in it are a pair of pointer-events classes, a number that is wrong on purpose, and the fact that app/layout.tsx does not render it.

The layout renders fonts and a JSON-LD block, and then stops

Here is everything inside <body> in the root layout:

<body className="bg-[#0a0a0a] text-[#fafafa] antialiased font-sans">
  {/* Who is behind this site, in the form a crawler reads. */}
  <script type="application/ld+json" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ ... }} />
  {children}
</body>

No nav. No footer. Both are imported and rendered by each page:

$ grep -rl --include="*.tsx" "<Nav" src | wc -l
15

Fifteen files, each opening with the same three lines. The App Router's whole pitch is that shared chrome belongs in a layout, so this needs a reason, and the honest one is a shape rather than a rule: a layout wraps every route under it, and opting out of a layout means moving a route into a different segment. Putting the header in the page means a page that should not have one simply does not import it.

Today, all fifteen import it. The payment success page imports it, the maintenance page imports it, and so the opt-out I am describing is currently used by nothing, which makes the duplication a cost with a hypothetical benefit. The part that keeps it from being a real problem is that fifteen files is not 38 pages: one of them is ArticleLayout, which renders all eight long-form pages, the five listed at notifio.app/guides plus three audience pages, and two more are dynamic routes covering the fifteen entries at notifio.app/alerts and the five at notifio.app/compare. The number of files that would need editing to change the chrome is fifteen; the number of pages is 38.

If I were starting again I would put it in the layout and use a route group for anything that needs to escape. I am writing down the trade rather than the conclusion, because the version in the repo works and has never once been the reason a change was hard.

Two classes so a transparent header does not eat clicks

The header is fixed, full width, and centres its contents:

<div
  className={`fixed top-0 inset-x-0 z-50 flex justify-center pointer-events-none transition-all duration-300 ease-out ${
    scrolled ? "pt-3 px-4" : "pt-0 px-0"
  }`}
>
  <nav className="pointer-events-auto w-full ...">

pointer-events-none on the outer div, pointer-events-auto on the nav inside it. This is the entire reason the design works.

Once scrolled, the nav is a rounded pill with max-w-6xl and 12px of padding above it. The outer div is still the full width of the viewport and roughly 60 pixels tall, sitting at z-50 above everything. Without those two classes, that invisible rectangle swallows every click and hover in the top strip of the page, including the ones aimed at the gap either side of the pill. Nothing in the UI tells you why. You just find a dead zone at the top of a page, usually on a wide monitor, usually weeks later.

The pair is the smallest fix available: the container keeps its layout job and gives up its hit-testing job, and the one child that needs to be clickable takes hit-testing back. Worth remembering as a shape, because every floating or inset fixed element has this problem: a fixed positioning container is as clickable as it is wide, not as wide as it looks.

The scroll state is a boolean, and that is a throttle 

const [scrolled, setScrolled] = useState(false);

useEffect(() => {
  const onScroll = () => setScrolled(window.scrollY > 20);
  window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });
  return () => window.removeEventListener("scroll", onScroll);
}, []);

No requestAnimationFrame, no debounce, no IntersectionObserver sentinel. The listener runs on every scroll event, which during a trackpad flick is a lot of events, and it reads window.scrollY each time, which is a layout read.

What it does not do is re-render. setScrolled(false) while the state is already false is a no-op as far as the rendered output goes, because React bails out when the next state is identical to the current one. The component re-renders when the value flips, so a long scroll down the pricing page produces one state change rather than four hundred. The derived class strings change at exactly the moment the appearance is supposed to change, and the CSS transition does the 300ms of work between the two states.

That leaves the cost of the handler itself, which is why { passive: true } is there: it promises the browser that this listener will never call preventDefault, so scrolling is not blocked waiting to find out. A boolean threshold plus a passive listener is enough for this. The version with a rAF-throttled handler and a ref holding the last value is more code that produces the same pixels.

The one thing I would change: the handler never runs on mount. Load the page already scrolled, which happens on a refresh or when following a link to an anchor, and the header renders in its unscrolled state until you move. One extra onScroll() call before the addEventListener fixes it, and it is a genuine bug rather than a trade.

The number 56, seventeen times

The nav's inner row is h-12, which is 48 pixels. When scrolled it gains pt-3, 12 more, for 60. Every page then pushes its content down by this:

<main className="pt-14">

pt-14 is 56 pixels. Not 48, not 60, in between.

$ grep -rn --include="*.tsx" "pt-14" src | wc -l
16
$ grep -rn --include="*.tsx" "100vh-56" src | wc -l
2

Fifteen of those sixteen pt-14 matches are a page clearing the header, the sixteenth is the footer's own padding, and the two calc matches are this, on the success and maintenance pages:

<main className="pt-14">
  <section className="flex min-h-[calc(100vh-56px)] items-center justify-center px-6 py-20">

The same constant written twice in two notations, in two files, for pages whose single card is supposed to be vertically centred in whatever is left under the header. Seventeen places that know how tall the header is, and the one match that is not about the header at all is the footer, which is its own small hazard: the string is not searchable for the thing it means.

The defensible part is that the header is position: fixed, so it is out of flow and the gap under it has to come from somewhere. The indefensible part is the value. 48 and 60 are both real heights depending on scroll position, 56 is neither, and the reason it works is that pages have 80 pixels of their own top padding under it so an 8 pixel error is invisible.

A CSS variable, --nav-height, set once and used by both the component and the pages, would make the relationship explicit and let the two states disagree honestly. The reason it has not happened is the reason most of these do not: nothing has gone wrong yet. Writing it down is the cheap half of fixing it.

Three links out of 38 URLs 

<Link href="/alerts">Sites</Link>
<Link href="/pricing">Pricing</Link>
<Link href="/download">Get Notifio</Link>

That is the whole menu, with no mobile variant because three short links fit. The hub pages for guides and comparisons are not in it, which is deliberate: the header carries the path a visitor is on, which is "what does it watch", "what does it cost", "give me the app". Everything else is reachable from the footer, which has its own set of trade-offs that I wrote up in the footer post, and from in-page links.

The one detail in the markup worth copying:

<Image src="/icon-light.svg" alt="" width={18} height={18} priority className="opacity-90" />
Notifio

alt="" on the logo, because the word "Notifio" is right there in the same link as text. An alt="Notifio" here makes a screen reader announce the brand twice for one link. The priority is because this is the only image above the fold on every route.

What the component is, in total

A fixed container that does not take clicks, a pill inside it that does, one boolean of state, three links, and a hardcoded offset repeated in every page. The interesting work in a site header is almost never the markup. It is the two classes that keep an invisible rectangle from stealing input, and the constant that quietly knows how tall everything is.

The 38 URLs it sits on are mostly generated rather than written, which is a different post: our sitemap is 38 URLs and only ten of them are typed out by hand. The app the header is advertising is at notifio.app/download.

title: 40 font-face blocks, 10 files, and the word bold appears nowhere: three typefaces reaching a Next.js site and an Expo app
description:
Munchable uses three typefaces, and each has exactly one job. Fredoka, which is round and friendly, is allowed on the wordmark and hero headlines and nowhere else. Outfit does every other heading. Nunito does body text. The sizes come from a tokens package shared by the website, the phone app and the renderer that produces our video, so a heading is 27/33 in all three.

Two of those consumers load the fonts in completely different ways, and the second one surprised me more than it should have.

The web half, and why it is self-hosted 

const nunito = Nunito({
  subsets: ['latin'],
  weight: ['400', '500', '600', '700'],
  variable: '--font-nunito',
  display: 'swap',
});

Three of those, one per family, each exposing a CSS variable that globals.css consumes through role names rather than family names:

--font-display: var(--font-outfit), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;
--font-body: var(--font-nunito), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;
--font-brand: var(--font-fredoka), var(--font-nunito), ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif;

--font-brand falling back to Nunito before the system stack is deliberate: if the display face fails, the wordmark should land on the font the rest of the page is already using rather than on whatever Helvetica the device has.

next/font/google downloads the font files at build time and serves them from our own origin. That is a privacy decision before it is a performance one. A <link> to fonts.googleapis.com means every page load reports the visitor's IP address to a third party, and this is a site where the page somebody is reading can be the IBD page or the SIBO page. The URL is a health disclosure. There is no third-party request in the critical path of any page here, and the privacy policy says so, which means the fonts had to come along.

What that actually ships

You can count this yourself on any page of the site. Pull the stylesheet and look at the @font-face blocks:

  • 40 @font-face blocks
  • 10 distinct .woff2 files
  • 3 of the blocks are not web fonts at all

The three odd ones are named Nunito Fallback, Outfit Fallback and Fredoka Fallback. They are synthetic faces pointing at a local system font with adjusted metrics, generated so that the text drawn before the real font arrives occupies close to the same space. That is the mechanism that keeps display: swap from shoving your layout sideways, and it is the main reason to use the font loader rather than hand-writing the @font-face rules.

Forty blocks for ten files because the same file is declared under several weights and several unicode ranges. The browser then fetches only the ones a page actually asks for. On the homepage, in a fresh profile:

performance.getEntriesByType('resource')
  .filter(r => /\.woff2/.test(r.name))
  .map(r => [r.name.split('/').pop().slice(0, 12), r.encodedBodySize]);

Three files, 101,084 bytes in total, all from munchable.app.

The audit this led to

Eleven weights are declared across the three families: four of Nunito, four of Outfit, three of Fredoka.

The public stylesheet contains exactly three numeric weights: 600, 700 and 800. Body copy inherits 400 and never says so. Grep it and that is the whole list, inline SVG demos included.

Which means at least two declared weights are never referenced by the site: font-weight: 500 appears nowhere in the public CSS at all. It appears in exactly one file in the repository, the admin panel's own stylesheet, which is behind authentication and noindexed.

The honest accounting here matters, because it explains why nobody noticed. A declared and unreferenced weight costs a visitor nothing in bandwidth: no rule asks for it, so the file is never fetched. It costs build output, a slightly bigger stylesheet, and a wrong answer to the question "which weights does this product use". It is a one-line fix in each of three calls, and the reason to make it is tidiness rather than speed, which is worth saying out loud instead of dressing it up as a performance win.

The React Native half, where weight is not a number

Here is the part that trips up anybody moving a design system onto React Native. On the web, you ask for a family and a weight and the browser picks a face. In React Native with custom fonts, the weight is part of the family's name:

export const fontMap = {
  Fredoka_600SemiBold,
  Fredoka_700Bold,
  Outfit_500Medium,
  Outfit_600SemiBold,
  Outfit_700Bold,
  Nunito_400Regular,
  Nunito_600SemiBold,
  Nunito_700Bold,
};

Eight named faces, handed to expo-font's useFonts. Then the type scale attaches a family to each variant rather than a weight:

export const typography = {
  brand: { fontFamily: 'Fredoka_700Bold', ...typeScale.brand },
  hero: { fontFamily: 'Fredoka_700Bold', ...typeScale.hero },
  display: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_700Bold', ...typeScale.display },
  h1: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_700Bold', ...typeScale.h1 },
  h2: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_600SemiBold', ...typeScale.h2 },
  title: { fontFamily: 'Outfit_600SemiBold', ...typeScale.title },
  body: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_400Regular', ...typeScale.body },
  bodyStrong: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_700Bold', ...typeScale.bodyStrong },
  label: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_700Bold', ...typeScale.label },
  caption: { fontFamily: 'Nunito_600SemiBold', ...typeScale.caption },
};

fontWeight appears nowhere in the app. Not in the tokens, not in a component, not in a screen. Grep returns nothing, and that is the design: setting fontWeight: '700' on a custom family asks the platform to synthesise a bold, which on Android is a smeared version of the regular face and on iOS is sometimes ignored entirely. Two platforms, two different wrong answers. Naming the face is the only portable instruction.

The ...typeScale.h2 spread is where the two halves meet. The sizes and line heights live in a platform-free package, so h2 is 21/27 on a phone, in the browser build of the same app, and in the rendered video frames, without anybody retyping a number.

One <Text variant="h2"> component reads that table. No screen picks a family, so there is no screen that can pick the wrong one.

Boot, briefly

Fonts block the splash screen, because the app's first screen is a scanner and text reflowing under somebody's thumb in a supermarket aisle is worse than a slightly longer splash. But the gate is fontsLoaded || fontError: a font that fails to load must not hold the app hostage, and the fallback stack exists precisely so that case is merely uglier rather than broken.

Where to see all three

The homepage is the only page with the brand face at full size, so munchable.app is where Fredoka actually earns its place. A content page such as the congee recipe is the ordinary case: Outfit for the headings, Nunito for everything you read, and nothing from a third-party domain in the network panel.

title: A 3% zoom hid a one-pixel rounding gap for 372 cards, then cut the first letters off the 373rd
description:
A while ago I wrote about
putting a real screenshot at the top of 372 practice test cards:
a dev-only capture route, a crop script, and a manifest the build generates so a
card can never point at a file that is not there.

This post is what happened when a second kind of content needed the same
treatment, which is the point at which you find out which of your decisions were
decisions and which were coincidences.

The frame, and the arithmetic in it

The screenshot does not sit flush at the top of the card. It sits inset, like
the screen of a handheld console, with the card acting as the case around it:

<div className="shrink-0 p-2 pb-0">
  <div className="bg-muted ring-border relative aspect-[16/10] overflow-hidden rounded-[12px] ring-1">
    <div className="absolute -inset-px">
      <Image src={src} alt={alt} fill sizes={sizes} className="object-cover" />
    </div>
    {badge && <div className="absolute top-2.5 right-2.5 shadow-sm">{badge}</div>}
  </div>
</div>

The radius is not a taste choice, it is subtraction. The card is
rounded-[20px]. The frame around the screen is p-2, so 8px. A rounded corner
inset by 8px only stays parallel to its parent if its own radius is 8px smaller:
20 - 8 = 12, hence rounded-[12px]. Use the same radius for both and the inner
corner looks tighter than the outer one; use a bigger one and the gap between
the curves visibly fattens at 45 degrees. This is the single most common
giveaway in nested rounded rectangles and it costs one subtraction to get right.

The aspect ratio is 16/10 because that is the capture ratio, so the box and
the image agree and object-cover has nothing to crop. I did try a shorter box
on phones, on the theory that a card is mostly text. It cut off the bottom strip
of the screen, which in most of our tests is where the answer controls live, so
the screenshot stopped showing the thing it was there to show.

The bug the extraction exposed

Look at that inner wrapper again:

<div className="absolute -inset-px">

A negative one pixel inset on every side, so the image overhangs its box by a
pixel all round and gets clipped by overflow-hidden. It used to be this:

className="scale-[1.03] object-cover"

Both exist to solve the same real problem. At some card widths the browser
rounds the image's layout box a fraction short of its container and leaves a
one-pixel grey sliver down the right edge. A 3% scale buries the sliver under
overflow, and for 372 game screenshots it was invisible and fine.

Then the same component rendered an assessment centre exercise, whose brief
panel starts hard against the left edge of the screen, and 3% of 1280 pixels is
about 19 pixels of horizontal zoom. The first letters of the panel went missing.

The two fixes look equivalent and are not. A scale is proportional, so it costs
you a percentage of the content at every edge, and the percentage you need is a
guess about rendering you cannot measure. A one-pixel bleed is absolute: it
covers exactly the sub-pixel rounding that caused the problem and nothing else.
I had reached for the proportional fix because it was one class, and it survived
only because no content was near enough to the edge to notice.

The general version, which I keep relearning: a fix sized in percent for a
problem measured in pixels works until the content changes.

Extracting it

Both surfaces now render the same component:

export function CardScreenshot({ src, alt, sizes, badge }: {
  src: string;
  alt: string;
  sizes: string;
  /** Pinned to the screen's top right corner. */
  badge?: ReactNode;
}) { /* ... */ }

Four props, and the choice of which four is the whole design. src and alt
are obviously the caller's. sizes is too, and it has to be, because
next/image needs a sizes string that describes the card's width at each
breakpoint and the two grids are different:

// game cards, three columns from lg
sizes="(min-width: 1024px) 400px, (min-width: 768px) 50vw, 100vw"
// exercise format cards, two columns from sm
sizes="(min-width: 896px) 440px, (min-width: 640px) 50vw, 100vw"

A shared component that guessed sizes for its callers would silently serve one
of them the wrong image width forever, and next/image gives you no warning
because it has no idea how wide your card is.

What is deliberately not a prop: the padding, the ratio, the radius, the ring,
the bleed, the badge position. Those are the frame. If a caller needed a
different one of those, it would not be this component.

The docstring carries the constraint the component cannot enforce:

The card must be overflow-hidden rounded-[20px]: the screen's corners are the
card's 20px less the 8px frame, so the curves run parallel.

That is a contract a type cannot express, so it is written where whoever breaks
it will be looking.

916 is not a round number

Generalising the capture script meant turning its constants into a record with
one entry per content type:

const TARGETS: Record<'game' | 'exercise', Target> = {
  game: {
    viewportHeight: 800,
    headerHeight: 64,
    footerHeight: 0,
    // ...
  },
  exercise: {
    // The e-tray's three panes run the full width, so a 16:10 trim would cut
    // text off both edges. 916 is 800 plus ExerciseContainer's h-14 header and
    // the workspace's 60px "Finish & score" bar, which leaves an area of exactly
    // 1280x800 to keep whole between them.
    viewportHeight: 916,
    headerHeight: 56,
    footerHeight: 60,
  },
};

Games capture at 1280x800 and the default crop takes a 16:10 box from the middle
of the play area. That works because most games are roughly centred.

An e-tray exercise is three panes side by side across the full width. Trimming
it to 16:10 from the centre would cut text off both edges, so these captures use
the mode that keeps the whole area and pads it instead. But "the whole area" has
to actually be 16:10 to avoid padding bars, and the area is the viewport minus
the chrome. So the viewport height is derived backwards from the area you want
to keep: 800 for the content, plus 56 for the header, plus 60 for the bottom
action bar, is 916.

Which means footerHeight had to exist as a concept at all. The game target has
footerHeight: 0 and the crop maths is the same for both:

const bottom = viewport.height - target.footerHeight;
const areaHeight = bottom - header;

Three fields and two subtractions where there used to be two constants. Adding a
second target to a script written for one is almost always this: the constants
you hardcoded were not wrong, they were just unnamed.

The ids are not the filenames

One detail worth a paragraph because it bit me. The generated manifest lists the
captures that exist:

/**
 * Exercises with a card screenshot at public/exercises/screenshots/<id>.webp.
 * Generated by `pnpm tsx scripts/game-screenshots.ts manifest`; do not edit by hand.
 */
export const EXERCISE_SCREENSHOTS: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set([
  'etray-product-launch',
  'group-discussion-scenarios',
  'intray-office-manager',
  'presentation-board-strategy',
  'roleplay-difficult-client',
  'written-recommendation-report',
]);

Four of those six do not match the source file they are defined in.
etray-marketing-launch.ts exports an exercise whose id is
etray-product-launch; written-consulting-report.ts is
written-recommendation-report. The files were named during drafting and the
ids were named for the reader.

Generating the manifest from the output directory rather than from the content
library is what makes that harmless. The capture is written as <id>.webp, the
manifest is read back from the filenames, and the card looks up its own id. At
no point does anything have to know what the file on my disk is called. Had I
written the list by hand from the content folder, four of the six would have
pointed at nothing.

And one line of selection logic

The public page shows one captured scenario per format:

/**
 * One captured scenario per format for the top of its card, the first in
 * library order, so the e-tray card shows the free sample. A format with no
 * capture keeps its icon.
 */

"The first in library order" is doing real work there. The library is ordered
with the free sample first, so the card for the format you can try without an
account shows the scenario you would actually get. And a format with no capture
is not broken, it keeps the icon treatment, which is also why the card's radius
is conditional: rounded-[20px] with a screenshot, rounded-xl without, because
the nested radius arithmetic only applies when there is something nested.

The game cards are live now, so you can see the frame on any provider page, for
example Aon's, where the cards lead with a
capture of the test they open. The exercise cards on the
assessment centre practice page
still show icons at the time of writing; the six captures above go out with the
next deploy. The free e-tray scenario on that page runs in full without an
account either way.

title: "4200subscribers": the content said "black" and the renderer believed it
description:
Our numerical reasoning practice shows you source material (a table, a bar
chart, a line graph) and asks you questions about it. The content that drives
those charts carries a unit alongside each value, because "4200" on its own
means nothing and "4200 subscribers" does.

For a while, several of our charts rendered that as:

4200subscribers

Which is the single most recognisable bug in the genre. Here is the code that
produced it, and if you have written a dashboard you have written this line:

<span className="font-semibold">
  {hasValue ? `${value}${unit}` : '-'}
</span>

Template literal, value, unit. Correct for 45 and %. Wrong for 4200 and
subscribers. And the fix is not "add a space", because then you get:

4200 %
£ 286000

Worse, the currency case is not a spacing problem at all. A pound symbol is a
prefix, so gluing it on in either direction gives you 286000£, which is not
how anyone writes money in English.

Three shapes, one function

The unit strings in our content fall into three groups, and they want three
different treatments:

shape examples rendering
currency £, $, £m symbol leads, remainder trails
symbol or one letter %, k, % per year attach directly
word or multi-letter hours, MWh, thousand households space between

So the concatenation became a function. All 32 lines of it, docstring included:

/**
 * Join a data value to the unit a question bank gives for it.
 *
 * Bank units come in three shapes, and gluing them straight on reads wrong for
 * two of them: "4200subscribers", "£4200" rendered as "4200£".
 */
export function formatWithUnit(value: number | string, unit = ''): string {
  if (!unit) return String(value);

  if (/^[£$€]/.test(unit)) {
    const symbol = unit[0];
    const rest = unit.slice(1);
    const n = typeof value === 'number' ? value : Number(value);
    // "-£5", not "£-5".
    return Number.isFinite(n) && n < 0
      ? `-${symbol}${Math.abs(n)}${rest}`
      : `${symbol}${value}${rest}`;
  }

  if (unit.startsWith('%') || unit.startsWith(' ') || unit.length === 1) {
    return `${value}${unit}`;
  }

  return `${value} ${unit}`;
}

Some notes on the decisions in there, because every branch is a judgement call
someone will want to argue with.

Currency is split, not matched whole. The unit £m is a symbol plus a
magnitude, and they go on opposite sides of the number: £12m. Taking
unit[0] as the symbol and unit.slice(1) as the remainder handles £, $m
and €bn with one branch.

Negative numbers move the sign outside the symbol. £-5 is the kind of
output that makes a reader stop and squint at a chart, which in a timed practice
test is a cost I am imposing on them for nothing. Three lines to produce -£5.

% per year attaches, per year would not. The rule is "starts with %",
not "is %", because a percentage of something still wants the sign tight
against the number: 2.5% per year.

length === 1 catches k and m without a list. Any one-character unit
attaches directly. It is a heuristic and I am comfortable with it: there is no
single-letter unit in English that wants a space.

A unit that already begins with a space is left exactly as written. This is
the escape hatch. If a piece of content needs spacing this function would not
give it, the content can say so and the function will not second-guess it.

The test file is all cases, which is the right shape for a pure function like
this:

expect(formatWithUnit(4200, 'subscribers')).toBe('4200 subscribers');
expect(formatWithUnit(1840, 'MWh')).toBe('1840 MWh');
expect(formatWithUnit(2.5, '% per year')).toBe('2.5% per year');
expect(formatWithUnit(12, '£m')).toBe('£12m');
expect(formatWithUnit(-5, '$')).toBe('-$5');
expect(formatWithUnit(7, ' units')).toBe('7 units');
expect(formatWithUnit('n/a', '')).toBe('n/a');

That last one is why the signature takes number | string. A value is not
always a number; sometimes a table cell says n/a, and Number('n/a') is NaN,
which is how you end up shipping a chart that reads "NaN%".

Two components were doing their own concatenation across five call sites, and
both now call this instead. The interesting part was not writing the function,
it was that the same mistake had been written twice independently, because
${value}${unit} looks so obviously right that nobody reviews it.

The same bug wearing a different hat

In the same commit, this:

const SHAPE_COLORS: Record<KFLogicalShape['color'], string> = {
  red: '#ef4444',
  blue: '#3b82f6',
  green: '#22c55e',
  yellow: '#eab308',
  black: '#1f2937',
};

Four of those are colours. The fifth is a role. Red means red, but "black"
means ink, and #1f2937 is a very dark grey that was effectively invisible
against the dark card those shapes are drawn on. In dark mode, the item that
the content called black was the one you could not see.

  // "Black" is the ink colour, so it follows the theme's foreground: a fixed
  // #1f2937 vanished into the dark card the frames sit on.
  black: 'currentColor',

With className="text-foreground" on the SVG, so currentColor resolves to
whatever the theme says text is. One word in a lookup table, and the shape is
dark on light and light on dark.

The thing both bugs have in common

Our content banks store descriptive strings: a unit, a colour name, a label.
Both of these bugs came from a renderer taking one of those strings literally.
unit was treated as a suffix because it usually is. black was treated as a
hex value because it usually is. In both cases the right move is for the
renderer to interpret the string as a declaration of intent rather than as
output.

That is an easy sentence to write after the fact and an annoying one to act on
in advance. The practical version: when a data field's name is a noun from the
problem domain rather than from the view layer, do not pipe it into the view
unexamined.

Both fixes are on live pages if you want to look at them. The charts and tables
that carry these units are what
numerical reasoning practice
is made of, the tabbed source documents are listed on
Aon's practice page, and the abstract shape
sequences whose "black" is now ink are the Elements Logical test on
Korn Ferry's. Each page says which of
its tests are free.

title: AWS Backup now supports Amazon FSx file systems in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region
description:
AWS Backup now supports Amazon FSx for Lustre, Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP, Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, and Amazon FSx for Windows File Server in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region.

With this launch, you can use AWS Backup to centrally automate and manage data protection for your Amazon FSx file systems in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region, alongside your other supported AWS resources. You can create policy-based backup plans to schedule backups and apply retention rules, store backups in encrypted vaults, and restore file systems when needed. This helps you meet business continuity, disaster recovery, and regulatory compliance requirements from a single, centralized service.

To get started, visit the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. For a complete list of supported Regions and features, visit the AWS Backup documentation. To learn more about AWS Backup, visit the product page and pricing page.

title: Announcing Blockchain Snapshots on AWS for node bootstrapping
description:
For blockchain node operators running Ethereum or Solana, AWS is announcing Blockchain Snapshots on AWS, an initiative that publishes pre-synced public blockchain node chain data in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) so you can bootstrap a node from a snapshot instead of peer-to-peer syncing from the network. These snapshots are hosted on Amazon S3 within AWS infrastructure, enabling customers running nodes on AWS benefit from reduced latency and optimized data transfer. Blockchain Snapshots on AWS republishes each network's authoritative snapshot in a format optimized for parallel extraction across multiple cores, reducing setup time, that an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance can use.

Snapshots cover Ethereum and Solana, are available at no charge, and refresh on the same cadence as the upstream provider. Use them to add capacity to a remote procedure call (RPC) fleet, recover a failed node, or re-sync a corrupted database.

You can use Blockchain Snapshots on AWS in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Europe (Ireland), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). Access requires an Amazon EC2 instance in the same Region with an Amazon S3 gateway VPC endpoint.

To get started, visit the Blockchain Snapshots on AWS documentation to access setup instructions and download the latest snapshots.

title: AWS Transfer Family console supports SVG logos and ICO favicons for web apps
description:
The AWS Transfer Family console now supports SVG files for logos and ICO files for favicons in web apps, with upload limits increased to 2 MB. This gives you more flexibility to use existing branding assets when customizing your web app.

Previously, the console accepted only JPG and PNG files and limited logo uploads to 50 KB and favicon uploads to 20 KB. The console automatically resizes images and converts them to JPG or PNG before saving them. Existing API upload limits and format requirements remain unchanged.

These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where Transfer Family web apps are offered. To learn more, see the Transfer Family web apps tutorial.

title: AWS Transfer Family now supports AWS Secrets Manager storage for SFTP server host keys
description:
AWS Transfer Family now lets you store SFTP server host keys in AWS Secrets Manager in your own AWS account. This gives you greater control over your server identity and helps simplify server migrations and failover.

Previously, Transfer Family stored host keys within the service, so you could not retrieve the associated private key material. With this launch, you can choose Secrets Manager as the storage type when creating a server or importing a host key. You can then retrieve the private key material and reuse the same host key across servers and AWS Regions. For example, you can use it on a standby server for failover or on a replacement server during migration, without requiring clients to trust a new host key. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies let you control who can retrieve the stored keys. You can also migrate existing host keys to Secrets Manager, which may require additional steps; see the AWS Transfer Family User Guide for details.

This capability is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transfer Family is available. To learn more, see Store SFTP server host keys in AWS Secrets Manager in the AWS Transfer Family User Guide. To get started, go to the AWS Transfer Family console.

title: Amazon RDS Proxy now supports SQL Server 2022
description:
Amazon RDS Proxy, a fully managed, highly available database proxy for Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS), now supports Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances running major version 2022.

Amazon RDS Proxy sits between your application and the database to pool and share established database connections, improving database efficiency and application scalability. For Amazon RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ databases, RDS Proxy automatically connects to the standby database instance during a failure, preserves application connections, and helps reduce failover times by up to 83%. RDS Proxy supports standard IAM authentication for SQL Server, where your applications authenticate to the proxy using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and RDS Proxy manages database connections using credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager.

You can enable Amazon RDS Proxy for your SQL Server 2022 database in a few steps on the Amazon RDS console, then connect by pointing your application to the RDS Proxy endpoint. To get started, see our documentation.

Resource criticality is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost and is always on for all customers.

title: Perseid 0.1.0 is now available
description:
I am very pleased to announce that, after a long hiatus, Perseid 0.1.0, a set of utilities for versioning PostgreSQL database schemas, has been released.

Perseid 0.1.0 is available from:

  • Codeberg
  • Git repository: https://codeberg.org/perseas/perseid

Documentation is available at: https://perseas.codeberg.page/perseid/

Perseid is the successor to Pyrseas. It provides dbtoyaml and yamltodb to extract a PostgreSQL database schema as YAML and to generate or apply SQL to bring a target database into agreement with a YAML specification.

This initial release supports SQL SCHEMAs, TABLEs, COLUMNs and CONSTRAINTs. PostgreSQL 17 or higher is required.

Many thanks to those who contributed code, ideas, and discussions to make this first release possible.

Best wishes,

Joe Abbate

title: psqlODBC 18.00.0005 released with security fix for CVE-2026-109448
description:
The psqlODBC team has released version 18.00.0005 of psqlODBC, the official ODBC driver for PostgreSQL. This release fixes one security vulnerability and two bugs. All users should upgrade.

Security issue

CVE-2026-109448: heap memory corruption when binding more than 32767 parameters

CVSS 3.1 base score: 5.9 (Medium)

Versions affected: 08.01.0102 through 18.00.0004.

psqlODBC stored the number of bound parameters on a statement in a signed 16-bit field. When an application bound more than 32768 parameters on one statement, the driver wrote zeros outside the memory that holds the parameter bindings. The application could crash, or keep running with corrupted memory. An application is exposed if it lets untrusted input decide how many parameters it binds, for example by building an IN (?, ?, ...) list from user-supplied values.

SQLBindParameter now rejects parameter numbers above 32767 with SQLSTATE 07009. ODBC cannot report more than 32767 parameters, because SQLNumParams and SQL_DESC_COUNT are 16-bit values. No earlier release could run a statement with more than 32767 parameters, so this change does not break any application that worked before.

If you cannot upgrade right away, limit the number of parameters your application builds from external input, or pass long value lists as a single array parameter, for example = ANY(?).

The psqlODBC team thanks Richard Kuesters for reporting this problem.

For more details, see the advisory GHSA-cmfx-rm3r-p2jr.

Bug fixes

  • Statements prepared on the server with 1000 or more parameters could fail with errors such as type "timestam" does not exist. From parameter 1000 on, the driver cut the type name that follows each parameter to fit a fixed-size buffer.
  • Since 18.00.0003, bytea parameters failed with "Type is invalid" when used through Microsoft's OLE DB Provider for ODBC (MSDASQL), for example from ADO.

The Windows packages are now built with OpenSSL 3.5.9.

Download

Windows installers and merge modules for x86, x64 and ARM64 are available from the PostgreSQL download site and from the GitHub release page. The source code is on GitHub.

The full list of changes is in the release notes.

Please report bugs on the psqlODBC issue tracker or the pgsql-odbc mailing list.

title: PgBouncer 1.26.1 released - Fixes three CVEs
description:
PgBouncer 1.26.1 has been released. This release fixes three CVEs:

  1. CVE-2026-107350: Authentication bypass, allowing a client that knows the password of one SCRAM user to log in as any other SCRAM user, including admins and backend superusers. Caused by a second StartupMessage being processed during SCRAM authentication when connecting to a non-existent database.
  2. CVE-2026-107349: DoS due to infinite loop, triggerable by unauthenticated clients. Caused by an empty option name in the startup options parameter, when ignore_startup_parameters is non-empty but does not contain options.
  3. CVE-2026-107348: DoS due to infinite loop, triggerable by unauthenticated clients. Caused by an integer overflow in the packet buffer growth logic, only when max_packet_size is set above its default.

It also makes ignore_startup_parameters take precedence over tracked parameters, so that ignore_startup_parameters = search_path restores the 1.25 behaviour of ignoring search_path.

See https://www.pgbouncer.org/2026/10/pgbouncer-1-26-1 for more information, the detailed changelog, and download links.

title: Introducing pglifecycle 2.0 beta
description:
I’m pleased to announce the first public release of pglifecycle, an open source schema management tool for PostgreSQL.

pglifecycle keeps your database schema in version control as structured YAML, with one file for each table, view, function, role, and other object. This makes the current schema easy to browse, review, and change without reconstructing it from years of migration files.

With pglifecycle, you can:

  • Pull an existing database into a schema project
  • Build that project into an archive for pg_restore
  • Compare it with a live database and generate the DDL needed to reconcile them

Deployment is plan first. Destructive changes are withheld unless explicitly allowed, making the generated SQL suitable for review in CI.

The companion pglifecycle GitHub Action can detect schema drift and post deployment plans directly to pull requests without applying them.

Version 2 is a Rust rewrite of the original tool, which has managed AWeber’s production schema for more than seven years. The beta release expands PostgreSQL object coverage and improves deployment convergence and safety.

  • Getting Started
  • Documentation
  • GitHub Action

Feedback and real world test cases are welcome as pglifecycle moves toward a stable 2.0 release.

title: Show HN: Pulse Local, a Mac budgeting app whose AI models run on your machine
description:
Hi HN, I'm Niz. Pulse Local is a budgeting app for Mac (Apple Silicon, beta) that answers questions about your spending with models that run on your machine. Local mode needs no account. The ledger and your questions stay on the machine, and the app sends no analytics or crash logs.

I felt there are not enough consumer apps that run locally with no calls to the outside world that help us manage sensitive corners of our lives. This app in its local variant only downloads a couple of models and occasional updates, it does not send any analytics nor data.

Features-wise, Pulse local is a complete budgeting app that offers an assistant built on top of a fine-tuned model and thousands of rules embedded in the code itself. I'm sharing it for free with options to help me continue experimenting with fine-tuning and expanding along this direction.

How it works: you import a CSV from any bank, in any currency. When you ask a question, a tuned Qwen3 0.6B model reads it into a structured query, and code, not the model, does the money math against the ledger. A 4B checker model double-checks each money answer; when the two readings disagree, the app says it is not sure instead of guessing. That change took wrong answers from about one in five to 5 in 494 questions across our last three tests. The write-up covers how we test, the designs that failed, and the limits of the claim: https://pulseos.finance/pulse-local/writing/agree-or-not-sur...

The tuned weights are on Hugging Face (PulseOS/pulse-local-qwen3-0.6b).

Limitations: the first start downloads about 2.9 GB of models. With the checker on, a money answer takes 12 to 14 seconds (you can turn the checker off). Small models can still misread an open-ended question. The app answers in English. Mac only for now; Windows is next.

The app is free. An optional Connected mode (Sync Pass, $29/year) syncs US banks through Plaid; transactions pass through our server's memory and are not stored.

Feedback welcome, especially on wrong answers and on questions it should handle but does not.
