title: Taste is not a design methodology
description:
It has become our favorite answer to AI-generated sameness. The reality is good products come from judgment built on facts, and the agency to use them when the room prefers opinions.

Ask Rick Rubin what he does and he’ll tell you he has “no technical ability” and knows nothing about music. In a 2023 interview with Anderson Cooper, the producer said artists pay him for confidence in his own taste.

https://medium.com/media/1f83a53654c7bc936b099303acddda54/href
“The confidence I have in my taste and my ability to express what I feel has proven helpful for artists.” — Rick Rubin

Everyone now wants that job.

Just typing this makes me squirm because I believe the field should be research and data driven as much as it can be. With humans even.

“Taste is the new moat” might be the industry’s favorite sentence of 2026: artificial intelligence made competent screens cheap, so the one thing left to sell is the judgment to pick the good one. A ProductLed interview in January went further, telling builders not to validate before they build. It’s about 45 minutes in.

I decided not to show the video inline because it adds fuel to the fire and their use of typography isn’t to my taste.

It’s come up with couple of authors I follow — The taste paradox by Nicole Alexandra Michaelis is a good read over at UX Collective, and Xinran Ma had a interview recently about it in UX — and it’s in the zeitgeist.

My point is that it’s the wrong word.

The moat crowd is right that judgment matters; they’re wrong about where it comes from:

  • Taste is a preference. It comes from what you’ve seen and who you admire, and two people with different taste can disagree with no way to settle it.
  • Judgment is a claim you can check. It rests on principles research has tested, plus evidence about your users, so it can be explained, taught, and shown wrong.

Judgment needs agency too, because someone has to raise those facts when the most senior voice would rather trade opinions. What Nicole Alexandra Michaelis and Xinran Ma are talking about Judgement i.e. experience they can back with facts and experience.

The short rule: if you can’t name the fact or research behind a call, it’s still an opinion, which is otherwise known as taste.

Admit taste is an opinion

In 2001, researchers in Bordeaux and Montpellier gave a panel of 54 tasters a white wine colored red with an odorless dye. The panel described it with the vocabulary of red wine.

Nothing had changed but the color, and that was enough to overwrite their noses.

That’s the trouble with treating taste as a standard: it’s an opinion that feels like a fact. Two skilled designers can look at the same screen, reach opposite conclusions, and neither can prove the other mistaken.

Taste feels like perception, but a lot of it is expectation. Apple Music is probably the best example, it’s Apple, but still a challenging application to use established as fact.

For example, I like driving Audi TTs. A lot.

The proportions, the way one sits on a highway on-ramp, the complete impracticality of the back seat, the beautifully designed cockpit, the race to 110 miles per hour in California.

That last part is just storytelling, really.

I don’t expect any of that to be anyone else’s taste, and nothing is wrong when it isn’t, because my taste in cars only has to satisfy only me. A product has to work for thousands of people who never met me for it to be profitable, and that’s where a preference stops being enough.

My expectation is that Audi TT’s are designed for my taste, and it doesn’t fail me, ever.

Design has its own version of the wine study.

In 1995, Masaaki Kurosu and Kaori Kashimura of Hitachi had people rate 26 ATM layouts and found that how usable a layout looked tracked its beauty far more than its inherent usability. The field now calls this the aesthetic-usability effect, and it cuts both ways.

Generative tools make this worse because they turn out polished screens by default, so every option in the review looks finished. That’s the blind spot in the moat argument: the less polish costs, the less polish can tell you.

It reminds me of a conversation I had with Scott Jenson — Generative AI makes a lot of beautifully just above average screens. I made that argument they’re still better than a lot of portfolios I have seen, even if the screens have less depth.

This is why “does it have taste?” makes a weak review question: it has no failure condition other than an opinion.

Ruiqi Zhou called taste unfalsifiable in a February essay named Taste Is the New Moat — And That’s the Problem. It’s a great read, and points out that a standard you can never fail works more like a status marker, and status markers reward whoever already holds status. Usually, that’s product management.

Build judgment on laws that have held for centuries

User experience borrowed its foundations from people who ran experiments, and they had computers in only some cases.

Here are examples:

  • Paul Fitts showed in 1954 that the time to hit a target depends on its size and distance using fighter cockpits for research, and William Edmund Hick showed that decision time climbs as options pile up. Both findings have held up for seven decades.
  • Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich developed heuristic evaluation in 1990, and the ten heuristics are still the default checklist. Each turns an opinion into a checkable claim, like a button too small for a thumb.
  • Dieter Rams and his ten principles took what could have stayed personal taste and wrote it down where other people could use it, which is why teams still audit work against them fifty years on.

They are normative rather than experimental, but a checklist can be argued with. I keep plain-language summaries of Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, Nielsen’s heuristics, and Rams’s principles on ux-guidelines.com, a reference site I maintain. Every law has conditions, and knowing them is part of judgment.

Hick’s Law describes a choice among equally likely options, and a 1985 study of its exceptions found cases where adding choices barely slowed people down. Fitts measured people tapping a stylus between two targets, not a thumb stretching across a phone.

A law applied outside its conditions is just another opinion with a citation.

Principles don’t settle everything.

At Microsoft, Ronny Kohavi’s team reported that only about a third of well-run experiments improved the metric they were designed to move. The laws tell you what’s likely, and testing tells you what happened.

User research earns its place next to the laws for the same reason.

A law is general and your users are specific, so only watching them shows which steps they repeat and where they give up. Teresa Torres makes the cadence the point, defining continuous discovery as weekly contact with customers by the team building the product, rather than a study that lands after the decision.

Test beauty with the people who will use it

None of this means beauty is decoration. The same aesthetic-usability effect explains why users forgive attractive products, and appearance shapes trust and first impressions.

Don Norman gave the effect a mechanism in Emotional Design: a positive mood broadens thinking and makes people more forgiving of small friction. Jony Ive’s teams built the most admired hardware of their era and also shipped the butterfly keyboard, which Apple settled a class action over for $50 million in 2022 after years of complaints.

Taste operating at that altitude still needed someone to check whether the thing worked.

The mistake is assuming the designer’s eye can stand in for the audience’s. Nielsen Norman Group showed the same five screenshots to 229 adults aged 18 to 25 and 228 aged 35 and older,

The results?

  • The younger group rated the flat designs slightly more attractive.
  • The older, slightly less attractive.

Whose taste was right? Each group’s, for itself.

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, especially in enterprise software, where the person who admires the demo is rarely the one who lives in the product eight hours a day.

Beauty is a user outcome, so measure it like one.

That’s where the line between fact and opinion falls here. What users report about a screen is a fact about your audience, while a design lead’s verdict is one more opinion, however practiced the eye behind it. The survey used a modified version of the Microsoft Desirability Toolkit, which asks people to pick words that describe what they see from a fixed list.

Score task success and time on task separately from those ratings, so a polished prototype can’t inflate the verdict on whether the thing works.

Teach the principles before the portfolio

In 2009, two researchers who had spent careers on opposite sides of this argument wrote a paper together. Daniel Kahneman had documented how judgment fails, while Gary Klein had defended expert intuition in the field.

Their joint answer on when intuition deserves trust came down to two conditions:

  • The environment has to be regular enough to learn about who they’re designing for
  • The person needs a real chance to learn it

Design taste rarely gets that chance. A designer ships a screen, moves on to the next project, and never finds out whether the choice helped anyone.

Confidence grows with years, but accuracy only grows with feedback.

Tell a designer two years out of school to trust their taste, after a portfolio course, maybe an internship, and very few closed loops between a decision and its outcome. What they have is exposure to showcase sites and admired apps, which produces taste that matches the feed, not the user.

Principles are the shortcut experience can’t hand out, and they come with standing. A junior designer who knows Hick’s Law can push back on a longer menu in her first critique, and a new hire who has studied the heuristics can flag a missing undo before anyone senior does.

Facts give people the agency that seniority usually keeps for itself.

Give everyone the agency to argue from facts

Taste has a politics problem.

When the standard is taste, the taste that counts usually belongs to the most senior person present. Ron Kohavi named it in a 2008 Stanford talk, Listen to Your Customers not to the HiPPO: the HiPPO is the highest-paid person’s opinion.

A taste culture is a HiPPO culture with better typography.

The fix isn’t to ban taste from the room, it’s to stop one person from owning it without evidence.

Everybody on a team has taste, and the new designer’s is worth as much as the vice president’s, which is exactly why it makes a poor standard: nothing decides whose version wins except rank. Facts don’t work that way, since a law or a session recording says the same thing no matter who reads it out.

Taste cultures have a patron saint they misappropriated: Steve Jobs.

He told BusinessWeek in 1998 that designing by focus group is hard. People, he said, “don’t know what they want until you show it to them.” It gets quoted as permission to skip research, though the same answer described watching trends and studying Apple’s installed base.

But even he met his match in Paul Rand.

When Steve Jobs needed a logo for NeXT in 1986, he hired Rand, whom he openly called the greatest living graphic designer. The friction came immediately: Jobs asked for a few options, and Rand refused, saying he would solve the problem and Jobs would pay him, and if he wanted options he could hire someone else.

Jobs agreed to the terms and the $100,000 fee. Rand returned with one design, the tilted black cube, presented in a hand-bound booklet that walked Jobs through the reasoning until the logo felt inevitable.

Jobs loved it, and later admitted that you don’t hand a genius a menu.

Because of this, Apple did research all the time and that gave Jobs credibility to make judgement calls. Those that claim they have the same truly understand the company, nor how to combine taste with judgement.

Even Steve Jobs’ famous 2x2 Matrix Strategy is rooted in science — Paradox of Choice.

The larger problem is survivorship bias, another old law. We remember the founder whose certainty paid off and forget the rooms where the same certainty sank the product with dollar amount attached to it.

Agency with receipts is the fix.

Session notes, retention data, and a heuristic all lose to a senior “that feels off,” unless the team agrees that facts outrank opinions.

With that agreement in place, the quietest person in the room can win by naming the law a design breaks or the data point it ignores. Peter Merholz argues that design executives earn that standing by making design their secondary concern.

The fair counterargument belongs to Doug Bowman, Google’s first visual designer.

In 2009 he left and explained why in Goodbye, Google: a team was testing 41 shades of blue, and he had been asked to prove whether a border should be three, four, or five pixels wide.

His complaint went past the trivia: with nobody senior who understood design, he argued, the company ran out of reasons for its decisions, and data became “a crutch for every decision” that kept anything daring from shipping.

$200 million later. Hard to argue that as an outcome.

Measuring everything is its own way of dodging judgment, so decisions slow to the test calendar, and designers who could settle a border width from a principle leave for places where that counts, as Bowman did.

Aim evidence at the choices that change what users can do. A corner radius needs no significance test, since a law settles it faster.

Choose facts over opinions

Judgment is knowing which facts apply, and where they stop applying: a law, a heuristic, a published study, or research on your own users. Where taste says “this feels right,” judgment points out that the target is too small to tap reliably and that Fitts showed why in 1954.

Agency is saying that out loud in the review, even when it cuts against the most senior opinion in the room.

Judgment tells you which facts matter, and agency is using them when the room prefers an opinion.

The new reality:

  • Generative tools can produce fifty layouts before my morning coffee.
  • Judgment cuts the pile fast, dropping the ones with targets too small to hit, menus too long to scan, and flows that ask people to hold too much in their heads.
  • What’s left goes to research, where users settle what the principles can’t.

Teams that run interviews and usability sessions on a schedule build a store of facts they can reach for in any review, and teams that skip them are left with preferences and a deadline. Dan Maccarone spent a year rebuilding his studio’s process around these tools and found that it didn’t make the work faster, which he counts as the point: what changed was where the thinking had to happen.

Rubin’s approach works because a record has no task to fail. A designer who borrows that job description claims the authority without the conditions that make it hold.

Judgment also improves in a way taste doesn’t, if somebody writes the call down. Jeff Gothelf formalizes that in the Lean UX canvas: state what you believe will happen, then name the evidence that would tell you whether you were right. It’s the equivalent of the Change My Mind meme, and it’s brilliant.

Picture two designers.

  • One moves a filter panel above the results because Hick’s Law favors fewer competing choices on the way to what people came for, predicts lower search abandonment, and checks the numbers six weeks after launch.
  • The other spends the same six weeks studying award-winning screen shots.

Only the first one learned something new about their users, and only their judgment got sharper.

Conclusion

Taste isn’t going away, and it isn’t the real enemy.

Opinions shape style, brand voice, and the small choices no principle covers. The trouble starts when an opinion gets treated as a fact and wins arguments it hasn’t earned.

The moat story is half right.

Artificial intelligence does make average output cheap, and plenty of products will look alike because of it. The scarce skill isn’t picking the prettiest variation, it’s knowing which ones break what the field already knows, which ones deserve a test, and what the result means for the next decision.

The wine panel in Bordeaux wasn’t foolish; its members were human, and so are we. That’s the whole reason design has laws and methods at all.

Human perception drifts toward what it expects to see, and principles are how a field keeps itself honest across decades of new tools.

So learn the laws, read the research carefully, and give your team the agency to use both. Then let your users decide the rest. Judgment you can explain, backed by the nerve to raise it, will outlast taste you can only defend, and teams built on it will ship the products everyone else ends up copying.

Action Items

  • Ask “what fact supports this?” instead of “does it have taste?” In critiques, every significant call should rest on a principle, a study, or something your users did. If nobody can name one, label the call an opinion and flag it for testing.
  • Teach the laws before the look. Give junior designers Fitts’s Law, Hick’s Law, cognitive load theory, and Nielsen’s heuristics before mood boards. Principles hand them decades of feedback, and the standing to use it.
  • Make it safe to push back with facts. Say plainly that a cited principle or data point outranks a job title, and back the junior designer who uses one against you. Agency that gets punished once rarely shows up twice.
  • Test where the facts run out. Brand feel, new interaction patterns, and cases where two laws conflict all need research. Run a usability session, a few interviews, or a first-click test that week, and log the prediction behind it. Leave the border widths alone.

Taste is not a design methodology was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Amazon ECS adds LiveTaskCount and removes the charge for RunningTaskCount metric
description:
Today, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) announces LiveTaskCount, a new ECS service metric that reports how many tasks are actively running in your service, available to all customers at no additional charge. Additionally, the existing RunningTaskCount metric in Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights no longer incurs a charge.

LiveTaskCount reports the number of actively running ECS tasks across all desired states (ACTIVATING, RUNNING, and DEACTIVATING), including tasks still running while transitioning to a stopped state, for example, tasks undergoing connection draining during a scale-in event. This comprehensive state coverage makes LiveTaskCount well suited for autoscaling policies and capacity planning where a complete view of active, metric-generating tasks is required. It is available at no charge as part of ECS service utilization metrics and does not require opting in to CloudWatch Container Insights. The existing CloudWatch Container Insights RunningTaskCount metric tracks tasks where both the current and desired state are RUNNING, and continues to serve as a health and stability signal for customers who depend on it. With today's update, RunningTaskCount is now available at no additional charge for all CloudWatch Container Insights users.

These updates are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECS is available. No action is required, and the pricing change for RunningTaskCount takes effect beginning October 1, 2026, and applies automatically. To learn more, see ECS CloudWatch metrics and ECS Container Insights metrics. For a pricing example, see Amazon CloudWatch pricing.

title: AWS Lambda durable functions increases durable operation and checkpoint payload limits
description:
Starting today, AWS Lambda durable functions increases the maximum number of durable operations per execution from 3,000 to 30,000, and the maximum checkpoint payload size from 256 KB to 1 MB. Higher operation limits let you safely do more work in a single execution including expanding iterative loops, polling for longer time periods, and building more complex rollback paths that run when a step fails. At 1 MB, checkpoint payloads match the maximum payload size of asynchronous Lambda invocations, and integration services such as Amazon SQS, and Amazon EventBridge, so a workflow can persist a full event from any of these sources in a single operation.

AWS Lambda durable functions helps you build resilient multi-step applications and AI workflows that execute for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing, automatic retries, and waits that suspend execution without incurring compute charges. Every durable operation counts toward the per-execution limit, including each step attempt, each poll of a wait-for-condition, and each branch of a parallel or map operation. With 30,000 operations, a single execution has more room to coordinate complex, multi-step workflows, iterate across thousands of items, or poll an external system for weeks, without exceeding checkpoint limits.

An agentic application can reason over thousands of model and tool calls, and with 1 MB checkpoints it persists larger conversation histories, model responses, and outputs from tools directly in the checkpoint instead of writing to external storage. For state larger than 1 MB, the JavaScript and Python SDKs include a FileSystem serializer that writes the payload to an Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files mount and checkpoints a pointer instead.

 The new limits apply in all AWS Regions where AWS Lambda durable functions is available. To learn more about these service limits, see the AWS Lambda developer guide.

title: AWS Agent Registry now supports custom metadata for registry records
description:
AWS Agent Registry is the centralized, governed catalog for agents, MCP servers, agent skills, gateways, and custom resources within your organization. As organizations scale to hundreds of such resources, a name and description alone are insufficient for effective governance and discovery. Custom metadata lets you extend every registry record with your organization's own structured fields, so both people and automated systems can find and govern resources consistently.

With custom metadata, publishers can record fields like team ownership, data classification, or review status directly on each registry record. You define a schema once per registry with common attributes, then extend it with type-specific fields — such as a model family for agent records. Each field supports free text, a URL, a Boolean, or a choice from a list of allowed values, and the registry validates required fields and values on every record creation or update. You can then filter search results on any custom metadata field from the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, the AWS SDKs, or the registry's MCP endpoint.

Custom metadata is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland).

To learn more, visit the AWS Agent Registry documentation. For detailed setup guidance, see Define a custom metadata schema and Set custom metadata values on a record.

title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
description:
Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects.

Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units.

GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked).

Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models.

GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony

Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.

title: Amazon DCV releases version 2026.0 with RHEL 10 support and new clients
description:
Amazon DCV 2026.0 is now available, adding support for RHEL 10, Rocky Linux 10, CentOS 10, and Ubuntu 26.04 along with a new macOS client and updated Windows and Linux clients. Amazon DCV is a high-performance remote display protocol that enables customers to securely access remote desktops and application sessions across Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Amazon DCV 2026.0 includes the following key features and improvements:

  • Support for RHEL 10, Rocky Linux 10, CentOS 10, and Ubuntu 26.04, with Linux hosts and sessions running on the modern Wayland display server

  • A new macOS client with gamepad support, and updated Windows and Linux clients

  • URL redirection on Windows hosts, so configured links opened in a remote session launch in the local browser on the client device

  • Printer preferences redirection on Windows, giving remote sessions access to client-side printer settings

  • Performance improvements, including H.264 frame slice support and slice-based multithreaded decoding on the Linux and macOS clients for lower latency

  • Support for new macOS server versions on Amazon EC2

For more information about the new features and enhancements in Amazon DCV 2026.0, see the release notes or visit the Amazon DCV webpage to learn more and get started.

Amazon Location Service now offers a complete, interactive API Playground that lets developers explore and test every Places, Routes, and Maps API visually without writing code. With this release, all 14 Amazon Location Service Places, Maps and Routes APIs are available in an interactive API Playground, where developers can make real API calls, see results rendered on an interactive map, adjust parameters, and copy ready-to-use request snippets directly into their applications.

title: New ways to drive smarter discovery, deeper engagement, and business growth on Google Play
description:
Posted by Paul Feng, VP of Product Management, Google Play, Google Play


Today, we shared how we’re taking our “More than a store” vision into its next chapter. From You tab—now a personalized home base for your favorite apps and content—to Play Games Sidekick connecting over 2 billion players, Google Play is meeting users wherever they are. [1] 

For developers, our goal is to help you connect with your audience and build a sustainable business. Below is a checklist to optimize your apps for our latest discovery features, new tools to deepen player engagement, and updates to our quality programs that reward great user experiences with lower service fees.

Reach the right users on Google Play and in the Gemini app

Earlier this year, we shared how new tools are transforming app and content discovery. Now, we’re expanding these features to make it easier for people to find your app.   

  • App comparisons on Ask Play: Ask Play already helps users find the right app through natural conversation, understanding context and adapting to follow-up questions. Now, it can generate dynamic, side-by-side app comparisons directly in search results. When a user compares details like subscription models or offline capabilities, Ask Play summarizes your store listing and user reviews to help them choose your app with confidence.
  • Game finder: Tailored by each player’s gameplay habits, favorite mechanics, and community reviews, Game finder explains why a title is recommended and highlights what similar players and profiles you follow are enjoying. It begins rolling out to English-language users in the US today. 
  • Play in Gemini: People are increasingly discovering apps directly through conversations in Gemini—driving over 6 million app installs in just two months since launch. [2] When someone describes a specific need, such as organizing family recipes or finding a collaborative task manager, Gemini matches their request to your store listing and key features, so they can evaluate and install your app with a single tap. And now, with Gemini Live, they can get these same app recommendations through voice conversations. 

To make sure your app is represented accurately everywhere users discover content—from Ask Play and Game finder to the Gemini app and Collections on home screens—review the following checklist: 

  1. Keep store listings and promotional events fresh: Regularly update your descriptions, tags, and events in Play Console to highlight new features, seasons, and timely offers.
  2. Upload high-resolution media assets: Use clean images and video previews that look great across different screen sizes and devices.
  3. Validate deep links in Play Console: Use the new built-in deep link emulator to preview and test your links without needing a physical device.
  4. Integrate Engage SDK: Bring users back to your app by delivering personalized content across surfaces, including Apps Home, You tab, and Android tablets—now supporting 9 categories, including Education and Health & Fitness.

Deepen player engagement with social competitions and rewards

Once players find a game they love, recognizing their progress and connecting them with a community keeps them coming back. We’re introducing new ways for players to share their favorite moments, compete with friends, and earn rewards: 

  • Playbacks in Sidekick: With Sidekick—our in-game overlay now reached over 285M users—we bring Quests, Leagues, Sprints, and community features just a tap away.[3]


  • Sprints: Building on Leagues, which turn in-game leaderboards into month-long competitive seasons, Sprints are fast-paced, 48-hour challenges that match 2 to 5 players of similar skills. It gives players an exciting reason to jump back into your game throughout the week.


  • Quests: Beyond competing on leaderboards, players want their time and progress rewarded. We’re expanding Quests beyond Play Points to include in-game rewards like character skins, performance boosters, and valuable currencies. 

You can turn on these competitive and social features by integrating Game Stats and Play Games Rewards:

  • Game Stats: By sharing basic gameplay event signals—such as match completions, score thresholds, or key milestones—your games can show daily Streaks and become eligible for platform-wide competitions like Leagues and Sprints. Game Stats connects seamlessly with your backend data , giving you access to our engagement mechanics without rebuilding matchmaking or leaderboard systems.
  • Play Games Rewards: Now generally available, you can set up ongoing in-game rewards that celebrate achievements and sync with Play Points. This helps you grow loyal players and keep them coming back.

Accelerate business growth with the Apps Experience and Level Up program

These new discovery and engagement tools help you deliver a better user experience while growing your business. For developers looking to go even further, our quality programs - Apps Experience and Level Up reward standout apps and games with lower service fees. 

Titles integrating Level Up guidelines, like Summoners War, PUBG MOBILE, and Fruit Ninja are already seeing strong results by polishing graphics performance, integrating Game Stats, and launching Leagues and Quests. For example, PUBG MOBILE drove 22% uplift in new installs from high-value players, and achieved a 62% uplift in spend per buyer among engaged players.[4]

Both programs are now available in Australia, Japan, the EEA, UK, and US, and will roll out to Korea by the end of the year.  We've also made it easier to submit and manage your program enrollment directly in Play Console.  

Explore these new tools in Play Console today—where you’ll also start seeing a visual refresh rolling out this month to streamline your everyday workflow. Please keep sharing your feedback with us as we build the future of Google Play together.

title: Bringing our latest frontier model to Android Developers
description:
Posted by Jason Buchel, Creative Technologist, Platform & Devices




As agentic development accelerates, Android engineering is reaching an exciting new frontier: moving from assistive code completion to agents executing end-to-end under your direction. You have total choice and flexibility in the models and agents you use. 

Gemini 4 Argon excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science.

Starting today, Android developers can access Gemini 4 Argon across their development surfaces, including Google Antigravity (standalone and in Android Studio Canary) for Google AI Ultra subscribers, and in Android Studio and Google AI Studio via the paid tier of the Gemini API.

Velocity & Autonomy: Closed-loop build self-correction

Argon has significant improvements in long-horizon autonomous execution and the ability to plan and run multi-step, complex software tasks over time.

  • Self-Healing Build Loops: When a local build fails, the Antigravity execution harness captures error streams directly from Gradle daemons and Kotlin compiler logs. Using this feedback, the model iteratively diagnoses the root-cause of build failures to arrive at a revised solution. Gemini 4 Argon's training dramatically improves on this process. It's engineered to maintain a consistent hypothesis across successive rounds of editing, as well as making use of internal Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) awareness to better inform edits. This means Gemini 4 Argon is more resilient and better able to address the true root-cause of build failures.

UI sophistication: Fluid motion & shader-backed Jetpack Compose

Argon demonstrates exceptional design craft, generating production-ready Jetpack Compose code out of the box:

  • AGSL Shaders on the GPU: Argon possesses the advanced mathematical reasoning needed to write complex, production-ready Android Graphics Shading Language (AGSL) directly into Compose Modifier.graphicsLayer blocks and shader brushes. From live frosted glass shaders to dynamic lighting and ripple effects, Argon can handle complicated vector and rendering math that produces lightweight GPU shaders that run alongside fluid 120 FPS Compose animations.

A flexible developer experience with Android CLI

Antigravity operates across multiple surfaces, from the desktop app and IDE extensions to the command line. No matter which surface you prefer, the official Android CLI plugin is the de-facto engine that connects your agent to local Android tools, enabling it to run programmatic commands for common tasks and execute custom developer skills.

Starting today, you can access and configure this agentic workspace in two primary ways:

  1. Setting up visually (Antigravity Desktop & Android Studio Canary)
    • In the Antigravity Desktop App: Go to Settings > Customizations > Build With Google Plugins (or the Antigravity Plugin Marketplace), locate android-cli-plugin, and toggle it to Enabled
    • In Android Studio Canary: Log in to your Antigravity account in the agent tool window to enable agentic workflows directly alongside your editor 
  2. Setting up via the Terminal CLI 

    For Google Antigravity, run:

    agy plugin install android-cli-plugin
  3. For any terminal agent (via Android CLI), run: 
    android init

Availability & getting started

Starting today, Argon is rolling out globally to developers in supported regions. You can access and begin building with the model in your local environment across three primary development surfaces:

  1. Google Antigravity: Google AI Ultra subscribers can build with Gemini 4 Argon in the standalone Antigravity desktop app (available for macOS, Windows, and Linux) or directly via the terminal CLI
  2. Android Studio:
    • Via Google Antigravity: Google AI Ultra subscribers can build with Gemini 4 Argon by logging into Antigravity within the latest Android Studio Canary.
    • Via the Gemini API: Developers on the paid tier of the Gemini API can build with Gemini 4 Argon in Android Studio.
  3. Google AI Studio: Google AI Ultra subscribers or developers on the paid tier of the Gemini API can build with Gemini 4 Argon via Playground and Build in Google AI Studio.
  1. Firebase AI Logic: Starting today, developers globally on the paid tier of the Gemini API can use Gemini 4 Argon client-side to build intelligent features in their mobile and web apps via Firebase AI Logic.

To begin building with Argon in your local environment:
    • Choose your path: Confirm you have an active Google AI Ultra subscription to use Antigravity, or ensure you are on the paid tier of the Gemini API to use standard API surfaces (with introductory pricing available through November 30, 2026).
    • Update your tools: Download the latest version of the Antigravity desktop app or CLI, and install the official Android CLI plugin (agy plugin install android-cli-plugin) to connect your agentic workspace directly to your Android Studio build tools.

We are eager to see the high-craft Android experiences you build at the frontier. Share your projects and feedback with us on X (@AndroidDev) and LinkedIn!

title: Create complex UI with a class library in PHP
description:
Despite the rise of JavaScript frameworks like React and Angular, building the UI on the backend is still a common feature in many web applications. This is generally done with a template library, like Twig, Blade or Latte, and often using a different language which is close or related to the main application language. A template engine then converts the template code into the application language, and generally caches the generated code for further reuse.

In the PHP ecosystem, there are many attempts to build application UIs using a class library.

Some of the most popular complements a template library. spatie/html extends Laravel Blade with functions to build HTML elements. Symfony Forms and Nette Forms can build forms, then validate and process their values.

Less known and less used, there are other PHP packages whose purpose is to build an application UI using a class library. ATK UI, Viewi, ui-awesome/html, danielescherzer/html-builder and Sirius HTML are a few examples of such libraries.

However, they don't match the advanced features of template libraries like Blade or Twig. Even when providing a fluent API, generally those libraries can only create chunks of HTML or individual HTML components, without being able to tie them together into a complete UI block. The user then needs to complement them with a template engine or plain PHP calls for string concatenation, iterative or conditional rendering.

The HTML Builder library

HTML Builder is a PHP library that provides classes to represent the HTML components, as well as an API to build UIs using those classes. A UI is built using a call tree, where each component receives its children as parameters. HTML tags are created by calling methods named after the tags, while attributes are set using methods named set followed by the attribute name in PascalCase.

    $this->html->div(
        $this->html->div(
            $this->html->label($this->html->text('Collation'))
                ->setFor('collation')
        )->setStyle('width: 30%;'),
        $this->html->div(
            $this->html->select(
                $this->html->option('(collation)')
                    ->setValue('')
                    ->setSelected(true),
                $this->html->each($collations, fn(array $groupCollations, $group) =>
                    $this->html->list(
                        $this->html->when($group === '', fn() =>
                            $this->html->each($groupCollations, $this->html->option(...))
                        ),
                        $this->html->when($group !== '', fn() =>
                            $this->html->optgroup(
                                $this->html->each($groupCollations, $this->html->option(...))
                            )->setLabel($group)
                        )
                    )
                )
            )->setName('collation')
        )->setStyle('width: 70%;')
    )->setStyle('display: flex; justify-content: space-between;')

This is the same template, built with Twig.

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between;">
    <div style="width: 30%;">
        <label for="collation">Collation</label>
    </div>
    <div style="width: 70%;">
        <select name="collation">
            <option value="" selected>(collation)</option>
            {% for group, groupCollations in groups %}
                {% if group == '' %}
                    {% for collation in groupCollations %}
                        <option>{{ collation }}</option>
                    {% endfor %}
                {% else %}
                    <optgroup label="{{ group }}">
                        {% for collation in groupCollations %}
                            <option>{{ collation }}</option>
                        {% endfor %}
                    </optgroup>
                {% endif %}
            {% endfor %}
        </select>
    </div>
</div>

The virtual components

What actually makes the HTML Builder library as powerful as a template library, is its virtual components.

A virtual component takes application data as input, and generates zero, one or more components as output. It generates no additional HTML tag, so its output is only composed of those of the generated components.

There is a bidirectional relation between virtual and real components. A real component can contain either real or virtual components as children, and a virtual component can generate a collection of real and virtual components.

Virtual components enable the HTML Builder library to generate HTML elements dynamically, a feature not available in the libraries mentioned above.

The types of virtual components

The HTML Builder library provides 5 types of virtual components.

Note: a closure passed to a virtual component must return a single component, which can be real or virtual.

The When component

The When component mimics the if clause of template languages. It takes a boolean condition and a closure as parameters, and calls the closure only when the condition is true.

    $this->html->when($user->isLoggedIn,
        fn() => $this->html->div($this->html->text($user->email)));

The List component

The List component groups a set of components into a single one. It then allows to pass a list of components in places where a single component is expected, for example as the return value of a function.

    $this->html->when($user->isLoggedIn,
        fn() => $this->html->list(
            $this->html->b($this->html->text('Welcome ')),
            $this->html->div($this->html->text($user->email))
        );

The Pick component

The Pick component mimics the PHP switch clause. It takes multiple When components as input, and calls the closure provided by the first true condition.

    $this->html->pick(
        $this->html->when($user === null,
            fn() => $this->html->html('Welcome')),
        $this->html->when($user->isAdmin,
            fn() => $this->html->html("Welcome <b>{$user->name}</b>")),
        $this->html->when(true,
            fn() => $this->html->html("Welcome {$user->name}"))
    );

The Each component

The Each component takes an array of items and a closure as parameters, and calls the closure with each item in the array. It then generates the same number of components, each of which can be either real or virtual.

    $this->html->select(
        $this->html->option('(Default)')->setValue(0),
        $this->html->each($choices,
            fn($choice) => $this->html->option($choice->label))
    );

The Each component can also take an iterator or a generator as parameter, and the closure also accepts the array key value as second parameter.

    $this->html->select(
        $this->html->option('(Default)')->setValue(0),
        $this->html->each($choices,
            fn($choice, $id) => $this->html->option($choice->label)->setValue($id))
    );

The Loop component

The Loop component is the same as the Each component, but its second parameter is a LoopItem object, which provides various information about the current loop.

    $this->html->select(
        $this->html->option('(Default)')->setValue(0),
        $this->html->loop($choices,
            fn($choice, $loop) => $this->list(
                $this->when($loop->current->group !== $loop->prev?->group,
                    fn() => $this->html->option($loop->current->group)
                        ->setClass('group-title disabled')),
                $this->html->option($choice->label)->setValue($id))
            )
    );

Note: The Loop component was inspired by this article on Twig.

Comparison with template engines

The HTML Builder library combines a fluent PHP API with a lightweight, object-oriented approach to HTML generation.

Its virtual components support dynamic content while deferring the execution of closures until rendering. This keeps UI construction entirely within PHP, using a consistent fluent API from start to finish, without requiring a separate template compilation step.

The combination of regular and virtual components provides the building blocks needed to implement the main features commonly found in template engines, including conditional rendering and iteration, while preserving the fluent API. Combined with PHP's object-oriented features, such as inheritance, traits, method overloading, and composition, this approach offers a flexible way to structure and reuse UI code.

Like template engines, HTML Builder can also be extended with custom functions to meet application-specific needs.

Why use HTML Builder?

When using the HTML Builder library, the application UI is organized as a library of PHP classes rather than a collection of template files. This makes the UI independent of any particular application framework and eliminates the need for a separate template engine.

UI classes can accept structured objects and domain-specific data types instead of relying solely on simple arrays. This allows the interfaces between the UI and other application components to be defined more explicitly, improving separation of concerns and making dependencies easier to understand.

A class-based UI can also benefit from familiar software engineering practices, including encapsulation, inheritance, code reuse, and unit testing. For applications where the UI is maintained as part of the codebase, this approach can make the code easier to organize, maintain, and test.

What changes with HTML Builder?

Template engines commonly compile templates into PHP code and cache the compiled result for reuse. This reduces the overhead of processing templates repeatedly and can provide a performance advantage over an object-based approach to HTML generation.

HTML Builder instantiates objects for HTML components and makes use of features such as magic methods, closures, and method calls to compose the final output. These mechanisms introduce some runtime overhead compared with executing precompiled PHP code.

However, performance depends on the implementation, the structure of the UI, and the amount of work involved in rendering it. The trade-off is an approach that emphasizes object-oriented composition, extensibility, and code reuse rather than minimizing runtime overhead.

Some template engines also provide a sandbox that allows untrusted templates to be executed with restricted capabilities, improving security. Developers can define which functions templates are allowed to call. This feature is particularly useful when an application needs to render templates provided by third parties.

HTML Builder does not provide a sandbox, as it is designed to build HTML directly from PHP code rather than to execute untrusted templates. Its UI classes are intended to be part of the application's codebase, not to serve as a restricted execution environment for externally supplied templates.

The UI Builder library

The UI Builder library extends the HTML Builder library with functions for creating UI components based on CSS frameworks. It provides a set of primitives for creating components such as buttons, cards, tabs, pagination, and more, as well as configuring their properties.

The UI Builder library is currently used to build the UI of the Jaxon DbAdmin application, and the example below is taken from its codebase.

    $this->html->build(
        $this->html->buttonGroup(
            $this->html->button(
                $this->html->text($this->trans->lang('Columns ')),
                $this->html->when($columnCount > 0, fn() =>
                    $this->html->badge("$columnCount")->primary())
            )->outline()
                ->secondary()
                ->fullWidth(),
            $this->html->button(
                $this->html->text($this->trans->lang('Filters ')),
                $this->html->when($filterCount > 0, fn() =>
                    $this->html->badge("$filterCount")->primary())
            )->outline()
                ->secondary()
                ->fullWidth(),
            $this->html->button(
                $this->html->text($this->trans->lang('Order ')),
                $this->html->when($sorterCount > 0, fn() =>
                    $this->html->badge("$sorterCount")->primary())
            )->outline()
                ->secondary()
                ->fullWidth()
        )->fullWidth()
    );

The UI Builder library is separated into multiple PHP packages.

The lagdo/ui-builder package provides the BuilderInterface interface, which defines the functions that each builder must implement. It also provides base classes for UI components and implements a common set of functions shared by the different builders.

Each supported CSS framework has its own package, which implements the Builder class and the corresponding UI component classes. Each component class defines how the component's HTML is generated for the target framework, using the functions provided by the lagdo/ui-builder and lagdo/html-builder packages.

The framework-specific Builder class extends the AbstractBuilder class provided by the UI Builder package and only needs to specify the names of the component classes it uses.

The following CSS frameworks are currently supported:

  • Bootstrap 5
  • Bootstrap 4

The Bootstrap 3 package is deprecated.

The packages for Tailwind CSS and Bulma are under development and will be available soon.

Closing thoughts

Generating an application UI entirely in PHP has always been challenging. PHP libraries designed for this purpose have traditionally lacked many of the features offered by template engines, often requiring developers to supplement them with a template engine or direct PHP calls.

Thanks to its virtual components, the HTML Builder library bridges this gap. Its fluent API and methods named after HTML tags make it easier to build complex application UIs entirely in PHP.

The UI Builder library takes this approach a step further by extending the HTML Builder library with higher-level UI components, such as buttons, cards, tabs, and pagination. Framework-specific packages generate the corresponding HTML for CSS frameworks such as Bootstrap, Tailwind CSS, and Bulma.

title: Tiny CSS Detail Stopped Countdown Button from Shaking
description:
While working on a session countdown, I noticed a small but annoying UI issue: the button slightly changed its width every time the counter updated.

With a senior developer’s eye, even the smallest movement becomes noticeable.

Why Does It Happen?

In most fonts, digits do not have the same width. For example, 1 is usually narrower than 8.

When the countdown changes:

Yes 4:50
Yes 4:49
Yes 4:48

the text width changes too. If the button does not have a fixed width, it grows and shrinks by a few pixels, creating a distracting shaking effect.

The Simple Fix: tabular-nums

The CSS property font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums gives every digit the same horizontal width.

With Tailwind CSS, we can enable it using one class:

<button className="tabular-nums">
  Yes {formattedTime}
</button>

Now, 1, 4, 8, and every other digit occupy the same amount of space. The countdown can change without affecting the button’s width.

Why Not Use a Fixed Width?

A fixed width may hide the issue, but it is not always flexible. It can break when the text changes, the interface is translated, or a different font size is used.

tabular-nums solves the actual problem while keeping the component responsive.

Where Is It Useful?

Use tabular-nums for any frequently changing numeric value:

  • Countdown timers
  • Digital clocks
  • Prices and financial values
  • Dashboard statistics
  • Live scores
  • Data tables
  • Progress indicators

It is a small CSS detail, but it makes the interface feel more stable and polished.

Notice the details. Read more. Code smart.

title: The synth everyone owned and few could program: a lesson for AI design
description:
AI made quality available to everyone, and made it average. What sets work apart now is a decision you can see.

An AI assistant helped me write this. The ideas, the data and the final edit are mine.

E.PIANO 1

In 1983, Yamaha released the DX7, the first digital synthesizer to sell in large numbers. It was powerful and almost impossible to program: no knobs to shape the sound, only menus on a small display that few musicians ever learned to navigate. So it shipped with factory sounds, 128 presets that two specialists had put together in less than four days. Most owners never went further.

One of those sounds, “E.PIANO 1”, imitates an electric piano. It sounds professional from the first note. The music theorist Megan Lavengood counted how often it shows up on the charts: in 1986, it is on 39% of the Billboard Hot 100 number ones, 40% of the country number ones and 61% of the R&B number ones. Her study is called “What makes it sound ‘80s?”: a quality sound handed to everyone became the signature of a decade, and then the surest way to date a record.

The same year, Brian Eno released Apollo with Daniel Lanois and his brother Roger, an ambient album written for a documentary about the Moon missions, and he used the DX7 on it. He was one of the few people who could program the machine in depth. Yet his case reads as a matter of order more than technique: music imagined for those images first, then the sounds to make it, which no preset contained.

The 2026 preset

Generative AI is doing to design what the DX7 did to sound. It gives a clean result to someone who doesn’t know how to adjust the tool, and that result converges.

I measured it on twelve app briefs, with seven models from three makers (results and public benchmark). For a corporate law firm, all seven pick navy blue with a touch of gold. The average gap between their colours is only 9, the same as for a funeral home, measured in ΔE, the distance between two colours as the eye perceives it: under 10, they are shades of the same colour. The category sets the look.

Prose is going the same way. In a 2024 study published in Science Advances, Anil Doshi and Oliver Hauser had people write short stories with or without ideas from a language model. With the help, stories were rated more creative and better written, especially among the less confident writers. They were also more similar to one another, what researchers call homogenization. In another field, selection decisions such as hiring, the computer scientists Jon Kleinberg and Manish Raghavan described a related effect in 2021, algorithmic monoculture: when everyone relies on the same algorithm, each of them can come out ahead while the group as a whole does worse.

The DX7 preset had at least been chosen, once, by two people, for no song in particular. The AI’s preset was chosen by nobody: it’s an average. What you recognize in a screen or a paragraph that looks AI-made is something nobody chose.

The preset looks good

Presets didn’t wait for models. In 2013, Paul Adams, then VP of Product at Intercom, was already warning against the Dribbblisation of design: interfaces polished for the shot rather than for the problem.

What’s new is elsewhere. For a long time, the preset showed: a template looked like a template, and moving away from it bought visible quality. The 2026 preset shows much less. It is coherent and polished on the surface, sometimes more finished than what a small team in a hurry would have shipped. As Tanya Donska put it in Built In: “All of it is correct. All of it could belong to anything.” Not all of it is correct, though: in the same measurement, 34 primary colours out of 84 fail the minimum contrast for white text on top, which you only see once you check.

So apparent quality has become the floor. Much of the value people saw in designers came from the gap between ordinary work and careful work, and the machine now closes that gap on demand. Whatever sets work apart has moved somewhere else.

Three ways out, and only one holds

The first idea is to do better than the machine. Two things need separating here. Fixing what it gets wrong, like that contrast, is still essential, but it’s verification: an audit tool flags it just as well, and it sets no one apart. What holds up badly is the race for finish, because the floor rises with every new model and this year’s extra polish will be next year’s average.

The second is to be original. It doesn’t hold up either, and the same data shows why. I asked the same models to avoid clichés. They did drop Playfair Display and Bebas Neue, but two-thirds of their new headings landed on a new repertoire, with Fraunces 19 times out of 84 and Space Grotesk 15 times. Originality pursued as a goal ends up averaged in turn, just a little later.

That leaves decisions. A decision differs from an instruction by its content: “avoid clichés” says nothing about the product, while a decision starts from what this particular product has, which the average doesn’t know. And it has to be held. The boxing gym brief said “a boxing gym in a working-class neighbourhood of Marseille, members are mostly young adults who train hard.” The seven models still returned roughly the same thing: bright red or orange on a near-black background, with condensed headings for six of them. To describe the mood they were going for, they chose words like “raw, intense, gritty”, with no trace of Marseille or of the neighbourhood, as if the category had covered up the context in the brief. Deciding, then, means defending what’s particular against the pull of the category, at every step where the preset comes back.

“It looks AI”

This changes the design review. “It looks AI” has become a common remark, about a mockup as much as a text. It sounds like a comment on quality, and it often works as an accusation.

Yet the look it points to doesn’t prove that a machine was involved. A person following the defaults produces the same thing, and a model given real decisions, a colour with its reason or a constraint specific to the product, can move away from it. The look only proves that the preset stayed. Treating it as evidence turns the review into a trial: people ask who made the screen, and nobody discusses what it should be.

The remark has a useful version, which is to name the preset. Maya Brennan’s guide to de-slopifying designs is a good list of what to name.
This gradient came with the tool: what should our colour say here? This card grid is the standard layout: what does this content actually need? Put that way, the question asks for a decision, and it applies just as much to a screen drawn by hand. As hipuku writes, with generative tools “the first version turns up before the opinion has formed”. Naming the preset reopens that frame.

For a team, that comes down to two habits. In review, ask what came from the preset before judging whether it works. In the design system, write the reason for each choice next to its value. An entry that reads “primary colour: #1B2A4A” says nothing more than the preset. “Primary colour: the blue of the firm’s original sign, darkened to hold contrast” shows a decision, and gives the next person a reason to keep it or change it.

A common objection is that you just need to give the AI a design system. That is indeed the right answer, as long as someone has made the decisions it contains.

The question to keep

E.PIANO 1 sounded great in 1986, which is exactly why it ended up everywhere, before it dated every record that kept it as it was. The 2026 look will probably go the same way. The preset was never a quality problem, and once quality is a given, only one question is left to ask in front of a screen: did someone decide this?

Cover photo: Leo-setä, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0), cropped.

Mathieu Poli is Head of Frontend Engineering at GoodBarber and writes about frontend engineering, product design and AI.

title: AWS DataSync Enhanced mode now supports FSx for OpenZFS, NFS 4.2, and object metadata controls
description:
AWS DataSync Enhanced mode now supports Amazon FSx for OpenZFS as a source or destination location, NFS version 4.2 for on-premises NFS servers and FSx for OpenZFS file systems, and a new ObjectMetadata option for object storage transfers. Previously, customers transferring data to or from FSx for OpenZFS were limited to Basic mode.

NFS 4.2 lets you transfer data from NFS servers on the latest version without reconfiguring them to an older protocol version. The ObjectMetadata option gives you control over whether an object's user metadata is copied to the destination, which helps when destination metadata must stay intact, such as buckets served by AWS Storage Gateway, or when source metadata keys are not compatible with the destination, such as Azure Blob Storage. Existing tasks remain unaffected and continue to run as scheduled.

These capabilities are available for Enhanced mode tasks in all AWS Regions where AWS DataSync Enhanced mode is supported. To learn more, visit the AWS DataSync documentation.

title: Amazon Route 53 now supports registrations, transfers, and renewals for Premium Domains
description:
Amazon Route 53 Domains now supports Premium Domain Names. Customers can now search for, register, transfer, renew, and restore registry premium names directly through Route 53.

Most domain registries set aside a selection of "premium" domains - names that are short, memorable, or in high demand. Previously, Route 53 Domains did not support these premium names, which meant customers who wanted them had to register and manage them through other registrars, fragmenting their portfolios across multiple providers. With this launch, customers can now discover and acquire premium domains directly in Route 53 Domains, consolidate their existing premium domains from other registrars, and manage premium and standard domains together through a single, unified experience. Finding and registering a premium domain works just like it does for standard domains. Premium domains appear automatically in domain search and availability results, with pricing shown upfront, so customers know the cost before they commit.

To learn more about Amazon Route 53 Domains and start registering premium domains, visit the Amazon Route 53 Domains page. For a complete list of supported top-level domains, see the Route 53 TLD list.

title: What are we willing to sacrifice for AI?
description:
Three paths forward, each challenging what we value most.

I suspect artificial intelligence may eventually accomplish what generations of socialists have struggled to achieve. And the irony is that capitalism may ultimately be responsible for making it happen.

What makes this possibility particularly uncomfortable for me is that my political instincts lean libertarian. I have never been particularly enthusiastic about government-supplemented incomes, wealth redistribution, or expanding the state’s role in economic life.

Yet the more I consider the potential consequences of AI-driven automation and its displacement of human labor, the more I recognize that a greater degree of centralized collective support may be necessary for society to continue to prosper.

The economic arrangements I have long defended, particularly free markets and the principle of individual economic independence, may become difficult to sustain—not because their underlying principles have been disproven, but because the technology we are developing could fundamentally change the conditions upon which they depend.

AI itself does not decide who benefits from its capabilities or who bears the costs. People do, through choices shaped by ambition, self-interest, competition, and greed. We may build machines capable of extraordinary intellectual achievements without becoming any wiser about the desires that govern their use. Those human incentives complicate every path forward.

We appear to be heading toward a future in which artificial intelligence allows companies to produce much of what we need with a fraction of today’s workforce. Previous technological revolutions displaced workers but also created new occupations, and if you’re feeling optimistic, AI may do the same.

But that optimism rests on the assumption that AI will follow a familiar historical pattern. Unlike previous technologies that automated particular forms of work, AI can perform an expanding range of intellectual tasks across industries, including some of the very capabilities people have historically relied upon to adapt to technological change.

What happens to an economic system built around the relationship between work and income when fewer people are needed to produce the goods and services society consumes? And more interestingly, what happens to our philosophical convictions when the conditions that once justified them fundamentally change?

As I see it, such a future points toward three broad directions, each requiring us to sacrifice one value in pursuit of another. Of course, some would argue that compromises are possible between the scenarios I’m about to present. Yet I question whether such compromises would offer more than temporary relief from the underlying tensions.

The First Path: Sacrifice Profits to Preserve Jobs

The first path forward would require businesses to sacrifice the additional profits AI could generate in order to preserve human employment and the economy built around it. This would not necessarily mean accepting losses or abandoning profitability, but rather voluntarily forgoing opportunities to earn more by replacing workers with AI. Companies would need to exercise restraint, even when doing so puts them at a competitive disadvantage.

The problem is that businesses have powerful incentives to maximize profits, often by reducing costs and improving efficiency. As AI becomes more capable, replacing human workers becomes an attractive way to accomplish both, particularly when competitors are doing the same. Yet workers are also customers, and if enough people lose their jobs, businesses could eventually undermine the consumer economy that supports their profits.

This is not simply a question of corporate greed, although in many cases it is. Some companies pursue greater profits, while others must reduce costs to remain competitive or survive. But companies are ultimately run by people, and the pursuit of wealth and power is as old as civilization itself.

Greed has been recognized as a moral failing for centuries, yet that recognition has done little to eliminate it from human behavior. Expecting business leaders to collectively resist opportunities for greater wealth, particularly when their competitors have every incentive to pursue them, strikes me as wishful thinking.

Sure, governments could attempt to impose such restraint through regulations, financial penalties, or incentives to retain workers. But businesses have spent generations minimizing taxes, relocating operations, lobbying lawmakers, and finding ways around regulations. Ultimately, such measures would do little to change the underlying incentive driving these decisions, as businesses will continue to seek opportunities to increase profits, even when doing so comes at the expense of human employment.

The Second Path: Turn Away from AI

Rather than continuing down our current path, relying on businesses to restrain their pursuit of profits, or implementing targeted government regulations that may prove difficult to enforce, we could take a far more drastic approach and severely restrict the development and use of AI altogether. The objective would be to preserve the jobs on which economic independence currently depends.

I understand the appeal of protecting people’s ability to support themselves through their own work, but consider what such a decision could cost us. AI might accelerate cancer research, develop more sustainable ways of producing food and energy, expand access to knowledge, and help solve problems that have resisted us for generations. I find it difficult to justify sacrificing those possibilities simply to preserve the way we currently earn a living.

The difficulty is that there is no obvious way to separate acceptable uses of AI from unacceptable ones. We might welcome a system that advances scientific research while objecting when the same capabilities replace analysts, administrators, or other workers.

Progress in one field can also disrupt employment in another. Someone would have to decide which benefits justify that disruption, which jobs deserve protection, and how much innovation society should forgo. Even if we agreed on those judgments today, new applications would make those boundaries harder to maintain tomorrow.

There is also the question of whether such restrictions could endure. The impulse to invent, explore, and overcome limitations is as much a part of human nature as the pursuit of wealth or status. Nations, businesses, and research institutions would have powerful incentives to continue developing AI, particularly if their competitors were doing so. This path might preserve familiar forms of employment, but it would also require us to deliberately constrain a technology whose greatest benefits we have yet to discover.

The Third Path: Reconsider What Liberty Requires

That leaves the possibility I find most uncomfortable. We continue developing AI, accept that substantial labor displacement may occur, and reconsider how people obtain the resources necessary to live. Some form of guaranteed income, broader ownership of productive technology, or another mechanism may be required.

I recognize that not every form of income support constitutes socialism, and I do not claim to know which approach would work best. But the deeper question is philosophical, not merely political. An economy built around the expectation that people earn their own living may have to confront a future in which opportunities to do so become increasingly scarce through no failure of individual effort.

My instinct is to resist any arrangement that makes people more dependent on government. Yet the freedom to support oneself presupposes a meaningful opportunity to do so. Keynes imagined technological progress relieving humanity of much of its economic burden. We may achieve something resembling that ambition while retaining an economic system that requires most people to sell their labor to survive. We could make work less necessary without making workers any less dependent on having work.

Considering greater economic intervention does not mean that replacing corporate power with government authority eliminates the human appetite for wealth, power, and control. Governments are no more immune to corruption than corporations, regardless of the virtues their political ideologies claim to represent. Changing the institutions that distribute resources does not change the human beings who operate them.

My instincts are closer to subsidiarity, the principle that individuals and smaller communities should address problems within their capacity, with larger institutions stepping in when necessary. That could mean exploring local cooperatives that own AI tools, community land trusts, or regional funds that share the gains from automation rather than assuming any response must come from a central government. I want people to retain as much freedom and responsibility over their lives as possible.

But if the means of earning a living become unavailable to large numbers of people, the problem may exceed what individuals or local communities can solve. Accepting that possibility would not require me to abandon liberty as a value. It would require me to question whether the institutions I have preferred can still protect it.

Of course, new occupations may emerge, and the scale of displacement remains uncertain. Yet I believe AI has the potential to fundamentally disrupt the relationship between human labor and economic independence. Whether that disruption unfolds as dramatically as I have suggested remains to be seen, but the possibility alone forces me to reconsider economic and political convictions I have long held.

What Are We Willing to Surrender?

The first path asks businesses to sacrifice potential profits to preserve employment. The second asks us to restrain our impulse to invent and discover. The third asks us to reconsider how much institutional dependence we are willing to accept in order to preserve economic independence. Each presents a different kind of sacrifice, raising difficult questions about what we value and what we are willing to give up.

I remain hopeful about what AI could make possible, and deeply uneasy about the society we might build around it. I have no desire to surrender my belief in individual liberty, but I am beginning to question whether the economic arrangements I have long defended will remain capable of protecting it. Perhaps the real test of our convictions is whether we can recognize when the means we have chosen no longer serve the ends we value.

title: Audit your UI before you redesign it: baseline first, then compare
description:
We just spent two weeks improving six dashboard pages in our research system. The tempting move was to open each page, feel what was wrong, and start fixing. That approach produces exactly what you expect: pages that each look individually fine but feel like they were designed by six different people.
Instead, we ran an audit first. Here is the method and what it caught.

The method: baseline, compare, classify

Step 1: Extract a baseline. Pick two or three pages in your system that already feel right — not because they are beautiful, but because they are consistent. Write down every convention they share: segmented controls, button styles, icon usage, font sizes, color semantics, spacing.
In our case, three pages shared a set of conventions we hadn't written down anywhere:

  • Segmented controls: gray track, pill-shaped, white floating active state
  • Back buttons: shared icon component, gray hover state
  • Icons: one shared icon library, no emoji
  • Text buttons: link-style gray-to-accent on hover
  • Loading: shared spinner component

Step 2: Compare every target page against the baseline. Not "does this look good?" but "does this match?" Each deviation gets written down as a specific, nameable difference.

Step 3: Classify each deviation. There are only two kinds:

  • The page is wrong — it should adopt the baseline convention
  • The baseline is wrong — the deviation reveals a better pattern that should be promoted to the system This classification prevents the two failure modes: inconsistency (everything is special) and rigidity (nothing can improve).

What the audit caught: 8 deviations in 6 pages

Deviation Fix
Square segmented controls Changed to gray-track pill with floating white active
Back button with red hover Changed to shared icon + gray hover
Three-line page headers Aligned to single-line pattern from reference page
Star icon in accent red Changed to neutral gray
Inline SVG chevron Changed to shared icon component
Outlined box button Changed to link-style text button
No loading indicator Added shared spinner
Inconsistent filter-clear hover Unified to same color token

None of these are dramatic individually. Together, they made six pages feel like six different products. After the audit, they feel like one system.

The color rule that fell out

One deviation taught us a principle worth keeping: a back button had red on hover. Red in UI means destructive — delete, danger, irreversible. A back button is none of those. Using red there trains users to hesitate on every red hover.
The rule we wrote down:
Accent red is reserved for numeric values and selected states. Icons and button hovers use neutral gray.

This is not a aesthetic preference. It is semantic hygiene: red should mean "pay attention to this number" or "you are here", never "this is clickable decoration".

The discipline part

After fixing, three things make it stick:

  1. Shared components only. Icons go through one file. Buttons go through one component. No page-local SVGs or ad-hoc button styles.
  2. Full verification after changes. TypeScript zero errors, all frontend tests pass, build succeeds, deployed chunk hash verified on both production ends.
  3. When a new pattern is better, promote it to the baseline. The point is not stasis — it is that changes happen at the system level, not scattered across pages.

The connection to agent governance

If you have been following this series, you will see the pattern: this is the same method as the shadow-to-gate pipeline from the previous post. In both cases:

  1. Measure before you change (shadow audit / UI baseline)
  2. Fix the mechanism, not individual instances (citation rebuild / shared components)
  3. Add a gate to prevent regression (citation gate / component-only rule) Whether you are governing agent output or UI consistency, the sequence is the same: baseline → compare → fix mechanism → gate.

Takeaway

If your multi-page application feels inconsistent, resist the urge to redesign page by page. Instead:

  1. Write down the conventions your best pages already share
  2. List every deviation in every other page
  3. Fix deviations — or promote better patterns to the baseline
  4. Enforce with shared components and full verification The audit itself took 30 minutes. The fixes took one afternoon. The result is six pages that feel like one system — something no amount of per-page tweaking had achieved.
